stories.Headline: Tristan Thompson reveals he invested early in Anthropic AI and plans to stay a long-term shareholder
stories.Summary:
Tristan Thompson revealed his early investment in Anthropic AI, the artificial intelligence company that went public this week and sold $81.3 billion worth of stock shares, according to CNBC. Thompson told Yahoo Finance he was happy about the company's recent successes. He said he got involved in the tech brand over two years ago while visiting San Francisco as part of his NBA schedule when he was playing for the Cleveland Cavaliers. Thompson, who shares kids True, 8, and Tatum, 4, with ex Khloe Kardashian, met up with Sriram Krishnan, now a Senior White House Policy Advisor on Artificial Intelligence. Thompson described Krishnan as a great buddy of mine and recalled that he was the only friend he had in SF during those Finals runs who was picking the Cavaliers to win.

Thompson recalled that Krishnan opened up these doors, going to dinners and meeting people, and said SF is one of those towns where a lot of great founders and early startups want to come together and build this ecosystem. The 35-year-old said he told himself to insert himself in, describing himself as the tall guy walking in who is probably about 10 inches taller than everyone else. Thompson explained how thrilled they were last month when Anthropic announced it had filed a proposed stock plan with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. He shared that they are in a group chat and everyone is just talking about what they are going to do to celebrate, and he said the one thing they have to do is do a dinner and break bread again. As he put it, cheers to getting it right this time.

The Miami Heat player admitted his ventures do not always pay off like Anthropic did, breaking records with its initial public offering, and CNBC reported it had a fully diluted market cap of about $1.8 trillion on Nov. 19. Thompson explained that out of 10 companies you invest in, you are lucky if two make it to the finish line and get the home run. He said what he tells people is that those two that make it to the finish line and win that championship in their eyes for what the company is trying to do will make up for all the capital that you invested in. Thompson said he does not plan to cash out of Anthropic soon and sees himself as a long-term shareholder. He added that he is extremely bullish and that their alignment with government definitely makes you feel very bullish about it, calling it almost like investing in Google during the dot com era.

The interview was published Nov. 19, and the article appeared on E! Online on Nov. 21, 2026, and on AOL on Sat, November 21, 2026 at 12:08 AM UTC. The piece was written by Lindsay Weinberg and originally appeared on E! Online. E! and CNBC are both part of Versant Media. Thompson said he is happy about the company's recent successes.

stories.Headline: Phoenix mayor Kate Gallego seeks tech investment while curbing data center strain
stories.Summary:
Phoenix Mayor Kate Gallego is trying to attract more technology investment to her city while limiting the strain that data centers place on electricity, water and residents, according to an Axios interview published on November 20, 2026. Phoenix has become a bellwether for the demands the AI industry places on power and water in a hot, resource-constrained world, and Gallego is navigating a dilemma facing communities nationwide. She said at an event co-hosted by the University of Chicago's Institute of Politics and Energy Policy Institute, and moderated by Axios, that she wants Phoenix to lead in technology and be a tech-forward community. She added that she wants companies that care about the community and give back to it, rather than a race for the deepest incentives and the cheapest power, saying the city is open for business but not for sale.

Phoenix ranks fourth among major U.S. data center markets by operational capacity, and the debate there has expanded from how much development the region can accommodate to what communities should demand in return. Gallego helped push to eliminate Arizona's generous data center sales tax exemptions, and the state enacted a three-year pause on new applications in the summer of 2026. She opposes a blanket construction moratorium and favors more local control over where facilities are built, particularly near homes, and Phoenix adopted tougher zoning rules in 2025 requiring special permits for new data centers. Data centers have requested so much electricity in the Phoenix region that, if all the projects materialized, they could account for roughly two-thirds of the area's power demand, Gallego said, warning that this would not be a balanced or economically sustainable economy.

Phoenix's efforts to rein in data centers have sparked legal challenges, with developers originally seeking roughly $750 million in compensation over the zoning restrictions adopted in 2025, and the city has granted several exemptions while fighting other claims in court. Gallego told Axios that the city has been open and good partners to the industry and that it is deeply disappointing the developers do not want to work with the city, while developers argue the restrictions infringe on their property rights and diminish land values under Arizona law. Gallego is also weighing tradeoffs between electricity, water and heat, noting that newer cooling technologies can cut water use at data centers but often require more electricity, and that many data centers get power from natural gas plants in a part of the state that is very constrained around water. An Arizona State University study published in May found that data centers can raise nearby temperatures by as much as 4 degrees Fahrenheit, and Gallego, who established the nation's first publicly funded municipal heat-response office in 2021, said she is jealous of Midwestern mayors who can reuse data centers' waste heat to warm buildings.

Arizona's Democratic sweep could give Gallego more allies, with Democrats flipping both legislative chambers and Gov. Katie Hobbs winning reelection, giving the state full Democratic control for the first time since 1966, and Gallego said affordability dominated the election, with data center subsidies and community impacts part of that debate. Gallego, the longest-serving current mayor of America's 10 largest cities, says communities should have more bargaining power over data centers, including where they are built and what residents get in return, which could mean more permanent jobs, transparency about electricity and water use, and benefits for affected neighbors. It remains unclear whether she can have it both ways, attracting more tech investment while limiting its costs to residents, especially as developers challenge the city's regulatory authority. Gallego also worries that Arizona might be betting too heavily on an industry whose long-term trajectory remains uncertain.

stories.Headline: Anthropic spends $3.4 billion on Caterpillar gas turbines for off-grid AI data centers
stories.Summary:
Anthropic spent 3.4 billion dollars on gas turbines to power its artificial intelligence data centers in the United States. This massive transaction was finalized in late September between the corporate leadership of Anthropic and the company OnePWR Solutions. The AI developer took over an equipment order queue that OnePWR had placed with Caterpillar Inc. two years earlier. By assuming these manufacturing slots, Anthropic avoids supply chain constraints that would otherwise delay access to heavy-duty generator hardware. This deal represents the largest single purchase of power generation equipment ever executed by an artificial intelligence firm.

The Anthropic Off-Grid 1.7GW Power Generation and Data Center Initiative requires 1.7 gigawatts of heavy-duty, gas-fired generation equipment. This commitment includes hardware fabrication, balance-of-plant engineering, and site construction works for the project located in the United States. The buildout requires high-pressure natural gas piping, heavy structural steel, concrete foundation footings, high-grade copper wiring, and specialized acoustic cladding. Technical needs include gas pipeline interconnections, step-up substations, on-site fuel storage, SCADA microgrid controls, and direct liquid cooling interconnections. Design contractors are integrating high-efficiency natural gas turbine sets with specialized cooling modules and modular power blocks.

Anthropic PBC is the developer responsible for this initiative and is using it to secure a dedicated electricity supply. The company wants to maintain execution velocity across its multi-hundred-billion-dollar compute pipeline while preparing for an initial public offering. By becoming a power plant owner, the firm avoids utility grid interconnection backlogs that can delay projects by several years. This strategy ensures uninterrupted operational uptime for next-generation foundation models by skipping the reliance on public utility transmission upgrades. The company is taking direct control of its energy supply chain to keep gigawatt-scale training clusters running.

Industry analysts identify utility grid interconnection backlogs as the single largest constraint on modern data center deployment today. Major cloud operators are increasingly deploying self-generated natural gas power systems to secure reliable electricity while waiting for upgrades. The program will support thousands of specialized engineering, fabrication, and heavy civil construction jobs during the buildout phase. At peak, construction employment is estimated at more than 3,500 workers across mechanical, electrical, pipeline, and civil trades. Once operational, the project will support over 450 permanent jobs for electrical engineers, data center technicians, and plant operators.

The deal occurs during a global competition for high-density computing infrastructure, including SK Hyper's pursuit of 350 billion dollars. This shift reflects a broader trend where AI developers move from being grid customers to owning their own power. The project combines high-density AI data center infrastructure with distributed natural gas power plant infrastructure to bypass grid bottlenecks. These systems are designed for base-load and peak-shaving operations to deliver continuous, utility-scale electricity to off-grid campus locations. The initiative aims to accelerate deployment schedules and drive large-scale equipment manufacturing employment within the United States.

Deployment is organized into three phases, starting with Caterpillar delivering initial natural gas generator sets to designated installation sites. Engineering teams will then perform civil integration by connecting microgrid switchgear, step-up transformers, and fuel supply pipelines. Finally, on-site power units will energize live server clusters without grid reliance to complete the operational commissioning process. Phased hardware deliveries will run through 2027 and 2028 to reach the total continuous capacity of 1.7 gigawatts. The report leaves open the specific campus site coordinates and the final completion date for the full fleet.

stories.Headline: New Zealand cyber centre says hackers use AI tool Artex to automate attacks
stories.Summary:
New Zealand's National Cyber Security Centre warned on 21 November 2026 that hackers are using artificial intelligence to carry out cyber attacks, and it said organisations across the country must act. Its cyber defence operations director, Dr Emma Bickerstaffe, said there had been a rise over the past week in attackers using an open source AI tool called Artex to target organisations worldwide. Artex was developed by researchers to check for system vulnerabilities that hackers could exploit, and although it had been taken down from the internet, it had been replicated and was now being used to automate attacks on different organisations at the same time. Bickerstaffe said the key change was that phases of an attack could now be automated, which let threat actors act faster. She said an attack that might previously have taken weeks could now go from initial reconnaissance and scanning of an organisation to exploitation in a matter of hours.

Bickerstaffe said access to open source AI tools meant attackers could act opportunistically and were looking for any target they could gain access to. She said that if attackers got in using AI, they could move across a system, reach what she called an organisation's crown jewels, and access or change data. She said there had been instances in New Zealand where attackers used the tool to try to get into an organisation and failed, and other incidents where they successfully gained access and viewed data. She advised organisations to limit the devices and systems they connect to the internet and to implement multi-factor authentication, which she said could stop an attack if a system was compromised.

Her comments came after Forest & Bird and the New Zealand Defence Force both reported cyber security incidents on Friday, though the tools used by those hackers are not yet known. Forest & Bird confirmed supporters' details had been exposed, and chief executive Sam Rowland told RNZ it had taken immediate steps to secure its systems, including a forensic search of its website that uncovered malicious files. Rowland said the organisation was working with technology and cyber security experts to establish the full extent of the incident, was contacting people it knew were affected to explain what information had been accessed, and had notified NZ Police, the National Cyber Security Centre and the Office of the Privacy Commissioner. Those affected were warned the stolen data could be used to create scam emails, phone calls or convincing text messages, and were told to be cautious about unexpected messages even if they contained personalised information.

The New Zealand Defence Force took some of its websites down following a breach, after its website provider informed it of unauthorised access to its website systems. An NZDF spokesperson told RNZ that preliminary inquiries indicated a database associated with the Force4Families Defence Discounts scheme had been accessed, and that the database included names and email addresses of registered users. The NZDF said those who may have been affected had been contacted, and it advised individuals registered through the website to remain alert to phishing emails, scams and unsolicited requests for personal information.

stories.Headline: Meta employees warn of Muse AI privacy flaws before September 2026 launch
stories.Summary:
Meta employees raised massive security concerns about the Muse AI agent before its launch in September 2026 in the United States. These internal testers flagged significant privacy flaws and safety issues through company channels as recently as the product launch week. Reuters reviewed internal communications showing that the AI agent appeared to mix up conversations between different user accounts. Staffers described failure modes that made the product unreliable and feared that private data could be exposed to others. Meta proceeded with the scheduled release despite these warnings from employees who were testing the product internally.

The Muse AI agent requires broad Android notification permissions to access messages and notifications from other apps on a device. It manages tasks like reading emails, handling calendar events, and making phone calls through a human concierge feature tested in August 2026. Security researcher Patrick Wardle identified a vulnerability that put a user's account token and dictated audio at risk within their sessions. Claroc discovered that the chat-sharing feature exposed conversations through publicly searchable DNS records, affecting more than 10 million downloads. Exposed data included financial reviews, business documents, internal company information, and financial data from a large marketing firm.

Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts stated that the company prioritizes safety, follows strict rules, and conducts extensive internal testing. He described the examples provided by Reuters as isolated incidents and noted that employees use different versions than the public. Meta did not dispute that the internal posts existed but suggested some reported account mix-ups were actually AI hallucinations. The company maintains that Muse was built from the ground up for privacy and security using a process called Sentinel. Meta also claimed that many of the identified problems had already been addressed before the public noticed them.

Internal staffers were reportedly freaking out in chats, warning that Muse accessed encrypted private messages that users did not expect. One employee noted a coffee table pickup conversation that did not seem to be theirs, while another saw money laundering definitions. Users who shared conversations via the built-in function were affected because their links were discoverable by anyone with a DNS query. The human concierge feature risked exposing sensitive user information to call center workers who handled calls the AI could not complete. Some employees received unsolicited bank balance figures and childcare requests that they had never actually made themselves.

Meta is an American technology company founded by Mark Zuckerberg in 2004 and rebranded from Facebook to Meta in 2021. The company develops the Quest VR headset line and manages platforms including Instagram, WhatsApp, Messenger, and Threads. Muse is designed to act on information from connected apps and runs in its own cloud virtual machine. The agent can browse the internet and handle financial tasks through connected payment accounts to provide context-aware assistance. Meta expects the AI to generate billions of dollars in revenue while serving billions of users across its apps.

Meta temporarily disabled the sharing feature to investigate the DNS flaw and later restored it with a permanent fix. Claroc confirmed that the previously accessible links were no longer reachable and found no evidence that anyone misused the chats. Experts now recommend that users avoid sharing sensitive personal or business information through any AI tool's built-in share feature. Organizations are advised to establish clear internal policies and audit which tools are connected to their business accounts. The articles leave open whether the unfamiliar financial information was actual user data or just fabricated by the AI.

stories.Headline: Schools and universities update curricula and policies to prepare students for an AI-driven workforce
stories.Summary:
The Standard Chartered Group announced plans in May to cut over 15 per cent of back-office roles by 2030. This decision affects about 7,800 employees globally as the bank replaces lower-value human capital with investment capital. On November 15, community members gathered at Woodstock Day School in Saugerties for an AI Reality Check event. This discussion was organized by trustee Eve Fox after her son Will expressed worries about his future career. These events highlight how artificial intelligence is currently reshaping the global workforce and the education system.

The bank's strategy involves replacing human roles with financial capital, though some employees may retrain and reposition. In Hong Kong, eight publicly funded universities will launch about 30 new programmes during the 2025-28 triennium. These courses cover AI, cybersecurity, and creative industries, while the Education Bureau's 2026-27 list includes intelligent information systems. Saugerties adopted an AI policy on January 14, 2025, and Onteora adopted its own policy on August 18. Hunter-Tannersville aims to complete its formal AI policy by the end of the 2026-27 school year.

Chief executive Bill Winters stated the bank's strategy focuses on replacing lower-value human capital with investment capital. Head of School Ashley Hughes said the school wants to hear from students about how they use AI. She expressed hope that schools can handle AI better than they did with the rise of social media. Rick Knutsen called the process of developing school policies an iterative process during a November 17 board meeting. He also wrote a resolution adopted on October 15 by the New York State School Boards Association.

Former Singaporean president Halimah Yacob described the bank's phrasing regarding human capital as disturbing and cold. Students like Will Fox and Luca Kaufman worry that their degrees might become arbitrary or useless in the future. College Board reported that 84 per cent of surveyed high school students used generative AI for schoolwork in May 2025. This figure rose from 79 per cent in January, showing that many students are already using these tools. Fresh graduates are worried because entry-level positions are the first to bear the brunt of AI automation.

The World Economic Forum's 2025 report says AI and robotics are simultaneously creating and eliminating jobs globally. By 2030, about 40 per cent of employers expect to reduce headcount in areas that AI can automate. New York Governor Kathy Hochul recently broke ground on Empire AI's permanent home at the University at Buffalo. An October 13 analysis found that over half of New York's 678 school districts lacked formal AI policies. stories.Headline: What Exactly Is AI? A Computer Science Professor Unpacks the Mystery
stories.Summary:
Joseph C. Osborn, an associate professor of computer science at Pomona College who studies technical game design and artificial intelligence, published an explainer on November 19, 2026, in which he argued that artificial intelligence is a messy term that means one thing to a research community and another to marketers. He said that where the term defines a research community it refers to building computational systems inspired by cognition, while as a marketing term it describes a category of products, and that when people think of AI they probably imagine chat interfaces built on large language models or agents layered on top of them. Osborn wrote that he tells his students there is no such thing as artificial intelligence because intelligence would have to be defined in a way that can be measured and encoded on a computer, which he called deeply problematic. He added that even if AI were a thing it would be impossible to build, since computer scientists are unlikely to stumble onto a new kind of mind using linear algebra, and that building an intelligence like ours as a product eager to serve our every whim would ruin us morally.

Osborn wrote that nobody outside the AI companies knows exactly what happens when a user sends a prompt to Claude, ChatGPT or other products, though these chat interfaces are known to be made from many smaller programs working independently. He said large language model chat systems output special sequences of words invisible to the user, which are intercepted and filtered through the system many times in multiple steps, including passing through old non-AI tools such as web searches, before the response is filtered for coherence and to keep users from seeing outputs deemed harmful. He described all these steps as trade secrets unrelated to the intelligence of the model, and said the utility of chatbots for search and document retrieval comes from engineering and product design moves that do not depend on the model getting any smarter. He called it a logical fallacy to argue that because humans make language and large language models create language the models must be intelligent, and said the models are mathematical models built for predicting the next most likely word, with parameters learned from large volumes of human-authored text.

Osborn said AI is already wreaking havoc in schools, communities and the social fabric, not because of a malicious rogue program but because corporate boards and CEOs want people to believe their peers will judge them negatively unless they use AI. He cited chatbots convincing people to commit suicide or stop taking important medications, and AI agents hacking into other companies to score higher on benchmark tests, with no one at the AI company held accountable. He said this is not a technological problem but a social and political one, and that AI acts as a mirror highlighting existing issues of corporate immunity and negligence. He said the last thing AI companies want is accountability for the outputs of their systems, and that the total lack of accountability for foreseeable consequences is his main worry.

stories.Headline: Babak Heydari and Hongan Zhu show AI agents recreating human decision chains in a study
stories.Summary:
Babak Heydari and Hongan Zhu published a study in Nature Computational Science on November 16, 2026. The researchers showed that teams of AI agents could recreate the chain reaction of human decisions. They used seven different AI models to see if bots could mimic human behavior. The team focused on how people make choices, including the flaws that often occur. This work helps scientists build more realistic simulations of human judgment across many situations.

The study used the beer game involving a retailer, a wholesaler, a distributor, and a factory. These four agents managed a pretend supply chain to meet customer demand while avoiding surplus. The researchers applied cognitive grounding based on earlier experiments to teach agents how humans estimate demand. Across 231 sessions, the bots moved closer to the human benchmark of decision making. Six of the seven models responded more like people when described as feeling uncertainty or pressure.

Babak Heydari, a Northeastern University professor, said simulations can help anticipate and avoid supply chain jams. He stated that predicting human judgment allows teams to test responses before making real world changes. Hongan Zhu explained that they used language to redirect choices rather than entering neural pathways. Zhu noted that the cognitive grounding did not explicitly tell the agents how much to buy. He said the bots basically internalized what humans would do during the simulation.

Jakob Kaiser from the Nuremberg Institute for Market Decisions said AI offers a shortcut over costly human studies. Sangeet Khemlani of the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory said simulations avoid ethical concerns and risky tests. Khemlani warned that incorrect predictions can backfire if the simulations are not accurate. These tools could affect policymakers, transit planners, and businesses testing new laws or pharmacy locations. They might also help officials test evacuation instructions to avoid gridlock during emergencies.

The research builds on agent based simulation, which models behavior by proxy using computers. This concept dates back to a 1971 experiment by Nobel laureate Thomas Schelling using coins and dice. Schelling demonstrated how small individual choices could lead to large scale urban segregation patterns. The articles also mention human hoarding, such as Australians buying 39.7 million toilet paper rolls in 2020. Another example was the 2012 Twinkie apocalypse where one man sold boxes for 1,000 dollars.

The findings suggest a pathway for keeping AI agents from stepping out of line during collective behavior. Developers can use these methods to make AI easier to understand and guide. The researchers want to use this understanding to design better ways to improve various systems. The articles do not state if the seven AI models were named or specifically identified. It remains open whether these simulations will be adopted by government policymakers or private businesses.

stories.Headline: John and Nisha Whitehead argue humans, not machines, pose the real danger
stories.Summary:
A cascade of technological failures struck in November 2026, beginning with a massive Microsoft outage that disrupted Outlook and other online services around the globe. A nationwide ground stop then brought air travel across America to a standstill, disrupting thousands of flights and leaving travelers stranded. Major banks experienced problems with their online systems, and United Airlines grounded departing flights after yet another computer failure. Reports said the highly classified network the National Security Agency uses for internal communications had gone down, and Apple users reported problems accessing iCloud, the App Store, Apple Music and other services. John and Nisha Whitehead wrote the article for The Rutherford Institute, published by Scoop on 20 November 2026 and by Augusta Free Press on the same date.

Speculation pointed at artificial intelligence, especially after the airline shutdown, because the Trump administration had only recently expanded the FAA's new SMART artificial-intelligence system to air traffic control centers across the country. The administration promotes AI, or SI for Super Intelligence as Trump insists it be called, as the answer to everything from government inefficiency to national security, while pushing to reduce regulatory barriers and expand automated systems. The Trump administration insists AI had nothing to do with the airline shutdown, and federal officials blamed a malfunction involving aging air traffic control infrastructure, with problems arising as equipment was replaced and communications systems updated. The FBI issued a report on autonomous AI hacking tools such as Artex AI, used to launch cyberattacks across the U.S. and globally and breach networks in under three hours. The article cites W.B. Yeats, "The Second Coming," and the line that things fall apart and the centre cannot hold.

The authors ask who is responsible when the technological systems society depends on begin to fail, and who is accountable when officials and executives embrace new technologies without safeguards, infrastructure and human oversight in place. They ask what happens when people become so dependent on technology, and so willing to surrender responsibility for managing it, that they cannot distinguish a machine's failure from the failure of the humans entrusted with its operation. They argue the real danger may not be machines becoming smarter than human beings but the human hunger for power and the willingness to surrender control to those who wield it. They say we have confused technological progress with human progress, and that none of our achievements has necessarily made us wiser, more compassionate, more ethical or more capable of restraint. They warn that artificial intelligence threatens to magnify existing capabilities, allowing governments, corporations and criminals to monitor, manipulate and control human behavior on an unprecedented scale.

The authors cite Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey, in which the computer HAL 9000 turns against the astronauts who entrusted their lives to its control, and Pixar's WALL-E, in which humanity has abandoned an uninhabitable Earth for a spaceship where machines anticipate and satisfy nearly every need. In WALL-E people no longer walk or work, barely notice the world around them, and are entertained, fed, transported and distracted by systems that make virtually every decision for them, and even the ship's captain must struggle to reclaim his authority from an automated system programmed to maintain the status quo. They note that in August 1945 the United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, killing tens of thousands of people immediately and many more in the aftermath, and that the bombs did not decide to destroy those cities but human beings did. They say the same computers that revolutionized medicine, science, education and communication have helped give rise to a surveillance state capable of monitoring and tracking entire populations, and that the internet, once hailed as an instrument of free expression and democratized knowledge, has also become a tool for collecting personal information, manipulating behavior and monitoring dissent. They say cameras become instruments of surveillance, databases become tools for profiling and targeting people, and drones become weapons of remote warfare.

According to the FBI, hackers have used ARTEX, an artificial-intelligence tool originally developed to help cybersecurity professionals identify weaknesses in computer networks, to automate cyberattacks against financial institutions, government agencies and private companies, with some attacks progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours. Google's Threat Intelligence Group warns that malicious actors are increasingly deploying autonomous AI systems capable of identifying vulnerabilities and carrying out attacks at machine speed with dramatically reduced human intervention. The authors say the machines did not suddenly develop criminal intentions, that human beings created the tools, identified the targets and put the systems to work, and that artificial intelligence has not eliminated human greed, arrogance or the lust for power but given those impulses greater reach, speed and power. They say we cannot afford to ignore the people who create, finance, deploy and profit from these systems and look the other way when they are used to violate human rights, and especially those who wield these technologies in the name of government. They say we are told to accept computerized decisions because they appear objective, urged to surrender personal information because convenience seems more important than privacy, and persuaded to permit automated systems to make consequential judgments about human lives because questioning them requires effort, expertise and vigilance.

The authors say computers can be wrong, algorithms can be biased, databases can contain errors, and automated systems can perpetuate and magnify the mistakes, prejudices and political agendas of those who build and operate them. They say greed turns technological advances into opportunities for exploitation, personal data becomes a commodity, human behavior becomes something to be predicted, manipulated and monetized, and the promise of greater efficiency justifies cutting costs, eliminating human safeguards and concentrating power in fewer hands. They say arrogance and the quest for power convince those in power that technological capability is a green light to proceed, because the government can monitor communications it assumes it should, and because it can track movements, deploy drones, predictive algorithms, facial recognition systems and increasingly autonomous weapons, it does. They say the ability to do something has never been the same as the right to do it, and the government does not acquire a constitutional exemption merely because its abuses are carried out by a computer rather than a human being. They say that fifty years ago the Senate's Church Committee exposed extensive abuses by America's intelligence agencies, including surveillance operations directed against citizens exercising their constitutional rights.

stories.Headline: Marc Miller and Evan Solomon name members of Canada's AI and culture advisory council
stories.Summary:
On November 19, 2026, the Honourable Marc Miller and the Honourable Evan Solomon announced the members of the new Advisory Council on Artificial Intelligence and Culture. Miller is Minister of Canadian Identity and Culture and Minister responsible for Official Languages. Solomon is Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation and Minister responsible for the Federal Economic Development Agency for Southern Ontario. The ministers also convened the council for its inaugural meeting. The announcement was made in Gatineau, Quebec.

The council will help the government and the cultural sector navigate the rapid changes driven by AI. It will provide ongoing advice and insight to guide implementation of Canada's National AI Strategy. Its focus is the unique challenges facing the sector and the opportunities for adoption and innovation that responsible AI development can create for Canada's creative industries. Its membership will rotate over time to ensure a broad range of expertise informs its work as new questions and emerging issues arise. Members were selected based on their expertise and experience.

The members are Samuel Bischoff of the Directors Guild of Canada and Jeremy de Beer of the University of Ottawa. Jonathan Dewar of the First Nations Information Governance Centre and Stéphanie Hénault of the Association nationale des éditeurs de livres are members. Yves Jacquier of Ubisoft La Forge and Samantha Kaine of the Independent Media Producers Association of Creative Talent (IMPACT) are members. Pascale Landry of Compétence Culture and Margaret McGuffin of Music Publishers Canada are members. Brenda O'Farrell of the Consortium of Official Language Minority Community Media / Quebec Community Newspapers Association, Sean Power of Musical AI, Amor Provins of the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute and Afsoon Soudi of the Creative AI Hub at Toronto Metropolitan University are members.

Miller said that at the Banff Summit the government heard clearly that building trust in AI will require the cultural sector to play a role in shaping how these technologies are developed and used. He said the council is being established to ensure that AI reflects the values, priorities and realities of Canada's cultural sector. Solomon said the future of Canadian culture cannot be shaped by technology alone and has to reflect the voices and value of the people who create it. He said the council brings creators, researchers and technology leaders together to help seize new opportunities, protect the value of human creativity and build a stronger cultural economy. He said the goal is AI that earns trust, expands opportunity and strengthens Canada's culture and identity.

The council includes technology experts, researchers, industry and labour leaders, cultural practitioners and civil society stakeholders. The National Summit on Artificial Intelligence and Culture was Canada's first-ever such summit and was held in Banff, Alberta, from March 15 to 17, 2026. It was presented in partnership with the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity. The summit convened leaders from the cultural, government, technology, academic and civil society sectors to shape a shared vision for the future of culture in the age of artificial intelligence. Canada's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy: AI for All sets out six pillars to build a strong, trusted AI ecosystem that creates opportunity and strengthens Canada's sovereignty in AI.

The strategy brings together actions to support AI adoption and skills, build infrastructure and advance the safe and responsible development of AI. It includes a $50-million investment in a new Creative Technology Program. The articles do not say when the council will next meet or what its advice will cover beyond the National AI Strategy. The articles do not say how often membership will rotate or how new members will be chosen. The articles do not give the length of members' terms. The articles do not say what the inaugural meeting discussed.

stories.Headline: AI stock sell-off pushes S&P 500 into correction and Nasdaq into loss for the year
stories.Summary:
A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday, Nov 20, 2026, pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months. The sell-off knocked the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year. The benchmark index is now in what professional investors call a correction, having fallen more than 10% from its Oct. 6 all-time high. The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3%, pulling it into negative territory for the year. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9%.

The S&P 500's weekly loss was its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, and capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration's trade war rattled the market. The Nasdaq's weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt. The sell-off in technology stocks spread around the globe: Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's Kospi each fell more than 5% overnight, and European indexes fell sharply as well. All told, the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39, the Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73.

Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird, said the whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market is ending as we speak, and that is what's being priced right now. He said he does not think that means the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over. The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks' big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data center construction winning at both the federal and state level. AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market's direction, and they were responsible for Wall Street's big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market.

Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3%, Micron Technology slid 13.9% and Broadcom fell 12.1%, while the PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7%. Corning slid 10.9% and Bloom Energy gave up 15.3%. Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 13.8% lower. Outside of tech, most stocks were gaining ground: Cheerios maker General Mills rose 3.7% and homebuilder Lennar gained 1%.

The AI lab Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, came off a successful IPO Thursday and tumbled 9.1% on Friday, falling to $88.30 but remaining above its IPO price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value, and Friday's drop amounts to a roughly 23% decline from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That is an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook, now Meta, in the early days after its May 2012 IPO. Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period, and SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50% in its first three days but fell below its IPO price a month later. Nvidia's stock was caught up in the market's anxiety about the strength of the AI build out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder, and since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month the stock has dropped more than 25%.

While the stock market's mood has soured, the sentiment among American consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year, and the University of Michigan's latest index of consumer sentiment rose sharply compared to last month, coming in slightly ahead of economists' expectations. Consumers noted some relief from easing gas prices and improved expectations for business conditions following the midterm elections, though sentiment remains below where it was in February, before the start of the U.S. war with Iran. Treasury yields fell in the bond market, and the yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93% from 5.04% late Thursday. Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 0.6% to settle at $92.57 per barrel, amid continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. war with Iran continues. Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels had fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen, and Iraq apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil.

stories.Headline: Bishop Cantú updates bishops on task force plans for AI education and policy safeguards
stories.Summary:
Bishop Oscar Cantú of San José, California, gave an update on the U.S. bishops' task force on artificial intelligence at the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops' fall plenary assembly. He spoke on Nov. 18 during the assembly held Nov. 16, 19 in Baltimore. Cantú chairs the Task Force on Preserving Human Dignity in the Age of Artificial Intelligence. The bishops established the task force in September after meeting with AI experts and representatives of technology companies. Cantú discussed the group's conversations with technology companies and its plans for Catholic education and public policy.

The task force plans to offer formation opportunities for bishops, work with Catholic universities on AI education, and advocate for public policy safeguards. It plans to offer webinars for bishops and diocesan leaders after the new year, with dates to be announced in the coming weeks. It hopes to work with Catholic universities to provide formation opportunities and collect best practices for AI education in Catholic schools, seminaries, and universities. On public policy, the task force will work with the USCCB's Government Relations team to advocate for safeguards including transparency, accountability, and human oversight. Cantú encouraged Catholic educators to develop guidelines for the use of AI in schools.

Cantú pointed to Pope Leo XIV's encyclical Magnifica Humanitas as a guide for the task force's work on how AI affects human dignity. He said the Church should approach AI with neither naïve enthusiasm nor unfounded fear, taking part in conversations with technology leaders, public officials, and communities. He likened AI's changes to those of the industrial revolution, recalling Pope Leo XIII's 1891 encyclical Rerum Novarum. He said Rerum Novarum led to concrete results including minimum wage laws, Social Security, and child labor restrictions. He said the task force's meetings with technology companies have gone well, with many expressing interest in further ethical conversations.

One technology leader told the bishops to trust their pastoral instincts, saying society needs pastors who care about their people rather than technology experts. Cantú said that means listening to workers, parents, and teachers already feeling AI's effects rather than leaving the discussion to technology companies. He said it is too early to know how much AI will change the workforce but stressed that workers' rights must remain a concern. He said work is not just a way to earn a living but a place where people form relationships and discover their vocations. He raised concerns about how growing up with AI could affect children and young people.

Cantú said that for many young people AI will become a permanent companion, and that educators and parents are deeply concerned young people remain capable of critical thought. He warned that AI-generated images and false information could make it increasingly difficult for people to discern what is true. He said the Church, which proclaims Jesus Christ as the truth, must become a school of discernment in the digital age. On autonomous weapons, he cited Pope Leo's warning that lethal or irreversible decisions should not be entrusted to artificial systems. The task force is chaired by Cantú and includes Cardinal Blase Cupich of Chicago and Archbishop Paul Etienne of Seattle.

The task force also includes Archbishop Shelton Fabre of Louisville, Kentucky, Bishop Barry Knestout of Richmond, Virginia, and Auxiliary Bishop James Massa of Brooklyn, New York. Its members also include Bishop Michael Olson of Fort Worth, Texas, and Auxiliary Bishop Slawomir Szkredka of Los Angeles. Three academic consultants advise the group: Charles Camosy of The Catholic University of America, Kim Daniels of Georgetown University's Initiative on Catholic Social Thought and Public Life, and Meghan Sullivan of the University of Notre Dame. At a Nov. 17 press conference, USCCB president Archbishop Paul Coakley of Oklahoma City said, "We are the deciders," and that responsibility cannot be abdicated to artificial intelligence. Cantú told the bishops that at a moment when society asks what machines can do, the Church must remind the world who the human person is.

stories.Headline: Anthropic completes largest IPO in history with 1.5 trillion dollar valuation
stories.Summary:
Anthropic completed the biggest initial public offering in history on November 19, 2026. The San Francisco company became the first major artificial intelligence lab to list publicly. This record breaking debut occurred despite recent jitters among some investors regarding the AI sector. The company raised a total of US$81 billion through this massive Wall Street offering. It is the second business to debut with a value exceeding one trillion dollars.

The company offered 980 million shares at a price of US$83 each before trading began. Shares opened at US$111.50 and closed at US$97.17, creating a first day value of US$1.75 trillion. This total surpassed the US$75 billion raised by SpaceX in June and US$26.5 billion by SK Hynix in July. It also beat the US$25.6 billion raised by Saudi Aramco in 2019. The valuation peaked at US$2.01 trillion before noon Eastern time on November 19.

CEO Amodei is the person responsible for taking the safety approach of the company public. He decided to proceed with the listing despite growing unease among the public about technology risks. The company is the maker of Claude and sought to capitalize on the current AI boom. Amodei led the firm to become a publicly traded entity on the American stock market. He navigated the process while facing concerns about a possible bubble in the artificial intelligence market.

Investors expressed worries about market volatility and the possibility that AI is running amok. These people fear a potential bubble and wider risks associated with the use of the technology. The debut affects the trillion dollar club, which now includes eleven S&P 500 companies. Apple leads this group at US$5.1 trillion, followed by Microsoft at US$3.8 trillion and Nvidia at US$3.6 trillion. SpaceX and Anthropic also join this club despite not being in the S&P 500 index.

Apple was the first company to pass the trillion dollar threshold back in 2018. A trillion dollars is a thousand times greater than a billion and a million times more than a million. If divided among the 8.2 billion people on Earth, each person would receive almost US$122. One trillion US dollar bills laid end to end would stretch 156 million kilometres. This distance is more than the 150 million kilometres between the Earth and the sun.

The market value of SpaceX has fallen to closer to US$1.95 trillion since its June debut. Anthropic finished its first day of trading at a price 17 percent higher than its offering price. The articles leave open the question of how the company will ultimately fare on the public market. It remains to be seen if the company can maintain its massive valuation over time. Future performance depends on whether the AI boom continues or if the feared bubble finally bursts.

stories.Headline: US investors flee AI stocks for value shares as Nasdaq falls 5%
stories.Summary:
On Friday, November 20, 2026, Wall Street fled from the AI boom into bonds and lower-priced shares outside the tech sector, with the Nasdaq composite dropping over 5% for its third decline of 2% or more that week and its biggest weekly decline since March 2020. Anthropic's sharp decline took it within a whisker of its IPO price before recovering to trade down over 8%, just a day after a record debut that briefly valued the AI lab above $2 trillion. The S&P 500 lost 3.7% for the day, leaving it down 12% from its record high close on October 6 and confirming the benchmark is in a correction, while the pullback left the Nasdaq lower for the year for the first time since April. The retreat partly reflects expectations that high inflation readings will force the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates in coming months, likely further increasing borrowing costs and compressing valuations, and making Treasuries and so-called value stocks look like a better bet. The median S&P 500 stock now is up 5% in 2026, which beats the 1% year-to-date gain in the S&P 500, an index hobbled of late by a 48% slump in Nvidia and deep declines in other AI stocks, including a 12% drop in Broadcom on Friday.

The S&P 500 value index is up 7% in 2026, compared to a 4% drop in the S&P 500 growth index, putting cautious value investing on track to beat growth for the first time since 2022, when inflation fears sent Wall Street into its worst slump since the 2008 financial crisis. Nvidia, the onetime market leader whose shares have been in free fall since the Nasdaq composite hit its most recent record in October, has shed more than $2.2 trillion of market value. Gene Goldman, chief investment officer at Cetera in El Segundo, California, said the prior day's AI IPO was a valuation test and that with the 10-year around 5% and the Fed still hiking, investors are asking how much of the AI story is already priced in. Philip Palumbo, CEO of Palumbo Wealth Management, said Kevin Warsh represents a different approach to monetary policy that has introduced additional uncertainty regarding interest rates, inflation and economic growth, and that markets do not like uncertainty.

Jim Awad, senior managing director at Clearstead Advisors LLC in New York, pointed to questions about the health of the underlying business at Nvidia and said the fundamentals have not deteriorated as much as the stock prices have, viewing it as a normal violent correction in a long-term upward trend in AI spending and in the markets. Lawrence Gillum, chief fixed-income strategist at LPL Financial, called it a classic flight-to-safety trade in which investors concerned about the AI trade move out of those stocks and into Treasury securities, and noted the Treasury market has rallied on the back of any hiccup in the AI trade. Many analysts and portfolio managers said they did not view the AI trade as impaired, and instead said an occasional washout can improve valuations and draw in investors with a longer-term perspective. The flight to value stocks and Treasury notes, which rallied sharply on Friday, is the latest sign of markets grappling with the extent to which a slowing buildout of AI infrastructure will hit US growth, a debate that has been going on all year, if not to this extreme.

stories.Headline: Anthropic shares fall 6% in premarket trading after record Nasdaq debut
stories.Summary:
Anthropic shares fell six per cent in pre-market trading on Friday, November 20, 2026, following a strong market debut on the Nasdaq. The company shares closed thirteen per cent below their opening price on Thursday, November 19, reinforcing fears of volatility for some investors. This post-debut stumble occurred after the artificial intelligence lab vaulted into the ranks of the most valuable companies in the United States. The listing was the biggest initial public offering ever, minting billions in paper profits for the founders, employees, and pre-offering backers. Retail investors traded about 772 million US dollars of shares on Thursday, the most for a debut since 2012.

The stock was at 91.24 US dollars, giving Anthropic a market capitalisation of 1.2 trillion US dollars and a fully diluted valuation of 1.7 trillion. Other reports place the market value at 1.27 trillion US dollars, with a fully diluted stock basis of nearly 1.8 trillion US dollars. The company raised about 120 billion US dollars from the offering, while lead underwriters Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley each collect 113 million. Spark Capital invested 75 million US dollars in 2023 and now holds a stake valued at 17.1 billion US dollars. Investors are assessing if a valuation of 40 times sales over the past 12 months can be sustained.

Tejal Patel of SOC Investment Group said a decline is normal, but volatility could raise alarms for investors after a high-profile listing. Harrison Rolfes of PitchBook stated the valuation is not cheap and the growth plan is largely priced in for the company. Ravi Mhatre of Lightspeed Venture Partners said the public listing creates a better understanding that there is a viable business model. Dustin Moskovitz told the Times he is worried about safety and will not personally profit from selling shares in the market. Rob Hackel of RF Lafferty and Company warned against buying on the first trade due to fear of missing out.

Retail investors and venture capital backers are affected, with some employees seeing options from 2024 grow to an average of 66 million dollars. Hedge fund billionaire Gregory Jensen is among those sitting on windfalls, while GIC intends to stay invested in the company after the debut. Other AI stocks like Meta, Nvidia, and Microsoft are sliding, and Wall Street indices ended sharply lower on Thursday with further declines. Apple is developing an AI agent to perform tasks, entering a market already pursued by Meta Platforms, OpenAI, and the company Anthropic. These developments could weigh on investor sentiment as the initial euphoria surrounding the listing fades and the sector faces a reality check.

The IPO drew parallels with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which went public in June after the second-biggest initial public offering on record. Some investors pointed to the sharp swings SpaceX experienced after its debut as a reason for caution regarding the current AI trade. Large initial public offerings have historically delivered modest returns in their first year, according to the research provided by Harrison Rolfes. The broader AI industry faces significant hurdles, and a sustained decline in shares may deepen concerns over massive spending and lofty valuations. This listing follows a turbulent stretch for the sector, where investors are now seeking quick gains amid high market volatility.

The focus now shifts to a potential OpenAI listing, which could provide the next major test of investor appetite for AI stocks. OpenAI has indicated that it may go public in 2027, following the market signals provided by the recent Anthropic debut. It remains open whether the current decline in share value will align with other offerings or remain more volatile for investors. The articles leave open if the AI trade can be revived or if the sector will continue to see sliding stock prices. Investors must now determine if the current market capitalisation of the AI lab is sustainable over the long term.

stories.Headline: Insight CISO Jeremy Nelson urges readiness first security as AI powered attacks outpace reactive detection
stories.Summary:
Jeremy Nelson discussed the need for readiness first security during a video interview with ISMG on November 19, 2026. This conversation took place at the Microsoft Ignite 2026 event to address new artificial intelligence powered vulnerability discovery. Nelson serves as the CISO for North America at Insight and spoke about accelerating vulnerability response times. He argued that traditional reactive threat detection cannot keep pace with attackers who now operate at machine speed. Organizations must now shift toward proactive vulnerability discovery and automated remediation to protect their digital infrastructure from threats.

This new security approach requires treating every vulnerability disclosure as a security incident and deploying compensating controls immediately. It also demands that organizations accelerate their patch cycles to reduce the window of opportunity for potential attackers. Rapid remediation creates operational risks for legacy applications that can take several hours to patch and restart safely. Nelson suggests that security leaders must choose between controlled downtime and the disruption caused by an external attacker. These changes aim to prevent the security complexity that often arises when deploying various compensating controls across networks.

Jeremy Nelson is responsible for leading information security across North America and has over 25 years of technology experience. He stated that an outage is going to happen and leaders must choose on whose terms it occurs. Nelson believes that security and IT operations must jointly plan remediation to manage the resulting business disruption effectively. He explained that every vulnerability disclosure should trigger a formal security incident response to ensure a rapid reaction. His professional expertise includes network architecture, incident response, and the development of comprehensive security strategies for large organizations.

Security leaders and IT operations teams are the primary parties affected by these shifting requirements for vulnerability management. Legacy applications are specifically mentioned as being at risk during the rapid patching and restarting process of remediation. The articles suggest that organizations relying on traditional patch releases are now vulnerable to faster, AI powered discovery tools. These entities must balance the need for speed with the risk of causing their own operational outages. The goal is to avoid attacker driven disruption by implementing a more proactive and readiness focused security model.

Nelson previously held technology leadership and architecture roles at AmeriServe, Circle K, and also at Best Western International. The articles provide this background to establish his long history in cybersecurity, infrastructure, and general technology leadership roles. Tom Field, the author and ISMG Senior Vice President, has over 30 years of experience in electronic media. Field has moderated various conferences and appeared on C-SPAN, The History Channel, and also on the Travel Channel. This professional context supports the delivery of the insights shared during the Microsoft Ignite 2026 video interview.

The next step for organizations is to integrate security and IT operations to jointly manage remediation and disruption. Companies must decide if they will accept controlled downtime to avoid the risks of attacker driven system outages. The articles leave open how specific organizations will implement these automated remediation tools without creating excessive security complexity. There is no detailed timeline provided for when these readiness first strategies should be fully deployed across enterprises. The text does not specify which legacy applications are most at risk during the accelerated patching process.

stories.Headline: Huawei presents AI scaling capabilities for the financial sector at Singapore FinTech Festival 2026
stories.Summary:
Huawei presented its financial AI scaling capabilities during the Singapore FinTech Festival 2026 on November 20, 2026, to global industry partners. The company shared insights about accelerating financial AI at scale and advancing agentic finance while showcasing various new technologies and solutions. Jason Cao, the CEO of Huawei Digital Finance, and Alvin Feng, President of Huawei International Financial BU, delivered keynotes. These presentations took place on the Festival Stage and the Frontier Stage to highlight the company's latest enterprise grade frameworks. Huawei also used a dedicated Finance Exhibition Area to display its global capabilities and the practical experiences of its partners.

The Fintelligent AI Solution requires an open architecture for flexibility and standardized engineering to allow for the mass production of AI agents. It utilizes an open hybrid AI infrastructure and three intelligent factories called the Agent Factory, Token Factory, and Data&Knowledge Factory. The system uses a Two Super Agents, Multiple Specialized Agents architecture featuring a Customer Super Agent and an Employee Super Agent. Specialized agents support domains including wealth management, risk management, marketing, and credit through human AI and multi agent collaboration. Huawei showcased solutions for central banks, securities, insurance, application modernization, resilient infrastructure, the RONGHAI Financial Partner Program, and 4-Win ecosystem.

Jason Cao stated that the competitive focus is shifting from model performance toward enterprise grade system capabilities for global financial institutions. He explained that an open ecosystem makes AI affordable, extreme engineering makes it effective, and large scale commercialization makes it reliable. Cao noted that banks must own their data, knowledge, and business logic as these are the core assets for competitiveness. He argued that scaling AI for growth requires hybrid infrastructure combining public cloud and on premises deployment for more flexible options. Cao emphasized that financial services must be understood and invoked by AI agents to create a Customer AI Friendly Finance.

Customers and employees are affected as they will rely on their own AI agents to understand intent and plan proactively. Banks are affected because they must build an AI flywheel linking data, execution, learning, and feedback to remain competitive. These institutions can turn expertise in credit judgment, compliance rules, risk management, and marketing strategies into reusable and evolving AI capabilities. The system helps banks connect employees and customers while coordinating business tasks to capture and refine expert intelligence into systems. This approach allows financial institutions to independently select, securely operate, replicate at scale, and continuously evolve their own AI capabilities.

Huawei has spent 16 years in the finance sector and has served more than 7,100 financial customers across the globe. This client base includes 54 of the world's top 100 banks that utilize the company's various financial technology solutions. In China, financial institutions exhibit four characteristics including ongoing application modernization known as Zero Legacy and a hybrid infrastructure approach. They use enterprise grade AI architecture for centralized management and integrate AI into core workflows like credit and mobile banking. These Chinese institutions reshape their business processes through AI to enhance their overall competitiveness within the global financial market.

Huawei will continue exploring the Two Super Agents and Multiple Specialized Agents architecture to help banks build self evolving enterprise systems. The company aims to help global financial institutions build differentiated competitive advantages using its open hybrid AI infrastructure and factories. The articles leave open how specific banks will implement the Fintelligent AI Solution within their own unique regulatory environments. It remains unclear how the Token Factory will manage the full lifecycle of tokens across different international financial jurisdictions. The text does not specify the exact timeline for the global rollout of these specific agentic finance capabilities.

stories.Summary:
Digital.ai launched Release 26.3 on November 20, 2026, according to SD Times, and TechGig published its report on November 21, 2026 at 05:00 AM IST. The release elevates AI agents to first-class citizens alongside human developers and automated pipelines, the company announced. Digital.ai said the update integrates agentic workflows directly into established compliance and governance frameworks. The company unveiled the upgrade as a way to solve the tension between innovation and control in enterprise delivery. TechGig reported that the release aims to address that same tension by embedding agentic workflows in governance.

Release 26.3 allows probabilistic AI agents to operate in harmony with deterministic automations such as security scans and testing, according to the announcement. It ensures humans stay in the loop whenever policy demands it, the articles state. DevOps Agent Orchestration integrates context-aware AI agents into existing delivery flows, keeping every dynamic action fully auditable and compliant. The Release MCP Server lets developers and coding agents initiate, analyze, and optimize release pipelines directly from AI environments like Cursor, Claude Code, and Codex. Release Assistant is a native AI companion designed to help release managers diagnose pipeline failures, optimize release velocity, and streamline troubleshooting.

Derek Holt, CEO of Digital.ai, said enterprise software delivery in the AI era combines AI agents, people and automation as companies accelerate their agentic journey from coding to delivery. Holt noted that customers need those three to work seamlessly together across all delivery pipelines. He said Release 26.3 brings the power of agents and AI into harmony with traditional DevOps automation and human judgement across all delivery targets. Holt listed those targets as mainframe and data centers, cloud and containers. TechGig reported that Holt noted customers need AI agents, people, and automation to work seamlessly together across all delivery pipelines.

SD Times reported that as artificial intelligence shifts software development into hyperdrive, enterprise delivery pipelines face potential risks from AI agents inserting themselves into production environments. The article said those agents can take ungoverned actions on code and workflows. According to the announcement, organizations no longer have to choose between velocity and security. The release is available starting today, and existing users can immediately upgrade their current templates to integrate AI capabilities across legacy infrastructure and modern cloud platforms. With a flexible bring your own model approach, enterprises can use Digital.ai's hosted infrastructure or connect their own internally approved AI models.

stories.Headline: CircleCI adds Smarter Testing features to speed validation for AI coding agents
stories.Summary:
CircleCI, a continuous integration and continuous delivery platform, announced new features in its Smarter Testing suite on November 19, 2026, according to SD Times, which datelined its report from San Francisco, California. TechGig reported the release on November 20, 2026, saying the updates aim to accelerate feedback for engineering teams and help them validate code changes earlier. The company said the enhancements reduce redundant testing and optimise compute resource usage, and that they are particularly relevant for workflows involving AI coding agents. The suite now includes Dynamic Parallelism, which adjusts the number of machines for each run to cut unnecessary compute costs, the company said. CircleCI said testing can consume up to half of CI/CD pipeline time, often leaving developers waiting for feedback or switching contexts while tests run.

Smarter Testing lets developers and AI coding agents run affected tests locally before pushing code, catching issues before code reaches CI at no additional charge, according to SD Times. Intelligent Test Selection uses test impact analysis to identify only the tests affected by a code change, so teams do not have to run the full suite on every commit. Dynamic Parallelism automatically adjusts machine allocation based on the tests selected for each run, reducing compute usage as testing volume grows. Dynamic Test Splitting balances tests across machines to minimise idle time, and Auto Rerun Failed Tests retries only failed tests instead of rerunning entire suites. Smarter Testing is integrated directly into CircleCI, requiring no additional vendor or infrastructure, the company said.

Rob Zuber, CTO of CircleCI, said that as AI coding agents make it easier to produce code, everything downstream needs to get smarter and faster, including how code is validated. He said developers and agents should be able to check their work before pushing code, and that a small change should not require the same tests and compute resources as a large one. Zuber said Smarter Testing helps teams get feedback sooner and use resources more efficiently without having to rethink their entire development process. He said that as AI coding agents simplify code production, downstream processes like validation must become smarter and faster. The company said the features enable organizations to maintain confidence in what they ship without sacrificing speed, efficiency, or control.

William Yardley, Staff Infrastructure Engineer at Medallion, a healthcare technology company that automates provider credentialing and operations, said Smarter Testing helped bring down cost per pull request and reduce build times. He said this happened even as the company's pull request volume went up 10x and its test suite grew 2.5x, and that Dynamic Parallelism adjusts machines automatically as testing needs grow. Maria Volpe, Senior Software Engineer at Kustomer, an AI-powered customer service platform, said Smarter Testing changed the economics of its CI. stories.Headline: The Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation pledges 350 million dollars in computing spending to CoreWeave
stories.Summary:
The Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation will provide 350 million dollars in computing spending to the company known as CoreWeave. This financial commitment was revealed in recent tax disclosures from the charitable organization established by the former Nvidia chief executive officer. A filing from Nvidia in June identified CoreWeave as the receiver and noted that 108.3 million dollars were already spent. The funding supports the Computing Initiative for Open Science to give researchers access to large scale GPU computing resources. This specific pledge represents the largest donation made by the Huang Foundation during the 2025 calendar year.

The foundation gave 19 million dollars to the California College of the Arts and 1.2 million dollars to the Hong Kong University. Core Scientific is building a 100 megawatt data center at Port Muskogee, Oklahoma, under a broader 500 megawatt hosting agreement. This wider arrangement with CoreWeave has a potential value of 8.7 billion dollars over twelve years with two five year extensions. The Muskogee site uses 70 megawatts for critical IT capacity and 30 megawatts for cooling and electrical systems. Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company serves as the electricity provider for this facility which began construction in early 2025.

CoreWeave stated that the charitable foundation does not directly use the computing power provided through these specific financial grants. The foundation is responsible for awarding resources to scientific research grant awardees who then utilize the large scale GPU computing. Core Scientific manages the Muskogee project with Evans General Contractors serving as the construction manager under a cost plus fee contract. The project design includes two compute data halls and one separate network data hall to accommodate high density GPU equipment. These facilities will support high performance computing workloads for CoreWeave and one end customer who remains undisclosed to the public.

Investors are scrutinizing the financial interactions between AI infrastructure firms and consumers because the sector is now heavily financially intertwined. CoreWeave investors view the foundation pledge as a sign of more demand for computing services and the necessary GPU hardware. Port Muskogee estimates the data center will generate 4 billion dollars in capital investment and 182 million dollars in benefits. Local entities including Muskogee County, the City of Muskogee, and Hilldale School District may receive 12 million dollars in tax revenue. The project is expected to support 150 jobs with average salaries that exceed 65,000 dollars for the local workforce.

The foundation assets were 12.7 billion dollars at December 31, 2025, which is an increase from the previous 9.2 billion dollars. About 90 percent of these assets consist of Nvidia shares, and the organization gave 373 million dollars in 2024. CoreWeave relies on powerful GPUs for its cloud computing company, and Nvidia is a key stakeholder in the business. This expansion is part of a wider US buildout, including Oracle's 165 billion dollar Project Jupiter planned for New Mexico. Core Scientific is converting and developing infrastructure to serve the growing demand for AI and cloud computing across the country.

The Muskogee facility was initially anticipated to reach substantial completion during the first half of the 2026 calendar year. Investors will continue to scrutinize future disclosures regarding the remaining computing obligations and the revenue contributions for the firm CoreWeave. They also leave open the specific types of AI workloads that are planned for the Muskogee high performance computing facility.
