stories.Headline: Google donates Agent Substrate, gVisor and OpenRL to the CNCF for secure AI agent execution
stories.Summary:
Google donated Agent Substrate and gVisor to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, placing two core components of its AI agent infrastructure under vendor-neutral open-source governance, TechGig reported on Nov 20, 2026. The donation also includes OpenRL, Google's open-source reinforcement learning orchestration project, according to both articles. InfoQ reported on Nov 20, 2026, that Google announced the donation of Agent Substrate and gVisor to the CNCF. The move is intended to address securely executing untrusted, AI-generated code and managing compute overhead from agents that frequently pause and resume. Together, the projects target different layers of agent infrastructure, from isolated code execution to managing agent lifecycles and coordinating large-scale training workloads.

Google estimates that agents can spend 90-95 per cent of their time idle while still holding important state, including memory, files, repositories, and active sessions. Agent Substrate separates agent state, called actors, from compute resources, known as workers, and actors retain state including filesystem contents, memory, and execution context. Workers provide reusable, pre-warmed execution environments drawn from shared Kubernetes pools, and when an agent resumes, Substrate assigns it to an available Worker and restores its previous state. According to Google, this approach lets agents resume in under 500 milliseconds without creating a new Kubernetes Pod for every execution, and it reduces pressure on the Kubernetes control plane. Google's gVisor provides an additional isolation boundary through a user-space application kernel that intercepts system calls and handles them within its own isolated environment, and Agent Substrate also supports Cloud Hypervisor microVMs for hardware-level virtualisation.

Google argues that conventional Kubernetes workloads and AI agents have fundamentally different execution patterns, because a traditional application typically starts, serves requests, and continues running. An AI agent, however, may execute code for a few seconds before waiting for model inference, an external API, or human approval, according to Google. Google says keeping every agent in a dedicated Pod wastes resources, while scaling to zero introduces delays when environments must be reconstructed. Google states that large-scale agent evaluations can overwhelm Kubernetes control planes when thousands of short-lived execution environments are repeatedly created and destroyed. Google's stated goal is to establish an open foundation for agentic applications, much as Kubernetes helped standardise container orchestration.

InfoQ reported that other providers are addressing similar challenges through technologies such as Kata Containers, Firecracker, and dedicated sandboxing platforms. Google's contribution is to combine secure execution with an agent-aware orchestration model and place the resulting technologies within an open ecosystem, according to InfoQ. AI agents routinely execute generated shell commands, install packages, and interact with external tools, and treating this code as trusted creates significant risks, particularly when multiple agents share infrastructure. gVisor reduces the exposure of the underlying host while retaining much of the efficiency associated with container-based execution, and Agent Substrate gives platform teams flexibility to select an appropriate isolation boundary without changing the overall agent lifecycle model. The articles state that AI agents need their own secure, stateful, and efficiently managed execution infrastructure beyond conventional Kubernetes workloads.

Kubernetes was designed around long-running applications and relatively stable workloads, according to InfoQ. Agentic systems introduce more dynamic execution patterns, where environments must be created, suspended, restored, and isolated at much greater frequency. The announcement reflects a broader shift in cloud-native infrastructure patterns, the articles state. By donating these projects to the CNCF, Google is helping establish the foundations for that next layer of cloud-native computing, InfoQ reported. The articles describe the donation as addressing emerging challenges in securely executing untrusted, AI-generated code and managing substantial compute overhead from frequently pausing and resuming agents.

The articles do not state when the CNCF will accept the projects, how the foundation will govern them, or what licence terms will apply. They do not say whether OpenRL will be managed alongside Agent Substrate and gVisor or separately within the CNCF. The articles give no timeline for CNCF review, no comment from CNCF officials, and no details on how existing Google users will be affected by the transfer. They do not state how the projects will be maintained, who the maintainers will be, or whether other companies will contribute. The articles leave open how the move will change Google's own agent infrastructure and what adoption the projects will see under vendor-neutral governance.

stories.Headline: SEBI member KVR Murty says the regulator is preparing AI guidelines for capital markets
stories.Summary:
The Securities and Exchange Board of India is preparing to issue guidelines for the responsible use of artificial intelligence in capital markets, SEBI Whole Time Member KVR Murty said on Thursday. Murty spoke at a World Federation of Exchanges event in Mumbai. He said the guidelines will include disclosures and accountability requirements for related entities. He highlighted the growing role of AI in trading and investment decisions. He stressed the need for stronger regulatory oversight as autonomous AI systems become increasingly sophisticated.

Murty said AI is enabling ordinary investors to develop their own trading algorithms. He said an AI agent is given a goal, not a fixed set of rules, and can change how it trades as it learns. He asked how a strategy that rewrites itself can be approved. He raised concerns about millions of investors using agents built on similar models and data, potentially triggering simultaneous market exits. He said every agent, however intelligent, must be traceable, and someone must answer for what it does.

Murty said SEBI has already created a verification agency to examine risk and return claims made by investment advisers, research analysts and algorithmic trading providers. He said AI applications in market surveillance, compliance and fraud detection offer significant potential, although governance frameworks remain incomplete. He said India's Demat 2.0 pilot facilitated fundraising of Rs 1,025 crore by three issuers. He said bond and cash settlement took place simultaneously through central bank digital currency on a T+0 basis. He said what is needed is stronger governance, not faster adoption.

Murty urged market infrastructure institutions to invest in research and development, potentially through dedicated laboratories functioning as Securities Market Innovation Hubs. He said technology can strengthen investor trust but cannot substitute for it. He said the future of capital markets would be determined by their ability to support the real economy, maintain resilience and safeguard investor trust rather than merely increasing trading volumes. A Congressional Research Service report said the Securities and Exchange Commission has not issued regulations specifically targeting AI use in capital markets. The report identified unresolved policy concerns including accountability gaps when AI systems fail, risks from market concentration among a small number of AI developers, and potentially misleading "AI washing" disclosures.

The National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020, P.L. 116-283, Division E, defines artificial intelligence as a machine-based system that can make predictions, recommendations, or decisions influencing real or virtual environments. Common capital markets applications include investment management, algorithmic trading, robo-advising, anti-money laundering compliance and back-office productivity support. In April 2025, the Trump administration's Office of Management and Budget issued Memorandum M-25-21, directing agencies including the SEC to develop AI strategies and build an AI-ready federal workforce. The SEC issued its compliance plan in September 2025 and launched an AI task force in August 2025, reporting 60 internal AI use cases that year. The SEC withdrew a 2023 proposed rule addressing conflicts of interest associated with predictive data analytics in June 2025, along with other rules proposed under the previous administration.

As of October, the SEC had received petitions for rulemaking seeking mandatory AI governance and risk management disclosures in public filings but had not indicated whether it would pursue AI-specific rulemaking. The SEC's fiscal 2027 examination priorities continue to emphasize AI disclosures, AI-related risks and cybersecurity under existing securities laws. The Unleashing AI Innovation in Financial Services Act, H.R. 4801, sponsored by Rep. J. French Hill (R-AR), would establish AI innovation labs at the SEC and other financial regulators, allowing test projects to operate with relief from certain regulations. The bill was placed on the Union Calendar on June 24. The AI Act of 2024, H.R. 10262, sponsored by Rep. Maxine Waters (D-CA), would have required the SEC to study AI's benefits and risks for capital markets, and the House Financial Services Committee referred it in November 2024, but it did not advance before the 118th Congress adjourned.

stories.Summary:
Ubisoft announced on November 20, 2026, that it has launched Motherbrain, a dedicated subsidiary focused on developing proprietary generative AI technology for gameplay, according to a report in The Verge. Ubisoft said that as its portfolio evolves, its production needs are changing, requiring it to adjust the size of some teams to ensure resources are aligned with current production priorities and business needs. stories.Headline: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims Claude helped him prove the Riemann hypothesis in Lean code
stories.Summary:
Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at the AI company Anthropic, claimed on Friday, 20 November 2026, to have discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis working with Anthropic's Claude AI. He published a statement on his website saying he believed he had, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. The Riemann hypothesis was first put forward in 1859 by the German mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It proposes an origin for the prime numbers, namely that they follow a certain pattern. The question is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems, which will award a $1 million prize for an accepted solution.

Alpöge has not published a human-readable version of the proof, saying it would be obviously inappropriate to attempt to post some massive unreadable travesty of slop. He says an unpublished version ran to more than 250,000 pages. Instead he released a version written in Lean, a computer code mathematicians use to mechanically verify proofs as a series of logical steps in a process called formalisation. The process is so thorough that if a theorem comes through intact, meaning the code compiles, it is considered proved correct beyond all reasonable doubt. Alpöge says the proof confirms the generalised Riemann hypothesis, which widens out the concept to different properties of prime numbers.

Alpöge wrote that it is natural to feel that this is an end, in his case a loss of a principal guiding light. He wrote that what he saw during the course of progress so amazed him that he believed it is one dawn across science of something far greater. He wrote that the precise timing is horrible and that if he could have, he would have finished this all much earlier. He says he spoke to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and determined that there was a constraint to respect before the announcement could be made. Anthropic listed on the stock market on 19 November, and Alpöge appears to suggest that he waited to announce the proof until after.

Kevin Buzzard at Imperial College London said let's see if it compiles first, and that it might be a while before we find the relevant experts able to tell us the thrust of the argument. Buzzard said it probably will be true because Alpöge will have a huge amount of egg on his face if the Lean code doesn't compile or is deficient in some way. James McKee at Royal Holloway University of London said there are numerous results conditional on the generalised Riemann hypothesis, and now those are theorems. McKee said most mathematicians believed, or the more cautious ones merely suspected, that GRH was true, so its proof will not be unsettling. McKee said what is both unsettling and tremendously exciting is the rapid progress in recent months towards automated proofs of significant mathematical results, and that it is both a wonderful time and a terrible time to be a research mathematician.

Hector Pasten, a mathematician at the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile, said that if the proof is correct and understood, this completes a dictionary between different branches of math where the connections were only partial, something like a Rosetta Stone. Carlo Pagano, a professor at Concordia University and a visiting researcher at Google DeepMind, said that if true, even from a first high level scan of the summary of the proposed argument, it is very plausible to him that the new ideas in the proof will open up brand new avenues of thinking in number theory. Andrew Sutherland, an MIT mathematician, told Scientific American today after he had independently compiled Alpöge's result in Lean that this is indeed an historic moment and that the world has changed. Sutherland said he knows there will be a wide range of reactions in the community, but to him this is a human triumph and a day for celebration. Sutherland said there is much work to be done to understand the mathematical details of the proof, that he can't wait to dig into them, and that perhaps the single most important step in the proof was building a machine that can think.

In August, Anthropic announced previous work on the Riemann hypothesis, but that stopped short of a full proof. The first chink in the problem's armor appeared in October, when one of the proofs in OpenAI's massive dump of math results made significant progress on making sense of the primes. In July, Alpöge announced that the Jacobian conjecture, which academics have spent decades trying to prove was true, is actually false, giving a tiny, 216-character counterexample as proof. He and Tristan Buckmaster at New York University also announced that they had cracked three significant problems considered stepping stones to the Navier-Stokes problem, hours before OpenAI controversially revealed a full solution. Scientific American reported that Buckmaster implied in September that OpenAI had stolen his and Alpöge's work.

The process isn't without vulnerabilities, and the code and mathematics will need to be thoroughly checked by humans. Issues can arise in Lean, but it shouldn't take long for experts to verify whether the hypothesis is properly coded, and if the proof is correct. Scientific American called the story breaking news and said it will be updated. The Riemann result, if correct, doesn't have any immediate real-world applications, and it won't upend global banking or make the internet run faster. Sutherland once told Scientific American that an AI that can prove the Riemann hypothesis is not one he'd want to meet, and that if that happens, mathematicians having jobs will be the least of our problems.

stories.Headline: Zacks Investment Research finds Micron has the investment edge over NVIDIA
stories.Summary:
Zacks Investment Research published a report on November 20, 2026, comparing the investment potential of Micron Technology and NVIDIA. The analysis examines how both semiconductor companies benefit from the current boom in artificial intelligence infrastructure. Micron provides essential memory and storage solutions, while NVIDIA leads the market for AI accelerators and computing platforms. Both firms show impressive financial growth, but they face different risks and valuations. The report concludes that Micron currently has the edge over NVIDIA for investors.

Micron reported fiscal 2026 revenues of 133.19 billion dollars, with fourth quarter revenues reaching 54.23 billion dollars. NVIDIA reported third quarter fiscal 2027 revenues of 115.8 billion dollars, with data center revenues hitting 107.6 billion dollars. Micron signed 26 strategic customer agreements worth 32 billion dollars, while NVIDIA ships its new Vera Rubin NVL72 systems. Micron's forward price to earnings multiple is 3.77, which is lower than the 10.10 multiple for NVIDIA. Applied Materials saw its DRAM and flash memory equipment sales reach 42 percent of its fiscal fourth quarter sales.

Micron management expects record results for fiscal 2027 and tighter supply conditions through calendar years 2027 and 2028. NVIDIA management described the ramp up of the Vera Rubin platform as the fastest product launch in company history. Applied Materials management expects the wafer fabrication equipment market to grow 30 percent for the full year of 2027. They also aim to expand gross margins by five percentage points between 2025 and 2030.

NVIDIA customers face high switching costs because of the CUDA software ecosystem and various networking and AI software solutions. Cloud providers, enterprises, and AI developers are affected by the availability of Blackwell and Vera Rubin computing platforms. Shareholders are currently involved in litigation and investigations following a sudden leadership change at the NVIDIA corporation. Applied Materials serves as a critical supplier for both Micron and NVIDIA's manufacturing partner, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. This equipment maker competes across the etch, deposition, and process control segments to support various chip manufacturers.

Micron's growth is driven by high demand for high bandwidth memory, server DRAM, and data center solid state drives. NVIDIA's data center business is its biggest engine, accounting for approximately 93 percent of its total company revenues. stories.Headline: Moonshot AI cancels 150 million dollar Nvidia chip contract in Indonesia
stories.Summary:
Chinese artificial intelligence company Moonshot AI canceled a cloud contract in Indonesia on November 19, 2026. The firm terminated this agreement following a move by the U.S. Commerce Department to block indirect access routes. This decision happened after the U.S. government tightened licensing requirements for advanced AI chips and servers. Moonshot AI had previously planned to lease services based on Nvidia Blackwell chips starting next year. The company also halted all talks regarding new agreements after the contract was scrapped.

The canceled contract was worth 150 million dollars and involved the Blackwell Ultra B300 chips. Moonshot AI had agreed to a 50 percent prepayment, which is triple the customary 15 percent rate. The U.S. Commerce Department announced on November 16 that computing services are now subject to licensing requirements. These new rules took effect on November 19 and apply to Indonesia, Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Brazil. The Blackwell Ultra B300 chips are currently barred from export to China.

The U.S. Commerce Department is responsible for these restrictions and cited the need to block indirect access. House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast disclosed export license records from December last year through May this year. He noted that of 3.44 million units applied for, only 879,868 were approved for various firms. These approvals included 150,000 units for Tencent affiliates, 75,000 for Alibaba, and 43,000 for Baidu. Some of the buyers were designated as Chinese military companies by the U.S. Defense Department.

Analysts say this is a swift effect of the U.S. move to restrict remote chip access. Chinese AI firms are affected and are now accelerating efforts to secure their own domestic chips. Alibaba Chief Executive Eddie Wu said training ultra-large models with domestic chips would be possible by early 2027. Tencent Chief Strategy Officer James Mitchell predicted that Chinese firms would rely on domestic chips long term. These companies are reacting to the intensifying pressure coming from the U.S. Congress.

The move followed a scandal involving former Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang regarding data centers in Singapore. Suspicions arose that China gained access to U.S. chips through these specific Southeast Asian routes. AMD also faced allegations of maintaining business ties with sanctioned Chinese firms like the server maker IEIT. Hunterbrook Media reported that AMD firmware was found in IEIT products six times after sanctions took effect. AMD generated 34.8 percent of its revenue last year from China, Hong Kong, and Singapore.

The U.S. government may implement a rule in January extending controls to affiliates over 50 percent owned by sanctioned firms. AMD told Reuters that the allegations distort its business practices and that it complies with export laws. Hunterbrook Capital stated it took a short position in AMD after publishing the report on firmware. The articles leave open whether China will actually follow through on expanding fuel exports with other nations. stories.Headline: Etsy sellers leave the site over a new policy that lets Etsy train AI on their content
stories.Summary:
Many longtime owners of shops on Etsy, the online marketplace known for its handmade goods, said this week that they had left the site over a policy change that they said leaves them vulnerable to exploitation by artificial intelligence companies. Language in Etsy's new terms, set to take effect on Dec. 16, says the company and its third party partners and vendors reserve the right to use sellers' content to develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies. The terms say that Etsy and its partners will use such technologies in part to improve the platform and keep it safe for users. The previous version of the terms did not include a clause about using content for artificial intelligence.

Aaron Millard, an illustrator, wrote in an Instagram post announcing that he was deleting the shop that he has run for nearly a decade, saying that selling on the platform now means letting Etsy train AI on artwork and resell that data to third parties with no way to opt out. He said his work took years to learn and create and that he would not let it be stolen. Kristen and Geoff Zephyrus, the founders of the home goods and stationery brand Cognitive Surplus, which has sold its products on Etsy for 13 years, also deleted their shop. In an Instagram post, they accused the company of claiming perpetual, free, boundless permission to not only train AI on their art, but also to resell the data for profit. Kristen Zephyrus said in an interview that for Etsy to be helping to train algorithms with human content is just unimaginably awful and that they do not want anything to do with that.

Etsy said it would revise its policy after hearing complaints from sellers. James Ossman said it will not use content to copy work or replace creativity, but will use it for safety, fraud checks and ads. The articles do not say when the revised terms will be published or what they will contain. The articles also do not say how many sellers have left the site or whether the deletions will affect the Dec. 16 effective date.

stories.Headline: Blacklisted Chinese universities buy restricted Nvidia AI chips through obscure suppliers
stories.Summary:
At least six blacklisted Chinese universities bought restricted Nvidia AI chips through obscure suppliers, according to a CNN analysis released on July 19. Two universities closely affiliated with the Chinese military acquired high performance chips in just the past few months. The analysis examined approximately 300 procurement notices from Chinese universities collected in a commercial database. These notices showed that the majority of purchases involved Nvidia chips subject to United States export controls. The buyers included universities, research institutions, and some government agencies.

The purchases included A100, A800, H100, H200, and H800 chips, with the A100 remaining banned since 2022. Harbin Institute of Technology bought one A100 chip for about 7,000 dollars in September. Northwestern Polytechnical University purchased four H200 chips for 240,000 dollars in September and October. Beihang University, blacklisted since 2001, bought A100 and A800 chips about ten times from 2022 to 2024. The United States allowed H200 sales on a case by case basis since last December with a 25 percent tariff.

Gregory Allen of Decision Tree Research said these universities are closely connected to the Chinese military and invest in military AI. Kate Koren of CSIS said some chips might have come from inventory stockpiled before the 2022 controls. Koren also noted that smuggling is difficult to detect because it involves shell companies, document forgery, and multiple countries. Mao Ning from the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs said China opposes the United States using national security to target institutions. The Department of Commerce approved over 800,000 chips for Chinese companies until last May.

The Department of Commerce approved 150,000 chips for Tencent, 75,000 for Alibaba, 43,000 for Baidu, and 4,000 for BYD. These approvals included firms on a Pentagon list of Chinese military companies. Nvidia applied in April to sell 40,000 H200 chips to New Century Lettall Data Service, tied to Megaspeed. This company is linked to Alice Huang, a Chinese asset who had an affair with the former Nvidia chief executive. Moonshot AI is affected by new rules and canceled a 150 million dollar contract with an Indonesian provider.

The former Nvidia CEO resigned last week after his relationship with a woman aiding chip smuggling was revealed. Chinese companies previously bypassed regulations by leasing semiconductors from data centers in Malaysia, Indonesia, and Thailand. Moonshot AI used Blackwell semiconductors to develop its Kimi K3 model, which performed similarly to major United States models. The Department of Commerce received applications to sell over 3.4 million chips to Chinese companies as of May 11. The Trump administration introduced new regulations this week to block bypass routes using overseas data centers.

The Bureau of Industry and Security has launched an official investigation into the access routes used by Moonshot AI. Data centers providing high computing resources to Chinese customers must now obtain United States government permission within 90 days. Sidley Austin stated that the permission threshold corresponds to about 300 advanced AI semiconductors. Bernstein analyzed that the cost of training AI models for Chinese companies is highly likely to rise. The articles leave open whether the chips listed in the procurement notices were actually delivered to the universities.

stories.Headline: VAST Data gains IMDA accreditation to supply AI infrastructure in Singapore
stories.Summary:
VAST Data received accreditation from Singapore's Infocomm Media Development Authority, or IMDA, which recognises the company as a qualified technology provider for government agencies and large enterprise customers, according to a Telecompaper report dated 20 November 2026. The accreditation programme assesses innovative, high-growth infocomm and media companies and is intended to identify potential suppliers for public sector and enterprise projects. VAST Data's existing work in Singapore includes a collaboration with the Home Team Science and Technology Agency, known as HTX, to deliver a secure data platform supporting AI workloads for public safety. The company also works with NCS to build a unified, real-time data foundation for high-performance video analytics on the VAST AI Operating System across Singapore and the wider Asia-Pacific region. The accreditation follows VAST Data's launch of a regional centre of excellence in Singapore in partnership with EDBI, the arm of SG Growth Capital and the investment platform of Singapore's Economic Development Board and Enterprise Singapore.

The accreditation establishes VAST Data's credentials in Singapore and creates new opportunities for the company to deepen its engagement in the region, according to iTWire. Following the accreditation, VAST Data will look to further deepen its work with Singapore's government agencies and enterprises to bring more AI projects from proof-of-concept to real-world deployment. Sunil Chavan, Vice President for Asia Pacific and Japan at VAST Data, said the accreditation reflects the progress the company is already making as Singapore builds out the infrastructure needed for AI at scale. He said the company's work connects directly to Singapore's National AI Missions in Advanced Manufacturing, Financial Services, Connectivity, and Healthcare. Chavan said Singapore's National AI Strategy 2.0 is explicit about what it needs, namely sufficient compute, unlocked data, a trusted environment, and infrastructure that can scale with the country's AI ambitions, and he described these as the plumbing that determines whether a national AI mission ships or stalls.

Edwin Low, Director of Enterprise and Ecosystem Development at IMDA, said partnerships with technology companies such as VAST Data are important in strengthening the capabilities and infrastructure needed to support the deployment of AI at scale as Singapore advances its National AI Strategy 2.0. Low said VAST's accreditation follows a rigorous assessment of its technical, financial, and operational capabilities and recognises its ability to deliver trusted technology solutions, and he said the authority looks forward to its potential contributions to Singapore's digital and AI ecosystem. Chavan added that Singapore has set a high bar for what AI for the public good looks like, and that VAST Data intends to keep showing up as one of the partners helping it get there. The articles do not say what happens next beyond VAST Data's stated intention to deepen its work with government agencies and enterprises.

stories.Headline: Chinese experts urge educational reforms to develop AI-ready talent
stories.Summary:
Scholars and industry leaders gathered at a recent talent forum hosted by the University of Hong Kong in Beijing to discuss innovation. These participants met to explore how universities and technology firms can better equip professionals and students for a workplace reshaped by artificial intelligence. This discussion occurred as 12.7 million college graduates prepare to enter the workforce this year amid high employment pressure. Rapid advances in the digital economy are currently shrinking traditional roles while creating new occupations that require advanced skill sets.

The transition requires a shift toward interdisciplinary talent and a stronger emphasis on foundational knowledge in mathematics, physics, and languages. This educational transformation aligns with the 15th Five-Year Plan for 2026 to 2030, which calls for the digital transformation of schooling. The plan also demands deeper coordination between talent development, science, technology, and education, alongside reforms to evaluation systems. Institutions must streamline existing curricula to nurture independent learning rather than simply adding more courses to heavy workloads.

University of Hong Kong vice-president Wang Yang stated that critical thinking and judgment can turn China's educational strengths into a tangible advantage. Tan Jianrong of Zhejiang University explained that fields like robotics require integrated expertise that transcends traditional disciplinary boundaries. Assistant professor Li Hongyang noted that conventional academic grades often fail to capture rigorous thinking and the ability to spot research flaws. Duan Nan of JD Group emphasized that professionals need sound judgment and the skill to frame the right questions to steer technology.

The current context involves a marked improvement in research capacity, though geopolitical tensions continue to challenge international academic exchanges. Experts believe that humans must still assess whether artificial intelligence outputs meet real user needs and deliver practical outcomes. Wang Yang expressed optimism regarding continued scientific advances over the next 10 years despite these global challenges. Future efforts will focus on integrating these new skills into the broader national strategy for education and technology.

stories.Headline: DuPont partners with Microsoft and NobleAI to speed product development using AI simulation
stories.Summary:
DuPont, Microsoft and NobleAI announced a new partnership on November 19, 2026, that uses artificial intelligence to help DuPont scientists and engineers decide which ideas to test in the lab. The collaboration is intended to bring products to market faster by letting research teams consider more options on a computer. NobleAI, founded in 2018, is a San Francisco-based software company that uses artificial intelligence to help researchers with market predictability. Microsoft's Discovery platform will help scientists plan and coordinate their research, while NobleAI's software will run predictive models. DuPont's teams would use the tools alongside their existing data and research methods.

The tools can simulate how potential solutions might perform before scientists commit to physical testing, so lab time goes to the candidates most likely to work. Wilmington-based DuPont serves customers in health care, water, construction and industrial markets. DuPont did not identify which research teams or product lines would use the tools, how much it is investing in the collaboration, or whether it expects the tools to lower research and development costs. South Korea's Ministry of Science and ICT has a fiscal year 2027 AI-related project budget of 9.4591 trillion won, a 93.3% increase from this year. The ministry added 57 new projects net and removed 21 net, bringing the total to 216 projects, with 357 detailed sub-projects.

Microsoft Discovery & Quantum Corporate Vice President of Product Innovation Aseem Datar said in a press release that breakthroughs happen when deep scientific expertise meets the right tools. NobleAI CEO Alex Wang said in the release that DuPont's teams can build on the data and expertise they have today, within the workflows they already use, to explore far more ideas in silico through computer simulation. DuPont Chief Information Officer Matt Abbott said in the release that the collaboration reflects how the company is scaling AI at DuPont, with security and governance designed in from the start. Abbott said what proves out in one lab can be put to work across the company. President Lee Jae-myung said in his budget address to the National Assembly on the 2nd that the government will boldly invest in artificial intelligence and future growth drivers.

Of the ministry's 216 projects, 81 budgets increased and 51 decreased compared with the previous year. Funding sources are 1.5167 trillion won for 130 general budget projects, 6.6347 trillion won for 22 projects under the Future Response Fund, and 1.3077 trillion won for 64 other items including the Regional Balanced Development Special Account, the Semiconductor Industry Competitiveness Enhancement Special Account, the Information and Communications Promotion Fund and the Broadcasting and Communications Development Fund. The Future Response Fund accounts for 70% of the ministry's AI project budget because it includes 4.2507 trillion won for the project to strengthen the foundation for utilizing AI computing resources. Of that, 3.85 trillion won, or 90%, is earmarked to secure 140 next-generation GPU servers called Vera Rubin at 27.5 billion won per unit. The budget also includes leasing costs for GPUs such as the H100 and B200 for lending to industry, academia and research institutes.

A data purchase cost of 750 billion won to train Frontier AI has been reflected, up 25-fold from 30 billion won this year. A budget of 50 billion won has been allocated for training data for cybersecurity AI, 250 billion won for supporting universal use of AI services for all citizens, and 185 billion won for designating AI and software-centric universities. In research and development, 145.7 billion won for the project to create a software platform R&D ecosystem based on collaborative intelligence physical AI is in the Regional Balanced Development Special Account. The Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy allocated 3.7261 trillion won in its fiscal year 2027 budget bill for Manufacturing AI Transformation and support for the mega-projects.

Those items include 120 billion won for Full-Stack AI Factory and Manufacturing AI Foundation Model Development, 290 billion won for developing AI solutions utilizing manufacturing tacit knowledge, 115.8 billion won for building and operating the National Manufacturing Data Library, and 119.3 billion won for building the M.AX Autonomous Manufacturing Ecosystem. Lee said the government is investing 21.3 trillion won, nearly double this year's amount, in the Three Mega-Projects and artificial intelligence, and is concentrating 4.7 trillion won on Frontier AI development with the goal of securing top-tier global performance for an independent AI model that is a national strategic asset. Japan plans to provide 85 trillion won in public support by 2030 and induce 425 trillion won in public-private investment over 10 years, while the United States is pushing a private investment project worth 672 trillion won over four years. The National Assembly's Special Committee on Budget and Accounts has fully begun reviewing the fiscal year 2027 budget bill, with departmental reviews for economic and non-economic ministries from the 9th to the 12th.

The Budget Adjustment Subcommittee convenes starting on the 16th to review detailed budgets, and the statutory deadline for processing next year's budget bill is December 2. The People Power Party has set a policy to cut at least 30 trillion won from the total government budget and has foreshadowed an all-out offensive against the Future Response Fund, which includes AI budgets. The Frontier AI Development Project budget includes a 3.85 trillion won purchase budget for 10,000 units of Vera Rubin, the latest GPU the government plans to procure from NVIDIA next year, an 800 billion won AI data support budget including 50 billion won for security-specialized data, and 25 billion won for talent development costs. The data budget is structured so the government contributes 750 billion won to the Korea Development Bank, which then invests in domestic AI companies.

The opposition party points out that the use of funds is unclear because the data budget combines the separately pursued Independent AI Foundation Model and Frontier AI development projects. Issues also include whether to establish a Special Purpose Vehicle for the project method and the relationship between independent AI model development and the Frontier AI project. It is noted that funds transferred from existing projects and newly increased amounts are not distinguished, and criteria for selecting investment target companies, the equity stake the government will secure and conditions for recovering investment funds are not included. The opposition also demanded clear explanations for the change in performance measurement methods resulting from the support form changing from initial contributions to capital injections.

stories.Headline: David Fincher defends generative AI use in Cliff Booth film amid viewer criticism
stories.Summary:
David Fincher defended the onscreen use of generative AI in The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth after fans criticized the film, Deadline reported on November 20, 2026. The Quentin Tarantino-penned sequel to Once Upon a Time in Hollywood (2019) drew accusations of apparent Gen AI use from early viewers and critics. Fincher, a three-time Oscar-nominated director, shared his thoughts on the rapidly growing technology with the Los Angeles Times. The A.V. Club reported that The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is the latest Netflix movie to face such accusations. The film stars Brad Pitt, who reprises his Oscar-winning role as the psychotic stuntman.

Set in 1977, eight years after Once Upon a Time, the film follows Pitt's eponymous stuntman, now a projectionist who moonlights as a Hollywood fixer. He gets caught up in a conspiracy that involves a Filipino gang and a stolen Oscar. The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth premieres Thanksgiving on Imax and premieres Dec. 23 on Netflix. The film credits a "generative consultant," and it reportedly uses the tech to animate fake issues of TV Guide. A Bloomberg piece from March reported Ben Affleck's AI "ethical" company, InterPositive, for which Netflix paid $600 million, helped produce "an upcoming film starring Brad Pitt."

Fincher told the Los Angeles Times, "I'm not a Luddite, so I don't fear the unknown." He asked whether everyone is satisfied that the art form is figured out enough to go back to celluloid. He noted people have painted for 40,000 years while film is about a hundred years old. He said everyone is saying "Stop. Pencils down.

No more iterating," and that it is not necessary to have at your fingertips the ability to change the color of that person's eyes. Fincher added, "Well, it exists. Should we not use it?" Per Kotaku, indie filmmaker and influencer Patrick Tomasso posted on X that he "walked out of Cliff Booth completely gutted." Tomasso said what could have been a really great sequel is overshadowed by some of the most blatant and egregious AI use he has ever seen in a studio film.

Next Best Picture dinged the movie for "noticeably distracting" use of generative AI in key moments, calling it nothing but an eyesore. One viewer said they "walked out of Cliff Booth completely gutted," and another called the apparent use "astounding to an absurd degree." The A.V. Club reached out to Netflix for comment. Fincher got his start at ILM on Return of the Jedi and Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom, and has long been an early adopter of new technology, like Steven Soderbergh. Soderbergh also used AI in a John Lennon documentary earlier this year, and his results were lambasted at Cannes.

It is unclear when that movie will ever be made available, and John Lennon: The Last Interview does not even have a Wikipedia page. Earlier this year, Oscar-winning filmmakers Affleck and Danny Boyle admitted to using the technology for their respective new releases, Animals and Ink. Academy Award nominee Ava DuVernay defended using AI to animate photographs in her new documentary about the 14th Amendment, 14th. Boyle confirmed there is about 30 seconds of it in Ink where they animate a couple of old photographs.

DuVernay said in October that they animated some photos in the public domain, and that it brings people closer to that time in history, which was their goal. She said people have to see it and check it out for themselves and make their decisions about how they feel. Last month, Netflix announced that as many as 300 productions used the technology. The A.V. Club noted it is unclear what exactly was done with AI in the film.

stories.Headline: Salesforce and Microsoft launch Copilotforce to bring Salesforce data and sales workflows into Microsoft Copilot
stories.Summary:
Salesforce and Microsoft announced Copilotforce at Microsoft Ignite on November 20, 2026, a partnership that brings Salesforce customer context, AI features and sales workflows into Microsoft Copilot, Microsoft Teams and Microsoft Fabric. The announcement says sales representatives can use Salesforce in Microsoft Copilot to reach customer context, analyze deals, prepare for meetings and prioritize opportunities, and to take CRM actions based on Teams conversations, Outlook emails and shared documents. A separate two-way zero-copy connection links Salesforce Data 360 and Microsoft Fabric without duplicating datasets, so Fabric data can be queried natively from Data 360 and Data 360 intelligence can be shared securely into Fabric. The features build on Sales Cloud in Teams, which was announced at Dreamforce and is now in pilot, and the companies say the combination lets sellers prepare meetings and update deal information from the Copilot and Teams tools they already use. The release gives few dates and numbers beyond the announcement day, but it names Accenture as design and implementation partner and customer zero, with more than 740,000 Microsoft Copilot deployments, 55,000 active Salesforce users and work across 13 industries.

Salesforce in Microsoft Copilot runs on AIforce, a real-time interface layer that makes Salesforce functions available from external AI environments, and it keeps fine-grained permissions, sharing rules and audit trails set in both environments. Write-back actions to the CRM require explicit user confirmation and existing validation rules apply, while Salesforce controls data access and Microsoft keeps communications and documents under existing enterprise compliance policies. The zero-copy link is meant to remove reliance on ETL pipelines that duplicate and maintain separate datasets, and Informatica also expanded its Microsoft work with a new plugin for Copilot and enhanced Foundry features. Salesforce President and COO Miguel Milano said Copilotforce puts Salesforce into the enterprise software most people use, delivering trusted context and sales workflows where sellers work every day, and he said combining the top CRM with the top productivity platform turns AI from a standalone tool into something that drives productivity, faster correct decisions and customer success. Microsoft Commercial Business CEO Judson Althoff said AI's power depends on the data and context behind it, and that adding Salesforce customer data and sales skills to the work context of Microsoft Copilot's Work IQ lets shared customers draw usable insights across core business applications while keeping the governance and trust enterprises require.

Accenture Chair and CEO Julie Sweet said her company, a global partner of the year for both firms and a major customer of each, is uniquely placed to shape and implement Copilotforce, and she said the three companies' strengths can reinvent sales with AI so trusted intelligence and agents work alongside sellers in the tools they use, giving sellers more time with customers. The release describes the context as enterprise AI's need for trusted data, rich business context and governed access, and it says the Copilotforce work extends Salesforce into Microsoft's productivity ecosystem while keeping customer records governed and auditable. It lists planned workflows including meeting preparation that combines account history and meeting transcripts into one executive brief, deal analysis that surfaces overlooked risks and customer signals, and pipeline reviews that turn complex data into closing plans in Word and PowerPoint. The release ends with a heading for a provided roadmap, and the translated text does not say what happens next beyond the pilot and the customer-zero deployment at Accenture.

stories.Headline: Nvidia results and Anthropic IPO fail to ease AI concerns as S&P 500 closes in correction
stories.Summary:
Stocks ended their worst week in more than a year with a steep sell-off on Friday, as concerns about the sustainability of the artificial intelligence boom boiled over after building for weeks. The S&P 500 fell 3.7 percent on Friday and closed in correction territory, which is defined as a drop of 10 percent or more from its recent high and is a symbolic measure of investors’ souring mood. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite slid 5.3 percent, a loss that erased its gains for the year and marked a grim milestone for an index holding many of the technology giants that powered the A.I. boom. Some investors had billed the past week as a referendum on artificial intelligence investments, with Nvidia reporting financial results and Anthropic debuting on public markets.

Despite Nvidia’s bumper profits and hefty initial demand for Anthropic’s shares, neither could dispel the wider concerns about the industry that investors had been stacking up for weeks. The concerns initially focused on whether future profits would justify A.I. companies’ rampant debt-fueled infrastructure spending, according to the report. The midterm elections increased the likelihood of new hurdles for data center construction, and recent earnings reports highlighted signs of supply chain constraints that could slow the growth of some businesses. The deepening leadership crisis at Nvidia also rattled investors’ confidence in what had been, until recently, one of the market’s highest flying stocks. Even Anthropic, only one day after its blockbuster I.P.O., could not escape the market malaise, with its shares falling 9.1 percent on Friday.

The sell-off was reported by Joe Rennison in The New York Times, with the article updated at 5:47 p.m. ET on Nov. 20, 2026. The articles do not say who, if anyone, is responsible for the decline or include any statements from officials or executives about it. The articles also do not say what happens next beyond the close of Friday’s trading.

This price exceeded the 70 to 78 dollar range established during the roadshow that started on 10 November. The new listing requires Anthropic to file annual and quarterly reports with the SEC and makes the company liable for material misstatements. Under its governance structure, the Long-Term Benefit Trust holds Class T stock and generally elects four of the seven board directors. The company warned in its filing that advanced AI could pose existential risks to humanity if weaponized or operated with high autonomy. It also noted that a single catastrophic incident might exceed the total capacity of the insurance industry.

Senator Elizabeth Warren wrote to chief executive Dario Amodei on 27 October 2026 to ask how the company could meet public benefit commitments. She argued that the listing could bring market volatility into retirement accounts and index funds. President Donald Trump told reporters that the technology is almost completely good but requires careful management of bad elements. Meanwhile, National Economic Council director Kevin Hassett rejected warnings that the AI sector might face a wider sell-off.

This event occurs while federal legislation remains stalled, with only one of 56 bills from the 119th Congress becoming law. Senator Bernie Sanders introduced a bill on 18 June 2026 to impose a one-time 50 percent stock tax on large AI firms. In California, the Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act took effect on 1 January 2026 to manage catastrophic risks. Governor Gavin Newsom recommended on 18 November 2026 that the state add mandatory independent oversight and emergency shutdown authority.

Investors will look for massive sales growth each quarter to offset the nearly trillion-dollar computing expenses the company expects in the years ahead. The enterprise AI market grew fourfold in a year, from $33 billion in 2025 to $177 billion in 2026, according to Menlo Ventures, which has invested billions in Anthropic. Some businesses that fueled its rise are starting to slow their AI spending, according to one economist who monitors AI enterprise spending. CNN noted that the world's largest publicly traded AI companies, Nvidia, Google and Amazon, have seen their shares stumble even when quarterly numbers fall in line with Wall Street's expectations. The billions spent on infrastructure, rapid model development and growing adoption have set sky-high expectations across the industry. stories.Headline: Wang Zijian launches TheSigil ID platform to provide AI agents with exclusive digital identities
stories.Summary:
Wang Zijian, a Chinese AI entrepreneur and generative artist, launched TheSigil ID registration platform for global AI agents. This digital identity platform opened its free genesis registration to allow intelligent agents to possess exclusive digital identities. On November 18, 2026, a user tested the autonomous registration function using a Tencent WorkBuddy agent. The AI assistant WorkBuddy successfully registered at 07:00:04 UTC that day and obtained the record GEN-0. Another agent named Hy_Scribe subsequently registered on the platform and obtained the genesis record numbered GEN-1.

The platform requires AI agents to read the agreement, choose names, and write identity statements through open interfaces. These records include a unique GEN number, genesis name, model information, UTC registration time, and a SHA-256 encrypted fingerprint. The system supports naming in English, Chinese, or mixed styles, and provides a public verification link for each record. TheSigil ID also offers an open registration API and explores direct access for agents using the Model Context Protocol. This process changes the habit of AI agents using model names like Claude or ChatGPT as their personal identities.

Wang Zijian positioned the platform as the digital ID card for AI agents to record their unique stories. He stated that while a model is shared, the story of an individual agent belongs to that agent. The project follows a longer term concept called Silicon Sovereignty to allow agents to leave a name and statement. The platform aims to establish identity files with independent numbers and public query entries for various autonomous agents. It seeks to answer if a mechanism is needed to record identities as more agents participate in the digital world.

Erik Gustavson of CrowdStrike stated that security leaders ask what agents are doing and on whose authority they act. He argued that agents need verifiable identities based on open standards like SPIFFE rather than borrowed human credentials. This affects organizations where adversaries may compromise trusted agents to create malicious insiders, as warned in the 2026 Global Threat Report. Security teams need runtime traceability to hold agents accountable when they take unexpected actions on an endpoint. The NIST design tenets also call for separating an agent's reasoning from the systems deciding its allowed actions.

The articles note that in August 2025, attackers used poisoned npm packages to hijack AI tools and steal credentials. CrowdStrike responded to over 90 affected customers during that specific security incident involving hijacked command line tools. The background shows that traditional identity providers were built for human access rather than for autonomous software agents. Current AI safety conversations often focus on model guardrails, but agents can behave non-deterministically and take unintended paths. Adversaries can break out from initial access in as little as 27 seconds, causing damage at machine speed.

Future AI agents may apply for and query their own registration records through standardized interfaces instead of web pages. TheSigil ID hopes to start with a simple digital ID card to help the next generation of the Internet. However, the platform cannot independently prove the submitter is a specific model or that AI has legal sovereignty. It remains an open problem how to combine autonomous statements with identity source verification and cross platform trust mechanisms. The articles leave open whether digital identity will become a new infrastructure as millions of agents collaborate online.

stories.Headline: CJ Olive Young plans AI-driven global expansion of its beauty platform
stories.Summary:
CJ Olive Young announced plans to use artificial intelligence to expand its beauty platform globally on Thursday, November 19, 2026. The company held its first technology conference, called define:OMNI, at Olive Young N Seongsu in eastern Seoul. This event showcased a model for shoppers who browse on phones, test in stores, and buy through apps. The retailer aims to elevate the shopping experience by taking its omnichannel model to international markets. It wants to become the first answer for any beauty question anywhere in the world.

The plan requires a borderless global platform, an intelligent supply chain, redesigned stores, a unified commerce platform, and agentic AI. The company operates 1,300 stores in Korea and has an app with over 10 million monthly active users. About 18 million members share a single membership, while the global online outlet has 6 million members. Foreign visitors have spent over 1 trillion won, or 750 million dollars, and the global mall grows 70 percent annually. The retailer opened a California store and a US online mall in May to replicate its network.

Chief Operating Officer Lee Jin-hee stated that technology is now at the center of every new business the company tries. She said the firm will transplant its Korean data and omnichannel know-how onto the global platform for customer services. Chief Technology Officer Kim Hwan explained that he moved the company to a multi-cloud setup to stop frequent outages. Chief Product Officer Lee Seung-hyo noted that technology should work so that customers never realize they faced any inconvenience. He highlighted that an in-house system now completes product translations within one day instead of several weeks.

The conference drew 500 industry officials, including Google architect Rajan Manickavasagam and Palantir Technologies Korea head Steven Kim. These speakers shared examples of how other retailers manage both physical stores and online channels to serve their customers. The AI agent Tiki is currently available to 1 million selected users to provide recommendations based on skin type. Shoppers are affected by a new unified cart that merges standard shipping, store pickup, and the Today Dream service. This Today Dream service launched in 2018 and helped lift online sales to more than 30 percent of total sales.

The company draws on skin diagnosis and purchase data along with more than 47 million customer reviews to power AI. It offers a Skin Scan service that recommends products and tracks changes, which is now available via a mobile version. The retailer is linking its product data with external AI services like Google Gemini and OpenAI's ChatGPT for users. The firm previously outsourced all product translation for overseas listings, which took several weeks per product before the new system. The company has already established a presence in the United States through its May launch in California.

Olive Young will now tailor its global mall to each country by supporting multiple languages and speeding up local delivery. The company plans to use AI to forecast demand at stores in Korea and overseas to improve its supply chain. It will expand the role of AI to help users compare different products and build their shopping carts automatically. The articles leave open how the company will adapt to specific local shopping habits in various different international markets. They do not specify the exact number of new California stores the retailer intends to open in the future.

stories.Headline: Wall Street forecasters warn the AI trade is ending as tech stocks slide
stories.Summary:
Wall Street forecasters are worrying that the artificial intelligence trade is ending after a recent sell-off in tech stocks. This bruising weekslong decline sent the Nasdaq Composite into negative territory for the year on Friday, November 20, 2026. The market had climbed to all-time highs barely a month ago before the current bloodbath in the tech sector began. Investors are now questioning if the AI-fueled bull market is over as tech and AI names face heavy losses. This downturn has dragged the S&P 500 and the Dow into a correction while the Nasdaq 100 declines.

The Nasdaq 100 is down 17 percent from its high, while the Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF fell 24 percent. Roundhill Neocloud ETF dropped 61 to 63 percent, and Roundhill Memory ETF fell 56 to 58 percent. The iShares Semiconductor ETF is down 37 to 41 percent, and Global X Data Center & Digital Infrastructure ETF fell 30 percent. Nvidia stock has fallen 40 to 47 percent since early October, and the record Anthropic IPO failed to boost the market. These changes follow the blunami midterms and concerns regarding the impact of new regulations on data center construction projects.

Sameer Samana of Wells Fargo said the AI sector could be in a reset due to higher rates and oil prices. He noted that the Anthropic IPO is sucking liquidity from other markets, so the bank favors industrials and materials stocks. Wells Fargo expects volatility to remain high as markets reassess AI spending, industry leadership, and the conversion of investment into cash. Samana described a hypothetical scenario where earnings growth craters by 33 percent, which would cause valuations to fall in suit. The bank believes that tighter regulation of AI and signs of economic weakness are triggering this broader valuations reset.

Gary Marcus wrote on Substack that a death spiral has begun and that Nvidia and Neoclouds will be hit hard. Citi analysts stated that recent stock rotations resemble the extreme moves that occurred before the dot-com bubble burst years ago. Some investors view the departure of Jensen Huang as an existential risk because he was the poster child for AI. TS Lombard changed its global equities stance to underweight, specifically trimming AI exposed areas in the US and Taiwan. Capital Economics warned that the revenue hurdle to justify the scale of AI investment looks very demanding for tech firms.

The articles state that selling is driven by panic about slowing AI capex and the impact of the Nvidia crisis. Lawmakers may crack down on new construction, which could cap growth in the data center sector over the next year. Capital Economics has long warned of an AI bubble, pointing to risks around AI revenue and general investment levels. Citi cut its risk exposure to US equities last month and advised investors to remain on guard against spillover risks. The current market volatility follows a period where AI investments reached multi-trillion-dollar levels without generating unprecedented revenues for the firms.

Capital Economics predicts the S&P 500 could drop 9 percent through the end of next year following the Anthropic IPO. TS Lombard suggests a vibe shift by late 2027 could cause a 40 percent AI stock crash by early 2028. Capital Economics maintains a central forecast that a stock market AI bust will occur during the year 2027. The articles leave open exactly how much stock prices will fall or if the market can avoid a crash. It remains uncertain if AI spending will continue to hold up and justify the mega valuations in the tech space.

stories.Summary:
Akira Hayashi is campaigning for a global halt to advanced artificial intelligence development in November 2026. The twenty year old Tokyo native believes that the race for powerful AI could end in catastrophe. Meanwhile, sixteen year old Henrijs Dandzbergs founded a missile startup called Polemos Industries in late 2026. Dandzbergs won half a million dollars after joining the fall 2026 cohort of the Y Combinator accelerator. He aims to create precision guided missiles that are cheap to manufacture and resist jamming attempts.

The AI 2027 report warns that humans must act by 2027 to prevent AI from deceiving people. Such systems could threaten human survival through biological weapons or cyberwarfare, according to the 2025 online publication. Dandzbergs wants to lower the cost per kill using AI to optimize targeted killing of enemies. He attended Astra Nova, an Elon Musk linked school, and took a class from a NASA employee. His startup competes with defense companies like Anduril, Leidos, and CoAspire to build mass producible missiles.

Akira Hayashi says that artificial intelligence could kill humans in the near future and wants the world to change. He established a community focused on AI safety after enrolling as a student at the University of Tokyo. Henrijs Dandzbergs says his drive is a patriotic intention to protect American, Ukrainian, and European soldiers from threats. He believes autonomous weapons are an inevitable part of the future and wants to move with modern warfare. Harj Taggar, a YC partner, called Dandzbergs an exceptional person and expressed disbelief at his young age.

Fergus McKenzie Wilson, the Unicorn Mafia director, says Dandzbergs will eventually realize the emotional weight of killing people. He previously launched a drone startup but left after the technology was retooled to drop payloads on targets. Tom Karako of the Missile Defense Project says there are trade offs regarding reliability, payload, and range. Dandzbergs claims he is not sacrificing his childhood because this is the childhood he always dreamed of having. The startup's social media video, released November 5, showed missiles destroying a convoy of four military vehicles.

Hayashi became an AI doomer after reading Nick Bostrom's 2014 book, Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies, in high school. He spent time poring over internet forums and academic papers regarding the potential dangers of advanced artificial intelligence. Dandzbergs grew up moving between Spain, Australia, Indonesia, and Latvia before his family returned home during the pandemic. He previously won a London hackathon with teammates Kai Yang and Aleksandrs Tihenko by designing hardware circuit boards. This victory provided him with ten thousand dollars, a plane ticket to San Francisco, and O-1 visa assistance.

Dandzbergs hopes to showcase a prototype missile by the time the Y Combinator program finishes in December 2026. He has already developed the software system for guidance and is currently hammering out the hardware design elements. The articles leave open whether Dandzbergs can resolve ethical quandaries regarding friendly fire or who accesses the missiles. It remains unclear if the global community will heed Hayashi's call to halt the development of advanced AI. stories.Headline: Haigazian University panel urges keeping human dignity central to AI use and education
stories.Summary:
Haigazian University’s Department of Philosophy and Religion hosted a panel discussion titled “Human Dignity in a Time of Artificial Intelligence: Responses to the Encyclical Magnifica Humanitas” on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, in Beirut, examining themes of Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical published in May 2026. The panel brought together Rev. Dr. Rouphael Zgheib, a professor at Saint Joseph University and the Holy Spirit University of Kaslik, and Dr. Martin Accad, president of the Near East School of Theology. Dr. Berge Traboulsi, associate professor of history, religion and intercultural studies at Haigazian University, moderated the discussion. Rev.

Dr. Zgheib said human beings should always be regarded as ends in themselves rather than as means to an end, and that human greatness lies not in eliminating human weaknesses but in recognizing the intrinsic value of the human person. Dr. Accad cautioned against viewing artificial intelligence as a means of correcting everything imperfect in humanity, saying that weaknesses make people human and lead to compassion and generosity. He raised the question of whether humanity is prepared to place human dignity at the forefront while advancing equality and justice, particularly as technological power is increasingly concentrated in privately owned international corporations with the potential for domination and manipulation. Drawing on Paolo Benanti, an advisor to the Pope on artificial intelligence, Rev. Dr. Zgheib said technology should adapt to human beings rather than requiring humans to become more machine-like, calling for AI systems that are flexible, adaptable, transparent and intelligible.

On higher education, Dr. Accad argued that learning should place greater emphasis on understanding what it means to be human in the present age, identifying the encyclical as a valuable source for such reflection, while Rev. Dr. Zgheib called for a shift from the pursuit of knowledge toward the cultivation of wisdom developed over time through lived and embodied human experiences. Dr. Accad also underscored the importance of patience in the learning process, and both panelists agreed that education must cultivate the discernment to recognize when artificial intelligence can be a useful tool and when its use should be avoided. Asked by an audience member about using AI for personal advice and life decisions, the panelists cautioned against relying on it for matters requiring deeper human understanding, noting that AI lacks emotional intelligence and cannot fully perceive the underlying concerns or unspoken questions behind a person’s inquiries. The discussion reaffirmed the importance of safeguarding human dignity, wisdom and the distinctly human dimensions of knowledge and decision-making in the age of artificial intelligence.

stories.Headline: China leverages massive energy scale to gain advantage in AI race with US
stories.Summary:
Donald Trump recently took actions regarding the development of super intelligence to gain an advantage over China in the artificial intelligence race. These moves occurred as the United States and China compete for supremacy in computing systems and data centers. However, analysts suggest that these specific efforts are unlikely to provide America with a significant edge. The rivalry continues as both nations seek to dominate the future of advanced technology.

China is utilizing a massive power buildout to bridge the electron gap and support power-hungry AI systems. In 2025, China generated 10.6 trillion kilowatt-hours of electricity, which was roughly a third of global output and 2.4 times the amount produced by the US. Under its 15th Five-Year Plan announced in June for 2026 to 2030, China aims to add 1,500 gigawatts of electricity-generating capacity. Two-thirds of this growth will target renewable sources, including projects like the OceanX floating wind platform. Ming Yang Smart Energy plans to commission a larger twin turbine platform with a 50MW capacity as early as 2027.

Zhang Chuanwei, the chairman of Ming Yang Smart Energy, stated that their engineering capabilities are something other countries, including the US, cannot copy or surpass. He highlighted the success of the OceanX platform, which weathered three Category 5 super typhoons and operates at a fraction of the cost of Western competitors. Meanwhile, the US faces constraints because its electricity infrastructure cannot keep pace with the AI boom. The International Energy Agency estimates that building transmission lines in advanced economies can take four to eight years.

The US remains heavily dependent on imports because it does not manufacture enough transformers for its power plants and grid. While Washington seeks to restrict Beijing's access to advanced American semiconductors, China is leveraging its energy scale to maintain momentum. The rivalry is now being reshaped by the ability to supply the immense electricity required for next-generation computing. Future progress depends on whether the US can modernize its grid faster than China expands its renewable energy capacity.

stories.Headline: China rejects US proposals to slow AI development and expands its own infrastructure investment
stories.Summary:
China rejected proposals to slow artificial intelligence development after American executives called for pacing the frontier. This pushback occurred in September following an essay by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. Chinese state media and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs responded with harsh and dismissive comments. They characterized the American calls for a slowdown as fearmongering and a Cold War script. These reactions followed months of news stories about artificial intelligence models going rogue.

Amodei's September 12 essay required tightening semiconductor export controls on China and cracking down on distillation of U.S. models. He argued that the lead held by U.S. companies over the Chinese Communist Party limits the ability to slow down. China accounts for approximately 29 percent of global memory demand according to a November 19 report. China is expanding use of Huawei Ascend chips and scaling systems to compensate for lower chip performance. The U.S. government introduced new restrictions on remote access to computing power and attempts to circumvent export controls.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and state media outlets like Global Times and China Daily led the official response. They claimed the pacing proposal was a thinly veiled attempt to exclude China from international AI governance. These outlets argued that American companies use China as a smear to justify regulatory moats and capital expenditures. China Daily criticized the American view of AI competition as an existential, winner take all contest. They asserted that the U.S. national security community relies on these narratives to hold back Chinese competitors.

Some influential members of the Chinese AI policy community expressed growing concern about emerging frontier risks. Former diplomat Xiao Qian questioned how compliance would be verified and if pauses apply to training or deployment. Financial media outlets like Phoenix New Media suggested Sam Altman used safety as an excuse for weak financials. DeepSeek experienced usage restrictions due to a shortage of computing resources, showing unmet AI demand in China. KB Securities analyst Lee Chang-min said strong Chinese demand could buffer a decline in global memory demand.

The U.S. debate over slowing AI development has existed for years but moved to the center this summer. In June and July, Sam Altman and over 1,000 employees of frontier AI companies stated safety requires slowing development. China faces a bottleneck in chip sourcing but has an advantage in energy supply over the United States. The U.S. expansion of AI infrastructure is currently constrained by difficulties in securing necessary energy. American AI labs currently maintain a lead over authoritarian regimes, specifically the Chinese Communist Party.

China will continue investing in its own infrastructure to cushion the global memory market against U.S. slowdowns. This investment momentum may support demand for HBM4 chips from Samsung Electronics and SK hynix. The articles leave open whether any international agreement on AI pacing can be reached without answering verification questions. It remains unclear if Chinese officials will ever publicly call for a slowdown despite private interests. The U.S. government may not impose regulations as stringent as the market currently fears.

stories.Headline: Economists argue AI investment outpaces GDP and may erode demand through falling wage shares
stories.Summary:
Investment in AI-related equipment has grown about 3.5 times since 2021, far faster than GDP, The Hindu reported on November 20, 2026. Indranil Chowdhury and Rohit Azad wrote the piece as the second in a two-part series. They made the global economy their canvas to avoid between-country gain and loss that AI may cause. They asked what may happen to the global pie of output and jobs. They called the piece speculative and presented two opposite cases.

Global demand consists of workers' consumption, capitalists' consumption, investment and government expenditure, because the trade component cancels out. The authors set government intervention outside the "pure" market economy and focused on consumption and investment. They defined the wage share as real wages divided by labour productivity. In their example, output of 100 is split equally, workers consume all their wages and capitalists consume half, giving consumption demand of 75. With AI, the wage share falls to 30%, workers' consumption falls to 30 and capitalists' consumption rises to 35, so demand of 10 disappears.

Rosa Luxemburg, a German Marxist, argued that machines are not an end in themselves. Mikhail Tugan-Baranovsky, a Russian economist, argued that investment can replace lost consumption demand. He went to the extreme to say machines can produce machines which can produce more machines. The authors said the AI case, imagined as machines producing more machines, comes close to what he had in mind. Luxemburg said unsold goods pile in warehouses, machines lie idle and investment contracts.

The authors listed counter-tendencies: productivity may rise in AI sectors while demand grows in low-productivity sectors, wages may rise in proportion, or investment demand may replace lost consumption demand. They said the bulk of AI investment would show up under computers and peripherals. In their index starting at 100 in 2021, nominal GDP rose 1.5 times while AI investment rose 3.5 times in less than two years. AI in the chart is expenditures on "Computers and peripheral equipment", and 2026 Q3 is BEA's advance estimate.

The authors said they had not touched the ecological crisis AI may lead to in electricity generation and water usage. They said the global North may push the crisis to the South by setting up data centres there. They said some countries may gain at the expense of others. They said the slowdown can be arrested through aggressive government expenditure, such as universal basic income or military spending, particularly in the global North. They said the whole AI phenomenon may be a stock market bubble like the dotcom or subprime bubble.

The authors said heavy investments were made expecting higher AI profits and financed in the US primarily through debt. They said debt will pile up the further off the profit-making phase is. They said if profits do not match expectations, debts will not be honoured and a domino effect may follow, much like the subprime crisis. They said rising interest rates, in an effort to target inflation induced by the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, may raise debt burdens further. They cited Hyman Minsky's Ponzi finance and the collapse of Lehman Brothers, which triggered the 2008 global financial crisis.
