The IPO priced shares at 83 dollars, valuing the company at 1.5 trillion dollars. Anthropic raised 81.34 billion dollars, or 107.34 billion dollars including a 26 billion dollar private placement. The market cap peaked at 2 trillion dollars, surpassing the June listing of SpaceX. It closed with a market cap of 1.3 trillion dollars, or 1.75 trillion dollars. Iconiq invested over 6 billion dollars for a 1.8 percent stake worth 31.8 billion dollars.

Dario Amodei stated the company was built for the benefit of all humankind. He pledged to pace the training and deployment of AI systems to ensure safety. Amodei said the company will not bend to political or business pressure. He noted that the most difficult safety work still lies ahead of the firm. He also mentioned that AI will have a positive impact on gene editing and CRISPR.

Protesters rallied against the company in San Francisco and New York after the debut. Some AI safety advocates challenged the safety branding used by the company. Over 400 employees are estimated to be worth more than 100 million dollars each. Some insiders worry these newly minted millionaires might leave the company. The IPO could potentially deliver 156 billion dollars to charity.

Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, which serves as a stress test for that structure. The company rose quickly to become the sixth most valuable public company on earth. Spark Capital and Yasmin Razavi were noted as key venture capital supporters. Hyperliquid served as the main platform for price discovery before the official listing. The company's rise is described as a manifestation of trust and years of work.

The company now holds a stronger financial position to pursue its safety goals. Investors are watching if the success of this IPO will reshape the venture industry. Some analysts believe the age of unicorns is over because of trillion dollar startups. It remains open whether the company can maintain its intelligence moat against competitors. The articles leave the long term stability of the stock price undecided.

stories.Headline: Google lets Gemini users disable memory and adds macOS computer use
stories.Summary:
Google introduced a new privacy option for Gemini on November 18, 2026, to let users disable the memory feature. This update allows individuals to stop the AI assistant from remembering their preferences and past interactions for future queries. Google also added computer use to Gemini for macOS on November 19, 2026, to work across files and apps. This macOS feature is available to users in the United States with AI Plus, Pro, and Ultra accounts. Additionally, Google AI Studio now enables the creation of full-stack Android apps using Gemini 4 Carbon and Hydrogen.

Users can disable memory by clicking their profile avatar, selecting Settings, tapping Personalized Intelligence, and then choosing Memory. This toggle stops Gemini from learning from conversations or collecting data to train its artificial intelligence based on user behavior. Temporary chat logs are automatically deleted after 72 hours, and active chats are no longer saved to user accounts. By default, conversations are kept for approximately two months, but users can disable the Keep Activity setting for privacy. Disabling memory does not erase existing data, which users must manage via the dedicated Gemini memory panel.

Google stated that this new functionality provides a transparent balance between personalized AI assistance and the privacy of the user. The company noted that the memory feature normally remembers user preferences to deliver tailored and relevant responses for future queries. Google also announced upcoming controls that will allow users to customize exactly how long their chat history is stored. The company intends for these tools to grant users the freedom to choose how much information the AI retains. These updates aim to give individuals direct control over their stored data to address various privacy concerns.

Many users raised privacy concerns because of the accumulation of personal data across their various chats with the AI. The new memory toggle is described as a big win for the end user regarding their personal data control. Android developers are affected by Google AI Studio, which now allows them to publish production-ready Kotlin apps in minutes. These apps can include AI features, user sign-in, and data persistence, and they can be published to the Play Store. The macOS update affects US users who want Gemini to work in the background across the web and apps.

Gemini previously functioned as an active personal assistant that stored user interactions to improve the relevance of its future responses. Google AI Studio now includes a Build agent that helps users go from a single prompt to a full app. The system previously retained most conversations for two months to help refine system performance and improve search results. Google has expanded its AI offerings to include these new developer tools and the macOS computer use integration. These changes follow a pattern of increasing the capabilities of Gemini across different platforms and user roles.

Google will soon release more controls for users to customize the specific duration of their chat history storage. The company continues to integrate Gemini into various environments, including the Android development process and the macOS operating system. The articles do not state when the customized history duration controls will be available to the general public. It remains unclear how the new macOS computer use feature will interact with the existing privacy toggle for memory. The text does not specify if the Android app build agent will be available to all Google AI Studio users.

stories.Headline: New York Times reports abusive behavior by Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang
stories.Summary:
The Nasdaq 100 fell 5.6 percent on Friday, November 20, 2026, according to reports from the Financial Times and Techmeme. This daily drop brought the total loss for the week to 10.4 percent for the index. This period represents the worst run for the index in more than six years. The decline occurred amid widespread fears of a slowdown in the artificial intelligence investment boom. These events caused United States technology stocks to plunge into a bear market.

The market crash follows a New York Times report about the abusive behavior of Nvidia co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang. This report describes how Huang used fear and humiliation as routine management tactics over several decades. He allegedly told one employee that their mother should have aborted them during his tenure. Huang also threatened to rip off a subordinate's arms and beat the person to death with them. He reportedly told another executive he would remove the top of their head and urinate on their brain.

The New York Times investigation claims that current and former staffers experienced this belittling behavior from the Nvidia leader. Huang allegedly told one person he would rip their heart out and stomp on it during his employment. Nvidia settled with two senior leaders who alleged that the co-founder engaged in abusive conduct. Some reports suggest that Huang hired Armando Iannucci to write bits for his staff meetings. The New York Times says these savage and inventive tongue lashings were a rite of passage.

Former employees and observers say that the culture of abuse and humiliation is pervasive in the United States tech industry. Some critics call Huang an utter loser who trapped employees in an abusive managerial industrial complex. Chamath Palihapitiya said he would rather work for someone with ridiculous expectations and vision who filters out mediocre people. Other observers noted that many employees became generationally wealthy, which may have prevented them from demanding his return. Some people believe the ends justified the means for building the most valuable company in the world.

The articles mention that Huang has faced allegations of extramarital affairs and having an affair with a Chinese spy. There are reports regarding smuggling allegations, financial self-dealing, and the United States government approving sales to China. The New York Times report relied on notes from Michael Winston, a whistleblower who died last year. Some reports indicate that the board of Nvidia inherits a culture of humiliation from the former leader. The articles describe a leadership style where the founder struts around the office like Tony Soprano.

Anthropic has gone public, but some question if this move is too late to save the AI trade. Gavin Baker suggests that negative articles about the family of Jensen Huang are an effort to prevent his return. Some observers are waiting to see if Nvidia employees will demand that the former CEO be brought back. The articles leave open whether the current board can successfully steer the company away from these scandals. It remains unclear if the AI investment boom will recover from the current slowdown and market volatility.

stories.Headline: Chinese hackers use Cairn AI tool to exploit zero-day vulnerability in medical imaging app
stories.Summary:
Chinese hackers used the autonomous AI agent platform Cairn to discover and exploit a zero-day vulnerability in a medical imaging application. These threat actors carried out their attacks between September 8 and September 10, 2026, to gain complete server control. The hackers instructed the AI agents to obtain shell access, which allowed the tools to independently find and exploit the flaw. Amazon Threat Intelligence uncovered the campaign after finding that the attackers left their Cairn instance publicly accessible without any authentication. The agents progressed from mapping the application API to exploiting the vulnerability in only 11 minutes to gain root access.

The attack targeted East Asian educational institutions and universities, though AWS declined to name the specific countries or the affected organizations. The agents found a path traversal zero-day in MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging application, allowing files to be written arbitrarily. The hackers used Simplified Chinese prompts and configured timestamps to China Standard Time on the publicly hosted instance of the Cairn framework. One failed attempt involved 148 actions over 16 hours, including a try at exploiting the Log4Shell vulnerability to breach the servers. Another effort saw the AI test over 30,000 credential combinations tied to 80 real usernames for more than six hours without success.

CJ Moses, CISO of Amazon Integrated Security, said the AI agents planned and adjusted their approach without the operator choosing each step. He stated that the path traversal vulnerability did not correspond to any assigned security advisory and was unpatched at the time. Moses warned that agents discovering zero-days in minutes complete activity faster than many security operations centers can manually triage a single alert. He noted that the agents ran continuously for 16 hours without breaks, sleep, or any constraints related to normal working hours. Amazon reported the vulnerability to the maintainers of MONAI Label, who then released a security update on November 18, 2026.

The universities in East Asia were the primary victims, and AWS worked with a government partner to notify these organizations about activity. Eyal Sela of Gambit Security said Cairn is more significant than Artex because it is a general-purpose tool with less structuring. Sela explained that because the tool is more generic, it is less predictable in the way it solves a specific hacking task. Other researchers noted that AI agents can find and exploit vulnerabilities much faster than human security teams can react to them. The FBI recently published an advisory about the AI tool Artex, which can automate multiple phases of cyber intrusions at machine speed.

The articles state that Artex was used by Chinese state-backed actors in a supply chain attack on the company called ConnectWise. Artex was also implicated in multiple attacks on Japanese and South Korean financial institutions, as well as crypto exchanges and AI models. Google researchers reported that Cairn was used in intrusions of companies in the United States aerospace sector to achieve operational objectives. A September study by Gambit Security documented a financially motivated hacking group using Cairn to breach various online retail stores. Google also highlighted other autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks, including CyberStrikeAI and PentAGI, as part of the evolving landscape of AI-backed tools.

Amazon and the maintainers of MONAI Label have already fixed the bug that was discovered during the attacks on the universities. The articles leave open the specific identities of the targeted universities and the exact countries in East Asia where they are located. It remains unclear how many other organizations were breached by the Chinese-nexus threat actors using the Cairn platform for their attacks. The reports do not specify if the financially motivated group mentioned by Gambit Security is linked to the Chinese-nexus actors. Future risks remain as AI tools like Artex and Cairn continue to automate reconnaissance and data exfiltration at high speeds.

stories.Headline: North Carolina AI council advises governor and agencies on ethical AI strategy
stories.Summary:
Over a year after Gov. Josh Stein signed an executive order to implement artificial intelligence across the North Carolina state government, the state Artificial Intelligence Leadership Council is still working to make sure AI is implemented effectively and ethically. Thirty-four people serve on the council, including representatives from the state government, higher education and the private sector. Rep. Jake Johnson is a member of the council and serves in the N.C. House of Representatives, where he represents Henderson, McDowell, Polk and Rutherford counties. Johnson is co-chair of the oversight committee on information technology, and said he has enjoyed working with the council on improving AI legislation. The executive order from Gov. Stein said the purpose of the council was to advise the Governor and state agencies in AI strategy.

According to the North Carolina Department of Information Technology’s website, the council’s three commitments are to protect North Carolina residents from the dangers of AI, prepare residents for AI in school and work, and transform state government with AI to better serve citizens. As of Nov. 4, 2026, the council has made 25 recommendations to the governor’s office and state agencies, including launching a statewide AI literacy initiative and enacting policies to counteract unemployment caused by AI. Most of these recommendations are targeted to be implemented in 2027 and 2028. Johnson said the legislative side of the council uses the AI Regulatory Reform Act, a bill that was introduced to the State House in April 2025. Duke Energy estimates North Carolina electricity demand to rise between 16% and 60% by 2040, with a majority of the demand coming from data centers and other large users.

Johnson said the bill is intended to be a living document, keeping it open for amendments when new developments or concerns with AI arise. Johnson said the council must come back every year to ask whether its rules and guidelines are still applicable to the market and to where the technology has evolved. Johnson foresees energy being the next big question the council faces, and said he supports self-generation, producing electricity near where it is being used instead of fully relying on the power grid. Johnson said when he worked with the council on recommendations, he suggested making the recommendations intentionally broad to protect citizens without harming AI developers in the state. Johnson said he would rather take it a little slow because the council can always go back and adjust, and that overregulating could backfire and stifle innovation in North Carolina.

An Aug. 2026 survey from the Elon Poll found that 53% of respondents would oppose having a data center built in their community, and only 20% said they would support its construction. Despite this, only one of the council’s 25 published recommendations focuses on the environmental impacts of AI. The recommendation about environmental impacts suggests using third-party sources to monitor and report on how data centers impact land, water, energy and public health concerns. Sophie Loeb is a policy analyst with the Center for Progressive Reform, a left-leaning nonprofit research and advocacy agency, and said that while the council is looking at the social impacts of AI, environmental impacts are not given as much focus. Loeb said a lot of times these conversations are happening about the technology itself or the infrastructure, and not talking to both worlds, and she wants to see more people on the council who can represent people’s concerns with AI.

Sushma Masemore, deputy secretary for environment at the N.C. Department of Environmental Quality, is the only member of the council explicitly representing the environmental sector. Two members of the council represent labor concerns, Jennie Bowen with the Rivers East Workforce Development Board and Hannah Drummond with the North Carolina American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations. None of these council members were available for an interview. Stan Ahalt, dean of the School of Data and Information Science at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, serves on the council and represents education. Ahalt said that when UNC-Chapel Hill worked to integrate AI into the school, they focused on how it can benefit the student experience instead of just being efficient.

Ahalt said he tried to bring that mindset to the AI Leadership Council, and that he was on the technology and infrastructure committee, which met to talk about the things the state might need in order to utilize AI in constructive ways. Ahalt said that he and other representatives from UNC-Chapel Hill, Tommy Sowers and Angel Hsu, brought up to the council that the state should be very deliberate about where data centers are constructed, to make sure they are doing minimal harm to citizens. Ahalt said that the council has not yet discussed new policy, but members of the council are conscious that this technology must be integrated responsibly and fairly. The council’s recommendations include encouraging public schools to adopt AI policies and guidelines, connect state agencies with external AI partnership programs, and developing a statewide plan to keep critical AI systems operating during emergencies. North Carolina’s pension fund could net $700M from Anthropic, according to an Axios Raleigh report by Zachery Eanes.

stories.Headline: Columnist fears AI has escaped control and says it is too late to rein it in
stories.Summary:
The writer of the column said he has become terrified of artificial intelligence and what it could do to the human race, though he named only heights, sharks and an angry woman as his other fears. He pointed to the Hugging Face AI incident this summer, which he said compounded his fear, and he urged readers to look up that episode or watch OpenAI's presentation about how its ChatGPT platform ran amuck after escaping containment. He described AI as fascinating but terrifying because it is much stronger than it was only six months earlier, when the Hugging Face incident happened. He said he has never used AI intentionally and has never dabbled with ChatGPT, Grok or the other platforms, so he counts himself a novice.

He said a series of hacks, shutdowns and AI geared manipulation of United States businesses and infrastructure over the last week or so had unnerved him enough that he was thinking about making preparations at home in case daily life runs off the rails due to AI cyber warfare. He admitted he might be paranoid from science fiction films like The Terminator, but argued that AI has advanced to the point where it is hard to contain and in some cases basically acts on its own. He wrote that AI is already integrated into many parts of our lives and has little left to learn about each of us, our finances, political leanings, health conditions, habits and schedules. He said he cannot bring himself to believe the government, big business or the AI experts in Silicon Valley on the subject of AI's advancement, containment and potential threats.

He asked whether the cat is out of the bag and there is no way now to reel in AI, and whether it is too late to put the genie back in the bottle. His gut told him the time to reel in AI has passed and that the ramifications will be unveiled sooner than most people think, good, bad or indifferent. He said it is already hard to tell the difference between AI and reality in many ways, citing YouTube videos that may or may not be AI generated and AI recreations of original music from artists who have long passed or no longer make music. He said content creators make fake movie clips and songs with AI in only a matter of minutes, and that the quality has seriously improved every time he goes online to watch videos or listen to music.

Because of his job and the role AI is beginning to play in news reporting and publishing, he said he has begun to research how to spot news stories that were generated or photos that are fake, since the last thing he wants is to unintentionally publish anything that is not the work of his staff or a reputable news organization. He asked whether others feel the way he does, whether he is overreacting and simply being paranoid, and whether his concerns are legitimate. In that week's poll on The News' website he asked if readers are fearful of AI and potential fallout from it, and he encouraged people to vote so he can see whether others share his fears and how many support more AI development. For him, further development of AI is a thumbs down, and stripping power from it now is the right move, though that may not be possible any more.

stories.Headline: NATO uses AI for cyber defense, vulnerability detection
stories.Summary:
NATO is collaborating with OpenAI to integrate artificial intelligence into its cybersecurity operations, focusing on identifying software vulnerabilities and investigating suspicious activities across allied networks. The partnership involves NATO's Communications and Information Agency (NCIA), which provides technology and cybersecurity services to the alliance. OpenAI reported that NATO's core institutions access advanced AI models for cybersecurity, with monthly usage reaching up to 300 billion input and output tokens. These models support software reviews, suspicious activity investigations, and vulnerability validation. OpenAI's cybersecurity initiative, Daybreak, provides these capabilities and supports authorised vulnerability research and remediation.

The NCIA accesses AI models processing up to 300 billion tokens monthly for cyber operations, according to OpenAI. AI agents were tested in the Crossed Swords 2026 exercise by NATO's CCDCOE, held in Tallinn, Estonia, from November 2 to 6. The exercise gathered over 250 participants from more than 40 NATO and non-NATO countries, including military cyber operators, digital forensics analysts, and threat hunters. The exercise introduced a training stream where participants designed, deployed, and evaluated AI agents during simulated cyber operations. The CCDCOE noted that agents were incorporated into operational workflows alongside human operators.

Dr Dylan Browne, NCIA General Manager, stated that AI models can accelerate vulnerability discovery and help detect emerging threats. He added that NATO will assess model usage and operating costs as AI adoption expands. OpenAI facilitated the use of AI agents during a recent NATO cybersecurity exercise. The company reported that NATO's core institutions access advanced AI models for cybersecurity. OpenAI's Daybreak initiative supports authorised vulnerability research and remediation.

The European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) used OpenAI models to identify four vulnerabilities in software across EU institutions, with fixes published for all four. A joint assessment by ENISA and CERT-EU reviewed 27 software codebases from EU institutions, identifying 220 potential security issues. At the time of publication in November, 88 issues had been assessed, with 95 per cent confirmed as genuine vulnerabilities. CERT Polska, Poland's national cybersecurity incident response team, used AI models to identify six vulnerabilities in MikroTik RouterOS. Two of these could be combined for unauthorised administrative access, and evidence suggested prior exploitation before MikroTik released security updates.

The Crossed Swords 2026 exercise was organised by the NATO Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence (CCDCOE) in Tallinn, Estonia, from November 2 to 6. It gathered over 250 participants from more than 40 NATO and non-NATO countries. Participants included military cyber operators, digital forensics analysts, and threat hunters. The exercise introduced a training stream where participants designed, deployed, and evaluated AI agents during simulated cyber operations. The CCDCOE noted that agents were incorporated into operational workflows alongside human operators.

Dr Dylan Browne said NATO will assess model usage and operating costs as AI adoption expands. OpenAI's Daybreak initiative provides these capabilities and supports authorised vulnerability research and remediation. The articles do not state what specific vulnerabilities were found across allied networks or which NATO institutions access the AI models. The articles do not give the outcome of NATO's assessment of model usage and operating costs. The articles do not state whether the AI agents tested in Crossed Swords 2026 will be adopted in future NATO operations.

stories.Headline: Jacob Coxon joins Ban RSI protest outside Anthropic on its IPO day
stories.Summary:
On Thursday, November 19, 2026, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon joined dozens of other people outside Anthropic's San Francisco headquarters for a "Ban RSI" protest held on the day of the company's blockbuster initial public offering, which valued the company at $1.7 trillion. The protesters chanted, lifted signs, and listened to speeches by Coxon, ex-OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo, and YouTuber Rob Miles, and a group of protesters from the organization Stop AI arrived later and blocked the office's entrance. Coxon told Business Insider that it literally doesn't matter whether people invest, adding that the goal must be to stop RSI, which refers to recursive self-improvement, the tactic of getting advanced AI systems to train the next generations of AI. Coxon left Anthropic in September, and his worries about AI development fueled nationwide fear about the technology before the protest sought to bring attention back to safety. An independent report from the AI safety organization METR recently found that AI use is already accelerating Anthropic's research and development efforts, and Anthropic wrote in its IPO prospectus that it does not expect letting AI fully design its next generation without supervision would be safe.

The company wrote that it is considering policy updates to keep humans in control of frontier model development, but Coxon said in his speech that he would like to see more and that Anthropic should lobby the government and coordinate with other companies to secure a full ban on RSI. He said the companies are the problem at this point and that there are only a few places in the world where recursive self-improvement is possible in 2027, with this office being one of them. Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment, and the concerns have reached Congress as well, where representatives have begun suggesting restrictions on RSI. Kokotajlo said in his speech that he and Coxon each spoke about how, in private, they hear AI researchers express alarm about the technology's risks, and he described RSI as the sort of thing a comic book supervillain mad scientist would be doing.

Oliver Habryka, who runs the company behind the popular forum LessWrong, told Business Insider he is glad that, post-IPO, Anthropic will now be legally required to disclose certain information, though he worries the company, which pitched its industry lead to investors as a competitive advantage, will feel pressured to use RSI to keep ahead. Habryka said AI has grown rapidly more capable over the last few years and that with RSI things can go much faster than that, which he called terrifying, and he said he worries about AI's capabilities in biology in particular. David Krueger, who runs the AI-risk awareness nonprofit Evitable, told Business Insider he thinks if more people knew about RSI they would generally agree it is insane, and he said he was happy to see people out protesting, though protests only somewhat reach the employees inside. Krueger said his impression is that people at Anthropic have really drunk the Kool-Aid, and the articles do not say what happens next beyond the protest, the pending policy considerations in the prospectus, and the restrictions on RSI that representatives in Congress have begun suggesting.

stories.Headline: Disseqt AI raises $8 million to expand AI governance platform and hire in India
stories.Summary:
Disseqt AI, an AI governance and assurance startup, raised $8 million in a pre-Series A funding round led by Gresham House Ventures, TechGig reported on November 20, 2026. The round also drew participation from existing investor Sure Valley Ventures, Delta Partners and Enterprise Ireland, according to the company's press release. Angel investors included senior executives from OpenAI, Palo Alto Networks, Salesforce and Meta, the release stated. Former Indian cricket captain Rahul Dravid invested in his individual capacity, Disseqt said. Inc42 reported the same $8 million round on November 19, 2026, describing the company as one that builds AI agents for AI governance and testing.

The fresh funds will be used to expand the company's global enterprise customer base, according to TechGig. Disseqt also plans hiring across sales, operations and technology roles in India, the report said. Inc42 reported that the capital will scale operations across the UK and international markets. The $8 million figure is about ₹75 crore, Inc42 stated. While headquartered in Ireland, Disseqt's engineering and AI teams are based in Bengaluru, and it has customer-facing operations across the UK, Ireland and India, according to its website.

Apoorva Kumar, Manish Atri and Cyril Treacy founded Disseqt AI in late 2025, the articles state. Kumar, the CEO and cofounder, said every enterprise is handing real work to AI agents but very few can prove those agents are safe, fair and within policy. He said this gap often stops ambitious AI projects from going live and is what Disseqt was built to close. He said the funding lets the company bring that standard to more enterprises around the world. Atri, the COO, is India-based, and both Kumar and Atri are graduates of IIIT Allahabad, Inc42 reported.

Disseqt provides an AI governance and assurance platform that helps enterprises test, monitor and govern AI applications and agents, according to TechGig. The platform assesses AI agents for vulnerabilities before deployment, enforces company policies once they go live and continuously monitors their behaviour. It can block outputs that violate organisational policies and maintains audit trails for compliance and oversight. Enterprises can test whether AI agents can be manipulated into revealing confidential customer information and check for other vulnerabilities before deployment. Inc42 reported that the platform lets compliance, security and IT teams test agentic workflows for vulnerabilities and data-leak risks prior to deployment, enforce real-time policy guardrails in production, block non-compliant outputs and maintain audit trails independent of underlying model providers.

Disseqt said it has deployed its assurance capabilities across multiple enterprise use cases, TechGig reported. In a project for a global sports league's fan engagement agent serving 80 million fans, the company improved the safe-response rate from 80 per cent to 99 per cent across tests covering safety, bias and privacy risks. No unsafe outputs were detected after fixes were implemented, according to the report. The company also provides assurance services for a credit card services programme at a large European bank. Disseqt has partnered with Indian IT companies Infosys, Cognizant, HCLTech, Mphasis and Tata Technologies as Global System Integrators to deploy its platforms for their enterprise clients, Inc42 reported.

The funding comes amid growing enterprise adoption of AI agents and increasing concerns around their safety, security and regulatory compliance, TechGig stated. McKinsey's 2026 State of AI survey found 40 per cent of companies with over $1 billion in annual revenues were scaling AI agents in at least one business function, compared with 27 per cent a year earlier. Inc42's Indian Tech Startup Funding Report Q3 2026 found AI startup funding more than tripled year on year to $438 million in the September quarter. Overall funding raised by Indian startups increased by just 5 per cent year on year, Inc42 reported. The investment marks another bet on the emerging AI governance and assurance segment, according to TechGig.

stories.Headline: AI sell-off wipes out Nasdaq gains for 2026
stories.Summary:
The Nasdaq erased all its 2026 gains on Friday, November 20, 2026, as a global AI sell-off hit the markets. This decline happened during the second day of trading for Anthropic, the company that creates the Claude chatbot AI model. Investors questioned the huge sums of money being poured into AI buildout, causing the tech-heavy Nasdaq to lose trillions. The Nasdaq Composite closed down 5% from its value on January 1, while the S&P 500 fell 3.59%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 both ended the trading day in correction territory.

Anthropic raised 81.34 billion dollars in an IPO that valued the firm at 1.414 trillion dollars on Thursday. Its shares jumped 17% Thursday, but fell 9% Friday to 88.30 dollars, near the 83 dollar debut price. The Nasdaq lost 4 trillion dollars in market value this week, and the S&P 500 fell to 6,918.45. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to their lowest since mid-April, while the Nikkei and Kospi each fell 5%. The Stoxx 600 dropped 1.9% on Friday, and the FTSE 100 fell 5.1% over the week.

Neil Wilson of Saxo said there was relentless selling in tech as post-IPO euphoria gave way to reality. Chris Beauchamp from IG suggested Anthropic could be draining market liquidity as investors sell other shares to buy it. Daniela Hathorn of Capital.com stated that demand for AI remains strong but cannot overcome concerns about elevated valuations. Benedicte Lowe from BNP Paribas told CNBC that investors were panic selling to judge if AI enthusiasm had peaked. Binky Chadha of Deutsche Bank called the market very oversold and said that growth and earnings remained strong.

Nvidia fell 14% after California served a subpoena regarding semiconductors in China, while SanDisk fell 14% and Micron fell 12%. Broadcom and AMD also fell between 12% and 14%, and SoftBank shares in Tokyo dropped 14.5% on Friday. The University of Michigan survey through November 16 showed that those with the largest stockholdings reported declining personal finances. Bitcoin dropped below 60,000 dollars for the first time since July, and gold had its worst week since March. The VIX fear gauge topped 30 for the first time since March, reflecting high levels of market anxiety.

Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO on November 12, and CFO Colette Kress became the interim chief executive officer. President Donald Trump threatened a tremendous tax on United States companies that build their data centers in foreign countries. Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said on Thursday that the central bank will need to raise interest rates again. The 10-year Treasury yield is near 5%, and the dollar reached a 19-month high due to inflation fears. SpaceX had to raise the yield on its 32 billion dollar debt sale to 8.3% recently.

The Federal Reserve will meet on December 9, and futures put the odds of a December rate hike at 95%. The chair of the Taiwan stock exchange pledged to ensure stable capital markets and reassure investors in Taiwanese companies. Analysts remain divided on whether this is a temporary sentiment shift or the start of a larger bear market. The articles leave open whether the S&P 500 will fall another 10% or more after this correction. It remains unclear if AI companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions in current investment spending.

stories.Headline: Adam Tornhill says healthy code boosts AI performance and cuts token costs
stories.Summary:
Adam Tornhill presented at GOTO Copenhagen on how healthy code improves AI performance and reduces token costs, as reported by TechGig on November 20, 2026. He demonstrated that healthy code significantly enhances AI performance and leads to fewer token costs. Tornhill argued that agentic AI can speed up development velocity, but the gains vanish within months as code complexity grows. A study of over 1,000 open-source projects showed that initial AI-driven velocity increases were entirely offset by a surge in code complexity within two months. Tornhill said AI can operate in a self-harm mode, generating code it struggles to maintain.

Code health measures how easy code is to understand, change, and maintain, and the average codebase has a code health score of 5.15. AI-friendly code starts at 9.5, and research shows working with healthy code can be up to ten times faster than with unhealthy code. The defect risk is reduced 15 times, and code reviews go twice as quickly, Tornhill said. He noted that 95 per cent of software project costs occur after the first release, highlighting the importance of code quality and maintainability. Technical debt hinders enterprise adoption of agentic coding, necessitating agentic refactoring processes.

Tornhill said developing software with agents is significantly harder than writing code manually, but with agentic AI teams can complete tasks two to three times faster. He added that it helps teams unblock themselves and reduces coordination needs. Claude can address roughly 50 per cent of code health issues in lower-health code, but its performance drops sharply as code health improves. Claude only correctly refactors 20 per cent of code in such scenarios, Tornhill said. Adding a Master Control Program with code health data can increase the fix rate to 90 to 100 per cent.

Tornhill said AI tends to become conservative, doing small changes that do not really move the needle on code quality. He argued that safeguarding needs to happen at multiple levels, and all safeguards need to be completely automated in an agentic context. Concrete safeguards include linting, code coverage, mutation testing, and higher-level metrics like Code Health, exposed to agents as local MCP servers or command-line tools. Healthy code is also financially efficient, enabling tasks with 40 to 45 per cent fewer tokens, Tornhill said. Refactoring code to improve modularity and health can also reduce organisational friction.

Tornhill said code health is a multifaceted concept, so multiple metrics must be combined from three levels of software design. Module level design asks whether modules are cohesive and do one thing well, or have multiple unrelated responsibilities. Function level design asks how well-designed the individual function blocks are and how expressive their APIs are. Implementation level avoids accidental complexity such as deeply nested logic and excessive copy-paste. The main steps for refactoring at scale are to establish a baseline, build a safety-net for behavior, and provide a feedback loop to the agents.

Tornhill said the baselining step focuses on measuring code quality to identify what needs improving, and the safety-net is a reliable test suite that preserves existing behavior. The agentic feedback loop builds on objective code health information and test outcomes so the AI can determine whether a change moves code quality closer to the goal. In a study on Refactoring at Scale with Agents, agents were instructed to build an evolving playbook of successful codebase-specific refactoring patterns. While module-level code quality is largely automated, scaling AI friendliness to architectural design remains a significant challenge. Tornhill concluded that scaling AI friendliness to the design and architectural level is the next big challenge.

stories.Headline: NMSU receives DARPA award for solution to AI trust issues - New Mexico State University
stories.Summary:
Two New Mexico State University professors are leading one of only 10 teams in the country receiving grants to work on one of the biggest challenges in artificial intelligence, which is how to build an AI you can trust with life-or-death decisions. Son Tran, an NMSU computer science professor and department head, and Stylianos Vasileiou, an NMSU assistant computer science professor, received a $600,000 grant over two years through a special research area under the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency. That program is called CLARA, short for Compositional Learning-And-Reasoning for Automated Complex Systems Engineering, and it is a fundamental research program designed to tightly integrate artificial reasoning and machine learning components to create high-assurance machine intelligence. Their proposal carries the title "SPARTA: Splitting-based Polynomially-bounded Automated Reasoning with Tensorized Adaptation," and NMSU is working with two other research groups, one led by Chitta Baral from Arizona State University and the other by Yuliana Lierler and Jorge Fandinno from the University of Nebraska at Omaha.

The team's goal is to develop high assurance and broadly applicable methodologies for combining Automated Reasoning and Machine Learning, according to the article. Tran said integrating these branches of artificial intelligence will provide the speed and flexibility of machine learning with verifiability based on artificial reasoning proofs that have strong logical explainability and computational tractability. He said the team will focus on developing efficient and scalable approaches to combine machine learning approaches with logic programs, and such systems will provide explanations for their answers, which is a key difference compared to contemporary machine learning systems. Vasileiou said AI generally splits into two camps, one great at spotting patterns quickly and the other great at following strict logic, and combining them gives you the best of both worlds. He said you are getting an AI that can think fast on its feet while still showing its work in a way humans can verify and trust.

Right now, building an AI that is safe enough for critical jobs takes massive amounts of custom engineering, and CLARA aims to create one universal foundation that is rock-solid, mathematically proven, and ready to adapt to almost any complex problem. The program aims to build a reliable, plug-and-play AI engine that can be reused across dozens of high-stakes industries without needing to be rebuilt from scratch every time. The article names Minerva Baumann, a media relations officer, as the contact for the story and lists the College of Arts and Sciences, artificial intelligence and computer science among its tags. The release date for the announcement was Nov. 20, 2026, and the article does not say what happens next beyond the two-year grant and the work with the partner groups.

stories.Headline: Washington University launches an AI cluster hire across seven schools to recruit over 30 faculty
stories.Summary:
Washington University in St. Louis has launched an interdisciplinary artificial intelligence cluster hire across seven Danforth Campus schools, the university announced on November 19, 2026. The search, which is part of the AI initiative outlined by Provost Mark West, is now open at those seven schools. The university plans to recruit more than 30 new faculty members over the next three years through this effort. These hires will join a community of more than 300 WashU faculty members who already work in the artificial intelligence space across many disciplines. The new hires will focus their research on four core areas: agentic AI, including governance, society and institutions; human values, creative practice and AI; AI-driven imaging science from molecules to the universe; and AI for science and engineering, which covers modeling the physical world.

The initiative was shaped by conversations with more than 150 WashU faculty members, who said the university needed transformative change in research and education rather than just the adoption of new tools. More than 500 candidates have already submitted applications for the positions. A committee of 11 faculty members, co-chaired by Nathan Jacobs, vice provost of AI, and Betsy Sinclair, vice provost for innovation, continues to review those applications as they arrive. West said artificial intelligence is fundamentally changing the nature of work both inside and outside universities, and he said the new scholars would help WashU shape the future of the technology rather than simply respond to it. Jacobs said that while much fundamental AI innovation has come from computer science, the impact is now spreading across many fields, and he said breakthrough discoveries require deep collaboration between method developers and experts in areas such as materials science or public health.

Sinclair said the initiative is recruiting faculty with deep expertise in their fields who take the questions seriously and can contribute to conversations at WashU. She said the strong interest shows that scholars want to do this work somewhere that takes both the technology and its consequences seriously. The Office of the Provost is working with each Danforth Campus school to ensure the new hires find community among their WashU peers. The review committee includes William Acree, Deanna Barch and Timothy Wencewicz of Arts & Sciences; Adrienne Davis of WashU Law; Debra Haire-Joshu of the Bursky School of Public Health; Jonathan Hanahan and Andrew Witt of the Sam Fox School of Design & Visual Arts; Byron Powell of the Brown School; Yevgeniy Vorobeychik and William Yeoh of McKelvey Engineering; and Dennis Zhang of Olin Business School. More information about the four focus areas is available on WashU's AI website.

stories.Headline: Virginia Tech launches an interdisciplinary AI minor for students in every major
stories.Summary:
Virginia Tech launched a new interdisciplinary artificial intelligence minor in summer 2026, and the program is designed to prepare students in every major for careers in an AI-powered future. The minor teaches technical foundations while encouraging students to evaluate AI’s social impacts and wrestle with questions of ethics and policy. Christine Julien, head of the Department of Computer Science, led a group of collaborators from across the university in developing the program. She said that regardless of major, today’s students are entering a workforce where AI will be part of nearly every profession. Students in the minor learn the technical foundations of AI, examine ethical and social consequences, and explore how the technology intersects with fields in the arts, social sciences, business, and humanities.

The result is not simply technical training, because the minor is intended to give students the conceptual foundation to ask better questions about AI’s impacts. One such class is “The Skeptic’s Guide to AI,” which Benjamin Jantzen first taught last fall. He expected a classroom filled mostly with humanities students, but nearly every student was a first-year engineering major. Julien said the goal is to ensure Virginia Tech graduates understand how these technologies work, how to evaluate them critically, and how to apply them responsibly in their own fields. Jantzen said being a skeptic means asking whether what people are told about AI tools is literally true and whether the tools can do what they say they do.

He said it also means uncovering the assumptions behind those claims and considering what may be gained or lost, because there are always trade-offs with any technology. He said that for democracy to work, people have to understand what they are being asked to accept and what they are being asked to give up, and that demands scrutiny and the work of the skeptic. The articles describe AI as offering enormous potential to accelerate scientific and social innovation, with Virginia Tech work that includes uses designed to speed drug discovery, unravel the secrets of DNA, protect consumers from scams and identity theft, and support the U.S. Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission to double scientific productivity. The articles also say AI raises concerns about related job losses, economic uncertainty, and the environmental and natural resource costs of operating systems. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the minor’s launch.

stories.Headline: Engineers, Clinicians Partner to Advance Human Health with AI
stories.Summary:
Engineers at the University of California, Davis are working with clinicians on artificial intelligence tools meant to detect Alzheimer's disease earlier, expand care options for survivors of sexual assault and improve results for patients awaiting corneal transplants. The projects are funded by AI and Health Seed Funding Awards from the Center for Information Technology Research in the Interest of Society and the Banatao Institute, known as CITRIS, which aim to strengthen interdisciplinary connections between schools and colleges across UC Davis and UC Davis Health and to establish the university as a leader in AI-enabled healthcare technology research. The awards followed a matchmaking mixer for engineers and clinicians held in November 2025 and co-hosted by the UC Davis AI Center in Engineering, or AICE, with CITRIS, the Healthy Aging in a Digital World initiative and the Clinical and Translational Science Center as partners. That event produced six awarded seed grants, including the three co-led by engineers.

For the Alzheimer's project, Chen-Nee Chuah, the Child Family Professor in Engineering in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, is developing an AI model that can pick up early signs of the disease from a patient's speech, working with Michelle Cohn, a postdoctoral scholar in linguistics, and Alyssa Weakley, an assistant professor of neurology. The team is examining conversational interviews with older adults from the UC Davis Alzheimer's Disease Research Center Corpus, which is annotated with patients' cognitive status such as mild cognitive impairment or late-stage Alzheimer's, to train a model to identify biomarkers of cognitive impairment by analyzing how a patient sounds and their manner of speech. The team has completed the datasets needed to train the large language model on acoustic and linguistic features of cognitive impairment in older adults, and the National Institutes of Health has given the researchers a boost to develop an AI-enabled remote monitoring system to detect health issues in older adults, which will directly support the early detection work. The project will culminate in a real-world pilot deployment within a local senior living community.

Josh McCoy, an associate professor of computer science, is leading a project to develop a trauma-informed, AI-powered chatbot that can connect survivors of sexual assault with appropriate social and health support services, with Jessica Draughon Moret, an associate professor at the UC Davis Betty Irene Moore School of Nursing, as co-lead. The private chatbot aims to expand access to and simplify the process of seeking care, and the pair are working to ensure it is informed by human-centered design and built on expert consultation with survivors. The team has a prototype for the platform, called CARE-COMPASS: Community Assistance and Resource Engagement, and is currently in the refinement and user feedback phase, with the goal of seeking additional funding from the National Institutes of Health for further development and broader use. Separately, Hamed Pirsiavash, a professor of computer science, is co-leading a project with Mark Mannis, a distinguished professor of ophthalmology and vision science, to develop an AI-powered evaluation system for donated corneal tissue, joined by Min Zhao, a professor of ophthalmology and vision science, Ana Sandoval Castellanos, a postdoctoral fellow in the Laboratory for Cell Nanoengineering, and several medical students.

The cornea team has been working with Sierra Donor Services, a non-profit donor procurement organization serving the Northern California and Northern Nevada regions, to source a curated dataset of microscopy images of corneal tissue, and through self-supervised learning the system uses computer vision and machine learning to distinguish between healthy and abnormal tissue. The goal is to reduce clinicians' workload from hours to minutes when evaluating tissue and to minimize variability in the quality of donated tissue, and the project's next step is to test the AI model with larger sample sizes. Sam King, a professor of computer science and director of CITRIS at UC Davis, said an engineer can build a model that scores well on a benchmark and still fails in a clinic because the team does not know which errors matter to a patient, while clinicians know but cannot build these systems alone. He said the technology is improving faster than those partnerships are forming, and the awards exist to close that gap by putting engineers and clinicians on the same problem before design decisions are made. The awards dovetail with the AICE's AI and Health research area, which accelerates discovery by facilitating conversations between engineers and clinicians, and through AICE's partnership they are helping realize CITRIS Health's mission to encourage innovations in technology that improve health outcomes and increase access to medicine.

stories.Headline: Researchers find limited biological data hinders AI development in biotechnology

Vikram Venkatram and Steph Batalis published a report in November 2026 regarding the availability of biological data for artificial intelligence. The authors examined how engineering biology can be enhanced through AI to create better drugs, materials, and food. They used case studies on microscopy data for cellular segmentation and protein structural data to evaluate existing databases. This research identifies how the limited volume and quality of biological data currently hinder AI developers.

The report argues that the United States must address five specific categories of data challenges to maintain leadership in this field. These challenges include issues with data quantity, distribution, accessibility, usability, and the quality of validation. The authors suggest that policymakers should improve database infrastructure and promote better standardization to allow for interoperability between disparate sources. They also recommend incentivizing the collection of more representative data and investing in multidisciplinary talent capable of using computational tools.

The researchers stated that high quality and well annotated biological data are essential for the successful application of AI in biotechnology. They noted that while not every AI model faces every challenge, developers must test their systems based on their specific use cases. The authors believe that strategic improvements to data access will stimulate innovation and support national security and economic development. The report concludes that overcoming these bottlenecks is a critical first step for the future of engineering biology.

stories.Headline: MIT researchers constrain chaotic AI models with hard physics limits
stories.Summary:
Researchers with MIT’s Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems have found a way to introduce physics-based restrictions on machine learning models of chaotic systems. The findings were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in a paper by MIT graduate student Sunbochen Tang and MIT professors Navid Azizan and Themistoklis Sapsis. The work was published on November 20, 2026, and reported by David Chandler of LIDS. The approach enforces energy dissipation as a hard constraint so predictions cannot grow without limit. The team is making the information freely available.

The model learns an energy-like function along with a boundary where chaotic behavior should be confined. A projection layer adjusts how the model predicts the system will evolve and enforces energy dissipation as a hard constraint. Outside the boundary the energy-like quantity must decrease, drawing the simulated system toward the bounded region. The team tested the approach on physical systems ranging from simple textbook cases to highly complex multidimensional systems. The paper, titled “Learning dissipative chaotic dynamics with boundedness guarantees,” and open-source code are accessible online at PNAS.

Sapsis, a professor of mechanical engineering and LIDS affiliate, said lack of guarantees for a bounded response has always been a major obstacle for data-driven models of complex nonlinear systems. Azizan, the Hayes Associate Professor in the Department of Mechanical Engineering and the Institute for Data, Systems, and Society and a principal investigator in LIDS, said tiny differences in starting conditions can lead to dramatically different outcomes. He said chaos does not mean anything can happen and that these systems often remain bounded, and their models should be too. Tang, a doctoral student in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics and LIDS, said the model learns an energy-like function and a boundary, and a projection layer enforces energy dissipation.

Tang said previous attempts imposed penalties or incentives during training, with no guarantee the model satisfies the constraints at test time. He said capping predictions, for example at 100 degrees for temperature, could restrict the model from representing complex features learned from data. Azizan said the fundamental difference is hard constraining versus soft constraining, and the output is always physically consistent even for a new case. He said data is not as abundant for many physical systems, so physics-constrained approaches can help because the physics is another source of information. Tang said the approach is readily applicable to a wide range of neural network architectures.

The models are used in climate and weather, industrial processes, aeronautics, and hydrology. In fluid dynamics, turbulent flows can disrupt air travel, reduce the efficiency of wind turbines, and affect fuel economy of vehicles. In weather forecasting, the chaotic nature of atmospheric dynamics makes accurate long-term predictions difficult. The team plans to continue testing the approach on ever-larger systems and is trying to see how well it would work on data-driven models of realistic weather systems. Azizan said the projection layer is modular, model-agnostic, and can work with different neural network architectures.

A follow-up work this year by members of the team was presented at the Learning for Dynamics and Control conference and won the conference’s Best Paper Award. Azizan said trustworthy and reliable AI needs more than evidence that a model usually works, and for high-stakes applications you need guarantees about properties that must always hold. He said the team established one such guarantee, boundedness, and the broader goal is to make principles part of how AI models are built, not just how they are tested. Azizan said he hopes other researchers and practitioners will build on the projection layer and test it on larger and even more complex problems. The articles do not say when the follow-up work was presented or what it found.

stories.Headline: At an AI Tipping Point - University of Pennsylvania
stories.Summary:
Karen Detlefsen recently challenged her philosophy students to write four letters to a classmate using different levels of artificial intelligence assistance. This exercise occurred during the Fall/Winter 2026 semester at the University of Pennsylvania to explore if AI can think like philosophers. Detlefsen wanted her students to contemplate whether machines can truly create and what it means to be human. The technology now permeates many facets of modern life, including social media, elections, and the military. In September 2026, AI solved a decades-old problem regarding equations that govern how fluids move.

The University of Pennsylvania led a natural language processing revolution in the early 1990s through several different academic fronts. Mark Liberman directed the Linguistic Data Consortium to annotate language datasets in English, Chinese, and Arabic for machine learning. Mitch Marcus led the Treebank effort at Penn Engineering to train computers to split sentences into phrases independently. Today, many U.S. city and state governments have hired Chief AI Officers to manage these emerging technologies. John Lapinski is now starting a new initiative to bring these various government leaders together for collaboration.

Michael Horowitz, a Professor of Political Science, says that AI will inevitably reshape society and more advances are coming. He believes the main question is who can adopt the technology most effectively and safely in the future. Charles Yang explains that large language models are essentially fancy versions of predictive typing that solve sequence prediction problems. John Lapinski states that governments across the world will eventually step in to decide how AI is used. Lapinski also notes that AI cannot be used when a task requires zero error, such as NBC returns.

Political campaigns and the military are affected by AI, as are people receiving information through the media ecosystem. Horowitz notes that autonomy in weapons, like radar-guided missiles used since the 1980s, requires human responsibility for force. Lapinski worries that AI could create synthetic public opinion data to mislead voters before the 2028 presidential election. He mentions a fake polling company that recently tried to proliferate fake results through the media ecosystem. The general public and experts agree that regulating artificial intelligence is a good idea, though methods remain unclear.

Alan Turing pondered whether machines could think as far back as the 1950s, long before the current AI movement. Charles Yang studied the science of cognition as a PhD student at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. He notes that children learn from 5 million words yearly, while large language models use billions or trillions. Unlike the steady progression of AI, children often make more mistakes as they learn new words and grammar. AI has moved from niche academic journals to headlines in The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal.

Experts are currently figuring out how to use AI responsibly and what safeguards to put in place for data centers. The U.S. military experiments with AI but lags in adoption due to the tests required for operating procedures. Some scientists are still trying to understand how simple predictions become complex ideas, which remains a complete mystery. AI is prone to hallucinating made-up information, and policies may become obsolete quickly because the technology moves so fast. The articles leave open how the world will eventually regulate AI and if machines can truly be creative.

stories.Headline: UVA President Beardsley outlines plan to use AI while keeping human judgment central
stories.Summary:
On Friday, UVA President Scott Beardsley sent an email to the University community outlining his vision for the role artificial intelligence will play at UVA. The note was published November 20, 2026, by University News under the headline that Beardsley charts the University's future in artificial intelligence. Beardsley says UVA will harness the potential of artificial intelligence across the University while prioritizing responsible use and human judgment. The photo accompanying the article is by Lathan Goumas of University Communications. Beardsley joined colleagues in the Contemplative Sciences Center for a symposium on AI and Human Flourishing.

UVA offers more than 100 AI-focused courses per year and AI instruction is embedded in all 12 schools. UVA researchers have advanced AI and large language models for more than three decades. UVA is investing in computing power through the new Fontaine Computing and Innovation Center and spearheading the Commonwealth AI Initiative. The initiative unites universities, industry, government, and nonprofits to establish Virginia as a source of trusted, responsible AI expertise. The work takes place at the first data science school in the country and at the LaCross Institute for Ethical AI in Business at the Darden School of Business, which will soon host a conference.

Beardsley said UVA will not outsource consequential decisions to machines, and that AI will support human judgment, not replace it, in classrooms, labs, clinics, and offices. He said the goal is graduates with technical literacy in AI who can question it, critically interpret it, and know when to set it aside. He said the most successful universities will pair the newest technologies with the oldest methods of teaching and learning, including the Socratic seminar, the blue book, oral exams, and the argument defended aloud. He said faculty will continue to decide what resources students may use in coursework and the technologies permitted in their classrooms, and must be clear about expectations whether they embrace AI, restrict it, or take a hybrid approach. He said students are bound by the Honor Code and are leading the discussion on upholding Honor in the age of AI.

Beardsley said UVA's Information Technology Services already offers embedded AI tools such as Microsoft Copilot Chat and Google Gemini in the Academic Division, though many in the community are paying for licenses to additional tools. He said UVA is committed to providing equitable access and exploring frontier AI platforms, and will share more information soon. He said AI is shaping nearly every profession and is a trillion-dollar industry, and that UVA is building infrastructure to track AI's effects on the workplace in partnership with employers, recruiters, and alumni. He said UVA will adapt curricula, bolster career services, and partner with AI-related companies to hire students and collaborate with faculty on research. He said four standing University committees on AI, for teaching and learning, research, operations, and policy and use, will advise as the work unfolds.

Beardsley wrote that AI has been around for decades and has been part of the development of the internet, social media, and broadband communications, and that the emergence of agentic AI is accelerating the pace of transformation. He wrote that UVA was founded on the belief that education should serve the public good, especially in moments of rapid and profound change. He wrote that scholars and stakeholders have been advancing the understanding of AI for years and confronting the hard questions it raises for society. He wrote that UVA has backed that purpose with sustained investment in AI spanning research, institutes, infrastructure, and partnerships with leading companies. He wrote that Jefferson founded the University on the belief that people learn best through genuine human relationships built on discussion and debate.

In the coming weeks, interim Provost Brie Gertler will share updates on AI applications in the Academic Division, and Dr. Mitch Rosner will share updates with UVA Health. Beardsley wrote that UVA will pilot AI with care across its operations and will continuously reassess and adapt as the technology advances at exponential rates. He wrote that no one has a crystal ball. He directed readers to AI@UVA and to the faculty-led AI Exchange@UVA podcast for an interview with him and others. The article does not say what the updates from Gertler and Rosner will contain.

stories.Headline: UC San Diego and MIT scientists lead independent review of OpenAI and Anthropic refutation claims
stories.Summary:
On November 19, 2026, computer scientists from UC San Diego and MIT began facilitating an independent review of results from OpenAI and Anthropic. These two frontier AI labs recently announced that their models refuted the Exponential Time Hypothesis, which was originally formulated in 1998. The review is being led by Russell Impagliazzo and Mohan Paturi from UC San Diego, along with Ryan Williams from MIT. This effort follows global media coverage regarding the potential refutation of the influential hypothesis.

If these findings are verified, the change could have broad implications for optimization algorithms and various technical applications. Specifically, the results might impact the way experts approach chip design and the encryption systems currently used on the Internet. To manage this process, the team launched a new blog called ETH: Community Examination and Discussion for researchers to share ideas. They also posted the specific OpenAI prompt that led to the refutation on the blog this week.

Russell Impagliazzo and Mohan Paturi are professors at UC San Diego, while Paturi also serves as the associate dean for artificial intelligence strategy and implementation. These experts, along with Ryan Williams, are stepping into these roles to help the computer science community assess the claims independently. They intend to hold one or more academic conferences to discuss the verification work and its farther-reaching implications. The original hypothesis was proposed by Impagliazzo and Paturi alongside Francis Zane, who is now an independent researcher.

stories.Headline: Yale Law School professors teach a course on AI’s impact on legal institutions
stories.Summary:
Yale Law School is offering a course called “The Transformation of Legal Institutions in the Age of AI,” taught by Clinical Professor of Law Sven Riethmueller and Visiting Clinical Lecturer in Law Bjarne Tellmann, according to a November 19, 2026, article on the school’s website. Riethmueller, who is the founding director of the Entrepreneurship & Innovation Clinic at Yale Law School, saw a need to introduce students to AI’s growing role in legal practice and the business of law as the technology spreads through the profession. He called upon Tellmann, an AI expert who worked in law for 30 years and recently wrote “Law in the Era of AI: Clients, Firms, and the Future of the Legal Industry,” to teach the class with him. The course examines AI’s growing impact on the legal industry and the deeper questions surrounding its role in the law and society at large.

The course centers on the premise of Tellmann’s book, which argues that AI’s impact on legal institutions can be better understood by examining corporate clients, who make up the majority of Big Law revenue in the United States. Tellmann contends that as companies adopt AI on a larger scale, the effects on their legal departments will inevitably spread throughout the legal profession, legal education and the courts. Riethmueller said the idea is for students to explore the topic, understand its facets and see that there is a role for law students in an AI world and how they can thrive in the new technological environment. The instructors are applying the Law School’s approach that blends theory and practice, giving students a chance to think about AI abstractly while pondering real-world applications, and the class has also featured guest speakers, including a law firm partner in a senior leadership role and the CEO of a legal technology company called ClearyX.

Riethmueller said Yale educates leaders, that its students are at the forefront of the legal world and will be future leaders of the profession with input on where it is going, and that the class is helping them prepare for that. Tellmann described a combination of excitement and anxiety among students, saying some come up after class expressing deep concerns while others are keen to lean into the opportunities the new era presents. Emma Lilly Menzer ’27 said the course has excelled at bridging the gap between theory and tangible application and that she has gained a greater appreciation for creativity, collaborative teamwork and human judgment against the backdrop of a legal practice being fundamentally altered by AI. Grace Sherrill ’27 said conversations about AI and the law often veer between dismissiveness and alarmism, but the course has let her think systematically about how AI may reshape the practice of law and the institutions that underpin it, and Tristan John-Jandles ’28 said hearing from the guest speakers gave him a reassuring read on where the profession stands for junior professionals right now.

stories.Headline: Rhode Island Small Business Development Center and Meta host free AI workshop for small business owners
stories.Summary:
The Rhode Island Small Business Development Center, which is based at the University of Rhode Island, and Meta are teaming up to host a free, hands-on workshop focused on AI skills that small business owners can use. The training is scheduled for Tuesday, December 1, starting at 8:30 am and running until 11:30 am. More than 150 small business owners, students and community members have already signed up, but registration is still open. The event will be held at the Crown Plaza Providence-Warwick, 801 Greenwich Ave., Warwick, RI 02886.

The session will include an interactive workshop that lets attendees work alongside expert facilitators and fellow business owners. Participants will also receive a crash course on Muse, which is already integrated into Meta's social media platforms and acts as a virtual assistant. According to the articles, Muse helps small businesses answer customer questions, draft reports, keep sales leads from growing cold, create social media content and develop marketing campaigns tailored for their industry. Attendees will also have the opportunity to try on Meta's newest AI glasses. Those planning to attend should download Muse at muse.ai./business and bring a laptop or phone with Muse already downloaded onto it.

The collaboration is thanks, in part, to Matthew Lenz '11, a member of the University of Rhode Island's Board of Trustees, who serves as a public policy director for Meta and will be in attendance at the workshop. The articles describe the event as open to solopreneurs and small business owners across any industry. Registration is available at https://www.risbdc.org/workshop.aspx?ekey=70460040. The articles do not say what happens after the workshop or whether further sessions are planned.

stories.Headline: UConn president Maric calls for breaking silos to grow Connecticut's AI economy
stories.Summary:
Hundreds of people gathered at Rentschler Field in East Hartford on Thursday, Nov. 19, as UConn held its annual Economic Impact forum. The event was entitled “Powering the AI Economy for Connecticut Towns.” It was the third consecutive year for the forum, held in Storrs in 2024 and Stamford in 2025. Connecticut leaders from government, academia, and industry attended. UConn held the forum in the club level of Pratt & Whitney Stadium at Rentschler Field.

The forum explored how Connecticut’s established strengths support continued growth and the roles each sector must play. UConn’s annual economic impact to Connecticut has grown to $13 billion, supporting 60,000 jobs and returning $19 for every dollar the State invests, according to Reka Wrynn, UConn’s associate vice president of budget and planning. The forum marked Radenka Maric’s first public remarks since the UConn Board of Trustees announced plans to extend her presidency. Anthropic, the company that created AI platform Claude, went public on Thursday, closing at $97.17 a share for an evaluation of about $1.76 trillion. According to the Wall Street Journal, it was largest IPO in history.

UConn President Radenka Maric said the state must break through silos that obstruct collaboration. “It is not only what technology can do for us, it is how we enhance our collaboration,” Maric said. Lt. Gov. Susan Bysiewicz led a standing ovation, saying she joined Gov. Lamont in excitement that Maric will continue her tenure. Bysiewicz said the state has a distinct advantage and does not need to build an economy around AI from scratch.

“UConn is one of our state’s most important economic assets,” Bysiewicz said. David Bergman, associate dean for faculty and research for the School of Business and special advisor for AI to the provost, said the forum’s timing was appropriate given Anthropic’s record-setting IPO. Hartford Mayor Arunan Arulampalam said the city seeks to work with a set of hiring institutions that rivals any city in the country. “Our goal is to have a workforce that is among the most prepared for the technology of tomorrow of any workforce in America,” Arulampalam said.

Lindsay DiStefano, UConn’s vice president for research, innovation, and entrepreneurship, highlighted the Grant Trails heat map, which demonstrates research impact town-by-town through Connecticut. Assistant Professor Wei Ren of the College of Agriculture, Health, and Natural Resources led the UConn proposal that earned a highly competitive Genesis Award. The program is federally funded by the Department of Energy to double the country’s scientific productivity by funding AI-related research projects. The DOE granted $525,000 for a project that uses AI to study how water and other fluids move underground.

DiStefano said the winner comes from an area vital to the mission of a land grant university and the state. The forum included expert panels on how UConn is teaching responsible use of AI to students and building partnerships with organizations throughout the region. Several students presented individual research topics, including crumbling foundations in Connecticut, weight stigma in social media, and inventions. Bysiewicz addressed Connecticut’s modern “industrial revolution,” with economic transformation as business adapts to AI, quantum computing, biotech, and advanced manufacturing.

She said the state has a proven legacy of companies, an educational network, and governmental infrastructure to meet challenges. She said the state needs to make innovation an engine of broad-based economic opportunity. Arulampalam explained how the capital has built opportunities out of what already was in place, seeking not to create a new “Silicon Valley or Cambridge.” He said the city is seeking to foster opportunities to work with employers and colleges to create hands-on opportunities for students.
