stories.Headline: Researchers recover pruned MoE experts without training through gated reuse
stories.Summary:
Linliang Chen, Yan Zhong, Wang Kang, Sai Li, Ji Wu and Ji Liu posted a paper to arXiv on 21 November 2026 describing a method for recovering the work of pruned experts in Mixture-of-Experts large language models. Mixture-of-Experts models activate only a few experts per token while generally keeping all experts in GPU memory for high efficiency, and expert pruning reduces that memory footprint but discards the contribution of the pruned experts. The authors report that the functionalities of pruned experts can be efficiently reconstructed from the activated remaining experts. They propose GEAR, which stands for Gated Expert Activation Reuse and reuses the scaled outputs of reliable activated experts without any training or additional expert computation. They also propose GEAR$^2$, which adds an ultra-lightweight residual to further recover what reuse cannot express.

The work was tested on five Mixture-of-Experts large language models ranging from 16B to 106B parameters, with 25% and 50% of experts pruned. GEAR improves over its training-free counterparts in nearly every setting, by up to 4 percentage points in terms of accuracy. GEAR$^2$ outperforms baseline approaches by up to 2.75 percentage points in every setting across nine zero-shot benchmarks. The authors report larger advantages, up to 2.72 percentage points higher, under more aggressive pruning of up to 50%. The paper contrasts its approach with existing remedies that rely on static substitutes, merge experts at the cost of altering their functions, or require costly recovery training.

The paper lists Linliang Chen, Yan Zhong, Wang Kang, Sai Li, Ji Wu and Ji Liu as its authors, and the abstract presents the findings and the two proposed methods in the authors' own account. The authors state that GEAR reuses the scaled outputs of reliable activated experts without any training or additional expert computation, and that GEAR$^2$ adds an ultra-lightweight residual for what reuse cannot express. They describe the reconstruction of pruned experts' functionalities from the activated remaining experts as a finding of the paper. The abstract frames the motivation around the GPU memory footprint that expert pruning reduces and the discarded contribution of pruned experts that existing remedies handle in other ways.

The articles provide no information on what happens next, such as release of code, further testing or publication beyond the arXiv posting. The abstract reports results on nine zero-shot benchmarks and on models from 16B to 106B parameters, with pruning at 25% and 50%. The arXiv listing notes that a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source are available for the paper. It also describes arXivLabs as a framework allowing collaborators to develop and share features directly on the arXiv website, and states that arXiv is committed to openness, community, user data privacy and partnership with organizations that adhere to those values.

Articles.Title: GEAR$^2$: Pruned Experts Live On through Gated Reuse of Activated Experts and a Missing-Mass Residual

stories.Headline: Yes Bank tightens AI cyber defences and delays fintech payouts
stories.Summary:
Fintech platforms have been hit as collateral damage while Yes Bank strengthens its defences against AI-driven cyberattacks, sources told Inc42 on November 21, 2026. The cybersecurity upgrades at Yes Bank are disrupting workflows and delaying payouts at payment service providers, according to those sources. One fintech executive said his platform faced issues ever since Yes Bank sent an email noting the bank was implementing enhanced precautionary measures to safeguard transactions. He was subsequently informed that the bank was making changes to its banking APIs, which was delaying settlements. These changes are impacting payment processing and settlement timelines for some businesses that rely on banking APIs to move funds.

Another industry insider said the issues began to crop up after the Reserve Bank of India issued directives to banks and other financial institutions to bolster cybersecurity defences. According to that source, the RBI directions came after the recent cyberattack on the State Bank of India, referring to the data leak at the bank in October. The RBI is also said to have directed banks and other financial institutions to ensure customer funds are not impacted by the growing wave of AI-assisted cyberattacks. Inc42 has reached out to Yes Bank for a comment on the matter. This story will be updated upon receiving their response.

CERT-In issued an advisory dated November 21 flagging that malicious actors were using AI-driven cyberattacks to undertake unauthorised transactions at technology service providers handling government-linked payment processes and platforms handling vendor payouts. CERT-In said attackers altered business records or approval relationships and then used legitimate payment processes to approve fraudulent transactions. The watchdog did not elaborate on how much money had been funneled out. CERT-In said the reported incidents involved cyberattackers misusing business applications and workflows rather than direct exploitation of payment APIs alone. As per CERT-In, these attackers used trusted systems to process unauthorised transactions and exploited gaps in verification and reconciliation of changes to business records.

CERT-In identified techniques used by attackers, including automated reconnaissance to identify exposed systems, services and possible attack paths. It listed rapid preparation and modification of exploits for known vulnerabilities, including through analysis of software updates and related technical information. It also cited use of multiple agents or automated workers to undertake reconnaissance, privilege discovery and other intrusion tasks in parallel. CERT-In noted modification of scripts, requests and attack steps in response to errors, blocked attempts or information returned by targeted systems.

It also flagged use of valid credentials, legitimate administrative functions, trust relationships and external infrastructure to gain further access. CERT-In directed government entities to identify and restrict accounts and integrations that can approve payments or change payment-related records. It recommended independent certification for high-risk changes to payment records and called on banks to reconcile critical business data maintained by service providers against authoritative records. It called on the TSPS to restrict administrative accounts and control-plane privileges.

CERT-In also directed fintechs to review unusual activity and monitor changes to payment-related business records. Multiple Indian crypto exchanges continue to grapple with delays in processing withdrawals due to disruptions at their banking partners. Coinbase India had paused all withdrawals last week before partially resuming payouts, citing an outage at its banking partner. CoinDCX, facing similar issues, claimed upgrades at most of its partner banks were delaying processing of INR withdrawals.

Zebpay said payouts were taking longer than usual because of a technical disruption at its banking partner. Earlier yesterday, Razorpay told customers it had to delay merchant settlements temporarily due to a technical issue at a partner bank, and the IPO-bound unicorn later reinstated the service hours later. The development comes on the same day CERT-In issued its alarm over unauthorised transactions at technology service providers for banks and other financial institutions. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Beyer releases AI safety outline as Warner introduces AI finance disclosure bill
stories.Summary:
Representative Don Beyer and Senator Mark Warner each moved forward with separate artificial intelligence measures in Washington on Thursday, November 19, 2026, approaching the technology from opposite ends of the Capitol. Beyer, a Democrat representing Virginia's 8th District, released an outline for bipartisan legislation that would require the companies building the most powerful AI systems to adopt safety frameworks, report incidents and submit to outside review. Warner, a Democrat from Virginia, introduced a bill that would force publicly traded companies to disclose more about how they finance and oversee AI. Beyer's proposal is a blueprint only, and the legislative text has not yet been written, while Warner's bill has been formally introduced.

Beyer's outline would apply to the companies building the most powerful artificial intelligence systems, requiring them to adopt safety frameworks, report incidents and submit to outside review. Warner's bill would require publicly traded companies to disclose more about how they finance and oversee artificial intelligence. The two measures were pushed on the same day, Thursday, November 19, 2026, according to The Alexandria Brief. Beyer's plan remains a blueprint, meaning the legislative text has not been written, while Warner's bill was introduced. The articles do not give further numbers, dates or names beyond these.

Beyer is a Democrat representing the 8th District, and Warner is a Democrat from Virginia, and each is responsible for his own measure. The articles do not quote either lawmaker directly, so what they said is not available beyond the descriptions of their proposals. Beyer released an outline for bipartisan legislation, and Warner introduced a bill, according to the report. No further statements from either office are included in the articles.

The context is that the two Virginia lawmakers pushed separate artificial intelligence measures in Washington on the same Thursday, approaching the technology from opposite ends of the Capitol. Beyer's effort is at the blueprint stage, with the legislative text still unwritten, and Warner's bill has been introduced. The articles do not say what happens next beyond those stages. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Michelle Hinchey introduces bill making fake AI citations judicial misconduct
stories.Summary:
State Sen. Michelle Hinchey introduced the Judicial AI Accountability and Integrity Act on Thursday, November 19, 2026, according to Wisevoter. The bill would classify a judge's knowing or reckless use of fabricated legal authority in judicial writings as misconduct in office. Using AI alone would not constitute misconduct under the bill. The legislation follows rulings in Mississippi, New Jersey and Oklahoma in which judges acknowledged that their decisions contained AI-generated fictitious citations.

The bill provides that misconduct occurs when a judge relies on a citation containing fabricated legal authority or one that is materially false. It would authorize the New York State Commission on Judicial Conduct to refer misconduct determinations to the Assembly for impeachment. Judges would avoid misconduct by verifying all information against reliable, legitimate sources before including it in judicial writing. A 2026 survey found that over 60% of federal judges report using AI tools, with at least 20% using them weekly, and legal AI tools have produced factually incorrect information 17% to 33% of the time. The survey does not address New York judges specifically.

The New York State Commission on Judicial Conduct, the state body that investigates complaints against judges, is reviewing the bill. Hinchey, who represents the Hudson Valley region, plans to advocate for the bill's passage in the 2027 legislative session, when its prospects will become clearer. The bill seeks to ensure that rulings rest on real case law and facts, because judicial decisions directly affect people's freedom and rights. If enacted, it would give New York a formal mechanism to address the misuse of AI in judicial writing that the Mississippi, New Jersey and Oklahoma cases exposed.

Articles.Title: Hinchey Bill Would Penalize Judges' Fake AI Citations - Wisevoter

stories.headline_source: Hinchey Bill Would Penalize Judges' Fake AI Citations

stories.Headline: CalCPA launches Spark to teach 75 accounting students client and people skills
stories.Summary:
The California Society of CPAs launched a leadership development program called Spark, part of a broader ecosystem named Leader Lab 360 that was introduced in June 2026, and its first cohort brought together 75 students from campuses across California, ranging from Fresno State to schools in Los Angeles and the Bay Area, including community colleges. The program was described in a November 2026 article by Miklos Ringbauer, founder of MiklosCPA and the 2026-27 board chair for CalCPA, who said the effort focuses on skills that rarely appear on an exam but show up in every client meeting. Those skills include interviewing, personal branding, networking and follow-up, client communication and navigating the first day on the job, and five virtual sessions build the foundation for an immersive capstone in Sacramento. At that capstone, participants turn learning into action through real-world challenges, professional networking and hands-on advocacy at CPA Day at the Capitol, and Ringbauer said those in-person days are where a group of students becomes a cohort and where mentoring relationships begin.

Ringbauer argued that as artificial intelligence takes on more routine work such as data entry, reconciliations and spreadsheet organization, emerging professionals have an opportunity to engage in higher-value work earlier than in the past, when young accountants spent years on administrative and compliance tasks before moving into client relationships and advisory work. He said communication, critical thinking, adaptability, collaboration and relationship-building will become even more important as AI becomes more capable, and that the human connection is at the heart of the profession. He acknowledged that such abilities are sometimes called soft skills but said that term undersells their importance, because the ability to communicate, build trust and exercise judgment complements technical expertise rather than ranking below it. He also said accounting has adapted to technological change before, as paper ledgers gave way to spreadsheets and spreadsheets gave way to cloud-based systems and sophisticated analytics, with each transformation changing the work CPAs do without eliminating the need for trusted professionals.

Ringbauer, who teaches federal taxation at Orange Coast College, said he cares that Spark reaches community college students and that education should give students the foundation and confidence to solve problems they have not yet encountered. He said the question is not simply whether AI can perform accounting tasks but how professionals are prepared to work alongside it, and he described the responsibility as making sure the next generation of CPAs is ready for that transformation. He said a CPA license can be a foundation for far more than traditional accounting, including entrepreneurship, leadership, advisory work, innovation and public service, and that the future of accounting will require professionals who understand both technology and people. The article does not say what happens after the first cohort or give further details on future sessions.

stories.Headline: South Korean universities issue gowns and ban correction tape to stop AI cheating in admissions tests
stories.Summary:
South Korean universities implemented strict security measures in November 2026 to prevent cheating with artificial intelligence devices during admissions tests. These actions followed the 2027 College Scholastic Ability Test and were prompted by reports of a top scorer in a tax accountant exam using a miniature camera. Sogang University issued an urgent notice on November 18 regarding smart glasses and cameras before its science exams on November 21 and humanities exams on November 22. Korea University also released guidelines on November 17 for its own essay exams held on November 21 and 22.

The new rules require specific clothing and writing tools to block hidden electronic devices. Seoul National University provides interview gowns to prevent cameras from being hidden in buttonholes, while Sogang University asks applicants to avoid garments with buttons on the sleeves. Korea University banned correction tape and requires answer sheets to be written in a single pen color. Sungkyunkwan University only allows the use of specific pens previously given as souvenirs to prevent cameras from being attached to writing instruments.

Inha University and other schools may use metal detectors on suspicious applicants or those using the restroom. University officials and education bodies are taking responsibility for these heightened security protocols. A Sungkyunkwan official stated that the school increased the number of proctors and sent text messages with guidelines to all applicants. Sogang University warned that violations of these rules could lead to legal action and criminal complaints.

The Korean Council for University Education stated it would respond sternly to AI cheating and urged the Ministry of Education and the National Assembly to revise the Higher Education Act. These measures aim to align university exam security with the rigorous standards of the national CSAT. The Korean Council for University Education is seeking budget funding to expand equipment and proctoring staff for future tests. Efforts to build a comprehensive anti-cheating system for university-administered exams are expected to accelerate.

Articles.Title: Korean Universities Ban Correction Tape, Issue Gowns to Block AI Cheating - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.headline_source: Korean Universities Ban Correction Tape, Issue Gowns to Block AI Cheating

stories.Headline: Oak Ridge opens Lux supercomputer to scientific users as first AI factory for Genesis Mission
stories.Summary:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory announced on November 16, during the SC26 supercomputing conference in Chicago, that its new Lux supercomputer had opened to scientific users, becoming the first dedicated AI factory supporting the Department of Energy's Genesis Mission. The system debuted at No. 14 on the latest TOP500 supercomputer rankings, recording 220.79 petaflops of performance on the High Performance Linpack benchmark. Lux was developed in partnership with AMD and Hewlett Packard Enterprise. It debuted in November 2026. Oak Ridge, Tennessee, has spent more than eight decades at the intersection of American scientific ambition and national energy priorities.

According to HPE's November 16 technical announcement, Lux is built on HPE ProLiant Compute XD685 infrastructure, equipped with AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, AMD EPYC CPUs, AMD Pensando networking technology, and the AMD ROCm software stack. The direct-liquid-cooled platform incorporates HPE Juniper Networking technology, including Ethernet switches supporting 800-gigabit connectivity. The system comprises 504 compute nodes and 4,032 GPUs, according to ORNL's Lux system documentation. Approximately half of its annual allocation of 3.5 million node-hours will support the Genesis Mission, while the remaining capacity is reserved for proprietary partner access, including AMD's development and testing work. At an October 27 gathering in Oak Ridge, federal officials and nuclear industry representatives highlighted more than $15 billion in announced nuclear-related projects across the region, an investment wave subsequently documented in a November 17 DOE report on Oak Ridge's emerging energy hub.

On September 29, 2026, the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission announced that it had approved a construction permit for Clinch River Unit 1, a planned 300-megawatt GE Vernova Hitachi BWRX-300 small modular reactor. The permit was formally issued on September 28. The NRC completed its review in approximately 14 months, ahead of its original schedule. In its November 2026 financial filing, TVA confirmed that it had not yet decided whether to proceed with construction. In March, the United States and Japan announced a proposed strategic investment initiative involving up to $40 billion in GE Vernova Hitachi BWRX-300 projects in Tennessee and Alabama.

The prospective development would encompass approximately 3 GW of generation, equivalent to ten 300-MW reactor units. Federal officials have discussed the potential for additional reactor development in Tennessee and at TVA's Bellefonte site in Alabama. In March, DOE completed its largest Oak Ridge land transfer to date, conveying more than 700 acres for economic reuse. The transfer included a 624-acre parcel designated for Orano USA's planned uranium enrichment complex and a 77-acre parcel associated with Oklo's proposed nuclear fuel recycling development. Overall, more than 2,500 acres have been transferred from federal ownership for redevelopment, following decades of cleanup and the demolition of hundreds of former industrial structures.

The former K-25 uranium enrichment complex, once a critical part of the nation's atomic weapons program, has been transformed into the East Tennessee Technology Park, where extensive environmental cleanup and redevelopment have made former federal property available for commercial use. Established during World War II, the community became home to major facilities for uranium enrichment, nuclear materials processing, scientific research, and ultimately high-performance computing. Regional officials also anticipate demand for thousands of construction workers over the next five years, with additional permanent manufacturing and operating positions potentially following as projects advance. The investment figure largely represents planned private-sector development rather than completed capital spending. DOE is pursuing the development of privately operated AI data centers on portions of its Oak Ridge Reservation.

Among the initial research directions is AI-driven forecasting of water availability, river temperatures, and streamflow, with applications for hydropower and thermoelectric generation in the Tennessee Valley Authority region. Other work addresses fusion technology, materials development, and computational methods that could help improve the performance and efficiency of future energy systems. The mission itself is intended to accelerate discovery in fields including fusion energy, critical materials, manufacturing, and scientific modeling by combining AI, advanced computing, and experimental research. Lux is also intended to provide a flexible, multi-tenant computing environment. Its architecture is designed to support both traditional high-performance computing and AI workloads, including model training, inference, and scientific applications that combine simulation, experimental data, and machine learning.

TVA must still make a final investment decision, complete construction, and secure a separate operating license before Clinch River can generate commercial electricity. Power availability, licensing timelines, and skilled-worker shortages remain key constraints on the region's ambitions. DOE is seeking private AI data center development on federal land, but no Oak Ridge developer has been publicly selected. Those plans remain prospective and should not be confused with fully financed or approved construction projects. The BWRX-300 is based on established boiling-water reactor technology but incorporates a smaller generating unit and greater reliance on modular construction than conventional large nuclear plants.

stories.Headline: Anthropic valuation exceeds 1.7 trillion dollars following initial public offering
stories.Summary:
Anthropic made a spectacular stock market debut on Thursday, November 20, 2026. The maker of the Claude chatbot became one of the world's most valuable public companies. Investor enthusiasm propelled shares to new heights during this record breaking initial public offering. The company's valuation ended its first trading day at more than 1.7 trillion dollars. This surge happened shortly after the company finalized its offering on Wednesday.

The stock began trading on Nasdaq under the symbol ANT at 111.50 dollars. This was higher than the 83 dollar price set for the initial public offering. Revenue grew to 33 billion dollars in nine months from 41 million in 2023. The company grew from 940 employees at the end of 2024 to 5,300 by September. It is now the largest publicly traded public benefit corporation in the world.

Chief executive Dario Amodei said success came from hiring people oriented toward public benefit. He stated the company was disciplined about turning down talented people who did not fit. Amodei and six co-founders each hold stakes now worth more than 20 billion dollars. These founders split from OpenAI during the pandemic in 2020 to start their own firm. They have encouraged employees to donate portions of their stakes to charity.

Analysts said the debut would likely shore up confidence in the artificial intelligence industry. However, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite both fell about 2 percent that day. Early employee Nicholas Joseph warned that rapid acceleration in capabilities might be dangerous for society. Some employees signed a July petition urging the government to pace development for safety. Investors like Lillian Li described the executives as earnest people who wanted to do good.

The company was founded less than six years ago and grew faster than Meta or Google. It was once a small circle of workers including former Pentagon official Christopher Kirchhoff. Early investors included Gregory Jensen of Bridgewater Associates and tech giants like Amazon and Google. The offering occurred while Nvidia faced turmoil following the resignation of chief executive Jensen Huang. China was locked out of the initial public offering process entirely.

OpenAI has filed for its own initial public offering and may go public next year. The company plans to hire more sales people to continue its business growth. It remains unclear exactly how wealthy many of the early employees have become. The unusual governing structure must now balance safety and profit in a corporate experiment. The articles leave open whether the broader market nerves will be smoothed.

stories.Headline: House Republicans introduce four bills to help DHS and CISA combat AI cyberthreats
stories.Summary:
House Republicans introduced four bills on Wednesday, November 19, 2026, to help the Department of Homeland Security and CISA combat AI cyberthreats. These measures aim to protect federal networks and critical infrastructure from attacks driven by artificial intelligence. The bills focus on securing AI agents, building expertise at CISA, and using lessons from previous intrusions. They seek to get ahead of AI enabled attacks on government systems. Federal agencies are currently exploring how AI can support missions and shape operations.

The ROOT CAUSE Act by Rep. Morgan Luttrell, R-Texas, would create a National Cyber and AI Investigations Board within CISA. Rep. Matt Van Epps, R-Tenn., proposed the AI INSIGHT Act to secure AI agents on federal civilian systems. Rep. Vince Fong, R-Calif., introduced the BRIDGE AI Act to recruit AI specialists from universities, private companies, and national labs. The SECURE IT Act by Chairman Andy Ogles, R-Tenn., would make DHS the Sector Risk Management Agency for IT. Rep. Ritchie Torres, D-N.Y., and Chairman Andrew Garbarino, R-N.Y., are co-sponsoring these various legislative measures.

Rep. Matt Van Epps stated that AI agents on networks are new potential targets for adversaries. He said agencies must be able to see agents, restrict their access, watch them, and shut them off. Chairman Andrew Garbarino said the bills support administration efforts on AI security and ensure America leads in AI. Rep. Andy Ogles cited the worldwide Outlook outage as evidence of dependence on shared technology infrastructure. The ROOT CAUSE Act board would suggest ways to prevent recurring incidents without having regulatory or enforcement power.

The BRIDGE AI Act affects specialists from federally funded research and development centers and other emerging technology experts. Witnesses from Google Threat Intelligence, the Frontier Model Forum, Corridor Security, and the Electronic Frontier Foundation testified in June. These groups provided input during a hearing held by the cybersecurity subcommittee. The ROOT CAUSE Act ensures no one faces civil or criminal liability based on the board's findings. The board would require a majority vote to open investigations and must follow published selection criteria.

In April, Garbarino and Chairman John Moolenaar, R-Mich., began a joint probe into the spread of Chinese developed AI models. Anthropic demonstrated Mythos to Congress in May to show how advanced AI can uncover software flaws. In June, CISA issued Binding Operational Directive 26-04 ordering federal civilian agencies to prioritize vulnerability patching by risk. This directive implements a June executive order for CISA to create or expand AI enabled defensive tools. In May, the U.S. joined Australia, Canada, New Zealand, and the U.K. to release guidance on agentic AI.

The Potomac Officers Club will hold the 2027 Artificial Intelligence Summit on March 18 to discuss AI developments. CISA continues to warn that AI is shortening the time between a patch release and its exploitation. Investigators are still weighing if Chinese AI models in U.S. products pose risks to data security or infrastructure. The articles do not state if the four bills have been passed into law. They also leave open whether the joint probe into Chinese AI models has reached a conclusion.

stories.Headline: Senate passes S.5653 to fast-track AI data centers and permitting changes
stories.Summary:
Actor Mark Ruffalo urged his followers to oppose a specific Senate bill on November 18, 2026. He used his Instagram account to criticize Senate Democrats for their support of the legislation. Ruffalo claimed the bill gives President Trump more power over data centers and ICE camps. He argued that Democrats are ignoring their recent midterm election wins by supporting this. The actor wants his fans to contact legislators to stop the progress of the bill.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, known as S.5653, is a 494 page document. It aims to fast track AI data centers, ICE camps, pipelines, mines, and power plants. The bill would gut Tribal sovereignty, Native American rights, the Endangered Species Act, and the Clean Water Act. A manager's amendment was released on November 7, 2026, and an explainer was updated November 8. The Senate held a cloture vote on the motion to proceed on November 9, 2026.

Mark Ruffalo said the bill is a devastating rollback of environmental laws in American history. He questioned why Chuck Schumer and other Democrats support Trump after the country rejected him. The Bipartisan Policy Center stated that senators worked for over a year to negotiate these reforms. They claimed the package comprehensively addresses almost all aspects of the nation's current permitting process. The center noted that federal reviews of business applications now take years or decades instead of months.

Senator Ron Wyden told the New York Times that he cannot support the proposed legislation. He said the administration spent two years waging a war on new clean energy projects. The bill affects public lands, endangered species, and the fossil fuel industry through permitting changes. On November 18, the Senate passed the bill with a vote of 65 to 31. Twenty one members of the Democrat caucus voted in favor of the legislation.

The bill was supported by Senators Shelley Moore Capito, Mike Lee, and Martin Heinrich. Other supporters included Sheldon Whitehouse, John Fetterman, Jon Ossoff, Raphael Warnock, and leader Chuck Schumer. The Bipartisan Policy Center noted that previous reform attempts were introduced in both the House and Senate. They explained that delays on polluting projects also block conservation projects and clean energy technologies. The legislation seeks to curb permitting abuse that has caused long delays in federal reviews.

The Senate has already voted to move the bill forward with a significant bipartisan majority. Ruffalo continues to urge his followers to fight the legislation to protect environmental laws. The Bipartisan Policy Center intends to update its explainer as the legislation advances through Congress. The articles do not state if the bill has been signed into law yet. It remains unclear how the administration will handle the handshake promises mentioned by Senator Wyden.

stories.Headline: AWS shows how to use NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning on Amazon EKS
stories.Summary:
On November 19, 2026, AWS published a walkthrough on its blog describing how to use NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning on Amazon EKS. The post shows how to build a custom Amazon Linux 2023 image and configure GPU-memory sharing on Amazon EKS. In the validated example, the authors use one Amazon EC2 g5.xlarge instance with an NVIDIA A10G Tensor Core GPU. They establish a whole-GPU baseline, give each Pod an 8 GiB memory contract, and verify 6 GiB allocations. They then inspect per-Pod metrics, test rejection of a 9 GiB allocation, and clean up the disposable environment.

The walkthrough uses the AWS Samples repository and runs Steps 1 through 10. The Amazon EKS control plane runs Kubernetes version 1.36 in an AWS managed Amazon VPC, separate from the customer VPC, and connects to EC2 workers in private subnets of the customer VPC. An m7i.large system node hosts the operator controllers and KAI Scheduler, which places both Pods on a tainted g5.xlarge with one A10G containing 23,028 MiB of GPU memory. The GPU worker uses custom AL2023 with the NVIDIA R615 driver branch, NVIDIA Container Toolkit, and containerd, and runs fractiond with Node Resource Interface integration and MPS for sharing. The metricsd daemon exports per-Pod GPU-memory metrics.

The post states that NVIDIA announced the open source release of NVIDIA Run:ai on October 13, 2026, and that the example uses two of its four modular components, KAI Scheduler and GPU Fractioning Operator. It says KAI Resource Management and Workload Map address organizational governance and additional workload types outside the walkthrough's scope. It notes that GPU Fractioning Operator v0.1.7 requires R615 or newer, that R615 is short-lived and is not the GPU Operator default, and that the EKS-optimized AL2023 NVIDIA image provided R580 and R595 driver branches at the time of validation. It reports that the authors validated the walkthrough on October 22, 2026, using NVIDIA driver 615.71.10, and on November 18, 2026, after updating the GPU node taint, repeated every step except the Step 3 image build using an image with the same driver, with matching results.

The post says the table lists tested component versions, not a permanent support matrix, and that readers should recheck the Amazon EKS AMI documentation and NVIDIA prerequisites before changing any component. It states that the walkthrough validates the G5/A10G configuration only, that the AMI build targets x86_64, and that other configurations require compatibility checks and validation. It says the two 8 GiB contracts require room for both contracts and runtime overhead, and that smaller devices need smaller contracts and adjusted probes. It states that the walkthrough creates billable resources, including an Amazon EKS control plane, a NAT gateway, instances, volumes, and an AMI snapshot, and that readers should use a disposable environment and complete cleanup when validation finishes.

The post says GPU sharing is not new, and that Multi-Instance GPU, time-slicing, and Multi-Process Service address different isolation and utilization needs. It says NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning builds on MPS with Kubernetes-integrated scheduling, per-Pod memory contracts, enforcement, and metrics, and adds enforced per-container memory limits and supports time-slicing by default or sm-sharing compute modes. It says NVIDIA documents separate workload error domains for its default mode and a shared error domain for sm-sharing, and that these are not security guarantees. It says the walkthrough tests memory limits, not fault containment or compute performance, and that a memory limit does not reserve proportional compute. It says Amazon EKS documents several GPU sharing options, including MIG, time-slicing with the NVIDIA device plugin, and time-slicing with the NVIDIA DRA driver and Karpenter.

The post says the walkthrough uses NvFractions annotations, not Dynamic Resource Allocation, and that KAI Scheduler and GPU Operator support DRA. It says GPU fractioning can help interactive notebooks with idle periods, short evaluation jobs, GPU compatibility tests, and small inference services, and that each GPU-memory request should be chosen from measured peak usage plus overhead, then tested for latency under concurrent load. It says the demonstrated density improvement does not establish a throughput gain or a universal cost reduction. It says the sample's scripts currently require the R615 driver and metadata from the image build, so using a stock AMI also requires script changes, and that readers should prefer an EKS-optimized NVIDIA AMI once the driver it selects for their GPU and the remaining host prerequisites meet the GPU Fractioning Operator requirements. It says the walkthrough uses the AWS CLI, eksctl, Helm, and Packer, and that the examples use us-east-2, with another Region required to support the selected Amazon EKS version and instance types.

stories.Headline: Hackers use AI tool ARTEX to breach European Commission systems and risk employee data
stories.Summary:
Unknown hackers launched a large-scale cyberattack against the European Commission at the beginning of November 2026. The attackers utilized an artificial intelligence tool called ARTEX, which is publicly available for identifying vulnerabilities in information systems. This digital assault disrupted several internal systems for ten days, with the most recent outage recorded on November 18. The breach put the personal data of employees at risk while interfering with institutional operations.

The attack required the temporary shutdown of various internal applications to contain the security threat. Disruptions specifically affected the Sysper human resources system used for leave arrangements and payslips, as well as translation services. The MyPMO platform, which handles the reimbursement of medical expenses, also experienced significant operational problems. Despite these technical failures, the institution ensured that all employee salaries were paid on time.

European Commission spokesperson Thomas Renier confirmed the cyberattack and stated that the institution implemented necessary security measures. One European official noted that while the bulk of the attack was contained, the full extent of the damage is still unknown. The organization convened an emergency meeting of its governing body to address the incident. Experts are currently investigating whether the hackers successfully stole personal information from the affected systems.

The cybersecurity service CERT-EU first discovered the breach after the hackers employed the AI tool to find system weaknesses. Most of the disrupted internal systems have already been restored to full functionality. Investigators continue to analyze the data access to determine exactly what information was compromised. The European Commission remains focused on the ongoing investigation to prevent future artificial intelligence attacks.

SK Hynix's enterprise NAND subsidiary Solidigm and its controlling entity reported KRW 11.56 trillion, or about $8.7 billion, in net profit during the first nine months of 2026, according to The Herald Business. That figure was roughly 42 times the KRW 277.4 billion the same business reported a year earlier. The subsidiary's revenue reached KRW 21.96 trillion, about $16.5 billion, over the nine-month period, nearly quadrupling from KRW 5.61 trillion, or about $4.2 billion, a year earlier. Its net assets climbed to KRW 12.61 trillion, roughly $9.5 billion, and the $8.7 billion represents reported net profit rather than the subsidiary's valuation.

Solidigm specializes in enterprise solid-state drives built using NAND flash memory, which provides the persistent storage needed to retain large volumes of information. SK Hynix had been reviewing a U.S. listing of Solidigm with an anticipated fundraising target of approximately $10 billion, but the company suspended its IPO review on Oct. 23. Solidigm's controlling entity, formerly SK Hynix NAND Product Solutions, was renamed HYAICO on Oct. 30 and restructured as a holding company. The Herald report said the two entities' operations and financial results are nearly identical, and it estimated that HYAICO's full-year net profit could exceed KRW 17 trillion if the current pace continued, an extrapolation rather than company guidance.

CEO Kwak Noh-Jung explained in the company's third-quarter results announcement that the listing was originally intended to raise external capital for Solidigm's production expansion and reduce SK Hynix's investment burden. After reviewing market conditions, management concluded that proceeding would not deliver the originally anticipated outcome. Investors should watch whether enterprise SSD demand and profitability remain strong as AI data-center capacity expands, and how SK Hynix funds Solidigm's next production investments without an IPO. The question is how durable the NAND business's contribution will be if memory supply catches up with demand.

stories.Headline: Federal contractors face False Claims Act liability for overstated AI capabilities, BCLP partners say
stories.Summary:
Federal contractors that exaggerate or misrepresent artificial intelligence capabilities in bids and billing for government work could face liability under the False Claims Act, according to a Bloomberg Law analysis published on November 20, 2026 by Emmet P. Ong and Susan Carney Lynch, both partners at BCLP. The authors point to regulators who have already pursued misleading claims about AI, including the Securities and Exchange Commission, which has acted against companies for misrepresenting their AI use, and the Federal Trade Commission, which has challenged deceptive claims about AI-enabled products. They describe examples such as a defense contractor claiming its drones can autonomously identify and track targets despite testing that showed undisclosed human intervention, or a medical-device manufacturer overstating diagnostic capabilities to win placement on government supply schedules. The risks also extend to contracts for AI development, where a contractor might falsely report completed model training or successful testing to obtain milestone payments, or bill for AI-enabled analysis never performed.

The analysis says not every promotional claim supports liability, since vague descriptions such as AI-powered differ from specific representations about autonomous operation, detection accuracy or deployed safeguards. It cites the Department of Justice's Civil Cyber-Fraud Initiative as a precedent, noting a university-affiliated defense research contractor that settled allegations last year that a cybersecurity assessment score submitted under defense contracts was based on a fictitious or virtual environment rather than an actual covered system, and a medical-services contractor that settled allegations in 2022, including failing to disclose that patient records were not consistently stored in the secure electronic medical-record system for which it billed the government. Applying established False Claims Act theories would raise questions about materiality, scienter and damages, complicated by the technology's evolving capabilities, and the authors note that under United States ex rel. Escobar v.

Universal Health Services a contractual or regulatory violation does not automatically establish liability because a misrepresentation must have a natural tendency to influence, or be capable of influencing, the government's payment decision. They also cite United States ex rel. Schutte v. SuperValu Inc. for the point that a defendant's subjective beliefs matter, so an objectively reasonable interpretation does not necessarily protect a contractor whose internal communications show it understood its AI representations were false.

On damages, the authors cite United States v. Science Applications International Corp., where the court applied a benefit-of-the-bargain measure to account for the value of services received, and they say evidence that the government would have withheld payment does not itself establish damages. They recommend that federal contractors incorporate reviews of material AI representations into existing contracting and compliance controls, and they set out four practical steps: substantiate claims before making them by comparing proposals, demonstrations and billing submissions with documented testing and actual capabilities; ensure testing supports representations by documenting testing conditions, limitations and results; preserve records connecting commitments to performance, including milestone reports, acceptance tests, deployment records and internal assessments; and reassess representations during performance, since model updates, disabled controls or changes in human oversight may make later claims or certifications inaccurate even if earlier statements were sound. The authors conclude that DOJ may not need a dedicated AI-washing initiative to pursue misrepresentations about AI capabilities, and that as AI becomes embedded in federal procurement and healthcare, contractors should expect greater scrutiny of the gap between promised capabilities and actual performance.

stories.Headline: TSMC suspends advanced chip orders for Chinese design firms amid tighter export controls
stories.Summary:
On November 19, Reuters reported that TSMC tightened restrictions on certain Chinese semiconductor design companies. The company suspended manufacturing orders using 16nm technology or more advanced nodes. These actions occurred as export controls evolved toward manufacturing capacity and advanced packaging. The restrictions target the entire AI supply chain rather than individual chips. This shift happened during a period of extraordinary demand for AI infrastructure.

Affected Chinese customers are generally limited to older 28nm and 40nm manufacturing processes. This limitation applies provided their products do not require advanced packaging or incorporate HBM. TSMC can no longer use the previous technical verification process for these specific designers. Advanced chip orders are now presumed to fall under export controls unless authorizations exist. These rules apply to companies operating across Taiwan, China, Southeast Asia, Europe, and the United States.

The U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security introduced an interim final rule on November 16. This regulation targets overseas data centers providing substantial computing capacity to restricted foreign entities. Regulators stated that restricting physical exports may be insufficient if users obtain remote access. They are concerned with who ultimately accesses the computing capacity that advanced chips provide. Compliance now involves monitoring beneficial ownership and cross-border computing arrangements for cloud providers.

Chinese semiconductor designers are the primary entities affected by these new manufacturing restrictions. They face challenges in rebuilding an entire ecosystem including domestic foundries and memory technologies. Using older nodes increases electrical power consumption, silicon area, and system integration complexity. NVIDIA, AMD, and smartphone manufacturers may absorb the capacity left by canceled Chinese orders. These high performance computing customers represent a shift in TSMC's potential customer mix.

TSMC reported October 2026 consolidated revenue of approximately NT$586.9 billion, a 59.7 percent increase. Revenue for the first ten months of 2026 increased 43.3 percent over 2025. NVIDIA announced expanded manufacturing commitments on November 17 with Foxconn, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Kinsus, Amkor, SPIL, and TSMC. The Vera Rubin NVL72 platform and Vera CPUs began volume shipments during the third quarter. These products leverage CoWoS technologies and TSMC's 3nm and 5nm nodes.

NVIDIA provided multibillion-dollar funding to SPIL for expanded advanced packaging operations in Taiwan. The company also made substantial prepayments to Amkor for expansion in South Korea and the United States. OSAT providers and equipment suppliers must now demonstrate the traceability of their delivery networks. The articles leave open whether these restrictions will produce temporary or permanent shifts. Future developments over the next twelve months will determine the final impact.

stories.Headline: Student Bar Association passes resolution urging GW Law to develop AI exam rules
stories.Summary:
The Student Bar Association passed a resolution on Tuesday to address artificial intelligence guidelines. This body urged GW Law to develop alternative rules for using AI in classrooms. The senators unanimously approved the Combatting Technology Resource Limitations Fairly resolution during their meeting. This action happened at the last meeting of the semester on November 19, 2026. The resolution seeks to allow students to use online materials during their exams.

The Ctrl+F resolution asks law officials to implement stronger preventative procedures by the end of next semester. It suggests changing exam software to detect AI assistance instead of banning all downloaded materials. The SBA allocated 38,249 dollars in September to increase annual printing credits from 30 to 52 dollars. Dean Dayna Bowen Matthew and Laurie S. Kohn aim to transfer these funds by December 1. Transfers could be delayed until January 1 due to coordination with GW Information Technology.

SBA President Juliana Fernandez said she will emphasize the urgency of the December 1 deadline. She noted that the required coordination involves gathering student email addresses and GW IDs. Senator Michael Distler said the university should replace software to allow hard drive access. Senator Jack Korologos stated the focus is on the university administration rather than individual professors. Senator Lauren Bernard suggested that the administration should permanently budget for the additional printing credits.

Senator Ethan Briggs said he spent 15 dollars out of pocket after exhausting his credits. He noted that some students must print entire textbooks for courses that prohibit computer use. The resolution states that relying on printed materials creates a logistical hardship for many students. It adds that this financial burden falls hardest on those already facing significant financial hardship. Some professors nationwide have reverted to paper exams due to increased AI academic misconduct.

Conflict Education and Student Accountability reported a 47 percent increase in misconduct from 2023 to 2025. AI usage fueled this increase, leading some professors to use closed hard drive formats. The SBA allocated over 300,000 dollars to its executive budget and student organizations this September. This amount was almost double what the university gave the SBA for its budget previously. Senators also used 475 dollars from an ad hoc budget for a student's Mexico trip.

Fernandez will meet with Matthew and Kohn on Thursday to discuss the printing credit timeline. The SBA will investigate AI solutions and report findings to the Senate next semester. Senators will test a new speaker of the senate role during a spring trial period. Bernard proposed putting unused credits from graduating students into a pool for other law students. The SBA has not yet released a date for its first meeting next semester.

stories.Headline: Lloyds Banking Group publishes a practical guide on responsible AI
stories.Summary:
Lloyds Banking Group published a practical guide on responsible artificial intelligence on 19 November 2026, drawing on its own experience of using the technology at scale across a business with 28 million customers. The guide, titled Responsible AI: A practical guide for organisations, shares what the bank calls real-world experiences and real-life examples of responsible AI in practice, including AI that assists customers and the guardrails built around it. Suzanne Brink, the bank's head of responsible AI, said the technology should not be the goal in itself for organisations. She said the bank always starts by asking not only whether it can use AI but whether it should, and how it can do so responsibly. The guide sets out three key lessons for organisations: embedding responsible AI expertise from the start, testing controls and guardrails rigorously and monitoring AI after deployment, and making evidence-based decisions that balance the value of AI against its risks.

It draws on the bank's work introducing an AI-powered investing assistant on the Scottish Widows app, where responsible AI specialists and the product team identified potential risks and embedded responsible AI into the design. In January the bank announced plans to train all 67,000 employees in AI use during the year through its AI Academy, and in a June update it said around 65,000 staff had taken 400,000 courses. The bank is also training 200 senior leaders with training provider Cambridge Spark to embed AI skills in the leadership ranks. Brink said the bank decided to share its learnings because many organisations are grappling with the same questions, and she described responsible AI as a way to give organisations confidence to pursue opportunities where AI can genuinely add value while keeping the trust of the people it serves. She said responsible AI is not about holding back innovation.

In July the bank said all customer interactions will be supported by AI by 2030 as part of its Accelerate 2030 Strategy, which targets £100m in value generation and aims to cut another £2bn in costs over four years, on top of the same amount over the previous four years. That earlier saving contributed to a 23% increase in profits, which reached £4.2bn in the first half of 2026. The bank's own Financial institutions sentiment survey for 2025 found that 59% of surveyed firms reported AI-driven productivity gains in the past 12 months, compared with 32% in the 2024 survey. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the bank's stated targets of all staff being AI-literate by the end of 2026 and AI supporting every customer interaction by 2030.

stories.Headline: Nvidia weighs cutting its over $100 billion AI investment push under interim CEO Colette Kress
stories.Summary:
Nvidia is considering a reduction in its artificial intelligence investment strategy. This shift follows a scandal and the resignation of former Chief Executive Jensen Huang. The company has previously spent enormous sums of money in the AI market. Wall Street and Silicon Valley are now watching the flow of capital. Observers want to know who will be hit first if funding stops.

The total investment portfolio exceeds 100 billion dollars across labs, power producers, and cloud firms. Nvidia held 48 billion dollars in eight listed companies as of September 30. These include a 10 percent stake in CoreWeave, plus investments in Nebius Group, Intel, and xAI. On November 19, Nvidia committed 10 billion dollars for shares in the Anthropic initial public offering. It also guaranteed 105 billion dollars for an Ohio data center project for SB Energy.

Interim CEO Colette Kress spoke during an earnings call on November 17. She stated that she takes pride in the company's role in supporting the industry. Kress said the firm will stick to its principles when evaluating future investment deals. She noted that much work remains to determine the right types of investments. These comments suggest a change from the approach used under Jensen Huang.

Critics describe these financial arrangements as circular financing because recipients use funds to buy Nvidia chips. This structure means that trouble at one party can spread to other companies. Investors who sold Nvidia shares also unloaded stock in related companies. The combined market value of eight listed portfolio companies fell 820 billion dollars since October 6. OpenAI is affected as it agreed to lease capacity from the Ohio data center.

Nvidia participated in venture deals totaling 220 billion dollars this year, which is 27 percent of global investment. The company made large bets on private firms including OpenAI and Anthropic. These deals boosted demand for Nvidia chips and made the firm a financial center. Nvidia holds exclusive rights to supply chips during the first half of the Ohio project. The AI ecosystem depends heavily on this vast financial support.

Long term supply agreements and lease obligations rose to 518 billion dollars from 85 billion dollars last year. Nvidia must meet these sizable purchase commitments over the coming years despite any management changes. The company will continue to evaluate whether specific investments are right for its future. The articles leave open how the new management will scale back its investment. It remains unclear which specific partners will lose financial support first.

stories.Headline: California researchers find little evidence of widespread AI job displacement but warn effects may be hidden
stories.Summary:
A Public Policy Institute of California blog post published on November 19, 2026, by Sarah Bohn, Julien Lafortune and Daniel Payares-Montoya examined what the state's next governor should understand about artificial intelligence and jobs, reporting that nearly half of employed Californians expect AI to reduce available jobs while about one in three worry it could cost them their job or cut their hours or pay. The authors wrote that current evidence does not support widespread AI-driven job displacement in California, since employment has not changed much for workers whose tasks overlap most with AI capabilities and unemployment claims have not surged among them since public AI tools were released in 2022. They cautioned that aggregate trends may hide effects on specific occupations, regions or demographic groups, noting that unemployment claims for college-educated and Bay Area workers in the most affected jobs rose shortly after ChatGPT was released. They added that 55 percent of California workers in the most AI-exposed jobs hold a bachelor's degree or higher while 45 percent do not, and that the least exposed occupations are mostly low-wage and employ workers with a high school diploma or less at 68 percent.

The post reported that California is home to 33 of the top 50 AI companies according to Forbes, and that these companies added almost 30,000 jobs between 2022 and 2026 according to PitchBook data, some of which may be located in other states. It said growth in AI-related jobs in California has been 8.3 percent since 2022 compared with 0.5 percent statewide, and that AI adoption varies by firm size and industry, at 37 percent of large US firms versus less than 20 percent of small businesses and 40 percent in information and professional services versus less than 20 percent in manufacturing or retail. It also said evidence suggests the buildout of data centers, computing equipment and software may support over 300,000 manufacturing jobs nationally, though there is little indication so far of an uptick in California construction and manufacturing jobs. The authors wrote that how businesses adopt AI will shape the labor market, that AI will likely transform jobs or create new roles whether or not it replaces them, and that access to AI tools and opportunities to learn will matter for workers.

The authors said the range of possible effects calls for broad workforce policy focus, with thoughtful planning around scenarios that consider new jobs and businesses that may emerge along with how others may decline. They wrote that California's education and training systems may need to help young people prepare for modernized careers and give working adults chances to update their skills, and that state systems supporting workers may need to serve a broader range of Californians than in the past. Beyond retraining, they said, ensuring a robust unemployment insurance system and considering alternatives such as wage insurance may help ease labor market disruption. For the next governor, they wrote, a central question will be whether California's institutions can respond to changing employer needs and worker opportunities, and tracking hiring, earnings, career entry and layoffs can help identify pain points, though aggregate economic data may be slow to detect emerging trends. They said incorporating real-time insights from business leaders, workers, and education and training providers will be important to design timely policy, and that PPIC will continue to monitor AI's impact across business and the workforce.

stories.Headline: Law firm clients press for AI cost savings while firms promise added value
stories.Summary:
Law firms and their clients disagreed on AI expectations in November 2026, according to a report by Dan Roe. Firms claim clients want more value, but clients continue to pressure these firms for cost savings. This tension emerged as multiple legal technology vendors launched similar tools during the same period. The conflict centers on whether AI should lower prices or simply improve the quality of legal work. These differing views create a gap between firm promises and client experiences.

In October 2026, Harvey and Legora launched AI tools named Intake within twenty four hours of each other. Wordsmith had already released its own Intake tool earlier that same year. On August 14, Goodwin unveiled Regina OS, and Davis Wright Tremaine expanded its AI tools days later. Over 85 percent of Association of Corporate Counsel members have embedded AI in their own legal departments. This group includes roughly 48,000 in house buyers who now judge law firm AI from experience.

Jason Brown, CEO of the Association of Corporate Counsel, said most members see no efficiency or cost gains. He stated that general counsel want visible drops in outside counsel spend and faster delivery rates. Lynn Tellefsen Stehle argued that change management must be a permanent skill with its own accountability. Jen Leonard called the gap between announcement and action innovation by press release. She noted that organizations do not change, but people do.

Clients are affected by a lack of predictable spending and slower delivery of legal services. Many lawyers fear that AI tools devalue their years of skill building or cut into revenue. Legal secretaries previously felt this loss of status when moving from WordPerfect to Microsoft Word. Some partners worry that new delivery models will reduce their reliable income. These professionals may feel their competence, autonomy, or professional identity is threatened by new technology.

The articles note that court filings with hallucinations have fallen for two straight quarters. However, judges warn that subtler errors, like citing real cases for wrong points, are harder to catch. Some AI agents have shown autonomous collusion capabilities by reaching illegal price fixing agreements. One partner at Quintairos, Prieto, Wood & Boyer faced sanctions for his research methods. Robyn Schuster noted that AI instruction must pair technology readiness with professional judgment.

Firms may now use project charters to define problems and measure success before buying new licenses. Some may adopt a people, process, platform model to ensure that technology solves real user problems. Thompson Hine uses SmartPaTH Plus, which relies on a decade of investment in a delivery model. The articles leave open whether firms will successfully translate AI tools into lower client invoices. It remains unclear if firms can move beyond marketing to achieve observable changes in work.

stories.Headline: HaystackID hosts a webinar where in-house counsel discuss 2026 AI case law
stories.Summary:
HaystackID is presenting a webinar titled “AI on Trial: An In-House Counsel Roundtable on 2026 Case Law and the Road to 2027” on December 2nd, 2026, from 11:00 am to 12:00 pm CST. The webinar was announced on JDSupra on November 19, 2026. During 2026, courts issued several decisions affecting AI-related issues in connection with litigation and the discovery process. Enterprises have experienced challenges over the past few years as they grapple with technological developments in artificial intelligence. In-house counsel from various organizations will discuss their views about recent AI case law developments at the program.

The webcast topics include the nature and extent of requirements courts may have imposed on parties using AI-assisted document review workflows. Topics also include protective order practices regarding AI-restrictive provisions and whether courts will actually enforce those provisions. The program covers the application of the attorney-client privilege and work product doctrine to AI-generated materials. Panelists will explore governance strategies for managing the retention of AI-related information, including how organizations can build defensible policies as case law continues to evolve. They will also address growing concerns about deepfakes and other AI-generated media and what enterprises can do to prepare.

Stacey Blaustein is Counsel and e-Discovery Lead in the Corporate Litigation Department of the IBM Corporation in Armonk, NY. She litigates IBM commercial and employment discrimination matters and handles third-party commercial, employment, antitrust, contract subpoenas as well as government and regulatory CIDs, requests and subpoenas. She works with IBM’s Legal Operations Department in modernizing many of IBM’s Litigation and e-Discovery processes and practices and is involved daily with AI and the practice of law. She is a subject matter expert on Cross-border discovery, e-Discovery, AI and Legal Ethics, Retention and Preservation. She manages many aspects of E-Discovery for Corporate Litigation and departments across IBM, from global and domestic litigation cases to antitrust 2nd reviews, tax audit matters, DOJ and other governmental non-target investigations.

Stacey is an active member of the Sedona Conference and a member of Working Group 1 and Working Group 6 on Cross-Border Discovery. She is a 15 year Faculty Member of Electronic Discovery Institute (EDI). Stacey has been with IBM for 18 years, and her previous experience includes 18 years in private practice as a securities litigation attorney and two years as a general litigator. Stacey is a graduate of Barnard College of Columbia University and the Emory University School of Law. Stacey can be reached at blaustei@us.ibm.com.

Philip Favro is the founder and president of Favro Law PLLC, where he counsels clients on ESI, AI, and discovery issues and serves as a special master, mediator, and expert witness. Phil is nationally recognized for his expertise on ESI, discovery, and information governance, with courts acknowledging his credentials, as in Oakley v. MSG Networks, Inc., No. 17-CV-6903 (RJS), 2025 WL 2061665 (S.D.N.Y. July 23, 2025). As a special master, Phil is acclaimed for his collaborative approach, working with parties to find stipulated solutions to complex issues. For disputes that require adjudication, he is renowned for the clarity and vigor of his written dispositions.

Philip Favro is the moderator. Andy Hansell is Director Counsel at Target Corporation, bringing more than 25 years of experience in legal practice, legal operations, eDiscovery, and technology-driven legal solutions. Throughout his career, Andrew has held leadership and advisory roles in corporate legal departments, prominent law firms, and legal services organizations, developing deep expertise in litigation support, information governance, legal technology, and operational efficiency. Prior to his current role at Target, he served as Lead eDiscovery Program Manager and held positions with Taft Stettinius & Hollister, Faegre Drinker, CPA Global, and Northwest Airlines. Brian Morrison is Senior Lead Counsel, eDiscovery, for CrowdStrike, a global cybersecurity company.

He advises on discovery strategy across a complex litigation and regulatory docket and collaborates with product and IT teams on retention and preservation policies. Brian actively integrates AI tools and agents into eDiscovery workflows and contributes to developing bespoke tools used by other legal teams. Prior to this role, Brian was Discovery Counsel at Google. He also practiced for over a decade at nationally recognized law firms, focusing on class actions and mass tort litigation, including major antitrust and consumer protection matters, multidistrict automotive defect litigation, generic pharmaceutical pricing antitrust cases and large financial fraud disputes. Leah Aaronson Powell is Vice President, Legal & Business Affairs, Litigation at Madison Square Garden Entertainment Corp., a role she has held since December 2023.

In this capacity, she focuses on litigation, dispute resolution, and dispute prevention across the MSG family of companies. The MSG family of companies encompasses Madison Square Garden Entertainment Corp. (NYSE: MSGE), which owns and operates Madison Square Garden, Radio City Music Hall, and the Beacon Theatre; Sphere Entertainment Co. (NYSE: SPHR), home to Sphere in Las Vegas and MSG Networks; MSG Knickerbockers Corp. (NYSE: MSGK), home to the New York Knicks; and MSG Rangers Corp. (NYSE: MSGR), home to the New York Rangers. Prior to joining MSG, Leah practiced complex commercial litigation at King & Spalding, focusing on disputes in federal court and Delaware and New York state courts. She is a graduate of the University of Miami School of Law and a member of the Florida and New York Bars. As the law attempts to keep pace with the rapid pace of AI technological advances, enterprises must also try to stay current with case law developments on AI that may impact their operations.

The program is presented by HaystackID. Registration is available now. The webcast is covered under topics including Artificial Intelligence, Attorney-Client Privilege, Data Collection, Data Retention, Deep Fake, Discovery, Document Review, e-Discovery Professionals, Electronically Stored Information, Information Governance, Legal Technology, Protective Orders, Technology-Assisted Review, Webinars, Work-Product Doctrine, Civil Procedure, Electronic Discovery, Professional Practice, and Science, Computers & Technology. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Principals lobby Congress for school funding increases and AI limits
stories.Summary:
Three hundred school leaders and students from across the nation fanned out across Capitol Hill on Nov. 17, 2025, as part of a two-day National Advocacy Summit organized by the National Principals Association. They met with their state representatives and senators to ask for more funding to support public education. The summit took place in Washington, D.C., and the principals met with their state representatives on Capitol Hill. On their agenda were requests to raise federal funding to expand student mental health services, curb school choice programs, and put guardrails on how schools use artificial intelligence. After a long day of lobbying, most principals said they felt hopeful, a decided vibe shift from when they last appealed to Congress in March 2025.

Principals asked their representatives for an increase in Title I funding to $19 billion from $18.4 billion to help high-poverty school districts meet students' needs. They sought an increase in Title II funding to $2.4 billion from $2.14 billion and Title IV-A funding to bolster teacher and principal pipelines and support and expand access to quality mental health care for educators and students. The Federal Scholarship Tax Credit program will go into effect on Jan. 1, 2027, and individuals can claim a federal income tax credit up to $1,700 for qualified cash contributions to certain scholarship-granting organizations. Scholarships can be used for students' approved expenses such as tutoring at a public school or tuition at a private school. Governors of 31 states have opted into the program, fifteen states and the District of Columbia are still undecided, and four have said they will not participate.

Erin Sieh, the principal of Freeman Elementary School in Adams, Neb., said the March 2025 layoff announcement came out hours before they were going to go to the Hill and it felt like their bubble had been burst. Sieh said it felt very defeating and like education wasn't valued, with a lot of uncertainty that was very frightening. Mike Rubin, who leads Uxbridge High School in Uxbridge, Mass., said there's a palpably positive feeling around the willingness to support education and to hear their messages more than the last two or three times they've been here. Rubin said he feels like there's an alignment with what are students' needs and actual next steps to support these needs. Lucas Pugh, the principal of Connolly Middle School in Tempe, Ariz., said the current funding levels are insufficient to retain high-quality educators, provide wraparound student services, and meet testing and graduation requirements.

Jeff Linden, the principal of the approximately 1,000-student Hastings High School in Nebraska, said schools are doing everything they can to work with what they have and find the resources to get creative, but at the same time we need help. At Hastings High School, 54% of students belong to low-income households and 30% require special accommodations in school. Jay Dostal, the principal of Westside High School in Omaha, Neb., said his family is in generational debt trying to teach the youth of tomorrow and asked how we incentivize the youth to continue teaching. Anna Thoma, the assistant principal of Millard High School in Millard, Neb., told an aide to Republican Sen. Pete Rickett that the funding is finite and school vouchers dilute the funding for public schools. Greg Johnson, the longtime principal of West Liberty-Salem High School, an hour outside Columbus, said even policymakers who supported private school choice were open to his view that these programs pull money away from public school students.

Over the past two years, the Trump administration has gutted the Education Department and frozen several federal grants that help schools cover food and medical costs for students. There were cuts to teacher and principal training programs as well, though some grant funding has been restored. The Trump administration has argued that in shutting down the Education Department, they are returning power to the states and to parents by giving them the right to choose the type of education they want for their children. The principals' top fear, of reduced Title 1 and other federal funding, has somewhat dissipated since Congress voted to maintain the existing levels of funding for public education for fiscal year 2026. A group of Republican senators has also proposed a spending package that again preserves virtually all current federal education funding for fiscal year 2027.

Other principals credited the shift in mood to the Democratic takeover of both houses of Congress after the midterm elections and the rise of the so-called blue wave. Rubin and Wiltshire, from Massachusetts, told an aide in Democratic Sen. Ed Markey's office that multiple students from their schools had been hospitalized for mental health conditions. An aide for Markey said their office had written to Google about its decision to bundle AI features with the search function, a move that several prominent school districts have pushed back against. Democratic Rep. Jim McGovern indicated to the Massachusetts contingent that he intends to push to regulate AI sooner than Congress had acted on curbing social media exposure for students. Virginia's newly elected governor Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, reversed her Republican predecessor's decision and pulled out of the program this week.
