stories.Headline: Global lenders reduce AI funding amid bubble concerns
stories.Summary:
Global lenders are pulling back from bankrolling the artificial intelligence boom due to growing fears of a bubble. Banks are now scrutinizing data center loans more closely to avoid holding bad debt. Some lenders are selling loans and passing risks to insurers to mitigate financial losses. This shift could hit Korea hard because its chip exports depend on AI investment. These changes are occurring as of November 2026.

Funding costs for data center asset-backed securities rose over 1 percentage point this year per Morgan Stanley. Spreads on single-A-rated securities averaged 2.57 percentage points over Treasurys recently, up from 1.95 percentage points. U.S. issuance reached 21.9 billion dollars by November 6, but fell 19.9 percent in three months. Hyperscalers issued 296 billion dollars in bonds, exceeding the 250 billion dollar Goldman Sachs forecast. Goldman Sachs raised its next year forecast to 440 billion dollars from 420 billion dollars.

Chris Poggi of Ropes & Gray said there was unbridled enthusiasm to provide debt to neoclouds. He noted that debt investors have full books and are assessing their current extensions. Marija Veitmane of State Street Markets said big tech earnings failed to impress investors. The Bank of Korea warned that AI-driven shocks could spread with greater intensity than before. This bank also warned about heavy debt carried by AI cloud service providers.

Institutional investors are reducing exposure to risky assets, including semiconductor stocks and shares in Korea and Taiwan. State Street reported its Risk Appetite Index stood at minus 0.09 in October. Bank of America noted spreads on hyperscalers' 10-year bonds widened by about 0.5 percentage points. This rise is two and a half times the 0.2 percentage point rise for industrial companies. Korean financial institutions are affected as they expanded data center and GPU secured loans.

The Bank of England modeled a shock where U.S. stocks fall 45 percent over six quarters. Such a shock could lower Britain's GDP by 2.2 percentage points, the central bank estimated. Dutch lender ING put 500 million dollars in data center loans up for sale. Barclays bought credit insurance, and HSBC looked into doing the same for infrastructure loans. These deals typically transfer 20 to 50 percent of loan risk to insurers.

More than 70 insurers now offer credit insurance for project finance, up from a few. Higher interest burdens may make it hard for indebted companies to borrow or roll over debt. Slower data center construction could delay revenue and create a vicious cycle of financial decline. The Bank of Korea noted circular deals make it harder to gauge real demand and risk. The articles leave open if the AI investment web will hold without Jensen Huang.

Articles.Title: AI bubble fears push lenders that bankrolled boom to pull back

stories.Headline: AI assistants disrupt online discovery and force businesses to adapt to agent-driven interactions
stories.Summary:
AI assistants are disrupting traditional online discovery and reshaping how users interact with the internet as of November 19, 2026. These agents are evolving to perform complex actions like booking flights, comparing insurance, and negotiating purchases on behalf of their users. This shift allows people to bypass conventional websites, search engines, and social platforms for product recommendations and decision making. Consequently, startups and businesses that rely on search engine optimization and curated feeds are facing a new battle for visibility.

The transition requires businesses to adapt to an agent-driven internet where AI agents evaluate options and provide personalized recommendations. OpenAI has introduced Businesses in ChatGPT for eligible US companies to claim profiles and create Business Agents that interact directly with customers. Additionally, OpenAI has developed Dots, which are always-on AI agents that connect to thousands of applications to learn user preferences. In India, Sarvam AI launched Token Factory, an inference platform providing developers access to models like Sarvam 105B, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, and Gemma.

Kushal Bhagia, a founding partner at All In Capital, stated that platforms focused on helping users discover information could face significant pressure. He believes that traditional discovery mechanisms and top-of-funnel platforms might become casualties as AI retrieves and summarizes information directly. Anuj Gupta, the founder and CEO of KiteFishAI, sees new opportunities emerging in digital identities, AI-driven communities, and agent-to-agent commerce. These leaders suggest that companies will soon have to compete for the attention of both human users and AI agents.

Research from WARC and Nature Human Behaviour in August and September 2026 shows that users are forming emotional attachments to chatbots for companionship. This suggests that AI assistants are occupying social spaces previously held by personal relationships and traditional social networks. While social media may shift toward entertainment, AI agents are becoming the primary personalized interfaces for advice and conversation. Future revenue for businesses may depend on transaction fees and recommendations conducted through these autonomous AI agents.

Articles.Title: AI assistants challenge online discovery, reshape user interactions

stories.Headline: Datavault AI founder Bradley sues over CEO removal and alleged concealment of $90m to $100m funding offer
stories.Summary:
Datavault AI's share price has fallen 99.9% over the past five years, and the stock now trades at a price to sales ratio of about 0.4x, according to Simply Wall St. The article, published on 20 November 2026, ties part of that low multiple to a boardroom dispute involving founder Nathaniel Bradley. Bradley has sued over his removal as CEO and over the alleged concealment of a proposed funding package worth between US$90m and US$100m. The piece weighs whether the remaining market value is justified by the sales the company currently generates. The 0.4x ratio sits far below the wider semiconductor group at roughly 5.3x and below similar peers at about 0.9x, the article states. It says the gap suggests the market attaches a modest value to each dollar of Datavault AI's sales compared with both the sector and closer comparables.

On the publication's preferred valuation model, which blends growth, profitability, scale and risk into a tailored fair multiple, the shares screen as undervalued on this metric. The article adds that part of the low multiple may reflect governance and funding concerns rather than only the revenue base. The article attributes the lawsuit to Bradley, the founder, and says it concerns his removal as CEO and the alleged concealment of the funding offer. It reports that a community narrative on Simply Wall St, written by an investor posting as DrFountain, argues the current market value overlooks key pieces of the company's commercial progress. That narrative says a clear disconnect emerges when Datavault AI is compared with other publicly traded AI and data infrastructure companies, many of which trade at significantly higher market capitalizations.

The article presents this as one of the top community narratives, which puts the company at 100% undervalued. The article notes that Datavault AI is still loss making on free cash flow, which is why it says revenue is the clearest anchor for the share price. It also points readers to a separate lens comparing the current price with where professional models think the business could be in a few years. Beyond that, the piece does not say what happens next in the lawsuit or the funding dispute.

stories.Headline: EU AI Act amendment delays high-risk rules but adds new prohibitions and enforcement powers
stories.Summary:
The Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, entered into force on 27 July 2026 and amends the AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, on a number of points. It is widely described as a postponement, and in one important respect it is, because the obligations for high-risk AI systems will now apply later than originally planned. That description is incomplete, however, because much of the AI Act already applies and the Omnibus also introduces new prohibitions and stronger enforcement tools. The note by Logan & Partners sets out the main changes and what they mean in practice for companies that develop, procure or use AI systems in the European Union. The AI Act is not a future regime, since its first provisions have applied since 2 February 2025.

Since 2 February 2025 the practices prohibited under Article 5 have been unlawful, including manipulative or deceptive techniques, social scoring, untargeted scraping of facial images, and emotion recognition in the workplace and in education, subject to limited exceptions. Infringements may lead to fines of up to EUR 35 million or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. Providers of general-purpose AI models have been subject to Chapter V since 2 August 2025 and must maintain technical documentation, put in place a copyright policy and publish a summary of the content used for training. The Commission's power to fine these providers has applied since 2 August 2026, and the transparency obligations in Article 50 have also applied since that date. Users must be informed when they interact with an AI system, synthetic content must be marked in a machine-readable format, and deepfakes must be disclosed.

Under new Article 111(4), providers of generative AI systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 have until 2 December 2026 to comply with the marking obligation in Article 50(2). The requirements and obligations in Sections 1 to 3 of Chapter III will apply from 2 December 2027 to the systems listed in Annex III, which covers areas such as recruitment and workforce management, creditworthiness assessment, risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance, education, biometrics, critical infrastructure, law enforcement, migration and the administration of justice. They apply from 2 August 2028 to AI systems that are safety components of products, or are themselves products, covered by the EU legislation listed in Annex I, such as medical devices, toys and lifts. The recitals explain that the postponement responds to the late availability of harmonised standards and to delays in setting up national authorities, and the legislator chose fixed dates. The Omnibus does not link application to the publication of standards, so companies should not plan on the assumption of a further extension.

The transitional rule in Article 111(2) has also been adjusted, so high-risk systems placed on the market or put into service before the relevant application date fall within the AI Act only if their design is significantly changed after that date. According to the recitals, this assessment is made per type and model, and systems intended for use by public authorities must in any event comply by 2 August 2030. The Omnibus adds two prohibitions to Article 5, which apply from 2 December 2026, the first covering AI systems that generate or manipulate realistic intimate images or sexually explicit content of an identifiable person without that person's explicit consent and the second covering AI-generated child sexual abuse material. Under new Article 5(1a), a provider may be caught even where its system was not designed for this purpose, where such output is a reasonably foreseeable outcome that can be reproduced without significant technical modification and the system lacks adequate safeguards to prevent it. A deployer, by contrast, is caught only where it uses the system for the purpose of generating such material, so providers of general-purpose image and video generation tools should review their technical safeguards.

Article 25 now specifies the information, technical access and assistance that an initial provider must give to the party that becomes the provider of a high-risk system, and it also requires written agreements with suppliers of AI models, tools and components. A breach of these obligations may now be fined up to EUR 15 million or 3% of turnover under new Article 99(4)(da). At EU level, the AI Office has obtained exclusive competence over certain AI systems, including systems based on a general-purpose AI model where the model and the system are developed by the same provider, and AI systems that constitute or are integrated into very large online platforms or search engines, with some exceptions. The AI Office now has inspection powers and may impose periodic penalty payments. Article 4 on AI literacy now requires providers and deployers to take measures to support the AI literacy of their staff, and it states expressly that no specific level of literacy has to be guaranteed.

SMEs and the new category of small mid-cap enterprises may provide technical documentation in a simplified form and apply a quality management system proportionate to their size, and where they are fined, the lower of the fixed amount and the percentage of turnover applies. New Article 4a allows providers of high-risk systems to process special categories of personal data where this is strictly necessary to detect and correct bias, subject to specific safeguards, and in exceptional cases the same possibility extends to deployers of high-risk systems and to providers and deployers of other AI systems and models. The Commission has published draft guidelines on classification under Article 6, the consultation closed in July 2026 and, at the time of writing, the final guidelines have not been adopted. Article 6(3) allows certain Annex III systems to be treated as not high-risk, for example where they perform only a narrow procedural or preparatory task, but this exception never applies to systems that perform profiling. Providers relying on it must document their assessment before placing the system on the market and register the system.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Ukrainian citizens sue Texas Instruments, Intel and AMD over chips in Russian weapons
stories.Summary:
Five Ukrainian citizens sued Texas Instruments, Intel, AMD and Mouser Electronics in December 2025 in Dallas County state court. They claim the companies' components wound up guiding Russian weapons used against Ukrainian civilians. The case has already been dismissed once, revived once, and fought over twice in federal court. Plaintiffs seek more than $1 million each in damages. Lawyers on both sides include some of the biggest names in American trial law.

The complaints cite five missile and drone strikes between 2023 and 2025 that killed or wounded dozens of people in Ukrainian cities. The original filing date was December 11, 2025, in Dallas County District Court. The case moved to the US District Court for the Northern District of Texas. The lead case is Liudmyla Dmytrivina v. Texas Instruments.

The filings state that the war makes it impossible to bring the cases before Ukrainian courts. The plaintiffs are five named Ukrainian citizens representing dozens of civilians hurt or killed in specific attacks. Lead counsel are Mikal Watts and Charla Aldous, with supporting firm BakerHostetler, including attorneys Robert Julian, Dustin Dow and Lauren Attard. Watts said the plaintiffs no longer opposed the case being handled in federal court. Watts called the US companies "merchants of death" making a "farce" of US sanctions law.

Mouser, based in Mansfield, Texas, was acquired by Berkshire in 2007 when it bought Mouser's parent company TTI Inc. Texas Instruments is represented by attorney Tom Melsheimer in dismissal hearings. Melsheimer argued that Texans made a deal with the Ukrainian people that if they gave up their nuclear weapons, the US would protect them. TI has denied wrongdoing throughout the litigation and argues the claims rest on speculation rather than direct proof. Intel's leadership, including CEO Lip-Bu Tan, has publicly denied knowledge of misuse, while AMD echoes commitments to ethical supply chains.

Both companies argue liability should fall on illegal resellers, not manufacturers. The lawsuits detail a network of third-party resellers and shell companies that facilitated the transfer of restricted chips to Russian entities. One attack allegedly involved Iranian-made drones with components associated with Intel and AMD. Others involved Russian-made KH-101 cruise missiles and Iskander ballistic missiles. The companies counter that thousands of resellers worldwide handle their products, making it nearly impossible to track every final buyer.

Plaintiffs' lawyers claimed they learned that TI, Intel and AMD were told by the federal government that their practices did not follow US rules. Defendants filed removal motions within hours of being sued in December 2025. At a hearing in February 2026, lawyers for the plaintiffs told the judge they would not oppose having the case tried in his federal courtroom. US District Judge Sidney Fitzwater is overseeing the entire litigation, and his rulings on dismissal motions have shaped the case. The judge gave plaintiffs a chance to fix the problems in their complaint rather than ending the case.

stories.Headline: SEBI Explores India-Made AI Model for Stock Market Regulation, Says Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey
stories.Summary:
The Securities and Exchange Board of India is exploring the development of an India-made artificial intelligence model for the securities market, Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said on Friday, November 20, 2026. Speaking at the CII DFS Financing Summit in Mumbai, Pandey said a committee was examining whether a domestically governed SEBI AI model could be developed jointly with market participants. The proposed system is intended to make AI-based regulatory tools more affordable, secure and accessible, particularly for smaller regulated entities. The regulator is considering whether the model could be developed as part of India's Digital Public Infrastructure.

The committee is assessing the costs, opportunities and risks involved, along with the safeguards required before such a system can be introduced, and Pandey said the proposal remains at an initial stage with consultations underway. No development or implementation timeline has been announced, and SEBI has not specified how such a system would be operated or which entities would be involved. The committee is also looking at the risks associated with AI, including the possibility of systems producing incorrect or misleading information, often referred to as AI hallucinations. SEBI has not announced whether the proposed model would be used for surveillance, compliance reporting, risk assessment or other specific regulatory functions, as these details would depend on the outcome of the feasibility assessment.

Pandey said appropriate safeguards would be necessary while examining the opportunities offered by the technology. The discussions come as SEBI expands the use of technology in market supervision and compliance monitoring, and the regulator has already introduced AI-based tools to monitor advertisements issued by market intermediaries and examine compliance reports. The latest comments follow an earlier announcement in October, when Pandey said the regulator was considering a domestically governed AI model for the securities market and outlined plans to strengthen AI risk management through international regulatory cooperation. SEBI is working on implementing the International Organization of Securities Commissions' supervisory toolkit for artificial intelligence, which focuses on improving oversight of AI systems and managing the risks arising from their use in financial markets.

SEBI has separately been examining the responsible use of AI and machine learning by regulated entities, and its June 2025 consultation paper proposed principles covering accountability, governance and oversight of AI applications in the securities market. The proposed domestic model would be a separate initiative and remains under consideration. For now, the committee's assessment will determine whether the model can be developed collaboratively and what safeguards would be needed. SEBI has not announced a formal rollout plan or a date for completing the exercise.

Articles.Title: SEBI Explores India-Made AI Model for Stock Market Regulation, Says Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey

stories.Headline: Incoming Democratic Congress plans stricter AI oversight and safety regulations
stories.Summary:
The artificial intelligence industry is preparing for more aggressive oversight as a Democratic-controlled Congress takes power on November 20, 2026. These incoming lawmakers intend to use their control over congressional committees to investigate tech companies and demand that executives testify in hearings. The new majority plans to introduce various bills that establish safety guidelines for capable models, protect the labor force, and address child safety. These legislative efforts require federal safety requirements for advanced developers and the mandatory reporting of safety breaches. Some proposed rules would force companies to maintain the ability to shut down AI systems if they spiral out of human control.

This shift follows two years of minimal regulation under a Republican-led Congress and President Donald Trump, who believes the industry can self-police. Trump has prioritized winning the AI race against China and has favored voluntary commitments over federal restrictions. Representative Don Beyer of Virginia stated that the government cannot wait for a major catastrophe before implementing meaningful safeguards. Representative Nathaniel Moran of Texas argued that the United States does not have to choose between innovation and safety. Senators Maria Cantwell of Washington and Mike Rounds of South Dakota recently urged National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton to take immediate action against cyberattacks.

They claimed that current defenses are not keeping pace with the ability of AI to exploit software weaknesses. The push for regulation comes as voters express negative attitudes regarding how data centers impact electricity prices and jobs. Recent tech outages at Apple, JPMorgan Chase, and Microsoft have further highlighted the vulnerabilities of interconnected digital infrastructure. While these outages were not linked to cyberattacks, they have spurred calls for a more proactive federal role in protecting financial institutions. Lawmakers are now forming bipartisan caucuses to create legislation that balances industry growth with necessary risk mitigation.

Articles.Title: AI industry braces for tougher oversight under incoming Democratic Congress - WBFF

stories.Headline: Akamai turns away AI infrastructure deals as power limits constrain capacity
stories.Summary:
Akamai Technologies is turning away some potential AI infrastructure business because of limited power availability, Chief Financial Officer Ed McGowan said at an event hosted by RBC software analyst Rishi Jaluria, MarketBeat reported on Saturday, November 21, 2026. The company has signed $14 billion in large deals this year, McGowan said. He said its pipeline is the largest he has seen in its history. Demand comes from enterprises, foundation-model developers, startups and other AI companies. Power constraints make it difficult to take on additional large projects requiring capacity in 2027.

McGowan said power is the most important and scarcest element today, and that availability should improve in the second half of 2028 and into 2029. Akamai closed a $2.5 billion offering the prior week and is funded for its committed deals without returning to debt markets through 2028, Jaluria said, and McGowan confirmed that. McGowan said Akamai has investment-grade ratings from Fitch and Moody's, while S&P downgraded the company. He attributed the difference to the agencies' assumptions about future leverage and growth. He said Akamai expects to deleverage over the next two years as it pays down debt and expands EBITDA margins.

McGowan declined to set a firm date for a sustainable return to positive free cash flow, saying faster cloud infrastructure growth would require more capital spending before revenue arrives. Depending on the pace of growth, he said, the company could reach that point in 2028 or later. He said three large customer projects expected to start in the fourth quarter are now generating revenue. Data center construction, customer-specific fit-outs and equipment issues can affect the precise date revenue begins, he said, calling it spreadsheet risk. Asked about an approximately 13% internal rate of return calculation for a large infrastructure contract, McGowan said Akamai included data center fit-out and network connection costs, as well as spare capacity, in its analysis.

McGowan said those costs could be shared as other customers are added to the same facilities. He said the calculation assumed revenue only for the contract's duration, although the company may be able to continue using the equipment afterward. He described the return as a floor, noting that a customer committing to a deal of that size receives Akamai's best pricing. McGowan said Akamai sees substantial demand for CPUs alongside GPUs in AI applications and will supply the hardware customers need. He pointed to potential uses for its distributed infrastructure in latency-sensitive applications, including robotics and other forms of physical AI.

Akamai is already supporting workloads from central cloud to the edge, including post-training work, McGowan said, but does not plan to build gigawatt-scale facilities for large-scale model training. Its development work includes making applications easier for customers to run without specifying the underlying hardware. In security, McGowan said AI-related bot activity is increasing demand for bot management tools, although traffic volume does not translate directly into revenue. Customers are also seeking broader web application firewall coverage, he said. McGowan described security as a healthy, recurring-revenue business but stopped short of predicting an acceleration in its growth rate.

Akamai acquired cloud provider Linode in March 2022, and McGowan said the company has since more than quadrupled the revenue it acquired in that transaction. McGowan said Akamai's own rising third-party cloud costs, along with customer requests to run their code on Akamai's platform, helped prompt its entry into the broader compute market. He said Akamai would continue to consider acquisitions, while weighing potential deals against returns from investing in its fast-growing cloud infrastructure business. McGowan said the company's financing needs after 2028 would depend largely on how quickly it chooses to grow. Akamai provides cloud computing, cybersecurity and content delivery services through Akamai Connected Cloud.

stories.Headline: Federal court rules police cannot arrest on an uncorroborated AI facial recognition match
stories.Summary:
A federal court ruled that police cannot arrest someone on an uncorroborated AI facial recognition match, and it denied qualified immunity to a Kentucky detective who jailed a Nebraska man on a bad-check charge, according to LavX News. Officers arrested Alain Osorio over a charge of passing a bad check at a bank in Florence, Kentucky, where detectives had only the bank's CCTV footage as a source for the suspect's image. Detective Ryan Kilmer of the Florence Police Department ran a screenshot from that footage through the department's facial recognition program, which matched the suspect to photos on Facebook belonging to a profile named "Yony Smith Npoles Charon." Kilmer concluded that "Yony" was Alain Vizcay Osorio, a man whose booking photo appeared in police files, and the court did not name the facial recognition program.

The use of Facebook photos suggests Clearview AI, a company that has scraped hundreds of billions of images from the open web. Osorio lived in Nebraska, and officers arrested him there and extradited him to Kentucky, where he posted bond on Jan. 24, 2025, the day after his arrest. A grand jury indicted him in March 2025, a court arraigned him two months later, and he pleaded not guilty, while the state attorney's office dismissed the charges after Osorio proved he was working in Nebraska when the suspect passed the bad check. Osorio does not resemble the man in the security footage or the Facebook profile, since he has a different head shape, haircut, facial features and complexion, though both men are Black with facial hair.

Kilmer told the court in an affidavit that he used "investigative tools" to "match" Osorio to the suspect, but the court found he used one tool, the facial recognition program. Under Florence Police Department policy, facial recognition AI alone cannot establish probable cause, and Kilmer used it despite the policy. The court wrote that the Fourth Amendment does not allow a detective to delegate to AI the task of assessing probable cause, and that the Constitution does not permit an arrest based on nothing more than an uncorroborated conclusion by AI that the individual committed a crime. The judge stripped Kilmer of qualified immunity, the legal doctrine that shields officers from civil liability unless they violate clearly established law, and Kilmer can appeal.

A higher court could affirm the decision or reverse it, and if Kilmer loses his appeal, the ruling would apply beyond facial recognition. Police departments use AI to steer patrols through predictive policing software, officers use AI to generate reports from body camera footage, and Axon has added AI tools to its body cameras. The article states that running a photo through an algorithm does not constitute detective work, that a match is a lead rather than a conclusion, and that departments across the country use facial recognition as an investigative shortcut. Detectives cannot treat an algorithm match as detective work, according to the piece, which cites Techdirt as its source.

stories.Headline: EU AI Act amendments push high-risk HR system obligations to December 2027
stories.Summary:
The EU Digital Omnibus Package amended the EU AI Act and entered into force on July 27, 2026, Mary T. Costigan of Jackson Lewis P.C. wrote on November 19, 2026. The Commission presented the Digital Omnibus in November 2025 as a package to simplify EU digital law, Éric Le Quellenec of Flichy Grangé Avocats said. The package has two parts, and the first reopens the GDPR, which is still being negotiated, Le Quellenec said. The second part amends the AI Act, and that one is now law, he said. Luís Neto Galvão of SRS Legal and Le Quellenec offered five practical steps for general counsel and HR leaders at multinational businesses.

Obligations for systems listed in Annex III, including recruitment and career management, were due to apply in August of this year, Le Quellenec said. They now apply from December 2, 2027, and from August 2, 2028, for AI built into regulated products, he said. The prohibitions have applied since February 2025, the AI literacy obligations as well, and the transparency rules since August 2026, he said. High-risk systems in use before December 2, 2027, only fall under the Act if their design is significantly changed afterward, he said. Point 4 of Annex III covers recruitment, including targeting job ads, filtering applications, and evaluating candidates, and decisions on the employment relationship, including promotion, termination, task allocation based on behavior or personal traits, and monitoring and evaluating performance.

The five steps are inventory and classify AI-enabled HR tools, strengthen oversight and vendor contracts, mitigate bias, train relevant teams, and prepare recruitment practices for compliance, the article said. Neto Galvão said clients should not think they have nothing to do until 2027 and that now is the time to put a compliance plan in place. He said a year goes very quickly when you have to map your tools, renegotiate vendor contracts, and train your teams. Le Quellenec said the vendor is usually the provider and the employer is the deployer, but this can change.

He said that if the employer puts its name on the tool, modifies it substantially, or changes its intended purpose so that it becomes high risk, it becomes a provider, which brings much heavier obligations. Le Quellenec said the employer should check the conformity assessment, CE marking, EU declaration of conformity, and registration in the EU database before buying. He said the employer must use the system in line with the instructions, assign human oversight to people with the competence, training, and authority to overrule it, and make sure the input data the employer controls are relevant and representative. He said the employer must monitor the system, suspend use immediately and inform the provider if a risk appears, report serious incidents, and keep the logs for at least six months.

He said the employer must inform candidates and employees who are subject to decisions and, before the tool is introduced, inform workers' representatives and the workers concerned. He said individuals have a right to an explanation of the role AI played in a decision that significantly affects them, and a rejected candidate can ask for it. Le Quellenec said the fundamental rights impact assessment introduced by the AI Act applies to public bodies, private entities providing public services, and credit and insurance uses. He said a private employer generally does not have to do it, and for them the key assessment remains the GDPR DPIA.

Neto Galvão said human oversight must be designed into the process, not added as a label, and a manager who can only confirm the system's output is not providing meaningful oversight. Le Quellenec said HR owns the use case, IT owns integration and security, the data protection officer owns data protection and privacy, and legal owns the contracts. He said the French Lawyers' Guide on Ethics and AI was adopted in March this year and draws attention to how the way you phrase a question shapes the answer. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Bloomington mayor Kerry Thomson vetoes a city council ordinance banning artificial superintelligence
stories.Summary:
Bloomington mayor Kerry Thomson announced on Thursday afternoon, Nov. 19, 2026, that she will not sign an ordinance the city council approved 7, 0 earlier that month, which would prohibit the distribution and deployment of artificial superintelligence within city limits. The ordinance was presented to the mayor on Nov. 9 at 5:13 p.m., according to the city clerk’s office, giving her until 5:13 p.m. Thursday to sign it or return it to the council with a veto message. Because she did neither, the ordinance is considered vetoed under Indiana law. Seven councilmembers voted for the ordinance on Nov. 4, when two members, Sydney Zulich and Kate Rosenbarger, were absent.

Councilmember Dave Rollo introduced the ordinance and put forward all four amendments the council adopted before its final vote. The ordinance would add a new chapter to Bloomington’s municipal code under Title 14, which governs peace and safety, and would prohibit distribution and deployment of ASI within the city, including through websites, software and other electronic interfaces, even when the computers hosting those systems are physically located elsewhere. It defines superintelligence in terms of agency, generality and intelligence, describing autonomous systems capable of modifying their own algorithms, executing computer code outside restricted environments and undertaking complex tasks without continuous human oversight, combined with capabilities vastly exceeding human cognitive performance. The ordinance does not establish a testing procedure or designate an independent authority to determine when a particular AI system has crossed the threshold into superintelligence. It invokes the city’s powers under Indiana’s Home Rule Act and compares superintelligence to hazardous substances and industrial processes that local governments can regulate in the interest of public safety, and it would authorize the city’s legal and police departments to seek civil penalties and court orders against violators, with enforcement discretionary rather than mandatory.

One amendment explicitly excluded end-user access from the prohibition, so a Bloomington resident would not violate the ordinance merely by accessing an AI system through an electronic interface, and another removed Rollo’s original proposal to require approval from more than 95% of Bloomington’s registered voters, along with findings establishing an extremely high level of scientific certainty about the safety of superintelligence, before the ban could be lifted, retaining a scientific-safety objective in the preamble but no longer making the finding and referendum requirements for repeal. Thomson said, “Bloomington is working hard to grow our innovation economy, and artificial intelligence plays an important role in that work,” and that “AI already contributes to advances in research, medicine, education and many other fields.” She added, “We also need to be careful about creating unnecessary barriers that discourage those very people from investing in our community.” Thomson said, “As mayor, I have a responsibility to lead the team that implements and enforces our ordinances,” and that “This ordinance leaves significant questions about how the City would identify violations, what authority we have to regulate them and what enforcement would require.” She said, “The potential need to monitor private digital activity is especially troubling given our recent work to strengthen protections against government surveillance,” and that “Passing a law carries responsibilities beyond stating a principle,” adding, “We need to be confident that we can implement and enforce the laws we adopt.”

Thomson acknowledged the risks Rollo is attempting to address, saying, “I appreciate Council’s efforts to address the risks of increasingly autonomous AI systems and the national conversation this legislation has helped advance,” and that “Those risks deserve serious consideration.” Rollo told The B Square he is still optimistic about working with the mayor on a version of the ordinance she might eventually be willing to sign, because superintelligent AI is “a deadly risk for everyone,” and he added, “Obviously, we’re racing forward as the horizon is racing at us. I mean, this is madness. And there are huge consequences.” Rollo said at the start of the Wednesday night, Nov. 18, council meeting, less than 24 hours before the mayor’s deadline, that the ordinance “is emphatically not what tech businesses are using here or at IU,” and he said, “This particular AI, ASI, hasn’t yet arrived,” while contending that developing such systems is the goal of leading AI companies and that the technology could arrive soon.

Rollo contrasted that goal with work at Indiana University, which he characterized as human-centered artificial intelligence emphasizing ethical deployment, human oversight and beneficial social impacts, and he said, “Local tech applications and IU are to be lauded for their approach.” Rollo rebutted Thomson’s surveillance concern, saying, “We don’t need to surveil anyone,” and suggested violations could be reported through complaints or investigated by testing whether a prohibited system was accessible from a city-operated computer. The ordinance vetoed by Thomson represents a third effort by Rollo to persuade Bloomington’s city government to address what he and others warn is the existential danger to the human species posed by increasingly powerful artificial intelligence. In July 2023, Rollo proposed a resolution calling for a moratorium on developing artificial general intelligence until adequate safeguards could be established, and he withdrew it after officials with Indiana University raised concerns about possible implications for research funding, and sufficient support from council colleagues appeared unlikely.

On June 10 of this year, the council unanimously adopted a resolution calling on governments at other levels to address the existential risks of artificial intelligence and urging a moratorium on developing advanced AI until the technology could be aligned with human values and well-being, and that resolution was nonbinding, expressing the council’s position without establishing a local prohibition. The ordinance approved by the council in early November goes further by attempting to make distribution and deployment of superintelligence a violation of Bloomington law. Rollo’s goals extend beyond Bloomington, and the ordinance is part of a strategy he envisions being replicated by hundreds of municipalities, with local prohibitions eventually generating enough pressure to prompt state, federal and international restrictions on advanced AI development. The council could attempt to override the veto at its next regular meeting, scheduled for Wednesday, Dec. 2, at 6:30 p.m., and an override would require six votes in favor from the nine-member council.

Thomson’s objections come despite several amendments the council adopted before its final vote, intended in part to narrow the ordinance’s scope, address concerns that it could affect ordinary users of AI technology, and other issues identified soon after Rollo introduced it. The amendments reduced the potential reach of the ordinance but did not resolve the underlying question of how Bloomington would identify prohibited systems or determine whether companies outside its boundaries were distributing them within the city. Whether Indiana’s Home Rule Act powers would support a prohibition extending to remotely operated digital systems is an unresolved legal question. Thomson’s surveillance concern comes just five weeks after the city council voted 7, 0 on Oct. 14 to prohibit automated license plate readers and certain surveillance camera systems that allow outside entities to access recordings and data, and the superintelligence ordinance does not itself authorize new surveillance of internet activity.

stories.Headline: Researchers argue that security generalization error is U-shaped and minimized at a finite optimal model size
stories.Summary:
Qi Tan, Tianyu Cui, Qi Li and Ke Xu posted a paper titled Condensing Law of Security Information on arXiv on 20 November 2026, arguing that the common belief that larger language models always perform better does not hold for security work. They say security decisions depend on unusual inputs such as zero-day attacks, which are long-tailed and poorly served by likelihood fitting, so scale does not help in the way it does elsewhere. They add that the capability that comes with scale, such as inferring an intended whole from a corrupted part, can lead a model to silently repair an anomaly before any downstream security head sees it. The authors formalize this as a tradeoff between the cognitive capability a model holds about the world distribution and the security-information retention that survives in its intermediate representation.

The paper derives three information-theoretic bounds that connect these two quantities, including an upper bound on restoration accuracy in terms of cognitive capability and an upper bound on retention in terms of restoration error. It also gives a Fano lower bound on security-task error in terms of retention, and the authors say these theorems approximately imply that usable security information is a product of how much security information survives and how well it can be extracted. They state the condensing law of security information, which says usable security information is unimodal in model size, so security generalization error is U-shaped and is minimized at a finite optimal size rather than decreasing without bound. Experiments on various real-world language models validate the law, and the authors conclude that there is an optimal model size for solving security issues.

The work is listed under Cryptography and Security, with Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning as additional categories, and the full paper is available as a PDF, as experimental HTML and as TeX source. The posting appears on arXiv, which describes arXivLabs as a framework that lets collaborators develop and share features directly on the site and states that partners in it have embraced its values of openness, community, excellence and user data privacy. arXiv says it is committed to working only with partners who adhere to those values and invites ideas for projects that would add value to its community. The articles give no further details on the experiments, the specific models tested or any planned follow-up work.

stories.Headline: Dan Ives views recent AI sell-off as a generational buying opportunity
stories.Summary:
Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives discussed a significant artificial intelligence sell-off during a CNBC interview on Friday, November 21, 2026. He described this recent downturn as one of the most disconnected technology crashes he has witnessed since starting his career in the late 1990s. The market experienced a sharp swing in investor expectations, causing the Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF to drop over 6 percent. Meanwhile, the iShares U.S. Technology ETF fell nearly 7 percent during the same trading session.

This volatility requires investors to look past current political uncertainty and concerns regarding chip export restrictions to China. Ives believes the market is incorrectly pricing stocks as if the AI revolution will not happen, despite the cycle being less than 15 percent complete. He noted that demand for chips from Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Nvidia Corp. remains so high that new orders might not be filled until the end of 2028. Furthermore, he stated that roughly 75 percent of data center projects have already received the necessary permits.

The Yorkville Ives partner argued that the current market sentiment is an overreaction to spending concerns and a political backlash against data center expansion. He characterized the situation as a white-knuckle roller-coaster moment but maintained that the broader technology bull market remains intact. Ives suggested that this period represents a generational opportunity to buy winning companies before the market realizes its mistake in eighteen months. He believes the infrastructure boom will eventually benefit financial services, industrials, and energy companies.

The current turbulence follows a blue tidal wave of political opposition that acted as a gut punch to technology investors. While retail sentiment on Stocktwits remained bearish toward the S&P 500 ETF, some indices showed recovery in after-hours trading. The Invesco QQQ Trust ETF rose 1.53 percent, and the SPDR S&P 500 ETF gained 1.11 percent. Ives expects the long-term potential of the industry to eventually outweigh these temporary shocks.

stories.Headline: ICC re-elects Jay Shah as Silicon Valley Unicorns use AI to make mid-match cricket decisions
stories.Summary:
The article, a Guardian opinion column by Barney Ronay published on 20 November 2026, concerns Jay Shah, who was re-elected unopposed this week as president of the International Cricket Council. The article also concerns the San Francisco Unicorns, a Major League Cricket team that uses artificial intelligence in making mid-match decisions on the field. Ronay first heard about this in an interview with Ravichandran Ashwin in the Cricketer Magazine. The article also discusses Jensen Huang, president of Nvidia, and proposals to regulate new global T20 leagues.

The proposals to regulate more aggressively the rush of new global T20 leagues were postponed to the next ICC conference. The Unicorns are the brainchild of Anand Rajaraman and Venky Harinarayan, Silicon Valley types whose stated aim is treating a cricket team like a startup. Their key tool is called Cric Lens, which provides real-time stats, pitch data and player information plus the predictive power of every T20 game ever played. The process is described as Human-in-the-Loop Execution. The Unicorns' roster includes celebrity endorsements such as Pat Cummins.

Shah was re-elected unopposed at a meeting in Bali, where the article says he wore his usual glazed facial expression. The article says Shah is the son of Indian prime minister Narendra Modi's oldest political ally. Rajaraman and Harinarayan are Stanford graduates of the mid-90s turned Bay-Area digital rainmaker types, like Huang. One of the founders says the ideas are at the level of human civilisation and cannot be kept contained, and that it is cricket for now but why not the NFL, football or soccer. The article says Huang has spent years perfecting a machine that can make every other person's job vanish.

Finn Allen, a New Zealand batsman for the Unicorns, spoke enthusiastically about the effect of the tool in the season just past. Allen said it is not all AI or no AI but the perfect amount of contribution, after an eight-wicket win against Washington Freedom. The article says the Unicorns' backstory reads like a pitch for an app, with endless giddy chat about scaling up the product. The article says AI is already present in elite football scouting systems, and that Formula One is already a machine-led activity now embracing robo-integration. The article says there is a theory big tech companies have begun to buy into sport, citing Bezos at Liverpool, as a hedge against AI.

The article says the latest suggestion being punted about is that Huang is irreplaceable as president of Nvidia. The article says the ICC conference was widely seen as disappointingly inconclusive. The article says captaincy is a skill and sport is a live test of human capacity, and that using a machine to make captaincy decisions should obviously be regulated, understood, debated and capped at source. The article says the Unicorns may be the tiniest twinkle in the sporting sky right now but carry a potentially significant contagion. The article says AI would undoubtedly be better at managing Manchester United than the lost souls currently passing through those gates.

The article says the 20th century gave visions of a flowering of culture and the death of human drudgery. The article says the current version is one in which four people become incredibly wealthy while the rest live in an asbestos box, face clamped into a smartphone. The article says the Luddites actually had some pretty good points about the industrial loom. The article says sport, the human spectacle, is seen as safe from new technology, like buying gold when currencies go haywire. The article says so much of football is essentially guesswork, sniff-test and hunch-based, all of the stuff artificial intelligence exists to replace.

The article asks whether we will ever have the will and the collective backbone to resist and regulate this stuff and police its limits. The article ends by urging readers to resist the machines and release Finn Allen from the Phantom Zone. The article says the proposals on T20 leagues will go to the next disappointingly inconclusive ICC conference. The article does not say when that conference will be held. The article gives no response from Shah, the ICC, the Unicorns or Huang to its claims.

Articles.Title: Forget rogue robots, it’s tech billionaires and AI cricket that should really terrify us | Barney Ronay

stories.headline_source: Forget rogue robots, it’s tech billionaires and AI cricket that should really terrify us | Barney Ronay

stories.Headline: Scholars Keller and Kilg argue personifying AI undermines human agency and urge human rights assessments for AI
stories.Summary:
Brazilian legal scholar Clara Iglesias Keller and German AI expert Marie Kilg spoke at an online session of the Bonn Symposium, organised by the Germany-based Development and Peace Foundation in September 2026, where they argued that personifying artificial intelligence undermines human agency and that the conversation should focus instead on the real people responsible for the technology. They stressed the need to discuss the concentration of power in the hands of a few private companies, and they described AI as a multidimensional tool embedded in society, politics, economics and science that is increasingly shaping decision-making and social interaction. The article says AI regulation is currently composed mainly of voluntary frameworks rather than binding mandates, with legislation falling behind and allowing Big Tech to fill the governance vacuum. Private corporations are dictating the rules of the AI conversation and granting themselves the responsibility of abiding by them.

Keller and Kilg called for the public sector to join in and steer the private sector towards democratic values of transparency and accountability, and they argued that the widespread approach to digital governance based on risk assessment is limited and obscures the political construction of the technology. They are therefore calling for AI technologies to be subject to a human rights assessment obligation. Keller stressed that people need to know what could happen and what their rights are where technology and inequalities overlap, while Kilg said the history of product regulation could be useful in building an AI framework based on the idea of rights. Kilg described repositories in charge of monitoring and creating best practice baselines, such as the African Observatory on Responsible Artificial Intelligence, as a positive first step, although an institution for reinforcing compliance with existing policies is still lacking in many places.

Keller sees little space for global governance on the matter, while Kilg contends that this is a positive thing, arguing that meaningful AI governance cannot be globally imposed and must be attentive to each country's public-sector capabilities and socioeconomic asymmetries. Kilg favours regional and multilateral agreements that foster a broader diversity of approaches, and she points to gaps in digital and AI readiness across nations that may lead to economic, social and political shifts disproportionately affecting vulnerable communities and lower-income countries. The article says Big Tech is strengthening its political lobby while states fear regulation would impede innovation and market competition. It concludes that AI is a tool built by humans for human purposes, that every aspect of it is man-made, and that human rules and obligations therefore apply.

stories.Headline: Google ties school access to AI tools as administrators gain opt-out control
stories.Summary:
Google announced on Nov. 3 that students using its classroom software will lose access to Google Search if their school administrators opt out of the company's artificial intelligence tools altogether, according to Associated Press reporting cited by Newstalk KZRG. The decision follows Google's move in August to activate its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students using Google Classroom. Google said it will no longer automatically enable AI tools for K-12 student accounts, and administrators will be able to individually enable or disable tools including Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Google Search, with the features off by default until administrators turn them on. Because Google's Search tools are integrated with AI, schools that choose not to use AI will also lose access to Google Search through those student accounts.

The policy could affect school districts across southwest Missouri, southeast Kansas, northeast Oklahoma and northwest Arkansas, where schools rely on digital platforms, Chromebooks and online search tools for everyday instruction. Google says about 150 million students and teachers worldwide use Google Classroom, and many students rely on school-issued Chromebook computers. Google Vice President and General Manager of Education Chris Phillips said the company believes schools should have control over AI in classrooms and the ability to manage how the technology is used. The company also said it is updating Search to better support learning, including offering step-by-step guidance through problems rather than simply providing quick answers to assignments.

Former Federal Trade Commission Chair Lina Khan criticized the decision, arguing Google is using its influence over school technology to encourage AI adoption. Josh Golin, executive director of children's advocacy group Fairplay, also criticized the policy, arguing that schools should consider privacy-protective alternatives to Google and encourage more substantive research methods. Missouri's U.S. Sen. Josh Hawley joined Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut in sending a letter to Google CEO Sundar Pichai demanding answers about AI integration into school technology. The senators set a Nov. 2 deadline for Google to respond to nine questions, including why AI features were made the default in some school settings, what research the company has conducted into AI's effects on children's mental and emotional well-being, and how the company responds to concerns raised by teachers, parents and school administrators.

Google's Nov. 3 announcement addressed changes to its AI settings for school administrators, but did not directly respond to the senators' letter or address all nine questions. The debate continues over whether AI should be a tool schools choose to implement or a technology they must accept to maintain access to services students already rely on. School systems nationwide are navigating how to incorporate emerging technology while maintaining safeguards for students and preserving educators' authority over classroom instruction. For schools across the four-state region, the discussion could ultimately center on whether districts retain the flexibility to decide how students access information, what technology they use and how AI fits into the learning environment.

Articles.Title: Google’s AI Policy Raises Questions for Schools Across Four-State Region

stories.Headline: Performativ links bank staff AI assistants to client records under existing permissions
stories.Summary:
Performativ connected AI assistants used by bank staff to client and portfolio records on November 19, 2026. This release allows employees to query business systems using tools like ChatGPT and Claude. The company used the Model Context Protocol to create these links for existing clients. This update is specifically for bank staff and not for the bank clients themselves. The service is off by default and requires a firm to enable it.

The system uses the Model Context Protocol to link assistants to records hosted in the EU. Administrators decide who can use the service, and each employee uses an individual login. Existing Performativ permissions apply to every user, and the company logs every request for audit. The platform connects to more than 150 custodians and supports over 1,500 advisors. It manages more than 100 billion euros in client assets across its broader platform.

CEO Albert Geisler Fox stated that the current release is for staff at client firms. He described letting bank clients query their own portfolios through AI assistants as a future ambition. The company says this setup prevents staff from manually copying client data into outside assistants. Performativ claims these controls ensure security and regulatory compliance for the firms using the service. The company says the system keeps data access tied to the firm's existing rules.

The service affects relationship managers, portfolio managers, back office teams, and compliance staff. Relationship managers can use the tool to create briefings that compare portfolio progress with projections. Portfolio managers can examine performance and risk alongside the advice a client previously received. Compliance teams can review risk profiles, regulatory status, and recent changes to client records. These workflows use data including meeting notes, account activity, and the identities of responsible advisors.

The MCP capability builds on governed agent workflows introduced with Custom Agents in November 2025. Performativ provides a platform for portfolio management, customer relationship management, compliance, and reporting. The company aims to move AI queries into the assistants that employees already use. This builds on the existing platform where firms manage their client relationships and records. The new version changes where staff can ask questions about their business data.

The next step is the ambition to let bank clients use their preferred AI assistants. This future direction would allow clients to ask about portfolios under the bank's controls. The articles do not state when this client facing feature will be released. They do not provide the specific adoption numbers for the new MCP service release. It remains open how many firms have enabled the service since November 19.

stories.Headline: Walmart reports 25% rise in global ad revenue as AI tools and connected TV deals gain traction
stories.Summary:
Walmart reported on November 20, 2026, that its global advertising revenue rose 25% in the latest period, while U.S. ad sales climbed 37%, according to a Simply Wall St article published on Yahoo Finance. Management tied the advertising gains to recent moves in connected TV, including acquisitions involving Vizio and Vibe.co, and the retailer also highlighted new AI powered retail media tools and conversational commerce features as part of its advertising push. The article said Walmart runs a global network of stores, clubs, websites and apps that generate vast shopper data, which gives its advertising unit a direct line to purchase behavior across consumer retailing. The piece was described as general in nature and produced with the assistance of AI automation, based on data and analysis from Simply Wall St.

The article said the 25% advertising jump feeds into a broader pattern its research has tracked, and it noted that its analysis turns up one warning sign for Walmart as well. It framed the ad rise as fitting Walmart's narrative that higher margin businesses such as advertising, marketplace services and memberships gradually matter more to earnings than low margin store sales, and it said the main factor that has to go right is continued growth and profitability of those alternative profit pools. The article also said the news sharpens a key risk already flagged in that narrative, that regulators are scrutinising Walmart's use of AI and digital pricing, and that tighter rules on how Sparky or digital shelf tools work could slow the profit streams investors are now cheering. It pointed readers to a full story suggesting a $129 fair value for Walmart.

The article did not name any Walmart executive or provide direct statements from the company, attributing the advertising figures and the connected TV and AI details to management and the retailer generally. It said the advertising surge gives bulls fresh evidence that the ad unit is not just an add-on but a material earnings contributor that differs from traditional retailers such as Target or Costco. It also said that to judge what the headline really means for Walmart, readers need a clear view of where its mix of low margin retailing and higher margin services is heading over time, which it said is exactly what a narrative tries to spell out. The article stated that Simply Wall St has no position in any stocks mentioned and that the piece does not constitute a recommendation to buy or sell any stock.

The context the article gave is Walmart's effort to build higher margin income streams alongside its store sales, with advertising, marketplace services and memberships expected to matter more to earnings over time. It said the advertising gains were supported by AI tools and connected TV deals and described the ad unit as increasingly material rather than incidental. The article did not say what happens next beyond inviting readers to add Walmart to a watchlist and get alerts as these catalysts play out, and it noted that its analysis may not factor in the latest price-sensitive company announcements or qualitative material. It also said the article does not take account of readers' objectives or financial situations.

stories.Headline: Cognizant executive says legacy systems absorb up to 80% of banks IT budgets
stories.Summary:
Ashish Bhatnagar, Head of Banking & Financial Services for Cognizant in the UK & Ireland, gave a Q&A to FinTech Magazine published on November 20, 2026, about how banks can turn legacy systems into an AI advantage. He said legacy technology is a major constraint on banks' modernisation efforts. He said legacy systems can absorb up to 80% of banks' IT budgets through simple maintenance. He said many of these systems support critical services and contain decades of business rules and institutional knowledge. He said it can be difficult to scale or transition to new technology.

He said architecture reviews, risk assessments and security approvals were designed to provide essential control but often cannot scale with the volume and pace of a major transformation programme. He said this produces late-stage delays, fragmented delivery and a reluctance to experiment. He said fear of failure can create paralysis, because if a new system fails it can affect whether people can pay bills or access their money. He said in the UK alone banks spend an estimated £3.3bn (US$4.3bn) annually managing core legacy systems. The article states core banking management and maintenance consumes an average of 24% of UK banks' IT budgets, nearly a quarter.

He said the true cost of legacy extends beyond licence fees, upgrades and system run rates to substantial below-the-line costs from additional employees and the specialist knowledge and manual processes required to keep systems operating. He said every hour and pound devoted to maintaining ageing infrastructure cannot be used to improve customer experiences, introduce new products or integrate AI. He said legacy environments can make banks less attractive to scarce technology talent. He said governance, security and regulatory controls are indispensable in banking but the processes used to apply them can become bottlenecks. He said the answer is not to weaken oversight but to embed it into delivery from the beginning.

He said security, compliance, data permissions and usage rights should be designed into the architecture and supported by repeatable, automated controls. He said an AI-ready bank has moved beyond isolated pilots and created the conditions to deploy AI securely, responsibly and at enterprise scale. He said that requires infrastructure capable of supporting AI, accessible contextual data, and robust permissions and governance built into the architecture from the outset. He said the bank also needs a culture that permits controlled experimentation, supported by the right engineering, data and AI skills.

He said AI readiness means AI becomes part of how the organisation operates, not simply another tool, and can support complete workflows while meeting security, compliance and customer expectations. He said existing systems often contain valuable assets including business rules, customer context, historical data and institutional knowledge. He said AI can help surface and apply that intelligence while accelerating modernisation itself. He said AI-driven automation, predictive DevOps, automated testing and self-healing systems can improve productivity and reduce the burden of technical debt.

He said banks can then modernise in controlled stages, focusing investment on the value streams that matter most and minimising disruption to critical services. He said this approach creates value sooner, makes transformation decisions better informed and frees up resources for further innovation. He said leaders should first reduce structural friction by identifying where legacy complexity, manual controls and approval bottlenecks create drag, then simplify or automate them. He said teams should second organise delivery around value streams, focusing on complete customer or business outcomes rather than isolated technology components.

He said this improves delivery speed and reliability, increases straight-through processing and prevents risk, security or architecture issues emerging late. He said banks should third build intelligence from existing systems, using AI to extract value from the data, business rules and institutional knowledge already embedded in their estates, with security, compliance, permissions and responsible-AI controls designed in from the outset. The article lists Cognizant's partners as Microsoft, AWS, Google Cloud, Temenos and ACI Worldwide, and says Cognizant and ACI Worldwide demonstrated ACI's BASE24-eps card-processing platform running at scale on AWS, processing more than 4.6 million transactions without failure in performance testing. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Salt Security finds 77 percent of firms using AI see agents act outside authorized behavior
stories.Summary:
Salt Security reported on November 19 that 77 percent of organizations using or exploring AI saw agents act outside authorized behavior. This finding came from a poll of 500 C-suite professionals conducted by Censuswide from September 10 to 18. The respondents included 250 leaders from the US and 250 from the UK. These professionals worked at organizations with 50 or more employees. Most executives, specifically 92 percent, would still allow agents to take some independent action.

The poll found 64 percent of leaders restricted, delayed, or canceled AI projects over regulatory, governance, or security concerns. While 97 percent of AI users keep agent inventories, 19 percent admit these lists are not consistently updated. Salt sells tools to discover agents, MCP servers, and APIs to monitor runtime behavior and govern connections. Other surveys show different results, such as a 49.8 percent rate from Salt's October 13 report. EMA reported 65 percent of agents acted outside scope, while CSA found 53 percent exceeded permissions.

Salt co-founder and COO Michael Nicosia stated that executives give agents authority over money, data, code, and customer relationships. He argued that governance cannot be a one-time approval process for these systems. Nicosia said organizations need continuous visibility into what every agent can reach and actually does. He believes a static inventory or single sign-off is a weak foundation for governance. This view contrasts with Microsoft, which points to identity, permissions, and policy controls.

The CSA survey affected 445 IT and security professionals and was fielded in September and November 2025. Illumio and Sapio Research polled 1,100 decision-makers in 10 markets, finding 26 percent of agents connected without approval. EY surveyed 202 senior AI executives at US public companies with at least one billion dollars in revenue. Their data showed 26 percent of organizations using agentic AI cannot detect unauthorized internal agents. These various figures reflect different respondent groups, denominators, and definitions of unauthorized action.

The articles note that agents often inherit access through existing APIs, identities, and applications across separate teams. This relates to the mid-1970s least privilege concept by Jerome Saltzer and the 1988 confused deputy problem by Norm Hardy. The UK National Cyber Security Centre warned in December 2025 that language models are inherently confusable deputies. Salt Labs also found that the Manus platform, based in Singapore, was vulnerable to hidden email prompts. TechRadar reported on October 2 that Manus fixed this issue after JavaScript ran in the runtime.

Next, buyers should ask five questions about who answered, the denominator, what counted, the timing, and who paid. The articles leave open whether control belongs at the moment access is granted or during agent runtime. They also leave the exact definition of an AI agent open, as no standard definition exists. It remains unclear how serious the incidents were for the 77 percent of firms. Finally, the reports do not state exactly how many projects were affected by governance concerns.

stories.Headline: Tristan Harrison urges comms teams to ask six questions before commissioning AI video
stories.Summary:
The article is a set of six questions for PR and comms teams to ask before commissioning AI video, written by Tristan Harrison, who spent years in PR agencies before running a production company that combines AI with live action and traditional filmmaking. He says the Christmas season ended the theoretical stage of the AI advertising debate, pointing to the backlash over Dior's animated holiday short and to Very, which was upfront about combining CGI with AI-assisted animation and achieved its highest-ever pre-launch audience-testing score. He also notes that the IAB has updated its industry framework on AI transparency and disclosure and that the EU AI Act's transparency rules are already in force. His conclusion is that audiences are not necessarily against AI, since they want good creative and honesty about how it is made, and that AI video is a reputational decision for comms teams rather than only a creative or production one.

The six questions cover who is actually making the film and who is responsible for the final cut, since the software is not an acceptable answer, and where AI genuinely adds value, since it is not always quicker or cheaper and the technology should serve the idea. They also cover approval points, because a small change such as a shirt going from green to red can mean rebuilding an entire sequence, and Harrison describes getting clients to approve static AI-generated frames before animation and asking for a PPM meeting as with traditional film making. Ownership is the fourth question, covering likeness rights, consent, synthetic voices, music licensing, the tools used and ownership of the finished assets, with the warning not to assume a supplier's software licence covers the brand's intended use. Disclosure is the fifth, which he says should not be an awkward conversation after the film is finished, since not every AI-assisted production task requires a public label but nobody involved should be left guessing, and discussing it only at launch is too late. The sixth asks whether the supplier can deliver beyond the demo, with advice to see completed client projects rather than showreels and to find out how revisions are handled when AI does not deliver what was expected.

Harrison gives one example from his own experience, a brief involving precise eye movements that proved difficult to control with AI, where an actor and a camera would have been simpler. He says the best approach might be fully AI-generated, live action or a hybrid, and that suppliers should be asked why they recommend a particular route and whether they considered the alternatives. He describes comms teams as often the last line of defence for a brand's reputation and says that with AI video they should also be the first people asking the right questions. The article ends with an invitation to sign up for the publication's free twice-weekly editorial alert and to register for free analysis on techniques and campaigns in the PR sector.

stories.Headline: Rep. Vince Fong introduces bipartisan bill to place private AI experts inside CISA
stories.Summary:
Representative Vince Fong introduced a bipartisan bill on November 20, 2026, to strengthen cybersecurity in the United States. This legislation follows several widespread technical outages that have recently impacted various systems across the entire country. The Bridging Resources for Innovative Defense and Government Expertise in Artificial Intelligence Act would authorize the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to collaborate with private professionals. This bill calls for a pilot project involving about 100 private sector workers to serve within the CISA. It also requires a semi-annual report on the status of the program and ways the agency could improve it.

Republican Representative Vince Fong of Bakersfield stated that communities and critical industries are struggling to keep up with a surge in AI-related cyberattacks. He noted that attacks in the Central Valley have targeted water systems, hospitals, and schools to steal sensitive data. Fong argued that bringing in private sector specialists ensures that national experts have the tools needed to modernize systems. Democratic Representative Josh Gottheimer of New Jersey co-authored the bill and said that adversaries are using AI to attack American networks.

He claimed that the agency on the front lines of defense does not have enough capacity to keep pace. Gottheimer stated that the act is a common sense fix to help the agency hunt intruders and patch vulnerabilities. The bill follows a nationwide plane ground stop and outages impacting the National Security Agency and Microsoft Outlook. Other affected entities include Apple, United Airlines, and multiple banks that experienced technical failures.

These events highlight the vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure that the new legislation aims to address through private sector expertise. The bill must be approved before the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency can begin collaborating with the private sector AI professionals. The legislation aims to stress-test AI tools before they are exploited by adversaries to protect national security. The articles do not state when the bill will be debated or if it has passed.
