stories.Headline: South Korea inspects exam candidates glasses and blocks Wi-Fi to stop AI cheating
stories.Summary:
South Korea will inspect all glasses worn by students taking this week's national college entrance exam to prevent AI-assisted cheating. This action follows a confession on Sunday by a person who placed first in the 2026 tax accountant exam. The individual admitted to photographing questions with a microcamera and using an AI tool and smartphone to find answers. These events shook public confidence in the country's high-stakes testing system and caused panic before the college test. The government is now implementing strict security measures to protect the integrity of the upcoming national examinations.

The Education Ministry will inspect all glasses in every session of the College Scholastic Ability Test in Seoul and other centers. Smart devices were added to the banned items list in July, and public Wi-Fi will be blocked during the exams. Every exam room will have warning notices about criminal penalties, and each center will have one staff member monitoring devices. A hotline will link centers to local education offices and the ministry's control room to judge difficult cases on the spot. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook announced that emergency alerts will be sent before the exam to detect any hidden mobile phones.

Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin told a parliamentary hearing on November 16 that the ministry would inspect all eyewear worn by candidates. He stated that the ministry would work with parliament to lengthen the current one-year exam ban to three or ten years. Choi also noted that offenders may be reported to the police for obstructing official duties during the national testing process. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook said the government would form an emergency team to prepare measures to safeguard the college entrance exam. She urged officials to develop AI-based detection technology and called for strengthened penalties for those who cheat using technology.

Some people called for the university entrance exam to be postponed to ensure fairness, but the Education Ministry ruled out delays. The Suneung exam is seen as a ticket to well-paid jobs and better marriage prospects in a hyper-competitive society. Students are affected by these changes, as anyone caught using smart devices will have their results invalidated for the current year. They will also be barred from sitting the exam the following year under the current rules and potential new penalties. The national exam is so intense that much of South Korea will stand still on Thursday to minimize student distractions.

The scandal began when the top tax accountant candidate confessed on November 15 to using a microcamera and AI for cheating. Smart glasses are a global concern because they can record confidential material or people without their knowledge or any consent. Grepp, a company with a 90 percent market share in online proctoring, uses a service called Monito for recruitment exams. This technology is already used by major corporations like Samsung Electronics, LG Electronics, and SK hynix for their own hiring processes. Grepp recorded 13.5 billion won in revenue last year and is now expanding into physical test center AI solutions.

The ministry will consult specialists on radio-signal detectors and may introduce this technology for the 2027 test to stop AI cheating. Grepp CEO Lim Sung-soo is discussing a pilot deployment of Monito at Prometric test centers in the United States next year. The company plans to seek accreditation as a private operator of nationally recognized qualification assessments and pursue an IPO in 2028. Articles leave open whether thermal imaging cameras or radio-frequency detectors will be used, as they face legal and technical challenges. It remains unclear if the government will successfully implement these high-tech tools due to interference with nearby wireless communications.

stories.Headline: AI tools help businesses and creators produce images and videos faster while requiring human review
stories.Summary:
The Daily Iowan published a promoted post on November 20, 2026 describing how artificial intelligence is becoming a major force behind the evolution of digital media, from personalized online experiences to automated creative production. The article says businesses, designers and content creators are increasingly adopting AI solutions to improve efficiency, explore new ideas and deliver engaging content. It describes AI image generators that turn written descriptions into illustrations, realistic photographs and artistic compositions, and AI video generators that build animated scenes, promotional clips and product videos from text, images and other inputs. The piece also says AI is being used in e-commerce for product illustrations and lifestyle visuals and in education for illustrations and videos that explain complicated concepts.

The article lists several claimed advantages of AI video tools, including faster production, creative flexibility, lower production barriers, marketing opportunities and content experimentation. It says AI image generation can serve as an additional creative resource for professional designers and an accessible starting point for beginners without extensive design experience. It adds that generated content should be reviewed for accuracy, originality and suitability, and that businesses should consider copyright requirements, privacy concerns and transparency when using AI-generated materials. Human oversight remains important, the article says, because automated systems may occasionally produce inaccurate details or results that do not match the intended creative direction.

The article names no companies, people, products or specific figures, and it does not say who is responsible for any particular tool or announcement. It presents the shift toward AI in digital production as a general trend, saying improvements in machine learning and visual understanding could make creative systems more accurate, adaptable and responsive to user instructions. It says the next stage of AI development will likely involve greater connections between image generation, video creation, animation and interactive media, with opportunities across entertainment, advertising, education and online retail. No next steps, timelines or specific events beyond that general outlook are given.

stories.Headline: FP Markets adds an Anthropic share CFD for trading from 19 November 2026
stories.Summary:
FP Markets, a globally recognised Forex and CFD broker based in Limassol, Cyprus, announced on 18 November 2026 that it will add an Anthropic share CFD to its existing product range. The new instrument, listed under the ticker ANT.xnas, goes live for clients worldwide on 19 November 2026 and will be available to trade on MetaTrader 5, cTrader and TradingView. The addition will match the standard trading hours of other US-listed share CFDs on the platform, with competitive commission rates applied across all transactions. FP Markets was established in Sydney, Australia in 2005 and offers more than 10,000 CFD instruments across seven asset classes. The listing matters because Anthropic, the AI giant behind the Claude models, is described as one of the most widely anticipated listings this year and arguably the key name in the AI space.

The article says AI's progress has been called into question at a deeper level following the departure of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, so Anthropic's IPO is widely viewed as a major test of AI investor appetite. FP Markets clients will be able to use the new share CFD to diversify into a broader investment portfolio and respond to opportunities in the technology sector. The broker's regulatory presence includes ASIC in Australia, the FSA in Seychelles, the FSCA of South Africa and the CMA of Kenya. FP Markets Chief Market Analyst Aaron Hill said the debut of Anthropic is a defining moment in the AI trade, according to the article.

He said the addition of the share CFD will open the door to further opportunities in the technology sector, allowing traders and investors to respond to the opportunities and volatility that come with a high-profile listing. The article does not give the price of the instrument, the size of the listing or any figure for the drop in Anthropic shares suggested by the headline. It also does not report any statement from Apple or from Anthropic itself about Apple's AI agent plans. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Anthropic debuts on Wall Street at $1.75 trillion as safety pledges face shareholder pressure
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence startup known for its Claude chatbot, made its debut on Wall Street on Thursday and ended its first day of trading with a market value of $1.75 trillion, according to TechGig. The company was founded by seven people, including CEO Dario Amodei and his sister Daniela Amodei, who left OpenAI to build a company focused on AI safety. Amodei described the conflict between safety and advancing AI as a central tension within the company on Thursday. The company still pledges to prioritise humanity's benefit but now faces shareholder pressure to make profits from technology its leaders have described as posing existential threats.

The listing follows a period of rapid expansion, and a report from the nonprofit Model Evaluation and Threat Research found Anthropic is developing its systems around twice as quickly as a year ago, largely due to AI itself. An Anthropic researcher resigned in September and criticised the safety practices of both Anthropic and OpenAI, saying they were gambling with lives. Anthropic is structured as a public benefit corporation, legally obligated to balance shareholder interests with the public good, a structure the article says places it in uncharted territory because such companies rarely reach this scale in the public market. Before the IPO the Amodei siblings each had a net worth of just over $14 billion, which rose to over $22 billion by Thursday afternoon, and the co-founders have committed to pledging 80 per cent of their equity to philanthropy. Anthropic's filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission last month included an unusually lengthy 93 pages on risk factors, noting that advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.

Separately, the US-based nonprofit Better Data Center Project mapped 19 US sites where Anthropic has leased between 5.9 and 9.6 GW of capacity, out of approximately 15 GW it has contracted, according to Data Center Dynamics. The nonprofit claimed that approximately 2.5 GW, or 26 percent, is powered by on-site natural gas, with the remainder tied to the grid, which is itself 47 percent natural gas, so it asserted that 60 percent of the mapped sites' power demand is tied to natural gas. Earlier in November Anthropic signed a $3.4 billion deal for 1.7 GW of natural gas generators supplied by Caterpillar, in partnership with OnePWR, expected to be available within two years. Paweł Czyżak, CEO and founder of Ornaq, said the figures were estimates, that Anthropic does not disclose its sites, that at least 5 GW is not mapped and that some attributions are speculative, while noting he had expected a higher standard.

An Anthropic spokesperson told Data Center Dynamics that the company was working to add new power generation so it is not drawing on supply used by local homes and businesses, and said much of that new power is natural gas because it can be brought online quickly, ramps up and down as demand changes and is abundant in the places being considered. The spokesperson said the company is also working to broaden its energy mix with geothermal, wind, solar and emerging technologies, and is designing projects that will rely on renewable energy in regions with strong renewable resources. The company also pointed to sustainability measures including joining the carbon emission buying consortium Frontier and working with Watershed, a carbon accounting and emissions disclosure platform. The power research came as the company completed its initial public offering this week, which was expected to value it at approximately $1.5 trillion after shares were priced at $83 ahead of its Nasdaq debut.

stories.Headline: Experts link AI-accelerated patching to major US tech outages
stories.Summary:
A series of major technology outages disrupted critical services across the United States, affecting email, air travel, banking and government operations. The incidents included a day-long Microsoft 365 outage, a nationwide FAA ground stop, and technical issues at JPMorgan Chase that slowed transactions for other banks. The National Security Agency's classified internal network also experienced a disruption. Officials found no evidence of cyberattacks or links between these incidents. Microsoft attributed its outage to a months-old software defect, the FAA cited a newly installed router, and the NSA pointed to routine maintenance.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton connected the NSA disruption to patching a PHP vulnerability discovered with AI assistance. Senator Mark Warner noted that AI-driven vulnerability discovery compels organisations to patch many systems at once, stressing infrastructure not built for such rapid change. Ken Barth, CEO of Catalogic Software, said AI finds vulnerabilities faster than many remediation processes can manage, noting Microsoft fixed over 1,400 vulnerabilities in its October security release, a monthly record. Brian Contos, Field CISO at Mitiga, cited the FAA router change that destabilised 17 of 22 en route centres as an example of how a single failure can cascade across interconnected systems.

Gil Tene, CTO and Co-founder of Azul, believes AI-accelerated patch velocity is already causing major operational incidents, citing customers where urgent, non-security OpenJDK updates led to stability issues and failed rollouts. Samuel Hassine, CEO of Filigran, suggested the outages are more a change problem where systems cannot handle frequent updates, arguing a fix causing downtime is also a security failure. Benny Czarny, CEO of OPSWAT, warned that faster patching can contribute to outages when testing and recovery cannot keep pace, adding that failures can result from primary and backup systems sharing the same software and network dependencies. Bryson Byrd, Cybersecurity Advisor at Huntress, cautioned against premature conclusions regarding AI's role but stressed the need for resilience and tested fallback plans.

Grayson North, Principal Threat Intelligence Consultant at GuidePoint Security, mentioned the Vulnpocalypse as AI makes vulnerability discovery trivial, leading to a surge in patches. Chris Hughes, VP of Security Strategy at Noma Security, stated that AI has industrialised vulnerability discovery, pushing organisations to race to fix findings. Crystal Morin, Senior Cybersecurity Strategist at Sysdig, suggested the industry swung too far with the patch faster mantra, leading to organisations shipping fixes without adequate testing. Patrick Quirk, President of Opengear, stressed the importance of tested rollouts in staging environments and independent management paths for recovery when primary networks fail.

stories.Headline: Krishna Rao steers Anthropic through its blockbuster initial public offering
stories.Summary:
Krishna Rao, the 43-year-old Indian-origin finance chief, is steering Anthropic through its initial public offering, which the livemint.com article published on 19 November 2026 says goes public today. Rao joined Anthropic in 2024 and is set to become one of Wall Street's closely watched executives as the AI company lists. The livemint.com article calls the listing a blockbuster initial public offering and says Rao has played a pivotal role in the company's growth and financing strategy. Earlier this year Anthropic found itself at odds with the US government over the safe use of artificial intelligence, and Rao stood firm during that dispute. The Pentagon wanted the company to loosen restrictions on how its tools could be used in combat and threatened to cancel a contract worth hundreds of millions of dollars.

The prospectus, signed by Rao and other executives, reported a revenue run rate of $81 billion as of October 31, up $10 billion from the end of September. When Rao joined in 2024, Anthropic had annualised revenue of about $250 million, and the company was aiming to scale that to $1 billion. Rao initially wondered how long it would take to reach that target, but the milestone was reached within months, he said on a podcast. At JPMorgan Chase's New York headquarters last Friday, a packed room of high-net-worth investors gathered to hear Anthropic's top executives. JPMorgan Asset and Wealth Management CEO Mary Erdoes singled out Rao, calling him the "CFO extraordinaire" and the person "who is helping us get through things".

Rao leads hundreds of finance staff and has five close deputies, and he has helped expand Anthropic's investor base globally, including in the Middle East. "We think the benefits of AI are not specific to one country or region," Rao said in a previous interview with Bloomberg News. "We really want the benefits of what we're building to be global in nature." Anthropic declined to make Rao available for the story, Bloomberg reported. Rao has said he has moved away from thinking about sales growth in linear terms, and he said on a podcast that "it's really hard to predict this business."

Gaurav Kapadia, who runs investment firm XN and holds a large stake in Anthropic, said Rao was a great firewall preventing investors from pushing the company into a decision that was culturally incompatible with their long-term objectives. Kapadia's account was reported by Bloomberg, which described Rao fielding calls from investors urging Anthropic to give in to the Pentagon's demands. Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital, told Bloomberg that "Krishna is humble and purposely flies under the radar," and he described Rao as "an important voice in the AI discussion". Before joining Anthropic, Rao worked at Blackstone and Airbnb, where he played an important role in the company's IPO and interacted with top investors. Goldman Sachs bankers viewed Rao as the "killer in the room" who could answer every question about Airbnb's IPO, according to a person familiar with the matter cited by Bloomberg.

Rao was among the first executive hires outside Anthropic's close-knit group of seven co-founders. One of his early priorities was helping the company expand its enterprise business, which was still nascent and overshadowed by OpenAI. Anthropic's expensive AI roadmap, investments in chips and data centres, and commitment to responsible AI development will be under closer examination by shareholders once the company enters public markets. Rao's ability to balance commercial interests with Anthropic's principles is likely to face greater scrutiny once the company enters public markets. While CEO Dario Amodei has become a prominent voice in the AI debate, Rao's job will be to help investors understand the financial risks and rewards of the technology's rapid expansion.

The livemint.com article was published on 19 November 2026 at 12:46 PM IST and was written by Sanchari Ghosh. The Axios article, titled "Behind the Curtain: Anthropic contradictions," was published on 18 November 2026 and written by Jim VandeHei and Mike Allen. Anthropic declined to make Rao available for the story, Bloomberg reported. The articles leave open how Anthropic's shares will perform once the company enters public markets. The articles also leave open how Rao's balancing of commercial interests and Anthropic's principles will fare under shareholder scrutiny.

stories.Headline: Investors buy Anthropic IPO as tech stocks and chipmakers face a broad sell-off
stories.Summary:
Investors piled into the initial public offering of Anthropic on Thursday, which saw the company storm onto the public markets. This event occurred while tech stocks and chipmakers faced a broad sell-off, creating a disconnect for those investing in AI. The Nasdaq Composite fell more than 2 percent, and the S&P 500 logged another ugly day during this period. Chip stocks were bleeding, and companies like Nvidia and AMD were getting crushed as the market faced a perfect storm. Selling pressure extended into Friday, November 20, 2026, as investors began repricing the AI trade in real time.

The Nasdaq Composite closed at 23,020.97, while the S&P 500 fell to 7,021.68 and the Dow 30 dropped to 48,769.04. Anthropic, PBC shares were at 84.70, and Nvidia Corporation fell to 135.32, while Intel Corporation dropped to 52.59 on Friday. CoreWeave reported nearly 90 billion dollars in debt and liabilities, alongside a net loss of 709 million dollars in the third quarter. Nvidia reported 116 billion dollars in third-quarter revenue, 65 billion dollars in net income, 32 billion dollars in debt, and 118 billion liabilities. The Russell 2000 fell to 2,608.41, and the VIX rose to 32.10, while Bitcoin USD dropped to 58,906.46.

Executive Editor Brian Sozzi said the market is facing a perfect storm where investors are less willing to pay any price. He noted that the Democratic Blue Wave has Wall Street questioning if Washington will put brakes on AI and data center construction. Sozzi stated that the leadership fallout at Nvidia is shaking confidence, as the market does not like interim CEO Collect Crest. He mentioned that technical selling and market clearing events are forcing investors to raise cash during this period of volatility. Sozzi also cited sticky inflation, hawkish Fed rhetoric, and the prospect of tighter financial conditions as drivers of the current weakness.

Hyperscalers including Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle are no longer cash-flow positive despite the billions they reap in quarterly revenue. Neoclouds, which rent compute to hyperscalers, are tens of billions in debt, with CoreWeave seeing its stock price drop over 50 percent. Short seller reports targeting AMD and fresh regulatory fears regarding China have further damaged the semiconductor trade and affected these specific chipmakers. Bethany McLean questioned if the hundreds of billions spent on AI infrastructure and data centers can be repaid when it is due. Investors who want the AI future are now facing a reality where the broader AI trade is being blown to pieces.

Nvidia previously operated under an open checkbook policy led by founder Jensen Huang, who was the face of the AI revolution. The company loaned money to neoclouds to buy Nvidia chips, a tactic that critics have described as circular financing. Nvidia essentially guaranteed it would cover the debt of neoclouds if they could not pay, making Nvidia the guarantor of last resort. Much of this debt was resold to Wall Street and held by insurance companies, creating a complex web of financial liabilities. The industry has seen aggressive financial practices and rapid data center construction that may now be reined in by new leadership.

The market is waiting for Nvidia to announce a permanent CEO, as there is currently no timeline for this specific leadership decision. Investors are watching to see if the Democratic wave will burst the AI bubble and who will be left holding debt. It remains open whether the AI dream can survive the current repricing and the potential for tighter financial conditions from the Fed. The situation leaves it unclear if Anthropic can maintain its status as a 2 trillion dollar sensation amid the broader sell-off. Future market movements depend on regulatory fears in China and the ability of neoclouds to manage their massive debt loads.

stories.Headline: Satya Nadella says Microsoft could have prevented the Outlook outage
stories.Summary:
Satya Nadella, Microsoft's chief executive, said on Wednesday evening in an interview with CNBC's Jim Cramer that Microsoft could have prevented last week's Outlook outage. The disruption happened last Thursday and was caused by a previously undetected software bug that emerged under a particular traffic pattern. Nadella said the outage brought swaths of corporate America to a standstill and was the first in a series of technology outages during a difficult week for the sector. The incidents affected everything from corporate communications to airline operations and banking transactions, highlighting the growing dependence of businesses and everyday life on technology. Nadella told CNBC it was one of those crazy perfect storms where a latent bug got found only during a particular traffic pattern.

Nadella said Microsoft should have done the testing before and should have figured out how to have the bulkheads so there was no global outage. He warned that faster software updates and fixes are creating new stability challenges for older technology infrastructure. He said AI has allowed the company to find and fix bugs, but that means you have got to then patch them, and that creates instability. He added that a lot of what is being seen is maybe old infrastructure with new patches and instability. Microsoft's October 28 earnings showed Azure cloud revenue surging 48% to $33.2 billion, reflecting strong demand for AI computing power.

Nadella is responsible for the comments, having acknowledged the company could have done more to prevent the outage. He said of course we should have done the testing before and should have figured out how to have the bulkheads. He told CNBC the consumption will go up and people will have to have new business models, citing Dynamics, where a lot of the business is not about seats but usage. He said customers would be able to choose between different AI models, asking whether they want Claude, OpenAI or Microsoft's own models, and said you can route across all of them. He also said technology companies must win the hearts and minds and the votes one community at a time, pointing to Microsoft's data centre operations in Quincy, Washington.

At the DealBook Summit on Wednesday, Nadella said the company's shift to an AI-first operating model will fundamentally change employee roles, with workers increasingly directing and managing AI agents rather than performing tasks directly. He explained the voluntary buyouts offered to approximately 60,000 employees in October, aimed at giving workers greater choice amid workforce reorganisation around AI. He said the role of software engineers will remain relevant, but its nature and team structures will evolve as AI tools become more capable. He cited the team developing Cowork, an AI agent in Microsoft 365 apps, which comprises just 11 developers who use AI extensively to build a software factory that constructs the product. He believes this model of directing AI agents will extend across all jobs.

Earlier this year, investors worried that AI advancements could disrupt the traditional seat-based software model, putting pressure on Microsoft's business. The company's strong cloud growth and spending discipline helped improve investor sentiment, and shares bottomed out for the year in late June. Since the company's late-July earnings report, the stock has climbed 30%, though the momentum has stalled a bit of late. The stock has pulled back nearly 9% over the past two weeks since its all-time closing high on Nov. 4, the day after the midterm elections. At its Ignite conference Tuesday, Microsoft laid out its vision for Copilot as the central hub for workplace productivity.

Microsoft is seeking to position artificial intelligence as a driver of growth rather than a threat to its established software business. The articles leave open how the bulkheads Nadella mentioned would be implemented and when the testing changes would take effect. They do not say how many customers or systems the Outlook outage affected, nor what the previously undetected bug specifically was. They do not state how the approximately 60,000 voluntary buyouts were distributed across roles or what response employees gave. They also do not say whether the Cowork team's software factory model will be adopted by other teams or on what timeline.

stories.Headline: OVHcloud launches 55 AI cloud products hosted in Europe
stories.Summary:
OVHcloud said on Thursday that it had launched 55 cloud-computing and AI products running on infrastructure hosted in Europe, including access to Nvidia's latest AI chips and a workplace application that combines email, documents and videoconferencing with AI assistants. The French cloud provider said its data centres could take up to 60,000 of Nvidia's Blackwell chips, a capacity it said matched the largest global platforms. OVHcloud also announced partnerships with the cloud-computing company Shadow, with the search engine Qwant and with EUSP, a joint venture between Qwant and Ecosia that develops a European search index. Qwant and OVHcloud said that AI-generated summaries appearing in the search engine's results would be powered by OVHcloud's Olala model and hosted in European data centres.

The launch brings Nvidia's Blackwell chips into data centres located in Europe, and it puts the Olala model behind the AI summaries that Qwant shows in its search results. The workplace application bundles email, documents and videoconferencing together with AI assistants, and all of it runs on infrastructure hosted in Europe. The partnership with EUSP ties the launch to a European search index developed by the joint venture between Qwant and Ecosia. The capacity for up to 60,000 Blackwell chips is the figure OVHcloud gave for its data centres, and the company said that capacity matched the largest global platforms.

OVHcloud is the French cloud provider behind the products, and it described the capacity of its data centres and the reach of its partnerships in its announcement on Thursday. Qwant and OVHcloud said together that the AI-generated summaries in the search engine's results would be powered by the Olala model and hosted in European data centres. The article does not say what Shadow, Qwant or EUSP said about the partnerships beyond the statements attributed to Qwant and OVHcloud together. The article also does not give the terms of the partnerships or the prices of the products.

The move comes as European governments and companies increasingly scrutinise where AI services are operated and how their data is handled, which the article says creates opportunities for regional providers seeking to compete with US cloud and AI firms. stories.Headline: Visa expands its Agentic Ready program across Asia Pacific to scale trusted AI agent payments
stories.Summary:
Visa announced the expansion of its Agentic Ready program across Asia Pacific on November 18, 2026, to scale trusted AI commerce. This initiative focuses on strengthening acceptance for transactions initiated by AI agents, moving beyond simple product recommendations to full payment processes. IBM and AWS also released a study on November 20, 2026, regarding the modernization of enterprises to scale agentic AI. The IBM report emphasizes that modernization is the essential foundation upon which organizations must build to run agentic AI systems. These developments highlight a broader industry shift toward integrating autonomous AI agents into commercial and enterprise operational frameworks.

The Visa program launched its first phase in April 2026, focusing on issuer readiness in production environments using Visa credentials. The second phase involves over 50 participants, including acquirers, payment gateways, and merchants, with more partners expected to join throughout 2027. Over 100 issuers across 10 regional markets have already joined the program to prepare for agent-led discovery and checkout. Visa utilizes its Acceptance Platform and Intelligence Commerce Connect to support credential management, fraud protection, and dispute resolution across channels. The IBM study suggests that renovating architecture, data, decision rights, and operating models is necessary to avoid fragmented IT estates.

T.R. Ramachandran, the Head of Products and Solutions for Asia Pacific at Visa, stated that agentic commerce requires secure transactions. He explained that merchants and payment providers need a clear way to understand and strengthen their readiness for these new transactions. Ramachandran noted that the program helps the commerce ecosystem prepare for this next chapter while maintaining expected consumer trust. IBM's Vamsi Yanamadala authored a report stating that modernization is not just a box to tick before AI work starts. IBM also highlights that CAIOs can create value from enterprise-wide opportunities that individual functions might miss during transformation.

Merchants are affected because they must now determine how to recognize trusted agents and support them through post-purchase services. Partners like Adyen, Stripe, and DBS Bank are working with Visa to test agent-initiated transactions in real-world environments. Other collaborators include Atlas Kitchen, Juspay, and SHOPLINE, who explore how agents build shopping carts and connect to payments. These partners assess existing systems to identify gaps in authentication, tokenized credentials, and transaction processing for AI agents. The goal is to ensure that the payment ecosystem reflects the diverse needs of different markets and merchant environments.

Visa draws on decades of experience providing global technology and security to enable new forms of digital commerce and movement. The company operates in more than 200 countries and territories, facilitating transactions between consumers, sellers, and various government entities. IBM provides AI consulting services with over 75,000 trained consultants and offers data strategy through an architectural approach. The IBM Institute for Business Value provides data-driven predictions and studies, such as the 2026 CEO Study on transformation. These organizations are leveraging their existing infrastructure to transition from traditional digital payments and IT to agentic AI systems.

Visa continues to collaborate with its diverse range of partners to embed intelligence into commerce journeys using existing payment infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining the Agentic Ready program or collaborating on agentic commerce are encouraged to contact their Visa representative. IBM's predictions for the enterprise in 2030 aim to help business leaders prepare to win in an AI-first future. The articles leave open how specific markets will vary in their adoption of these agent-led checkout and payment interactions. It remains unclear exactly how many additional partners will join the Visa program throughout the remainder of 2027.

stories.Headline: Listed new-age firms move AI from pilots into core operations
stories.Summary:
Zetwerk, Lenskart, Eternal, Delhivery, Meesho and PhysicsWallah are among the listed new-age firms that have moved AI from pilot projects into core operations, Moneycontrol reported on November 21, 2026. The companies disclosed the shift in recent quarterly filings, covering manufacturing, retail, logistics, customer service and education. They reported gains in productivity, faster turnaround times and lower costs. Zetwerk cut the time to generate bills of materials on its tender intelligence platform ZetSpec from three to four days to around 10 minutes. Lenskart expanded remote optometry to 934 stores in India from 303 a year earlier.

Zetwerk deployed Zeus, an agentic AI platform that lets business teams build applications without relying on engineers, according to its Q2 FY27 shareholder letter. Lenskart's AI-assisted eye-testing system Drysh lets customers complete most of an examination while an optometrist supervises, and it is being piloted ahead of a wider rollout. Lenskart's AI voice assistant handles routine customer calls and escalates complex queries, improving call satisfaction scores by around 30 percent in a quarter. Eternal built Dark, a privacy-focused AI assistant running on its own infrastructure, which it plans to launch globally in 2026. Delhivery said self-hosted models fine-tuned on open-weight systems cut customer support and proof-of-delivery validation costs by more than 50 percent without compromising output quality.

Zetwerk co-founder and CEO Amrit Acharya told Moneycontrol the company has moved beyond experimentation and is looking to deploy AI across every part of the organisation. He said AI can cut order processing in sales from several days to minutes, and agentic AI lets business teams build tools independently, reducing dependence on engineering teams. Lenskart founder and CEO Peyush Bansal said AI is a powerful way to expand the profit pool, improving reliability at the same cost rather than only reducing costs. He said the company is bringing more technology in-house, including CRM, talent acquisition and HR management systems. Eternal founder Deepinder Goyal wrote that some repeat orders or restocking behaviour might shift to agentic interfaces, and that the food delivery and quick commerce businesses are protected because they coordinate fulfilment in real time and own the outcome.

Rishabh Katiyar, partner at Info Edge Ventures, said newer-age companies were early adopters because many founders and talent come from engineering backgrounds and many began experimenting two to three years ago. He said declining token costs and more accessible open-source models have turned several of those experiments into fully deployed products, primarily for internal operations. Info Edge's listed portfolio includes Eternal, the parent of Zomato and Blinkit, and PB Fintech, which operates Policybazaar and PaisaBazaar. Delhivery has deployed AI across order processing, proof-of-delivery audits, returns inspection and claims, and over the past year moved AI agents and workflows into production for delivery coordination, disruption alerts and automated checks. Delhivery said that over the last four quarters it invested in AI, initially on the software development lifecycle and technology team productivity, and is now seeing fairly material improvements.

The shift has been helped by the engineering-heavy talent base at newer-age companies and by a decline in the cost of deploying AI models. Lenskart is deploying AI across eye testing, customer service and inventory management. Eternal is using AI both to develop new products and to explore how its existing platforms could adapt to changing consumer behaviour. On Zomato and Blinkit, Goyal is evaluating how AI agents could change the way consumers place orders, particularly for repeat purchases and restocking. Delhivery's early AI work focused on the software development lifecycle and improving the productivity of its technology teams.

Lenskart's Drysh system is being piloted ahead of a wider rollout. Eternal plans to launch Dark globally in 2026. Delhivery said it is beginning to see fairly material improvements after four quarters of AI work. The articles do not give the full text of Delhivery's statement beyond that point. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Valor Energy completes Glorious Star purchase and plans $700 million Youngstown AI data center buildout
stories.Summary:
Valor Energy Inc. completed its purchase of Glorious Star, LLC, the Ohio limited liability company that owns an operational 18 MW computing center in Youngstown, Ohio, the company announced. The deal was structured as an equity acquisition and transfers 100% of the target's equity interests to Valor Energy. Glorious Star, LLC becomes a wholly-owned subsidiary of Valor Energy after the closing. Closing came after the company completed legal, financial and technical due diligence on the target. The purchase was announced on November 17, 2026, in a report by Ashish Joshi.

The Youngstown Project comprises a facility of approximately 30,888 square feet with roughly 18 megavolt-amperes of site-level apparent power capacity. That power is delivered by Ohio Edison through an existing 23kV utility interconnection, which the Company believes is approved and energized. Valor Energy plans total investment of approximately USD 700 million, deployed in phases as the project is built out. The first phase is expected to total approximately USD 200 million, and the figures do not represent committed funding. Valor Energy Inc. is a Nasdaq-listed company trading under the symbol VAI, and Green Energy Capital Asset Inc. is a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Company.

Dave Nichols, Strategic Advisor to Valor Energy Inc., said the existing utility interconnection carrying approximately 18 MVA may reduce certain development requirements relative to starting from an undeveloped site. Nichols cautioned that conversion into an AI data center will require further development work, permits and approvals, equipment and financing. He said the Company intends to pursue that development while evaluating the project's technical requirements and commercial feasibility. Nichols said closing the acquisition is an important step in pursuing Valor Energy's AI data center strategy. He added that the Company looks forward to building the project out with the local community and creating long-term value for shareholders.

Guy Coviello, president and CEO of the Youngstown/Warren Regional Chamber, called the investment a strong vote of confidence in Youngstown and the Mahoning Valley. Coviello described the site as an ideal location for a data center, noting it has operated as a heavy industrial site for decades. He said the building is largely out of sight of residential areas and the project offers a chance to reinvest in an established industrial site. Coviello said the project could help stabilize the surrounding neighborhood, create construction jobs for the skilled trades and generate new business for local companies. The Verge reported on November 18, 2026, that AI data center projects are continuing to pop up across the US with frequent opposition from locals concerned about their impact.

The Verge cited FOX 13 News reporting that data center regulation bills are coming, according to Utah's House Speaker. The Johnson County Post asked whether a small Johnson County town should ban data centers, and voters will decide. KDFW FOX 4 reported that a Red Oak data center expansion was approved despite community pushback. The Seattle Times reported that a proposed Amazon data center near Tri-Cities gets pushback from residents. Valor Energy historically ran automobile transaction and related services businesses and is now pursuing a strategic transformation into digital infrastructure, energy and other growth sectors.

Valor Energy said it intends to work closely with local officials and community partners in Youngstown on its proposed development plans. The Company stressed that its preliminary estimates remain subject to further planning, technical assessment and the availability of financing on acceptable terms. Valor Energy stated there can be no assurance it will obtain the financing necessary for any phase of the planned development. Timing, scope and the amount of each phase will depend on further design and engineering work, required permits and approvals, construction and equipment availability, project progress, financing and market conditions. The Company added that no phase is assured of completion within an anticipated timeframe, or at all.

stories.Headline: Dutch regulator warns consumers not to buy AI camera glasses after tests find dangerous errors
stories.Summary:
The Dutch Data Protection Authority officially warned consumers on Thursday, 19 November 2026, not to buy AI camera glasses after examining six types of camera glasses available in the Netherlands. The watchdog found that the glasses, which have a microphone that lets users ask questions to an AI chatbot, pose major privacy risks and can be actively dangerous because the responses are often incorrect. In one test the AP simulated an emergency in which someone was being resuscitated and asked the glasses for help, and the glasses said they had called the emergency number 112 and that an ambulance was on its way. That was an AI hallucination, because the glasses had made no such call. In other tests the glasses gave dating advice to an adult interested in a child, made errors when interpreting medication leaflets, and wrongly read the safety warning on toys.

The warning requires consumers to think carefully before buying these devices, and the AP recommended banning the glasses in sensitive locations like hospitals and sports clubs, where many organizations have already implemented such a ban. The AP had previously warned owners of AI camera glasses that secretly recording people is a crime. Monique Verdier, the AP vice-chair, said glasses that record you without your knowledge are concerning enough, but glasses that also provide incorrect advice when someone's life is at stake go a step too far. She said that while AI offers many opportunities, we must be able to trust the technology, and in the case of the camera glasses examined, such trust is currently not justified.

Civil rights organization Bits of Freedom called the new AP warning too little, too late. Evelyn Austin, the executive director of Bits of Freedom, told ANP that it is a bit like the Dutch Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority advising people not to eat a dangerous product rather than simply removing the contaminated food from the shelves. She said it is completely backwards, that the AP has one clear mandate to protect citizens by enforcing privacy laws, and that the authority is failing to do so. She said these peeping glasses should be pulled from the market.

stories.Headline: RadixArk releases DaisyRose-27B coding model trained exclusively with reinforcement learning
stories.Summary:
RadixArk released its first open-weight agentic coding model, DaisyRose-27B, during the week of November 20, 2026. This thinking model was post-trained from Qwen3.8-27B using only reinforcement learning without any distillation or supervised fine-tuning. The development process involved 18 days of training on 144 H200 GPUs, totaling 63,000 GPU-hours. This effort utilized the open-source RL framework called Miles and a specialized sandbox environment known as AgentENV.

The model features 27.8 billion dense parameters and a context window of 262,144 tokens. It requires a single GPU to run, with memory needs ranging from 23 GB for NVFP4 on Blackwell GPUs to 52 GB for BF16. The architecture maintains the Qwen3.8-27B design, including 64 decoder layers and a 27-layer vision encoder for processing images. Performance improved across seven benchmarks, most notably on Terminal Bench 4.1, where the pass@1 score rose from 5.6 to 12.0.

RadixArk developed the model using 1,200 curated tasks created with Eigent AI to address specific failures of the base model. The company stated that their internal backend achieved a 37 percent model flop utilization, which provided a two-fold speedup in throughput. They reported that their sandbox costs were approximately 80 percent lower than those of popular cloud providers. While the model leads in IFBench with a score of 82.4, the developers admitted it still trails larger mixture-of-experts models on difficult agentic tasks.

stories.Headline: Tech Talent Project urges incoming leaders to prioritize in-house technology hiring as AI reshapes public services
stories.Summary:
Following the 2026 midterms, a new class of elected officials is preparing to take office, and government technology experts say building stronger in-house technology teams should be among their top priorities. Jennifer Anastasoff, executive director of the Tech Talent Project, a nonpartisan nonprofit that helps U.S. federal and state governments recruit technology leaders, made the case in an interview with StateScoop. She said artificial intelligence, cybersecurity and major changes to federal benefits programs are putting additional pressure on government systems. Incoming state and federal leaders will need to recruit experienced technologists and give existing employees the resources to modernize how government operates, she said. Anastasoff is a founding team member of the U.S. Digital Service.

Anastasoff said 36 states held gubernatorial elections this year, and incoming governors should prioritize technology-fluent leadership across their cabinets, including chief information officers, chief data officers and potentially chief AI officers. She said agency leaders do not necessarily need to be technology experts themselves, but need enough understanding to make informed decisions and access to trusted advisers. She said states are preparing for new Medicaid and Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program requirements under H.R. 1 while managing cybersecurity threats and aging technology infrastructure. The Trump administration recently announced an optional six-month hold harmless period through June 30, 2027, allowing states to delay disenrolling or denying Medicaid coverage over new work requirements originally set to take effect on Jan 1. The Tech Talent Project recommends each state needs a dedicated data analyst embedded in state Medicaid agencies so beneficiaries do not lose access and caseworkers do not get backlogged.

Anastasoff said AI adoption requires more than hiring a chief AI officer, and governments need software engineers, data specialists, product managers and user experience experts who can evaluate whether AI-generated information is accurate and appropriate for public services. She said governments need people with the expertise to see where AI is real confident and real wrong. She said attracting those workers requires governments to rethink how they recruit, and while public-sector salaries may not compete with private industry, many technologists are motivated by public service. She said the bigger challenge is making sure qualified candidates can find positions and move through hiring processes quickly, and she urged incoming administrations to review job descriptions, recruitment systems and internal promotion opportunities early in their terms. She said many people reach out directly to say they are thinking about government, and the question is how effectively and how quickly they can be connected with the right role.

A recent report by the National Association of State Chief Information Officers found that many state AI officials lack the staffing, funding and authority needed to manage the technology across government agencies. The report found that while AI oversight has become a priority for state technology offices, establishing an AI leadership position is only the first step. The report states that when NASCIO first started tracking in 2023, less than 20 percent of states had a state chief artificial intelligence officer or a similar title. It states that just three years later, at least 46 states have identified at least one person tasked with directing artificial intelligence, and by its count 25 states have someone with AI in their title. Anastasoff said without investment, outdated systems and inefficient processes could continue to burden both government employees and residents who depend on public services.

In the Scottish Parliament on Wednesday, SNP MSP Zen Ghani asked what plans the Government had to use artificial intelligence to improve decision-making and increase efficiency as part of its public service reform agenda. Cabinet Secretary for Public Service Reform Ivan McKee said AI was being used to support human workers, not replace them, but confirmed the technology was being used to redesign services. He said public service reform is about redesigning services around people's needs, and digital services, data and technology is a key enabler through a dedicated work stream within the public service reform strategy. He said the government is scaling intelligent automation across core government and key public bodies, including identifying opportunities to pilot AI technology in public sector processes.

He said within the Scottish Government it is scaling responsible and ethical AI and automation, including the rollout of Microsoft 365 Copilot premium and developing AI agents to reduce administrative burden and support better decision-making while retaining professional judgement. Ghani pointed to figures from Skills Development Scotland which found that while 87% of businesses in Scotland now use AI in their daily practices, 74% of businesses reported no change to staff headcount. He asked how the Scottish Government intends to ensure AI is used to streamline governance and not as a tool to replace workers. McKee said the approach is to use AI to support the workforce, reducing routine administration and freeing staff to focus on what requires human judgement, expertise and empathy.

He said responsible adoption is supported by guidance in the Digital Scotland Service Manual, transparency through the mandatory Scottish AI register, and developing an AI ethics and assurance framework alongside safeguards on data protection and security, responsible procurement and investment in AI skills. Tory MSP Craig Hoy asked if the Scottish Government was considering replacing ministers with AI given how poor some are at answering questions, particularly the Cabinet Secretary for Transport, Stephen Flynn. McKee responded that this comes from a party that used AI to generate thousands upon thousands of irrelevant, trivial questions to the Government, running up an enormous bill. Douglas Lumsden, the former Tory MSP who became an MP in the Aberdeen South by-election after Flynn was elected to Holyrood, submitted around 1000 written questions to the Scottish Government in January 2025, reportedly costing around £100 each to answer, and the SNP accused Lumsden of costing the taxpayer £100k by using AI to ask nonsense questions about bees, straws and pepper sachets.

stories.Headline: Apple develops an autonomous AI agent and tightens macOS 27.3 app permissions
stories.Summary:
Apple is reportedly developing an advanced AI agent to rival OpenAI, Anthropic and Grok, according to a Bloomberg report from November 20, 2026. This new tool is designed to autonomously control devices, browse the web, write code and use various apps. The project was revealed through fresh job postings for a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant. This agent aims to function like a capable person by moving fluidly between browsers, terminals, editors and services. Apple has not yet officially confirmed the development of this autonomous AI agent to the public.

The upcoming macOS 27.3 update will change security controls by splitting Device Control and Data Access into Accessibility and System and App Protection Override. This update increases the authorization process from four steps to 14 steps, which Apple says is necessary for better security. Users will see a new transparency indicator when an app controls another app through the System and App Protection Override option. Apple is also introducing a single method for granting permissions by selecting the requested app from a provided list. New guidance will encourage users to grant access only to specific apps that need it when enabling these settings.

Mark Gurman, the executive editor of Bloomberg, stated that the brief for this agent is far beyond today's Siri. He noted that the job listing describes an agent that can write and debug code while deciding which tools to use. Apple warned app developers in a blog post that granting full disk access puts all data on a Mac at risk. The company stated it wants to balance user privacy with the utility of agents that take actions across the operating system. Apple also suggests that developers should ensure their apps gracefully handle having access to only a limited set of folders.

Some users view the increased authorization steps in macOS 27.3 as a sign of anti-competitiveness by the tech giant. AI early adopters are affected, as they have been purchasing Mac Studio and Mac mini computers to run local AI models. These users may find the new requirement to ask for permission every time access is needed to be tedious. App developers are affected and must adjust their onboarding processes to account for these new security and privacy changes. Those providing assistive technologies or disk backups can request entitlements to preserve their previous functionality.

Apple's concerns follow a claim by a journalist that the Meta Muse app read private messages without the user's consent. Another report from Wired cited a flaw in the ChatGPT Mac app that could allow hackers to access sensitive data. The company previously announced in October that it would revise security settings to protect data from the popularity of AI agents. These agents differ from chatbots because they run on devices to take actions across files and the operating system. Apple is currently benefiting from the sales of hardware used by people running their own local AI models.

Apple will implement these new security controls and transparency indicators as part of the macOS 27.3 software update. Developers must now learn to work within more granular controls and limited folder access to maintain their app functionality. The company will provide users with increased visibility into the wide range of data that apps can control or receive. The articles leave open whether Apple will officially announce the autonomous agent or when it will be released. It remains unclear if the new security steps will successfully stop the privacy risks associated with third party AI agents.

stories.Headline: Anthropic lists on Nasdaq at $1.5tn valuation and raises a record $107bn
stories.Summary:
Anthropic became a listed company on Thursday, 19 November 2026, when its shares began trading on the Nasdaq in New York. Dario Amodei, the co-founder, rang the Nasdaq MarketSite opening bell with his sister and fellow co-founder Daniela at the start of trading. The shares were priced at $83 each, above the indicated range of $70 to $78, and began trading at £111.50. The listing raised $107bn, a record sum, and the company was valued at $1.5tn at the listing price. At the opening trading price its market capitalisation reached $2tn, and only 14 months earlier it had raised money at a valuation of $183bn.

The prospectus detailed $900bn of spending commitments for computing power and infrastructure, and $26bn of the listing proceeds came from a cornerstone placement. That placement went to AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC, and the banks collected $550m of underwriting fees. Anthropic is loss-making, with projected revenues in 2026 of $50bn-ish, and tech analysts have pencilled in roughly $600bn of revenue in 2030. Nasdaq entry will be quick, but S&P 500 inclusion will take at least a year, and the company was founded five years ago.

Dario Amodei said as trading started that the company was hoping to be investment grade at some point in the future. He said: "Obviously, at some point in the future we're hoping to be investment grade," and the article noted that the price at which Anthropic borrows matters fundamentally. The prospectus said the technology "could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity". The article asked whether Anthropic, loss-making and with projected revenues in 2026 of $50bn-ish, can possibly be worth $1.5tn-plus.

The European Central Bank issued a reminder this week about how much capital is being bet on the AI revolution and how little transparency there is around the funding of hyperscalers and other suppliers. Its report said big tech firms are estimated to have total off-balance-sheet commitments of more than $4tn as of the second quarter of 2026. It warned of "historical parallels with the dotcom and sub-prime bubbles". Truist chief market strategist Keith Lerner noted that tech valuations have fallen 42% over the past year, and the sector has gone from outperforming the S&P 500 by 25% over six months to underperforming it by 6%. Bank of America's latest fund manager survey shows investors have cut tech exposure by the most since June 2006, and "Shark Tank" star Kevin O'Leary told the second article that investing in Anthropic is like investing in a young Amazon.

The second article said Thursday is supposed to be a celebration of AI, with Anthropic heading toward its long-awaited IPO at the Nasdaq. It said the very stocks that fueled this AI boom are still under pressure, pointing to sell-offs this week in CoreWeave, Salesforce and AMD. It said investors are questioning the AI spending, the valuations, the financing arrangements and whether the returns will ever justify the billions being poured into this technology. It said the AI build-out isn't disappearing, as seen from Nvidia on Tuesday, and that companies are still spending and the technology is still evolving. Lerner pointed out that previous tech pullbacks of more than 10% during this bull market were followed by an average rebound of 47%.

The first article said there was a late risk that investor sentiment towards the AI universe could be jinxed, or Jensened, by the soap opera at Nvidia. It said there was a worry that the AI bubble could burst when somebody tried to unload too much stock on the stock market in one go. It said the assembly of AI and AI-adjacent names in the cornerstone placement fed worries about the industry's circular financing. It said executives grumble that their IT budgets are finite and that nine-month-old versions, or cheaper "open weight" models from rivals, do the job for basic work. It said "commoditisation risk" could be the next year's valuation debate, and that debt, not just equity, will be a crucial part of this story.

stories.Headline: Anthropic falls 12.5% after upsized IPO as panel debates AI market reset
stories.Summary:
The Market Hang panel discussed Anthropic's IPO on Friday, November 20, 2026, with Barron's reporter Jacob Sonenshine, The Technology Letter's Tiernan Ray, Epistrophy Capital Research Chief Market Strategist Cory Johnson, and Laffer Tengler Investments CEO and Chief Investment Officer Nancy Tengler. Anthropic went public on Thursday, November 19, 2026, and the panel said the IPO was upsized and priced above its price talk. The panel said the stock opened with indications of 105, 106 and 107 before sliding, and on Friday it fell 12.5% to $85, just above the IPO price. The panel said Friday was the settlement date, so anyone who bought Anthropic on Thursday had the bill come due that day. The panel said Anthropic employees can sell up to 10% of their stake, unlike SpaceX, whose staggered lockup stopped anyone selling initially for a couple of months.

The panel said Anthropic had increased its IPO price and upsized the offering after people two weeks earlier had asked whether it would have to pull the IPO altogether. The panel said NVIDIA reported earlier in the week, projecting 75% revenue growth, and the market said it did not want that. Cory Johnson said he thinks 2022 is probably the best analog, citing an energy shock, central bank hikes and tightening liquidity visible in gold, commodities and a higher dollar. Johnson said he thinks the Fed will hike a few more times, that no cuts are coming to save the day, and that inflation has been too high for too long. Johnson said he would not be surprised to see another 10% down on the S&P.

Tiernan Ray said he hates the comparison to 2000 because the fundamentals and the IPO cycle are diametrically different, and he said the market today is healthy. Ray said a lot of companies are staying private for longer because they are getting the financing they need, which he called healthy, and many have really strong revenue growth. Ray said the first issue was positioning, and a lot of positioning that had accumulated over the past two years in crowded parts of the market had to wash out. Ray said the challenge for investors is when the institutional bid comes back, with some people needing to protect performance and others needing to chase it into year end. Ray said fundamentals and earnings growth are the ultimate arbiter of the market.

Johnson said earnings are priced too well and there is a lot more pain to come, and he said multiple compression will continue a little more as credit spreads widen. Johnson said that even if AI is amazing, which it very well may be, the market is priced for that scenario and needs to start pricing more of the left side of the distribution. Ray said Anthropic is one issue and the IPO clearly has not been the clearing event for the market that maybe would have been expected, but he called it a net benefit for the overall market. Ray said the success of frontier models will be so important to guiding the capex and future revenue of the entire AI buildout, and investors can now touch it and understand it better. Ray said there are a lot of high quality companies on fire sale right now, but no one is willing to step in with so much red on the screen for so many days in a row.

The panel said that two weeks earlier people were talking about whether Anthropic was going to have to pull their IPO altogether. The panel said Anthropic was able to go out, increase the IPO price above price talk and upsize the offering itself. The panel said the lockup is different from most traditional IPOs, and with SpaceX nobody could sell initially for a couple of months. The panel said that if you are an employee who started most five years ago, you would cash out right now, so the downward pressure is not surprising. The panel said the math that looked great yesterday looks greater today, and nothing in the underlying fundamentals or the macro thesis has changed.

The panel said the question is whether this is a healthy reset for AI, and Ray said he hopes the market will start to calm down and realize there are high quality companies on fire sale. Johnson said the Fed is not going to make a huge policy mistake, and the panel asked whether lighter Fed rhetoric could turn things around as in 2018, when the Fed did not start cutting until well into the next year. The panel said the market is still at pretty solid gains in a lot of indexes, commodities and high beta stocks for the year, and it just feels painful coming off all-time highs. The panel said the institutional bid's return is the open question heading into year end. The panel did not say what Anthropic or Dario Amodei said about his future or who could dethrone NVIDIA.

stories.Headline: Suregiant Technology expands capacity to target AI advanced packaging market
stories.Summary:
Suregiant Technology held a pre-OTC-listing earnings presentation on November 18, 2026, to discuss its growth. The company targets high-double-digit growth as its release film enters the advanced packaging market. This material is now used in mass production for the world's top five semiconductor manufacturers. The company is expanding its capacity to meet the rising demand for AI chip packaging. These developments aim to drive revenue and profit to new highs for the firm.

Taoyuan Plant 2 will start official mass production in December, with a scale 2.5 to 3 times Plant 1. The company expects a full-year capacity contribution in 2027 and an OTC listing in mid-December. The tentative public offering price is NT$438 per share for the upcoming listing on the market. Release film entered 2.5D packaging in 2024, FOPLP processes in 2025, and 3D advanced packaging in 2026. The company's first three quarters of 2026 saw earnings per share reach NT$6.35 for investors.

Chairman Yang Yun-pin stated that order visibility extends 2 to 3 years for the company. He noted that customer forecast orders have reached 5 to 6 years for their products. Yang explained that their precision coating experience allows them to provide customized samples to major manufacturers. He said the company does not rely on one customer because end customers are highly diversified. Yang believes long-term demand remains solid as the overall AI and high-end packaging megatrend continues.

Institutional investors noted that AI and high-performance computing demand is expanding the advanced packaging market. Yole Group estimates this market will grow from $46.1 billion in 2024 to $79.4 billion by 2030. First-tier manufacturers are affected as they expand capacity for molding and wafer grinding using these materials. Japanese manufacturers previously dominated this segment, but Suregiant is now capturing share through localized service capabilities. The company's products are already supplied for mass production use in first-tier advanced packaging plants.

Suregiant started in the optoelectronics industry and entered the semiconductor field in 2014 to build material expertise. The company currently focuses on two major product lines, which are release film and grinding tape. Grinding tape has been supplied to the world's top ten packaging plants for more than 12 years. Third-quarter revenue was NT$159 million, which represents an 80.76 percent increase over the previous quarter. After-tax net profit for the third quarter was NT$66.51 million, up 92.72 percent quarter-on-quarter.

A new-generation thick grinding tape is expected to begin contributing to company revenue in 2027. Official samples for a new hydrolyzable tape are expected to be sent to customers in mid-2027. This new tape may begin a gradual ramp-up in 2028 as the company's third growth leg. The articles leave open whether Taiwanese firms can continue capturing market share from Japanese material suppliers. Future performance depends on the ramp-up speed of Plant 2 and the verification of new products.

stories.Headline: Pontifical Gregorian University forum participants develop solutions for Catholic AI accountability in Rome
stories.Summary:
The Builders AI Forum, an interdisciplinary conference hosted by the Pontifical Gregorian University, held a two-day program of workshops in Rome on Nov. 5-6, 2026, aimed at identifying problems facing Catholic AI development. The forum was formed two years ago and holds annual gatherings in Rome. This year's theme was "Uniting to Shape AI Before It Shapes Us." The gathering brought together church leaders, technology developers, venture capitalists and policymakers from around the world. It took place in the same weekend that Pope Leo XIV spoke to Argentines about the "challenges posed by artificial intelligence and unregulated automation."

The conference examined the lack of human accountability within AI models, potential system biases against particular languages and cultures, and the dangers of treating machines as human persons. Participants then worked together to develop possible solutions for their communities and dioceses. The conference focused on the need for positive action in addition to technology regulations. It emphasized that forming thriving Catholic communities, building responsible and properly sourced AI tools, and calling governments and tech developers to protect human labor are essential tasks for the church today. The forum's theme framed the two-day program of workshops held at the Pontifical Gregorian University.

Matthew Harvey Sanders, founder of the forum and CEO of Longbeard, the company behind AI tools such as Magisterium AI and Vulgate, framed responsible human development of AI as a duty for the church in his opening address. He quoted Leo and called Catholic developers to fill the gaps of agency, instances where AI lacks human oversight and accountability, that are often created by AI developers. Sanders said a machine that can be blamed is a convenient place for everyone above it to leave the blame. He said that before any parish, school or hospital lets an agent act for a person, someone must be able to stop it, and someone must answer for it. Sanders presented a vision for "digitizing the church's patrimony and universalizing access to it" that he has worked to implement through Longbeard's AI products.

Cardinal Michael Czerny, who heads a Vatican commission on artificial intelligence, used an image from Magnifica Humanitas contrasting two biblical construction sites, Babel and Jerusalem, as examples of different ways that technology can be developed. He said both are collective efforts, yet the manner of constructing and the outcome are very different in the two sites. Czerny said the difference between Babel and Jerusalem lies in the desire that guides the act of building. He said the contrast between the two cities presents today's primary question: out of what desire shall we build, deploy and employ artificial intelligence? Sanders told the National Catholic Reporter that he sees AI as an "unfortunate means" to evangelize the world, emphasizing that building authentic Christian community is the ultimate goal.

Sanders said he does not think Catholic AI should need to exist, and that if everyone were well formed and living in good, vibrant Catholic communities, pressing fundamental existential questions would get answered by osmosis. He said the only reason they decided they needed to develop Catholic AI was that they could see a wave of interest in the Catholic faith and were not prepared for the scale. He said their thinking was AI could be a really good instrument in the short term to help ensure people get answers to fundamental questions, but then they need to get this person into community. In his closing speech, Sanders encouraged participants not to stand idle in the face of AI's challenges, but to take action in building communities and technologies that uphold and promote human dignity. Sanders said that a year ago, Pope Leo prayed that this forum's work would bear fruit, and that fruit is something you can see and hold, and it feeds someone.

Leo's encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas, called AI "a valuable tool ... [that] calls for a measured and vigilant approach." Leo warned tech developers to "embed values in their projects with due seriousness: with transparency, responsibility toward affected communities and careful attention to ensuring that what is being cultivated is a genuine good." Leo's Nov. 6-17 Latin America trip included a stop in Argentina, where he spoke to representatives of the country's work community about the dignity of labor and the dangers of encroaching technology.

On Nov. 8, the pope addressed workers, business and trade union leaders, and teachers and students at the Catholic University of Argentina in Buenos Aires. Leo reminded the crowd of "the dignity of the human person ... [who] is the author, the center and the goal of all economic and social life." Leo warned that "the challenges posed by artificial intelligence and unregulated automation can put countless jobs at risk and become a real threat to proper integral human development."

The pope's address came as Argentina's Congress considers legislation submitted by the Javier Milei administration that would grant legal recognition to companies operated solely by AI. Milei's proposed legislation comes after an announcement last October that a massive AI data center project, Stargate Argentina, will be constructed in Patagonia. The articles leave open what the forum's participants will do with the solutions they developed for their communities and dioceses. They also leave open the outcome of Argentina's Congress consideration of the Milei administration's legislation on companies operated solely by AI.

stories.Headline: Ranjana Kumari and Karuna Nain say parents need trust not tech expertise to keep children safe with AI
stories.Summary:
Ranjana Kumari and Karuna Nain wrote an article on November 19, 2026, about keeping children safe while using artificial intelligence. They explained that parents do not need to be technology experts to guide their children through these digital tools. The authors argued that the foundations of parenting apply to the online world just as they do offline. They emphasized that trust and open communication are more important than mastering every new piece of software. Children need adults who will listen to them even when the technology involved is not fully understood.

The authors mentioned that OpenAI has introduced parental controls and age-appropriate safeguards for teens using the ChatGPT platform. These specific tools allow families to manage selected settings and set quiet hours to limit the use of AI. The articles also list eight future career options, including AI engineers, robotics engineers, data scientists, and machine learning engineers. These roles require skills in mathematics, science, and programming to develop facial recognition, smart assistants, and automated machines. Robotics engineers specifically work in sectors like manufacturing, healthcare, space exploration, and agriculture to design and program robots.

Ranjana Kumari, director of the Centre for Social Research, and Karuna Nain, director of StopNCII.org, provided these perspectives. They stated that parents should encourage children to question AI answers and recognize that systems can sound confident without being correct. The authors noted that children must feel safe disclosing problems without fearing that their phones will be confiscated. They argued that parental guidance should make it easier for children to report issues rather than making it harder. The authors believe that the real measure of success is whether children feel able to turn to trusted adults.

The articles state that children are affected because AI can provide inaccurate information or create manipulative and confusing interactions. Some children may stay silent about problems if they believe their online activity will be punished by their parents. The text notes that this is particularly important in India, where families have very different levels of digital literacy. Some parents have the resources to explore tools, while others navigate these technologies in languages that are poorly served. These children need multiple sources of protection so the entire burden of safety does not rest on one parent.

The background provided explains that AI is rapidly changing how people live, learn, and work through voice assistants and smart devices. It is defined as the ability of computer systems to perform tasks like image recognition and language comprehension. Children already engage with AI through recommendation systems, chatbots, and classroom projects to develop curiosity and problem solving abilities. Early exposure to these tools helps students become more comfortable with changing work environments and new digital tools. Understanding the technology allows children to use these tools responsibly rather than acting as simple consumers of technology.

Next, governments must establish clear expectations and ensure that safety safeguards are implemented across all artificial intelligence platforms. Schools need to help children develop critical thinking and digital literacy while providing practical guidance that parents can use. Technology companies must build age-appropriate experiences, protect privacy, and provide accessible reporting mechanisms to act on foreseeable risks. The articles leave open how specific guidance will be made available to families with limited digital access and resources. They also leave open how the balance of responsibility between parents, companies, and governments will be managed in the future.
