stories.Headline: AI chip developers shift HBM production to a shared design and manufacturing model
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA unveiled its Custom HBM platform called NVHBM in August 2026 to integrate into the NVLink Fusion lineup for AI accelerators. This new platform will be deployed in NVIDIA's own Feynman GPU and also within AWS's Trainium 4 AI hardware. In October, Marvell presented a system for custom HBM at the OCP Global Summit to discuss new design tradeoffs. This shift moves the industry from a memory maker led model toward a three way division of labor for production. Memory makers like Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron previously controlled both the design and manufacturing of the entire HBM stack.

The new layout moves the memory controller into a custom base die beneath each DRAM stack instead of on the XPU. A narrower die to die physical interface replaces the wide HBM interface at the XPU edge to connect the components. Marvell estimates this change provides up to 25 percent more compute area and room for 33 percent more HBM stacks. Memory interface power could be 70 percent lower, while adaptive power management reduces interface power by 75 percent under normal workloads. These changes shift base die production to advanced logic processes, which increases the importance of TSMC in the supply chain.

Marvell stated that no single company can build custom HBM alone because it requires a coordinated effort from several partners. They argued that the base die, die to die interface, and package thermals must be co designed as one system. Marvell noted that the die to die PHY is a heat hotspot, making package cooling a central design constraint. They suggested using silicon heat paths, copper to copper hybrid bonding, or coolant channels etched into silicon to manage heat. Marvell also mentioned that adaptive power management can reduce interface power by 42 percent during periods of peak traffic.

AI chip developers are evaluating custom HBM because standard HBM must prioritize compatibility, which leaves limited room for individual accelerator optimization. GPU and ASIC designers are now helping define the foundation of HBM, which affects how these critical AI components function. IBM Technology's Kaoutar El Maghraoui explained that some workloads are limited by memory bandwidth rather than by the available computing capacity. This means adding more compute area may not speed up tasks if data movement remains the primary bottleneck for workloads. Marvell cited a Samsung study showing internal thermal resistance accounts for 57 percent of the HBM stack's total resistance.

HBM has traditionally been the home turf for memory makers who controlled everything from DRAM dies to the bottom base die. Marvell estimates HBM now takes up roughly 30 percent of a typical AI accelerator die area in the current market. At 2026 memory prices, HBM accounts for more than half of the total cost of a typical XPU AI accelerator. The roofline model and arithmetic intensity are used to distinguish whether a workload is constrained by compute or memory bandwidth. Samsung's thermal study also found that internal thermal resistance accounts for 13 percent of the total for an adjacent ASIC.

Custom HBM appears to be on the final stretch toward mass production as developers continue to evaluate these new design options. For next generation HBM running above 28 Gbps, Marvell expects the heat flux to exceed 2.0 watts per square millimeter. Marvell relays a projection that internal temperatures in 16 high HBM stacks will exceed the thermal budget by the year 2028. TrendForce will provide more insights on HBM and custom ASICs at the Roadshow Japan 2026 event in Tokyo on December 8. The articles leave open how fast CPO will scale and how a split US China market will reshape 2027 servers.

stories.Headline: Ouray County commissioners approve the county's first AI policy for employees
stories.Summary:
Ouray County commissioners on Tuesday approved the county's first-ever artificial intelligence policy, the Ouray County Plaindealer reported on November 18, 2026. The guidelines restrict employee use of AI and require training, and they take effect for county employees starting in January. The story was reported by James Hanlon and Gabrielle Porter. The approval came at a Tuesday commissioners meeting. The policy covers how county employees use artificial intelligence tools in their work.

The policy gives Ouray County employees new guardrails for AI use beginning in January. It is the county's first AI policy. It restricts employee use of the tools. It requires training for employees. The commissioners approved it on Tuesday.

Pittsylvania County Schools superintendent Steve Mayhew said the goal is a human-centered policy that is ethical and equitable, protects users and the school division, and provides adequate training for those most in need of it. He said the goal is also for students to develop important life skills and succeed academically without using AI to do the work, while balancing digital literacy and education. He said people use AI for a lot of things and that it is a tool but not supposed to be used instead of creativity. He suggested forming a taskforce on AI and its regulation made up of teachers, principals, division administrators, parents and potentially a school board member. Emily Reynolds, chief information technology officer with Pittsylvania County Schools, said students do not have access to AI and teachers only have access right now to MagicSchool, which is geared toward instructional purposes.

Kevin Mills, Westover district representative, was concerned with AI's reputation for spitting out erroneous information or producing information that aligned with user bias, telling individuals what they want to hear rather than strict facts, and said use of the technology could mislead students trying to use it as a study aid. Mark Shields, school board chair and Chatham-Blairs district representative, said his biggest concern with AI in schools was growing reports of students using AI programs such as ChatGPT to write essays. Kelly Merricks, Dan River district representative, pointed out that if teachers give students assignments to complete on the spot during class, it gives educators the chance to recognize students' authentic work, and that familiarity makes it easier to spot a student's use of artificial intelligence to complete essays or other assignments. The impacts and implications of AI relate not only to students but also to educators. Privacy and security are two major concerns in the dialogue surrounding AI in schools, staff said.

Pittsylvania County Schools has joined other school divisions in Virginia and across the nation in contending with the rise of artificial intelligence and its impacts within the education realm. Division administrators acknowledged that AI is not going anywhere and that school divisions have to craft policy and regulation around its usage, seeking to be strategic, careful and responsible as the technology changes many aspects of life and education. PCS has kept tight reins on unrolling AI in the division so far, administrators said, and that has been much to their benefit as other school divisions in the Commonwealth are trying to rein the technology in. The issue is something IT directors in school divisions everywhere are talking about, Reynolds said. Within MagicSchool, teachers can create AI-resistant assignments for students, and Reynolds said that really is the way, the push, to go, rather than trying to determine whether or not AI was utilized, to teach teachers how to build assignments that are more resistant to a student putting a prompt into a chat bot and getting some type of output of an assignment from that.

While programs do exist where teachers could upload content to see whether it has AI-generated components or not, Reynolds said even that gets murky, because effectively it is AI telling users whether something was AI generated. In the broader education realm, proposals have been made to begin introducing digital citizenship to students beginning in Kindergarten, effectively starting to teach five-year-olds about AI, computer technology and responsible use, and the premise of this push would level up digital literacy and AI education through the grade levels. Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, in part of her administration's recently announced Moving Virginia Forward agenda, aims to target finding a better balance that limits student screen time in school and encourages use of more traditional educational methods where possible, and this agenda is set to get in motion in 2027, per the governor's office. The memo reads that the agenda would require school divisions to minimize unnecessary student screen time, prioritize teacher-led and high-quality instruction, and regularly assess and develop plans to reduce excessive or low-value use of instructional technology. Adopting an AI policy was the first official step into the fray, and regulation and implementation will follow that baseline as the situation develops.

The Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors approved a policy Tuesday governing the safe, ethical and transparent use of artificial intelligence technologies across county government. The policy establishes standards, responsibilities and governance requirements for AI systems developed by the county, procured from outside vendors or accessed through third-party platforms. According to a board letter from the county's chief executive officer, AI technologies are increasingly used across county departments to enhance service delivery, improve operational efficiency and support data driven decision making, and as these technologies advance it is critical for the county to maintain clear governance structures, safeguard sensitive information and ensure that AI is deployed responsibly and ethically. The policy requires county departments to follow its terms.

stories.Headline: Viz.ai and rural health group run AI education events for hospitals
stories.Summary:
Viz.ai, an artificial intelligence disease detection and care coordination platform, entered a partnership with the National Rural Health Association about seven months before HLTH 2026, which the organizations marked at the conference in November 2026. Viz.ai Chief Clinical Officer Andrew Ibrahim discussed the collaboration with Fierce Healthcare at HLTH, describing its first year and his goals as it approaches the one-year mark. Since the partnership began in April, the two organizations have held three educational events for rural health systems. These sessions aim to show rural health administrators the specifics of AI tools and help them decide whether to adopt such technology.

Ibrahim said many rural hospitals lack the information technology expertise and infrastructure to adopt some AI tools, and he described the partnership as a force function to strengthen their hub and spoke relationships. He said it has been beautiful to see those relationships strengthened with the AI tool as the conduit, giving the hospitals a reason to interact more and a way to build their capabilities. In addition to the educational series, frameworks are in development to help rural health systems navigate, implement and deploy AI, and those frameworks will be built into a toolkit. One of Ibrahim's personal goals for the partnership's one-year mark is to ensure any rural health administrator can understand what an AI tool is when it is pitched to them. He said getting to 100% of hospitals at year one would be ideal but probably unrealistic, calling it the ultimate goal.

For measuring the collaboration, Ibrahim said he is looking for numbers showing that participants are keeping more care local and retaining their workforces. He said it would be great to connect the dots and understand whether adoption of an AI tool gives rural clinicians confidence, enthusiasm and a willingness to stay in their community rather than dropping services and moving back. Ibrahim also pointed to a new Viz.ai partnership with Wolters Kluwer Health to integrate the Viz.ai One platform into UpToDate Expert AI, which he said has disproportionate benefit in rural communities. He said he is excited about bringing that level of clinical decision support into rural hospitals.

stories.Headline: Legora adds Teams legal intake and Microsoft 365 AI search
stories.Summary:
Legora added legal request intake in Microsoft Teams and AI search across Outlook and Calendar to its Microsoft 365 offering, and the features are now generally available, IT Brief Australia reported on 20 November 2026. Staff can submit legal requests by tagging @Legora in Teams, while lawyers can search relevant email and meeting context from Microsoft 365 as they prepare responses and next steps. Existing user permissions remain in place when lawyers use the tools. The update expands Legora's existing Microsoft integrations, which include SharePoint, OneDrive and a plug-in for Copilot for Legal. It is intended to reduce the time legal teams spend gathering background material from chats, inboxes, calendars and documents before they can begin substantive work.

Legora's Teams intake tool allows a request to begin in the collaboration platform and flow into its legal workflow, and lawyers can then use the Microsoft 365 search function within Legora to identify relevant emails and calendar information linked to the matter. Lawyers can use that context to help draft a response and prepare follow-up actions, and check source material as needed. Legora's SharePoint integration remains in beta and allows the system to use stored documents to support agreement review and save edits back to SharePoint as a new version. Its plug-in for Copilot for Legal is generally available and allows users to begin legal work from Microsoft 365 Copilot. Legora said its products are used by more than 140,000 legal professionals at more than 2,500 law firms and in-house legal teams across more than 80 markets.

Max Junestrand, Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder of Legora, said legal work is shifting from executing tasks to directing them and standing behind the results. He said that only holds up if requests arrive with context and stay inside the controls legal teams already trust. He said that with Microsoft, Legora is making that possible, so legal professionals can spend more of their time on the judgment their stakeholders depend on them for. Tom Quoroll, Partner at Linklaters, said ensuring that its use of AI enhances the quality that Linklaters' clients expect is central to its strategy. Quoroll said Legora's integration with the wealth of Microsoft 365 context transforms its lawyers' ability to leverage that data, and that Linklaters is excited to connect two of the most powerful tools in its technology stack.

Samer Abu-Ltaif, President, Microsoft EMEA, said Legora is a great example of the bold AI innovation changing how legal work gets done, and that Microsoft is proud to help bring its solutions to lawyers around the world. He said Microsoft's customers want AI that works where they already work, and that Legora helps legal teams move from intake to finished work with relevant organizational context, ensuring enterprise security and governance. He said it is a clear example of how Microsoft's partner ecosystem turns AI into real impact. Linklaters, which uses the software, said the integration could help its lawyers make more direct use of information held within Microsoft 365. In practice, legal requests often reach in-house teams and law firms through several channels at once, including chat messages, emails and meetings, and supporting material may then sit across Outlook inboxes, calendar entries and document libraries, requiring lawyers to re-enter requests, forward files or create copies in separate systems.

Profound announced Profound for Microsoft Teams and Microsoft 365, together with new integrations that connect Your AI Marketer in Profound to SharePoint, OneDrive, Outlook and Microsoft Work IQ, GlobeNewswire reported from New York on 19 November 2026. By mentioning @Profound in a channel or messaging it directly, teams can ask what changed in their AI Search visibility, accuracy and citation share, why it changed, and what to do about it. From the same Teams message, they can create and run agents or start a new Profound Project, then use the Open project button to jump directly to the work, and they can also open direct-message conversations in Profound to continue working there. Your AI Marketer in Profound can find and read files in SharePoint and OneDrive, create and edit Word and Excel documents, bring selected SharePoint content into a Profound Knowledge Base and Context Manager, read email and write drafts in the connected user's Outlook mailbox, send completed reports from Outlook, and draw on a user's Microsoft 365 work context through Microsoft Work IQ. Everything Profound produces is reviewed and approved by the team before it goes live.

James Cadwallader, CEO and Co-founder of Profound, said marketing teams should not have to leave the conversation to get an answer or get work moving. He said Microsoft 365 is where much of that work already happens, so building on it was the natural choice, and that Your AI Marketer in Profound sits alongside the team, works from the content they already have and hands back results where they will be used. Sujeet Meha, VP of Teams Engineering, Microsoft, said AI is most useful when people can put it to work in the tools they already rely on. He said Profound's integration with Microsoft Teams and Microsoft 365 gives marketing teams a way to connect their AI marketing workflows with the conversations, documents and information they use every day, and that it is a practical example of how companies can extend Microsoft 365 to help people get more done. Profound for Microsoft Teams is available now to customers with an active Profound subscription and can be installed directly from the Microsoft Marketplace.

stories.Headline: Dell and Microsoft expand private cloud partnership to run enterprise AI inference on Nvidia HGX B300 systems
stories.Summary:
Dell Technologies and Microsoft expanded their private cloud partnership to support enterprise AI workloads on Nvidia HGX B300 systems, targeting organizations that want to run inference closer to sensitive data. The integration combines Dell infrastructure, Nvidia's HGX accelerated computing platform and Microsoft's Azure Local and Foundry Local software. It gives enterprises another option for deploying AI workloads outside public cloud environments while retaining control over data processing and infrastructure. The market opportunity is hybrid infrastructure, not a retreat from cloud services. Dell announced new additions to its Dell AI Factory with NVIDIA, extending a portfolio it says now includes more than 420 offerings and serves more than 6,500 customers.

Microsoft announced at its Ignite conference Nov. 17 that Foundry Local is generally available on Azure Local, and confirmed expanded Azure Local hardware support for Nvidia HGX B300 systems, enabling large-scale, multi-GPU inference and agentic workloads. Microsoft identified Dell, HPE and Lenovo as hardware partners with validated systems but did not provide specific delivery dates for those configurations. In IDC's June 2026 Worldwide Digital Infrastructure Sentiment Survey, 85% of enterprises said their AI workloads require both on-premises and public cloud infrastructure, according to Dave McCarthy, group vice president for cloud and data centers at IDC. Sovereignty and latency each influenced 51% of respondents, ahead of cost at 42%, McCarthy said. In IDC's June survey, 73% of respondents said AI infrastructure complexity delays the move to production, McCarthy said.

McCarthy said enterprises are rebalancing and public cloud stays in the mix. Steven Dickens, CEO and principal analyst at HyperFrame Research, said tokenomics and sovereignty concerns are driving a hybrid AI model, and that open-weight models give enterprises more deployment choices while organizations seek greater control over data and AI costs. McCarthy said IDC expects sovereign private cloud to be among the fastest-growing private cloud segments through 2028, and identified Azure Local as a platform scaling to support GPU-based sovereign inference, with Dell among its validated hardware partners. McCarthy said the Dell-Microsoft integration simplifies some of the companies' infrastructure layers, including lifecycle management, firmware coordination and support. Holger Mueller, vice president and principal analyst at Constellation Research, said integrated platforms also reduce implementation work and eliminate integration risks that enterprises would otherwise have to manage themselves.

Mueller said that does not remove the need for IT teams to manage capacity, optimize workloads and maintain the underlying infrastructure, and that the value of an integrated platform depends on how much operational work it actually removes. McCarthy said on-premises infrastructure makes economic sense when inference workloads are large, steady and predictable, and that for large and frontier models running sustained workloads, IDC finds on-premises total cost of ownership can be significantly lower than cloud infrastructure as a service once power, cooling and facilities costs are included. Mueller said organizations that understand their capacity requirements can often run workloads cheaper on owned infrastructure, but that many enterprises are still determining which AI workloads they will run and how much computing capacity those applications will need. Mueller said there is some doubt these can be reasonably sized at the current state of AI adoption in the enterprise. Mueller also cautioned against treating data sovereignty as the primary reason to move AI workloads on premises, saying public cloud providers offer data controls and the commercial advantage of running workloads in a particular environment remains the more important consideration.

Deploying AI locally gives enterprises greater control over workload placement, but it also makes them responsible for operating the infrastructure supporting those applications, including GPU capacity, storage, networking, power and cooling, along with the software needed to manage model execution and infrastructure utilization. For regulated organizations, control over data processing and workload placement can influence infrastructure decisions, and financial services, healthcare and government organizations face requirements governing where data resides and how they process it. Azure Local provides the infrastructure platform for running workloads in customer-controlled environments, and Foundry Local enables organizations to deploy and run AI models locally, keeping inference close to enterprise data. The expanded architecture brings Nvidia HGX B300 accelerated computing into Microsoft's Azure Local environment through validated hardware partners, including Dell. The broader Dell AI Factory architecture includes modular infrastructure built around Dell PowerStore, Dell PowerEdge XE9785 systems with NVIDIA HGX B300 GPUs, and Dell-supported NVIDIA AI Enterprise software.

Dell's announcements focus on four areas: data preparation for AI, management software for AI infrastructure, partner-built validated solutions, and new storage options for large AI workloads, intended to help companies move agentic AI projects from pilot stages into production. Among the additions is Agentic Data Gateway, which Dell says gives AI agents a single governed route to enterprise data and context, and in internal testing reusing context reduced token consumption by as much as 76% and increased answer accuracy from 60% to 94%. Dell is also adding hybrid data pipeline orchestration so pipelines can run where data already sits, including on-premises private clouds, Dell AI Factory with NVIDIA environments, non-Dell systems and public clouds, intended to reduce the need to move large unstructured datasets between environments. Dell is expanding its Exascale portfolio with a liquid-cooled 2OU platform supporting up to 32 NVMe drives and a 1U platform offering 67% higher drive density per rack unit than the previous generation, and says software-defined PowerScale on Dell Exascale has achieved NVIDIA-Certified Storage validation at the Foundation level. Dell introduced Dell OpenManage Rack Scale, which it says can manage up to 100,000 devices, up from 8,000 in the previous generation, and Dell Fabric Manager, which internal lab analysis found could cut Day-2 operational effort by up to 80% while maintaining a fully accurate device inventory.

stories.Headline: Guidepoint partners with Rogo to bring cited expert transcripts into AI financial research
stories.Summary:
Guidepoint announced a partnership with Rogo on Nov. 19, 2026, in New York, NY, according to a GlobeNewswire release. The partnership lets bankers and investors using Rogo access Guidepoint Library insights, including more than 150,000 compliance-reviewed expert transcripts. Answers that draw on Guidepoint content are cited to the original conversation. Guidepoint described itself as a global pioneer in access to expert insight. Rogo was described as the leading AI operating system for financial services and a trusted partner to the world's most prestigious financial institutions.

Through the Guidepoint MCP connector, Guidepoint clients who use Rogo can access Library insights from vetted Advisors in the same platform where they build comps, models, memos, and pitchbooks. The Guidepoint Library includes more than 150,000 compliance-reviewed transcripts of moderated conversations with vetted Advisors, and more than 5,000 new expert interviews are added every month. Guidepoint curates the content around topics relevant to clients' research needs, helping deal teams and investors screen opportunities, evaluate theses, and prepare client deliverables. Every transcript is compliance-reviewed, and Guidepoint implements custom compliance controls tailored to each firm's requirements. The connector is available now to Guidepoint clients using Rogo, who can contact their Guidepoint account team or email the address given.

Ameesh Shah, Chief Commercial Officer of Guidepoint Insights at Guidepoint, said it was clear from the first conversation that Rogo and Guidepoint share a commitment to reliable insight grounded in the firsthand experience of vetted practitioners. Shah said combining the strengths streamlines critical workflows, reduces everyday friction, and helps clients get answers faster. Shah said the partnership creates a more unified experience that helps users focus on what matters most. Strib Walker, Head of Product at Rogo, said some of the most valuable insights in finance come from people who have operated the businesses and navigated the markets customers are analyzing. Walker said the partnership brings that expertise directly into Rogo so teams can incorporate firsthand industry perspectives from diligence to investment decisions without interrupting workflows.

The partnership overview lists expert perspectives from vetted Advisors with direct operating, customer, and competitor experience. It lists traceable answers, where Guidepoint-informed answers in Rogo cite the original transcript, which users can open to validate the answer. It lists compliance review of every transcript and custom compliance controls tailored to each firm's requirements. It lists insights built into existing workflows, appearing where bankers and investors already work with no need to switch tools. The partnership is part of Guidepoint's broader effort to make its expert research available across the AI platforms and workflows its clients rely on, and Guidepoint is backed by a global network of more than 2M+ subject-matter experts serving institutional investors, consulting firms, and corporations.

Guidepoint announced Guidepoint MCP on Nov. 17, 2026, in New York, NY, a connector bringing its expert transcript Library and Advisor Network into AI platforms research teams already use. Guidepoint MCP connects Guidepoint360 to Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity, and is built on the Model Context Protocol, an open standard for connecting data sources to AI applications. Guidepoint CEO Albert Sebag said AI has made public information easy to access but firsthand practitioner insight is still the hard part. Sebag said a general-purpose AI assistant may draw on public filings, news, and web content but does not usually have access to firsthand practitioner perspectives. Sebag said a standalone research platform can provide primary research but may require teams to work in a separate environment, and Guidepoint MCP bridges both gaps subject to the firm's own entitlements and compliance protocols.

Guidepoint MCP capabilities include seamless AI incorporation, full source attribution tracing every answer to the source transcript in Guidepoint360 with a complete audit trail, compliance by design configurable to client-specific controls and topic restrictions, and a compounding dataset with 150,000+ transcripts now and 5,000+ added every month. An analyst can pull up the full transcript to confirm a quote or paraphrase, read the surrounding conversation for context, and reference the source in an investment committee memo or client deliverable. Teams can search their own completed consultations and query those transcripts in one place, subject to their permissions. Clients can pull up open projects, see Advisors submitted to them, read screening answers, filter by responses, check availability, and request or decline a consultation with a confirmation before each step. Clients can also ask about upcoming curated insights and register for roundtables, teleconferences, and moderated calls without leaving the workflow.

Sebag said one challenge researchers face is the friction of working in multiple AI environments, and he called Guidepoint MCP the first end-to-end workflow facilitator to interface with all the major existing AI platforms. Sebag said it is designed to work from a 360-degree vantage point, handling curation and selection of the right experts, booking them, and gathering the research. Guidepoint said its network of more than two million subject-matter experts serves institutional investors, consulting firms, and corporations across companies, markets, and trends. Guidepoint said it embeds expert knowledge into decision-making through live, asynchronous, and agentic workflows. The articles leave open the terms of the partnership and any further platforms Guidepoint MCP may connect to.

stories.Headline: Paul Meinshausen says a personal AI agent grades marketing messages more ruthlessly than he would
stories.Summary:
Paul Meinshausen, Head of Agentic Decisioning at MoEngage and Co-Founder of Aampe, asked Meta's Muse to check his notifications from marketing brands while listening to a conference talk in New York. He loaded up the personal AI agent because he was curious whether brands were responding to customers who now have software reading on their behalf. The verdict was harsher than he expected, and he said it gave a rundown on them that was sort of even more ruthless than he would have. He shared the experiment in a conversation with CX Today, published on 20 November 2026. For marketers, that small experiment points to a bigger problem, because if a customer's agent is reviewing every message, relevance stops being a nice-to-have.

Meinshausen said executives have long had human assistants who watch over their affairs even more obsessively than they do themselves, and agents are now making that available to everyone. He said most people are not just a professional in their job, they are also a parent or a partner or family member and a friend, and they give each task a small amount of focus, whereas an agent can spend far longer on a single decision. He said the expectation for detail, for relevance, and for personalization is just a lot higher, and that it is a good thing, but it just means that the rate of work has increased as well for everybody involved. He called messaging across every channel the previous wave of automation, where the aim was just to make machines do things. He defined intelligent activity as the ability to take an action, observe a result, and then update the action.

Meinshausen said activity should be intelligent activity, and that for marketers this means giving agents a way to read the response, not only the authority to send. He pointed to a much wider set of signals before and after a purchase, including how customers read material, how they click around, and direct feedback such as whether something was relevant. He compared it to everyday use of tools like ChatGPT, where people learn to prompt and then correct the system, and said businesses need their agents to be correctable in the same way, sometimes directly and explicitly and sometimes indirectly and kind of implicitly. He said one form of response can be a negative form, saying I don't like this, unsubscribing, or not responding when you kind of were expected to respond, and those are really important to learn from. He said the agent that over-messages is the one that ignores those signals.

CX Today has previously explored how suppression and next-best actions can reduce personalization fatigue, and the principle is similar. Meinshausen sees AI decisioning arriving quickly in lifecycle and CRM marketing, and spreading into orchestration and content production. He admitted there is too much to do, so teams will need to prioritize and calibrate which adoption decisions they make first. He was clear on one point, that there is definitely no time to do nothing. He suggested marketers consider how a customer's agent would grade their last week of messages and what it would say.

Genesys launched Standalone AI Agents and Genesys Arena on 18 November 2026 for organisations that want to deploy agentic AI in customer service without replacing their existing systems. Standalone AI Agents lets organisations deploy the Genesys Cloud Agentic Virtual Agent within existing customer service environments in a few days, without first migrating more widely to Genesys Cloud. The software can operate within defined business rules and hand an interaction to a human employee, along with the conversation context, if a request needs further expertise. Genesys Arena is built around prebuilt Agent Kits covering more than 50 industry-specific scenarios, and teams can create a functional AI agent in as little as 10 minutes before customising it with natural language and deploying it into Genesys Cloud. The announcement includes a new pricing structure that groups interactions into simple, moderate or complex tasks and measures usage in Experience Units, the new name for what Genesys previously called AI Tokens.

Tony Bates, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer at Genesys, said enterprises want to move faster with AI but need the flexibility to do it on their own terms without compromising trust and governance. Bates said that with Standalone AI Agents, Genesys Arena and a new effort-based pricing model, the company is giving organisations more choice in how they put agentic AI to work today and scale it as their needs evolve. Youssef Nokta, Senior Vice President of AI Forward Deployed Engineering at Genesys, said AI is advancing quickly and enterprises shouldn't have to start from zero every time they want to put a new idea to work. Nokta said Genesys Arena gives teams a practical head start so they can spend less time on the foundational work and more time shaping AI around their customers, business and the results they want to achieve. Each Agent Kit includes a working model with prebuilt knowledge, integrations, skills and guardrails for a given use case, according to Genesys.

Voice customisation tools are due to be added to Arena and the Genesys Cloud platform, letting organisations choose and adapt how AI agents sound by adjusting personality, tone and delivery using natural language prompts. Genesys cited Charles Sturt University as an existing user of its agentic virtual agent technology, and Michael Buttsworth, Associate Director, Student Experience Service Centre at the university, said using Genesys Agentic Virtual Agent has shown them how AI can improve the customer experience and drive efficiency by resolving more interactions autonomously. Buttsworth said getting that value into production depends on how quickly teams can move from an idea to an experience that works in the real world, and that Genesys Arena and Agent Kits will make that path easier. Mila D'Antonio, Principal Analyst, Customer Engagement at Omdia, said enterprises are under pressure to move agentic AI from experimentation into production quickly, but they aren't all starting from the same place, with some operating in the cloud while others navigate complex hybrid or on-premises environments. D'Antonio said Genesys Arena and Genesys Standalone AI Agents give organisations different paths to deploy agentic AI based on their existing environment and requirements, and the introduction of effort-based pricing highlights how commercial models are evolving.

Genesys said Standalone AI Agents are generally available now, while Agent Kits through Genesys Arena are due to become generally available later this month. Insight launched an online Agent Store for business customers, now generally available in 14 countries, offering a catalogue of AI agents, platforms and related services designed to automate routine work across business functions. Customers can deploy the tools in days or weeks rather than months, either as standalone products or alongside consulting, implementation and managed services. The launch adds six new agentic products to Insight's AI portfolio, bringing the total in its library to 15, and nine products were introduced earlier this year. Products listed in the store include Insight AI Flight Academy, focused on training and change management, and TokenScope, which tracks token usage and AI consumption costs for finance teams.

Insight said the offerings were first developed for clients or used internally in areas including security, finance and legal. New products available at launch include Quote Advisor, which assesses pricing, inventory, freight and contract requirements to produce sourced quotes, NDA Review Agent, designed to review non-disclosure agreements against a company's legal policies, and Parts Order Assist, which helps warehouse, maintenance and field staff search catalogues and place parts orders. Jack Azagury, Chief Executive Officer of Insight, said organisations are feeling the pressure to move AI from isolated pilots into production, and that as Client Zero, Insight has built a repeatable approach proven first across its own organisation. Azagury said that having driven over 90% internal AI adoption, Insight knows firsthand what it takes to deploy and scale agentic AI rapidly and responsibly, and that combining the solutions offered in Agent Store with its consulting and managed services expertise empowers clients to move from hype to how with AI. Culligan International is the first external customer to implement Flight Academy, according to Insight, and the water services company is using a mix of AI tools including Microsoft Copilot, Cowork, Copilot Studio, Azure and Microsoft Fabric while putting governance in place around cost and responsible use.

Laura Walsh, Global Chief Information Officer of Culligan International, said at Culligan they believe technology doesn't transform a company, people do, and that generative AI adoption is far ahead of the learning curve, so it is their responsibility to arm teams with the best tools to lead now into the future. Walsh said that with partners at Insight, Culligan has prioritised AI education so teams can confidently leverage AI productively and responsibly, and that they are leveraging Insight's best practice and have established a functional champ. The deployment centres on workforce education and internal adoption rather than a single operational use case, and Insight said the training-led approach is intended to help organisations build confidence in AI tools across teams and geographies. Insight is positioning the store as a way for businesses to move AI projects beyond the pilot stage and into wider use, and said it applied the approach within its own operations before making the products available more broadly. The articles leave open how a customer's agent would grade any particular brand's messages, and what it would say.

stories.Headline: Saudi Data and AI Authority launches Year of Artificial Intelligence initiative across universities
stories.Summary:
The Saudi Data and AI Authority launched the Year of Artificial Intelligence initiative across universities in the Kingdom on November 19, 2026. This program aims to spread knowledge about new technologies and promote their responsible use while developing national skills for the future. The initiative includes a range of scientific seminars, panel discussions, training workshops, interactive booths, and specialized consultations for the students. It seeks to transform academic ideas and projects into innovative solutions that support the digital transformation journey of the Kingdom. These efforts cultivate national talent capable of keeping pace with technological shifts to strengthen global leadership in data and AI.

The program operates in collaboration with universities across the country, including Umm Al-Qura University, to align with the goals of Saudi Vision 2030. It requires the integration of academic research with real-world industrial applications to create market-ready technologies and intellectual property for the nation. The scheme focuses on developing homegrown capabilities and fostering innovation to move beyond the simple adoption of existing artificial intelligence technologies. It emphasizes investing in human capital through specialized education, research opportunities, interdisciplinary collaboration, and practical training for the next generation. These steps aim to create high-value economic opportunities and position Saudi Arabia as a leading international hub for AI research.

The Saudi Data and AI Authority is responsible for the initiative and stated it will help strengthen the Kingdom's global leadership. They said the program will transform academic ideas into innovative solutions that support the digital transformation journey of the Saudi state. The authority believes these efforts will cultivate national talent capable of contributing to a future built on knowledge and innovation. They intend to develop national skills and promote the responsible use of AI technologies across all participating universities in the Kingdom. The authority views this as a way to align national technological growth with the broader strategic goals of Saudi Vision 2030.

Muhammad Khurram Khan, a cybersecurity professor at King Saud University, said the designation of 2026 as the Year of AI is an important milestone. He stated that the initiative reflects a commitment to harness AI as a driver of economic diversification and sustainable development. Khan noted that Saudi universities possess a wealth of research talent and scientific expertise that could address challenges across various sectors. He believes stronger collaboration between universities, government institutions, and the private sector can help transform research projects into innovative products. The professor argued that developing Saudi AI researchers and entrepreneurs is essential for building sustainable national capabilities and global competitiveness.

The background provided is that the Kingdom seeks to become a globally competitive, knowledge-based economy through the use of advanced technology. Saudi Arabia aims to move toward developing indigenous technologies and generating intellectual property rather than just deploying existing foreign AI solutions. The initiative is part of a larger strategy to foster innovation and contribute more significantly to the global AI landscape. It builds on the existing research talent found within the university system to address national priorities and various global challenges. This effort is designed to accelerate the digital transformation of the country while creating new economic opportunities for its citizens.

The next steps involve implementing the initiative across universities to strengthen the link between academic research and real-world industrial applications. The program will continue to provide specialized education and practical training to develop the next generation of Saudi AI engineers. The articles leave open how the private sector will specifically collaborate with universities and the authority to commercialize these research projects. They do not specify the exact number of universities participating or the specific timeline for the various workshops and seminars. It remains unclear what specific metrics will be used to measure the success of the Year of Artificial Intelligence initiative.

stories.Headline: Google picks Blue Origin to launch TPU-equipped Project Suncatcher satellites in early 2029
stories.Summary:
Google has selected Blue Origin for the first heavy-lift launch of Project Suncatcher, and the New Glenn rocket is scheduled to place satellites equipped with TPUs into a sun-synchronous orbit in early 2029. Each of those satellites will carry computing power comparable to a data center rack, according to the company. The two companies have signed an agreement for launch services, and this will be the first launch dedicated entirely to Project Suncatcher. Through this project, Google is investigating whether a network of solar-powered satellites, equipped with its own Tensor Processing Units, can scale up machine learning compute in space.

According to Google, the launch builds on its collaboration with other satellite and launch partners, and the company says solar panels in Earth orbit can generate up to eight times as much energy as comparable panels on Earth. Google also says the approach would reduce demand for computing power on terrestrial power grids. The first step was more modest, because Google worked with Planet on a prototype satellite that was launched on a SpaceX mission to determine whether TPUs could survive launch, radiation, vacuum, and extreme temperatures. That test was explicitly a hardware experiment and not a functioning data center in space, and Google plans to test laser links between satellites using two satellites in 2027. The 2029 launch is on a different scale, with the satellites interconnected via optical links to create a distributed data center.

Travis Beals, Senior Director of Project Suncatcher at Google, calls the agreement a crucial milestone on the roadmap and describes Project Suncatcher as a long-term moonshot to scale AI infrastructure in space by tapping into the abundant solar power in orbit. Jordan Charles, Senior Vice President of New Glenn at Blue Origin, says the rocket's heavy-lift capacity and large payload volume give customers the flexibility to bring new capabilities to orbit. Google wants to take advantage of sunlight, which is available almost continuously in orbit, and the company frames the effort as a way to scale machine learning compute in space. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the planned 2027 laser link test and the early 2029 launch.

stories.Headline: Zscaler partners with Anthropic and Mistral to secure enterprise AI adoption
stories.Summary:
Zscaler announced collaborations with frontier AI model providers on November 20, 2026, in Santa Clara, California. The company is partnering with Anthropic and Mistral to help enterprises adopt AI securely. These efforts aim to defend against AI-driven attacks and secure the agentic enterprise. Zscaler combines its security expertise with frontier AI innovation to protect customers. The goal is to stay ahead of emerging threats while embracing AI.

The collaborations integrate Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5.1 into Zscaler's Endpoint AI Security to power Exploit Paths. Zscaler also works with Anthropic's Cyber Verification Program to advance vulnerability discovery and security research. In Europe, Zscaler's Security for AI solution integrates with Mistral through a sovereign Zero Trust Exchange. This allows European enterprises to meet their data protection, sovereignty, and security requirements. A limited preview of the Exploit Paths capability is planned.

Zscaler CEO, chairman, and founder Jay Chaudhry stated that AI is fundamentally changing the threat landscape. He argued that Zero Trust is more critical than ever to eliminate attack surfaces. Chaudhry said that lateral movement must be prevented and AI agents must only access needed tools. He believes combining Zero Trust architecture with frontier AI innovations helps customers defend against attacks. This approach ensures agents never access the entire corporate network.

Traditional firewalls and VPNs cannot adequately protect enterprises as AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and exploitation. Zscaler's Zero Trust architecture affects users, workloads, devices, and AI agents by connecting them directly to authorized tools. This method reduces risk by eliminating internet-facing attack surfaces and preventing lateral movement. The platform protects thousands of customers from data loss and cyberattacks globally. It operates across thousands of private sites and over 200 public service locations.

Zscaler is a SASE-based Zero Trust Exchange and the world's largest inline cloud security platform. The company focuses on accelerating digital transformation to make customers more agile, resilient, and secure. The platform connects applications, devices, and users securely regardless of their physical location. These security solutions are designed for the AI era to provide visibility and control. They help enterprises uncover attack paths and protect sensitive data as they scale.

Zscaler will unveil new innovations to secure the agentic enterprise on December 9, 2026, at 1:00PM ET. This launch will showcase a unified Zero Trust Platform with capabilities to protect sensitive data and AI agents. The articles do not state when the limited preview for Exploit Paths will begin. They leave open the specific details of the upcoming December innovations. The text does not mention the specific terms of the Anthropic and Mistral partnerships.

stories.Headline: Microsoft unveils cheaper in-house AI models for coding and cybersecurity at Ignite
stories.Summary:
Microsoft introduced several in-house AI models for coding and cybersecurity at its Ignite conference in San Francisco. These announcements occurred on November 17, 2026, to target software development and digital security tasks. The company aims to reduce its reliance on external AI providers like OpenAI and Anthropic. These new tools provide comparable performance to rivals but at significantly lower costs for users. Microsoft also launched models for image editing, audio processing, and healthcare transcription during the event.

MAI Code 2 delivers 98 per cent of GPT-6.1 Sol performance at 40 per cent cost. It matches Claude Opus 5.5 at 96 per cent performance for only 5 per cent cost. MAI Code 2 Flash matches GPT-6 Luna performance at 65 per cent price and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 20 per cent. MAI Cyber 2 Flash outperforms GPT-6 Astra for less than 2 per cent of the cost per task. Other models include MAI Image 2.7, MAI Realtime 1, and MAI Transcribe 2 for various specialized business applications.

Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman said the system co-optimizes performance and price and is not a flash in the pan. He also stated that preventing AI from taking harmful actions remains a top priority for the company. CEO Satya Nadella posted on X that the goal is to turn technological advances into real outcomes. The company plans to integrate MAI Code 2 into GitHub Copilot for developers and Azure for enterprises. Customers can license model weights to fine-tune and customize these tools using their own private data.

Secure Code Warrior tested over 30 models and found that lower-cost systems can sometimes be safer than flagship models. Their research involved building 15,000 applications and 41.3 million lines of code across 11 different programming languages. The study found that curated security rule sets reduced measured risk in AI-generated code by as much as 70 per cent. GPT-6 Luna had a mean risk score of 19.4 at 0.10 dollars, while Claude Opus 5.5 scored 43.6 at 8.17 dollars. Software teams are affected as AI is expected to account for 65 per cent of committed code by 2027.

Secure Code Warrior CEO Pieter Danhieux said assumptions that newer or more expensive models are more secure do not always hold. He noted that models do not use secure coding by default and rely on the prompts and rules provided. Stanford University research found human-only commits introduced roughly 0.08 vulnerabilities per 1,000 lines of code. The AI benchmark showed a 15-fold gap between the best and worst performers, ranging from 0.24 to 3.66 vulnerabilities. This background suggests that procurement decisions based only on branding or price may not reflect actual security outcomes.

Microsoft is currently developing a general-purpose frontier AI model to compete with broader systems beyond task-specific tools. Access to the MAI Cyber 2 Flash model is initially limited to a small group of select customers. The company has not yet announced specific pricing or availability timelines for all of the new AI models. It remains open whether the pricing advantages are due to promotional discounts or actual operational cost reductions. The articles leave open how these specialized models will perform against general models in scientific research problems.

stories.Headline: Hickenlooper urges Senate Democratic leader candidates to plan for AI regulation on day one
stories.Summary:
Colorado Sen. John Hickenlooper said this week that the person leading the Senate Democratic majority next year should have a day one plan for responsible regulation of artificial intelligence. Hickenlooper has so far withheld an endorsement in the race between Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer and Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen. Hickenlooper said Friday that there has not been enough progress in Congress since Democrats formed a working group on AI three years ago. He said the working group convened tech leaders from across the country to figure out next steps. Hickenlooper said there is a perception that Congress has not done anything on AI.

Democrats have been publicly and privately discussing what their first steps could be on artificial intelligence when they take the majority in January. Top policy proposals could be regulating data centers, safety standards and stepping up monitoring and research. Hickenlooper said his priorities are robust third-party evaluation requirements, mitigation of national security challenges and clear rules of the road to hold AI companies accountable. Hickenlooper said he proposed a select committee on artificial intelligence to consolidate the conversation. In letters to both Schumer and Van Hollen, Hickenlooper wrote that with the presidential election two years away, there is a two-year audition to show Americans Democrats can deliver on affordability, accountability and AI safety.

Schumer is favored to win reelection in the closed-door Dec. 1 caucus leadership vote. A spokeswoman for Schumer, Allison Biasotti, said he has been working closely with the incoming heads of committees to develop an ambitious AI agenda and hit the ground running in January. Biasotti said Senate Democrats will make AI a top priority of the new Democratic majority. She said they are working to deliver comprehensive legislation that addresses the serious risks AI poses to national security, workers and consumers while keeping America at the forefront of innovation. Hickenlooper said his proposal would consolidate the conversation on AI.

Van Hollen said he supports the idea and that he does think a joint committee is needed because AI covers so many different areas impacting lives. It is unclear if other Democrats, especially the heads of committees already working on AI proposals, will support it. Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, the incoming chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, said he would want to see the specifics and what topics would be covered. Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, who is expected to become chairman of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, did not immediately endorse the idea and said Democrats have to make it a priority no matter what particular way they approach it. Sanders said Congress has been way behind where it should be in protecting the American people.

Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, the current Republican chairman of the Senate Commerce Committee, said a plan to take the issue out of his committee and others makes no sense. Cruz said there were already bipartisan conversations about the issue looking forward to next year, and he hopes the next Congress can see Republicans and Democrats finding common ground on addressing catastrophic risk. President Joe Biden's administration called on lawmakers to develop policies after a 2023 executive order on AI oversight, which President Donald Trump rescinded soon after returning to office. The bipartisan working group on artificial intelligence formed by Schumer released a report in 2024 recommending the U.S. spend at least $32 billion over the next three years to develop artificial intelligence and implement safeguards around it. Trump, who will hold the power of the veto, has repeatedly maintained that little regulation is needed even as the technology has progressed at a rapid clip.

Republicans who have led the House and Senate for the last two years have said AI should be a priority but have focused mostly on innovation, with no major push to establish safeguards or increase monitoring. House Democrats have also been discussing a way forward on AI and have proposed a robust package of proposals. This week, three Democrats announced the launch of the House AI Safety and Innovation caucus to address security risks. The Senate Democratic leadership vote is set for Dec. 1 in a closed-door caucus. It remains open whether other Democrats, especially committee heads already working on AI proposals, will support Hickenlooper's select committee.

stories.Headline: Newsom proposes a kill switch letting state officials shut down dangerous AI systems
stories.Summary:
Gov. Gavin Newsom released a wide-ranging set of policy recommendations today to mitigate risks from artificial intelligence, including letting state officials order an immediate emergency shutdown of AI systems they deem dangerous. The recommendations were drawn up by a panel of experts Newsom brought together earlier this fall. They followed high-profile cyberattacks by AI agents on governments, banks, and private companies. Newsom touted the recommendations as a blueprint for state legislation during a recent visit to Washington, according to a report in Politico. The recommendations came the same week as a lawsuit by Attorney General Rob Bonta against OpenAI to hold the company legally responsible for cybersecurity attacks carried out by agents it made.

The shutdown power, popularly known as a “kill switch,” would apply when companies like ChatGPT maker OpenAI and Claude maker Anthropic refuse to take action to contain systems that go awry. Other recommendations would mandate that independent auditors test AI models and establish safety and security standards. The group recommends licensing auditors, known as independent verification organizations, and giving the state power to revoke the licenses of those who fail to maintain sufficient independence or technical expertise. It also recommends considering having state officials assign evaluations to auditors instead of AI companies hiring auditors, to maintain independence. The group recommends funding CalCompute, a public cloud initiative intended to provide equitable access to AI, with a surcharge on fees AI companies pay to auditors.

The group recommends expanding existing protections for AI whistleblowers to include contractors and former employees. It recommends expanding reporting of AI safety incidents to government agencies and shortening the window to report critical safety incidents to 48 hours from 15 days. It recommends allowing government limits on the use of AI to design AI, since some experts believe this practice makes systems more dangerous. It recommends requiring developers to disclose the amount of computing resources they are using to automate AI development. It recommends requiring developers of large AI systems to demonstrate the ability to shut down models in emergencies and establishing state standards for safety, security, and transparency while referring to national and international standards.

The four-person panel includes Alondra Nelson, who ran the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy during the Biden administration, and Stanford University professor Rob Reich, who studies the governance of science and technology. It also includes former Google and Twitter executive Jason Goldman, the first White House Chief Digital Officer, and Gillian Hadfield, a Johns Hopkins professor who studies various issues related to AI. Newsom said in a press release that “instead of protecting the public, Donald Trump shrugs his shoulders and leaves AI regulation up to the companies themselves.” Governor-elect Xavier Becerra said in a written statement that he will move quickly with the Legislature to put “full incident reporting and real shutdown authority into law.” Becerra supported CalCompute funding during his campaign.

Anthropic, which makes the Claude AI system, is encouraged to see the report move the conversation forward on issues like the independent evaluation of AI models, according to the company’s chief global affairs officer, Tino Cuéllar. Cuéllar wrote that “we will continue working with leaders in California and throughout the world to make sure we keep making progress on these issues at a critical time.” Rif Saurous, a staffer at auditing nonprofit METR, said during a California Senate hearing last month that auditors are “under soft pressure to maintain good relationships with the [AI] labs so that they want to continue to work with us.” State Senator Scott Wiener, who wrote a state law to mitigate catastrophic AI dangers and was recently elected to take Nancy Pelosi’s seat in Congress, has pledged to introduce AI safety regulation after he is sworn in. State law currently defines catastrophic risk as a single event capable of killing more than 50 people or $1 billion in theft or property damage through a cyber attack or activity of an autonomous system.

California is home to some of the largest AI companies in the world, and the California Legislature has passed more bills to regulate AI than any other state in the country. Newsom signed dozens of bills passed by the Legislature into law in September to protect kids, workers, and people living near data centers from AI and related impacts. He also accelerated implementation of laws to create an AI auditor registry and set standards for auditors. A late 2023 executive order required the state to compile and assess the opportunities and risks associated with government use of generative AI, and a subsequent state report assessed the impact of generative AI on vulnerable and marginalized communities. A June 2025 expert panel report concluded that to balance innovation and safety, the AI industry needs evaluations by an independent, outside party.

Legislators can propose new bills when they return to Sacramento on December 7. The report out today focuses only on catastrophic risk and does not explore ways to protect people from other AI harms, such as automated discrimination, job loss, or threats to the safety or mental health of children. Coauthors of the recommendations argue that building a system for credentialed auditors to test models for catastrophic risk will make it easier to evaluate models for other forms of harm. The recommendations by the governor’s panel and by auditors in recent weeks provide fodder to an incoming class of lawmakers in the California Legislature and Congress. The articles leave open whether the Legislature will adopt the recommendations and what the lawsuit by Bonta against OpenAI will yield.

stories.Headline: J.S. Held Applies Multidisciplinary Expertise to Physical AI Claims and Disputes
stories.Summary:
J.S. Held announced on November 20, 2026, that it applies multidisciplinary expertise to Physical AI claims and disputes, according to a press release issued from New York. The firm said Physical AI moves artificial intelligence beyond digital outputs and into systems that sense, decide, control, or act in the physical world. Those systems include AI-enabled and autonomous vehicles, robotics, industrial equipment, building systems, medical technology, drones, and other technologies in which digital decisions can affect people, property, infrastructure, and business operations. The release said autonomous and AI-enabled systems are creating new investigative questions when digital decisions produce physical consequences. J.S. Held published the announcement through PR Newswire, and The Manila Times carried it on November 20, 2026.

J.S. Held said a Physical AI investigation may examine the complete system chain, from the data the system received and what its sensors perceived to what the AI decided and how software, controls, and equipment translated that decision into action. The firm said these matters do not necessarily require new investigative disciplines but require established disciplines to work across increasingly complex systems. J.S. Held said it is publishing two perspectives, one in Insurance Journal titled When AI Leaves the Screen, the Stakes Change, and one to be published as Expert Analysis in Law360 titled When AI Leaves the Screen, the Evidence Changes: What In-House and Outside Counsel Should Do Before a Physical AI Incident. The firm said the Law360 piece discusses evidence ownership and preservation, system and software changes, sensor data, operating logs, telemetry, contractual responsibility, privilege, regulatory reporting, and coordination among technical and legal teams. J.S. Held said more than 1,500 professionals serve organizations across six continents, including 84% of the Global 200 Law Firms, 75% of the Forbes Top 20 Insurance Companies, 90% of the NAIC Top 50 Property & Casualty Insurers, and 71% of Fortune 100 Companies.

James E. Malackowski, Chief Intellectual Property Officer, Intellectual Property Practice Lead, and co-lead of the AI Disputes practice at J.S. Held, said AI is moving from generating information to influencing and controlling physical systems. Malackowski said that when those systems are involved in an accident or loss, the investigation cannot stop with the algorithm. He said understanding what happened may require examining the data and sensors, controls and equipment, human interaction, and the resulting physical and economic consequences. He said Physical AI is where those disciplines increasingly converge. Stephen Fenton, PE, Executive Vice President and Accident Reconstruction Practice Lead at J.S. Held, said that when an AI-enabled or autonomous system is involved in an accident, investigators still have to reconstruct the physical event.

Fenton said reconstruction covers what happened in the moments leading to the incident, how the system or vehicle behaved, and how the available physical and digital evidence explains the outcome. He said the technology may change but rigorous reconstruction remains essential to determining how and why an event occurred, and his work includes forensic engineering, vehicle dynamics, photogrammetry, computer modeling, and vehicle and product testing. Scott Armstrong, Executive Vice President and Equipment Practice Lead at J.S. Held, said Physical AI incidents can create complex equipment and insurance questions after the cause of an event is established. Armstrong, who has more than 25 years of experience in equipment loss consulting involving high-technology equipment and systems, said a physical loss can raise questions about whether the problem was the equipment itself, the sensors or connected systems, the power supply or physical infrastructure, a manufacturing issue, or some combination of factors. He said separating those issues is important for insurers to understand the damage, determine what can be repaired or recovered, assess whether replacement is necessary, and evaluate the operational impact.

J.S. Held said its Physical AI perspective builds on its work involving artificial intelligence in industrial and operational environments. The firm said its experts examine AI implementation in the energy, manufacturing, and natural-resources sectors in Enterprise AI Implementation in Heavy Industry: A Digital Transformation Strategy for Sustainable Growth. Their analysis addresses data governance, digital architecture, analytics, system integration, and the organizational foundations required to deploy AI in complex operations. The publication includes a case study involving an AI readiness assessment for a major energy operator, which considered the digital, data, governance, and organizational foundations needed to support scalable AI implementation. J.S. Held said this experience is relevant to Physical AI because the reliability of an AI-enabled physical system may depend not only on an algorithm but also on the data architecture, connected systems, implementation decisions, operating environment, and human processes surrounding it.

Alastair Mckenzie-Kerr, PhD, Regional Director of Health, Safety & Human Factors, EMEA at J.S. Held, said the important transition is not simply that companies are adopting AI but that AI is being integrated into operational environments where people, equipment, and safety-critical processes already interact. Mckenzie-Kerr, whose work includes implementing AI-enabled EHS solutions and integrating human factors into design engineering and operational systems, said organizations need to understand not only whether the technology works as intended but how it performs within the broader operating system and how people respond to it. J.S. Held said it is publishing the two perspectives as part of its ongoing examination of Physical AI risk, addressing how organizations, insurers, and legal counsel can prepare for incidents involving AI-enabled and autonomous systems. The firm said the Insurance Journal article examines what organizations and insurers should consider when an AI-enabled system contributes to an accident, equipment failure, operational interruption, or other physical loss, and explains why engineering, digital, human factors, insurance, legal, and financial investigations may need to proceed together. J.S. Held said it is not a law firm and does not provide legal advice, and that its affiliates and subsidiaries are not certified public accounting firms and do not provide audit, attest, or other public accounting services.

stories.Headline: Alibaba beats revenue estimates as AI cloud demand and investment gains boost profits
stories.Summary:
Alibaba reported its September quarter financial results on November 19, showing revenue that exceeded analyst expectations. The company experienced a significant surge in demand for its artificial intelligence cloud and computing services. Reported profits more than tripled during this period, which was largely supported by gains from various investments. These results highlight the growing financial returns from the company's heavy investments in AI infrastructure and products.

Quarterly revenue reached 271.52 billion yuan, surpassing the average analyst estimate of 269.81 billion yuan. Revenue from AI cloud and computing services jumped 53 percent to 60.97 billion yuan, while non-GAAP net income rose 92 percent to 19.9 billion yuan. Capital expenditure increased 60 percent to 50.48 billion yuan, contributing to a negative free cash flow of 34.47 billion yuan. Adjusted earnings per American Depositary Share were 8.10 yuan, which fell short of the 11.16 yuan expected by analysts.

Chief Financial Officer Toby Xu stated that the business achieved strong growth in revenue and earnings through a strategic focus on AI and cloud services. He also noted that the company prioritized profit sustainability within the Alibaba E-commerce Group. The company has reorganized into four main units covering e-commerce, AI cloud and computing, AI model applications, and other businesses. This restructuring supports their goal of using technology as a primary driver for future growth.

Alibaba plans to expand its global data center capacity to over 20 gigawatts by 2032 and is currently training its Qwen 4 model. Its chip design unit, T-Head, recently filed for a Hong Kong listing and plans to release a new AI processor in early 2027. Despite these advancements, shares have dropped about 40 percent this year due to concerns over Chinese consumer demand. The company previously launched a 10 billion US dollar share placement in August to fund its AI data centers.

stories.Headline: Fed rate hike signal and AI stock selloff push gold to biggest weekly drop since March
stories.Summary:
Gold fell for a fifth straight day and was heading for its biggest weekly decline since March, after the US Federal Reserve signalled more interest rate hikes and a selloff in artificial intelligence stocks pushed investors to sell the metal to cover losses. Bullion dropped as much as 3.1% on Nov 20 to below US$3,515 an ounce, and was on track to lose nearly 9% over a week that saw it slide to the lowest level since September 2025. Spot gold was down 2% at US$3,552.06 an ounce at 3.10pm Singapore time, after falling 0.8% to US$3,596.09 an ounce at 9.01am in Singapore. Silver fell around 14% over the same period, dropping 2.5% to US$41.88 an ounce after sinking nearly 5% in the previous session, while platinum and palladium also declined. The prospect of tighter monetary policy kept Treasury yields elevated, with 10-year borrowing costs poised to match a 2007 run of 29 closes above 5% in the same year.

Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago president Austan Goolsbee joined a number of central bank officials on Nov 19 who have hinted at interest rate hikes, saying he would consider all options to counter stubborn US inflation. A gauge of the dollar rose 0.5% this week, making bullion priced in the US currency more expensive for most buyers. Globally, investors are betting that major central banks, including the Fed, the European Central Bank and the Bank of England, will keep rates largely unchanged for years once they have finished hiking at the end of 2027. Justin Lin, a strategist at Global X ETFs, said gold is now firmly in an air pocket, with very little technical support until the US$3,300 and US$3,400 region. He said the metal looks very fragile now and that he struggles to see what could turn momentum around just yet.

Analysts said gold looks very fragile now, with little support until US$3,300 to US$3,400, as silver, platinum and palladium also fell. Higher interest rates and yields are typically negative for gold, which does not pay interest. Bullion has fallen by about a third since the US-Iran war began in late February, as higher energy costs fuelled inflation. The precious metal has also been caught up in a rout in technology stocks, with Asian equities tracking a decline on Wall Street driven by concerns around the AI trade. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the levels and forecasts above.

stories.Headline: China and ASEAN launch a legal secretariat and AI research alliance in Chongqing
stories.Summary:
The 8th China-ASEAN Legal Cooperation Forum opened in Chongqing on November 19, 2026, gathering various judges, legal officials, and experts. These participants met to discuss how improved judicial cooperation could assist businesses in resolving commercial disputes and navigating local laws. The event featured the official launch of a permanent secretariat and a research alliance dedicated to the intersection of law and artificial intelligence. This gathering occurred during a year celebrating 35 years of China-ASEAN dialogue relations and five years of their comprehensive strategic partnership.

The new China-ASEAN Alliance for Artificial Intelligence and Law Research, started by Southwest University of Political Science and Law, will unite industry groups, legal practitioners, and research institutions. This alliance intends to study corporate compliance, cross-border data flows, digital governance, and the impact of AI. Additionally, the forum highlighted the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor, which connects western China to other markets and ASEAN. Courts along this corridor have utilized a 13+2 judicial cooperation mechanism since May 2024 to coordinate the resolution of cross-jurisdictional commercial disputes.

Parulian Paidi Aritonang, the dean of the Faculty of Law at the University of Indonesia, stated that a reliable legal environment is necessary to sustain trade links. He welcomed the permanent secretariat as a tool for maintaining dialogue and supporting long-term cooperation in legal practice and education. Tran Anh Tu, director of Hoa Viet Tin International Law Firm in Vietnam, noted that Chinese investment in Vietnam has grown and urged companies to follow investment law changes. Shaun Wong, managing director of Shaun Wong LLC in Singapore, suggested regular exchanges on trade, contract, and company laws to address differences among ASEAN legal systems.

Organizers noted that Chongqing's trade with ASEAN grew 17 percent from the previous year, reaching 116.41 billion yuan, or about 17.4 billion US dollars, in the first three quarters of 2026. Tran added that the new secretariat could provide businesses with better access to essential legal information. The forum emphasized that incentives in Vietnam are now increasingly tied to the ability of companies to meet eligibility requirements and maintain long-term operations. Participants concluded that these institutional frameworks would help foreign parties and transactions be handled more efficiently across different jurisdictions.
