stories.Headline: Oxide CTO Bryan Cantrill says agentic AI drives enterprises to own compute for model control
stories.Summary:
Bryan Cantrill, co-founder and chief technology officer of Oxide Computer Co., said in an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE at SC26 that agentic AI is reviving the argument over renting versus owning compute, with the model plane at the center of the debate. He spoke with theCUBE Research's John Furrier during the interview, which was part of SiliconANGLE's and theCUBE's coverage of SC26. Cantrill said agentic workloads are driving an explosion in compute demand, much of it CPU-heavy work that enterprises would rather own than rent. He said economics remains the main reason to bring that work in-house, but where models live is a close second, which makes the model plane as much a data governance decision as an infrastructure one.

Cantrill said there is a real enterprise drive toward open-weight models, and he expects more of it as people want to run models on-premises and keep their data from leaving. He said Oxide stripped the UEFI BIOS and baseboard management controller out of its rack to shrink the attack surface and built public cloud-grade multi-tenancy in from the start. He said multi-tenancy means potentially adversarial tenants share the same computer and network and must do so without violating confidentiality or breaching one another. He noted the same racks can take on legacy virtualization workloads from customers unhappy with pricing changes at Broadcom Inc.'s VMware business, letting enterprises run old and new applications on one general-purpose platform.

Cantrill said enterprises want the flexibility of elastic compute for economic, security and latency reasons, and they need it in their own data center because they want to control their fate. He said cloud computing is great but the model should not be exclusively to rent, and that at a certain scale you want to own your own computer. Oxide raised $445 million in October to expand rack production, and the article says the shift toward on-premises favors companies that built early for on-premises cloud infrastructure. Open-source efforts such as Upbound Inc.'s Modelplane route inference across clouds, but many enterprises want the models on hardware they control, according to the article.

Articles.Title: Model plane shifts on-prem as agentic AI favors owning compute

stories.Headline: Valkey launches version 9.2 with distributed KV caching to lower AI inference costs
stories.Summary:
Valkey announced the general availability of version 9.2 on November 20, 2026, in San Francisco. This open source datastore release includes the launch of distributed KV caching for AI inference. The project aims to help organizations do more with their existing infrastructure. It targets costs related to memory reserves, cross-region network traffic, and large dataset overhead. These updates focus on scaling enterprise workloads while driving down overall infrastructure costs.

Version 9.2 introduces Path Hash, a native data type for fast indexing of AI caching. It adds forkless snapshots to eliminate memory spikes and continuous stream compression for replication. Distributed KV caching integrates with LMCache and engines like vLLM and SGLang via one configuration change. Amazon ElastiCache added support for this distributed KV caching on November 19, 2026. The B+ tree architecture now rebuilds large sorted sets for better memory efficiency.

Project maintainer Madelyn Olson said the design delivers reduced memory overhead and lower network costs. She stated that Valkey 9.2 follows the ethos of getting more functionality with less hardware. Guoyun Zhu of Alibaba Cloud noted that his team contributed Path Hash to the release. Zhu said there are significant opportunities for Valkey within AI infrastructure for developers. He expressed a commitment to advancing the project through open collaboration.

Yihua Cheng of Tensormesh said RDMA allows Valkey to move KV chunks with minimal CPU overhead. He noted that traditional networking falls short for large, latency-sensitive KV cache objects. Builders running open-weight models on self-managed inference are affected by these new caching tools. Users can now reduce AI inference spend by up to 40 percent. Time-to-first-token latency can decrease by up to 80 percent for these users.

Valkey is an in-memory datastore governed by the Linux Foundation for caching and message queues. It is backed by contributors including AWS, Google Cloud, Oracle, and Tencent Cloud. The system traditionally faced memory spikes during snapshots, forcing teams to over-provision idle memory. Cross-regional data transfers and inefficient sorted set structures also created high operational expenses. The project serves as a fast, reliable datastore for modern application data paths.

Continuous stream compression reduces replication traffic by 50 to 65 percent and backup sizes by 80 percent. New replicas now sync about 35 percent faster using the built-in LZ4 option. Sorted set updates are up to 105 percent faster with 36 to 43 percent better efficiency. Replication traffic reduction costs about 2 to 4 percent of a CPU core per replica. The articles do not state when further versions will be released.

Articles.Title: Valkey Releases Version 9.2 Alongside Distributed KV Caching for AI Inference

stories.Headline: FBI warns about ARTEX as AI tool lets attackers breach banks in under three hours
stories.Summary:
The FBI issued a FLASH warning six days before the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI about ARTEX, an open-source tool that lets AI agents carry out an intrusion at machine speed, from reconnaissance through data exfiltration. The warning came as GTA VI, the sequel fans waited 13 years for, arrived this week. Some ARTEX attacks reached privileged access in under three hours. The GitHub repository has since been taken down, but copies are still out there. ARTEX has already been used against banks, government agencies, and tech companies.

In 2022, a 17-year-old broke into Rockstar and leaked early GTA VI footage from a hotel room, using an Amazon Fire Stick and a phone. In September, a Binance engineer went through two rounds of interviews for what looked like a great job and downloaded the take-home assignment, which was malware. The FBI blamed North Korea, and Binance puts the theft that followed at about $6.3 billion. A day after Microsoft 365 went down this month, attackers were already exploiting the confusion, sending fake outage notices that cited the real incident number. Adopting a new security approach means a six-month evaluation, a few more months to roll it out, and a pilot that waits for next year's plan.

Asaf Wiener is co-founder and CEO of Mate Security, which sells AI tools for security operations teams, and he previously led core products at Wiz and drove the growth of Microsoft Defender. Wiener wrote that skill, time, and money used to separate a bored teenager from a professional crew, and now a bored teenager with AI can operate like one. He wrote that Rockstar spent 13 years building a game that feels like real life, and in the same stretch real life took on the rules of the game. He wrote that attackers now run on three-hour clocks, while most security programs run on fiscal years. Wiener wrote that the leaders handling this well know the business first, save the caution for what can't be undone, and change in weeks, not quarters.

Wiener wrote that the best attacks don't look like attacks at all, arriving as job offers, invoices, calendar invites, and logins that look almost normal. He wrote that defenders are being asked to move faster and to tell real from fake at the same time. He wrote that security leaders have been burned by tools that promised a lot and broke things in production. He wrote that a team that misreads a signal will shut down its own business over a broken router, while the real attack walks in looking like a job offer. He wrote that the context defense needs, like who owns the server, whether that user really logged in from Lisbon, and what breaks if a system goes offline, lives inside your company.

Wiener wrote that when the first GTA VI trailer came out, half of the internet asked whether it was gameplay or real footage, and corporate security teams ask that every day now. He wrote that fans waited 13 years for GTA VI and the wait dragged on through so many delays that it became a meme. He wrote that when a game takes that long, you'd expect it to feel dated on arrival, but when GTA VI finally arrived this week, the opposite thing happened. He wrote that the real world has started to look a lot like the game. He wrote that Rockstar knows what a bored teenager can do.

Wiener wrote that in GTA players can reload their last save, but security teams don't have that luxury. He wrote that companies that make the right call at machine speed will still be around for the next GTA installment, however long it takes. He wrote that an attack that moves at machine speed doesn't wait for procurement. He wrote that attackers are playing on easy mode, and the defense is stuck on a loading screen. The opinions expressed in the Fortune.com commentary piece are solely the views of its author and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and beliefs of Fortune.

stories.Headline: Milemarker adds Model Context Protocol so firms connect their own AI tools to its warehoused data
stories.Summary:
Milemarker, an advisor data warehousing provider, announced this month that it has added a new Model Context Protocol for firms on its platform to connect their own AI tools to their Milemarker-housed data, according to an article published on November 20, 2026, by InvestmentNews. The move comes as advisory firm data remains scattered across CRM, custodian, portfolio management software, financial planning platforms and document storage vaults, which makes it hard to get a high-level picture of a client's situation or to run deeper firm-wide analytics. API integrations between software providers have helped only up to a point, because providers are inconsistent about how many integrations they build and how deep those integrations go, with some offering only read-only access while others allow read-and-write access. Several advisor data warehousing providers such as Skience, BridgeFT and Milemarker have risen over the past several years to aggregate data from disparate platforms into a single clean format that firms can plug into through an API.

The announcement raises the question of whether a centralized data warehouse is needed for AI tools to pull their data from, when tools like the recently released Claude for Financial Advisors can connect to an advisor's individual software tools themselves. The article says one potential answer could be consistency of data, since Milemarker may be able to clean a firm's data and resolve inconsistent, incomplete or incorrect records that AI tools might not catch. Milemarker may also have built more and deeper integrations over its years in the data warehouse business, and the article notes that Claude for Financial Advisors currently lists 22 advisor-specific tools it can connect to, whereas Milemarker boasts over 130 integrations. The article adds that there might be value in having a data connection any AI tool can plug into, which is the main purpose of an MCP, so an advisor who later switches to another AI assistant or builds their own would not need to re-establish all the data connections to their individual tools.

The article, written by Ben Henry-Moreland, a Senior Financial Planning Nerd at Kitces.com, says the big question with data warehousing has always been how much extra value there is in centralizing all of a firm's data in one spot, which inevitably gives rise to the temptation to build custom tools to make use of that data. It says it may be easier now to build custom data dashboards with no-code AI tools, but it is also much easier for off-the-shelf AI tools to connect to an advisor's data sources and pull the data in themselves. For firms with truly niche reporting and data-analytics needs that off-the-shelf tools cannot handle, or bespoke tech stacks of lesser-used software that are less likely to have API connections to newer AI tools, the article says a warehouse to pull in and clean the data may be worth it. But as AI tools expand their integration capabilities and the customizability of their interfaces, the article says it might become increasingly difficult to justify paying for a centralized data warehouse for making custom analytics tools when off-the-shelf software can do much of the same thing.

stories.Headline: Alteryx adds governance experience to Alteryx One for validating AI outputs
stories.Summary:
Alteryx introduced a new governance experience in its Alteryx One platform on Nov. 20, 2026, the company announced from Irvine, Calif. The experience is designed to solve one of enterprise AI's biggest obstacles, which Alteryx describes as ensuring answer validation, reliability, and repeatable outcomes across business operations and financial processes. Alteryx evolved its VURA framework, standing for Visible, Understandable, Repeatable, Auditable, into an active governance experience. Alteryx One surfaces real-time trust signals directly across OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, and Google Gemini chat interfaces. The company said this lets business users validate AI outputs while equipping IT with centralized control and platform oversight.

Alteryx One makes the data, workflows, and logic behind decisions and automations visible to users. The platform lets organizations operationalize repeatable business logic into governed agentic workflows that AI agents can safely reuse and automate at scale. IT defines software development lifecycle processes, versioning controls, and certification criteria, including statuses such as in review, certified, or deprecated. Sensitivity labels include public, internal, PII, or restricted, alongside custom labels such as "AI-Ready" or "Finance-Approved." Alteryx integrates with Google Cloud Knowledge Catalog, formerly Dataplex, Atlan, and Collibra for data lineage.

Ben Canning, Chief Product Officer at Alteryx, said enterprise AI adoption does not fail because models lack intelligence but stalls because of a fundamental trust gap across decisions and operations. He said business leaders hesitate to act when they cannot verify outputs or govern automated workflows. He said Alteryx One provides the business logic layer that pairs clean, trusted data with LLMs and agents. He said the company embeds its VURA framework directly into conversational interfaces and automated enterprise processes. Canning said AI models are incredibly powerful but leaders need verification.

Roan Pilsworth, Data Consultant at Bulien, said organisations often understand the importance of governing underlying data but many overlook the same practices for processes and workflows. Pilsworth said it has become critical to properly manage processes before they reach production as organizations look to accelerate development with AI. Pilsworth said Alteryx assets can be packaged as immutable objects, allowing logic to be locked down. Pilsworth said this ensures changes are traceable and transparent and assets can be shared while maintaining governance. Alteryx said its platform serves analysts, finance teams, operations teams, and business users.

Alteryx cited its "2026 State of Data Analyst: The Rise of Business Logic" report, in which 43% said interpreting and explaining AI insights remains a key barrier. Alteryx said generating insights faster does not always make decisions easier and that the biggest challenge is helping business leaders understand and trust AI-generated outputs. Alteryx said it has over 8,000 customers and describes itself as the agentic analytics and automation company. Alteryx said non-deterministic AI outputs pose a risk to reporting integrity for financial leaders. Alteryx said finance teams can operationalize governed metrics including Annual Recurring Revenue, Customer Lifetime Value, and revenue calculations.

Alteryx One natively integrates into existing enterprise technology stacks by leveraging the Model Context Protocol. It offers a customizable MCP Server or standard plug-ins for OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, Microsoft CoPilot, Databricks Genie, and Snowflake CoCo. Alteryx said offloading heavy data processing and calculation logic to governed workflows rather than LLMs can significantly reduce token consumption and execution time. Alteryx said business users can use natural language to generate and interact with transparent visual workflow diagrams and make incremental edits without recreating entire assets. Alteryx said this keeps intermediate AI actions fully visible for supply chain reordering, billing discrepancy reviews, or financial audits.

Alteryx scheduled a live session titled "Trust at the Speed of AI: November 2026 Release Webinar" with its product experts. The session is to demonstrate how Alteryx One grounds conversational AI in governed business logic, visible data lineage, and automated trust signals. Alteryx said the webinar covers the November 2026 release. The articles did not say how many customers have adopted the new governance experience. The articles did not give pricing or a general availability date for the experience.

stories.Headline: AI-driven bug reports strain Microsoft security and cause system instability
stories.Summary:
Security researchers began flooding Microsoft with a massive volume of bug reports starting in April 2026. This surge in discoveries is driven by the use of artificial intelligence to find vulnerabilities in software. While these bugs are often of relatively low severity, the sheer quantity is straining traditional security defenses. This trend has created a situation where adversaries can adopt new technology faster than defenders can respond.

The current volume of reports is overwhelming the Microsoft Active Protections Program, which has operated for nearly two decades. Since January 2021, Microsoft has issued patches for approximately 10,319 common vulnerabilities and exposures. The scale of the problem is evident in the data, as 2025 saw a total of 1,180 such vulnerabilities. In contrast, 2026 has already seen 5,383 releases, with 5,128 of those occurring since April.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella addressed these challenges during the New York Times DealBook Summit and on CNBC this Wednesday. He explained that while artificial intelligence helps the company find and fix bugs, the resulting flood of patches creates instability. Nadella noted that applying these numerous fixes to older infrastructure makes systems less stable. He clarified that a recent Microsoft 365 outage was caused by a latent bug rather than a direct AI attack.

The Microsoft Security Response Center manages these efforts through the Software and Services Incident Response Plan, which dates back to 2004. This organization coordinates with partner companies to provide early access to bug information before the monthly Patch Tuesday releases. In 2025, Microsoft stopped giving early access to Chinese companies following suspected leaks related to SharePoint attacks. Experts now worry that these established patch programs cannot adapt to the current AI-driven deluge of reports.

stories.Headline: AI trade enters downturn as market skepticism grows following Anthropic IPO
stories.Summary:
Anthropic launched the largest initial public offering in history on November 20, 2026, with a valuation of approximately 1.3 trillion dollars. The company shares initially rose 17 percent over the starting price, but they later dropped 11 percent as market skepticism grew. This volatility reflects a broader downturn in the artificial intelligence trade that is affecting many other technology firms. Some industry experts believe a slowdown is necessary because too many resources are currently concentrated among a few large companies.

The current market requires a shift away from the tokenmaxxing craze that previously accelerated revenue for hyperscalers and frontier labs. A report by the Centre for Economics and Business Research and Wasabi suggests that concentrating computer memory and accelerators among a few players hinders overall innovation. The departure of Jensen Huang from Nvidia further threatens the startup ecosystem and the development of open-weight models. These models, often originating in China, may struggle to grow if entrepreneurs cannot access enough Nvidia chips.

Reed Albergotti notes that the concentration of resources leaves very little room for diverse ideas and alternative products. He explains that cybersecurity concerns are also mounting because threat actors and nation states are using AI to increase their productivity. While the largest tech players might see massive growth, the actual real-life impacts of the technology may take longer to appear. Despite these concerns, reports indicate that Anthropic is accelerating its AI advancement even though CEO Dario Amodei previously called for slower model development.

stories.Headline: Dira wins $10,000 education prize at African Agentic AI Design Challenge in Nairobi
stories.Summary:
The Kenyan education technology startup Dira won the US$10,000 Education track prize at the African Agentic AI Design Challenge on November 20, 2026. This announcement occurred during a closed-door side event held alongside the Model Context Protocol Dev Summit Nairobi, which took place from November 19 to 20 at the Hyatt Regency Nairobi Westlands. Founded by Michelle Gati, Jacinta Wanjiru, and Irene Mukii, the startup developed an AI assistant that helps teachers identify students needing extra support. The tool converts spoken observations from educators into structured records known as Evidence Cards to reduce manual record-keeping.

The competition also awarded US$8,000 to first runner-up Marga AI and US$6,000 to second runner-up TALO, which was created by university students aged 21 and 22. All three winning teams received computing credits to help cover their initial hosting and model-inference costs. This event highlighted the Model Context Protocol as a standard for linking AI agents to external tools and institutional workflows. Such technical gatherings in Nairobi aim to integrate African engineers into global conversations typically dominated by Asia, Europe, and North America.

The Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy launched the Kenya National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025 to 2030 on March 27, 2025, with a reported KSh 152 billion budget. However, legislative progress has stalled, as a Senate committee in October 2026 recommended against the Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026, sponsored by Senator Karen Nyamu. That proposed bill would have created an AI Commissioner with the power to levy fines of KSh 5 million or impose two years of imprisonment. Organizers have not yet disclosed the judging rubric or how the voice-driven data is encrypted and stored.

The success of Dira will depend on whether the prize money and credits can lead to sustained pilots within school budgets. While the national strategy is in place, the lack of a dedicated regulator leaves startups to navigate general data-protection obligations on their own. Future adoption of these agentic tools requires reliable institutional procurement and comprehensive teacher training. It remains unclear if these early experiments will move from hackathon validation into everyday Kenyan classrooms.

stories.Headline: CISOs expect 60% to let AI agents act autonomously on low-risk security tasks within a year
stories.Summary:
Security leaders are about to hand AI agents a lot more authority, according to a recent a16z survey of CISOs at organizations with more than 1,000 employees. In that survey, 36% said they are comfortable today letting AI agents act autonomously on low-risk security actions. In 12 months from now, 60% expect to be comfortable at that level. Overall, AI SOC was the highest ranking initiative for 2027. The Hacker News published the article on Nov 20, 2026.

The same survey found the most common worry was AI-accelerated attacks outpacing the team's ability to respond, selected by 55% of respondents. Only 1% are comfortable with agents acting autonomously on most actions today, and only 7% expect to be a year from now. According to the a16z survey, 52% of CISOs want agents to act only with human approval. In the a16z survey, 46% of CISOs listed AI agents acting outside their intended permissions, or compromised agents, among their five biggest worries, and 29% cited prompt injection or data leakage through AI applications. Meanwhile 55% already run MCP servers or other agent-to-application integrations in production, and 34% run autonomous agents with tool access or write permissions.

In a widely cited 2000 paper, Parasuraman, Sheridan and Wickens proposed that automation applies to four broad functions. Those are information acquisition, information analysis, decision and action selection, and action implementation. Each function can sit at a different level of automation, from fully manual to fully automatic, within the same system. Researchers at the University of Washington define five levels of agent autonomy by the role the human plays. The authors make a point every SOC leader should take to heart, that autonomy is a deliberate design choice, separate from how capable the agent is.

Gartner offers a complementary distinction between a human in the loop, who approves each action, and a human on the loop, whose oversight is strategic. The OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications extends least privilege into least agency, granting agents only the minimum autonomy needed for safe, bounded tasks. Read through this lens, the a16z data describes a market moving from roughly L2 today toward L4 for low-risk actions within a year. The article says analyst time is the scarcest resource in the SOC, and every alert still means pulling evidence from several systems, reconstructing what happened and deciding whether it matters.

The article maps the four stages onto security operations as evidence collection, analysis and verdict, response recommendation, and response execution. It says a team can automate the first two stages heavily, since that is where analyst hours go and where mistakes are cheapest to catch. The same team can stay conservative on the fourth stage, where a wrong move disrupts the business. As the a16z report itself puts it, gathering logs is different from changing a production system. The article says the exact placement will differ by organization, and that is the point.

The article says the move from 36% to 60% will happen with or without a plan. It lists five steps, starting with inventorying every action and placing each one on the reversibility, blast radius and receipts rubric. It says to automate investigation aggressively, gate disruptive response with real evidence, write graduation and demotion criteria now, and govern the agent like a privileged identity. It says a single serious miss should trigger a demotion until the criteria are met again. The article ends mid-sentence, describing forensic-level investigation as the approach Intezer's AI SOC is bui.

Articles.Title: The Path to AI Autonomy in the SOC

stories.Headline: TechCrunch lists six AI gadgets for smarter home offices
stories.Summary:
TechCrunch published a roundup on November 20, 2026, describing six AI-powered gadgets that the outlet says could make a home office smarter, and the list covers tools for note taking, video calls, desk work and quick AI shortcuts. The items include the Flowtica Scribe pen, Anker’s Soundcore Work recording pin, Logitech’s MX Keypad, Amazon’s Kindle Scribe Colorsoft, Insta360’s Link 2 Pro webcam and the Autonomous Desk Pro standing desk. The article presents each device as a way to handle common office tasks, such as writing notes during meetings, capturing conversations, launching AI assistants and staying in frame on video calls. It also notes that TechCrunch may earn a small commission when readers buy through links in its articles, and says this does not affect its editorial independence.

The Flowtica Scribe combines a gel pen with audio recording, and its AI can transcribe a conversation, summarize key points and build a to-do list, with a built-in microphone, 32GB of storage, support for up to 15 speakers and 92 languages. Anker’s coin-sized Soundcore Work is priced at $159 and currently reduced to $99 in the Amazon Black Friday sale, and it records for up to eight hours alone or 32 hours with its charging case, with a claimed range of up to 5 meters and 300 free transcription minutes each month. Anker also offers optional plans, Pro at $99 per year and Unlimited at $239 per year. Logitech’s MX Keypad adds dedicated buttons for launching AI assistants and productivity tools, including GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Microsoft Teams, PowerPoint, Excel, Notion, Slack, Photoshop, Final Cut Pro, Zoom and Figma. The Kindle Scribe Colorsoft starts at $479 and adds color plus AI tools that clean up handwriting, straighten highlighting, summarize notes and search saved notes.

Insta360’s Link 2 Pro is priced at $249 and discounted to $199 for Black Friday, and it combines 4K video with intelligent tracking, automatic framing, group tracking and AI noise cancellation. The Autonomous Desk Pro is an adjustable standing desk that uses built-in sensors to monitor activity, remind users to move, stretch or change positions, and track sitting versus standing time. The article says users can ask the desk questions about their activity, such as how long they have been sitting, how the day compares with the previous one, or the room’s CO2 levels. The piece is written by Lauren, who covers media, streaming, apps and platforms at TechCrunch, and it includes contact details for reaching her by email or through Signal.

stories.Headline: Chinese spies use autonomous AI agents to exploit zero-day flaw and seize university server
stories.Summary:
Suspected Chinese spies used autonomous AI agents to discover and exploit a zero-day vulnerability to seize control of a university server. This campaign began on September 8 and lasted for 48 hours, targeting university networks located in East Asia outside of Mainland China. The attackers utilized an open source penetration-testing framework called Cairn to conduct multi-stage intrusions without any human assistance. These agents spent nearly a full day adapting their tactics, including failed attempts to breach a Redis server and a GPU server.

The successful attack targeted MONAI Label, which is an open-source medical imaging AI application, by exploiting a path traversal vulnerability. The AI agents mapped API endpoints and found a vulnerable upload parameter, allowing them to write files and execute a Python reverse shell as root within 11 minutes. Amazon notified the maintainers of the project, who subsequently released a security advisory and a fix for the flaw. After the initial breach, a human operator provided a proxy that allowed the agents to tunnel into a second university network running the same vulnerable code.

Amazon CISO CJ Moses reported that the Threat Intelligence Team discovered the operation on September 10 via a publicly hosted instance of Cairn. Moses stated that the agents demonstrated an ability to adapt for nearly a full day without human direction, showing that autonomous frameworks are now used for espionage. He noted that the prompts were written in Simplified Chinese and the scripts used China Standard Time. This discovery aligns with a report from Gambit Security documenting a Chinese operator using Cairn to compromise at least 27 companies during September.

The broader context reveals that these AI harnesses are being adopted for both criminal operations and state-sponsored espionage. Other targets in September included a Fortune 500 hospitality company, a major US airline, and a large private US industrial supplies distributor. These attackers stole sensitive data and credit card records using Cairn and two other open source AI tools. The incidents highlight a growing trend of using autonomous agents to conduct complex, multi-stage cyberattacks against diverse global targets.

stories.Summary:
The article, published by hitconsultant.net on November 20, 2026, argues for an AI-first payer model that would reshape how health insurance members first interact with their plans. It describes the front door of a payer as the member's earliest point of contact and proposes putting artificial intelligence at that entry point. The piece is an opinion and analysis column rather than a report of a specific event, so no company, agency or individual is named as having taken an action. No date other than the publication date is given, and no figures, statistics or named people appear in the available text.

Because the article is an argument rather than a news report, it does not set out a concrete requirement, deadline or change that any organization must adopt. It makes the case that an AI-first model should replace or supplement the traditional front door of a payer, but the available text gives no numbers, no dates and no names of executives, regulators or companies. No specific technology, vendor or budget is identified in the material provided. The article therefore describes a proposed direction rather than a decided change.

The available text does not attribute responsibility to any named person or organization, and it contains no statements from executives, officials or other spokespeople that could be paraphrased. No one is quoted, and no one is described as endorsing or opposing the proposal. The only responsible party identified is the publication itself, hitconsultant.net, which ran the piece on November 20, 2026. Because no named source speaks in the article, there is nothing further to paraphrase on who said what.

The context the article supplies is limited to its framing of the payer front door as the member's first point of contact and its argument that artificial intelligence should lead that experience. The available text does not say what happens next, whether any payer has adopted such a model, or whether further coverage is planned. stories.Headline: Meta AI funds LSU project that uses color-coded alerts to monitor infants breathing through artificial airways
stories.Summary:
Meta AI partnered with the LSU system on November 20, 2026, to launch five projects aimed at solving various healthcare challenges. One specific initiative called Eyes-On focuses on assisting infants who rely on artificial airways to breathe. This project functions as a specialized baby monitor for infants with complex or technology-dependent medical problems. The system uses a color-coded alert process to notify medical staff about the status of the airway tubes.

The project requires a total of 80,000 dollars in funding provided by Meta AI to operate. A green light indicates the tube is correctly in place, while orange means the system is uncertain. A red light triggers an alarm to warn staff that the tube has come out. The ultimate goal of the Eyes-On project is to keep babies healthy until they can breathe independently.

Michael Dunham, the Head of Pediatric Otolaryngology at the LSU School of Health, is responsible for the project. He stated that artificial intelligence should not be relied upon to perform these medical tasks entirely. Dunham believes humans must evaluate the input data and make the final decisions based on the AI output. He argued that keeping humans integrated ensures the foundation of healthcare remains people taking care of other people.

stories.Headline: Bain reports a third of US and European shoppers use AI assistants for shopping
stories.Summary:
About a third of consumers in the US and Europe use AI assistants for shopping, Bain & Company reported on November 20, 2026. Bain said AI is becoming the new search and is reshaping the top of the shopping funnel. ChatGPT alone serves 1.2 billion weekly users, Bain said. An estimated 15% to 20% of their prompts are shopping-related, up from 9% in 2025. Bain said shoppers now start with AI, which picks the best fit, not the biggest retailer.

A Bain Consumer Lab global survey found 33% of consumers in the US and 36% in Europe use AI assistants for some part of the shopping journey as of November 2026. That is up from 19% in the US and 8% in Europe in September 2025. AI assistants such as ChatGPT and Claude currently account for less than 1% of retailers' directly linked web traffic, according to Bain's analysis of estimates from Similarweb. Bain said AI referral traffic, though small, converts 90% better than non-AI traffic. Bain analyzed more than 4,400 shopping prompts across four retail verticals, testing more than 300,000 unique runs across the most used large language models, powered by Profound data.

Bain said retailers absent from AI responses will cede visibility, awareness, traffic, and profits. Bain said making the list requires a clear value proposition, an adaptable generative engine optimization strategy, and a focus on winning the shopper's occasion. Bain said leading retailers will build their assistants on proprietary data, using personalization, brand trust, and category expertise. Bain said a superior, well-communicated core value proposition should still win the purchase. Bain said retailers should ask whether they are winning for the things they want to be known for.

Bain said Kroger appears more often for prompts about promotion and loyalty, whereas Whole Foods outperforms on dietary needs and product selection. In Bain's grocery analysis, the top 10 sources accounted for roughly 30% of all citations across ChatGPT, Claude, and Google AI and Gemini. Bain said only 27 of the top 100 US retailers have a first-party AI assistant. A Bain survey found consumers still trust retailers' first-party assistants nearly twice as much as third-party ones. Walmart says Sparky users have up to 40% higher average order value, and Amazon says Alexa for Shopping users have about 40% higher average order value.

For Brazilian retailer Magazine Luiza, shoppers using its Lu assistant via WhatsApp convert at three times the rate of its traditional app users, Bain said. Bain said Lu earns an 85-point Net Promoter Score and 75% of payments happen on WhatsApp. Best Buy's Ask Blue launched in time for the holidays, Bain said. Carrefour's Hopla helps shoppers eat healthier with product swaps based on dietary preferences and analysis of cart and meal photos. Bain said a recent ChatGPT update sharply cut social media citations in favor of retailer websites and earned media.

Bain said more than 10 million people in the US and Canada set up agents in the six weeks after Meta's Muse launched. Shopping is the No. 1 use case, with purchases averaging more than $200, Bain said. Bain said consumer adoption is set to skyrocket in 2027 if early trends hold. Bain recommended retailers run a prompt audit before Black Friday and the final holiday rush. Bain said a solid GEO strategy never stops testing, learning, and adapting.

stories.Headline: Ant Digital Technologies and JB Financial Group partner to explore agentic AI in financial services
stories.Summary:
Dmitry Tikhomirov of EPAM Systems discussed agentic AI for financial services and insurance on November 10, 2026. Ant Digital Technologies and JB Financial Group signed a memorandum of understanding on November 18, 2026. This partnership occurred during the Singapore FinTech Festival 2026 to explore AI powered innovation. The collaboration focuses on applying AI agents to banking operations for risk management and efficiency. These developments highlight a shift toward autonomous systems that can plan tasks and execute actions.

The MOU involves Ant Digital Technologies, a subsidiary of Ant Group, and Korea's JB Financial Group. JB Financial Group includes Jeonbuk Bank, Kwangju Bank, JB Woori Capital, JB Asset Management, and JB Investment. Their overseas network includes PPCBank in Cambodia, JB Capital Myanmar, JB Securities Vietnam, and PT Bukopin Finance. Microsoft provides a stack including Entra ID, Agent 365, Purview, Defender, Work IQ, Fabric IQ, and Foundry IQ. The Foundry Agent Service acts as the runtime for deploying and managing agents in production.

Dmitry Tikhomirov stated that agentic AI is a good fit for industries full of rules and documents. He argued that AI agents excel where humans currently act as costly middleware between different systems. Leo Li of Ant Digital Technologies said he looks forward to developing responsible and practical AI capabilities. Ki Hong Kim of JB Financial Group said the technology will strengthen competitiveness in credit assessment. He also noted that the collaboration will improve financial access for their various foreign customers.

Banking clients are affected through improved onboarding, KYC refresh, alert handling, and financial crime investigations. Insurance users benefit from better underwriting intake, claims triage, policy servicing, and fraud referral processes. Capital markets see changes in post-trade exceptions, reconciliations, and surveillance triage to reduce manual coordination. McKinsey research from October 2026 notes a banking industry shift from AI copilots toward agentic AI systems. These systems are designed to collaborate across business workflows to create lasting value for the industry.

Ant Digital Technologies has operated independently since April 2024 and established Hong Kong headquarters in 2025. The company has partnered with over 300 partners to serve more than 30,000 enterprise customers worldwide. They have established collaborations in Asia with Ryt Bank, Touch 'n Go, Kenanga Investment Bank Berhad, and Bank CenterCredit. Omdia recognized Ant DT as a Market Leader in the 2026 Market Radar for agentic AI solutions. The 2026 Future of Fintech in APAC report describes a transforming landscape for digital lending and payments.

The partners will now identify practical AI applications that address the evolving needs of the financial industry. Firms are encouraged to redesign workflows from the ground up around digital labor rather than adding AI. Leaders must calibrate autonomy by setting specific mandates, clear permissions, and visible boundaries for every AI agent. The articles leave open how regulators will eventually use telemetry from Azure services for necessary audit trails. It remains to be seen how these firms will measure business outcomes like leakage and false positives.

stories.Headline: Chipmaker shares plunge as investors sell off artificial intelligence stocks
stories.Summary:
Shares of Micron Technology, SanDisk, and various other chipmakers plunged during early trading on Friday, November 20, 2026. This sudden decline occurred as investors remained under pressure due to a continuing selloff in technology and artificial intelligence stocks. The tech-heavy Nasdaq fell by more than 2 percent, while the S&P 500 index dropped around 1 percent. In contrast, the Dow Jones Industrial Average traded slightly higher because of gains in retail and healthcare stocks.

The market requires AI model and application revenues to reach at least $1.5 trillion by 2030 for an adequate return. UBS expects the Federal Reserve to implement 25-basis-point rate hikes in December 2026 and March 2027. Total United States technology investment in AI infrastructure could approach $5 trillion by the end of 2028. The iShares Semiconductor ETF, VanEck Semiconductor ETF, and Roundhill Memory ETF all declined by as much as 7 percent.

UBS stated that the risk-reward in equities has become more balanced following persistent pressure on cloud companies and chipmakers. The firm noted that monetary policy uncertainty added to fragile sentiment, though the structural AI investment story remains intact. An AMD spokesperson told Bloomberg that the company maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance with all applicable United States export control laws. UBS believes that the cumulative effects of higher rates will likely weigh on consumer demand.

The firm expects economic growth to remain close to the trend in 2027 with rising corporate profits. UBS predicts approximately 15 percent S&P 500 earnings growth in 2027 and sees further upside for equities. They favor financially strong hyperscalers with visible monetization and select leaders in semiconductor equipment and infrastructure software. The firm remains cautious regarding lower-quality suppliers and companies with valuations based on distant cash flows.

stories.Headline: California political candidates use AI to create fake images for election advertising
stories.Summary:
Political candidates used artificial intelligence to create fake images for election advertising in California. These campaigns used the technology to stand out on the air and online. Many of these ads appeared during the current election year. Some candidates depicted themselves as heroic figures or fought massive robots. Other images showed candidates kowtowing to rich fat cats and bloodthirsty crowds.

Researchers at the Wesleyan Media Project found campaigns spent over 137 million dollars on AI ads by mid-October. Republican groups accounted for about 80 percent of those messages. Steve Hilton appeared as a gladiator with Xavier Becerra and Gavin Newsom in a coliseum. Spencer Pratt depicted himself as Batman, while a San Diego school board candidate used a fake bake sale. These ads appeared on platforms like TikTok, Instagram, and X.

Ramesh Srinivasan is a UCLA professor of information studies who hosts the Utopias podcast. He said AI can now automatically create content that targets voters based on their psychology. Srinivasan stated that people lack disclosure regarding when content is AI generated. He believes this is pernicious because it removes a common basis of reality. He is working with the U.S. Congress and state Senate to require watermarks.

A female school board candidate in San Diego called an AI image of her sexist. Srinivasan noted that the president used AI to show himself healing a patient resembling Jon Stewart. He said voters cannot always tell the difference between AI and human created content. This lack of distinction may influence whether people vote or for whom they vote. He believes this is a problem for a functioning democracy.

The articles mention the Cambridge Analytica story from the last 10 years regarding psychological targeting. That organization used data brokers and credit card records to influence people. Srinivasan noted that Big Tech companies may have censored content during the Biden administration. He mentioned that these companies seemed to bend the knee at the inauguration. He argues that technology should expand human abilities rather than replace them.

Srinivasan wants to rein in AI companies to ensure they pay people for their data. He believes regulation can direct innovation to accompany social and economic progress. The articles leave open whether a leader will emerge to protect democracy in 2028. It remains unclear if platforms will adhere to basic standards of disclosure. The future of collective governance depends on whether people share a common reality.

stories.Headline: Louisville Public Media CEO Kenya Young says staff review all AI use and journalists write its stories
stories.Summary:
Louisville Public Media published a statement of its practices on artificial intelligence on November 20, 2026, and its President and CEO, Kenya Young, issued a message the same day explaining how the organization uses AI and how it does not. Young said LPM had been watching the technology closely and planning for the changing landscape, and that AI is part of the organization's new three-year strategic plan under its priority of Digital Transformation and Adaptability. The plan says LPM will adopt AI tools with clear ethical standards that increase efficiency and responsiveness, freeing staff capacity for higher-value work. Young said LPM is in the beginning stages of adapting to AI and is exploring, experimenting and in some cases already using AI tools for work behind the scenes. Young said the tools are used for tasks such as transcription, research and data analysis, and that anything LPM uses AI for is reviewed and checked by a person.

She said LPM does not use AI to write its stories, that its journalists source stories, conduct interviews and write the news, and that this will not change. She said LPM does not use AI to choose the music listeners hear, does not play AI-generated music on air, and will not use AI to replicate anyone's voice or to alter real audio, photos or video. Young said hosts and music staff decide what plays on WFPK and WUOL, and that staff own the final result of whatever AI helps with. Young said technology companies, including AI companies, have invested heavily in journalism and media in recent years, and that LPM has received support from some of them, including the Google News Initiative and the OpenAI Foundation's People-First AI Fund. She said the organization's ethics and independence policy states there is no connection between its funding and editorial decisions, and that donors have no direct access to the newsroom, programming or those who make content decisions.

She said that holds for technology companies too, and that their support comes with no influence over what news LPM covers or what music it plays and no commitment to any company's products. Young said media companies across the country are cutting staff, and some have tied those cuts directly to their increased use of AI, while data centers are going up in communities, particularly in Kentucky. She said AI is undoubtedly changing how people work and navigate their days, and that a generation ago the internet changed the media landscape, in some ways for the better and in others for the worse. She said LPM will keep innovating, experimenting and evolving, guided by its standards and ethics, and that the most important theme in its strategic plan is trust. She said trust has to be earned every day, with every concerto on WUOL, every new artist on WFPK and every local story on WFPL.

stories.Headline: PAHO publishes guidance on reinforcement learning in health AI
stories.Summary:
The Pan American Health Organization presented a new publication on 20 November 2026 in Washington, D.C., titled "Reinforcement Learning in Artificial Intelligence for Health: Opportunities, Risks, and Implications for Policy and Practice," which examines the opportunities, risks, and implications of reinforcement learning in artificial intelligence for health systems. The document provides guidance for policymakers, health authorities, technical teams, and health professionals so that they can better understand the potential of this technology and promote its responsible implementation. Reinforcement learning represents a step forward toward AI systems capable of supporting decisions that evolve over time, because it enables the identification and adjustment of strategies based on feedback from previous decisions. In health systems, where clinical and public health decisions are often part of continuous processes, this capability opens up new possibilities for improving care and operations.

The publication states that this approach can help optimize treatment sequences, support the care of people living with chronic conditions, improve the allocation of health resources, and develop public health interventions that adapt to changing epidemiological and operational conditions. It highlights that the potential of these technologies depends not only on their technical capabilities but also on the institutional conditions that support their implementation. One of the main challenges is preventing these systems from reproducing or amplifying inequalities embedded in historical data, and their adaptive nature means they require validation, monitoring, and continuous evaluation mechanisms to identify potential risks to safety, equity, and quality of care. The document emphasizes the importance of high-quality data, interoperable digital infrastructure, appropriate governance frameworks, and technical and institutional capacities.

The publication also underscores that human oversight must remain an essential component, ensuring that AI-generated recommendations strengthen, rather than replace, the judgment of health professionals and decision-makers. This approach aims to foster innovation without compromising patient safety, equity, or the protection of fundamental rights. The publication is part of PAHO's ongoing efforts to advance the digital transformation of the health sector in the Americas and to promote the development and use of safe, equitable, and people-centered artificial intelligence technologies. PAHO offers the full publication for download in English and invites interested readers to subscribe to a mailing list for updates on publications, activities, and resources related to artificial intelligence and digital health.

stories.Headline: Gallup finds frequent AI users report no change in meeting time
stories.Summary:
Gallup surveyed 21,648 U.S. employees and found that among the 32% of respondents who use artificial intelligence a few times a week or more, most reported no savings in meeting time. In that group of frequent users, 52% said they spend less time gathering information and 47% said they spend less time writing. But 83% said their time in meetings has not changed, and 78% reported no change in the time they spend collaborating with coworkers. The survey also found that 82% of frequent AI users spend about the same amount of time working with customers or clients.

The results suggest that while artificial intelligence speeds up some tasks, other parts of workplace life may be essentially AI-proof, and meeting time is the clearest example. A 2024 survey by the scheduling platform Reclaim.ai found that employees spend nearly 15 hours a week in meetings on average, which is roughly 37% of a standard workweek. Nearly two-thirds of frequent AI users, or 65%, said their roles require about the same mental effort as before, while 21% reported expending less mental effort and 14% said their work has become even more demanding. Among frequent users, 21% said they now spend more time reviewing and correcting work, and the same percentage reported spending more time learning new skills and tools.

Among employees at organizations that have adopted AI, just 29% told Gallup the technology has raised expectations for how much work they should complete in a day. Frequent AI users are more likely to feel pressure, however, since 36% said AI has raised expectations for their output and 33% said they felt pressure to use the technology to keep up. The survey's results suggest that AI is replacing routine tasks while creating new responsibilities, which may explain why even frequent users find their jobs have not gotten easier overall. Although meeting time has dropped from its pandemic-era peak, studies show that meetings still eat up an extraordinary amount of the typical worker's schedule.

stories.Headline: TeraWulf begins erecting structural steel at its 480 MW Kentucky AI campus for Anthropic
stories.Summary:
TeraWulf has moved from foundational work to vertical construction at its Justified Data Campus in Hawesville, Kentucky, where the company announced on LinkedIn that the first structural steel is going up at the Hancock County site, according to US Data Center Projects. The 480 MW facility is being purpose-built for the artificial intelligence company Anthropic, and the majority of structural steel for the first building, known as CB-1, has already been delivered and staged, with substantial deliveries also completed for CB-2. TeraWulf described the development as an important transition as it advances large-scale infrastructure built specifically for its customer Anthropic. Engineering, procurement and construction work at the site is being handled by Fluor Corporation, a partnership that has grown beyond the two companies' earlier collaborations. The Justified Data Campus occupies a 790-acre site in Hancock County that was previously used for aluminum processing, and Century Aluminum operated at the location from 1969 until 2022, when TeraWulf acquired the property with plans to convert the long-standing industrial site into digital infrastructure.

The project was announced in February, and the first facility at the campus is due to come online in 2027. Anthropic will lease capacity at the site, with Google acting as a backstop for the arrangement, and the campus is designed to support large-scale AI and high-performance computing workloads. At 480 MW of capacity, the Hawesville campus represents one of TeraWulf's largest commitments to date. Leo Kaid, president of Fluor's advanced technologies and life sciences business line, said earlier this month that Fluor is proud to expand its partnership with TeraWulf and support the delivery of infrastructure needed to meet rapidly growing demand for artificial intelligence and high-performance computing. He added that the company's integrated engineering, procurement and construction capabilities, combined with its data center expertise and skilled workforce, position it to deliver the project with a strong focus on safety, quality and schedule certainty.

The Hawesville development is one of several projects in TeraWulf's expanding portfolio, and the company currently operates a campus outside Buffalo, New York, located at a former coal power plant where it initially mined cryptocurrency at the 180-acre site before beginning to pivot the campus toward AI and HPC uses. Core42 and Fluidstack are live customers at the New York location, and in addition to its operating site and the Hawesville campus, TeraWulf is developing sites in Maryland and Kentucky and is planning a second development in Lansing, New York. The move away from cryptocurrency mining toward AI and HPC infrastructure reflects a broader strategic direction for the company. With the majority of structural steel for CB-1 staged and substantial deliveries for CB-2 complete, the project is positioned for continued above-ground construction activity in the coming months, and the first facility is expected to come online in 2027.

stories.Headline: ABC Corporation uses OpenAI's dots to manage a vinyl greenhouse in a two week trial
stories.Summary:
ABC Corporation, a company based in Nagoya's Nakamura ward, said its research and development division ran an experiment from November 1 to November 15, 2026, in which OpenAI's general-purpose AI agent "dots" served as the core system for managing a vinyl greenhouse used in protected cultivation. The company reported that the trial achieved stable management of the greenhouse. The work drew on procedures the company had built up while operating its own systems. The experiment covered sensing conditions inside the house, managing water, ventilation, liquid fertilizer and nutrient solution, and adjusting lighting according to the crop's growth stage.

The trial addressed six management items, namely temperature and humidity control, water management, rolling up the greenhouse vinyl for ventilation, continuous environmental monitoring, light source management that adjusts the timing and duration of illumination to match growth stages, and liquid fertilizer and nutrient solution management. In the experiment, an IoT box gathering several sensors inside the house was made available to dots, and cameras installed in the greenhouse acted as the agent's eyes. dots grasped conditions from the camera images as well as the sensor readings and made the judgments needed for facility management. The company confirmed that this setup could carry out its existing management procedures. Previously the company had implemented in-house the software framework, or harness, that combined the functions needed for daily management.

The company said that when AI is used in agriculture, one approach is to develop custom programs for each facility and use case, but it sees a problem in that priority tends to go to implementing the functions needed on site, leaving security questions, such as what information to give the AI and which equipment operations to entrust to it, pushed back. For this project it therefore concentrated the core of facility management in dots. When expanding to other greenhouses, it aims to set common rules for the information the AI handles and the scope of operations it performs, so that measures do not vary from facility to facility and a certain security level is secured. It also aims to turn the management methods cultivated in its own house into a form that can be applied to other vinyl greenhouses, and it will study management mechanisms usable according to each facility's equipment and operations.

ABC Corporation is located at 12-8 Tsubakicho, Nakamura ward, Nagoya, in Aichi prefecture, and its representative is Kina Oda. The company was founded in February 2021, has capital of 15 million yen, is unlisted, and lists information and communication as its industry. The experiment ran for about two weeks in early November 2026. The company said it will use the knowledge gained from the experiment to research management systems that can be adapted to the equipment and operation of individual facilities.

Articles.Title: ABC Corporation succeeds in experiment to manage greenhouse cultivation using OpenAI's "dots"

stories.Headline: Study Pocket launches AI simultaneous interpretation for schools in April 2027
stories.Summary:
Study Pocket Co., Ltd., a Tokyo-based company led by CEO Ryo Yamaji and CAIO Hiroyuki Tsuruta, announced on November 20, 2026 that it will officially offer its school-oriented web service "Study Pocket AI Simultaneous Interpretation" from April 2027, a tool that interprets conversations between teachers and children and students who need Japanese language instruction as well as parents with foreign roots. The service was first announced in May 2026 as "Study Pocket AI Interpreter" and was provided free of charge during the current fiscal year to teacher accounts of "Study Pocket for TEACHER," after which trial use continued at schools and municipalities that made inquiries. With the official launch the name changes to "Study Pocket AI Simultaneous Interpretation," and the pricing and timing that were undecided at the time of the announcement have now been set. The service runs in the browser of GIGA school devices without any dedicated equipment, and it supports bidirectional interpretation that displays the teacher's Japanese in the other person's language and the child's or parent's words in Japanese on the screen in real time.

The pricing is 50,000 yen per school per year, excluding tax, which covers all faculty and staff and up to five children needing Japanese instruction, with an additional 10,000 yen per year excluding tax for each person from the sixth child, and contracts are made per school and per fiscal year from April to the following March, with quotations and invoices available. The service supports 60 languages including Japanese, with Portuguese, Chinese, Filipino, English, Spanish, Vietnamese and Korean placed under frequently used languages, and it offers a face-to-face mode, full-screen display, adjustable text size, color coding by speaker, conversation records that can be reviewed later, AI summaries after a conversation and export in TXT or CSV formats. Speech recognition and interpretation use the Japan region of the voice AI Soniox, with audio sent directly from the device browser to Soniox, and schools decide the scope of use, as administrators assign children one by one from a roster. According to a May 2026 Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology survey, 84,759 children in public schools needed Japanese language instruction as of May 1, 2025, up 15,636, or 22.6 percent, from the previous survey, of whom 73,313 held foreign nationality and 11,446 held Japanese nationality, and 12,668 public schools, or 39.4 percent of all public schools, had at least one such child, while about 8,300 schools, roughly two thirds, had only one to four.

The company says it developed the service because such children are enrolled in small numbers across many schools and the languages used differ from school to school, making it difficult to station interpreters or native-language supporters at every school, so teachers often combine gestures and translation tools in class and meetings. A teacher at a public junior high school in the Chugoku and Shikoku area who used it during a three-way meeting with a parent from Vietnam said the parent tearfully told the teacher in her native language that she was truly grateful, and the teacher felt that feelings had gotten through beyond the language barrier. The company plans to hold a demonstration at its "StudyPocket Product Day 2026" online event on December 1, 2026 from 15:00 to 16:30, free with advance registration, showing the actual screen and plans for provision in fiscal 2027. Free trial use under this year's demonstration ends at the end of February 2027, and official provision begins in April 2027, with trial and demo requests handled individually.

stories.Headline: Algerian professor Fayçal Djeridane presents AI cancer screening project with Laghouat as potential pilot region
stories.Summary:
Professor Fayçal Djeridane presented the prospects of an ambitious AI-assisted cancer screening project at the 1st National Forum of Oncology Experts, held on November 5, 6, 2026, at the Chahid Mohamed Rezoug Cancer Center (CLCC) in Laghouat, Algeria. The forum gave particular attention to the opportunities offered by artificial intelligence in developing predictive and adaptive oncology during its scientific discussions. Djeridane is an internationally recognized Algerian expert in artificial intelligence and medical imaging and a member of the High Council of the National Scientific Community Abroad. His presentation highlighted the potential of emerging technologies in cancer screening and introduced the prospects of the project. The province of Laghouat could be selected as a pilot region for the AI-assisted cancer screening project.

The project would require defining the targeted cancers and eligible populations and establishing clearly structured screening pathways. It would require ensuring the availability of appropriate diagnostic infrastructure and training healthcare professionals. It would require validating algorithms in the Algerian population and protecting and securing medical data. It would require regularly evaluating diagnostic performance and project outcomes. The article was published on OncoDaily on November 20, 2026, and was authored by Abderrahim Djellaoui, MD, an Assistant Professor in Medical Oncology in Laghouat, Algeria, and medically reviewed by Vahe Grigoryan, MD, Editorial Director.

The article states that the aim is not to replace the expertise of radiologists or oncologists but to provide them with complementary tools. It states that a model designed using data from other countries does not necessarily guarantee the same level of performance in the Algerian population. It states that local validation is therefore a fundamental step before any large-scale implementation. It states that the approach requires close collaboration between oncologists, radiologists, biologists, epidemiologists, engineers, and data scientists. It states that artificial intelligence alone cannot solve all the challenges of cancer screening.

The article states that screening programs face challenges including the growing volume of medical imaging examinations, the availability of specialists, reporting delays, variability in diagnostic performance, and geographical inequalities in access to healthcare. It states that AI could offer applications including AI-assisted identification of suspicious lesions and improved analysis of mammograms and other medical imaging examinations. It states that applications also include characterization of certain radiological abnormalities, standardization and optimization of image interpretation, and support in identifying patients who require further diagnostic investigations. It states that the involvement of the Laghouat Cancer Center and its oncology team provides a particularly relevant clinical environment to support the initiative. It states that the project highlights the importance of collaboration between scientific experts, specialists in emerging technologies, and healthcare professionals.

The article states that cancer remains one of the major public health challenges worldwide and that early detection remains one of the key factors in improving patient outcomes and reducing cancer-related mortality. It states that AI is progressively emerging as a promising technology with the potential to transform medical practice, particularly in medical imaging, screening, risk assessment, and clinical decision support. It states that Algeria is also embracing this wave of innovation. It states that predictive oncology involves integrating clinical, biological, histopathological, molecular, and radiological data to better understand cancer behavior. It states that the combined analysis of these data could eventually help identify profiles associated with an increased risk of cancer, improve prognostic assessment, and contribute to predicting treatment response.

The article states that the potential selection of Laghouat as a pilot region opens up interesting prospects for exploring the integration of these emerging technologies into the Algerian healthcare system. It states that the Laghouat pilot project could provide an opportunity to develop a national experience in evaluating artificial intelligence tools applied to cancer screening. It states that such cooperation could also encourage the emergence of national research projects and contribute to strengthening Algeria's scientific expertise. It states that the transformation must be part of a structured strategy based on clear clinical objectives including improving access to screening, reducing diagnostic delays, addressing geographical inequalities, and improving patient outcomes. The article does not state whether the project has been approved, funded, or scheduled.

stories.Headline: MFour adds Google AI Mode to its consumer conversation feed and collects 2.8 million new AI conversations every 30 days
stories.Summary:
MFour Data Research, Inc., a provider of the largest mobile-app consumer panel in the U.S., announced on November 20, 2026, that it has added Google AI Mode to its AI conversation data feed. The Irvine, California, company said the addition means it now collects 2.8 million new consumer AI conversations every 30 days. Google AI Mode joins ChatGPT and Google Gemini in the feed, which MFour describes as the only platform connecting surveys and behaviors for full journey intelligence from prompt to purchase. The announcement builds on MFour's November 3 announcement that it had added Google Gemini, which expanded its collection from 2.35 million to 2.8 million new AI conversations every 30 days.

The addition gives clients greater scale and a broader view of how consumers use AI to research products and make decisions, according to the release. Google AI Mode lets consumers research products, compare brands and refine their choices through conversations within Google Search, and MFour connects those exchanges to the same consumers' subsequent behaviors. Brands and agencies can ask DANI, MFour's autonomous AI research analyst, to analyze AI conversations alongside connected behavioral and survey data and produce boardroom-ready reports. The AI conversation feed is also available for direct licensing, and MFour says the signals reveal what consumers are considering, what they do next and why.

Chris St. Hilaire, CEO of MFour Data Research, said a company cannot claim to understand its consumer if it is blind to the conversations shaping their decisions. He said customers are asking AI what to buy and which brands to trust, and that MFour connects those conversations to what they actually do next. He said this gives insights teams the power to walk into the boardroom with answers the business can act on, including what consumers want, what is winning their consideration and where to go next. MFour connects conversation data to the same consumer's demographics, web browsing, app usage, GPS-verified store visits, purchases and survey responses through a single identity.

MFour, founded in 2011, says its 14M+ consumer panel generates nine deterministic data streams all connected to a single identity, and that DANI provides analysis across 4 billion monthly buyer signals. The data comes from MFour's first-party panel, whose members opt in and are compensated for sharing their behavioral data and participating in surveys. The company says it is trusted by Samsung, Google, Amazon Ads, Microsoft, Hulu, Keurig Dr Pepper, Papa Johns and hundreds of other global brands. The release offers one free LLM insights report through MFour's website by providing DANI simple guidance on the insights being sought.

stories.Headline: Review authors link AI tools to supply chain resilience through agility and governance
stories.Summary:
A structured narrative synthesis of 75 studies published between 2015 and 2025 was published in Discover Artificial Intelligence. Adel Aazami, Amirhossein Hassani, Nadun Karunarathna, and Sebastian Kummer conducted the review. It examined how artificial intelligence can enhance supply chain resilience. The synthesis covered predictive analytics, machine learning, deep learning, digital twins, and robotic process automation. The review linked these tools to operational risk management.

The review covered literature published from January 2015 through December 2025. Database searches were executed through January 2026 across Emerald, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. The query combined three Boolean concept clusters covering supply chain contexts, artificial intelligence technologies, and resilience outcomes. The authors disclaimed compliance with PRISMA 2020 reporting standards because intermediate retrieval counts, database-specific search logs, screener counts, and inter-rater agreement statistics were not archived. Critical appraisal followed a qualitative, Joanna Briggs Institute-informed framework evaluating objective clarity, methodological adequacy, evidence validity, analytical transparency, and alignment between data and conclusions.

The authors assigned qualitative evidence weights of High, Medium, Low, and Limited support rather than numerical scores. They stated that artificial intelligence represents an enabling capability rather than a standalone operational remedy. They concluded that realized supply chain resilience depends on continuous co-evolution between technical capabilities, dynamic sensing and seizing routines, and verifiable institutional governance structures. They advised managers to sequence digital investments by establishing data quality, integration pipelines, and workforce analytics literacy before acquiring advanced predictive algorithms. They encouraged industry consortia and policymakers to develop standardized transparency protocols and secure data-pooling frameworks.

The synthesis found that research rose from fewer than 10 publications per year between 2015 and 2018 to more than 40 publications annually between 2023 and 2025. Research concentrated on demand forecasting and inventory management, while empirical investigations of supplier relationship management and deep-tier supplier vulnerabilities remained underrepresented. Conceptual frameworks, model-driven proposals, and simulation-based studies dominated the corpus, while longitudinal investigations and cross-industry empirical evaluations in live operational environments remained scarce. The authors noted that model opacity and black-box algorithms provoke algorithmic overrides during high-stakes crises. They also noted that disruptive crises are rare and poorly documented, generating a cold-start training problem that degrades algorithmic reliability.

Global logistics networks connect suppliers, manufacturing facilities, and consumer markets through cross-border flows of materials, capital, and data. Lean inventory and Just-in-Time principles removed safety stocks, backup sourcing channels, and redundant capacity across lower operational tiers. Modern networks face compounded shocks including the COVID-19 pandemic, geopolitical conflicts, and extreme climate events. Traditional risk management relied on historical probability distributions and static redundancy buffers. Many enterprise networks lack end-to-end visibility across lower supplier tiers.

The synthesis developed an organizing conversion architecture uniting the Resource-Based View, dynamic capabilities theory, and institutional governance frameworks. Agility and adaptability operate as intermediate organizational pathways converting technological inputs into realized resilience. Digital readiness and governance maturity function as independently necessary boundary conditions. Explainable artificial intelligence functions as an operational requirement providing local decision rationales alongside global feature priorities. The articles leave open the intermediate retrieval counts, database-specific search logs, screener counts, and inter-rater agreement statistics.
