stories.Headline: Ondas, Palantir and Regna AI convene defense leaders to speed AI into the field
stories.Summary:
Ondas Inc., Palantir Technologies Inc. and Regna AI co-hosted the Ondas Defense Technology Summit, a small, invitation-only executive session, on November 18 in Las Vegas. Ondas shared highlights from the summit in a press release dated November 20, 2026, issued from West Palm Beach, Florida and Miami, Florida. Executives and leaders from Ondas, Palantir, Regna AI and Aston Martin Performance Technologies attended, along with other defense technology and AI innovators and industry experts. The day opened with remarks from Ryan Hartman, President and Chief Executive Officer of Ondas Sentinel and Interim Chief Executive Officer of Regna AI. Palantir followed with a demonstration and presentation on sovereign AI for mission-critical operations.

The summit is one of the first activations of Ondas' Global Partner relationship with Aston Martin Aramco Formula One Team, announced as the "Speed to Decision" partnership. The partnership is a multi-year global partnership in the autonomous systems sector that extends through 2029. The Las Vegas Grand Prix will showcase Ondas through brand visibility, engineering collaboration and stakeholder engagement. Four panels covered autonomy in the air and at sea and where unmanned systems go next, investing in defense tech, how industry and the Department of Defense partner to deliver, and defense tech capital markets and mergers and acquisitions. Bob Bell, Business Development Consultant at Aston Martin Performance Technologies, led the session on Manufacturing and Supply Chains for Defense.

Eric Brock, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Ondas Inc., said defense technology is attracting growing demand and investment, and capital is following companies that can pair AI and autonomy with the ability to manufacture at scale. Brock said convening leaders from technology, defense and capital markets with Palantir and Regna AI reflects how Ondas is positioning itself at the center of that shift, turning innovation into fielded capability and creating long-term value for stockholders. Elias Davis, Office of the CEO at Palantir Technologies, said the companies are helping defense partners deploy sovereign AI on their own terms, with control over their data and operations. Davis said co-hosting the summit with Ondas and Regna AI reflects a deep and expanding partnership. Ryan Hartman said bringing the leaders into one room let them focus on how AI is changing the mission and what it will take to get capability into the field sooner.

Hartman said that across the demo and the panels the message was consistent: AI and autonomy only matter if operators can trust them, control them and rely on them. Hartman said that is where industry and government have to keep working side by side. The day closed with Q&A and closing remarks from Hartman. The focused, executive-level format allowed for candid conversations about AI across defense missions, including sovereign AI. The summit reflects Ondas' strategy of bringing together the software, autonomous platforms and production capability that modern warfare requires.

Ondas Inc. (NASDAQ:ONDS) describes itself as a leading provider of advanced autonomous systems and next-generation defense and security technologies. Ondas develops and deploys integrated unmanned and autonomous platforms across air, ground and stratospheric environments, including autonomous drone systems, counter-UAS technologies, robotic ground systems, advanced unmanned aircraft and propulsion solutions, demining and engineering systems, and integrated sensing and communications technologies. Ondas' solutions are deployed globally by government, defense and commercial customers to protect infrastructure, borders, transportation networks, personnel and strategic assets. Regna AI says it is building the sovereign AI layer for defense, putting mission intelligence under the customer's command through specialized AI models that governments and defense organizations can own, control and deploy wherever the mission demands. Formula One is one of the most technology-driven sports in the world, and the engineering, data and rapid manufacturing developed for the track are increasingly being applied in other industries.

stories.Headline: Review authors say AI can help close epilepsy diagnosis gaps in low-income countries
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a Review published in Nature Reviews Neurology on 20 November 2026 examining how artificial intelligence could address global disparities in epilepsy diagnosis and treatment, particularly in resource-limited settings. The Review was written by authors publishing in Nature Reviews Neurology, and it examines AI-based analysis of electroencephalography recordings captured with affordable open-source systems, smartphone data and electronic health records. It states that the convergence of AI and health care offers unprecedented opportunities to address disparities in access to specialized epilepsy diagnosis and treatment. It also states that advances in AI models, combined with increasing internet connectivity and smartphone usage in low-income and middle-income countries, offer promising solutions for epilepsy diagnosis and monitoring. The Review says this technological revolution raises important questions about the preservation and expansion of clinical expertise, AI algorithm transparency and health-care equity.

The Review states that most people with epilepsy live in low-income and middle-income countries, where shortages of neurologists, electroencephalography and MRI contribute to large diagnostic and treatment gaps. It says low-cost, open-source EEG systems combined with deep learning models that match expert performance in specific EEG tasks could enable minimally trained health workers to screen for epilepsy in resource-limited settings. It states that smartphone-based approaches, including video recordings of seizures and passive analysis of touchscreen interaction dynamics, are candidate tools for screening and monitoring but are not yet established diagnostic tests. It says multimodal and reasoning-capable large language models could integrate clinical histories in local languages with EEG data and explain their reasoning, and that affordable open-source models can run offline on local devices. It states that AI models trained in high-income settings often generalize poorly to other populations, so local data collection, external validation and attention to bias, data protection and cultural applicability are essential.

The Review states that responsible implementation requires a phased approach of hardware validation, local model adaptation, clinical trials and sustainable scaling that strengthens clinical expertise and community-based care. It says the authors examine how AI can help to address disparities and improve global epilepsy care while maintaining high clinical standards and addressing systemic challenges. The article presents figures on global internet penetration and on AI processing in epilepsy diagnosis with and without internet access. The article lists references including a 2024 Lancet Neurology analysis of the global burden of disorders affecting the nervous system from 1990 to 2021 and a 2018 Nature Reviews Disease Primers paper on epilepsy. It also lists a 2024 World Health Organization fact sheet on epilepsy and a 2017 Epilepsia review on premature mortality of epilepsy in low- and middle-income countries.

The article lists a 2017 ILAE position paper on classification of the epilepsies and a 2023 Epilepsy Research paper on challenges in epilepsy diagnosis and management in Bhutan. It lists the WHO 2017 Atlas of Country Resources for Neurological Disorders and a 2024 Seizure review on perceived and self-stigma in people with epilepsy in East Africa. It lists the WHO Intersectoral Global Action Plan on Epilepsy and Other Neurological Disorders 2022, 2031 and the WHO 2019 report Epilepsy: A Public Health Imperative. It lists a 2022 Epilepsia report from the ILAE Epidemiology Commission on the worldwide epilepsy treatment gap and a 2022 npj Digital Medicine review on AI for strengthening healthcare systems in low- and middle-income countries. It lists a 2024 Nature Reviews Neurology paper on AI in epilepsy and a 2023 JAMA Neurology paper on automated interpretation of clinical electroencephalograms using AI.

The article lists a 2022 Epilepsia paper on accurate identification of EEG recordings with interictal epileptiform discharges using a hybrid approach of AI supervised by human experts and a 2025 Epilepsia paper on expert level detection of interictal discharges with a deep neural network. It lists a 2024 Frontiers in Neuroscience review of epilepsy detection and prediction methods based on EEG signal processing and deep learning and a 2025 Epilepsy & Behavior survey of fellowship education in epilepsy in Latin America and Africa. It lists a 2010 IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Magazine paper on wearable electroencephalography and a 2022 Epilepsia systematic review on noninvasive mobile EEG for seizure monitoring and management. It lists a 2023 Sensors comparison of high-end and low-cost EEG amplifiers and a 2021 IEEE conference paper on a wearable system with in-ear EEG electrodes for monitoring brain activities. The article lists a 2025 IEEE Access paper on remote epilepsy monitoring signal quality and reliability and a 2014 PLoS ONE paper on the smartphone brain scanner.

It lists a 2017 Scientific Reports validation of smartphone-based EEG among people with epilepsy and a 2020 European Journal of Neurology paper on tablet-based EEG diagnostics in the West African Republic of Guinea. It lists a 2015 Nature paper on deep learning and a 2023 Archives of Computational Methods in Engineering review of convolutional neural network-based EEG signal analysis. It lists a 2025 Sensors review of transformers in EEG analysis and a 2025 IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics paper on a hybrid AI system for automated EEG background analysis and report generation. It lists a 2024 Epilepsia external validation study on generalizability of EEG interpretation using AI and a 2020 International Journal of Neural Systems paper on automated detection of interictal epileptiform discharges by convolutional neural networks. The article lists a 2022 Scientific Reports method for AI-assisted human interpretation of neonatal EEG and a 2021 Neurocritical Care paper on monitoring seizure burden and highly epileptiform patterns in critical care with a machine learning method.

It lists a 2025 IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics paper on EEG-Deformer and a 2024 PLoS ONE paper on epilepsy detection based on a multi-head self-attention mechanism. It lists a 2024 BioMedical Engineering OnLine paper on automatic detection of epilepsy from EEGs using a temporal convolutional network with a self-attention layer and a 2020 JAMA Neurology paper on expert-level automated detection of epileptiform discharges during EEG interpretation. It lists a 2023 Epilepsy & Behavior paper on epilepsy diagnosis using a clinical decision tool and artificially intelligent electroencephalography and a preprint on bioRxiv on reliable and automatic epilepsy classification with affordable consumer-grade electroencephalography in rural sub-Saharan Africa. The article states that the full text is available only through subscription or purchase. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Researchers launch autonomous AI agent to analyze neutron scattering data at China Spallation Neutron Source
stories.Summary:
Researchers recently introduced DrSai-Rongzai, an autonomous AI agent designed to analyze neutron scattering data at the China Spallation Neutron Source. This agent utilizes a large language model to perform joint neutron powder diffraction and pair-distribution-function analysis without any human intervention. By employing a hierarchical framework of reasoning and acting, the system orchestrates established refinement software to interpret complex materials data. The tool aims to eliminate the time-consuming iterative cycles of data reduction and modeling that typically challenge both experts and novices.

The system relies on Agentic Context Operation to maintain a working memory of file paths, domain rules, and intermediate results during processing. In tests using Si, CsAgTe, and Bi2MoO6, the agent produced structural parameters that were statistically indistinguishable from those derived by human experts. An 18-run factorial ablation study on two high-entropy alloys evaluated the MemoWrite and CoreSkillWrite mechanisms under 50k-token context compression. Full implementation of these components yielded a mean composite score of 0.9316 and a repeatability stability of 0.9905, while Memo alone improved performance by 20.2 percent.

The developers integrated the agent with a permission-controlled data interface at the facility to ensure the secure analysis of proprietary user data. They stated that the agent can move beyond simple recommendations to become a reliable partner in complex structural science. This integration allows for on-demand analysis and automatic archiving of results within the secure facility environment. The researchers believe this technology could potentially accelerate the overall rate of materials discovery at pulsed neutron sources across the entire world.

stories.Headline: Researchers propose a clinician-supervised hybrid AI framework to optimize medication regimens for multimorbid patients
stories.Summary:
An interdisciplinary research group formulated a conceptual framework to optimize pharmacotherapy in multimorbid patients through a clinician-supervised hybrid artificial intelligence system, published in the International Journal of Clinical Pharmacy. The framework was formulated between June 2025 and February 2026 by a team comprising specialists in clinical pharmacy, pharmacotherapy, artificial intelligence, digital health, and medication management. The authors adopted a design science-informed approach guided by problem identification, artifact design, and iterative refinement rather than a formal consensus methodology or clinical trial. The work responds to increasing clinical complexity driven by polypharmacy, fragmented patient records, expanding electronic health records, drug shortages, and healthcare workforce constraints. The investigators were informed by earlier feasibility work in artificial intelligence-supported pharmacotherapy, existing literature on clinical decision support platforms, and recurrent challenges observed in clinical practice.

The framework defines hybrid artificial intelligence as an operational integration uniting retrieval-augmented generation, deterministic safety rules, and contextual large language model reasoning. The researchers derived seven primary design principles, the first mandating decomposition of complex clinical workflows into distinct tasks with separate risk profiles and documentation needs, such as data acquisition, patient assessment, therapeutic goal formulation, safety checks, and guideline adherence reviews. The second principle establishes relevance-based prioritization by patient vulnerability and clinical urgency, such as highlighting severe drug-related problems over minor informational alerts. The third principle requires hybrid reasoning under strict human oversight, cross-referenced against established risk models and deterministic constraints, while the remaining four address patient alignment, professional agency, ongoing governance, and methodological evaluation. The data foundation incorporates structured electronic health record data, laboratory panels, vital signs, comorbidities, organ function metrics such as renal and hepatic assessments, and pharmacogenomic markers where available, alongside natural language processing of unstructured narratives and computer vision-based representation learning of guideline artifacts such as visual algorithms, decision flowcharts, and therapeutic tables.

The authors emphasize that the study presents a conceptual blueprint and does not provide empirical validation, performance metrics, or clinical trial outcomes. They state that stand-alone artificial intelligence models, especially general-purpose large language models, remain insufficiently reliable when deployed independently in complex medication management. They note that large language models demonstrate utility in answering isolated biomedical inquiries and categorizing descriptive data but present substantial clinical risks without structured clinical context, verification mechanisms, and explicit justifications. The authors stress that clinicians must actively shape the governance and clinical logic of these emerging digital tools to ensure future artificial intelligence implementations remain safely grounded in patient-centered pharmacotherapeutic reasoning. They also note that previous evaluative literature has disproportionately examined the outputs of off-the-shelf commercial language models rather than purpose-built clinical architectures.

Professional oversight and legal accountability remain anchored entirely with human healthcare providers, with physicians, clinical pharmacists, and allied health professionals retaining uncompromised authority to accept, modify, or reject system recommendations based on independent clinical assessments. Every recommendation is coupled with transparent rationales, explicit evidentiary citations, and visual uncertainty signaling indicating when data gaps warrant further investigation. Clinicians also record override justifications and performance feedback, establishing a traceable audit trail that supports continuous model refinement, helps prevent uncontrolled model drift, and aligns digital decision support with medical device regulatory requirements. The framework incorporates patient preferences, treatment burden thresholds, symptom severity, and adherence barriers, and envisions digital patient interfaces, potentially utilizing interactive avatar-based digital assistants on mobile devices, to gather longitudinal symptom reports, track well-being, and clarify medication concerns between clinical appointments. Key limitations include the absence of standardized consensus procedures during framework formulation, lack of direct patient involvement in design stages, and technical barriers surrounding electronic health record interoperability and secure data processing.

The authors aligned their structural design with the recently introduced MedinAI guidance, which mandates explicit documentation of model architectures, data provenance, ethical considerations, and verifiable human oversight in pharmacotherapy applications. They note that established reporting recommendations such as CONSORT-AI and TRIPOD-AI have advanced general reporting rigor. Citing broader evidence highlighting the absence of standardized testing protocols for retrieval-augmented generation in medicine, the investigators emphasized that their framework grew out of direct developmental experience with a de novo system engineered specifically to resolve complex drug-therapy trade-offs. The conceptual model positions its architectural safeguards within an evolving landscape of clinical artificial intelligence standards. The authors state that conventional clinical decision support systems remain primarily static and rule-based, frequently emitting non-contextual alerts that cause alert fatigue and exhibit limited clinical utility.

Implementation is expected to proceed modularly, beginning with deterministic safety rules before layering advanced retrieval-augmented components. System validation must proceed sequentially across multiple assessment layers, with initial evaluation phases focusing strictly on technical reliability, user interface ergonomics, alert relevance, workflow integration, and clinicians' trust in uncertainty signaling. Only after decision-support tools achieve stable, reproducible performance under real-world clinical constraints should trials proceed to quantify downstream clinical endpoints, including reductions in preventable adverse drug events. The articles leave open the empirical validation, performance metrics, and clinical trial outcomes the authors say the study does not provide. The articles also leave open how electronic health record interoperability and secure data processing barriers will be resolved.

stories.Headline: Abdullahi Hassan Elmi argues AI and ERAS protocols can jointly cut preventable surgical harm in low-resource hospitals
stories.Summary:
Abdullahi Hassan Elmi argued in a correspondence published in Patient Safety in Surgery that integrating Enhanced Recovery After Surgery pathways with artificial intelligence tools is a promising strategy to mitigate preventable harm in resource-limited surgical environments. The correspondence appeared on November 21, 2026, and was reported by Blake Davidson through Scienmag. Elmi's article is titled "Challenges for implementation of 'Enhanced Recovery After Surgery' (ERAS) protocols and artificial intelligence support tools in resource-limited countries." It was published in Patient Safety in Surgery, volume 20, issue 1, Article 24, with DOI 10.1186/s13037-026-00492-0. The article addresses surgical patient safety in developing and low-resource healthcare systems.

The correspondence states that surgical safety in these systems is compromised by delayed diagnostic assessments, restricted postoperative monitoring capacity, severe workforce deficits, incomplete clinical documentation, and inconsistent implementation of standardized perioperative protocols. It says ERAS pathways begin with comprehensive preoperative patient counselling and thorough nutritional optimization before surgery. It notes that formalized recommendations have been modified for elective abdominal and pelvic surgical procedures in primary and secondary hospitals in low- and middle-income nations. It cites a recent systematic meta-analysis confirming that rigorous application of enhanced recovery guidelines is statistically associated with shorter overall hospital lengths of stay and significant reductions in postoperative complications. It names the World Health Organization Surgical Safety Checklist as foremost among indispensable safeguards.

Elmi contends that artificial intelligence and structured surgical recovery pathways should be deployed as complementary components of a unified perioperative safety infrastructure rather than as separate, competing interventions. He argues that this combined paradigm could enhance institutional reliability, facilitate earlier recognition of patient deterioration, and foster sustainable quality improvement in environments operating under profound material constraints. He says the unified architecture is not designed to displace trained surgical professionals or substitute autonomous technology for human clinical judgment, but to supply frontline clinicians with practical digital aids. He emphasizes that artificial intelligence must never be introduced before basic clinical safety systems are firmly established and consistently maintained. He advocates a gradual, realistic, phased implementation roadmap tailored to the institutional constraints of resource-limited facilities.

The correspondence states that algorithmic tools can be trained for automated preoperative risk stratification, predicting delayed physiological recovery, evaluating susceptibility to specific surgical complications, and operating theater planning. It says such digital applications might include automated risk assessment algorithms, complication alert dashboards, digital audit feedback summaries, and structured outpatient follow-up notification systems. It cites a closed-loop audit study from Somalia examining adherence to the World Health Organization Surgical Safety Checklist, which underscored how iterative cycles of local audit, structured peer feedback, and systematic quality improvement can elevate checklist compliance. It warns that algorithms trained predominantly on data from well-resourced, high-income institutions and exported to low-resource hospitals without extensive local adaptation and validation create a primary hazard. It states that artificial intelligence applications in health must adhere to World Health Organization governance principles emphasizing transparency, accountability, patient safety, algorithmic equity, and ethical oversight.

The correspondence states that clinicians in underfunded hospitals must navigate acute shortages of specialized surgical and nursing personnel, fragile and fragmented referral pathways, and inadequate physiological monitoring technology. It says Enhanced Recovery After Surgery protocols provide a structured, evidence-based methodology that consolidates high-value clinical interventions into a coordinated continuum of care. It says the empirical foundation supporting these pathways has expanded considerably, demonstrating substantial clinical utility across varied socioeconomic and clinical contexts. It says rigorous international assessments across diverse high-income and low-income healthcare environments have repeatedly linked consistent checklist utilization to dramatic reductions in perioperative morbidity and surgical mortality rates. It says lessons from the Somali experience indicate that technological interventions achieve lasting clinical efficacy only when embedded within an organizational culture of open interdisciplinary communication, mutual accountability, and dedicated teamwork.

Under the advocated approach, hospitals in Somalia and analogous settings must first direct primary efforts toward fortifying fundamental clinical practices, including core recovery principles, checklist compliance, meticulous clinical documentation, infection prevention standards, postoperative monitoring routines, and multidisciplinary teamwork. Once these core processes operate reliably, institutions can judiciously integrate simple, affordable, and explainable artificial intelligence tools designed to execute specific, high-priority safety functions. The correspondence states that artificial intelligence algorithms cannot rectify deep-seated communication dysfunctions and that their clinical value is realized only within teams that already respect systematic verification and transparent peer review. It concludes that marrying resilient clinical care pathways with locally tested, ethically governed digital assistance can build a sustainable, reliable perioperative safety model that systematically reduces preventable operative harm. The articles leave open which specific hospitals would adopt the phased roadmap and when.

stories.Headline: A juvenile uses AI to make nude images of 61 students and staff at Woods Charter School
stories.Summary:
A juvenile is accused of using artificial intelligence to create nude images and videos of students and staff at Woods Charter School in Chatham County, according to a letter Principal Cotton Bryan sent to parents that WRAL News obtained. Bryan wrote that Chatham County deputies told school administrators the person used artificial intelligence to transform normal photos of dozens of students and staff into nude photos and videos. Some of the AI-altered material was then traded on the internet, Bryan wrote. According to Bryan, the person had pictures or videos of 47 current and former students and 14 current and former faculty members. Bryan added that there are other victims outside the school community, but the school has not received any additional details about them, and it is unclear which AI program the minor used.

Bryan said deputies told him the person they believe is responsible is a juvenile and that the school understood the person would be charged and taken into custody soon. The Chatham County Sheriff's Office declined to share specifics when asked about the case, stating only that it was conducting a criminal investigation involving the juvenile. Bryan said the school is cooperating fully with the Sheriff's Office and has reached out to outside expertise, specifically the Orange County Rape Crisis Center and Second Bloom of Chatham, two groups with experience supporting students, adults and families through traumatic experiences. Those groups will be on hand at Woods this week and in the weeks ahead to assist with support, Bryan wrote. He also said the school is fully committed to walking alongside all of its families and that the community has the heart and the skill to respond with deep care.

In 2024, state lawmakers updated North Carolina's sexual extortion laws to include language prohibiting the use of artificial intelligence as a means of producing pornographic material. It is not the first case this year involving a juvenile accused of using AI to make nude images of teens. In July, Wake County authorities charged a boy with 10 counts of sexual exploitation of a minor, saying he used AI to create sexually explicit images of underage girls. In that case, parents who spoke with WRAL on the condition of anonymity expressed concern that content the general public would view as sexually explicit is not considered the same in the eyes of the law.

stories.Headline: Ivo D. Dinov compares AI development to nuclear fission and fusion in a published analysis
stories.Summary:
Ivo D. Dinov published a perspective analysis in AI Perspectives & Advances examining developmental and societal parallels connecting controlled nuclear fission, nuclear fusion, and artificial intelligence, as reported by bioengineer.org on November 20, 2026. The analysis states that both technological fields originated from fundamental breakthroughs in theoretical science before evolving from conceptual principles into disruptive socio-technical forces. Contemporary artificial intelligence, driven by deep learning architectures and generative pretrained transformers, mirrors the historical trajectory of classical nuclear fission, according to the analysis. The long-term prospects of sustainable next-generation artificial intelligence reflect humanity's prolonged pursuit of controlled nuclear fusion, the analysis states. The analysis characterizes both frontiers as pseudorealistic technological revolutions, paradigm shifts that transform what is technically possible yet continually expose practical limitations, overpromises, and algorithmic recalibrations.

The analysis describes three chronological phases of nuclear energy, the first extending from 1890 to 1935 and focused on deciphering basic physical principles, fostering quantum physics, and formulating the fundamental matter-energy paradigm. Phase two, spanning 1935 to 1945, concentrated on controlling nuclear fission chain reactions and developing atomic weaponry under wartime urgency. The period from 1945 to 1960 pivoted these advances toward peaceful civilian applications, including fission reactors, nuclear submarine propulsion, and commercial electricity generation. Later nuclear research shifted toward operational safety, reliability, and long-term sustainability, including accident prevention, phenomenological modelling of nuclear fission observables, linking intrinsic-system models to symmetry-conserved observables, and managing long-lasting radioactive waste. The analysis traces artificial intelligence from 300 BC, when ancient Greek artisans conceived the mythological bronze guardian Talos, and 1206 AD, when Persian scholar Al-Jazari envisioned programmable mechanical automata.

In the 1680s, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz and René Descartes proposed that rational human thought could be systematized like algebra and reduced to mechanical calculations, the analysis states. By 1940, Alan Turing invented the programmable digital computer, leading to algorithmic machine abstractions of mathematical reasoning and the formal articulation of artificial intelligence at the 1955 Dartmouth Summer Research Project. Decades of computational and energetic constraints induced a prolonged artificial intelligence winter before IBM's Deep Blue defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov in 1997, initiating an artificial intelligence spring. Generative artificial intelligence gained momentum in 2012 with hardware deployment of graphics and tensor processing units augmenting central processing units. This expansion culminated in 2022 with the public release of ChatGPT, a generative pretrained transformer chat-bot demonstrating human-machine textual communication.

The analysis states that global energy consumption will not subside, with projections indicating worldwide energy demands may double by the end of the twenty-first century. Controlled nuclear fission currently satisfies approximately 11 percent of global electricity demand and provides between 20 and 80 percent of local energy supplies across numerous regional jurisdictions. The second law of thermodynamics restricts thermal efficiency of all heat engine power plants, including coal and nuclear facilities, to roughly 33 to 37 percent, and marginal engineering enhancements might elevate fission efficiency to 45 percent with substantial operational trade-offs. Kryder's law dictates that digital data storage volume doubles every 12 to 14 months, while Moore's law observes that computing power doubles approximately every 18 months. Sustainable augmented intelligence depends on four prerequisites: uninterrupted electrical energy, unhindered open scientific communication, unrestricted access to training information, and favorable regulatory frameworks.

Nuclear fusion merges lighter atoms into heavier elements, releasing vast energy while producing low-level radioactive waste, primarily tritium and activation isotopes, without transuranic elements or long-lived radionuclides, the analysis states. One kilogram of fusion fuel yields energy equivalent to 10,000 tons of fossil fuel, enabling a projected one-gigawatt fusion power plant to operate on only one ton of nuclear fuel annually. Replicating solar core conditions requires sustaining temperatures of 100 million degrees Celsius alongside immense gravitational pressure. Nuclear fusion reactors incur an irreducible baseline electrical power drain averaging approximately 20 percent of total generated power to maintain continuous reactions, while neutron activation contaminates non-structural components and generates substantial physical waste volumes. The analysis states that regulatory controls frequently lag behind technological adoption, as shown by past struggles to restrict nuclear fuel enrichment, ballistic missile proliferation, marine plastic accumulation, and orbital space debris.

Future horizons encompass next-generation artificial intelligence systems incorporating novel cognitive architectures, cumulative learning, ampliative reasoning, episodic learning, meta-reasoning, active perception, and proactive self-regeneration, according to the analysis. Because these developments follow non-linear pathways governed by unknown biosocial and environmental parameters, probabilistic inference remains the primary analytical tool for evaluating systemic risks and anticipated benefits. These emerging cognitive models intersect with nuclear fusion and quantum computing, forming what the author describes as a powerful technological trifecta capable of solving complex epidemiological, climatic, and other challenges. The analysis states that equivalent social mechanisms and accountability structures for algorithmic failure remain nascent and ill-defined. The articles leave open the full scope of the technological trifecta and the specific pathways by which the four prerequisites for sustainable augmented intelligence would be secured.

stories.Headline: Researchers find AI models accurately predict anaesthesia complications despite limited clinical validation
stories.Summary:
A research team published a scoping review in the Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing on November 20, 2026. This systematic investigation examined fifty-one published studies regarding artificial intelligence in anaesthesia. The authors evaluated how machine learning and deep learning architectures forecast adverse clinical events. These models were tested on adult surgical patients across various operative phases. The review found that these models achieve moderate to high predictive accuracy.

The review analyzed English studies from PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science published between January 2015 and March 2025. Researchers used the Joanna Briggs Institute framework, the Arksey and O’Malley foundation, and PRISMA-ScR guidelines. The team screened 1,332 titles and abstracts after removing 103 duplicate records from 1,435 citations. They excluded 1,232 studies initially and later removed 49 more from 100 full texts. The final synthesis focused on 51 primary studies meeting all eligibility criteria.

The authors stated that translation into routine surgical care is constrained by methodological shortcomings. They noted that retrospective study designs predominate and real-world clinical validation is markedly short. The researchers concluded that future work must prioritize prospective, multicentre trial designs and robust external validation. They argued for standardized outcome definitions and clear regulatory frameworks to address algorithmic bias. The team emphasized the need for clinical accountability and reduced technological dependency.

Patients are affected by perioperative complications, which occur in 15% to 20% of surgical cases globally. In one European cohort of 44,000 cases, 16.8% of patients had complications and 0.5% died. These events contribute to higher mortality, longer hospital stays, more readmissions, and increased healthcare costs. Intraoperative hypotension affects 30% to 40% of patients receiving general anaesthesia and causes kidney damage. Such instability correlates directly with myocardial injury and elevated postoperative mortality rates.

Three hundred million surgical procedures are conducted globally every year, creating a public health challenge. Traditional risk tools rely on linear relationships and manual predictor selection, failing in dynamic environments. Most current AI research originates from North America, Europe, and Asia, specifically China, South Korea, and the United States. Classical machine learning like Random Forest and XGBoost is common for tabular clinical variables. Deep learning is used for continuous physiological waveforms and real-time intraoperative data streams.

Future research must move toward multi-agent coordination rather than single-task, isolated, and outcome-specific tools. AI could help hospital administrators and surgical teams optimize resource allocation and coordinate clinical pathways. The articles leave open how to bridge the divide between theoretical accuracy and tangible benefit. They do not specify the exact regulatory frameworks needed for safe clinical workflows. The review does not provide a formal risk of bias or methodological quality assessment.

stories.Headline: UN and Barbados co-host summit to develop multilateral AI risk management framework
stories.Summary:
United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres is traveling to Barbados to co-host a special summit on artificial intelligence safety this coming Monday. This event aims to bridge the widening gap between the accelerating risks of technology and the limited capacity of many nations to manage such rapid development. Amandeep Singh Gill, the UN Special Envoy for Digital and Emerging Technologies, noted that 135 leaders expressed AI concerns during the recent UN General Assembly high-level week. This represents a massive increase from 2017, when only three leaders raised similar issues during the same annual gathering. The summit builds on momentum from calls for frontier model control signed by 32 States and the European Commission.

The Bridgetown Special Summit on AI Safety, co-hosted with Barbadian Prime Minister Mia Mottley, will focus on a proposed multilateral AI risk management framework. This framework is designed to provide independent and credible oversight without acting as a formal treaty or a set of rigid regulations. Instead, it offers a foundation that different countries can use to build their own national AI safety infrastructure. The meeting will include approximately 150 participants, such as ministers from Norway and Finland, AI industry leaders, and members of the UN Independent International Scientific Panel on AI. A senior diplomat from the United States and various Chinese experts are also expected to attend the hybrid event.

Secretary-General Guterres will emphasize that while AI can transform education and improve hurricane forecasting, the associated risks are growing just as quickly. Mr. Gill explained that many countries lack the computing power, talent, and capacity to test models developed in other geographies. He cited the World Development Report 2026, which shows high-income countries have 500 incident response teams compared to only six in low-income nations. Because these risks do not recognize borders, the UN believes that national approaches to safety must be strengthened immediately. Mr. Gill stated that while the world is in a good position, actual action must now catch up with the existing analysis.

The summit will not cover the military uses of artificial intelligence during its scheduled discussions. A second roundtable will specifically address issues of access, inclusion, and linguistic diversity to ensure developing countries do not miss out on benefits. Although the organizers have not planned a negotiated outcome, they expect the participants to make various pledges and calls to action. The event also recognizes that no single safety model can fit every country due to differing national needs and capacities. These efforts follow a previous summit hosted by French President Emmanuel Macron that was endorsed by 17 States and 10 AI developers.

Articles.Title: Bridgetown AI summit to tackle safety as risks outpace capacity to respond

stories.Headline: Brands prioritize data sovereignty to reduce dependence on external AI providers
stories.Summary:
Laura Islas wrote an article on November 20, 2026, about how brands are increasingly using artificial intelligence to manage consumer data. These companies are now prioritizing the secure management of information to ensure business competitiveness and compliance with all applicable global regulations. Brands use these tools to personalize customer experiences, automate various business processes, and analyze the purchasing behavior of their consumers. They are facing a new challenge to maintain control over data and reduce their dependence on external technology providers. This shift is part of a global trend toward sovereign artificial intelligence to ensure greater autonomy over digital infrastructure.

The Statista report Sovereign AI 2026: Infrastructure, Investment, and Strategy says 72 percent of respondents identify data sovereignty as a priority. This study, based on Linux Foundation and Futurewei Technologies data, notes 69 percent value national security and 48 percent value competitiveness. Additionally, 44 percent cite regulatory compliance, while 28 percent of technology leaders and policymakers want control over critical AI models. About 46 percent of those surveyed cite compliance with local regulations as a main factor driving these specific technology decisions. The report also notes that 61 percent of leaders are more likely to adopt sovereign technologies due to geopolitical developments.

The authors of the report state that data has become one of the most valuable resources for modern digital marketing strategies. They explain that companies use this data to understand habits, identify preferences, develop personalized campaigns, and strengthen their customer relationships. However, the report warns that using artificial intelligence raises significant challenges related to privacy, cybersecurity, and access to strategic information. When organizations use external platforms, they must evaluate the conditions under which their sensitive information is stored, used, and protected. The report suggests that the selection of providers can influence both operating costs and the capabilities of data protection.

The report notes that these issues are particularly relevant for companies in retail, e-commerce, and financial services with millions of consumers. These businesses use AI to automate audience segmentation, content creation, and performance analysis, as well as to develop virtual assistants. Many companies are concerned about the concentration of the technology market, which creates a heavy dependence on a few providers. The United States could generate 521.8 billion dollars in cloud revenue in 2026, compared to 90.8 billion dollars for China. Furthermore, organizations in the United States and China developed 80 of the 89 notable AI models in 2025.

The articles explain that sovereign artificial intelligence is a model designed to give companies and governments more autonomy over their systems. This approach allows brands to leverage the capabilities of artificial intelligence without compromising the control of their own strategic information. However, this autonomy comes with economic challenges, as more than half of respondents expect sovereign models to cost more. Specifically, they expect sovereign AI models and hardware to cost at least 20 percent more than the non-sovereign alternatives. Additionally, 55 percent of those surveyed believe that non-sovereign AI applications offer a wider variety of available solutions.

Statista estimates the sovereign artificial intelligence market could reach between 500 billion and 600 billion dollars by the year 2030. This is a significant increase from the projected range of 150 billion to 200 billion dollars estimated for the year 2025. Companies must now evaluate which specific business processes justify investing in these more expensive technologies to provide greater digital autonomy. The report does not specifically measure the current level of AI adoption among brands or the associated advertising spending. It leaves open how individual companies will balance the higher costs of sovereignty against the benefits of data control.

Articles.Title: As brands increasingly use artificial intelligence, controlling consumer data is becoming a business priority

stories.Headline: Independent researchers find 27.6% of advisor brochures cite AI risk while 23.7% disclose AI use
stories.Summary:
A peer-reviewed study published on October 14, 2026, in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence examined 388 Form ADV Part 2A brochures from a stratified random sample of 400 SEC-registered advisors drawn from 16,223 firms active at year-end 2024, and it found that 23.7% of the brochures disclose AI use while 27.6% contain AI-related risk language. The co-authors, Samir Chincholikar and Robin Chawla, independent researchers in New York City who work in the finance industry, used GPT-4o to sort each brochure under five prespecified labels and checked the model against a blinded recoding by Anthropic's Claude and human review. Within the sample, 77 brochures carry both risk language and disclosed use, 30 carry risk language only, 15 disclose use only and 266 mention neither, and the 3.9-percentage-point gap between risk language and use is statistically significant at a McNemar p of 0.036. The authors also warned that depending on how AI disclosure is defined, which advisors are counted and how results are weighted, the same brochures support estimates anywhere from 9.9% to 31.7%.

Disclosure rises steeply with assets under management, from 10.4% of brochures in the smallest quartile to 43.8% in the largest, and among private-fund advisors it climbs from 12% to 56% while among wealth and retail advisors it goes from 8.7% to 30.4%. The authors cite Charles Schwab's 2026 RIA and AI Research Study, which found 63% of 533 Schwab-custodied RIAs surveyed in October 2025 using AI in some capacity, and they call the roughly 39-point gap with brochure disclosure a benchmark divergence rather than a nondisclosure rate. Among 283 firms observed in both places, 23.0% of brochures but only 5.7% of websites disclosed AI use, yet the authors draw no conclusion about candor because brochures carry 7.3 times as much text and the gap disappears once document length is accounted for. A screen built from language in the SEC's March 2024 orders against Delphia and Global Predictions flagged five of the 388 brochures, of which two were false matches and three contained real AI references qualified by context or risk language, and none was judged an unsubstantiated promotional claim.

Chincholikar said that having just the word artificial intelligence in a brochure does not mean the firm is using it, since it can be for a specific purpose such as AI as a risk for investments, and he called the 2024 cases a case of overselling while saying the question now is whether firms are telling people exactly where they are using AI. He attributed the size gap to compliance capacity, saying large advisors have very large compliance teams with more capacity to understand their own processes, and Chawla cautioned that the data cannot show smaller firms are hiding anything because there is no statistical proof that small investment advisors are using AI but not reporting it. The authors' practical answer for advisors is a firmwide AI inventory that says plainly where each tool is used, and the study notes that the pattern fits a document built to describe material risks rather than to promote. The SEC's fiscal 2027 examination priorities, released on October 23, 2026, add AI-related cyber risk and, following a September 2026 executive order, refer to the technology as super intelligence throughout, which the study says makes the disclosure gap a compliance problem too.

stories.Headline: Review authors report AI matches expert tuberculosis detection from radiographs and genomic data
stories.Summary:
A review published in Molecular Medicine on November 20, 2026, reports that deep learning and machine learning algorithms match or exceed expert performance in detecting tuberculosis from radiological and genomic data. The synthesized evidence shows that artificial intelligence models reading chest radiographs reach near-expert diagnostic accuracy, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve values approaching 0.95 to 0.99. In parallel, computational prediction systems analyzing whole-genome sequencing datasets identify complex bacterial drug-resistance profiles with F1-scores surpassing 90 percent. The authors of the review are W. Ali, S. Prandiyal, A. Alam, M. Shariq, N. Z. Ehtesham, S. E. Hasnain and S. Ahmad, and the article is titled Methods and applications of artificial intelligence in tuberculosis diagnostics: advances, opportunities, and challenges.

The review states that tuberculosis causes more than ten million active cases each year, and that conventional workflows rely on sputum microscopy, microbiological culture and nucleic acid amplification assays, which face limitations such as suboptimal sensitivity, prolonged turnaround times, substantial infrastructure requirements and dependence on highly trained laboratory personnel. These constraints fall hardest on high-burden and resource-limited regions, where diagnostic delays hinder case detection and prolong community transmission. Traditional phenotypic drug-susceptibility testing is also limited by slow turnaround and demanding laboratory infrastructure, while artificial intelligence trained on whole-genome sequencing data predicts resistance patterns with F1-scores exceeding 90 percent. Researchers are further developing integrative multimodal frameworks that combine radiological imaging, whole-genome sequencing and clinical parameters into unified predictive pipelines for earlier, patient-specific assessments.

The review highlights substantial ethical, regulatory and practical barriers that impede translation of artificial intelligence into routine clinical practice, and the authors identify a widespread lack of regulatory harmonization across international jurisdictions as a major obstacle to equitable, standardized deployment of the software in global tuberculosis care. The authors say that overcoming these deployment hurdles requires robust governance structures, transparent model validation and representative clinical training datasets. They add that successful, sustainable adoption will depend on structured multidisciplinary collaboration among clinicians, microbiologists, data scientists, engineers and public health policymakers. With thoughtful governance and context-sensitive implementation, the authors conclude, artificial intelligence could transform tuberculosis diagnosis into an accurate, efficient, unbiased and patient-centered continuum supporting international efforts toward global tuberculosis elimination by 2030.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence Matches Expert Performance in Tuberculosis Radiography and Genomic Diagnostics

stories.Headline: Raleigh landlord blames AI agent for eviction after bot grants renter payment extension
stories.Summary:
Laura Mack, a Raleigh renter, says she received an email on Nov. 8 from the leasing office at Colony Townhome Apartments offering her until the end of the month to pay an overdue rent balance of almost $4,000, and then received an eviction notice on Monday, Nov. 16. Her landlord blamed the confusion on an AI-powered property management service, according to Mack, who says she was told the company's AI agent, called Olivia, had mistakenly given her permission by email to pay on Nov. 30. WRAL Investigates reviewed documents Mack provided, and the purported emails did not disclose that they were generated by artificial intelligence, with one message including sympathetic language about a hole in her downstairs bathroom ceiling. Mack was evicted on Thursday, Nov. 19, and is staying at a hotel through the weekend while she figures out her next steps.

State Sen. Jim Burgin, R-Harnett, said in an interview Friday that the eviction underscores what can go wrong when companies use AI bots for business decisions, and he plans to continue a push for AI-focused consumer protections in the next legislative session. Burgin said the Nov. 8 email to Mack should have notified her that it was written by Olivia, and he said the landlord will have to defend the fact that the bot told her in writing that she could have the extension. His "Bot Bill" would require a user to be alerted if they are speaking with or interacting with AI, and he has introduced legislation in each of the past three years, but it has not advanced in the legislature. Burgin said AI is like Pinocchio, with no conscience, morals or ethics, and that humans have to make sure there is a human component, adding that before someone evicted Mack, they should have reviewed their documents.

Colony Townhome Apartments disclosed to residents that it was using an AI agent in a December 2025 email, with section headings like "Who is Olivia?" and "Why we're excited," and in the following months emails from Olivia to residents were clearly marked, but the emails to Mack on Nov. 8 were signed "Best regards, Colony Townhome Apartments." Mack said she thought she was dealing with someone from the office and had plans to have until the 30th to either get the payment made or go, because that is what her email said. Mack said her overdue rent payment is her problem and that it is her fault, and she is taking full responsibility for that, but she said someone in that office has to take responsibility for the mixed messages. A spokesperson for the apartment complex, Alfred Leach, told WRAL on Friday that its owners are looking into the eviction and that Colony Townhome Apartments is gathering all information related to the matter and will be providing an update to WRAL next week.

Articles.Title: 'It's ridiculous': Raleigh eviction after AI bot’s promise reinvigorates push for protections

stories.Headline: NextEra uses Grid Composer AI to save Florida customers over $20 million in 2026
stories.Summary:
NextEra Energy has reported more than $20 million in savings for its Florida customers during 2026 from using artificial intelligence to decide which power plants run, how much fuel they burn and when repairs happen, according to a company executive. Rich Argentieri, president of NextEra Analytics, gave the figure at a September 2 virtual media roundtable hosted by Google Cloud, where he said the savings came from better choices about plant operation and maintenance timing. The tool behind the savings is called Grid Composer, and it runs across the generating fleet of Florida Power & Light, the NextEra utility that serves about 12 million people in Florida. NextEra built the first version of Grid Composer in less than 12 weeks and then rolled it out across the FPL plants, according to Argentieri. Grid Composer combines live equipment readings, customer demand data and plant output data into a single model that processes roughly half a trillion data points every day, Argentieri said.

The tool compares the choices employees made manually with the choices the AI would have made and makes real-time recommendations on plant, fuel and maintenance decisions in one place, according to Chairman, President and CEO John Ketchum, who described it on the company's first-quarter earnings call on April 23. Ketchum said the tool uses AI to optimize and orchestrate all aspects of the power generation process. The savings arrive as power demand climbs, with 21 of the 23 regions tracked by the North American Electric Reliability Corp. expecting higher electricity demand this winter, the grid's reliability watchdog said. NextEra is now selling the technology to other utilities as a commercial software suite called Optos, which was developed with Google Cloud's Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Google Cloud said in a September 3 post. One product in the suite, Optos Composer, pulls six jobs into one system, namely running plants, buying fuel, scheduling maintenance, trading energy, holding backup capacity and managing battery storage, tasks that separate teams have traditionally handled, Argentieri said.

NextEra said in its October 21 third-quarter earnings presentation that it has more than 100 strategic AI initiatives underway. The company has already put a dollar figure on its AI, while most large companies are still waiting for theirs. In a June survey of 60 senior technology executives at U.S. companies with at least $1 billion in annual revenue, at least 90% said AI has produced some return, according to the PYMNTS Intelligence report "The Enterprise AI Payback Curve: Adoption Accelerates as Returns Take Shape." No more than 10% said AI has fully paid for itself, and at least half expect AI to take five to six years to pay for itself. The articles do not say what further steps NextEra or Florida Power & Light plan beyond the Optos rollout and the continuing AI initiatives.

stories.Headline: Council of Europe trains 20 local authority teams to govern AI responsibly
stories.Summary:
The Congress of Local and Regional Authorities of the Council of Europe organised the first-ever Academy on responsible AI governance at local level, held in Paris from 17 to 19 November 2026. Twenty teams from local and regional authorities, selected in an open call, took part in the academy. The teams came from 18 municipalities and two counties, spanning the continent from Diyarbakır in Türkiye to Fingal in Ireland. The academy was organised by the Centre of expertise for multilevel governance (CEMG) at the Congress, in partnership with the Council of Europe's Steering Committee for new and emerging digital technologies (CDNET). It put into practice the Congress's call to strengthen local and regional authorities' capacity to use and manage AI.

Participants were provided with practical tools for responsible AI governance, based on the Council of Europe's HUDERIA methodology for assessing the impact of AI systems. Over three days, participants applied the methodology to a fictional AI-supported public consultation, identifying and analysing risks, mapping stakeholders and developing mitigation measures. The programme was designed to strengthen authorities' capacity to assess the impact of AI in public services on everyone they serve, from a human-rights, democracy and rule-of-law perspective. The participating authorities were Amaroussion (Greece), Bălți (Republic of Moldova), Bergen (Norway), Bitola (North Macedonia), City of Arezzo (Italy), City of Vigo (Spain), Diyarbakır (Türkiye), Fingal County (Ireland), Harghita County (Romania), Kutaisi (Georgia), London Borough of Camden (United Kingdom), Lviv (Ukraine), Nõo (Estonia), Resen (North Macedonia), Rivne (Ukraine), Shkodër (Albania), Szentendre (Hungary), Turnišče (Slovenia), Valongo (Portugal), and Ventspils Education Board (Latvia). The academy was also an official part of the "Road to Geneva" programme, leading up to the 2027 Geneva AI summit.

Opening the discussions, Congress co-rapporteur on AI Annika Vaikla (Estonia, ILDG), Deputy Mayor of Viimsi, urged authorities to use AI to give public servants more time for people, while keeping people in control. She called for AI literacy among political leaders, staff and citizens. She also called for smaller municipalities to have access to shared expertise. Deputy Mayor Vaikla is co-rapporteur for the 2026 Congress report on strengthening the capacities of local and regional authorities in the use of artificial intelligence. The articles give no further remarks from her.

The articles state that local and regional authorities are on the frontline of the AI revolution in Europe's town halls. Faced with shrinking budgets, they see real potential in efficiency gains promised by AI. They also face hard questions such as planning applications for data centres and democratic accountability for decisions informed by AI. The articles say they lack capacity in understanding and governing AI technologies, particularly smaller municipalities. The academy served as a Congress contribution to the Council of Europe's New Democratic Pact for Europe and was held in support of the implementation of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence.

The articles give no further background beyond the academy's organisation and aims. They state that artificial intelligence is already in Europe's town halls. They describe the academy as the first-ever of its kind at local level. They state that the twenty teams were selected in an open call. They state that the programme was designed to strengthen authorities' capacity to assess the impact of AI in public services. They give no further details on the Congress report or the Framework Convention.

The articles state that the academy was an official part of the "Road to Geneva" programme, leading up to the 2027 Geneva AI summit. They state that it was held in support of the implementation of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence. They state that it served as a Congress contribution to the Council of Europe's New Democratic Pact for Europe. They give no further details on what follows the academy. They leave open what the participating authorities will do next and what the 2026 Congress report will contain.

stories.Headline: Senators question whether Meta's AI data centers qualify for $6.6 billion in research tax credits
stories.Summary:
A New York Times article has renewed attention on the tax credits that Meta claimed for its artificial intelligence data centers, according to a report published by Accounting Today on November 20, 2026. In a letter dated October 14, 2026, Senate Finance Committee ranking member Ron Wyden of Oregon and six other senators said Meta claimed about $6.6 billion in federal research and development tax credits between 2023 and 2025. The senators questioned whether Meta described its AI data centers as experimental pilot models in those claims and asked the company for a breakdown of the credits tied to the data centers. The inquiry highlights two separate questions, which are whether the development activities count as qualified research and whether the claimed expenditures count as qualified research expenditures for the credit.

Treasury Regulation 1.174-2(a)(4) defines a pilot model as any representation or model of a product that is produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty about the product during its development or improvement. The rules say production costs paid or incurred after the uncertainty is eliminated are not eligible, and a pilot model must involve genuine uncertainty in the design that the model is needed to resolve. Meeting that definition does not by itself satisfy Section 41 of the tax code, which sets additional requirements for the credit and for eligible expenses. Only wages, supplies, computer leasing and contractor costs tied to qualifying research activities can be claimed as qualified research expenses. Section 41(b)(2)(C) excludes land, improvements to land and property subject to depreciation from the definition of qualified supplies, so a taxpayer cannot turn depreciable equipment into qualified supplies by calling it experimental or by not claiming depreciation on it.

For Meta's data centers, the treatment of purchased servers, chips and other equipment is a central issue, because using equipment for qualified research does not by itself make its purchase price a qualified supply expense. Meta asserts that uncertainty existed in the data centers and that it could only be resolved by building a physical data center and testing it. To support that claim, Meta would need to show the technical uncertainty that existed before the data center was built and how building it resolved that uncertainty. The article says taxpayers claiming pilot model costs should build a record that connects the technical work to the claimed expenditures, including initial design questions, alternative designs, simulation results, test plans, test findings and engineering designs. Cost records for employee activities, materials and contractor charges should be traceable to the relevant development work and should complement the technical evidence.

The article, written by David Seibel, a senior manager in the research and development tax credit practice at Indianapolis-based McGuire Sponsel, says the credit is one of the most fact-intensive and subjective areas of tax law. It says the questions raised by the Meta claim extend well beyond AI infrastructure, because manufacturers, equipment developers and other businesses face similar challenges in showing why a model was built, how its development involved experimentation and which costs the credit permits. The articles do not say what happens next in the Senate inquiry or whether Meta has responded to the senators' request.

stories.Headline: Governor Kathy Hochul pauses a proposed AI data center project in Niagara Falls
stories.Summary:
Governor Kathy Hochul ordered a freeze on certain state environmental permits for new data centers on July 14. This action paused the proposed Niagara Digital Campus project in Niagara Falls. A private developer wants to spend 1.5 billion dollars on this facility. The project aims to build a hub for artificial intelligence. This freeze happened while America competes with China in an AI race.

The pause affects data centers using at least 50 megawatts of power and can last one year. The Niagara Digital Campus would include nine buildings using 140 megawatts near the Robert Moses plant. The project requires a state air permit for backup diesel generators. The Responsible Data Center Development Act would lower the permit pause threshold to 20 megawatts. Governor Hochul must act on this legislative bill by December 31.

Governor Hochul said the pause allows the state to study effects on water, environment, and electric bills. She stated that developers should pay for required infrastructure rather than households. Niagara Falls Redevelopment, owned by the Milstein family, says it will pay for grid upgrades. The state council of building trades urged the governor not to adopt the freeze. NFR first proposed this data center project in 2021.

Opponents of the project express concerns regarding noise, water usage, and local electric bills. A consultant projects 675 annual construction jobs for nine years and 550 permanent positions. The project could generate 414.9 million dollars in taxes. Residents across the country are fighting data centers over water and power costs. Data Center Watch reports 75 projects worth 130 billion dollars were blocked in early 2026.

China added 543 gigawatts of generating capacity in 2025, mostly through wind and solar power. Chinese data centers pay about 3 cents per kilowatt-hour, which is one third of the American price. Morgan Stanley projects a 44-gigawatt power shortfall for American data centers by 2028. Stanford University found American and Chinese chatbots were nearly equal by March 2026. Liu Liehong called electricity a competitive advantage for China in March.

The project awaits a decision on its merits regarding generators, infrastructure, and environmental effects. The developer's builder, Urbacon, uses cooling systems that require little or no water. The project could move to states like Texas, Ohio, or Virginia if New York declines. Lawmakers in 16 states have considered bans, and Pennsylvania proposed a three-year moratorium. The articles leave open whether the state will ultimately approve the permits.

stories.Headline: US export rules restrict a wider range of chips including those for consumer electronics
stories.Summary:
The United States government introduced tighter export controls on Thursday, November 20, 2026, to restrict the flow of semiconductor technology. Industry insiders report that these new rules are causing a much wider disruption across the global supply chain than was first anticipated. The restrictions are not limited to advanced artificial intelligence chips but also impact system on chips used in common consumer electronics. Consequently, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. has already suspended some of its shipments to various clients.

These updated regulations affect a diverse range of developers, including those who are not based in China and do not create AI hardware. The rules target mobile and everyday consumer applications, which forces companies to change how they source and distribute their semiconductor components. Because the world's largest contract chipmaker is involved, the changes impact major customers like Nvidia who rely on leading-edge processors. Every developer using these specific types of integrated circuits must now navigate these stricter American trade requirements.

Multiple industry executives told Nikkei Asia that the scope of these controls is unexpectedly broad and damaging to the supply chain. They expressed concern that the rules extend far beyond the intended targets of high-end AI technology to hit general electronics. These leaders believe the current environment creates significant uncertainty for developers who were previously unaffected by trade wars. They warned that the sudden suspension of shipments could lead to larger shortages of essential components for mobile devices.

stories.Headline: Shanghai AI Laboratory releases Sage S2.1 Flash science multimodal agent
stories.Summary:
The Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory released Sage S2.1 Flash on November 16, 2026. This science multimodal agent combines tool use, coding, and search with instrument and molecular inputs. The lab published a benchmark table comparing it to Claude Opus, GPT-5.6 Sol, Qwen, and GLM. Weights for the model are available on Hugging Face under the InternLM organization. It is a full-stack science agent SKU designed for automating notebook-style machine learning engineering.

The 320B MoE model requires FP8 builds or full precision shards for hosting. It unifies ten scientific modalities, including crystal structures, molecular graphs, and protein or nucleic acid sequences. It also ingests light curves, ECG, EEG, spectra, mass spectrometry, and X-ray diffraction. The model uses a shared agent harness for tool-use and search after modality encoders. Demos show the agent using CAD, QGIS, Blender, and 3D Slicer for scientific workflows.

The Shanghai AI Laboratory claims the model is a single-model story rather than a chain. They report a 90.3 score on MLE-bench Lite and 72.2 on OfficeQA Pro. The lab states the model achieved 37.1 on SpreadsheetBench 2 and 25.0 on Harvey LAB. They report a 60.6 on SWE-bench Pro and 87.9 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The lab frames the agent as a tool for multi-step workflows with visual feedback.

Third-party commentators noted that weights appeared on Hugging Face before the official marketing site launched. ML engineers are affected by the model's positioning for automating machine learning engineering tasks. Finance and operations teams may use the SpreadsheetBench 2 and Workspace-Bench productivity capabilities. Users in regulated industries must align usage with institutional IRB and export rules. Some reports mention promotional API pricing relative to GLM-5.3-Flash through early December 2026.

The lab's release follows an open-weight push similar to DeepSeek usage limits and Alibaba Qwen4 Max. Science agents intersect with biosafety and export debates, including DHS DeepSeek removal orders. Western labs have released different science agents, such as Periodic Labs Neon and Nvidia Nemotron. Terminal-Bench-Science previously showed that leading Western agents had sub-30% resolution on real research tasks. The model's design mimics how graduate students work across various tools in one afternoon.

Users should now confirm licenses, VRAM needs, and data residency rules for their jurisdictions. Teams are encouraged to run private benchmarks on their own instrument suites for verification. The articles leave open whether the vendor-reported benchmarks will be matched by independent harness logs. It remains unclear if the promotional API pricing will be maintained after December. The actual reliability of the agent depends on governed chat patterns and MCP hygiene.

stories.Headline: Scholars and election officials examine how AI affects electoral integrity at a University of Ottawa workshop
stories.Summary:
On October 23rd, 2026, scholars, civil servants, election officials, and policy experts from around the globe gathered at the University of Ottawa for a one-day workshop focused on the upcoming edited volume Securing Elections in an Age of Artificial Intelligence by Michael Pal and Holly Ann Garnett. The project was supported in part by the National Cybersecurity Consortium and the Government of Canada (CSIN). The main goal of the workshop was to combine academic research and practical experience to explore how AI is impacting electoral integrity. Each panel included presentations on chapters from the volume and opportunities for academic and practitioner discussants to provide feedback on the presented research. These exchanges allowed authors to consider different perspectives, identify areas for further research, and explore how academic findings could inform practical approaches to the challenges facing election administrators and policymakers.

Four panels were held during the workshop examining various aspects of how AI can affect democratic elections. The opening panel discussed how the public and experts view the effects of AI on electoral integrity, including the increased use of AI by various actors in the electoral process and how AI-driven disinformation and persuasion tools can impact voters' capacity to make educated decisions. The second panel examined the advantages and disadvantages of Electoral Management Bodies' use of AI, addressing the hazards of depending on emerging technology while considering possible applications for increasing administrative efficiency and how EMBs are integrating AI into their operations. The third panel looked at generative AI chatbots, altered advertisements, and deepfakes of political figures in political campaigns, discussing how political actors are using generative AI in their campaign strategies and how an increase in AI use might sway public opinion. The final panel discussed the difficulties in developing efficient legal frameworks to govern the use of AI in elections, examining current regulatory strategies in various jurisdictions, concerns about deepfakes and malicious impersonation generated by AI, and the responsibilities of tech companies and other actors in the AI supply chain.

Discussion at the workshop highlighted the challenges of responding to disinformation, keeping up with rapid technological advancements, and making sure AI systems can meet the accuracy and reliability required in a "no fail" electoral environment. Participants also highlighted the difficulties of allocating blame for AI-related electoral damages and striking a balance between election integrity and the right to free speech. The wider implications of AI-driven political persuasion for democracy were considered, as well as possible regulatory solutions. Overall, the workshop offered participants the opportunity to further their knowledge and research on AI and democratic elections, and the chapters presented at the workshop are currently being developed into an edited volume on the topic.
