stories.Headline: AI power systems integrate lighting and industrial electronics to meet rising data center energy demands
stories.Summary:
Modern AI power supply systems emerged from a mixed evolution of lighting, automotive, and industrial electronics capabilities. This technological convergence happened as AI chip power consumption and cabinet power density rose to megawatt levels. The process integrates gallium nitride, silicon carbide, and silicon based power technologies into computing infrastructure. These older industrial capabilities became important again to meet the massive power demands of AI data centers. This evolution allows for more GPUs to be deployed in the same computer room space.

The system requires rectification, backup power, and multi-level DC conversion to deliver power to GPUs. Google released a plus or minus 400V DC solution for 1MW cabinets in 2025. NVIDIA promoted an 800V high-voltage DC architecture in 2026 with Google, Microsoft, and the Open Compute Project. Texas Instruments estimates that 48V architectures for 1MW cabinets would require nearly 200 kg of copper. Higher voltages like 800V reduce current from 20833 amperes to about 1250 amperes to lower resistance loss.

Texas Instruments launched high-density power devices integrating 650V gallium nitride power transistors in 2025. Infineon released a high-voltage intermediate bus conversion reference design based on 650V gallium nitride in 2026. Innoscience cooperates with NVIDIA to promote 800V DC AI data center power supplies. These companies aim to reduce copper loss and space burdens caused by large currents. They use different materials to divide work based on voltages, power densities, and switching frequencies.

AI data center operators and GPU manufacturers are affected by these power supply architecture changes. Gallium nitride is used for high-frequency and high-power density conversion links in these systems. Silicon carbide provides advantages in high power and voltage resistance for the infrastructure. Silicon remains necessary for low-cost control, protection, and power management functions. These materials ensure that input power is effectively delivered to the chips without excessive heat.

Gallium nitride technology grew from the semiconductor lighting industry and the development of blue LEDs. Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano, and Shuji Nakamura won the 2014 Nobel Prize for their early achievements. Japan invested 550 million yen between 1987 and 1990 to commercialize blue LEDs through Toyoda Gosei. China launched the National Semiconductor Lighting Project in June 2003 to expand this industrial scale. China's semiconductor lighting industry grew from 90 billion yuan in 2003 to 4.245 trillion yuan by 2015.

Jingcan Semiconductor enabled the production of 12-inch gallium nitride wafers in China as early as 2021. Shanghai New Micro Semiconductor is building a gallium nitride power foundry platform for various voltages. Shenzhen Pinghu Laboratory provides a public pilot platform for 8-inch silicon carbide and gallium nitride chips. The articles leave open how these global technology competitions will evolve between China, the US, and Japan. Future developments will determine how these materials further integrate into the global AI power chain.

stories.Headline: Maryland comptroller Brooke Lierman launches dashboard projecting AI job displacement
stories.Summary:
Maryland's comptroller's office launched a public dashboard tracking how artificial intelligence could reshape the state's economy, and the tracker includes a projection that Maryland faces the third-highest rate of job displacement from AI automation in the nation. The Maryland AI Economic Impact Tracker brings together data and forecasts from government agencies, universities and private-sector researchers to follow AI-related job creation, potential job losses and business adoption. The dashboard was reported on Friday, November 20, 2026, by The Baltimore Sun staff, and the comptroller's office is behind the launch. Among its most striking findings, research from Tufts University's American AI Jobs Risk Index projects that Maryland could see 7.2% of its jobs displaced by AI automation over the next two to five years under a median adoption scenario. That would be the third-highest projected rate among states, behind Massachusetts and Virginia, both at 7.3%.

The tracker is meant to give state and local leaders information to help shape policies affecting Maryland residents and businesses, according to the comptroller's office. Comptroller Brooke E. Lierman said in a statement that AI is reshaping the economy and that Maryland must meet this moment to support its workers and businesses. The dashboard combines data and forecasts from government agencies, universities and private-sector researchers, and it tracks AI-related job creation, potential job losses and business adoption. The projection of 7.2% displacement rests on Tufts University's American AI Jobs Risk Index and a median adoption scenario over the next two to five years. Massachusetts and Virginia sit just ahead of Maryland at 7.3% each in the same projection.

Lierman is the official responsible for the dashboard, and she framed it as a tool for state and local leaders rather than a final verdict on the state's economy. She said the dashboard will give those leaders information to help shape policies affecting Maryland residents and businesses. The comptroller's office described the tracker as bringing together data and forecasts from government agencies, universities and private-sector researchers. The articles do not say what policies, if any, the dashboard has already prompted or when the office will update its figures. The full story is available by visiting The Baltimore Sun website, according to the WBFF report.

Barr stated that on-balance-sheet debt for the seven largest AI firms could exceed 800 billion dollars by the end of the year. stories.Headline: US and Singapore authorities investigate Megaspeed International over AI chip trade
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Department of Commerce and Singapore Police Force investigated Megaspeed International for its AI chip trade. This company, formerly 7 Road International, grew rapidly into a high-profile player in the NVIDIA supply chain. Investigations peaked in June 2025 with raids on the company's business site in Singapore. Investigators questioned the then CEO, Huang Le, regarding the destination of advanced chips. The probe spanned the United States, Singapore, and Malaysia.

Megaspeed shifted to cloud computing in 2023 and joined the NVIDIA Cloud Partner ecosystem. From May 2024 to February 2026, related businesses imported NVIDIA products worth 4.13 billion U.S. dollars. In November 2025, it imported 17,454 GB300 units worth approximately 787 million U.S. dollars. Total NVIDIA hardware imports reached 4.6 billion U.S. dollars and 136,000 GPUs by November 2025. Assets grew from 32.9 million U.S. dollars in 2023 to nearly 3 billion U.S. dollars in 2024.

The U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security checked if chips reached restricted end users. Singapore Police investigated false declarations and whether equipment was shipped to undeclared locations. Huang Le provided inaccurate information to downplay her role and received a stern warning. She had her passport confiscated and was later barred from re-entering Singapore. The Singapore Police sought limited support from the FBI and server supplier Supermicro.

Clients used remote access to obtain computing power without owning chips or building computer rooms. Some users flew 80TB of training data on hard drives to Malaysia to rent servers. The Malaysian government now requires a strategic trade license for U.S. high-performance AI chips. This regulation, announced July 14, 2025, focuses on whether chips flow to other destinations. The business model affected brokers who converted hardware into rentable cloud computing power.

Megaspeed began as a gaming firm focused on overseas game distribution and operation. It utilized Malaysia's abundant land and power resources, especially in the state of Johor. The company posted a post-tax loss of 20 million U.S. dollars in 2024. High upfront costs included GPU procurement, data center leasing, and electricity prepayments. This growth occurred during a global GPU shortage and rapid Southeast Asian data center expansion.

The investigation into Megaspeed and six other related individuals is still ongoing. A gap of 50,000 chips exists between NVIDIA's government reports and external trade records. NVIDIA claimed this discrepancy resulted from equipment in other warehouses not previously counted. It remains unclear if the company violated specific export control requirements. stories.Headline: Nan Huang finds quantitative CT and radiomics may support CIP differential diagnosis
stories.Summary:
Nan Huang published a systematic review on November 18, 2026, regarding imaging biomarkers for immune checkpoint inhibitor-related pneumonitis. The researcher investigated whether quantitative computed tomography and radiomics could support the differential diagnosis of this specific condition. This study focused on identifying the cause of pulmonary abnormalities rather than predicting future risks for patients. The author conducted this review to see if these tools could help clinicians distinguish between different lung injuries. The final report was published in the journal Frontiers in Oncology within the Cancer Immunity and Immunotherapy section.

The author searched six databases in June 2026 and updated the public index through August 31, 2026. The review analyzed 17 reports, including 13 full publications, three abstracts, and one indexed preprint. Huang used the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies version 3 to reassess the risk of bias. The data included 21 areas under the receiver operating-characteristic curve and 10 sensitivity and specificity pairs. One hold-out operating point for 40 patients showed a sensitivity of 0.75 and a specificity of 0.60.

Nan Huang is affiliated with Yidu Cloud Technology in Beijing and the National Cancer Center in China. The author stated that quantitative computed tomography and radiomics may support the differential diagnosis of established pneumonitis. However, the researcher noted that the clinical utility and transportable accuracy of these imaging biomarkers remain uncertain. Huang explained that the current evidence supports discrimination within a dataset but not established diagnostic utility. The author concluded that the evidence is constrained by unavailable full texts and historical validation limitations.

Clinicians are affected because they must decide whether to withhold anticancer treatment or administer corticosteroids to patients. Misclassifying infection or radiation injury as pneumonitis can expose patients to unnecessary steroids and interrupt cancer treatment. Patients with limited pulmonary reserve are particularly vulnerable when CT abnormalities evolve before microbiological evidence is available. Thoracic radiotherapy creates a competing explanation because radiation pneumonitis can produce similar ground-glass opacity and consolidation patterns. Pulmonary infections also create overlapping phenotypes that make etiologic attribution difficult in routine clinical practice.

Immune checkpoint inhibitors are now standard treatments for many solid tumors, especially for those patients with lung cancer. These treatments can cause immune-mediated toxicities that require rapid intervention to manage the resulting lung inflammation. Quantitative CT describes spatial and textural variations that are only partly represented by standard visual descriptors. Radiomics and machine-learning methods combine these measurements into imaging signatures to complement treatment history and laboratory findings. The CIPHER foundation model is a separate tool that uses baseline CT to predict future risk.

Future priorities include independent attribution, locked patient-level testing, and genuinely external validation of the imaging biomarkers. Researchers must also conduct prospective evaluations to determine the actual clinical impact and management benefits of AI. The articles leave open whether these tools can reliably replace or supplement traditional microbiological and longitudinal evidence. No meta-analysis was performed in this review, leaving the overall statistical strength of the findings open. The study did not identify any prospective AI-assisted reader evaluations among the included reports.

stories.Headline: Researchers propose Vision-as-a-Tool to let text-only agents offload visual reasoning
stories.Summary:
Haolin Yang, Wenshan Wu, Jin Jiang, Yu Cheng, Yan Xia, Ting Song, Yangyu Huang, Zhiliang Peng, Wenhui Wang, Hangbo Bao, Yuzhe Zhang, Wen-Da Wei, Tengchao Lv, Li Dong, Lei Cui and Furu Wei posted a paper titled Vision-as-a-Tool: Visual Harness for Multimodal Agentic Coding to arXiv on 20 November 2026. The paper argues that multimodal agentic coding needs strong visual reasoning to analyze observations and to evaluate the artifacts that agents generate. Current frameworks mostly rely on a Thinking-with-Images paradigm, in which agents depend on their own intrinsic vision to carry out visually grounded tasks. That architectural coupling creates a fundamental bottleneck, because agent performance stays strictly bounded by internal perceptual limits, and text-only agents lack native perception entirely.

The authors introduce the Vision-as-a-Tool paradigm, which reframes general-purpose multimodal large language models as callable external utilities rather than as the agent's own eyes. Earlier visual tool use merely manipulated images for an agent's intrinsic vision to read, whereas this approach lets text-only agents completely offload visual reasoning during agentic execution. Vision-capable agents can meanwhile augment their native perception on demand, and the authors instantiate the paradigm in VHarness, a unified framework driven by five atomic actions. They evaluate VHarness across Image-to-HTML, Image-to-SVG and Image-to-3D generation tasks, and the results show that it consistently improves visual fidelity and geometric accuracy for both text-only and multimodal coding agents.

The paper is listed under Artificial Intelligence and Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, and its authors conclude that modularizing visual reasoning into callable utilities gives a flexible and scalable foundation for future agentic coding systems. The abstract does not assign responsibility for any failure to a named person or organization, and it reports no statements beyond the authors' own framing of the bottleneck and their proposed fix. The article also carries standard arXivLabs boilerplate describing a framework through which collaborators develop and share features on the site, and noting that arXiv works only with partners who adhere to its values of openness, community, excellence and user data privacy. The posting invites ideas for projects that would add value to the arXiv community through arXivLabs, but the articles give no further details on deployment, timelines or follow-up work.

stories.Headline: Online literature platforms crack down on AI generated content to protect human creators
stories.Summary:
A viral statement calling for a one day pause on AI updates earned 43,000 likes on November 20, 2026. This movement reflects a deep divide between the short drama industry and the online literature circle. While short dramas embrace the technology, literature platforms are actively fighting against AI generated content. Multiple purges of AI texts have occurred throughout the current year. These actions aim to protect original creators from being replaced by automated systems.

Tomato targeted low quality AI content in February and May of this year. Qidian banned AI written texts in July and processed hundreds of novels in August. On October 30, Qidian and QQ Reading announced further crackdowns on AI abuse in contracted works. These platforms will now cancel welfare benefits for authors who use AI. These rules apply to works with over ten thousand paid subscribers on the Qidian platform.

Platform editors and administrators are responsible for these governance rounds to stop AI abuse. They state that AI generated works are often not good to read. Officials argue that substantial cash rewards are flowing to the wrong recipients. They believe AI books seize benefits that should belong to original human creators. Platforms want to ensure that paid readers are not paying for machine generated words.

Readers complain that works on the leaderboards are still written by AI. Nigerian writer Jerry Adedayo Farad lost a 2 million US dollar deal for his novel. Publishers now avoid novels suspected of being AI generated to protect their investments. Some penalized authors claim they only used AI for grammar and polishing. These creators feel wronged because they wrote the original manuscripts manually.

High output was once a core competition threshold for online literature authors. Top creators like Tangjiasanshao and Mai Bao Xiao Lang Jun updated 8,000 words daily. Qidian previously required 4,000 words for VIP attendance bonuses, while Jinjiang required 3,000. One Qidian author averaged 20,000 words daily using the Doubao large language model. This high volume removed the competitive edge previously held by manual writers.

Qidian uses an AI detection tool called Motong to identify machine written texts. A Nature study showed humans only identify AI poems with 46.6 percent accuracy. Research in Science Advances suggests AI makes stories similar, reducing collective creativity. Another study found AI polishing decreases writing complexity by 21 to 50 percent. The articles leave open whether AI detection tools are truly reliable for platforms.

stories.Headline: Researchers find no AI dependency tool reports responsiveness or cross-cultural validity
stories.Summary:
Wenhai Fan and five other researchers conducted a systematic review of AI dependency tools. The study was published on November 20, 2026, in Psychology Research and Behavior Management. The team evaluated instruments used to measure AI dependency among college students. They searched eight databases from their inception until January 21, 2026. The researchers used the COSMIN Risk of Bias Checklist for their evaluation.

The review examined nine studies evaluating nine different AI dependency assessment instruments. The AI dependence scale and the reliance on ChatGPT scale for nursing students earned category A. Other instruments were classified as category B, while the scale for dependence on artificial intelligence was category C. No tools reported measurement error, responsiveness, or cross-cultural validity. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO under the number CRD420251269989. Mingming Yu and the authors stated that reliable assessment instruments are needed for students. They noted that existing tools assess dependency from psychological, pedagogical, and functional angles.

The researchers said that most tools showed acceptable basic quality but had gaps. They recommended the category A tools for evaluating AI dependency among college students. The authors called for more robust and theoretically grounded instruments in the future. The researchers noted that 78.3 percent of university students in the United Arab Emirates depend on AI. A study by Kaabi found that 94.5 percent of those students reported detrimental effects.

These effects include damage to linguistic skills and critical thinking for the affected students. AI dependency is defined as behavioral attachment and cognitive inertia toward AI generated content. This state makes it difficult for students to independently verify or correct AI outputs. AI tools like ChatGPT support learning but may reduce independent thinking and create psychological problems. Dependency is associated with academic procrastination, sleep disturbances, and negative emotions for some students.

It may lead to superficial learning, academic dishonesty, ethical dilemmas, and technology induced anxiety. Some scales were adapted from tools for internet addiction or problematic social media use. Others were developed as context specific scales tailored specifically to the use of AI. Future research should more comprehensively evaluate the psychometric properties of these measurement tools.

Improved tools will help researchers study psychological mechanisms and academic consequences of AI dependency. Better instruments will also support the development of interventions to reduce this dependency. The articles leave open how to unify concepts of addiction and problematic use. They do not provide a single, universally validated tool for all cultures.

stories.Headline: Nicholas Matsakis introduces Symposium and Agent Client Protocol to guide AI agents in using Rust
stories.Summary:
Nicholas Matsakis, a lead designer of the Rust programming language and a senior principal engineer at Amazon, introduced two new projects on November 20, 2026, according to TechGig. The first is Symposium, an agent-oriented toolchain designed to guide AI agents in using Rust, and the second is the Agent Client Protocol, which proposes a standardised way for AI agents and clients to communicate. Matsakis presented the projects as a way to integrate Rust with artificial intelligence more effectively. The report was published by TechGig on that date.

Symposium aims to give AI agents tailored Rust guidance, such as recommending Rust 2024 and the latest crate versions, while letting crate authors write skills that instruct agents on how to use their libraries. The Agent Client Protocol is intended to improve interoperability across various agents and front-end tools, moving beyond current vendor-specific implementations. The projects address current large language model limitations, including agents using outdated library versions or older Rust editions, because current LLMs often struggle to keep up with the fast pace of software development and library updates. By embedding skills directly within Rust crates, Symposium aims to prevent agents from hallucinating application programming interfaces or generating non-compiling code. Matsakis also introduced the concept of battery packs, which provide best-practice guidance for recommended sets of libraries such as an opinionated network service pack.

Matsakis emphasised Rust's memory safety as a significant advantage, noting its adoption in critical systems like the Linux kernel and at companies such as Microsoft and Amazon. He cited statistics indicating that switching to Rust reduces memory-safety-related vulnerabilities, which account for a large percentage of overall software flaws. The initiatives are part of a broader vision for a more extensible ecosystem that supports open-source maintainers through a Rust commercial network. The stated goal is to streamline language choice for developers by offering robust tooling and community support for Rust development, particularly when combined with AI.

stories.Headline: Nadella warns AI replacing workers could undermine democracy and the economy
stories.Summary:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella warned on November 20, 2026, that widespread AI adoption replacing human workers could damage both the economy and democracy, according to TechGig. Speaking at a roundtable after his Microsoft Ignite 2026 keynote, he said an economy run entirely on AI would leave democracy without a foundation. He questioned how elections could be won in a democracy if only capital exists without labor. Nadella rejected the view that AI is merely a race among tech giants for market value, calling that one of the strangest and narrowest ways to consider AI's potential.

Nadella argued that an AI model has no inherent limits and could evolve into a healthcare company, a financial services firm, or even take over the government. He raised concerns about the role of companies and individuals if all of human capital collapses into token capital. He had previously posted on X in June advocating that every company needs token capital, its own AI capability, alongside its employees' human capital. He suggested that human capital becomes more valuable as token capital increases, and he compared the risk of a few AI models capturing all value to how outsourcing affected industrial economies during globalisation.

Microsoft's Ignite announcements align with this perspective, offering tools for businesses to select cost-effective AI models, operate their own, and maintain data control. Nadella asserted that if the world's economy requires more than one or two firms, then there must be as many models as there are firms. The article does not say what actions, if any, Microsoft or governments plan to take in response to his warning. It also gives no date for any next step beyond the Ignite keynote and the roundtable that followed it.

stories.Headline: Polygon Labs CEO Marc Boiron tells staff to automate their jobs with AI or risk their roles
stories.Summary:
Polygon Labs CEO Marc Boiron has instructed employees to automate their jobs using artificial intelligence, according to a post he made on X, and he warned that those who decline to automate tasks capable of AI execution might risk their positions. Boiron argued that employees who successfully automate their responsibilities would become more valuable to the company, and he added that Polygon would be willing to pay these employees significantly more for other work. The directive has raised concerns about job security and drawn comparisons to Meta's past AI-driven workforce plans. Some users criticised the statement and questioned whether companies were asking employees to develop technology that could make their roles redundant, while other users supported the idea and suggested AI could free employees from repetitive work.

The discussion recalls a similar strategy considered by Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, and a Reuters investigation published in August 2026 revealed that Meta had explored using AI for a large part of employees' daily work, with smaller teams supervising virtual workers. This plan, known as Project OT, was discussed by Zuckerberg and senior executives in January, and internal scenarios reportedly considered reducing several team sizes by up to 60 per cent through layoffs and role reassignments. Meta proceeded with a 10 per cent workforce reduction in May but abandoned plans for a second restructuring round, following growing employee resistance and concerns that the company's AI agents were not delivering expected productivity improvements. Employees were particularly worried that Meta's AI initiatives could train the technology to replace them, and the company also faced criticism over plans to collect mouse clicks and keystrokes from employees' computers for AI system training.

Zuckerberg later acknowledged that AI agent technology had not progressed as quickly as he anticipated, and Meta stated that Project OT aimed to cut costs and reorganise teams, not eliminate 60 per cent of its overall workforce. Boiron's directive at Polygon Labs has drawn criticism from some users, who questioned whether companies were asking employees to develop technology that could make their roles redundant, while other users supported the idea. The articles do not say what response Polygon Labs has given to the criticism or whether any employees have declined to automate their tasks. The articles also do not say what happens next at Polygon Labs beyond Boiron's statement.

stories.Headline: Security leaders shift focus to securing how employees use AI as enterprises balance adoption with data leak risks
stories.Summary:
Enterprises are facing a conflict between adopting generative and agentic AI for tasks such as debugging code, summarizing contracts and automating decision-making, and preventing proprietary data from leaking into unauthorized models. Security and compliance leaders are working at the same time to stop proprietary source code, financial projections and regulated customer records from leaking into unauthorized AI models. For most Chief Information Security Officers the question is no longer whether employees are using AI, because that use is now acknowledged. Their focus has shifted to understanding what employees are doing with AI and to securing that use rather than blocking it. Semantic DLP is presented as a way to secure enterprise generative AI data without hindering adoption.

The story requires enterprises to balance the adoption of generative and agentic AI against the risk of data leakage, and it changes the focus of security leaders from whether AI is used to how it is used. The tasks named in the articles are debugging code, summarizing contracts and automating decision-making, and the data at risk includes proprietary source code, financial projections and regulated customer records. The articles give no numbers, no dates beyond the publication date of November 20, 2026, and no named individuals. The only named technology is semantic DLP, which the articles say helps secure enterprise generative AI without hindering adoption. The articles do not describe how semantic DLP works or what it costs.

Chief Information Security Officers are the people responsible, and the articles say they acknowledge that employees use AI and have shifted their focus to securing it. Security and compliance leaders are also described as working to prevent proprietary data from leaking into unauthorized models. The articles paraphrase no individual by name and carry no direct statement from any officer or company. The context is a tug-of-war between adopting generative and agentic AI for everyday work and keeping sensitive data inside authorized systems. stories.Headline: McGill librarian Kristen Howard uses a hidden AI-generated source to teach history students critical source evaluation
stories.Summary:
Kristen Howard, the Liaison Librarian for Religious Studies, Indigenous Studies and History and Classics at McGill, created a workshop for history undergraduates that merges primary source literacy with AI literacy, with the support of Professor Elsbeth Heaman. In the workshop Howard presents a variety of sources and analyzes them with the participants, and unbeknownst to the students one of the sources is completely AI-generated, such as a diary entry by someone living in a remote location in Ontario or Quebec in the distant past, usually including a fake citation. Each time she gives the workshop Howard generates a new fake primary source, which allows her to monitor the tool's evolution, and she finds it gets better every time. So far, she said, no one has been quick to guess that the source was AI-generated, and she then reveals its true nature to address both how large language models work and how to think critically about sources regardless of their origin.

Howard said that from a historian's perspective the interesting thing about generative AI is that there have always been fakes and forgeries in the documentary record, and she cited The Awful Disclosures of Maria Monk, an 1836 book by someone who claimed to be a former nun at the Hôtel-Dieu convent in Montreal and reported shocking depravities she allegedly witnessed there after escaping to Boston. The testimony initially caused a great public outcry but was quickly contested, and today the book, published when anti-Catholic sentiment was already running high in the United States, is largely regarded as a hoax. Howard said the book is a terrible primary source for studying the life of nuns in Montreal in the 19th century but a great source for studying what people feared was taking place in Catholic convents at the time, which is part of what she calls the Spectrum of Authority, a pedagogical device she created for the workshop. The Spectrum was inspired by part of the Association of College and Research Libraries's Framework for Information Literacy for Higher Education, Authority Is Constructed and Contextual, and Howard explained that it is not a binary, that there aren't sources that are true and sources that are false, and that most things are somewhere in the middle depending on the context, including the research question being asked.

Howard said she believes her role is not only to teach skills that have always been part of the history curriculum but also to prepare students to work in the world that exists now, as a historian or not. In the workshop she leads a discussion about generative AI and the ways it can be useful in historical studies or other humanities and the ways it can't, and she finds students are more willing to talk openly about AI once the conversation about primary sources has taken place. Howard has published a paper on the Spectrum of Authority in Communications in Information Literacy and turned it into an open educational resource available on the Libraries' website, and she has presented her work at various conferences. She has just completed a project with fellow librarian Sandy Hervieux testing generative AI platforms' capacities to identify relevant primary sources, and as LLMs continue to evolve she said she plans to continue to evaluate their use as research tools.

stories.Headline: Snowflake's Vivek Raghunathan says skipping rollout stages causes uneven AI coding results
stories.Summary:
Many engineering organisations have deployed AI coding tools but frequently encounter uneven results, according to insights from industry leaders reported by TechGig on November 20, 2026. This outcome is often attributed to overlooking critical phases in the rollout, specifically the transition from initial experimentation to codified best practices. Vivek Raghunathan, senior vice president of engineering at Snowflake, outlined a five-stage progression for AI rollouts that draws inspiration from Intel's Andy Grove. The initial phase involves allowing chaos to reign, followed by discovering effective practices, codifying them into a shared language, scaling that language across the organisation, and finally reorganising around the new operational reality.

Organisations often bypass the second and third stages, which involve discovering and codifying what actually works, because of an eagerness to demonstrate a quick return on investment for new tool purchases. Skipped stages frequently lead to measuring inappropriate metrics too early, such as lines of code or merged pull requests, instead of focusing on tool adoption across diverse tasks. A lack of a shared vocabulary for effective practices also prevents individual successes from becoming organisational knowledge. Raghunathan's team at Snowflake identified approximately 14 named patterns, including plan in writing before you write code and fence agents into separate git worktrees, which provide a concrete framework for teaching and measuring AI-assisted work.

Scaling AI adoption through mechanisms like regular focus weeks, where dedicated time is allocated for learning or innovation, proved more effective than relying on mandates. Reorganising roles and responsibilities, the final stage, should only occur once a clear understanding of reliable AI-assisted work is established within the company. The article attributes the uneven results to skipped rollout stages rather than to problems with talent or the tools themselves. It does not say what happens next for organisations that follow the model or what further steps Snowflake plans.

stories.Headline: EU consortium 2DFIRE develops graphene and barium titanate modulators for AI data center optics
stories.Summary:
A new European Union project called 2DFIRE has officially started with seven partners from five European countries, and the Universitat Politècnica de València in Spain coordinates the consortium. The other partners are Lumiphase from Switzerland, KU Leuven from Belgium, Graphenea from Spain, Annealsys from France, Riga Technical University from Latvia and PNO Innovation from Spain. The project has a total budget of €4.92 million, which is about US$5.4 million, and it will run for 36 months. The work is funded by the European Union under the Graphene Flagship.

The project aims to develop faster, smaller and more energy-efficient photonic devices for artificial intelligence and high-performance computing. Its approach is a hybrid platform that combines barium titanate, a ferroelectric material, with two-dimensional materials such as graphene and MoS₂. The core target is electro-optic modulators for optical interconnects in data centers, and the consortium points to electricity use in AI data centers, which it expects to more than double by 2030. According to the project page, the devices are barium titanate coupled-modulated ring modulators, and the target is data transmission at 400 Gbps per wavelength.

Besides graphene and MoS₂, the work covers hydrogen-doped indium oxide as a transparent conducting oxide. The aims include thermal phase shifting with low optical losses and new electrode designs that cut driving voltage and energy use. The partners will work on reliable methods to deposit and transfer the two-dimensional materials and integrate them with barium titanate devices. The project also aims to show that the modulators are compatible with existing semiconductor manufacturing processes and value chains, including 200 mm wafer technology.

The consortium says this compatibility should support industrial adoption and strengthen Europe's semiconductor and photonics supply chains. The articles do not name individual people or give direct statements beyond the consortium's published positions on the project page. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the 36-month work plan and the stated aims.

Those teams develop platforms, products, and AI-driven experiences for consumers, businesses, and accountants worldwide. stories.Headline: Anthropic researcher warns superhuman AI may arrive by late 2027
stories.Summary:
Anthropic AI researcher Tao Lin predicted on November 20, 2026, that broadly superhuman artificial intelligence could emerge within about 1.3 years, potentially by the end of 2027. Lin said this AI would rival or surpass human skills in fields such as programming, medicine, law, and filmmaking. He highlighted risks including major workforce displacement and permanent reliance on state welfare. Automation-driven job cuts are already affecting technology firms like Salesforce, Amazon, and Oracle, according to the report.

The forecast sets a timeline of roughly 1.3 years from the November 2026 report to a possible arrival by late 2027. Lin cautioned about losing control over autonomous systems as one of the risks of rapid progress. He urged AI developers to slow progress so that comprehensive safety testing can take place. The article names programming, medicine, law, and filmmaking as the fields where such a system could match or exceed human skills.

Lin, an AI researcher at Anthropic, is the person responsible for the prediction and the warnings that came with it. He said developers should slow down to allow for comprehensive safety testing before such systems arrive. He also pointed to workforce displacement and permanent reliance on state welfare as risks of the technology. The article does not say what Anthropic itself plans to do in response to his remarks.

The context is that automation-driven job cuts are already affecting technology firms including Salesforce, Amazon, and Oracle. Lin's warning comes as those cuts show the workforce effects that he says could grow much larger. The article does not say what happens next beyond his call for slower progress and safety testing. stories.Headline: OpenAI requires prior approval for platforms that give third parties direct access to its models
stories.Summary:
OpenAI began requiring operators of platforms that give third parties direct access to its models to obtain the company's prior review and approval, under a rewritten version of its Usage Policies. The new text carries an effective date of November 20, 2026, and replaces the version that had applied since October 29, 2025. OpenAI announced the changes in a changelog entry dated October 21, 2026, which gave customers 30 days before the rules took hold. The rewrite also adds a section barring the use of OpenAI models and outputs to prepare training material for rival AI systems. The policy body grew from about 830 words in the October 2025 version to about 1,400 words in the new one, according to a PPC Land count of the two texts.

The policy states that operators of a model-access intermediary platform or other service enabling third parties to directly access OpenAI models must obtain prior review and approval. It states that this requirement does not apply solely because an application integrates OpenAI models to power its features or functionality. The rewrite rewrites the child safety rules and widens the human review rule from automated decisions to automated actions, with a definition covering actions, decisions, transactions, submissions, and other steps. Three headed sections are new: Training and developing models, OpenAI-approved use, and Providing access to our models. The training section states its restrictions do not prohibit uses expressly permitted by an applicable Agreement with OpenAI, including any Permitted Exception under the Services Agreement.

The changelog entry states that OpenAI updated its Usage Policies to clarify restrictions on using OpenAI models and outputs to train other models. It states that OpenAI also clarified protections for children and teens and requirements for high-stakes uses, and that the update incorporates existing national security principles and sets out approval requirements for national security and law enforcement uses, as well as for model-access intermediaries. A help center notice titled "We're updating our Usage Policies" lists the same four themes and describes the training language as a clarification of restrictions that already existed rather than a new prohibition. It describes the intermediary rule as an added approval requirement and states that existing agreements and other applicable terms, including any express permissions granted in them, continue to apply. Under the heading "OpenAI-approved use," the policy states that OpenAI may grant specific partners case-by-case exceptions to certain restrictions, naming the factors reviewed as the partner, proposed use, applicable safeguards, and the partner's compliance commitments.

Elena Gurevich, an AI and intellectual property attorney who advises companies on AI governance, wrote in a LinkedIn post on November 20 that OpenAI's updated usage policies kicked in that day. She summarized the intermediary rule as meaning that a business providing customers direct access to OpenAI's models needs OpenAI's approval first, while using the models to power an application's features does not trigger the requirement. She gave OpenRouter, which she described as a platform that streamlines access to multiple AI models from different providers, as an example of the kind of service in scope, and OpenAI's policy names no company. The changelog records that on October 25, 2022, developers no longer needed to wait for approval after submitting as long as they complied with the policies. It records that on November 9, 2022, OpenAI no longer required developers to register their applications, using a combination of automated and manual methods to monitor for policy violations instead.

In August, data drawn from OpenRouter showed AI agents using nearly five times as many tokens per task as human users, with agent usage up about 14 times since February 2026 and more than 85% of agent token spend going to cached prompts. When Anthropic's rewritten Usage Policy took effect on November 12, 2026, it added a prohibition on reselling, proxying or otherwise providing access to Claude through unauthorized means, naming services that route requests through consumer subscriptions or misrepresent which product or client is in use. The training section opens with a rationale stating that capable models must have safeguards proportionate to the risks they pose before they are deployed, and that training another model on OpenAI outputs can transfer capabilities without carrying those safeguards over. The operative prohibition states that users must not use OpenAI models or their outputs to generate, prepare, select, or supply training material or signals for models intended as alternatives to or substitutes for OpenAI models or services. The policy lists what that covers, including creating or preparing training data, training tasks, rubrics, or reinforcement-learning environments, and providing feedback used in training, including labels, scores, rankings, preferences, rewards, or corrections.

Neither the policy page nor the help notice describes how to apply, how long a review takes, whether services already running on November 20 have a transition window, or whether any intermediary has already been approved. The policy gives no application route, form or review time for the access rule. OpenAI's documents do not state a rationale for the intermediary section. The introductory text remains unchanged word for word, including the statement that OpenAI reserves all rights to withhold access where it reasonably believes it necessary to protect its service or users or anyone else. The privacy section still bars uses such as facial recognition databases built without data subject consent and reads exactly as before.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Razorpay plans updated DRHP filing next week for February 2027 IPO
stories.Summary:
Razorpay plans to file its updated Draft Red Herring Prospectus next week, targeting a potential initial public offering by February 2027, according to a Bloomberg report cited by TechGig. The Bengaluru-based fintech firm had confidentially filed its draft IPO papers in June 2026, and the Securities and Exchange Board of India cleared that confidential filing on November 3. Investor roadshows are expected to begin immediately after the public filing of the updated prospectus. The public issue is reportedly planned at around $600 million, comprising fresh shares and an Offer For Sale component.

The IPO could value Razorpay at approximately $5 billion, or about ₹47,000 crore, which marks a markdown from its $7.5 billion valuation in 2021. Razorpay reported a 65 per cent year-on-year increase in operating revenue to ₹3,783 crore in FY25, but it recorded a loss due to ₹1,209 crore in ESOP expenses and one-time costs linked to its domicile shift from the US to India. The company is also exploring a 0.4 per cent merchant discount rate on eligible UPI transactions above ₹2,000 to boost monetisation, though its rollout might be delayed until after the 2027 state elections due to concerns over merchant backlash. Beyond payments, Razorpay is expanding into AI-led products, including its Agent Studio platform for deploying task-specific AI agents.

Razorpay was founded in 2014 by Shashank Kumar and Harshil Mathur, and it offers payment processing, business banking, payroll, and lending solutions. The company has raised over $800 million from investors including Tiger Global Management, Y Combinator, Ribbit Capital, and Lightspeed. India's IPO market has seen firms raise around $18.6 billion through initial share sales so far in 2026. stories.Headline: Open-source BehaviorLock blocks unproven API behavior to counter AI-driven attacks
stories.Summary:
BehaviorLock, a new open-source library for ASP.NET Core, was released to block unproven API behavior as a defense against fast-moving, AI-driven exploitation of vulnerabilities, according to a TechGig report published on November 20, 2026. The library records SQL statements and outbound HTTP calls for each API endpoint into a behavior.lock.json file while running in a Learn mode. In an Enforce mode, it blocks any access not present in that recorded profile, returning a 403 error and raising an alert. The approach is meant to counter attacks that outpace traditional patching cycles, including SQL injection, mass assignment, forgotten debug switches, Server-Side Request Forgery and compromised dependencies, whenever those attacks produce new endpoint behaviors.

The articles give several numbers on how quickly exploitation now follows disclosure, and they show why the library's authors see patching alone as insufficient. Attackers needed 63 days on average to exploit a vulnerability after its patch release in 2018-2019, according to Google's Mandiant team, but that duration dropped to 5 days in 2023 and was negative for 2024 and 2025 estimates. In August 2025, DARPA's AI Cyber Challenge saw automatic systems find 54 of 63 planted vulnerabilities and patch 43 of them, while also discovering 18 real vulnerabilities at a cost of about $152 per task. Anthropic announced in April 2026 that its Mythos Preview model found thousands of zero-day vulnerabilities in major operating systems and web browsers, with the count exceeding 10,000 high or critical findings by May 2026.

BehaviorLock runs inside the application process and currently supports EF Core and IHttpClientFactory for .NET 11, with future plans to extend coverage to Dapper, raw ADO.NET, direct HttpClient, file access and background jobs. The library does not replace existing security practices such as parameters, authorization checks or patching, and instead serves as an additional defensive layer against rapid, unknown attacks. Its code is available on GitHub under the Apache-2.0 license. The report does not name the individuals behind the library or attribute any statements to them, so responsibility for the project rests with its open-source contributors as a whole.

stories.Headline: AI agents make Spec-Driven Development effective again by shortening feedback loops
stories.Summary:
AI agents are making Spec-Driven Development effective again by shortening the feedback loops that long challenged the Waterfall Model, according to a recent analysis reported by TechGig on November 20, 2026. The approach moves the main effort from writing code to the discovery and design phases of software development, which enables faster iteration. Better large language models over the past year fixed earlier problems where correcting generated code cost more time than it saved. The method closely mirrors the sequential phases of the Waterfall Model, including specification, requirement analysis, technical planning and system design. Both methodologies stress structured, detailed documentation and move to the next phase only after the current one is completed and approved.

The historical problem with the Waterfall Model was feedback loops lasting weeks or months, along with unclear upfront requirements. AI agents cut individual phase durations to minutes or hours, letting developers quickly rework specifications, turn intents into structured documents and check that requirements stay consistent. The faster cycles allow iterative work on smaller increments, so unsatisfactory outcomes can be easily reverted or discarded. Documentation such as specifications and decision logs is now cheap and central to the method, a benefit that often suffered in agile environments because of time constraints. The articles do not name who is responsible for the analysis or attribute any statements to a person.

The analysis says the improved quality of large language models over the past year addressed the earlier issue where fixing generated code outweighed the time savings. It also says AI helps quickly rework specifications and validate requirement consistency. No further context or next steps are given beyond these points. More to follow.

stories.Summary:
A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year. The benchmark index is now in what professional investors call a “correction,” having fallen more than 10% from its Oct. 6 all-time high. The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration’s trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3%, pulling it into negative territory for the year.

Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt. The Dow Jones industrial average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9%. Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 9.1%. The sell-off in technology stocks spread around the globe: Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s Kospi each fell more than 5% overnight.

European indexes fell sharply as well. AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market’s direction. They were responsible for Wall Street’s big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market. The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks’ big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data center construction winning at both the federal and state level.

“The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that’s what’s being priced right now,” said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. “But I don’t think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over.” Much of the AI rout was centered among chip stocks, which have been big beneficiaries of the build-out of AI data centers. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3%, Micron Technology slid 13.9% and Broadcom fell 12.1%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7%.

Corning slid 10.9% and Bloom Energy gave up 15.3%. Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 13.8% lower. The chip company’s stock was caught up in the market’s anxiety about the strength of the AI build-out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 25%. The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled Friday with the rest of the tech sector.

The stock fell 9.1% to $88.30, but remains above its IPO price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value. Anthropic’s share price drop on Friday amounts to a roughly 23% decline from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That’s an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook (now Meta) in the early days after its May 2012 IPO. Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period.

SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50% in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later. Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills rose 3.7% and homebuilder Lennar gained 1%. All told, the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39.

The Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73. While the stock market’s mood has soured, the sentiment among American consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year. The University of Michigan’s latest index of consumer sentiment rose sharply compared with last month, coming in slightly ahead of economists’ expectations. Consumers noted some relief from easing gas prices and improved expectations for business conditions following the midterm elections.

Still, sentiment remains below where it was in February, before the start of the U.S. war with Iran. Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93% from 5.04% late Thursday. Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 0.6% to settle at $92.57 per barrel, amid continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. war with Iran continues.

Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels had fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen. Iraq apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil. Troise and Veiga write for the Associated Press. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Nasdaq goes negative for the year, tech stocks slammed by AI swoon

stories.Headline: Onlook lets designers build and edit real app code visually with AI
stories.Summary:
Onlook, an open-source AI-first design tool, was published on GitHub by the onlook-dev organisation, and TechGig reported on it on November 20, 2026. The tool lets designers and visual engineers build, style and edit code visually with AI on a canvas. It works directly with real app code running live from any Git repository on a user's machine. The GitHub repository, onlook-dev/onlook, had 1,644 commits, 27.3k stars, 121 watchers and 2.2k forks when the articles were written. TechGig published its report on November 20, 2026 at 04:51 AM IST, and the GitHub page was dated November 19, 2026.

Onlook is released under the Apache 2.0 License, and the license covers source code but not every asset in the repository. Artifacts can be exported as self-contained HTML, PNG, JPEG or PDF files, with PNG and JPEG captured through Electron capturePage and PDF through Electron printToPDF and pdf-lib. The macOS desktop application is available for download for Apple Silicon and Intel x64, while Windows and Linux versions are planned, with waitlists for both. The source build needs no Onlook account, cloud keys or .env file, and a build from source asks before collecting usage analytics, which can be turned off in Settings or with STUDIO_TELEMETRY=0. The desktop app is built with Electron, React 19, Astryx, React Flow, Zustand and CodeMirror, and uses Git, node-pty, Bun and Turborepo.

The GitHub page says Onlook is the developer tool for designers and describes it as a free, local-first editor where designers craft exceptional experiences in code. It states that Onlook does not ship its own model, and that users connect the Claude Code or ChatGPT/Codex account they already have so that agent does the work inside their project. It says Onlook opens any Git repository on a machine and runs the user's own dev server, so what is designed is the actual product, not a mockup someone has to rebuild later. It says the app runs on the user's computer, code stays there, and more tools can be plugged in through MCP connectors. The page also says the team is hiring engineers and designers in SF.

TechGig describes Onlook as an open-source alternative to Figma, V0, Replit Agent, Base 44 and Webflow, and the GitHub page lists the same alternatives. The GitHub page says users can design apps, websites, posters and graphics with local fonts and assets, work on multiple design tasks at once across repos and pages, and use mobile, tablet and desktop frames side by side. It says a safe worktree copy means the user's folder is never touched, and that projects run as parallel tabs. It says users can ask about any element on the canvas, have the agent arrange the canvas for variations, states and flows, reference images on the canvas, and sketch and share artifacts for quick HTML sketches outside the repo. It says users can import a GitHub repo, start entirely new codebases from scratch, and make one-press pull requests from checks to merge.

The GitHub page says Onlook works with all web frameworks or languages the user's dev server already supports, because it runs the project with its own tooling. It describes a workflow where a user starts a new empty project with the New Draft button in the upper left corner of the projects page and writes a request in the input box in the lower right corner. It says the user answers clarifying questions from the agent and waits for it to build, then clicks frames for context in follow-up prompts or double-clicks an element to use inline chat. It says the user selects a frame, asks the agent to convert it into an Artifact, exports it as HTML/CSS or PNG with the export button in the upper right corner of the frame, and pastes it into Slack, email or any messaging tool. It says changes show up on the canvas as the dev server reloads, and Git keeps track of everything that changed.

The GitHub page says the previous browser-based version of Onlook, v1, lives on the v1 branch of the repository, and the first desktop version is at onlook-dev/desktop. It says Onlook's icons come from Central Icons by Iconists and are licensed to Onlook for its own product, a license that does not extend to forks, and that brand marks, DMG art and sounds are not covered either. It points to ASSETS.md for what is covered and what to replace when forking, and to NOTICE for third-party notices. It says the official download has product usage analytics on by default, and points to the privacy policy for details. It lists contact channels including Discord, email, Twitter, LinkedIn, YouTube and Substack, and the website onlook.com.

The GitHub page invites users to fork the repo and create a pull request, browse open issues, and read CONTRIBUTING.md for instructions and a code of conduct. It says security issues should be reported by following SECURITY.md instead of opening a public issue. It says Windows and Linux users can join waitlists to be emailed when there are updates, and that the team is still gauging demand for Linux. It says SOURCE_BUILD.md covers building and running Onlook on a Mac. The articles do not say when Windows or Linux versions will be released, and they do not give a release date for the macOS app.

stories.Headline: The New York Times Opinion section hires Jasmine Sun to cover AI and technology
stories.Summary:
The New York Times has appointed Jasmine Sun to its Opinion section, where she will cover artificial intelligence and technology, according to a report published by citybiz on November 20, 2026. Sun brings experience in Silicon Valley, product management and technology journalism to the publication. In her new role, she will lead a weekly newsletter focused on artificial intelligence and contribute to the development of editorials addressing technology and related issues. She will also participate in the publication's expanding audio and video programming and appear as an occasional guest on the relaunched Hard Fork podcast. The appointment requires Sun to contribute to Opinion Shows and extend her coverage across multiple editorial formats at the publication.

Before joining The New York Times, she worked as a product manager at Substack, the digital publishing platform that enables writers and creators to distribute newsletters and subscription-based content. During her tenure at Substack, Sun helped develop strategies supporting the platform's growth and gained firsthand experience with digital publishing, audience development and the technology industry's business models. She also co-founded Reboot, a publication focused on young technologists and their perspectives on technology, culture and the industry's broader influence. Her editorial experience also includes helping research and edit The A.G.I. Chronicles, the latest book by Kevin Roose, a technology journalist at The New York Times. Sun is a graduate of Stanford University and is based in San Francisco, placing her near the center of the Silicon Valley technology industry.

The report says her appointment comes as artificial intelligence continues to reshape the technology industry, creating demand for reporting and commentary that examines the development, commercialization and broader consequences of emerging AI systems. Her background combines direct experience working inside a technology company with independent editorial work, providing perspectives on both the business and cultural dimensions of technological change. At The New York Times Opinion, Sun will focus on artificial intelligence while contributing to broader editorial discussions about technology. Her weekly newsletter will provide a dedicated outlet for her analysis, while her involvement in Hard Fork and Opinion Shows will expand her presence across the publication's multimedia offerings. The report says her appointment adds a technology-focused writer to The New York Times Opinion team as the publication expands its coverage and commentary on artificial intelligence and the rapidly evolving technology sector.

Articles.Title: The New York Times Opinion Hires Jasmine Sun to Cover Artificial Intelligence and Technology

stories.Headline: AI bug hunting prompts rushed patches that overwhelm systems and cause outages
stories.Summary:
A series of recent technology outages affecting JPMorgan Chase transactions, Microsoft Outlook and a classified National Security Agency network may stem from a rapid effort to patch security vulnerabilities, according to officials who briefed members of Congress. Wall Street executives and the NSA told lawmakers that the disruptions were caused by attempts to fix flaws identified by artificial intelligence models, The Washington Sun reported. The outages do not appear to be cyberattacks, and officials said the sheer volume of fixes temporarily overwhelmed the systems they were designed to protect. A congressional official noted that AI models are identifying massive vulnerabilities, which increases the urgency for immediate patching.

Microsoft fixed a record 1,400 security flaws in a single monthly update recently, a significant jump from about 170 a year earlier, The Wall Street Journal reported. That increase is linked to AI bug-hunting models such as Anthropic's Mythos and similar models from OpenAI. The NSA's classified internal network, NSANet, went offline because of a software patch for major PHP vulnerabilities discovered last month, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton confirmed. PHP powers approximately 70 per cent of the world's websites, and Clayton stated that the incident was not a cyberattack or a coordinated nation-state action.

Not all the outages fit that explanation, since Microsoft's Outlook disruption, which affected over 450 million Microsoft 365 users, was traced to a latent bug on its networking gateway servers. The Federal Aviation Administration's nationwide ground stop resulted from a data flood hitting its network, possibly linked to a new router, and the FAA blamed legacy equipment. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin indicated that pushing new technology onto older systems seems to overwhelm them, suggesting more such incidents are likely. Companies and government agencies are using powerful AI models to find weak spots before hackers exploit them, and that pressure has led to faster rollout of fixes, according to The Washington Sun.

Articles.Title: AI-driven bug fixes overwhelm systems, causing major outages

stories.Headline: Google gives AI Ultra subscribers Genie 4 with real-time world editing
stories.Summary:
Google made Genie 4 available to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers on November 20, 2026, introducing a new Project Genie experience for those users. Project Genie is an experimental research prototype that lets users generate and explore interactive worlds, and the update provides first-time access to Genie 4 along with upgrades to Genie 3. Genie 4, which Google describes as its most realistic world model, enables users to prompt mid-session to alter worlds they have created. This allows for real-time editing of environments while users are navigating them, and users can change weather conditions, add characters, or redirect actions within their worlds.

Genie 4 also integrates real-time native audio that adapts as scenes unfold, including ambient soundscapes and character dialogue. The Project Genie agent assists users in building their visions, and a community gallery is available for discovering, exploring, and remixing worlds. Project Genie combines advanced world models with Gemini models, allowing users to generate, step inside, and shape worlds directly from their browser. The update enhances the Project Genie experience by enabling users to generate and explore interactive worlds with real-time editing and audio.

Google is the company responsible for the rollout, and it made Genie 4 available to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers as the article reports. Google describes Genie 4 as its most realistic world model, and the article says the model enables users to prompt mid-session to alter worlds they have created. The article does not include any further statements from Google or from named individuals about the release. The rollout gives subscribers first-time access to Genie 4 and upgrades to Genie 3, according to the article.

The context is that Project Genie is an experimental research prototype that combines advanced world models with Gemini models for browser-based world shaping. The article does not say what happens next beyond the availability of Genie 4 to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers and the features described. The community gallery remains available for discovering, exploring, and remixing worlds, and the Project Genie agent assists users in building their visions. The article gives no further dates, numbers, or names beyond those already stated.

stories.Headline: Calif researchers use GPT-6 Cyber to find a critical Java memory bug
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the cybersecurity startup Calif used OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber to uncover a critical memory corruption bug in Java, a programming language widely used across banking, aviation and other critical sectors, according to TechGig. The vulnerability affects the memory safety of Java's base64 decoder, which is a common method for representing binary data as text. Calif stated that malformed input, specifically 64 "A" characters followed by one equal sign, can overwrite neighbouring memory. That corruption can reveal sensitive memory or lead to remote code execution, which grants unauthorised access to the underlying system. The discovery was published on November 20, 2026.

Oracle, Java's current steward, has issued patches for the flaw and urged customers to apply them without delay. The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, known as CERT-In, has issued a high-severity advisory and urged Indian organisations across public sector, private banking, fintech and consumer internet verticals to apply the Oracle patch. Java powers 90 per cent of Fortune 500 companies and is used in critical sectors globally. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency also urged users to identify all Java installations and monitor for security patches.

Calif's researcher Quang Luong used AI to find and weaponise the Java vulnerability, and the startup coined the term "centaur hacker" for human-AI collaboration in security research. The company said the approach combines AI and human expertise to discover the flaw. This discovery follows Calif's AI-assisted research that exposed critical flaws in PHP a month prior. The articles do not say what further steps, beyond patching and monitoring, are planned.

Articles.Title: AI finds critical Java vulnerability, CERT-In issues advisory

stories.headline_source: AI finds critical Java vulnerability, CERT-In issues advisory

stories.Headline: Trina Storage unveils Elementa Hybrid Genset for AI data centers at RE+ 2026
stories.Summary:
Trina Storage introduced a new hybrid power product on Nov. 18, 2026 at RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas, combining gas-fired generation with the company's battery storage platforms under a single hybrid plant controller. The Elementa Hybrid Genset is aimed at data center developers that need on-site power while grid interconnection is delayed, limited, or unavailable. The launch follows a preview of the solution at Data Center World Power in September. Trina Storage unveiled Elementa Hybrid Genset at RE+ 2026, according to a PR Newswire release dated Nov. 19, 2026 in Las Vegas. The solution combines gas-fired generation from qualified partners with Trina Storage's Elementa DC battery systems and Electra AC platform, coordinated by a hybrid plant controller.

The system consists of three main components, with gas generation providing sustained power using reciprocating engines rated up to 2.5 MW in modular configurations. Trina Storage acts as the system integrator, while qualified engine partners supply the generation equipment. The Elementa and Electra BESS solution provides rapid power response and grid-forming capabilities, with reference configurations based on 5 MW/10 MWh building blocks. A hybrid plant controller coordinates all power sources in real time, and its scalable control architecture is designed to support applications ranging from 5 MW to 1 GW. The solution supports four reference scenarios: grid-connected with backup generation, grid-constrained, bridge-to-grid, and off-grid, and solar PV can also be integrated where appropriate.

Load Transient Sensing uses the power plant controller to predict changes in power demand and coordinate a rapid BESS response, allowing the system to accommodate swift load fluctuations before slower-responding power sources can adjust. Hybrid Power Coordination dynamically coordinates power output between the BESS and gas generators, so when a sudden load increase occurs the BESS responds immediately while the gas generators gradually ramp up. Fault Isolation and Resilient Power Supply addresses failures, and when a fault occurs the control system identifies and isolates the affected equipment while the BESS and remaining available gas generators respond to support critical loads. Two system architectures are available, with Load Sensing prioritizing cost efficiency and system performance while Double Conversion provides full electrical isolation and enhanced power quality. The choice between the two depends on the IT load profile and grid conditions at a given site.

Eric Cao, Vice President of Trina North American PV and BESS Business, said AI data centers have demanding power requirements, particularly when grid capacity is constrained or workloads fluctuate rapidly. Cao said Elementa Hybrid Genset brings gas generation, battery storage, and hybrid controls together in one system architecture, designed to coordinate these resources according to project needs. Trina Storage describes itself as a global leader in energy storage solutions and enters the growing field of hybrid power solutions for data centers where grid access cannot keep pace with demand. The company framed the product as a response to a pairing of limitations, since AI workloads can cause rapid and substantial fluctuations in power demand that gas generators alone may struggle to follow. Battery storage responds quickly to those fluctuations but is not designed to supply energy through extended outages on its own, according to Trina Storage.

Trina Storage says it continues to develop and validate the product through simulation, hardware-in-the-loop testing, and an integrated validation platform incorporating real power generation, conversion, and storage equipment. Further testing of grid-forming functionality and hybrid control strategies is ongoing, alongside relevant certification activities. Final system configurations and performance specifications will be assessed based on individual project requirements. The company describes the product as designed to accommodate different power requirements and grid conditions, from grid-connected sites seeking additional power flexibility to projects operating with limited or no grid access. System architecture and equipment selection can be tailored to each project's load profile, site conditions, and operational requirements.

Trina Storage is currently engaging with data center developers and project partners to explore potential applications and develop project-specific configurations. The articles state that these capabilities help coordinate different power sources within one system, with the specific operating strategy depending on the project configuration and requirements. The articles leave open the final system configurations and performance specifications, which will be assessed based on individual project requirements. The articles also leave open the outcomes of the ongoing grid-forming functionality testing, hybrid control strategy testing, and relevant certification activities. The articles do not state when the Elementa Hybrid Genset will be commercially available or which specific projects will use it.
