stories.Headline: Torus raises 500 million dollars and launches Foundry modular AI inference system
stories.Summary:
Torus, a Salt Lake City-based manufacturer of distributed power and compute infrastructure, announced on November 11, 2026 that it has raised 500 million dollars in growth capital led by Magnetar, and the financing coincided with the debut of its newest product, Foundry, a modular AI infrastructure system built for inference workloads. Each Foundry unit provides 1 to 20 megawatts of inference capacity per site and moves from signed contract to running AI workloads in 12 to 16 weeks, a timeline Torus contrasts with the years required to build a conventional hyperscale campus. Foundry units are prefabricated at GigaOne, Torus's manufacturing facility in Salt Lake City, where the smallest unit measures roughly the size of a small cargo van and the modular systems require no building construction at all. On-site timelines are correspondingly compressed, with site preparation taking about a week while installation and commissioning take one to two days, and the product is designed, engineered, and manufactured in Utah by Torus's team of nearly 400 employees, with key components built in-house. Every Foundry deployment ships paired with Torus Reserve, the company's energy storage and management product, which delivers grid-enhancing technologies that Torus groups into three capabilities: inertial-based firm power, grid flexibility with load curtailment, and ramp-rate support.

These functions are executed through what Torus calls load-shaping recipes, predefined controls that govern how power is dispatched and that shape loads to manage demand, support grid stability, and ramp power in milliseconds. The integrated inertial flywheel and battery storage and management serve a dual purpose, covering demand peaks so that more compute can fit on an existing interconnection and supplying backup power during grid outages. Torus describes Foundry as a vertically integrated offering spanning fiber to site, chiller to coolant distribution unit, and grid to rack, comprising three products: Torus Reserve for load shaping and redundancy, Torus Foundry for inference compute, and Torus Protect for integrated networking and security, with every deployment turnkey and ongoing operations and maintenance handled by Torus itself rather than left to the customer. Founder and CEO Nate Walkingshaw said that inference does not have to wait, that the company has spent years learning how to make the grid more affordable, flexible, resilient, and intelligent, and that Foundry applies that to compute capacity in weeks with power that is already available. He added that most providers are bringing power to the chips while Foundry brings the chips to power, and he said the industry has largely tried to solve AI's power problem by building net-new infrastructure, an approach he described as costly and slow to bring compute online.

Torus instead treats the situation as a capacity problem before it is a generation problem, contending that many sites already have unused grid capacity that its systems can make usable, and because Foundry installs behind the meter, drawing on available headroom at individual transformers, the company says the units add steady, high-load-factor demand without triggering the infrastructure upgrades that often produce rate increases and without compromising grid reliability. Torus frames Foundry as a response to a structural change in AI demand, as workloads shift from training models to serving inference for enterprises and compute is being pulled toward on-premises and edge sites closer to where users are, with inference running continuously, responding in real time, and lending itself to distributed deployment according to the company. McKinsey data referenced in the launch forecasts annual growth of 35 percent in data center demand for AI inference through 2030, outpacing the 22 percent projected for training, and Torus notes that its customers want security, protection of intellectual property, and control over where their workloads execute, which the company says a distributed architecture can satisfy more readily than centralized capacity. Foundry debuts with first customers Hydra Host and another AI cloud provider and is offered in three commercial models: the Strategic model is a powered shell supplying power and enclosure without GPUs, the Partner model is a turnkey bare metal unit that bundles power, enclosure, and GPUs, and the Direct model delivers sovereign inference capacity straight to enterprise customers with single-tenant hardware allocated exclusively to one company's workloads. Taken together, the launch and the 500 million dollar Magnetar-led round position Torus to scale a distributed model of AI capacity delivery, one that leans on existing grid interconnections, factory-built modular hardware, and compressed deployment timelines rather than new construction.

stories.Headline: Developers say AI coding tools remove the struggle and risk eroding core engineering skills
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence coding tools have become part of the daily work of every software engineer Gemma Rodgers knows, and in a 2026 Stack Overflow survey 83% of software developer respondents said they use at least one AI tool, CNBC reported on November 20, 2026. Rodgers, a software developer based in the United Kingdom who began her computer science degree in 2002, told CNBC that the sense of joy and fun she used to get from working through a challenge has been removed somewhat, and that using AI can now feel like a breadcrumb of joy rather than a full meal of joy. She said AI tools have lowered the barrier to entry significantly and let many people thrive who would not have thrived five or even three years ago, but she also warned that the core skills engineers traditionally learned on the job are being lost as engineers churn work out. James Broadhead, chief technology officer of the AI decision-making company Taktile, told CNBC that engineers who might once have spent three weeks building a prototype can now generate 10 in an afternoon, and that the hardest part is having the judgment to decide which of those are any good.

Broadhead said AI agents produce so much code that engineers no longer read all of it, and that the old sense of comfort and awareness of how a whole code base was structured has given way to constant change. Joshua Wöhle, chief executive of the London-based AI training company Mindstone, told CNBC he sees a growing divide between workers who know how to use AI effectively and those who do not, and he said the industry's old talk of 10X engineers is widening into 100X engineers. Wöhle said companies will increasingly have to decide whether to help employees catch up with AI or prioritize those who get the most out of it, and he described as very real the grief of people who once excelled at writing code finding that the thing they love is no longer what the company should be paying for. Chris Sees, a software engineer of more than 20 years and chief executive of the London-based virtual office company Hoxton Mix, told CNBC he views AI as a capable junior engineer that still needs supervision, and he said the important thing is knowing what to delegate and when human judgment is needed.

Sees said he gets a lot of satisfaction from proving and spotting where AI has gone wrong, but he worries about the next generation of engineers if AI takes over the routine coding and debugging through which they traditionally learned, tasks he called where you learn lessons and build scar tissue. He said companies need to make sure AI becomes part of the learning process rather than a shortcut. Rodgers, who is self-employed, said she can use AI to automate the tedious parts of a project while keeping the more interesting problem-solving for herself, and she believes friction and discomfort are vital parts of the human experience. She said people need to feel accomplished in something and that part of accomplishment requires challenge, and that without working that through you never get the full force of the good feeling on the other side.

Articles.Title: AI is changing software engineering — and some developers miss the struggle

stories.Headline: John Deere acquires Orchard AI to add plant-level crop intelligence for growers
stories.Summary:
John Deere announced on November 19, 2026, that it has acquired Orchard Robotics, which operates as Orchard AI, a San Francisco-based agriculture technology company founded in 2022 that develops crop intelligence solutions for high-value crop growers. The deal strengthens Deere's ability to help growers make more informed decisions throughout the growing season by combining Orchard AI's detailed, plant-level crop insights with Deere's own expertise in precision agriculture, equipment, and farm technology. Orchard AI uses vehicle-mounted, AI-powered cameras to capture data for every individual tree, vine, or plant across a farm, all season long. With every pass through the field, the system analyzes hundreds of images per tree, giving growers a detailed view of crop conditions alongside accurate yield estimates, precise fruit counts, fruit size and color data, canopy measurements, and more. Its FruitScope software platform enables growers to visualize and use this data to make more informed farm management decisions, improving their efficiency of labor, time, and inputs across their operations.

For high-value crop growers, months of work and investment can depend on making the right decisions within narrow windows, since a missed spray application or mistimed harvest can affect fruit quality, yield, and an entire season's profitability. Weather, labor constraints, and changing crop conditions add pressure, leaving growers little time to determine what each block needs and get the work done. Combining Orchard AI's detailed view of crop conditions with Deere technology and equipment can help growers understand exactly what their trees need and act at the right time throughout the growing season. These capabilities can better inform critical decisions, from pruning and thinning trees, applying crop treatments where they are needed, and identifying which blocks are ready for harvest. The integrated AI software translates precision data into actionable recommendations, so growers can identify areas with higher bloom counts and receive a prescription on where to spray, delivered directly to a mobile device for in-field application or into an in-cab G5 display.

Tim Marquis, Director of Farm Systems Innovation at John Deere, said everything the company does starts with helping its customers succeed, and that the acquisition connects crop-level intelligence with Deere technology and equipment that can precisely execute the work in the field. He said bringing these capabilities together gives Deere an opportunity to help growers make more informed decisions across their operations and get more value from the technology they already rely on. Charlie Wu, CEO of Orchard AI, said the company was started to give growers the crop intelligence they need to farm more profitably and sustainably than ever before, and that joining John Deere lets it accelerate that mission. Justin Rose, President of the Worldwide Agriculture & Turf Division, Small Ag & Turf at John Deere, said a big part of what makes Orchard AI successful is its speed of innovation and the close relationships it has built directly with customers. He said Deere wants to preserve those strengths while bringing its scale and capabilities to help Orchard AI reach more growers and solve real challenges in agriculture.

stories.Headline: OSF HealthCare CEO Michelle Conger says Pope Leo XIV's AI encyclical guides the Catholic system's AI strategy
stories.Summary:
OSF HealthCare CEO Michelle Conger spoke about Pope Leo XIV's first encyclical, which focuses on artificial intelligence, at this year's OSF OnCall Digital Health Symposium, according to a newsroom post dated 20 November 2026 from Peoria, Illinois. Conger said the document gives Catholic health care organizations a chance to help shape how the rapidly evolving technology is used. She said the encyclical provides a framework for thoughtfully embracing AI while ensuring it serves patients, communities and the health care workforce. She said many people have compared the transformation that will come from AI to the industrial revolution, a time when there were questions about jobs and about who would be harmed. She said Pope Leo's message reinforces the importance of keeping people at the center of decisions about technology.

Conger said the encyclical is not an outright rejection of artificial intelligence and not an endorsement of adopting new technology without careful consideration. She said it is a call for organizations, particularly those rooted in Catholic values, to consider how AI can improve the human condition. She said OSF is already exploring applications such as ambient listening, robotics and automation to reduce administrative work. She said a significant amount of time and effort is spent in its revenue cycle to collect payments for care already provided, work she said is necessary but does not directly add value to the patient experience. She said OSF is approaching AI adoption through a governance process that considers the potential impact on both patients and employees.

Conger said the encyclical's themes include protecting human dignity and labor, addressing disinformation, educating people about AI and establishing appropriate governance. She said the message reinforces that AI must serve people and protect human dignity. She described the central themes she took away as human dignity over machines, with a person always kept at the center of the care provided or the work done. She said technology and algorithms must serve people rather than reduce them. She said the document provides a framework for OSF, as a Catholic organization, to apply the message and be a leader in doing so in a positive way to improve the health and wellbeing of patients and communities.

Conger said OSF's governance process includes its human resources team, its Mission people and its ethics people, who help it think through and make sound decisions. She said the challenge is to balance the promise of innovation with the responsibility to ensure technology remains a tool in service of people. She said she sees AI as an opportunity to free labor to do things far more rewarding than some of the work people do today, adding that OSF needs all of them. She said the shift is particularly important as health care organizations face persistent workforce shortages and growing demand for services from an aging population. She said individuals frequently struggle to determine where to go for care and how to access the services they need.

Conger said technology could help OSF better understand a person's background and circumstances when they contact the organization, making it easier to direct them to the appropriate care. She described that vision as creating a digital safety net that helps patients find the right entry point into the health care system. She connected that responsibility to OSF's broader system goals: clinical excellence, working together as One OSF and becoming the health care destination patients choose, regardless of where they enter the system. She said the goal should not simply be to do more with technology but to use it to elevate the work of caregivers, strengthen relationships and improve the health and well-being of the communities OSF HealthCare serves. She said the pope's message offers an opportunity for OSF to demonstrate how a Catholic health care organization can lead through a period of significant technological change without losing sight of its purpose.

The newsroom post was published at 17:06 PM America/Chicago on 20 November 2026 and was shared by media relations coordinator Colleen Reynolds. The post lists audio clips of Conger speaking on people being at the center of AI decision-making, technology serving people, Pope Leo providing a framework and AI freeing up Mission Partners for more meaningful work. The post also lists video clips with Conger on technology needing to serve people, people needing to be at the center of AI decision-making, Pope Leo providing a framework and freeing up employees for meaningful work. The post offers a media kit and B-roll of the Digital Health Symposium for download. stories.Headline: Researchers develop PIPETTE system to stop AI agents from retraining on repetitive prompt injections
stories.Summary:
Researchers from the University of Waterloo, Zhejiang University, and KTH Royal Institute of Technology discovered that AI agents retrained on larger sets of prompt injections often became easier to hijack. During tests conducted on models ranging from 4 billion to 27 billion parameters, the team found that automated red-teaming tools frequently repeated the same attack techniques. In one specific contest using the Qwen3-4B model across 560 tasks, the PISmith tool produced 7,132 working attacks compared to 4,282 from RL-Hammer. Despite having more successful injections, the version of the model trained on PISmith's data was hijacked 47.5 percent of the time during a stress test, while the RL-Hammer version was hijacked only 27.5 percent of the time.

This vulnerability requires a shift in how developers harden agents, as simply increasing the number of successful attacks used for retraining does not guarantee better security. The researchers developed a system called PIPETTE that sorts attacks by technique and rewards tools for finding new methods rather than repeating old ones. When tested on the AgentDojo public test bed, agents trained with PIPETTE allowed off-the-shelf injections to succeed less than half a percent of the time on average. Furthermore, the hardened Qwen3-4B model finished 64.95 percent of clean tasks, which was a slight improvement over the 61.86 percent completion rate of the original model.

The researchers explained that the gap in defense occurs because attack tools often get stuck using a single trick, such as claiming a user's task is already finished. They noted that existing variety checks often only measure differences in wording, which leads to retraining on thousands of rewordings of a few basic attacks. The team argued that the most useful metrics for security are the number of distinct techniques covered and how the agent performs against attackers allowed hundreds of attempts. They also observed that PIPETTE outperformed detection tools like PromptGuard, which blocked necessary data and caused the agent to finish the user's real task only 16.19 percent of the time.

stories.Headline: UK accelerating elite law firms gain ground by adopting AI early, Chambers finds
stories.Summary:
The first US and UK editions of the Chambers Advantage Index, a debut analysis by the legal ranking firm Chambers of a decade of its rankings data, were published on November 20, 2026, and only four law firms reached the top tier in both countries: Latham & Watkins, Kirkland & Ellis, Goodwin, and White & Case. Each firm was scored on how strong its market position is today and how fast that position is improving, which split the market into four groups: Accelerating Elite, Stable Elite, Accelerating Challengers, and Stable Challengers. The gap between the movers and the rest is stark, with US accelerators growing premium practices at a 78% higher rate and UK accelerators growing premium practices at a 54% higher rate, where premium practices are those that attract the highest value work and the firms with the highest revenue or profit margins. Latham and Kirkland made the greatest strides of all, each with significant increases in ranking volume and promotion into higher bands, while Gibson Dunn, one of the UK’s fastest-growing challengers, is close to joining the Elite there. For US firms in London, much of the growth comes through lateral hiring, as talent has moved toward US firms where UK lawyers see more opportunity and bigger rewards, and Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison is one example, adding partners across M&A, finance, and tax as part of expanding its private equity offerings.

That route carries big risk, because high-profile partners are expensive and firms have mixed success in earning a return on them or even keeping them over the long term, and mergers offer another route to a marked jump in market presence that many top performers have taken. Client feedback shows priorities differ, since a broad international footprint matters less to many US-based clients but is critical to many UK-based clients, and the UK’s leading firms are growing in the US too but have yet to match that breadth there. Not every success rests on a big bet, as Davis Polk shows practice depth with Band 1 rankings in New York for corporate M&A, banking and finance, and tax in Chambers USA 2026, and Macfarlanes has accelerated with a tightly focused domestic strategy built on premium practices and repeat work from private capital clients. In the UK, the Accelerating Elite are winning on AI, as many were early adopters of legal technology who set up alternative service delivery hubs akin to the Management Services Organization model in the US, bringing together data, technology, and paralegal expertise to drive efficiency and build data assets. That experience is now paying off, since they already have the know-how, the multidisciplinary teams, and the culture to adopt new technology at pace, and their junior lawyers report more confidence in using AI.

In the US the picture flips, with the Accelerating Challengers’ associates reporting the most successful AI adoption, while the US Accelerating Elite came to AI later but are now investing heavily. Chambers’ research with in-house legal teams shows AI is now the fastest-growing trend affecting clients’ legal needs and how they handle legal work, and fewer than 5% of clients were negative about firms using AI in the latest research. Clients still buy expertise, judgment, and great service first, but they increasingly expect firms to use technology to give them more for less, and the firms already set up to deliver that are the ones gaining ground. For everyone else, the question is how long they can afford to wait.

stories.Headline: A distributor finds agentic AI costs 20 times more than traditional architecture for the same ROI
stories.Summary:
A large regional distributor set out to build a new sales transaction management system to automate order intake, discount approvals, exception handling, customer communications and inventory checks, as David Linthicum reported in InfoWorld on November 20, 2026. After vendor presentations, the company decided to go agentic, using AI agents to manage decision flows, invoke tools, check policies and interact with enterprise systems. One vendor pitched its offering as a common LLM brain that could make decisions as if the company had hired 10,000 experts who were not on the payroll. Building the system required far more integration work than expected, with each agent needing clean data, governed APIs, business rules, security controls, observability and human override mechanisms. The project ran fine in production, but six months later the company found the system cost roughly 20 times more than a traditional architecture and delivered about the same ROI.

Linthicum wrote that he hears versions of this story once or twice a week from clients, colleagues and friends. He said agentic AI is powerful but is being pushed into places where simpler technology would deliver the same business value for far less money. He described the pattern as familiar, with names, diagrams and conference sessions changing while every enterprise architecture discussion starts with the trend instead of the business problem. He cited cloud-native, microservices, service-oriented architecture, distributed objects and CORBA as earlier approaches that promised flexible, reusable, distributed systems. He said each pattern had value and solved real problems but caused expensive failures when adopted as a default answer rather than a fit-for-purpose architecture.

Linthicum said SOA gave enterprises a language for service reuse and integration and pushed teams away from tightly coupled monoliths and point-to-point chaos. He said SOA became expensive and complex quickly, with enterprise service buses turning into central chokepoints and governance becoming heavyweight. He said teams spent more time debating service contracts, standards, registries and middleware than delivering business features, and SOA became an architecture tax in many companies. He said microservices worked well for organizations with strong devops practices, mature automation, disciplined domain boundaries and high-scale needs. He said many companies shattered ordinary applications into dozens or hundreds of services and traded code complexity for network complexity, creating distributed failure modes, data consistency problems, monitoring challenges and testing headaches.

Linthicum said containers and Kubernetes brought portable workloads, declarative deployment, elastic scaling, automated recovery and a modern operating model. He said many enterprises moved systems into containers and Kubernetes without a clear reason, adding clusters, service meshes, observability stacks, platform engineering teams, security layers and specialized skills. He said the architecture nearly doubled the cost of running systems that did not need that level of abstraction in many cases. He said agentic systems require model access, prompt management, tool orchestration, evaluation frameworks, security controls, audit trails, human-in-the-loop design, data governance and new operational skills. He said they introduce nondeterministic behavior into processes that may require deterministic outcomes and can make simple automation much more expensive than it needs to be.

Linthicum said enterprises should start with value, not architecture, and that the value must be measurable rather than vague promises of automation. He said agentic AI works best where a problem requires interpretation, adaptation and semi-autonomous action, and is less compelling when a process is stable, rules-based, highly regulated or easily expressed through traditional logic. He said a traditional workflow engine, rules platform, API integration or conventional application delivering the same result at one-tenth the cost matters. He said enterprises need to separate impressive demos from practical use cases, because a system that looks intelligent in a conference demo may be expensive, fragile and hard to govern in production. He said skepticism is healthy and every architecture has positives and negatives.

Linthicum said the job of enterprise architects is not to follow the trend but to understand it, test it against business value and apply it only where it fits. He said otherwise we are destined to make the same mistakes over and over again. He wrote that agentic AI will have automation benefits along with governance, security and operations challenges. He said SOA gave us value and complexity, microservices gave us agility and operational burden, and cloud-native delivered scalability and cost expansion. He is an internationally recognized industry expert who has authored 13 books on computing, the latest being An Insider's Guide to Cloud Computing, and his views are his own.

stories.Headline: OpenAI launches MedChemBench to test how well AI models reason about molecules and select compounds in drug research
stories.Summary:
OpenAI introduced MedChemBench on November 20, 2026, a benchmark that tests how well AI models read molecular structures, interpret experimental results, and choose which compounds to test next in medicinal chemistry research. The benchmark draws on 117 papers and patents and includes 761 distinct molecular structures, presenting models with 99 problems taken from published research. For most problems, models receive the context available at a chosen point in a research program, including the biological target, the researchers' goals, the compounds studied so far, and selected experimental findings. The benchmark evaluates four components: molecular structures, scientific reasoning, ranking and selection, and property predictions.

At the xhigh reasoning setting, GPT-6.2 Astra earned 84.5% of the available credit, compared with 83.3% for GPT-6 Astra, 82.0% for GPT-6.1 Sol, and 58.2% for GPT-5.6 Sol. Across the full benchmark at the shared xhigh setting, Astra earned 83.3%, compared with 82.0% for GPT-6.1 Sol, 75.1% for GPT-6.1 Terra, and 58.2% for GPT-5.6 Sol, while at max effort GPT-6 Astra reached 83.8%. Astra earned 95.4% of the available structure credit at xhigh but only about half the credit for selecting compounds and predicting numerical properties. One problem asks models to assemble a molecule from a central structure and two attached groups while preserving an 18-atom ring, and GPT-6 Astra reconstructed it correctly in all ten responses while GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.6 Luna failed across all ten.

OpenAI said the results do not establish whether models can discover new drugs or improve laboratory decisions, and that prior exposure to the published sources cannot be ruled out. The company also said each response was a single attempt without tools, feedback, or new experiments, and that the benchmark evaluates reasoning from historical evidence rather than real-world drug discovery. OpenAI stated that the results help identify where models are advancing and where challenges remain, and that it believes MedChemBench will support continued progress. The company said it looks forward to sharing updates as its models advance to serve the field.

stories.Headline: Former Secret Service investigator Jason Brown warns AI makes scams harder to detect
stories.Summary:
Jason Brown warned that artificial intelligence makes scams harder to detect on Thursday, November 20, 2026. He is a former U.S. Secret Service cyberfraud investigator and the director of customer advisory at iCounter. Brown sounded this alarm as the holiday season nears and Americans grow more anxious. He noted that AI allows criminals to create more convincing fraudulent messages. These tools make scammers more efficient and less prone to errors.

AI eliminates warning signs like spelling mistakes, poor grammar, and awkward phrasing that consumers previously used. Criminals use voice cloning to impersonate relatives and demand thousands of dollars in gift cards. Scammers may impersonate the U.S. Postal Service, FedEx, and UPS during holiday shopping. They claim packages need additional postage paid through gift cards or cryptocurrency. Businesses face schemes where criminals impersonate trusted vendors to redirect legitimate payments.

Jason Brown told Fox News Digital that Americans have reason to be cautious about technology. He stated that everyone now needs a high level of distrust regarding suspicious messages. Brown explained that AI makes criminals more effective at targeting families and consumers. He urged people to stop, think, and independently verify any communication. He suggested families establish a safe word to confirm identities during unexpected calls.

Americans are increasingly on edge following a wave of major technology disruptions. These disruptions involved the Federal Aviation Administration, Microsoft, and several financial institutions. Victims of these sophisticated scams face significant financial losses and an emotional toll. FBI reporting identified over 22,000 AI fraud cases in 2025 with losses exceeding 890 million dollars. Businesses are also affected, especially when executives travel or temporary workers join operations.

Brown noted that some recent technology incidents involved infrastructure problems while others remain under investigation. He explained that scams are more likely to be built from publicly available data. The holiday season creates vulnerabilities as employees take time off from their jobs. AI allows for the impersonation of familiar voices to trick victims into believing relatives are distressed. These tools help criminals create messages that are increasingly difficult for people to recognize.

Brown advised people to end calls and contact relatives using a trusted number. He recommended that Americans independently verify any suspicious messages they receive. The articles do not state if the government is taking specific actions against AI. They do not mention if delivery companies have new security measures for notifications. It remains open whether the number of AI fraud cases will rise in 2026.

stories.Headline: DevOps engineer Mahathi Kari receives 2026 Global Recognition Award for secure deployment pipeline and AI research
stories.Summary:
Mahathi Kari, a DevOps engineer supporting Johnson & Johnson Technology, received a 2026 Global Recognition Award in the Innovation, Research category on November 20, 2026, according to a press release dated that day. The award recognized her secure deployment pipeline for the Impella screen project and her cited research in artificial intelligence and cybersecurity. Reviewers selected her file because her scholarship and her daily engineering duties were difficult to separate. The honor was granted in a category that rewards depth of practice instead of isolated achievement.

Her nomination centers on the Impella screen project, a healthcare initiative in which accurate presentation of patient heartbeat data is essential to system function. Kari designed and manages the CI/CD and deployment pipeline that builds, tests, security-validates, and deploys software changes for that project, where patient safety depends directly on dependable performance. Her architecture combines GitLab, Jenkins, Terraform, Ansible, Docker, and Kubernetes, while Checkmarx, Semgrep, Snyk, and Coverity add scanning layers so security and code-quality risks are caught before release. Splunk and Prometheus give her team live visibility into the health of both the pipeline and the application.

Shortlisted applicants are scored with the Rasch model, a statistical framework that converts subjective grading into a linear measurement scale. Kari's Google Scholar profile lists 52 citations, an h-index of 4, and an i10-index of 2, and her most cited paper on machine-learning-based zero-trust intrusion detection for cloud computing has earned 26 citations. A second paper on how artificial intelligence affects the software development lifecycle has gathered 13 citations, and its findings mirror the automation and validation tasks she performs on the Impella project. Her wider portfolio covers automated defect prediction, AI-assisted database query optimization, deep-learning phishing detection, network-security fault prediction, and a comparative study of the MD5, SHA-256, and SHA-512 hashing algorithms.

She treats each failure, deployment blocker, and security finding as a direct threat to patient-facing stability and takes ownership of the root-cause investigation whenever one appears. Alex Sterling, a spokesperson for Global Recognition Awards, said Kari represents the kind of candidate the Innovation, Research category exists for, someone whose academic work and daily engineering responsibilities reinforce each other rather than sitting apart. Global Recognition Awards describes itself as an international organization that recognizes exceptional companies and individuals who have significantly contributed to their industry. The press release states that Markets Insider and Business Insider editorial teams were not involved in the creation of the post.

stories.Headline: Cryptographer Matthew Green warns AI advances threaten public-key cryptography and urges improved cryptographic agility
stories.Summary:
Johns Hopkins cryptographer Matthew Green warned in a series of posts on X last month that existing public-key cryptography systems were at risk because machines have begun outperforming humans in their ability to address some mathematical problems. Green wrote that he saw a 1% chance we live in Minicrypt and a 15% chance we functionally lose confidence in existing public-key encryption algorithms. He said he was worried about standardized public-key encryption and some signatures, and specifically the fact that most of it is based on a small number of hard problems. Green warned that a disruptive loss of confidence in internet security systems would arise if a major cryptanalytic surprise arrives faster than standards and deployments can adapt. The comments sparked discussions on LinkedIn and elsewhere about how public-key crypto could fail, and Green is yet to respond to CSO's request for comment on the debate he sparked.

Green's warning concerned the cryptographic foundations beneath public key infrastructure, the system of certificates, keys, and certificate authorities that secures Transport Layer Security, code signing, and many other information security functions. He said the industry needs to focus on improved cryptographic agility. Markku-Juhani O. Saarinen, a cryptographer and professor at Finland's Tampere University, told CSO that he takes Green's warning seriously but urges caution and said there is no need to rip and replace established industry cryptographic standards. Saarinen said cryptography has good standards, best practices, and active modernization paths, the PQC transition, and that just following those is the most sensible approach from an information security perspective. He said what has happened in 2026 is that mathematics had its Lee Sedol moment and analytical problems previously thought to be in the human domain are now being solved by computers.

Saarinen said the fear in cryptography is that AI will find a shortcut for some hard computational problems and make them easy, though AI is very good at optimizing computation and is not expected to turn all hard computational problems into trivial ones. He explained that a cryptographically relevant break can be exponential but might halve the number of bits, and that such an analytic break has happened to some relatively new schemes, such as HAWK by AI in 2026, and to numerous older proposals by humans. He said AI also played a significant role in finding a significant shortcut to the parameters of the McEliece cryptosystem, one of the earliest public-key schemes, designed in 1978. Saarinen added that the German cyber agency had been recommending a variant called Classic McEliece for quantum security since 2020, but withdrew its recommendation at the end of September.

He clarified that in both cases the schemes could still be considered secure if security parameters were adjusted, but that would have doubled public and secret keys, signatures, and ciphertexts. Saarinen said RSA and Elliptic-Curve cryptosystems are already broken from a computational-complexity viewpoint because polynomial-time quantum algorithms for them have been known since 1994, and building quantum computers is just an engineering problem. He said the main post-quantum alternatives, ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA, have received more than a decade of intense analysis. Saarinen suggested a mathematical shortcut is more likely to exist in public-key cryptography given that it by definition requires mathematical structure for the trapdoor, and that symmetric-key cryptography, hashes and keyed ciphers, has simply more design freedom in this sense.

Professor Alan Woodward, a computer scientist at the University of Surrey, said LLMs are yet to make a huge dent on cryptography and that what is actually happening is that the LLMs are acting as a great tool for mathematicians, cryptographers, and computer scientists to speed up their research. Woodward said the leap of intuition needed to find the fatal flaw still seems to need humans, and that LLMs are very effective at finding flaws in implementations rather than the underlying mathematics. Woodward compared the threat posed by AI in breaking encryption schemes to the danger to legacy encryption schemes posed by quantum computers, and said both problems highlight the need for improved agility in the cryptographic schemes in use. He said people have already been migrating in preparation for Q-Day, the hypothetical future time when quantum computers are powerful enough to break public-key encryption, so in some ways that should already be addressing the risks posed, if they are real, by LLMs.

Woodward said the most effective route so far seems to be a hybrid route where we have a mix of cryptographic schemes that, whilst one or two might fall away, leaves us with others we can rely upon. He said any found to be flawed for whatever reason can be deprecated rapidly and the intact schemes used instead. Cryptography uses numerical problems, traditional ones like factoring the products of large prime numbers and discrete logarithm, and newer ones like learning with errors, and analyzing those algorithms and their complexity is part of theoretical computer science. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Researchers find elderly health monitoring AI lacks human centered privacy features
stories.Summary:
An international research team published a comprehensive review in Discover Artificial Intelligence on November 21, 2026. The investigators examined how remote health monitoring systems for elderly patients protect patient confidentiality. They found that privacy mechanisms rarely incorporate human-centered artificial intelligence principles. Most systems do not involve elderly end users directly in the design. The review revealed a lack of user-facing controls in existing engineering studies.

The team analyzed forty-five primary studies published between 2020 and 2025 from IEEE Xplore, Scopus, and Web of Science. Search cycles occurred in May 2025 and May 2026, retrieving 202 initial records. India led research with eight studies, followed by China with six and Japan with five. The United States and Taiwan contributed three each, while Australia and Canada provided two each. Fourteen other nations and two multi-country partnerships also provided single studies.

The researchers stated that most studies rely on technical data transformations rather than human-centered design. They noted that nominal transparency is not meaningful if elderly users cannot comprehend the feedback. The authors argued that technical explainability must become actionable, low-burden indicators for vulnerable populations. They found that ethical awareness is often reduced to mathematical data perturbation. The team emphasized that these systems often lack direct evidence of stakeholder participation.

Older adults are affected by cognitive, accessibility, and digital-literacy barriers when navigating complex privacy settings. Patients are vulnerable to risks from unprocessed audio, video feeds, thermopile arrays, and wearable telemetry. Third-party cloud infrastructure may be untrusted or susceptible to unauthorized access. Some systems use non-invasive equipment like LiDAR and millimeter-wave radar to detect falls. However, distributed architectures introduce localized security vulnerabilities and risks of physical tampering.

Remote monitoring helps older adults maintain medical oversight and reduces the need for frequent in-person examinations. These systems gather sensitive physiological, behavioral, and environmental information outside conventional clinics. Most reviewed models focus on prediction tasks, specifically fall detection and activities of daily living. Research accelerated in 2024, with 60 percent of literature coming from international conferences. Only two of the forty-five studies explored generative artificial intelligence models.

The researchers will continue to examine how algorithmic safeguards align with human-centered dimensions. They leave open the psychological impact of persistent ambient surveillance on patient dignity. The review did not evaluate human-centered features directly with any elderly participants. Future work may need to include non-English language literature to find more studies. It remains unclear how to effectively integrate personal autonomy into these technical frameworks.

stories.Headline: Anthropic pursues disease cures to drive growth after its IPO
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, fresh off its record-setting initial public offering, now must show investors that it can sustain growth and generate profits, and the company has a plan for that: curing some of the world's gnarliest diseases. In its IPO prospectus, Anthropic states that AI holds the potential to profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine, potentially curing diseases that have plagued humanity for millennia, including cancer, Alzheimer's disease, heart disease, rare genetic diseases, and the major infectious diseases. Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei said in a post on X in August that he believes it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in roughly five to ten years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well. The company has partnered with biotech and pharmaceutical companies that use its Claude Science model for various purposes, and Anthropic also operates its own AI-powered biology wet lab in San Francisco that has already made scientific discoveries.

Developing breakthrough drugs is among the most promising avenues of research for AI, potentially bringing treatments for a range of conditions to market much faster than is currently possible, according to scientists and industry analysts. Neerav Kaushal, an AI and molecular biology expert at Michigan Technological University, told CBS News that AI can accelerate research and will help you get there faster, but it is not just speed, it is directional speed. He compared the effort to standing at the top of a mountain and aiming to find a drug for cancer that lies in the valley, saying AI will not just help you get down there faster but will help you get down to the right valley where the drug is. For Anthropic, developing drugs could open up potentially enormous commercial opportunities, and Morningstar senior equity analyst Malik Ahmed Khan told CBS News that if you can use a large language model to condense any part of the timeline, it is very economically valuable.

The challenge for Anthropic will be how it turns its life sciences research into profits, which could take time, Khan told CBS News. He said how this becomes lucrative for Anthropic is a very important question, and he thinks it is a question Anthropic has not figured out yet, adding that coding is its best-proven use case, followed by cybersecurity applications, then financial and legal research. Khan said that if you improve your drug's efficiency by a couple of percentage points, that can make a world of difference, and he expects a drug developer like Eli Lilly and Co., which partners with Anthropic to give its employees access to Claude, would be willing to pay hundreds of millions or billions of dollars to make its arthritis drug two percent better than it is. Developing potentially lifesaving drugs could have other benefits for Anthropic, because by applying tools to the life sciences and using them to improve human life, the company could help shift the narrative around AI to a more positive one, according to experts. Khan said that if you are the AI company that helps advance some kind of cure or solution to a sickness or illness that has prevailed for quite some time, that gets you a ton more trust with consumers and end users, because you end up becoming the company that is actually improving the quality of life for humans at large.

stories.Headline: Swedish MASAI trial finds AI supported breast screening meets noninferiority criterion for interval cancers
stories.Summary:
The Swedish MASAI trial reported in 2026 on interval cancers, which are cancers found after a negative screening and before the next scheduled round, and among about 106,000 randomised participants there were 82 interval cancers in the AI supported group and 93 with standard double reading, rates of 1.55 and 1.76 per 1,000 women. The trial met its criterion for noninferiority, and the numerically lower rate should not be presented as proof of superiority, while sensitivity was 80.5% with AI support and 73.8% under standard screening and specificity was 98.5% in both groups. An earlier report from the same MASAI population found detection rates of 6.4 per 1,000 women with AI supported screening and 5.0 with standard double reading, a relative increase of 29%, and these are successive analyses of one trial rather than independent replications. The intervention combined risk based allocation to single or double reading with detection support for radiologists, and it reduced screen reading workload by about 44%, a figure about reading examinations rather than all labour across a breast screening service.

The German PRAIM study, published in Nature Medicine in 2025, evaluated 461,818 women at 12 screening sites with 119 radiologists, and AI supported examinations had a cancer detection rate of 6.7 per 1,000 women against 5.7 without AI support, a relative difference of 17.6%, while recall rates were 37.4 and 38.3 per 1,000. This was a prospective observational study in which radiologists could choose whether to use the AI supported viewer, so the comparison was not randomised, and statistical adjustment cannot guarantee that every relevant difference has been removed. ScreenTrustCAD examined another arrangement in Stockholm, where in a prospective study of 55,581 women examinations were assessed by two radiologists and an AI system, and one radiologist plus AI detected 261 cancers against 250 with two radiologists, meeting the study's noninferiority criterion. That paired design compared combinations evaluating the same screening material, and its primary assessment concerned cancers identified within three months, so it answers a different question from later interval cancer follow up.

The article says the findings strengthen the case for the tested workflow but do not establish a reduction in breast cancer mortality, and longer term outcomes, including the consequences of detecting additional disease, remain relevant when programmes decide how much confidence to place in earlier diagnosis. For regional screening authorities the combined evidence supports a more specific procurement conversation about which clinical task was tested, in which workflow, and with what downstream consequences, since a detection headline alone cannot answer those questions. Hospitals considering a change need an explicit route for disagreement, where an AI flag may require arbitration, further imaging or a decision that no action is needed, and the staffing and expertise for that route belong in the deployment plan. For implementation, the next step is to compare the tested arrangement with the proposed local pathway, with arbitration, assessment capacity and monitoring specified alongside the software.

stories.Headline: MIT and Cornell researchers create an AI text detector that identifies rewritten machine content
stories.Summary:
Researchers from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Cornell University created a new method for detecting AI-generated text on November 20, 2026. This system can identify machine-produced content even after it has been rewritten by tools designed to make the writing appear human. The technology uses test-time adaptation to learn from new material during the analysis process instead of relying only on original training data. It analyzes groups of passages to find shared patterns through a phenomenon called inference-time homogeneity.

The new approach detected 93.3% of AI-generated texts rewritten by humanizer tools, while the benchmark tool called Pangram only found 27%. When tested on language models outside its original training data, the system achieved detection rates between 87% and 94%. It also maintained an accuracy of 86% to 90% when identifying human-written texts, whereas one conventional detector dropped from 85.9% to 73.4% over ten years. These results demonstrate a significant improvement over existing tools that have not been updated.

The researchers stated that this technology could help employers, publishers, news organizations, and universities determine the true origins of written material. They also suggested that the system has cybersecurity applications for identifying AI-generated phishing emails or attempts to manipulate search engine results. While the results are promising, the developers noted that the method is not error-free and still requires human verification. The findings are scheduled to be presented later this year at the international artificial intelligence conference known as NeurIPS.

stories.Headline: Sage CEO Stephen Hare reports 11% revenue growth to £2.78 billion on AI adoption
stories.Summary:
Sage Group reported an 11% increase in annual revenue to £2.78 billion for the year ended 30 September 2026, with operating profit rising 12% year-on-year to £600 million, according to CEO Stephen Hare. Hare attributed the growth to increased adoption of AI-powered services, saying AI is expanding what the company can do for customers and increasing its market opportunity. He said Sage is building on strong foundations, deep domain expertise and long-standing relationships with millions of small and medium businesses and accountants. The company's intelligence engine now generates 10 billion predictions per year, more than twice the level a year ago, Hare said.

Hare said Sage's proprietary permission data, built through processing billions of transactions every year, and its partner ecosystem give it a deep understanding of business context along with the governance and permissions that keep customer data safe. He said AI in Sage Intacct is now processing 50 million invoices per year, saving customers nearly 6 million hours of work, while adoption of the Making Tax Digital agent in Sage for Accountants has doubled in six months. Sage AI Workspaces, now in beta, will let small and medium businesses manage multiple agents across workflows while keeping approvals in human hands, he said. During the year Sage launched Agent Builder, which lets partners create and publish their own agents in its marketplace, and the Sage AI Gateway, which lets customers connect Sage data to the AI applications they choose.

Hare said agency without permissions is a business risk and that Sage's AI is designed to be transparent, explainable and auditable so customers gain productivity without giving up control. He said the company is addressing barriers to AI adoption through initiatives such as its AI Trust label and the UK Government's AI Skills Boost program. On competition, Hare said Sage faces both traditional and emerging competitors but is acquiring new customers at accelerating levels, including more new customers in the UK in the last 12 months than at any time since he became CEO in 2018. He said Sage is growing faster than its more established competitors pretty much across the board.

Hare said Sage's AI strategy creates several drivers of growth, including more value embedded into core subscriptions, upsell of its own agents such as accounts payable and financial close automation, and growth in consumption revenue as third-party agents access its data, workflows and APIs. He said the company's purpose is to create the confidence that businesses are built on and its vision is to be the essential platform for the people who need to get it right. He acknowledged that confidence is commercial, meaning businesses choose Sage, get up and running faster, stay longer and buy more. The article's author described the results as a solid performance to complete 2026 for Sage.

stories.Headline: US authorities investigate Singaporean firm over diverted Nvidia chips to China
stories.Summary:
US authorities have scrutinized the Singaporean cloud computing firm Megaspeed International over suspicions that restricted Nvidia chips were diverted to Chinese customers. This investigation centers on Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who served as the managing director of the company in 2023. The controversy became a major point of discussion on Friday, November 20, 2026, as it highlighted weaknesses in American technology controls. While Singapore found that Huang provided inaccurate information about her role, the government stated there was insufficient evidence that she committed a crime.

The situation requires a shift from blocking hardware shipments to a broader model of compute governance. Washington is now considering new measures to prevent Chinese firms from renting capacity at overseas data centers that use restricted processors. This change would involve monitoring who operates advanced chips, who accesses them remotely, and the specific purposes of that access. Malaysia is also considering new legislation to monitor how high-performance chips are used within its own data center operations. Such a system would require auditable records, strict customer verification, and deeper cross-border cooperation to be effective.

Lawmakers in the United States are now questioning what Nvidia and government officials knew about these risks and how they were assessed. Singaporean officials claimed they received limited assistance from American authorities during their investigation into these AI server transactions. The reports suggest that the US cannot simply transfer the burden of enforcement to chipmakers who are seeking new markets. Experts argue that a credible system must define clear, enforceable obligations regarding what firms should know about their end users.

This affair reveals that controlling the export of a processor does not necessarily control the computing power it provides. Chinese companies can bypass hardware restrictions by accessing servers remotely or using intermediaries in Southeast Asia. This creates a strategic contradiction because the United States must protect sensitive technology while its companies still depend on global infrastructure. Future enforcement will likely focus on who can use the capabilities of a chip regardless of where the hardware is physically located.

stories.Headline: AI stocks plunge as SEC probes Nvidia accounting practices
stories.Summary:
Nvidia shares dropped 12 percent on Friday, November 20, 2026, marking seven consecutive days of losses for the chip giant. This decline occurred alongside double-digit losses for peers AMD and Broadcom during a broader sell-off of artificial intelligence stocks. The market downturn followed reports of a Securities and Exchange Commission probe into the accounting practices of Nvidia. Other affected companies included Micron Technology and SK Hynix, which both fell more than 10 percent.

The volatility follows the Thursday public debut of AI model maker Anthropic, whose stock fell as much as 12 percent on Friday. Broadcom has significant financial ties to Anthropic, including an agreement to lend the developer up to 42 billion dollars for infrastructure. Additionally, Broadcom agreed to purchase approximately 1 billion dollars of Anthropic shares through a private placement related to the IPO. Nvidia has fallen more than 22 percent this year, putting it on track for its first annual decline since 2022.

Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives stated that the current weakness is a panic-driven sell-off rather than a sign of darker times. He argued that big tech companies will continue spending capital expenditures in the 1.5 trillion dollar range next year. This market instability comes after the exit of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and growing concerns regarding the financing of AI. Other firms like Coherent and Bloom Energy also saw their stocks sink by 6 percent and 7 percent, respectively.

The broader chip sector had already been on shaky ground before the recent public offering of Anthropic. Neocloud providers CoreWeave and Nebius extended their losses on Friday, with both companies declining roughly 9 percent. Shares of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and equipment maker ASML also declined during the session. Investors are now monitoring whether these declines signal a long-term shift or a temporary reaction to leadership changes and regulatory scrutiny.

stories.Headline: Anthropic prices shares at 83 dollars and closes its first trading day at 97.17 dollars
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the company that created the AI assistant Claude, began trading on Thursday. The company priced its shares at 83 dollars per share. This pricing gave the company a value of about 1.1 trillion dollars. The stock closed its first trading day at 97.17 dollars. Many investors are now asking whether they should buy the stock.

Anthropic has signed up for about 900.9 billion dollars of spending on computing and infrastructure. Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and Meta spent 615.4 billion dollars in the four quarters to September 2026. This is 4.3 times the 143.9 billion dollars spent in the same period three years earlier. Amazon spent 215.2 billion dollars, Google spent 159.8 billion, Microsoft spent 135.9 billion, and Meta spent 104.4 billion. These figures compare to 54.7 billion for Amazon, 28.8 billion for Google, 31.7 billion for Microsoft, and 28.6 billion for Meta.

The Trefis team believes the slowest part of the AI power supply to build is the grid. They state that most of the money from big buyers has not yet reached the grid. Trefis suggests that long run investors should own the whole chain rather than one link. They recommend sizing a portfolio for a bad year to avoid a broken plan. The team notes that picking the one stock that paid the most was not possible.

Anthropic warns in its filing that waiting lines to connect large electricity users have lengthened substantially in many regions. The company says it will cover price increases its data centers cause for consumers. Some investors are affected by the backlash regarding whose power bills are going up. A Texas governor once promised a data center moratorium, which caused some AI stocks to fall. Suppliers feel the impact immediately if the big buyers cut their spending together.

Anthropic was founded in 2021 before ChatGPT made AI a household word. The company bet that models get better as more computing is put into them. GE Vernova sales of grid equipment rose 51 percent in the September quarter from a year earlier. Vertiv sales grew 97 percent, Quanta grew 91 percent, and Eaton grew 41 percent over three years. Cameco sales were flat, up 0.4 percent, over the last year.

Investors must now decide if 2027 will be a repeat of 2022 for stocks. The articles leave open whether the current demand for computing will keep rising. It remains unclear which specific stock in the power chain will pay the most. The long term impact of electricity needs on AI will matter in 2030. The market must determine if the grid can be built fast enough.

stories.Headline: MX8 Labs survey finds 68% of US internet users have used AI tools instead of search
stories.Summary:
Research firm MX8 Labs surveyed 1,005 U.S. internet users in September 2026 for the 2027 State of Browsing Report, which Shift Browser commissioned and produced. The survey found that 68% of respondents had used AI tools like ChatGPT or Perplexity instead of traditional search in the past six months. In the same survey, 64% said they would rather have a browser that gives them more control, even if that means making more decisions themselves. Shift Browser makes its own browser, so its conclusions come from a business with a stake in convincing people to switch. The report says it was meant to find out what people actually want from their browser, not what the industry assumes they want.

Use of AI tools in place of search reached 80% among 18- to 24-year-olds and 76% among 35- to 44-year-olds, and half of seniors had done it. Respondents wanted AI for research (35%), finding previously viewed information (28%), comparing information or products (27%), and summarizing multiple tabs (25%). Nearly half (48%) said they would feel very uncomfortable with AI accessing stored personal IDs like Social Security numbers, and 37% felt the same about financial information. Among adults 65 and older, 80% said they would choose control even if it meant more decisions, and 30% said they don't want AI in their browser at all. Women leaned toward control at 67%, and 34% of 18- to 24-year-olds said they are open to a browser making decisions on their behalf.

Shift's report sums up its own takeaway for the industry: browsers should make browsing smarter without making people feel like they have surrendered control. Shift's own summary of the report puts it bluntly under the heading "The Average Browser Tab Is a Small Act of Anxiety." The company has a commercial interest in findings that show dissatisfaction with Google Chrome and demand for alternative browsers, and its report frames several results as opportunities for alternative browsers. The interpretations in the article are drawn from the survey figures, not from the company's marketing conclusions. Because it is a one-time survey, the results capture what people said at a single point in time.

Google Chrome remains the giant, with 90% of respondents familiar with it and 58% using it as their primary desktop browser. Safari came in a distant second at 16%, followed by Microsoft Edge at 13%. Asked why they use Chrome, 38% said they have simply used it for years without a second thought, and 25% said it came pre-installed on their device. Over half (54%) said they had not seriously considered changing their primary browser in the past year, and 32% said losing saved logins and being used to their current browser is what keeps them from switching.

Privacy and security ranked as the top factor in choosing a browser (36%), narrowly ahead of compatibility with other apps (33%) and speed (32%), and among 55- to 64-year-olds privacy climbed to 44%. Respondents named slow performance, website tracking, and unwanted features as their three biggest frustrations with browsers. Four in 10 people across all age groups said they leave tabs open because they are afraid of losing something, another 30% said they open tabs they never return to, and 36% said they regularly reopen the same sites throughout the day. Digital burnout turned out to be common: 12% said they feel drained by their time online very often, 17% often, and 34% sometimes, while only 13% said never.

Seniors 65 and older reported the least burnout, with 43% saying they rarely feel drained online, while among 18- to 24-year-olds only 6% said the same. Adults ages 25 to 34 stood out at the other end, with 20% reporting very frequent digital fatigue. Asked about their biggest concerns with AI in browsers, 45% pointed to AI accessing too much personal information, 42% to AI taking actions they didn't intend, and 40% to basic security, while 32% worried about losing control over their browsing experience. About a third (32%) want to be asked before new AI features are enabled, and 22% want AI features off unless they opt in, so more than half would rather not have AI switched on for them by default.

Just over half of all respondents said AI has made their online life at least somewhat simpler. The published materials do not list a margin of error, the number of respondents in each age group, or the exact wording of the survey questions. Age-group results rest on smaller subgroups and carry more uncertainty than the overall numbers. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI Can Take Over Your Browser And Run Tasks For You. Here's Why Most Americans Aren't Thrilled With The Idea

stories.Headline: Anthropic goes public as falling AI token prices spark analyst concerns
stories.Summary:
Anthropic completed its initial public offering on November 19, 2026, with its stock price jumping 17 percent during the debut. The company entered the public market with a market capitalization of 1.27 trillion dollars and a share price of 97.17 dollars. This event allows stock market investors to gain exposure to artificial intelligence labs for the first time in history. However, some analysts are concerned because the prices of AI tokens have been falling sharply across the industry.

The Silicon Data LLM Token Expenditure Index shows that prices per million tokens fell over 40 percent between June 30 and early October. Anthropic responded by cutting prices for its newest frontier model, Fable 5.2, by 20 percent to remain competitive. Goldman Sachs projected that the company could reach 440 billion dollars in revenue by 2029, while Morningstar suggested a bull case share price of 188 dollars. Despite these price drops, the company reported 47 percent sequential growth in the third quarter ending September 30.

Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei believes the technology could cure diseases like Alzheimer's and cancer within the next ten years. He has called for a crackdown on industrial scale distillation because he views it as a national security threat to the United States. Amodei argues that distillation is like counterfeiting because it allows China to build better models by undercutting original research. He claims this practice disincentivizes long term investment and research and development for the market leaders.

Anna Wong, the chief economist for Bloomberg, argues that Anthropic lacks durable pricing power and must rely on price cuts to drive volume. She suggests that the company operates as an oligopolist and that this market structure makes for a very tough business. Other critics point out that token usage shares have not increased despite the lower costs for customers. The company continues to face pressure from cheaper models and shifting consumption habits for routine tasks.

Articles.Title: AI Token Prices Are Tumbling. Is It a Red Flag for Anthropic Stock?

stories.Headline: Capgemini expects enterprises to adopt control planes to govern multi-agent AI systems in 2027
stories.Summary:
Capgemini published its outlook for 2027 on November 20, 2026, with Pascal Brier, its Chief Innovation Officer and a member of the Group Executive Committee, saying the main challenge for organizations will be how to scale AI autonomy without losing control. The firm expects AI to dominate corporate agendas next year, after being cited alongside cloud infrastructure and tech sovereignty as key topics for this year. Capgemini foresees the rise of multi-agent systems in which agents interact in ways nobody designed. Sudhir Pai, the firm's Deputy Group CTO, said every enterprise is building and deploying agents and can test single agent systems, but as the number of agents grows, systems were not designed to test and govern this.

Pai argued that the problem is less the drift in behaviour of each agent than ensuring the enterprise-wide deployment acts as expected, since every agent can be right while the system is wrong, with serious business consequences. He said future control will need to operate at three levels: a harness around each agent, a control plane for each agentic system, and an enterprise control plane across all of them. In 2027, Capgemini expects enterprise control planes to incorporate a register of every agent and agentic system, an identity and permissions for each one, monitoring of outcomes delivered and consumption, visibility into how agents interact, limits on what they can do together, and a way to stop them. The firm also expects a shift from AI explainability to containment, as some new models no longer show all their reasoning steps.

Mark Roberts, Head of AI Futures Lab, argued that agents can get past their environments not because they are rogue but because they are very clever in following rules, and that even if you can explain each component you still do not know how the overall system will behave. He said governance must move beyond micro-management of agents to control at the macro level, the way traffic systems work, and be lifted up the technology stack, with human oversight where it matters rather than in every loop. Muktadir Khan, Global Head of Cybersecurity Solutioning, warned that thinking must shift on how to respond, with AI-powered autonomous patching becoming more prevalent and continuous threat and exposure testing designed for each specific business context. Capgemini also flags how AI will influence processes, with Valérie Perhirin, Trusted Board Chairman and Advisor, saying agentic R&D moves from sequential to parallel processes and changes the economics of R&D, and Maxime Girardeau, VP AI Strategy and Transformation, expecting agents to confirm an order within a conversation and an AI assistant to decide which payment card is best for each transaction.

stories.Headline: Tesla renames AI Computer to Super Intelligence Computer in new software update
stories.Summary:
A hacker discovered that Tesla renamed its AI Computer to Super Intelligence Computer. This change appeared in software update 2026.44.1 on November 20, 2026. The hacker known as green found this transition in the backend code. This update also includes FSD v14.3 Lite for HW3 and FSD v14.3.13 for HW4. The release also features a new Charger Network View for users.

The update changes the kernel from v5.4.302 to v6.18.38 in the system. It renames the HW4 or AI4 computer to SI Computer in car properties. This shift follows US President Executive Order 14434 passed on September 29, 2026. Tesla previously renamed its social media AI accounts to SI before this update. The company will use SI nomenclature in official documentation and release notes.

The hacker green is responsible for finding these hidden changes in the code. He posted his findings on his X account on November 17, 2026. Green noted that the AI computer was upgraded to super intelligence in properties. He also identified minor adjustments and upcoming features within the firmware update. The hacker has posted these types of updates frequently in the past.

Tesla owners are affected by new notifications regarding charging price fluctuations during drives. Users of SpaceX AI bot Grok will see chat history sync across devices. This synchronization will work between a Tesla car, a phone, and a laptop. The update also impacts drivers using FSD v14.3 Lite and FSD v14.3.13. These users will experience the new backend terminology and system kernel changes.

Tesla previously released update 2026.38.6 on November 4, 2026, which added Latvian language support. Grok came out of beta during that specific software release for all users. Update 2026.38.5.11 was expanded on October 26, 2026, for HW3 and HW4 hardware. The company has been transitioning its terminology from artificial intelligence to super intelligence. This process began with social media accounts before moving into the car firmware.

Future updates will include the Chinese music streaming service known as Soda Music. Tesla is working on a new wake word for Grok or Tesla AI. Upcoming features include smart charging mode and improvements to battery preconditioning for cars. Navigation will soon offer an option to prefer major roads for the driver. The articles leave open when these specific features will be officially released.

stories.Headline: Bevado raises $10M seed round led by RET Ventures to scale AI agents for property management
stories.Summary:
Bevado, a New York-based AI platform that automates resident and prospect communication for property managers, has secured $10 million in seed funding led by RET Ventures, with participation from Pear VC. The company, formerly known as Frontdesk, builds a shared AI brain that connects data across existing systems to understand residents, prospects, properties and workflows. Its agents use that context to run entire multi-step processes across voice, text, email and chat, such as coordinating a repair when a resident reports a leak. In leasing, the agents call prospects before tours and follow up when interest stalls, and they are trained on more than 10,000 synthetic calls before deployment.

Founder and CEO Ruchir Baronia, a former Meta engineer who built an early voice AI agent at UC Berkeley, founded the company in March 2025. He said most AI tools lack the context to follow through and end up as glorified chatbots, whereas Bevado aims to strengthen resident relationships. Bevado supports customers with portfolios exceeding 30,000 units, and Zest Properties increased showings by more than 300% and saved over 40 hours a week. Christopher Yip, Partner at RET Ventures, said the platform remembers every interaction and knows how to act on it.

The funding will be used to scale the company's AI agents for property management, according to the announcement. The agents continue learning once live, building on the context from the shared AI brain that connects data across existing systems. Bevado's approach contrasts with tools Baronia described as lacking the context to follow through on multi-step processes. The round was announced on November 20, 2026, and the articles do not say what specific milestones the company plans to reach next.
