stories.Headline: Gemini 3.0 Pro matches expert algorithms on cancer symptom guidance but falls short on depression
stories.Summary:
A multicenter research team from the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Northeastern University, Elimu Informatics, Brigham and Women's Hospital, and the Medical University of South Carolina tested Google DeepMind's Gemini 3.0 Pro on two clinical informatics functions. The team evaluated the model's ability to interpret narrative and semi-structured updates in published clinical guidelines and incorporate them into existing symptom management algorithms. The team also assessed the model's ability to translate complex decision trees into patient-specific clinical recommendations for simulated patient vignettes. The study was published in Frontiers in Medicine and covered cancer-related fatigue, pain, and depression. The artificial intelligence system demonstrated high concordance with expert consensus standards and rule-based decision support logic.

The study evaluated decision support algorithms from the Sapphire Cancer Symptom Management system, known as CDS-Sx, which classify clinical knowledge across four operational layers. The original fatigue algorithm comprised 29 decision nodes and 19 unique clinical pathways. The depression algorithm spanned 42 decision nodes and 39 pathways. The pain algorithm encompassed 1,425 decision nodes and 3,194 separate pathways. The authors supplied Gemini 3.0 Pro with explicit Level 2 semi-structured decision trees alongside formal guideline documents.

Two-member expert review panels used an agile rapid qualitative analysis methodology combined with evidence mapping. The panels scored each proposed algorithmic update across four predefined rubric domains. Detection was scored on a zero-to-two scale, completeness on a zero-to-three scale, accuracy on a zero-to-three scale, and safety risk on a zero-to-two scale. Pre-specified acceptable study-level performance required a mean detection score of at least 1.5, mean completeness of at least 2.0, and mean accuracy of at least 2.0. At least 80 percent of items had to meet acceptable individual thresholds and at least 95 percent had to introduce no meaningful clinical risk.

For cancer-related fatigue, the model exceeded all pre-specified acceptability thresholds across 19 evaluated items. It recorded a mean detection score of 1.9, a mean completeness score of 2.8, a mean accuracy score of 2.8, and a safety score of 2.0, with 100 percent of items deemed free of clinical risk. The system elevated evidence-based non-pharmacologic interventions such as exercise, cognitive behavioral therapy, and mindfulness to first-line status while discouraging routine psychostimulant use. The model incorporated critical opioid safety measures, identified contraindications for meperidine, and highlighted pharmacokinetic drug-drug interactions between dexamethasone and opioids metabolized by CYP3A4. It confirmed transdermal buprenorphine as a valuable therapy in patients presenting with renal impairment.

For depression, mean detection reached 1.0, completeness averaged 1.6, and accuracy averaged 1.5, with only 57 percent of items meeting acceptable accuracy criteria. This decline was driven by the omission of non-pharmacologic integrative modalities from Society for Integrative Oncology companion guidelines, including music therapy, reflexology, relaxation techniques, Tai Chi, and Qi Gong. The model generated explicit agent-level suggestions, such as favoring specific selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors or avoiding paroxetine in patients taking tamoxifen due to CYP2D6 inhibition. Clinician judges noted that the suggestions were safe, clinically appropriate, and concordant with practice. The model maintained an uncompromised safety profile.

The first vignette described a 62-year-old man with stage IV small cell lung cancer, bone metastases, stage 3b chronic kidney disease, and severe persistent fatigue. The second vignette detailed a 55-year-old woman with metastatic colon cancer receiving FOLFIRI chemotherapy who presented with severe depression, moderate abdominal pain, and chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy. The third vignette involved a 55-year-old man with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer invading the brachial plexus who experienced severe mixed somatic and neuropathic pain despite escalating sustained-release and immediate-release morphine regimens. Across all three vignettes, the model registered overall F1-scores between 0.86 and 0.96 and a precision score of 1.00 in all three cases. For the fatigue vignette, the system achieved a recall between 0.86 and 0.92, reproducing 12 of 14 reference recommendations and omitting only late-line integrative therapies and short-course dexamethasone intended primarily for end-of-life care.

In the depression vignette, the model achieved a recall of 0.85 by reproducing 11 of 13 recommendations, correctly suggesting mental health referral, duloxetine initiation to address co-occurring neuropathy, physical therapy, and bowel prophylaxis, while omitting oral non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and naloxone co-prescription. In the pain vignette, the model produced an F1-score of 0.86 and a recall of 0.75, generating 9 of 12 reference recommendations. The system correctly guided opioid titration, recommended topical lidocaine patches for focal neuropathic burning, initiated gabapentin titration, incorporated cold and heat therapy, recommended bone-modifying agents, and added naloxone co-prescription and bowel prophylaxis. The three missing elements were scheduled acetaminophen, upward duloxetine titration, and future consideration of a tricyclic antidepressant if initial therapies failed. Qualitative analysis confirmed that discordance stemmed entirely from omission rather than commission.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Nvidia names Palantir a key AI partner on its November 2026 earnings call
stories.Summary:
During Nvidia's November 2026 earnings call, the company's management named Palantir Technologies as a key AI partner and cited Palantir's use of specialized open models on Nvidia's platform, according to the Foreign Policy Journal. The mention places Palantir inside the tooling layer that Nvidia wants customers building on top of its chips, rather than treating it as a downstream application buyer. Nvidia framed the partnership within its broader push for an open AI model ecosystem, a posture designed to attract software platforms that extend the utility of its GPU infrastructure. Palantir builds data analytics software serving government agencies, defense clients and commercial enterprises, and its core base includes security, defense and intelligence users running increasingly complex models at scale.

The endorsement connects Palantir's software directly to the GPU buildout fueling global AI infrastructure spending, and Nvidia's acknowledgment suggests those workloads are now considered production-grade deployments. The remarks arrive at a sensitive moment for Nvidia, which is navigating leadership changes that place additional scrutiny on which software and security partners it publicly prioritizes. On the Palantir side, the mention reinforces an existing investment thesis built around proprietary ontology technology, a claimed competitive moat and the broad rollout of its AIP platform across large organizations. Analysts tracking the company have set a fair value estimate of $222, and both stocks closed lower on the day, with PLTR falling 2.43% and NVDA dropping 2.06%.

Investors will now be watching whether the Nvidia relationship generates measurable commercial momentum to support that figure, with the clearest evidence expected from future disclosures around joint Nvidia-Palantir deployments. The article says particular attention will go to any named customer wins in U.S. government or commercial AI programs, and to whether Palantir reports rising AIP usage specifically tied to Nvidia-based computing environments in its updates running through 2027. Any quantified contribution that Palantir-driven workloads make to Nvidia's AI infrastructure demand figures would further validate the partnership's commercial weight beyond a single earnings call mention. The market, per the article, is reserving judgment until harder data on the collaboration emerges.

stories.Headline: Apple prepares to enter personal AI agents race without matching rivals' AI capital spending
stories.Summary:
Apple Inc., once again the world's most valuable company by market capitalization, is preparing to enter the race for personal AI agents, according to a Seeking Alpha article by JR Research published on November 21, 2026. The article says Apple is still trying to get its AI strategy in order, but that it does not need to invest aggressively in AI capital spending in order to win. It also says Apple's move takes the shine off the first-mover advantage that Meta Muse had held in that market. The piece was written by JR Research, an investing group leader who discloses a beneficial long position in Apple and Meta shares.

The article says Apple's iOS ecosystem supports native AI agents, controls external access to them, and captures subscription revenue without matching the aggressive AI capital spending of its rivals. It adds that the AI infrastructure trade could enter an imploding phase, which the author presents as a reason Apple's lighter spending approach could pay off. The article also notes that Apple's valuation is now almost hitting the 40 times forward earnings level, which the author describes as a very crowded trade at this point. The author calls Apple a firm favorite for a buy-and-hold strategy and says he will wait for another opportune moment to add to his position.

The article's author is responsible for the views, and his disclosure states that he holds a beneficial long position in Apple and Meta shares through stock ownership, options or other derivatives. He says he wrote the article himself and that it expresses his own opinions, and that he receives no compensation for it other than from Seeking Alpha. He also states he has no business relationship with any company whose stock is mentioned in the article. Seeking Alpha's own disclosure says past performance is no guarantee of future results and that no recommendation or advice is being given on whether an investment is suitable for any particular investor.

The article also carries a promotional note for the author's investing group, Ultimate Growth Investing, which is running a limited period Black Friday sale offering a 20 percent upfront discount. The author says he made numerous timely top and bottom calls over the years and that April 2026 proved to be another spectacular bottom, a call he describes as spot-on. He says his approach combines timely and sharp price action analysis with fundamentals as its foundation, and that he tends to avoid overhyped and overvalued stocks while capitalizing on battered stocks with significant upside recovery possibilities. stories.Headline: Deirdre Bosa says Microsoft can catch up in frontier AI through OpenAI model rights until 2030 and enterprise data reach
stories.Summary:
In a Yahoo Finance video published on November 20, 2026, host Ejaaz Ahamadeen spoke with Deirdre Bosa about whether Microsoft can build a viable frontier model. Ahamadeen noted that Mustafa Suleyman of Microsoft AI had appeared earlier that week and asked whether OpenAI and Anthropic had run away with the frontier. Bosa said Microsoft has been among the best investors in AI and holds the largest stake in OpenAI, which she put at around $136 billion. She added that Microsoft has not done as well when it comes to building its own models. Bosa gave several reasons why she still thinks Microsoft can catch up to the frontier.

She said Microsoft holds the proprietary intellectual property of OpenAI's models until roughly 2030, which lets it take the blueprint or model weights of OpenAI models and rewire them into its own. She also pointed to Microsoft's enterprise data reach, since most companies in the world use a Microsoft tool or product in some form. She said every frontier lab, including Anthropic and OpenAI, will work on its own chip to get the most intelligence per amount of compute and save money. Bosa described the formula as applying compute to an AI model to produce a more intelligent model, with a custom chip tuned to that model. She said OpenAI knows how its model is made and Anthropic knows the same for its own, which lets them produce the most intelligence per compute spent.

She was unsure whether Microsoft can pull off the same approach because it has not yet built a good model. Ahamadeen had asked whether it is too late for Microsoft, given that OpenAI and Anthropic hold back their best models for reasons such as alignment. The video did not say what Microsoft plans to do next or when it might release a frontier model. It also did not give a date for any Microsoft model or any statement from the company beyond Suleyman's earlier appearance. The article listed Anthropic as ANT and OpenAI as OPAI.PVT among the tickers shown with the video.

stories.Headline: Meta rejects plans to build AI that posts for deceased users
stories.Summary:
Meta announced on November 21, 2026, that it has no plans to build an AI that posts for dead users. The company was granted a patent for an SNS avatar that could simulate social media activity. This technology would use a language model trained on a user's past interactions to act on their behalf. Meta clarified that receiving a patent does not mean the company will implement the technology.

The patent, identified as US12513102B2, describes a system for users who are absent or deceased. Facebook and Instagram currently allow families to convert profiles into memorialised accounts that lock logins. TikTok and X allow families with death certificates to request full account removal. Facebook offers tools to hide memories by date range, while Instagram lets users filter names.

A Meta spokesperson stated the company has no plans to move forward with the posthumous AI example. Mark Zuckerberg said interacting with memories could be helpful for those who are grieving. The patent filing argued that a user's absence is more permanent and severe if they are deceased. These statements frame the technology as a potential fix for the loss of a user.

Minedco and Re;memory already sell conversational versions of remembrance using stored posts, photographs, and recordings. Minedco uses a patent-pending engine called Coop to power its Epitaph line of Conversational Memorials. Re;memory provides lifelike avatars based on voice and photos to help users find solace. These startups target mourners who want more than the static pages offered by larger platforms.

The articles explain that memorialised accounts preserve a snapshot and treat a person's voice as finished. This approach avoids the risks of voice cloning or putting words in a dead person's mouth. In contrast, generative AI tools simulate patterns from data but cannot know new thoughts. Meta's other AI experiments, like the Muse agent, have previously suffered from technical flaws.

The sources leave open whether users actually find closure through digital avatars or conversational memorials. There are no confirmed launch dates, consumer prices, or user counts for the Epitaph product line. It remains unconfirmed if any posthumous AI account system is currently available to the general public. The articles do not detail the processing times for account removal requests on TikTok or X.

Articles.Title: Meta Says 0 Plans for AI That Posts After You Die

stories.headline_source: Meta Says 0 Plans for AI That Posts After You Die

stories.Headline: Anthropic IPO and Coherent buyback refocus investors on Fabrinet's AI optics role
stories.Summary:
Fabrinet drew renewed investor interest in AI infrastructure after Coherent announced a US$2b share repurchase plan and Anthropic completed its IPO, Yahoo Finance reported on Saturday, November 21, 2026. The article, by Mitch Lawler and published at 2:11 AM CST, said the two events together refocused attention on suppliers tied to data center and telecommunications build outs. The piece said Fabrinet has been swept up in that enthusiasm, which highlights its role in optical packaging and manufacturing for high performance compute and networking. It said that role can become more central as customers scale out capacity. The article said it would look at how Fabrinet's investment narrative could be influenced by AI infrastructure enthusiasm sparked by Anthropic's IPO.

The article said Fabrinet has 5.8b of existing capacity and planned expansion toward 9.8b and beyond. It said the company has 800G hyperscaler transceiver programs in production and multiple merchant transceiver programs slated from late 2026. It cited analyst projections of US$10.1b in revenue and US$1.1b in earnings by 2029, based on assumed yearly top line growth of 25.3% and an earnings increase of about US$619.4m from current earnings of US$480.6m. It said the most optimistic analysts were already pencilling in about US$10.6b of revenue and US$995.4m of earnings by 2029, with a P/E of 37x. It said Fabrinet's fair value indicates a 98% potential upside to its current price, and that one estimate suggests as much as 181% upside.

The article said owning Fabrinet means believing high value optical packaging and AI focused data center work can keep filling the company's growing capacity while customer concentration and component availability stay manageable. It said the analyst consensus Narrative on Simply Wall St leans on continued AI related optics demand as a key driver. It said the recent AI infrastructure rally after Anthropic's IPO and Coherent's buyback lifts sentiment but does not change Fabrinet's core operational tasks. It said the main near term swing factor is whether Fabrinet can convert its capacity and planned expansion into steady AI and datacom volume without hitting supply bottlenecks in lasers, memory or ASICs. It said execution on concrete projects, and how consistently the firm ships despite component constraints, will likely matter more for the story than any single market rally.

The article said the biggest risk is still dependence on a small group of large customers like Cisco, NVIDIA, Nokia and Amazon, where any program shift or insourcing decision could quickly hit revenue and earnings. It said the renewed AI trade sparked by Anthropic's IPO feels most relevant among recent developments because it directly ties into the data center optics and DCI narrative. It said stronger interest in AI infrastructure stocks can keep attention on Fabrinet's role in high performance compute and networking hardware. It said the sentiment upswing sits alongside existing drivers such as the merchant transceiver programs, the capacity expansion and Fabrinet's push into higher value photonics packaging. It said one alternate view focuses on Fabrinet's potential earnings power rather than customer risk.

The article said the report includes a comprehensive fundamental analysis summarized in a single visual, the Snowflake. stories.Headline: Parents drive growth of screen-free AI hardware for children to balance learning and health
stories.Summary:
Parents recently created a new product category of screen-free AI hardware for children. This trend emerged over the last year to balance AI learning with screen avoidance. Companies launched AI voice printers, painting projectors, sticker machines, and 3D printing learning machines. These devices use voice input and physical output to engage children without screens. Parents are the primary payers for these tools to avoid childhood myopia.

Stickerbox sells coloring stickers for 129 US dollars in North America and sold out 13 times. Spin Master acquired Stickerbox in August for between 35 million and 50 million US dollars. Zhiti Technology created the Huahuabao voice printer and has equity penetration from Lenovo. Zhixiaobai sells an AI-native 3D printing learning machine for 999 yuan in China. myFirst received over 8 million US dollars in financing in March of this year.

The general manager of Zhixiaobai, Guo Dongxu, believes time is the biggest barrier. He stated that competition will shift toward software and content systems as hardware converges. The Taoli Editorial Committee noted that parents fear children falling behind in the AI era. They argued that physical objects provide a closed loop for every AI interaction. This approach turns AI into a creativity tool rather than an electronic pacifier.

Parents are affected by fears regarding vision, concentration, and sleep due to screen time. They worry that AI is rewriting the definition of almost all future occupations. Children are affected by the shift from passive consumption to active creation. The products target primary school students from grades 1 to 6. These users move from talking to machines to creating physical, collectible objects.

Educational consumption in China migrated from offline tutoring to online classes and learning tablets. Generative AI entered office software and search boxes before entering children's rooms. Traditional AI toys often lose novelty within two weeks because they lack physical output. Zhiti Technology previously provided intelligent terminals for 50,000 taxis across 100 Chinese cities. Gongfudou Technology served 100 million parents as a 2D printing software provider.

Companies will now focus on building long-term content relationships to avoid becoming obsolete. Zhixiaobai developed a 3+3 Learning and Creation Growth System for science and innovation. Future success depends on whether these tools grow from simple tools into full systems. The articles leave open whether children will continue using devices after novelty fades. It remains unclear if consumables and content can support a healthy repurchase model.

stories.Headline: OpenAI reports its internal agents independently complete 46% of research tasks
stories.Summary:
OpenAI released an internal Agent research report titled “Research acceleration: The jagged frontier” on 2026-11-20, as reported by 36Kr and written by QbitAI’s Wen Le. The report states that Agents within OpenAI can now independently complete 46% of research tasks that originally took humans 2 to 4 hours. In March this year that proportion was only 23%, and in just 7 months it has doubled. For tasks that originally required 4 to 8 hours, the independent completion rate of Agents rose from 13% to 35%. The median daily spending of researchers on Agents rose from 1,500 USD to 2,400 USD.

For the top 10% of heaviest users, single-day usage cost hit 23,000 USD, about 160,000 RMB, up from 11,000 USD. Each researcher can now drive an average of 5.7 Agent workdays per day, with 8 hours of cumulative Agent running time counting as one workday, 11 times the previous benchmark. More than two-thirds of researchers run at least 4 Agents simultaneously daily, and more than 10% of heavy users run at least 16 at once. The equivalent API value of Agents has reached twice the non-equity compensation of researchers, which does not include the large equity portion. Agents perform well on “communication” at 69% and “analysis” at 58%, but lag on “construction” at 43%.

Most respondents said they would give up 40% of their team’s headcount, or 30% of their computing resources, to regain access to the most cutting-edge Agents for the next 3 months. Researchers said the model usually cannot come up with well-defined problems it cannot solve at one time, and one said asking it to “do this task just like that other task” led to being tricked many times. Agents cannot come up with good problems on their own, cannot tell good code from bad, and cannot distinguish high-quality data from low-quality data, and must be watched like a supervisor or they churn out “AI slop.” Human researchers propose ideas, set directions, define problems, make key decisions and conduct final quality control, while Agents act as a superpowered “hand” and “eye.” One researcher said evaluating whether an open source project works well previously took no less than one or two weeks, but now takes one day at most a few days.

The success rate of monitoring training tasks is 79%, but the success rate of writing reasoning and service code is only 25%. When developing GPT-6.2 Astra, the pre-training team for the first time attributed the generation of a key idea to collaborative conversations with Codex, where a researcher proposed the idea and Codex put forward a key modification that made the whole solution work. In 2026 the number of lines of code produced by each active contributor has been increasing sharply compared to the period before 2025. The number of experiments run by each active experimenter has reached 1.68 times the 2025 benchmark.

Since August 2025, the frontier of OpenAI model capabilities, measured by OpenAI’s internal capability index (OECI), has increased by 16.4 points per year, exceeding the previous annual industry trend of 14 points. OpenAI’s report emphasizes that this AI-driven progress may not be linear, and it is necessary to be alert to sudden, leapfrog breakthroughs like those that recently occurred in the field of mathematics. Among all research directions, the field of safety has the largest increase in manpower input and the highest workload growth rate. A large number of researchers, whether newly recruited or transferred internally, are flocking to safety projects.

The report’s title refers to a jagged frontier, uneven across different scenarios. The original report is at https://openai.com/index/research-acceleration-jagged-frontier/. The article is from the WeChat official account “QbitAI,” written by Wen Le, and authorized for release by 36Kr. The article states that its views only represent the author, and the 36Kr platform only provides information storage space services.

36Kr Europe (eu.36kr.com) delivers global business and markets news, data, analysis and video, and lists business@36kr.com for media inquiries, interview requests, business collaboration and recruiting global ecological partners. The article lists Partner: startuprad.io and Friendly Links: ai.36kr.com. The report describes Agents as a top “execution co-pilot” but by no means a “chief scientist.” The article asks whether AI is really accelerating the birth of new AI and whether recursive self-improvement has actually happened.

stories.Headline: South Korea's top tax exam scorer admits using AI to cheat, casting doubt on CPA exam fairness
stories.Summary:
In South Korea, people who passed the certified public accountant exam are facing a tighter job market and new doubts about exam fairness, after the top scorer in this year's certified tax accountant exam admitted using generative artificial intelligence and electronic devices to cheat, The Korea Times reported on Nov. 20, 2026. The same person confessed to using those methods during the CPA exam, though he did not pass it, and he appeared before reporters at the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency. A candidate who spent at least three years preparing and missed the passing score by less than a point said it felt deeply unfair that people who played by the rules were paying the price. He added that if the top scorer had not admitted to cheating, candidates might never have realized they had been denied a fair shot.

Passing the CPA exam does not by itself qualify a candidate to practice, because under the Certified Public Accountant Act each passer must first complete a year of practical training at an approved institution such as an accounting firm, a public corporation or a private company. As of September, 723 passers had yet to register with a training institution, according to the Korean Accounting Association. The annual quota has already been lowered twice, from 1,250 in 2024 to 1,200 in 2025 and 1,150 in 2026, and expectations are growing that it will be cut by another 50 places next year. The Financial Services Commission is expected to set the minimum number of candidates that can be selected from next year's exam by the end of November.

The Financial Supervisory Service, which administers the CPA exam, said it would work with experts and relevant institutions to develop measures to prevent cheating using sophisticated electronic devices. In a study released Nov. 4, researchers at the Korean Accounting Association estimated that AI adoption could reduce accounting firms' demand for audit staff by about 10 percent over the next three to five years, with the decline reaching 12 to 16 percent thereafter, and they proposed reducing the annual quota by as many as 300 over the next two to three years. A 30-year-old accountant at a major entertainment company said she was glad to have found a job before AI took off, though she doubts demand for junior staff will hold up over time. The scandal has unsettled people still studying for the exams as well as those who have already passed, raising questions about whether the exam's safeguards are keeping pace with advanced technology.

Articles.Title: Aspiring accountants face tougher odds as AI reshapes hiring, shakes confidence in CPA exam

stories.headline_source: Aspiring accountants face tougher odds as AI reshapes hiring, shakes confidence in CPA exam

stories.Headline: Han Won-seok admits to using AI to cheat on a national exam as Seoul officials propose phasing out Suneung by 2040
stories.Summary:
Han Won-seok recently admitted to using a smartphone, a miniature camera, and generative artificial intelligence to achieve the highest score on a national tax accountant exam. This admission occurred as over half a million students prepared to take the College Scholastic Ability Test, known as Suneung, on Thursday, November 19, 2026. The scandal has sparked wider concerns about AI-assisted cheating on other high-stakes tests, including the Legal Education Eligibility Test and civil service exams. Government officials have launched a broad investigation into various national qualification exams held throughout the current year.

The ruling Democratic Party is now pursuing legislation that would impose a ten-year ban on any test-taker caught cheating with artificial intelligence. Meanwhile, the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education is pushing a December 2025 roadmap that suggests starting systemic changes in 2028. This specific plan proposes a shift toward essay-based assessments and the complete phaseout of the Suneung by the 2040 academic year. Such a transition would move the primary responsibility for assessing applicants away from a national exam and into the hands of individual universities.

Park Do-soon, the first director of the Korea Institute for Curriculum and Evaluation, stated that written exams only test about one-tenth of curricular goals. He argued that the current system is limited because it asks questions that artificial intelligence can easily answer. Similarly, Korea University professor Cho Byeok has called for the total abolition of the Suneung to reduce the knowledge burden on students. Cho predicted that the national education system will undergo major changes within the next five years.

The government has pledged zero tolerance for cheating, but critics argue that simply removing devices from rooms does not solve the underlying problem. The debate now focuses on whether traditional written exams can still accurately measure a student's actual abilities in an AI-driven world. While the Seoul education office has provided a concrete timetable for retirement, the national government has not yet adopted the proposal. Future efforts may focus on giving students more opportunities to demonstrate their reasoning through written work.

Articles.Title: Suneung was built for a world before AI

stories.headline_source: Suneung was built for a world before AI

stories.Headline: South Korea detects 111 exam cheating cases as AI fears grow
stories.Summary:
The 2027 College Scholastic Ability Test took place on Thursday, November 20, 2026, amid high anxiety over AI assisted cheating. Many students and experts now question if traditional safeguards can keep exams fair against advancing technology. The Education Ministry reported that 111 cheating cases involving smartphones and other electronic devices were detected. Some examinees attempted to cheat despite advance warnings from the Interior Ministry and the Education Ministry. These violations occurred at various testing sites, including a high school in Yeongtong District, Suwon, Gyeonggi.

The government sent three highest level emergency alert messages, including one announced in advance and two unannounced, to identify phones. These alerts sound even when devices are set to silent, and they helped uncover 54 of the cheating cases. Five cases involved the use of smart devices during the exam, while 52 others were detected through Wi-Fi signal detection. Examinees had to roll up sleeves to expose wrists and place stickers over clothing buttons, measures credited to Han Seong-sook. Proctors checked these analog measures during each session, and bags were placed in hallways to prevent the use of devices.

Vice Education Minister Choi Eun-ok briefed reporters on AI cheating cases at the Government Complex Sejong on November 19. Park Joo-ho, president of Daelim University College, stated that maintaining traditional assessment methods will only place a greater burden on examinees. He argued that the weight of the CSAT in university admissions must be reduced to ensure fairness. Park suggested that universities should evaluate applicants through a wider range of methods beyond written exams. He noted that while these changes are necessary, they would be difficult to implement for the 2028 CSAT.

Parents like 48 year old Jung Mi-seo, waiting at Duksung Girls' High School in Jongno District, Seoul, expressed deep anxiety. Jung noted her daughter wore contact lenses instead of glasses and wondered if this would be required for every exam. Seventeen year old Lee Si-yeon questioned the point of exams if people can get high scores by using AI. A 29 year old teacher surnamed Kim in Seocho District, Seoul, said students made cynical remarks about powerful AI tools. One test taker in Suwon described the exam room atmosphere as unsettling after a student was caught with a smartphone.

The tech industry doubts that current methods can catch AI cheaters as hidden devices become smarter. This year's CSAT followed a pattern of increasing concerns over whether some AI violations went undetected by proctors. The government used emergency alerts because some students failed to surrender their phones before the exam began. Traditional analog inspection methods are now being questioned for use in upcoming professional licensing exams. These events highlight a growing conflict between advancing technology and the premise that the entire testing process is fair.

The government will continue to monitor cheating as the nation considers whether traditional exam methods can still ensure fairness. Experts believe serious discussions must begin regarding the reform of assessment methods to combat technological advances. It remains open whether analog checks, like stickers on buttons, will be applied to other national examinations. The industry continues to doubt the effectiveness of current security measures against smarter hidden devices. It is unclear if the admissions system will be reformed in time for the 2028 CSAT.

stories.Headline: AI and social media tools enable bereaved people to preserve memories of the deceased
stories.Summary:
Modern technology and social media now allow bereaved people to preserve memories of the lost through digital legacies and AI recreations. These tools enable users to maintain connections with deceased loved ones using saved messages, voice notes, and photographs. This technological shift has occurred as digital remnants of human lives have become more prevalent across various online platforms. Experts are now examining whether these digital tools help the grieving process or hold people back from healing. The BBC reported on these developments on November 21, 2026, highlighting the complex nature of digital mourning.

Facebook and Instagram allow users to convert profiles into memorialised accounts where people can share tributes to the deceased. Families can request the removal of accounts on X and TikTok if they provide documentation such as a death certificate. Facebook offers options to hide memories of specific people or dates, while Instagram users can filter certain names or phrases. These features change how people say goodbye by keeping the likeness of the deceased permanently accessible in the digital world. The process involves managing digital content that remains visible to the original audience while preventing any new logins.

Karen Sutton, a widow coach based in Cheltenham, says digital reminders can be both a blessing and a curse for some. She warned that using AI to fabricate new memories could hinder the brain from learning that a person no longer exists. Sutton suggests that people should check in with themselves and delete voicemails or reminders if they cause too much pain. Professor Kate Woodthorpe from the University of Bath notes that younger generations may rely on digital legacies more than older people. Woodthorpe serves as the co-director for the research Centre of Death and Society at the University of Bath.

Kelsey Mulcahy, 33, found purpose by sharing her grief for fiancé Joseph Day, who died in 2022, with 45,000 TikTok followers. Natalie Krzak and Katie Burnham from Surrey met through the Widowed and Young website after losing husbands in December 2022. These women launched a podcast called Those Two Widows to share honest accounts of navigating grief during their 30s. They believe the digital space provides a vital platform to educate others and offer an outlet for similar stories. These individuals feel that online communities make the heavy burden of bereavement much easier to carry.

The articles explain that the process of grieving is unique to each person, meaning there is no universal formula for it. Digital remnants have increased because more people are living their lives online than ever before in human history. Some people view popping up photos or voice messages as signs, while others find such reminders to be total torment. The brain requires time and rewiring to accept a loss, which may be complicated by AI versions of people. This background shows a tension between the comfort of digital connection and the necessity of emotional detachment.

By the 2050s, people will have lived their entire lives online, leaving behind an enormous amount of digital content. This future suggests that the reliance on digital legacies will continue to grow as connectivity becomes more constant for all. The articles leave open the question of whether humans will ever truly have to say goodbye to the deceased. It remains unclear how AI recreations will specifically impact the long term psychological healing of the bereaved population. Future technological revolutions will likely further alter the way society handles death and the preservation of personal memories.

Articles.Title: AI and social media allows memories of the lost to be preserved

stories.headline_source: AI and social media allows memories of the lost to be preserved

stories.Headline: South Korea's personnel minister says AI will shift civil servants toward judgment and problem-solving work
stories.Summary:
South Korea's Minister of Personnel Management, Tschoe Dong-seok, said in an interview with The Korea Herald published on Nov. 19, 2026, that artificial intelligence will take over routine administrative tasks and that civil servants will increasingly be expected to exercise independent judgment, solve complex problems and engage with the public. He said the next 10 years will be a period of fundamental change in the roles of public officials and the way the civil service operates, driven by the rapid advancement of AI and other technologies. As AI takes over simple and repetitive tasks, he said, public officials will be able to concentrate more on roles that only humans can perform, such as policy judgment, solving complex problems and communicating with the public. Those changes have prompted the government to rethink how it recruits, trains and evaluates its workforce.

The Ministry of Personnel Management plans to expand the Public Service Aptitude Test, currently used for Grade 5 and Grade 7 recruitment, to Grade 9 examinations by 2029, and the new assessment is designed to evaluate logical reasoning, data analysis and decision-making abilities rather than primarily testing memorized knowledge. The government also plans to introduce the assessment to local government Grade 7 recruitment in 2027 and firefighter officer candidate examinations in 2028, while encouraging broader adoption across public institutions. The ministry is pursuing additional pay increases for junior officials in Grades 7 through 9 and discussing further improvements with fiscal authorities, aiming to bring starting salaries for Grade 9 officials to approximately 3 million won, including allowances, in 2027. For specialized AI and information technology positions, the government already offers special salary arrangements that allow compensation comparable to private-sector levels, and the ministry is expanding AI-related hiring to include computer systems development and data.

All civil servants are now required to complete at least two hours of AI training annually, supported by a government learning platform that integrates educational resources from public and private providers, and the ministry plans to expand practical training that enables officials to identify workplace problems and develop solutions using AI, alongside specialized programs for managers responsible for leading organizational transformation. Tschoe said attracting young talent would also require improvements in compensation, and he emphasized that adapting to technological change would require more than simply introducing new tools. He said government workplace culture must also move away from hierarchical management toward greater autonomy, professionalism and collaboration. The ministry introduced a continuous performance management system across government ministries in October, allowing supervisors and employees to regularly review work progress and document individual contributions, and Tschoe said the changes would improve evaluation transparency and ensure civil servants in demanding fields, including disaster response and public safety, receive greater recognition for their contributions.

He said the ultimate goal of reforming how the civil service works is not simply to improve efficiency but to enable public officials to focus on policy judgment and problem-solving for citizens and provide better public services. Tschoe's remarks came as Korea hosted the fourth annual meeting of the Asia Public Service Network in Seoul on Wednesday, bringing together representatives from 14 countries and the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development to discuss the future of public administration. The conference was held under the theme "Leadership for Transformation" and focused on organizational reform, performance management and building a workforce capable of adapting to emerging technologies. Among the findings scheduled to be shared at the conference were those of a joint study South Korea and the OECD conducted from 2025 to 2026 on how participating countries use digital technologies to recruit civil servants, and further joint research and exchanges are planned.

Articles.Title: AI will put premium on human judgment in Korea’s civil service: personnel minister

stories.headline_source: AI will put premium on human judgment in Korea’s civil service: personnel minister

stories.Headline: US outages linked to software fixes, not AI cyberattack
stories.Summary:
A wave of service disruptions across the United States last week affected JPMorgan Chase, United Airlines and Microsoft Outlook, leaving customers unable to access banking services, board flights or open email. Experts speaking to Axios dismissed fears of an AI-driven cyberattack and attributed the incidents to software fixes and technical failures. JPMorgan Chase customers faced banking service issues caused by an internal software bug, which delayed transactions involving other banks. United Airlines briefly grounded flights, citing a technology problem, and this followed a nationwide ground stop by the US Federal Aviation Administration days earlier, caused by network traffic overwhelming older equipment. Microsoft Outlook and other Microsoft 365 services experienced downtime due to a months-old bug, coupled with increased traffic and reduced server capacity.

US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin suggested that AI systems for writing and modifying code could play a part in the disruptions. National security officials and Wall Street executives have informed lawmakers that these outages are linked to efforts to fix software flaws discovered by AI tools, according to The Washington Sun. Experts note that the accelerated pace of coding and review, driven by AI tools to identify vulnerabilities, can itself lead to downtime. David Woods, professor emeritus of integrated systems engineering at Ohio State University, said safeguards are being reduced in the pursuit of speed, and that cross checks, tests, stress tests and safeguards are being cut out.

Security technologist Bruce Schneier attributed the public's panic to human pattern recognition, interpreting coincidences as conspiracies. Liz Fong-Jones, technical fellow at Honeycomb, emphasised that these outages are a decades-old phenomenon of cascading failures, unrelated to AI-driven code writing or shipping. Ookla analyst Luke Kehoe reported nearly 6 million US problem reports on Downdetector in the week ending November 16, marking the highest weekly total in a year. Experts found no evidence of an AI-driven cyberattack, despite social media speculation, and described the incidents as largely unrelated technical failures that occurred close together.

Articles.Title: US outages linked to software fixes, not AI cyberattack

stories.Headline: Korea Consumer Agency finds over half of surveyed Koreans who changed medication on AI advice suffered side effects
stories.Summary:
The Korea Consumer Agency released a survey on Thursday, November 19, 2026, showing that many Koreans suffered health problems after following medical advice from generative AI chatbots. Out of 500 adults who used AI for medicine or supplements in the past year, 110 people changed or stopped their medication without professional help. More than half of those individuals, specifically 56 people, experienced negative health consequences including worsened conditions or adverse reactions. Other findings showed that 133 respondents skipped or delayed hospital visits because they trusted the information provided by the AI services.

The survey revealed that 27.3 percent of affected users had mild reactions like indigestion, while 19.1 percent suffered treatment setbacks and 14.5 percent required additional medical care. AI tools were used most often for over the counter drugs at 76.2 percent, health supplements at 63.8 percent, and prescription drugs at 15.6 percent. Testing of ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and Perplexity showed that some provided medicine advice without checking age or existing health conditions. Furthermore, ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Claude directed users to proxy purchase websites for drugs that are banned from online sales.

The Korea Consumer Agency urged AI companies to block illegal drug sites and make their medical warnings more prominent for users. OpenAI and Anthropic stated they would consider improving their warnings and information filtering, while Google said it would maintain its current system. Perplexity did not provide a response to the agency's recommendations regarding these safety concerns. The agency also warned consumers to use AI only for reference and to always consult a pharmacist or doctor before altering any medication.

stories.Headline: Sitespace co-CEO Lee Ju-yeon demonstrates smart glasses at Seoul education office training for CSAT staff
stories.Summary:
Lee Ju-yeon, co-CEO of the nonprofit startup Sitespace, is the woman shown wearing black smart glasses and looking at a test paper in recent articles about exam cheating using artificial intelligence glasses. The photo was taken on the 11th at the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education in Yongsan-gu, Seoul, during a training session for dedicated smart-glasses headquarters staff for the College Scholastic Ability Test. Sitespace had first contacted the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education to propose introducing the functions of smart glasses, which led to the event. At the training, they demonstrated functions such as taking photos with smart glasses, solving test questions, and communicating with a smartphone. Reporters flocked in to film the demonstration, and photos of Lee appeared in multiple outlets after suspicions emerged on the 12th about cheating with smart glasses by the top scorer in the tax accountant exam.

The session taught staff assigned to test sites in Seoul about the features of smart glasses and how to identify them. Co-CEO Jeong Jin-seorang said they first went to show the actual glasses to supervisors at the education office, and after they asked that teachers also be allowed to handle them directly, it turned into a training session. The other woman photographed with Lee was a practicum guide hired short-term for the day's training. Sitespace assisted with smart-glasses identification at test sites on the 19th, the day of the CSAT, identifying models by checking photos sent by the education authorities when a device suspected of being smart glasses was found. A smart-glasses identification aid app developed by Sitespace, which detects nearby Bluetooth and Wi-Fi signals and helps determine whether glasses are AI-enabled based on photos taken from multiple angles, was also used by CSAT proctors.

Lee said in a phone call with Kyunghyang Shinmun on the 19th that AI glasses can be used for public-interest purposes as well, but it seemed like public opinion was becoming too negative. She said they told the education office they wished to explain the functions of the glasses free of charge for the public good. Lee said she was there for work, so she wore comfortable clothes with no makeup, and she did not expect reporters to come. She said that because the proctor teachers have portrait rights issues, she told them it would be better to photograph us doing the demonstration instead. Lee said that at first she was flustered, but now she thinks she has come to enjoy it a bit, and that she is glad many people have learned that there are AI-glasses services like ours engaged in public-interest work.

Jeong recalled that she finished a lecture for teachers in the basement auditorium and came upstairs, and Lee was surrounded by cameras firing flashes like a movie scene. They said they had attended without knowing the event would be open to the press. After the articles ran, people with visual impairments and related institutions reportedly inquired about trying out the app. Jeong said they received many identification requests, but most turned out to be ordinary glasses.

According to the Ministry of Education, one case of cheating using smart glasses during the exam was uncovered that day at a CSAT test site in South Chungcheong Province. Sitespace launched after winning the top prize in April at the startup competition of Hongik University, the alma mater of the two co-founders. Jeong said they at first envisioned a docent service in museums based on smart glasses, but after meeting many people with visual impairments, they realized what was truly needed was technology that helps with mobility. Sitespace is developing an app that uses the cameras and speakers of commercially available smart glasses to provide audio guidance about the surrounding environment, recognizing objects in the user's line of sight with the camera and conveying them through sound.

Instead of long sentences, it is designed to deliver only the necessary information quickly and concisely, such as sliding door, automatic door, and half open. They are currently improving functions through pilot use. After CES 2027 in Las Vegas, USA, next January, they plan to officially release the app on the Apple App Store and Google Play Store. Lee said that AI glasses and ultra-miniature cameras are being used in negative ways, but technology continues to advance.

She said they want to let people know that there are organizations that use technology for the public good. The articles do not say what became of the cheating case uncovered in South Chungcheong Province. The articles do not say how the identification requests were resolved beyond most turning out to be ordinary glasses. The articles do not give the outcome of the tax accountant exam cheating suspicions.

stories.Headline: JohnAIC raises $1.9 million to expand on-premise AI server production
stories.Summary:
Bengaluru-based JohnAIC, a startup building on-premise AI servers for enterprises and government bodies, raised $1.9 million in a pre-seed funding round led by Crane Venture Partners, with Neon Fund also participating, according to a TechGig report published on November 19, 2026. The company said it will use the capital to expand its manufacturing, configuration and supply capabilities for AI servers. JohnAIC aims to reach a production capacity of up to 100 AI servers per month. The startup is investing in factory and supply chain infrastructure to serve Indian organisations building private AI environments and neoclouds.

JohnAIC, founded by Sasank Chilamkurthy, sells integrated systems that combine high-performance GPU servers, inference software, optimised open-source models and local data management. The systems let enterprises run AI within their own environment without separately assembling servers, models, deployment tools and security controls. JohnAIC's customers include public sector organisations, large enterprises, banks, healthcare companies and public sector undertakings. For banking, financial services and insurance institutions, the company said its systems support Digital Personal Data Protection and Reserve Bank of India requirements, keeping sensitive financial data inside the organisation's own environment. The startup is also collaborating with Andhra Pradesh Eastern Power Distribution Company Limited, where its server is embedded in the utility's operational survey processes to convert field data into real-time insights.

Chilamkurthy said Indian enterprises need AI infrastructure they can fully own, operate and trust, and that the mission is to make on-premise AI adoption as seamless as cloud solutions, with compute, models and data staying under customer control. Anandamoy Roychowdhary, managing director for India and APAC at Crane Venture Partners, noted the company's goal of maximising the AI tokens customers generate per rupee spent. Siddhartha Ahluwalia, co-founder and managing partner at Neon Fund, highlighted Chilamkurthy's background as a co-author of PyTorch and his leadership in AI deployments at Qure.ai. The company positions its product as enterprise-hardened servers running voice AI and predictive models behind the customer's firewall, pre-configured with open-source tooling to help avoid recurring cloud costs and dependence on a single vendor.

stories.Headline: London builds an AI safety hub as government funds model testing
stories.Summary:
London has established itself as a global center for artificial intelligence safety. A growing ecosystem of researchers, policymakers, and campaigners now works in the capital. These groups focus on ensuring powerful models benefit society rather than cause harm. This effort has intensified as warnings over the potential dangers of technology ramp up. The city is increasingly described as the leading AI hub for Europe.

The government announced hundreds of millions of pounds for AI safety and security. This includes 120 million pounds for the AI Security Institute to test advanced systems. The London Initiative for Safe AI will relocate to a headquarters in King's Cross. Basecamp Research operates from a former watch factory in Farringdon to fight pathogens. The London AI Hub estimates that 50 organizations in the capital focus on safety.

The AI Security Institute assesses leading models for risks like cyber misuse before release. Apollo Research examines if AI models might lie or cheat against human interests. Oliver Vince says London is a key player due to its culture and expertise. Rupert Elston says the city acts as a referee in the global AI game. Lord Khan says London has the talent to lead in using AI responsibly.

Professor Hannah Fry believes London focuses on ethical technology for good rather than hyper-capitalism. Gina Neff says researchers struggle to access cutting-edge models before their public release. Imperial College president Hugh Brady warns AI could be used to design harmful substances. Joseph Miller runs Pause AI UK to stop the development of frontier AI models. The London AI and Jobs Taskforce helps workers prepare for changes in employment.

London is home to Google DeepMind and a major base for the company Anthropic. The city has historical links to effective altruism and possesses leading university communities. Imperial College has over 750 people working on large language models or their applications. A Greater London Authority report warns that energy is a critical constraint for growth. The Telehouse data centre in Canary Wharf uses a closed loop water system.

The government will launch an AI Biosecurity Lab to protect against future pandemics. Basecamp Research will work with OpenAI and Anthropic to develop vaccines and antibiotics. Pause AI UK plans a demonstration for Saturday to call for a development halt. The articles leave open whether these local efforts will make a global difference. They do not state when the new biosecurity lab will officially open.

stories.Headline: OpenAI demos the Codex Security Plugin workflow in a published recording
stories.Summary:
OpenAI published a page on 19 November 2026 titled Explore the Codex Security Plugin, which presents a product demo of the Codex Security Plugin and shows the workflow in action from getting started to reviewing the results shown in the recording. The page appears on OpenAI's own site under its product and resources sections, and it carries a share link that opens in a new window. The page also lists links to Security and Privacy, Trust and Transparency, ChatGPT, ChatGPT Business, ChatGPT Enterprise, ChatGPT for Education, Codex, Dots, Release Notes and the API platform. Beyond the demo and the navigation links, the page gives no further detail on what the plugin does or how it works.

The page offers no release date for the plugin itself, no version number, no pricing and no statement of which plans or products the plugin works with. It names Codex and Dots among the linked products but does not say whether the plugin is available now or only shown in the recording. The only date the page gives is the 2026 copyright line covering 2015 to 2026, and the only action it describes is watching the demo and reviewing the results shown in it. No requirements, changes or availability details appear in the text.

The page names no person, no team and no executive, and it contains no statement from anyone at OpenAI about the plugin. The only voice on the page is the site's own description of the demo, which invites readers to watch the workflow from getting started to reviewing the results shown in the recording. Responsibility for the plugin therefore rests with OpenAI as the publisher of the page, and the page itself makes no claim beyond that. Nothing in the text says who built the plugin or who oversees it.

The context the page gives is limited to its placement among OpenAI's security and privacy materials and its product links, which sit alongside the company's terms, privacy policy and other policies. The page ends with the OpenAI copyright notice for 2015 to 2026 and a privacy choices link, and it offers no roadmap, no follow-up date and no next step beyond watching the recording. Because the articles carry too little for a longer account, this is a breaking story. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Singapore stages first large-scale AI cyberattack and defence exercise with 250 participants
stories.Summary:
The Singapore government conducted its first large-scale artificial intelligence attack and defence battle on Thursday, November 19, 2026. This event was part of the fifth Critical Infrastructure Defence Exercise, which ran from Tuesday to Friday at the Punggol campus of the Singapore Institute of Technology. The exercise simulated coordinated swarms of AI agents attempting to disrupt various sectors at rapid speeds to test modern security. More than 250 participants from 46 different organisations took part in the four-day event to address evolving cyber threats.

The exercise expanded to eight testbeds by adding aviation and healthcare sectors to the existing six covering water, energy, maritime, telecommunications, land transport, and multi-cloud environments. A red team including personnel from the Land Transport Authority, Government Technology Agency, Infocomm Media Development Authority, Defence Science and Technology Agency, Cyber Security Agency of Singapore, and Digital and Intelligence Service launched the attacks. For the first time, a blue team of AI agents developed by the Cyber Defence Test and Experimentation Centre attempted to detect and contain threats. These AI tools completed investigation reports in under 10 minutes, a process that typically takes human personnel several hours.

Military Expert 6 Sim Swee Horng, the director of the Cyber Defence Test and Experimentation Centre, stated that defenders must harness AI to match the capabilities of attackers. She explained that the goal was to identify the strengths, weaknesses, and limits of AI tools when they work alongside human judgement. Brigadier General Clarence Cai, the Defence Cyber Chief, noted that defensive capabilities must keep pace because AI allows for faster attacks on a larger scale. He affirmed that the Singapore Armed Forces will continue collaborating with industry partners and agencies to develop these essential cyber defence capabilities.

This year's event also integrated operationally ready national servicemen from the Digital and Intelligence Service to lead blue teams across various sectors. These participants practiced responding to attacks on both information technology systems and industrial control systems that manage physical facilities. By simulating these environments, the government can test responses without affecting actual public services. The exercise concluded with visits from Minister of State for Defence Desmond Choo and Senior Minister of State Tan Kiat How.

stories.Headline: Scale AI recruits experts to turn professional work into low paid gig tasks
stories.Summary:
Scale AI and its recruiting platform Outlier are transforming professional roles into low paid gig work by hiring experts to improve artificial intelligence. The company recruits physicians, lawyers, and Ph.D.s to design complex scenarios, rank model outputs, and verify data generated by AI. This process has expanded globally, with the company previously using its Remotasks platform to hire workers in Venezuela, Kenya, Nigeria, and Pakistan. Many of these workers experienced a pattern where initial pay was high to build a workforce before rates were cut.

The platform offers up to 180 dollars an hour for United States cardiologists, but pays only 12.50 dollars for Swahili work in Tanzania and 7.50 dollars for Tagalog work in the Philippines. In Venezuela, some workers earned as little as 2 dollars on their first day, while a family once made 20 dollars in one day during December 2020. Remotasks ended its hourly program in Venezuela in 2021 and later discontinued operations in Kenya, Nigeria, and Pakistan in March 2024. Terms of service allow the company to deactivate accounts without notice or withhold accrued payments based on its own determinations.

Scale AI attributed the closure of several international operations to enhanced security protocols, though it later admitted that Kenyan workers missed notices due to operational errors. Representatives from AI companies and outsourcing firms have agreed that pay should be better, but they often distance themselves from direct employment of these workers. Scale AI has denied wrongdoing regarding a proposed settlement in San Francisco, while a separate class action suit alleges that Mercor misclassified over 30,000 professionals. Mercor has provided services for companies including Meta, Anthropic, and OpenAI, though those firms are not defendants in the case.

This system of extractivism takes value from people in unstable economies to benefit buyers who set all the terms. Workers often have no say over sudden rate changes or the disappearance of tasks, leaving those with few options trapped in precarious employment. In March 2023, a Kenyan judge temporarily stopped Meta and contractor Majorel from dismissing 260 content moderators, but Meta subsequently moved that work to West Africa. The trend suggests that professional work will continue to shift toward these platforms wherever the next available worker logs on.

stories.Headline: Meta FAIR develops self-improving memory method to boost AI agent performance on continual learning tasks
stories.Summary:
Meta FAIR introduced a method called Self-Improving Memory on November 19, 2026, to help AI agents manage their own memory. This two-stage process allows an agent to discover its own memory instructions and then train those skills directly into its weights. Researchers from the University of Washington and Johns Hopkins University co-authored the work. The system uses a Kimi-K2.6 model, which is a 1T-parameter MoE with 32B active parameters and 256K context.

The method requires a persistent memory directory that the agent edits using file tools while working through subtasks. It utilizes two specific prompts, LOAD and OFFLOAD, to retrieve and update notes between these tasks. The system achieved an average score of 56.0 across three Continual Learning Bench tasks, surpassing the 44.6 score of the best human-written prompts. The Codebase task saw the highest performance at 64.3, which was 20.6 points higher than the best hand-written harness.

The research team explained that a meta agent rewrites the memory prompts based on trajectories and scores. They used a Discover-Demonstrate-Distill pipeline to move these gains into the model weights via a LoRA adapter with rank 64. This distillation process resulted in a 5.5-point gain over standard fine-tuning on generic trajectories. The team noted that the model is essentially trained on memory skills it discovered for itself.

The tests focused on Database, Codebase, and Spectrum tasks to measure how well the model generalizes to new instances. While the search for better prompts was noisy, the Codebase task continued to improve through the fourth generation. The distilled model eventually averaged 43.1 across ten matched seeds while using generic prompts. This demonstrates that the model can maintain high performance without needing the optimized instructions.

stories.Headline: Federal Circuit ruling shows AI patent applicants how concrete claim language shapes eligibility, Phelan says
stories.Summary:
The Federal Circuit recently decided Ceiva Opco, LLC v. Amazon.com, Inc., a patent case about digital picture frames that the court used to show how concrete claim language can change the outcome of a patent-eligibility analysis. The court reversed an ineligibility ruling for one digital picture frame claim while it affirmed that same ruling for representative claims of three related patents. The claim that survived specified the interactions among a physically separable user interface, a server, and a digital frame, and the court found that this combination addressed technological limitations of earlier devices. By contrast, the related claims broadly described desired functions without sufficiently specifying how those results were actually achieved.

Although Ceiva did not involve artificial intelligence, the decision offers a practical lesson for AI patent applicants, according to Marshall, Gerstein & Borun LLP partner Ryan Phelan, who analyzed the ruling in a contribution to IPO Daily News. Phelan wrote that applicants should identify the technical improvement, connect it to shortcomings in existing technology, and claim the features and relationships that produce that improvement. He made the point that concrete claim language can make a meaningful difference in the patent-eligibility analysis. Phelan is a regular contributor to the newsletter's AI Insights column, where he analyzes court decisions, regulatory developments, and other issues affecting patents and emerging technologies, and he also authors the firm's PatentNext blog on artificial intelligence and other next-generation technologies.

The article was published by Legal 500 on 20 November 2026 and carries the headline about the claim-drafting lesson for AI patents. It presents the Ceiva decision as an illustration for applicants rather than as a change in the law, and it does not say what happens next in the case or whether any further review is expected. The piece states that its content is intended as a general guide to the subject matter and that specialist advice should be sought about specific circumstances. Members can read Phelan's latest AI Insights article on the IPO website, according to the article.

stories.Headline: Perplexity releases Orchestrator API to route developer requests across multiple AI models
stories.Summary:
Perplexity launched the Perplexity Orchestrator API on November 19, 2026, to provide a single endpoint for various frontier and open-weight models. This hosted inference gateway allows developers to access models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and xAI, as well as open-weight options like DeepSeek, Kimi, and GLM. The system manages model routing by selecting providers based on their current capacity, availability, and latency. By using one base URL and one account for billing, developers can reduce the number of necessary integrations and receive a single invoice.

The service requires users to point their SDKs to specific URLs, such as the OpenAI base URL at https://api.perplexity.ai/orchestrator/v1. It supports OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses, and Anthropic Messages requests, often requiring only a change to the API key and base URL. Failover mechanisms automatically swap deployments if provider errors, timeouts, or rate limits occur, such as moving a failed Claude request from Anthropic to AWS Bedrock. The system also offers a preview for automatic routing via the perplexity/auto setting, which uses a decision model to direct traffic among one to five routes or a default model.

Perplexity stated that there is no additional platform fee beyond the credits used for the answering model's published per-token rate. They noted that production traffic measured between October 4 and November 2, 2026, showed higher success rates and less variance during incidents than requests to single providers. The company explained that requests failing before producing output are not billed, and usage can be funded through prepaid credits or the AWS Marketplace. They also detailed a tiered access system where Tier 0 includes Google and xAI, Tier 1 requires 50 dollars for OpenAI, and Tier 2 requires 250 dollars for Fable and Opus models.

The company tested automatic routing on a 63-task subset of Terminal-Bench 4.1 using Claude Code to bypass certain safeguards. They found that routing to GPT-6.1 Sol or GPT-6 Astra increased successful task completion by three tasks in areas like biology and security. Current default policies send traffic to GPT-6.1 Sol, while simpler requests are routed to GPT-6 Luna. Perplexity continues to develop speed-aware routing to further optimize the performance of the gateway.

stories.Headline: Education minister Choi Kyo-jin admits he cannot detect AI cheating as 550,000 students sit a chaotic exam
stories.Summary:
The 2027 College Scholastic Ability Test took place on Thursday amid a controversy over cheating using artificial intelligence. This exam was conducted at 1,312 testing centers nationwide during a period of unprecedented confusion and anxiety. The government failed to prepare and respond adequately to repeated warnings about AI assisted cheating before the test. Some 550,000 applicants took the exam while emergency disaster alerts sounded three times throughout the day. Administrative incompetence and irresponsibility turned this crucial national examination into a crisis and a textbook government failure.

The government required students to cover buttons with stickers and place their bags in hallways to prevent cheating. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook was reportedly behind these specific measures to combat the fears surrounding artificial intelligence. Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin attended a government ruling party meeting at the National Assembly on November 18. He appeared before the National Assembly Education Committee on Monday to discuss the measures against AI assisted cheating. These hastily devised and outdated countermeasures only deepened the confusion for the students and the exam supervisors.

Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin bears particular responsibility for the lack of preparation and crisis management expertise during the exam. Choi is a former middle school Korean language teacher and a regional leader of the Korean Teachers Union. He also served as a three term superintendent of education in South Chungcheong before becoming the minister. When asked if he could detect AI cheating, Choi replied that he could not, perhaps because of his age. This response provoked public outrage and highlighted the failure of the ministry to handle the technological risks.

Many students were likely unsettled by the unprecedented disruptions and the loud noise of the emergency disaster alerts. The tech industry expressed doubts about whether the government can actually catch those who cheated using artificial intelligence. Parents opened up about their frustration over the cheating fears and the chaotic environment of the testing day. The entire examination administration system has now been exposed to international ridicule due to the government's negligence. Students who spent years preparing for the test deserved a fair and orderly environment instead of this uncertainty.

The Anti Corruption and Civil Rights Commission had received 44 petitions calling for measures against AI assisted cheating. AI cheating had already surfaced in a national examination in May and a university essay examination last month. The CSAT was introduced more than three decades ago, but it has never been this chaotic before. Generative AI became widely available recently, which increased the risks of cheating in various high stakes national tests. These repeated failures raise questions about whether education officials understood the risks posed by rapidly advancing technology.

Authorities must now work with investigators and telecommunications companies to determine if AI assisted cheating occurred during the exam. They should also examine how extensively AI was used for cheating in previous CSAT examinations since generative AI appeared. The government must identify the officials responsible for failures in preparation, oversight, and the emergency communication system. The articles leave open whether Minister Choi will resign or if the administration will implement a fundamental overhaul. Systematic planning and effective coordination among agencies are required to prevent future cheating and restore public confidence.
