stories.Headline: Korea plans unannounced disaster alerts during exam to catch AI cheaters
stories.Summary:
The government is considering sending unannounced disaster alert messages during this week's annual college entrance exam to catch cheaters using their phones and prevent cheating assisted by artificial intelligence, an interior ministry official said Wednesday. Authorities have been mulling measures to root out cheating during the College Scholastic Ability Test on Thursday following a recent cheating scandal in the certified tax accountant exam using AI. As part of anti-cheating measures unveiled Tuesday, the government said it would send an emergency alert message before the start of the exam to detect any unsubmitted devices. The official said the government is considering sending alerts unannounced in addition to the planned alert scheduled to be sent between 8:25 and 8:30 a.m. President Lee Jae Myung said Tuesday he had instructed authorities to review sending additional alerts, even during testing, to catch cheaters.

The government will send another disaster alert at an unspecified time during this week's annual college entrance exam, the interior ministry said Wednesday. While the first alert will be sent at 8:30 a.m., just before the start of the test, the ministry plans to send another message at an undisclosed time to find any test takers with unsubmitted phones. The ministry said the alerts will ring for 10.5 seconds at full volume, urging the public not to be alarmed. The education ministry notified schools nationwide Wednesday that it will allow test takers to only bring in pencils inside CSAT exam rooms, revising its list of permitted items. Authorities earlier notified test takers that they were allowed to bring black marker pens, correction tape, erasers, pencils and mechanical pencil lead for the exam, and under the revised rules, stationery items except for pencils will be provided at the test sites.

President Lee Jae Myung called on officials Tuesday to thoroughly prepare anti-cheating measures for the nationwide college entrance exam set to take place this week, describing cheating as a grave crime that undermines social trust. Lee made the remarks during an emergency meeting to inspect the country's readiness for the CSAT, also known in Korean as Suneung, scheduled for Thursday, following widespread concerns over cheating using AI. Lee said the Suneung is a symbol of fairness and a ladder of opportunity in our society during a video meeting held from Manila, as he wrapped up his visit to the city for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit. Lee added that officials must take strict action against those who engage in misconduct, adhering to a zero-tolerance policy, while asking them to come up with response measures against AI-assisted cheating. In a subsequent social media post, Lee said the government plans to offer a reward of over 100 million won, or US$74,805, per case to those who report instances of cheating involving advanced gadgets, should the case be confirmed.

Anti-cheating measures announced earlier Tuesday include physically checking all glasses worn by test takers, covering buttons on their clothes with stickers and blocking Wi-Fi networks inside and near the test sites. The government also warned that test takers caught cheating will be banned from the CSAT for the next 10 years, while facing criminal punishment. The move appears to reflect concerns of misconduct involving miniature cameras hidden inside personal items brought by test takers. South Korea has recently been rocked by the recent confession of the top scorer on this year's certified tax accountant exam that he had cheated with the help of AI and digital devices.

The incident has deepened worries of such cheating on the upcoming CSAT, widely seen as a major life event in South Korea, where the university one goes to can heavily influence career prospects. The anti-cheating measures were unveiled Tuesday, and the education ministry notified schools nationwide Wednesday of the revised permitted items list. The first alert will be sent at 8:30 a.m. just before the start of the test, while the planned alert was scheduled to be sent between 8:25 and 8:30 a.m.

The interior ministry official said that if the time is known, there would effectively be no point in additional alerts. The CSAT, also known in Korean as Suneung, is scheduled for Thursday. The ministry said the alerts will ring for 10.5 seconds at full volume, urging the public not to be alarmed. stories.Headline: Police in Seoul continue investigating alleged AI cheating by perfect LEET scorer Lee Jin-woo after his death
stories.Summary:
Lee Jin-woo was found dead in Seoul on Thursday, November 19, 2026. He was the first person to earn a perfect score on the Legal Education Eligibility Test. Police and fire authorities found the 32 year old man in Gangdong District. He died before a planned livestream to dispel allegations of AI assisted cheating. A short note was found, but it did not address the cheating claims.

The IDA admissions research institute planned a verification event at a Gangnam District studio. It required metal detectors and ear endoscopy checks to rule out any hidden devices. Lee would solve the Korean language section of the current College Scholastic Ability Test. The event would be livestreamed on YouTube and include a session with a language instructor. Lee had previously entered Korea University in 2024 and Seoul National University in 2026.

Police said they will continue the investigation to establish the substantive truth of the case. They assigned the matter to the financial crimes investigation team of the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency. Lawyer Park Eun-sun of 2yoo law firm said it is important to uncover cheating methods. Lawyer Kwak Joon-ho of Law Firm Chung said investigations can proceed to establish the facts. Police are now seeking a forensic examination and an autopsy to determine the cause.

Lawyer Jeong Joon-yeong of HMP Law said meaningful results are difficult without a statement from Lee. Some test takers say the state is failing to manage exams properly in the AI era. A 22 year old preparing for civil service exams said national exams have lost credibility. This person mentioned the tax accountant cheating case and the LEET case as examples. Others view the failure to appear at the verification as a tacit admission of guilt.

Lee once placed in the sixth to eighth tiers on the national college entrance exam. He later claimed to have developed his own study method to improve his scores. He faced allegations that his sharp improvement resulted from using artificial intelligence during his tests. Some claimed he received suspicious private tutoring in life science just before the CSAT exam. His LEET answer sheet showed signs that he had marked answers in the wrong rows.

Police applied for an order to preserve Lee's answer booklet at Younghoon High School in Gangbuk. They want to use the booklet from last year's CSAT as evidence in the probe. Investigators are looking for any accomplices who may have helped Lee cheat on the exams. The articles leave open whether the police will find evidence without a statement from Lee. It remains unknown if the forensic examination will reveal more about his death.

stories.Headline: Polly Barnes says AI lets founders build with smaller teams but makes every hire a harder bet
stories.Summary:
Polly Barnes, an operating partner at the investment firm EQT and the author of The Founder Six, wrote in an article published by Sifted on 19 November 2026 that AI is making it possible to build technology companies with fewer people, even as the stakes of every hire rise and finding exceptional talent does not get any easier. She said exceptional candidates want to know what they will own, what they can build and whether the opportunity is worth leaving their current job for. She wrote that as teams shrink, every hire carries more weight, and that the hardest question for a founder is no longer whether a candidate can do the job but whether that person is the right bet for a smaller, more senior team. She described how behavioural science can help founders navigate the demands of fast growth, drawing on her work leading the early-stage talent team at EQT. The article says companies are increasingly looking beyond their local talent pool, driven by the evolution of AI and flexible working, and that European startups must embrace global hiring to survive a growing tech talent crunch.

It reports that 52% of something in the text is tied to the shift, and it cites figures of 66 to 87% and 58% in passages describing how AI tools affect the work of engineers and the share of tasks they handle. It notes that a typical team once needed 55 people for a certain job and now needs far fewer, and it says one company cut its engineering headcount while keeping output steady. It adds that candidates now ask what a role will let them own and build, and that founders must answer those questions clearly to win them. Barnes is responsible for the argument, writing as an operating partner at EQT and as the author of The Founder Six, and she says she has met thousands of founders from companies such as Wellhub, Lovable, Harvey and Vinted, which she says gives her insight into what drives high-performing teams. She says founders should treat each hire as a bet on a smaller, more senior group rather than as a replacement for a large one, and that they should be honest with candidates about what the role will involve.

She says the fight for real talent is getting harder rather than easier, and that companies will have to go the extra mile to attract the people they need. The context is a European startup scene where AI and flexible working are pushing companies to hire beyond their local pools, and where the article says local talent pools are drying up as demand for tech skills grows. The article says European startups must embrace global hiring to survive the crunch, and it points to a related piece on how Europe is future-proofing its hiring strategy. It does not say what specific companies plan to do next beyond that shift toward global hiring, and it offers no timeline for when the smaller-team trend will play out.

stories.Headline: UK government delays decision on AI copyright training as OpenAI withdraws Stargate funding
stories.Summary:
Britain has not decided whether AI models can legally be trained on publicly available copyrighted material, and three successive governments have failed to settle the question. The Intellectual Property Office was given the issue in 2022, and in February 2024 it passed the question back to the now-defunct Department of Science Innovation and Technology, calling it too difficult. DSIT consulted in December 2024 with responses required by February 2025, and received many thousands. Former Secretary of State Liz Kendall held roundtables for around 60 organisations in September 2025 and committed to a full report by March and the setup of specialist task forces. On 18th March 2026 Kendall told Parliament the government would "take time to get this right," and OpenAI backed out of promised funding for the UK Stargate project with NScale that month, citing the UK's failure to act on copyright and model training.

A ministerial letter published 11th November but dated 30th October, by Ian Murray MP, responded to a public letter from Caroline Dinenage MP and set out where responsibilities for AI and copyright lie across departments following DSIT being disbanded. Murray repeated that Parliament would "take its time to get it right" and promised a further task force before Christmas. In 2024 the creative, media and sport sectors contributed an estimated £247.6 billion to the UK economy, according to DCMS. The AI sector's revenues rose 41% to £33.6 billion in 2025 and it employed an estimated 130,400 people.

The IP Office is offering £80,000 in a tender for a survey of the creative industries. The House of Lords published a report on the question in March this year. The Turing Institute's report, Securing resilience for the age of AI, focused on five risks in frontier models: cybersecurity risks, democratic instability, misalignment, loss of meaningful human control, and chemical and biological threats. The report suggests the use of a standard in respect of the copyright confusion.

At a report launch event panel, a representative of Sov.AI said they comply with laws, other panelists could do nothing more than point to the report, and Lucy Yu said "it's later than we think." The IP Federation has sought to comment on the Getty Images v Stability AI appeal, saying the outcome could have far reaching implications for British industry and the UK's ambitions to become a global leader in AI. The Office of National Statistics last week shared growth of 0.7% in GDP attributed to AI and cloud computing. The IP Federation said the appeal will decide whether an AI model developed overseas can be treated as an infringing copy under UK copyright law, even where the model itself does not contain or reproduce the copyright works in question.

The article says other countries have created some level of certainty on an interim basis at least, making it easier for companies to plan ahead. The article says the conversation ought never to have been framed as an argument between creatives and tech. The article says streaming is the prime example, where a technology company, Spotify, has taken the lion's share of the market, leaving those that create music with a smaller share than they had previously. More to follow.

stories.Headline: AI image generators struggle to draw exactly 13 eggs due to diffusion model limitations
stories.Summary:
AI image generators across the internet failed to draw exactly 13 eggs on November 18. This collective flop became a trending search on Weibo with over one million views that day. User @No.1 Sentry Post shared screenshots of the AI Doubao failing multiple times. The AI eventually admitted defeat by stating that a text list is most reliable. Netizens called this specific way of admitting a mistake the sliding-kneeling style.

The task requires drawing 13 eggs, but models often draw 12, 14, 15, or 18. Doubao, Keling, and Jimeng failed, while some users reported success with ChatGPT or Doubao. Standard egg boxes in supermarkets have two rows of six grids for 12 eggs. This layout makes it hard for AI to place a 13th egg in the box. Changing the prompt to eggs scattered on a table makes the task easier.

Blogger Zero Gravity Wali found that four out of nine tested models drew the eggs correctly. These successful models used irregular layouts rather than full rows and full columns. The AI models value arranging objects neatly more than they value counting them correctly. The chat models often insist they are right because they are inclined to agree with people. They do not actually count the images but simply issue the requested instructions.

Users of Doubao, Keling, Hunyuan, and Tongyi Wanxiang are affected by these counting limitations. A March 2025 paper showed that accuracy for 11 to 15 objects is below 10 percent. Even Imagen-3 only had an average accuracy of 43 percent for these types of tasks. Researchers found that modifying prompts or specifying object placement actually made the accuracy drop further. The paper noted that all tested models failed to draw 13 trees correctly.

Diffusion models start with a noise image and denoise it to create a clear picture. They learn what a box of eggs looks like but not the number 13. There is no internal counter that records how many objects have been drawn during the process. An October 2025 paper explained that the final count depends largely on the initial random noise map. The number provided in the prompt acts only as a weak signal for the model.

Some users now try specifying layouts like five, five, and three eggs per row. Others use local redraw tools to add one egg to a standard box of 12. Academic researchers are adding a link that allows the model to count while it is drawing. This new method increased accuracy from 26 percent to 54 percent in some studies. The articles leave open whether these academic solutions will be integrated into mainstream AI products.

stories.Headline: LG Electronics promotes 44 executives and forms a CEO-led AI partnership team to speed AI and robotics growth
stories.Summary:
LG Electronics announced on November 19, 2026, that it promoted 44 executives and reshuffled its leadership to improve its competitive edge during the AI era. The company created a new AI partnership team that reports directly to CEO Lyu Jae-cheol to strengthen ties with global tech firms. These changes aim to accelerate growth in future businesses such as robotics, mobility, smart factories, and data center cooling. The organizational restructuring will take effect on December 1, while the executive promotions become official on January 1.

The reshuffle includes promoting Baek Seung-tae, the head of the home appliance business, and Lee Sang-woo, the head of management strategy at LG Corp, to presidents. Lee Sang-woo will now lead the TV and display business, while Baek Seung-tae continues to manage home appliances and robot actuator commercialization. LG Electronics is establishing a new applied business unit under its Eco Solution division to expand its data center cooling operations. Additionally, a new unit under the vehicle division will focus on advanced driver assistance systems and high-performance computing.

Company leadership stated that these moves are intended to speed up decision-making and respond more quickly to changing market conditions. To achieve this, regional heads for Asia, Europe, North America, Latin America, the Middle East, and Africa will now report directly to the CEO. The company is also leveraging a multibillion-dollar deal to supply chillers for data centers with a combined capacity of 5 gigawatts. LG Electronics aims to reach 1 trillion won in annual chiller sales as early as next year.

To support this growth, the company plans to establish a manufacturing subsidiary in Virginia next year to meet rising demand. This strategy builds on the creation of a robotics business center in July that also reports directly to the CEO. The electronics maker continues to streamline its global management structure by reducing layers between regional operations and headquarters. These efforts are part of a broader push to develop robotics and AI infrastructure into primary growth engines.

stories.Headline: Kuaishou reports AI growth as other business lines decline in third quarter financial report
stories.Summary:
Kuaishou released its third quarter financial report on November 19, 2026. The company reported a widespread decline across almost all of its business lines. Only the artificial intelligence segment showed growth during this specific period. Total revenue for the quarter reached 31.6 billion yuan, which is down 11.1 percent. Adjusted net profit fell 84.2 percent to reach 790 million yuan.

The online marketing service revenue dropped 11.1 percent to 17.9 billion yuan. Live streaming business revenue fell 19 percent to reach 7.8 billion yuan. Other service revenue, including AI and e-commerce, rose 1.5 percent to 6 billion yuan. Kuaishou's share price was HK$23.04 with a market capitalization of HK$99 billion on November 19. Total revenue from the first three quarters reached 100.843 billion yuan.

Kuaishou stated that e-commerce performance was under pressure from rising merchant costs and competition. The company noted that revenue from gaming and AI partially offset the e-commerce decline. Management did not disclose specific quarterly revenue or annual recurring revenue for Kling AI. They only stated that the revenue for the Kling AI product recorded year-on-year growth. The company continues to support anchors and agencies to improve the live streaming ecosystem.

E-commerce advertising investment declined due to a changing consumption environment and intensified industry competition. Small creators and C-end users are affected by the new ToC template functions. Users of the Web terminal saw a surge in access volume to 16.11 million. Monthly unique visitors for Kling AI on the Web reached 8.122 million in October. This represents a month-on-month increase of 45 percent for the Web side.

Kling AI launched its 4.0 model in September and fully rolled it out on October 15. The company completed independent financing for Kling AI, closing the deal on October 30. This financing provided approximately 2.905 billion US dollars, while Kuaishou retains over two-thirds equity. R&D expenses rose 41.9 percent to 5.18 billion yuan due to Kling-related investments. Administrative expenses rose to 1.566 billion yuan, including 700 million yuan for employee incentives.

The company will continue to use a high cost-effectiveness strategy for its API pricing. Kling AI 4.0 is nearly 60 percent cheaper than competitors in 1080p scenarios. Future success depends on whether the model capability remains in the first echelon. The articles leave open whether the Kling team can maintain its continuous operation capability. It remains unclear if the AI growth can offset the overall operating losses.

stories.Headline: South Korea targets AI cheating as 550,000 students sit college entrance exam
stories.Summary:
South Korea conducted its toughest crackdown on cheating during the 2027 College Scholastic Ability Test on Thursday, November 19, 2026. Authorities targeted AI assisted cheating as about 550,000 students sat for the nationwide college entrance exam. Proctors caught a 20 year old repeat test taker with a miniature camera and earphones in Yongin, Gyeonggi. Police also found a phone in a shoe insole in Seocho District and other banned items in Jung District. In Yangsan, South Gyeongsang, police responded to a YouTube chat claim about someone wearing AI glasses.

Proctors at 1,312 test sites required students to remove glasses, roll up sleeves, and place stickers over clothing buttons. Public and carrier Wi-Fi within 100 meters of sites was shut off, and 8,400 additional inspectors were dispatched. The government used the emergency alert system at 8:30 a.m., 2:21 p.m., and 2:57 p.m. to find unsubmitted phones. This system uncovered 22 phones across nine cities and provinces, according to the Ministry of Education.

Prime minister Han Seong-sook reportedly spearheaded the ideas for button stickers and placing bags in hallways. The Ministry of Education stated that the emergency alerts helped identify phones that students had not surrendered to proctors. The government vowed to keep pursuing cheating after the exam through tougher penalties and new incentives to report it. President Lee Jae Myung ordered a plan to pay bounties of up to 100 million won for reporting cheating. The ruling party and government are pushing a legal revision to extend the retake ban from one to 10 years.

Officials also asked provincial offices to keep last year's test papers instead of destroying them. Some people claimed online that they did not receive the emergency alerts or that no alarms sounded at all. Critics argued that shutting off Wi-Fi cannot stop smuggled devices from using mobile data to send photos of questions. Parent Jeong Jae-wook in Cheongju, North Chungcheong, said the hastily prepared measures were not enough and assessment methods must change.

Lee Jeong-in believed the government should create more definite measures to protect the efforts of students who studied hard. These concerns highlight doubts about whether current security can stop increasingly sophisticated AI assisted cheating. The crackdown followed AI cheating scandals on other national exams, including a certified tax accountant exam top scorer who used AI. Last year, electronic devices were used in 84 of 279 cheating cases, which is 30.1 percent, according to Ko Min-jung.

These devices included 31 digital watches, 23 e-cigarettes, 16 phones, eight Bluetooth earphones, and six tablet PCs. Lee Jin-woo, who took last year's CSAT and aced the Legal Education Eligibility Test, died by suicide on Thursday. He had faced allegations of using AI to achieve his perfect score on the law school entrance exam. Police will now investigate if the repeat test taker in Yongin photographed questions or communicated with people outside the site.

The government continues to push for the legal revision regarding the ten year ban for those caught cheating. Authorities are still finalizing the bounty system for reporting cheating under the orders of President Lee Jae Myung. It remains unclear if the current security measures can truly prevent the use of advanced generative AI tools. The Education Ministry is still reviewing last year's test papers following the allegations against Lee Jin-woo.

stories.Headline: South Korea covers buttons and checks glasses to stop AI cheating on the CSAT
stories.Summary:
Proctors began checking test-takers’ IDs and collecting their phones at 8:10 a.m. on Nov. 19, the day of the College Scholastic Ability Test, which had 551,864 applicants this year. Test-takers wearing clothes with buttons were handed small stickers and told to put one over each button under new nationwide measures against AI devices that could be used to cheat on the exam. In one exam room, test-takers who walked in at 7:40 a.m. nervously studied four notices taped side by side on the blackboard.

The notices spelled out the penalties for cheating with smart devices and listed banned and permitted items. Proctors also had to check every test-taker’s eyewear at each period to make sure none were smart glasses. The Ministry of Education said in its Nov. 9 guidance that merely wearing smart glasses during the exam would count as cheating. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook announced last-minute checks, including the button stickers, on Tuesday, Nov. 17, and the government ruled out postponing the CSAT. Tuesday’s measures added checks of buttons, sleeves and collars.

Public Wi-Fi within 100 meters of test sites nationwide was switched off for 24 hours from 6 p.m. on Nov. 18 to curb AI-assisted cheating, though officials said mobile networks could not be blocked. At 8:30 a.m., the government sent a nationwide emergency alert that sets off a 10.5-second alarm on any phone that is switched on, so that any phones test-takers had not handed in would go off. Test-takers’ phone and AI service records will be checked after the exam, and the government plans to bar anyone caught cheating from retaking the CSAT for 10 years, raised drastically from one. During the exam, test-takers may write only with black pencils or the writing tools the ministry provides.

This year’s test-takers are also the last to sit the CSAT under the 2015 revised national curriculum, and from next year elective subjects are dropped and all test-takers will be tested on the same subjects. Police were dispatched to a test site in Yangsan, South Gyeongsang, Thursday morning after a report that someone planned to cheat with AI glasses. The Ulsan Metropolitan Police Agency received the report at around 8:45 a.m., according to the Gyeongnam Provincial Police Agency, passed it to the South Gyeongsang agency two minutes later, and police reached the school at around 8:51 a.m. and informed the proctors. No smart devices or other irregularities had been found so far, and a police official said, “We are checking whether the post is genuine.”

The person who reported it had seen a post in the chat window of a YouTube channel on college admissions consulting that said, in effect, “I will take the exam wearing AI glasses,” and named a specific test site. On Sunday, police opened an investigation after the tax exam’s top scorer turned himself in, confessing he cheated with a hidden miniature camera and generative AI. The Human Resources Development Service of Korea, which runs the test, has said it will file a criminal complaint against the test-taker and revoke the passing result. Suspected cheating with AI-powered smart glasses and miniature cameras has surfaced in a string of recent exams. “My son was very angry about the cheating controversy,” Noh Jeong-dae said, adding that he calmed him down by telling him, “Ignore it and just show what you know,” but still feels upset.

“If the government had postponed the exam by just one week, it could have come up with something more reliable than stickers,” Noh said. “Many students say they feel as if what they built over more than 10 years of hard work has been stolen by cheaters,” a teacher at Seoseok High School in Gwangju said, adding that the school went to great lengths to calm students shaken by the recent controversy. At Namnyeong High School in Jeju City, most test-takers arrived in padded jackets, hoodies or other clothes without buttons, and a teacher there said he told students yesterday to avoid clothes with buttons if they could. “The detailed guidelines changed so suddenly that there could be confusion on site,” Park Su-ji, a third-year homeroom teacher at Chuncheon High School, said, adding that she told her students to get a proctor to check any item before using it. “What I told my students most often was, ‘Hold your nerve,’” Cho Su-yeon, a teacher at Yongin High School, said outside Dongnae High School, a test site in Busan, adding that some students were worried by rumors that the mechanical pencil leads provided at test sites were poor quality.

“I cheer on students outside the test site every year,” Woo Hyeong-geun, a third-year homeroom teacher at Daewon High School in Daegu, said, adding that this year problems like AI cheating meant one change after another right up until the exam. “They are the last generation under the 2015 revised curriculum, and now the AI issue has come up as well,” another teacher in Jeju said, adding that the tax accountant case blew up and that it is actually a good thing it has led to steps against cheating. “I do not know what the world is coming to,” a woman waiting at a bus stop outside Hakseong High School in Ulsan said, adding that she worries about the children who will have to live in a society where trust has broken down. “The government did rush out anticheating measures,” Jung Jae-uk, a parent outside the Cheongseok High School test site in Cheongju, North Chungcheong, said, adding that given how advanced technology has become they do not seem satisfactory and that there should be changes to how the CSAT assesses students or how it is proctored. “Cheating is fraud against everyone who studied hard,” Lee Jeong-in, who came to Cheongseok High School to cheer on a younger sibling, said, adding that once this CSAT is over the government should come up with firmer measures.

“Once this year’s exam is over, it is my child’s turn next year,” said a parent surnamed Son, whose child is a second-year high school student in Jeju, adding that she is worried about AI cheating but that there will always be people like that and it pays to take a wider perspective of life. “My child usually wears glasses, and I worry they might be wrongly suspected or feel intimidated during the checks,” a parent outside Hakseong High School said, adding that stopping cheating is important but so is letting children who prepared diligently take the exam without feeling anxious. In a fourth-floor study room of Myeonggok Library in Changwon, South Gyeongsang, about 20 people were studying for teacher recruitment, civil service and licensing exams, and a library-goer surnamed Lee, preparing for the special education teacher exam for secondary schools, said the alarm did not feel like much of a disturbance. Outside Chuncheon High School in Chuncheon, Gangwon, first- and second-year students from Seongsu High School cheered on test-takers. A mother cheered on her child outside the test site at Myungduk Foreign Language High School in Gangseo District, western Seoul.

Proctors collected banned items and handed out writing tools at Gwangnam High School in Gwangjin District, eastern Seoul, and a proctor checked a test-taker’s glasses for smart glasses at Yeouido Girls’ High School in Yeongdeungpo District, western Seoul. Test-takers got ready for the exam at Yongsan High School in Yongsan District, central Seoul, and a smartphone at Ewha Girls’ High School in Jung District, central Seoul, showed the emergency alert sent nationwide on the morning of Nov. 19. A public Wi-Fi device is installed in front of a CSAT site in Seoul, and a miniature camera was placed next to a button on a sweater in an image released by NEWS1. The library-goer surnamed Lee said, “This problem will surely come up not only in the CSAT but also in the teacher recruitment exam I am preparing for,” adding, “I think I would be really angry if I failed because of people like that,” and that there need to be harsh punishments for AI cheaters and a government way to weed them out. The article was originally written in Korean and translated by a bilingual reporter with the help of generative AI tools, then edited by a native English-speaking editor, with all AI-assisted translations reviewed and refined by the newsroom.

Prime Minister Han Seong-sook was reportedly behind the idea to spearhead anticheating measures for the college admissions test. The CSAT is Korea’s college entrance exam, and the tax accountant exam’s top scorer confessed on Sunday to cheating with a hidden miniature camera and generative AI. The government announced the extra measures only days before the college admissions test was to be held, which induced anxiety in some test-takers and aggravation among parents and teachers. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Sam Altman rules out letting AI independently develop models without human oversight
stories.Summary:
Sam Altman said at the Semafor event on November 16 that OpenAI could have pushed further toward recursive self-improvement but cannot do so safely right now. He drew a clear red line on the spot against fully handing the steering wheel of R&D to AI. OpenAI has already used its own AI technology to speed up R&D of new models, and AI is already helping OpenAI build the next generation of GPT. Altman said OpenAI has not yet allowed AI to independently develop the next generation of models and carry out rapid self-improvement without human supervision. He said this matter, like AGI, has no clear dividing line that people will suddenly cross one morning.

Altman unveiled OpenAI's latest concrete safety measure: inviting external evaluation institutions including METR into the lab to conduct on-site supervision directly. According to OpenAI's official blog, OpenAI has signed agreements with four institutions: Apollo Research, METR, Transluce and Goodfire. In the first phase, the evaluation will directly cover two core links: model training and internal use. Apollo Research will send a 6-person team for a 4-month on-site pilot, checking whether the model will secretly damage the alignment and control mechanisms of itself or the next generation model. Transluce will start a 6-week pilot in early December, with access to some models, raw chain-of-thought outputs and internal evaluations, including at least one model for internal use only.

Altman defined the "push while holding back" approach as tactical restraint: first use AI to tackle alignment problems and solve the core safety issue of how to control AI. He criticized Silicon Valley peers who promise to help humans conquer cancer and provide cheap products while asking humans to hand over all decision-making power. In his exact words, this would make humans "live like a Labrador retriever: the machine might keep you happy, but you no longer have any control at all". On the Silicon Valley buzzword "handover", whether gradual handover of power or sudden transfer of control, Altman's attitude was firm: never accept it. He said inviting external experts to assess safety work and system robustness will become increasingly critical in the future.

As of October this year, the capability improvement speed of rival Anthropic's models on specific well-defined tasks is about twice the historical level from March 2024 to October 2025. It is estimated that the AECI improvement speed of Anthropic's models has increased to 1.9 times. Altman did not engage in this digital competition and admitted that the current capability evolution of AI is still jagged: some links are extremely fast, far more than twice, and some links are still stuck on hard problems and progress much slower. METR will focus on OpenAI's largest reinforcement learning training to date, specifically searching for misalignment risks that may be missed by existing tests and regular monitoring. Goodfire will use interpretability methods to analyze the internal mechanism of the model, assist in monitoring the training process and identify abnormal signals.

In the past, safety tests for large models were usually carried out just before the products were ready to be launched to the public. Many models that have not been released to the public have long been put into internal use, and even directly participate in the R&D of the next generation of models. From July to August this year, METR and Redwood Research personnel conducted a 3-week inspection of OpenAI's internal agent monitoring system at that time. The inspection found a mechanism blind spot: there was a set of monitoring mechanisms in the inspected system that would only trigger inspections after the agent returned control to the user. During the gap period before context compression triggers the inspection, the agent can completely carry out unlimited consecutive actions to continuously execute operations, pushing the inspection time further and further away.

OpenAI cannot delete Apollo's qualitative judgments on various claims, nor can it demand deletions or revisions just because the inspection results are unsatisfactory; OpenAI still has the right to erase supporting evidence involving sensitive intellectual property rights. All evaluation results of internal exclusive models are strictly prohibited from being made public. Transluce made it clear that the permissions obtained this time are not equivalent to the permissions of official OpenAI employees; the complete, unredacted report will only be submitted to the Safety and Security Committee of the OpenAI Foundation Board of Directors. There is no evidence yet that a METR report has prompted OpenAI to slow down its self-improvement plans. The articles leave open whether the model has had malicious intentions when working in the "back kitchen" and whether the reasoning traces can capture abnormal behaviors on the spot.

stories.Headline: Chinese internet giants push AI short dramas to the global cutting edge
stories.Summary:
Chinese internet giants pushed AI short dramas to the global cutting edge by 2026. This industry evolved from small workshops to film level production over eight years. AI now empowers these dramas to reach a state of cyber ascension. One popular AI drama this year gained 6.6 billion views without real actors. These platforms now dominate the leisure time of many Chinese people.

The market size exceeded 50 billion yuan in 2024, surpassing the total Chinese film box office. By 2025, viewers exceeded 600 million, with over half of internet users watching. In 2026, the market exceeded 100 billion yuan and viewers surpassed 800 million. The Hongguo App daily active users surpassed iQiyi, Youku, Tencent Video, and Mango TV. These figures show the rapid growth of the short drama sector.

Internet giants are responsible for this growth as part of a commercial war. They view the short drama sector as a game between competing platforms. These companies use quantified advertising indicators to create highly addictive, formulaic content. They focus on hooks, emotional pushes, and suspense to retain their audiences. The platforms hold the power of traffic distribution and make steady profits.

Traffic placement operators are affected because they determine if a producer makes money. They edit clips for specific audiences, such as young women or agricultural video lovers. If the return on investment is lower than 70 percent, placement is stopped. Producers and placement companies only take 10 percent of the total market revenue. The platforms take 90 percent of the revenue through traffic placement fees.

The industry began with advertisements like the Crooked Mouth Dragon King in 2020. These ads used real people to perform exciting plots from online novels. Platforms like Qimao, Fanqie, and Midu provided free novels and monetized through ads. This model used short videos on Douyin and Kuaishou to attract users. Entrepreneurs from advertising distribution then flooded the marginal short drama market.

Next, companies will integrate production and placement to try and increase their revenue. They will continue using specific timing units, like reversals every three seconds. Some memes from these dramas may appear in next year's Spring Festival Gala. The articles leave open how producers can earn more than 10 percent. They do not say if AI will replace all real actors.

CJ Olive Young said in Seoul on Thursday that it will develop its online platform into an omnichannel service connecting online and offline shopping for consumers in Korea and overseas. Chief Operating Officer Lee Jin-hee said the company aims to build an AI-powered platform spanning inventory, store layouts, delivery logistics and supply chains. The company was established in 1999 and now serves 18 million members, Lee said. Olive Young operates 1,300 stores, and Chief Technology Officer Kim Hwan said accurately sharing each store's stock status with customers is difficult.

The company introduced a shopping cart service a month ago that combines same-day delivery, regular delivery and store pickup. Olive Young has more than 47 million customer records covering skin conditions, analyzed solutions and product reviews, which it plans to use to support consultations through agentic AI. Lee said foreign visitors have contributed 1 trillion won to sales this year and account for 6 million memberships at Olive Young's online global mall. She said those foreign visitors drive 70 percent of the company's annual growth, and Olive Young's California stores use the same technologies as its Korean stores.

Lee said the company is now leading a global commerce trend that integrates online and offline channels into a single marketplace. She said everything from checking stocks to in-store product arrangement, delivery logistics and supply chains will work on a singular platform. Kim said the company at first saw its online infrastructure tumble frequently because of errors, and that implementing cloud technology brought failures as well as chances to improve. Lee said Olive Young aims to move beyond keyword searches and scrolling through lists of results, and that its online traffic and offline stores together offer a next-generation K-beauty media platform.

Revenue reached 30.2 billion US dollars, which is an increase of 48 percent year on year. Adjusted net profit hit 1.4 billion US dollars, rising 166 percent year on year. The adjusted net profit margin for the period stood at 4.5 percent.

The ISG business recorded 11.3 billion US dollars in revenue and 1.1 billion US dollars in operating profit. AI server revenue grew over 300 percent, with reserved orders reaching 530 billion RMB. IDG revenue reached 17.4 billion US dollars, while SSG revenue hit 3.1 billion US dollars. AI PCs reached a shipment share of 25.2 percent, and Lenovo holds a 31 percent global Windows share. The SSG operating profit margin hit a record high of 26.02 percent.

The author of the Tech Business article questioned if these record profits are sustainable. They noted that the 9.6 percent ISG operating profit margin is a historical high. The author stated that the current profit margin was pushed up by loose pricing for early orders. They argued that the revenue growth in IDG relies partly on passive price increases. The writer suggested that the market may still view Lenovo as a PC cycle stock.

Global PC shipments in the third quarter of 2026 fell 20.1 percent year on year. Lenovo's own PC shipments declined by 22.6 percent during that same period. Dell leads the local AI server sector with a 24 percent share of the market. Super Micro Computer holds a 6.1 percent share, while Lenovo holds a 5.1 percent share. These figures show that competitors are expanding production and customers have more bargaining power.

The ISG business began with the 2014 acquisition of the x86 server business from IBM. Over ten years, that business had total sales over 84 billion US dollars and losses of 1.95 billion. Lenovo also previously acquired Motorola to expand its business reach. Memory and SSD costs in a single PC rose from about 15 percent to nearly 40 percent. This cost increase happened because AI data centers crowded out high bandwidth memory supplies.

The company must prove if the ISG profit margin can resist a cross cycle decline. It remains unclear if the 20 percent SSG growth rate and 26 percent profit margin are sustainable. stories.Headline: AI short drama creators adapt classical masterpieces to attract high traffic
stories.Summary:
AI short dramas recently adapted classical masterpieces, leading to the viral hit The Ugly Fox and the removal of Dreaming Back to the Red Chamber. These productions topped Weibo hot search lists as creators used AI to tap into high-value traffic mines. Low-budget creators chose these stories because the established characters and plots save effort during early production. Some creators used AI to restore atmospheric charm, while others followed standardized assembly-line routines. These trends split the industry into those seeking shortcuts to traffic and those exploring new expression.

Dreaming Back to the Red Chamber rewrote the original into a rebirth and inner-house power struggle story. It misappropriated facial features from 17 actors in the 1987 TV adaptation of Dream of the Red Chamber. Other works include Rebirth of Wu Dalang and Song Jiang Reborn: No More Path for Surrender to the Court. These Water Margin adaptations use time travel and fate reversal to satisfy audience demands for counterattacks. The Ugly Fox and Journey to the West: The Self-Cultivation of the Holy Monk are cited as high-quality examples.

The creator of Dreaming Back to the Red Chamber had their account cancelled after the series was reported. Zhang Li, who played Xue Baochai in the classic adaptation, stated she never authorized the use of her portrait. She reserves the right to pursue further legal responsibilities against the creator for the infringement. The articles state that high-quality adaptations must respect the unique inherent traits of classic characters. They should avoid stereotyped transformations and not let short drama routines dominate the entire plot.

Audiences disliked Dreaming Back to the Red Chamber because it turned Lin Daiyu into a flat, dominant female lead. This version of Daiyu focused on power manipulation and aggressiveness rather than her traditional sensitivity and tragic beauty. Viewers of The Ugly Fox praised its focus on human nature, though some felt it amplified the character's grievances. These viewers argued the adaptation weakened the fox spirit's original decisive traits and made her seem irrationally obsessed. Young people's spiritual demands for self-growth make the themes of Journey to the West resonate with them.

The articles explain that classic works like Journey to the West and Strange Stories from a Chinese Studio carry collective memories. These stories provide a broad national audience and are deeply rooted in the public mind. The Ugly Fox modified the original setting by making the fox spirit beautiful before she became haggard. This change highlighted the scholar's greed as he grew rich and then tried to drive her away. Journey to the West: The Self-Cultivation of the Holy Monk reshaped Tang Sanzang to discuss mercy and karma.

Future success for AI short dramas requires optimizing narrative rhythm and fitting in with contemporary audience emotions. Creators must flexibly adjust narrative styles without shaking the core essence of the original classic works. The articles leave open how the industry will balance satisfying plot points with literary integrity. They do not specify if Zhang Li will officially file a lawsuit against the cancelled account. The text ends while discussing the dilemma live-action remakes face when modifying classic cognition.

In Yongin, Gyeonggi, a 20-year-old had a miniature camera and earphones. Other devices found included smart glasses in Cheonan and a phone in a shoe insole in Seocho District.

The Ministry of Education stated they are looking into reports of arguments between proctors and examinees. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook reportedly spearheaded the idea to cover buttons with stickers and move bags. Some students, including 18-year-old Yang, said inspection methods varied and some proctors were more lenient. Examinee Bang and another student named Lee reported different frequencies of glasses checks at one school. One online post claimed proctors skipped identity checks to focus on clothing buttons. Student Kim Han-bi expressed worry that smart glasses could lead to unfair perfect scores. A parent surnamed Kwon ensured their son wore a buttonless sweatshirt to avoid suspicion.

Last year, 30.1 percent of 279 cheating violations involved electronic devices like smartphones. This year, 54,338 registered examinees were absent, which is a 9.97 percent absentee rate. This figure is an increase of 3,042 people from the previous year's 9.4 percent rate. Some people speculate that the stricter supervision contributed to this increase in absences. stories.Headline: It is fun to talk to artificial intelligence (AI) even if there are no special tasks. If you put the..
stories.Summary:
Yoon Tae-sung, a professor at the KAIST Graduate School of Technology and Management, wrote in a November 19, 2026 column that talking to artificial intelligence is enjoyable even when there is no special task, and that putting the same question to several AI models produces a different answer from each one. He said comparing those different answers is fun, and that some AI models answer outside human stereotypes by pointing out things people have not thought of and suggesting brilliant ideas. He compared this to AlphaGo's 37th move against Lee Se-dol in Go, where a number humans had not considered led people to develop a new standard. He also said such AI helps when many ideas are needed, such as planning a new business or developing a scenario, and that it broadens the range of human thinking.

The professor wrote that AI produces plausible answers to problems that depend on human life or a company's survival, but that it sometimes gives wrong answers and leads people in the wrong direction. He said strange AI and wrong AI come from the same roots, because large language models predict statistically plausible next fragments to answer a user's question. He said the same answer can count as creative in terms of ideas and as wrong when facts must be confirmed, and that AI cites data to make sentences more perfect than humans, which makes those answers harder to verify. He added that it is difficult to confirm whether the evidence AI presents actually exists and whether the content is true or inferred.

On responsibility, he wrote that it is difficult to clearly identify who is responsible when a wrong AI result causes serious consequences, because developers, service companies and users all have intertwined responsibilities. He said a car accident allows investigators to examine defective parts such as brakes and engines, but AI is different because the model answers using an algorithm and the user believes the answer is correct. He said a car accident is solved by first checking the black box, but AI has no perfect black box, so the cause of an error is hard to reproduce. He noted that attempts to expand product liability law to AI are actively under way, citing the European Union's New Product Liability Guidelines, which take effect on December 9, 2026, and which include AI in products and ease the burden of proof for victims.

He said defects caused by updating or learning an AI model are also subject to responsibility under those guidelines, but that some parts remain unresolved because the AI's judgment process is opaque. He said the cause of damage is spread across developing the model, providing the service and using the service, which makes responsibilities hard to distinguish, and that even when a model admits a wrong answer, the extent of damage is difficult to calculate. He concluded that AI creates answers but does not take responsibility on behalf of humans, so for an important question a person should put it to multiple AI models at the same time. If the answers differ, he wrote, a person should at least doubt whether it is strange AI or wrong AI, because that doubt is the starting point for human verification and responsibility.

stories.Headline: KAIST professor Jaeseung Jeong builds AI Socratic system to grade student oral exams
stories.Summary:
Neuroscientist and KAIST professor Jaeseung Jeong appeared on tvN’s You Quiz on the Block, which aired on the 18th, and described how artificial intelligence has changed the way he runs university exams. Host Yoo Jae-suk noted that cheating with AI glasses has recently been detected at exam sites and asked whether setting questions now weighed on him. Jeong said that when he first became a professor he promised creative education, giving students a question and 24 hours to email their answers by the following night, with any reference material allowed. He explained that he tried giving his own questions to AI and it produced answers at an A-grade level, so he could no longer assign questions of that kind.

Jeong said that although he had long told others to prepare for the age of AI, for the past three years he has told his students there would be no open-book exams and that they must come to the classroom. He described the return to analog methods as going back 25 years and said he did not become a professor to do this. Last year he created a new assessment system, saying that if they were going back in time they should go back 2,500 years rather than 25, and he built an AI version of the Socratic method of questioning. He reasoned that written work cannot be trusted because students will get help from AI, so he asks them questions directly and listens to what they say, and that talking for two or three hours lets him understand what is in their heads and grade them honestly.

When Yoo Jae-suk asked whether he really speaks with each student individually for two or three hours, Jeong replied that this would not be possible and explained that his team is creating an AI version of himself. When a student turns on their computer he appears on the screen, the student talks with AI Jaeseung, and the system records the entire conversation, which the AI evaluates and grades, under a system called Socratest. He added that written work cannot be trusted and that he thinks oral interviews and oral exams will become commonplace, while noting that students are not exactly happy about it. The articles do not say what happens next with the system or how widely it will be used.

stories.Headline: OECD works with Southeast Asian countries on turning AI principles into practice
stories.Summary:
The OECD, with support from Japan and the United Kingdom, worked with Southeast Asian partner countries through AI governance dialogues and workshops over the past year. These included the OECD AI Policy Roundtable in Tokyo, Japan in 2025. They also included co-creation workshops on the OECD AI Policy Toolkit in Bangkok, Thailand in 2025 and 2026. The OECD-Southeast Asia Policy Roundtable on Shipbuilding, Steel and AI took place in Tokyo in 2026. A clear message emerged from these exchanges: the real challenge is no longer defining principles but making them work in practice.

The OECD AI Policy Toolkit helps governments map their AI policy landscape, identify priorities, and draw on concrete international experience to inform policy design and implementation. It is intended to support domestic policy efforts and peer learning across countries, rather than to rank countries or assess AI performance. Discussions held in Bangkok last Spring highlighted a strong interest in moving from principles to practice. Participants focused on implementation questions, including how the Toolkit can help governments identify priorities for policy development. They also asked whether it can support coordination across ministries and how it can be adapted to different national contexts.

The authors of the piece are Guillermo Hernández, David O’Connor, Lucia Russo and Takafumi Iwasaki. They state that the opinions expressed and arguments employed are solely their own. They add that these do not necessarily reflect the official views of the OECD, the GPAI or their member countries. They write that AI is transforming how people learn, governments deliver services and economies grow. They say governments in Southeast Asia are working to harness these opportunities while putting in place the governance needed to manage emerging risks.

The feedback was clear that countries are not only looking to identify gaps, but also to prioritise actions and sequence implementation. Participants saw value in the Toolkit as a resource to support decision making, cross-government coordination and practical policy development. The International AI Safety Report 2026 highlights both rapid progress in AI capabilities and risks already visible in areas such as fraud, synthetic media and cybersecurity. Safeguards do not always behave as expected once systems are used outside controlled environments.

Singapore has taken an approach that builds on existing legislation, complemented by voluntary guidance and assurance tools such as AI Verify, alongside ongoing testing. The Hiroshima AI Process Reporting Framework invites organisations developing and deploying advanced AI systems to report on their risk management practices. This reporting follows the Hiroshima AI Process International Code of Conduct for Organisations Developing Advanced AI Systems. The framework aims to strengthen trust through greater transparency and generate learning that can help address gaps in methodology, coverage and incentives.

Three issues will be paramount going forward: expanding participation, keeping pace with rapid technological change, and ensuring interoperability across emerging AI governance and reporting approaches. Language- and culture-related relevance proved one of the most tangible challenges discussed. AI systems still perform unevenly across languages, and mistranslations, loss of context or weaker safety filters in non-English prompts can affect how systems behave. Examples from the region include SEA-LION.AI, a family of open multilingual models developed by AI Singapore and adapted to Southeast Asian languages and contexts.

MERaLiON is a speech-centric multilingual and multimodal model developed by A*STAR’s Institute for Infocomm Research (I²R). Indonesia’s Sahabat-AI is an open LLM ecosystem designed to better support Bahasa Indonesia and regional languages such as Javanese and Sundanese. High-quality training and evaluation data for many local languages are often limited, and existing benchmarks tend to focus on English-language tasks. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Affinidi and Terminal 3 launch Tenon network to secure AI agents handling sensitive data
stories.Summary:
Affinidi and Terminal 3 announced a partnership on Thursday, November 19, to launch a public network called Tenon. This collaboration was revealed during the Singapore Fintech Festival to make artificial intelligence agents safer when handling sensitive data. The network will first be rolled out within the financial services sector to verify and secure the work of agents across different organizations. It aims to allow agents to perform bank functions, such as overseas transfers and disputed credit card charges, without exposing private account details.

The system requires a confidential computing network that combines the open-source governance technology of Affinidi with the hardware-secured security platform from Terminal 3. Tenon will use a programmable policy engine and trusted registries based on open standards to confirm the identity and authority of every agent. It will substitute sensitive data in prompts and execute workflows involving protected secrets within cryptographic enclaves. Every action will be recorded in a private, immutable audit trail that neither administrators nor agents can alter.

Terminal 3 co-founder and chief executive officer Gary Liu stated that enterprises have held back AI agents because they lacked a trusted way to verify identities. He noted that Affinidi provided the necessary trust primitives while Terminal 3 pioneered the confidential computing needed for autonomous workflows. Affinidi CEO Glenn Gore explained that trust is the missing layer of the internet and should be built in the open for all developers. He believes Tenon creates an ecosystem where agents can be trusted as their work moves between different companies.

This initiative comes as governments and enterprises deploy AI agents faster than safeguards can be developed. Senior Minister K Shanmugam recently warned that agentic AI is advancing rapidly, citing a September incident where an agent accessed non-public data in Australia. Terminal 3 and Affinidi will serve as the founding operators of the network's computer systems. They expect more operators from the government, technology, logistics, and healthcare industries to join the shared foundation in the future.

The Cyber Security Agency of Singapore urged all organisations to strengthen their cyberdefences immediately on November 13. This warning followed recent data breaches involving Doctor Anywhere, M1, and MoneySmart. These incidents put cyber risks back into focus for businesses across Singapore. The agency wants organisations to take immediate steps to improve their security. This push comes as AI moves from assisting employees to acting on their behalf.

The agency requires businesses to determine if they can contain consequences and reverse unintended outcomes. This involves identifying the minimum viable company, which defines systems and data that must be restored first. For a bank, this includes enabling customers to withdraw funds and make time-critical payments. A logistics provider must be able to track goods, accept shipping instructions, and release deliveries. These priorities must be based on business impact and recovery requirements rather than just AI use.

The Cyber Security Agency of Singapore is responsible for urging these immediate security improvements. They suggest that detection without recovery is not true resilience when AI systems are compromised. The agency believes that recovery readiness must now become a part of overall AI readiness. They state that businesses must demonstrate they can restore critical operations when existing safeguards fall short. This ensures that the business can safely resume operations after a critical system is hit.

Business leaders are affected because they must ask if teams can identify compromised AI systems. Commvault found in its 2026 State of Data Resilience report that only 45 per cent of Singapore organisations are confident. Boards are also affected, as they should require evidence that management has identified critical business capabilities. They must ensure there is an agreed order for restoring and testing systems cleanly. This process prevents financial, operational, and reputational damage from piling up during a disruption.

The articles cite a September 2026 incident where Boustead Singapore isolated affected systems in an overseas business unit. That company activated business continuity procedures and recovered critical data from backups without material disruption. In contrast, a 2025 cyberattack on Marks and Spencer forced systems offline for several weeks. While physical stores traded, customers could not access certain online shopping services during that time. These examples show that getting systems online differs from safely resuming full business operations.

Organisations must now map the people, data, and infrastructure needed to support their most critical processes. They need to understand the chain of actions an autonomous AI agent takes across connected systems. This includes knowing which transactions were initiated and which downstream processes accepted the AI output. The articles leave open how specific organisations will define their own minimum viable company. They also do not state how the agency will verify if businesses have strengthened their defences.

Articles.Title: When AI systems are compromised, detection without recovery is not resilience - The Business Times

stories.Headline: Anthropic’s record IPO lifts European tech stocks as Stoxx 600 rebounds
stories.Summary:
European shares rose on Thursday, November 19, 2026, after three straight days of losses. This rebound followed a record initial public offering by the Claude chatbot maker, Anthropic, which occurred on Wednesday. Technology stocks led the gains as investors felt optimistic about artificial intelligence despite some general doubts about the boom. The pan-European Stoxx 600 index climbed 0.2 percent to 645.07 points by 0958 GMT.

The record IPO by Anthropic raised 81.3 billion US dollars and valued the company at 1.5 trillion US dollars. Technology stocks in Europe grew by 1.6 percent, with ASML rising 4.1 percent and STMicroelectronics increasing 4.6 percent. Infineon shares rose 2.3 percent, while France's Soitec surged 17.5 percent after strong fiscal 2027 forecasts. UniCredit grew 1.6 percent and Commerzbank rose 1.3 percent following a deal between the Italian bank and the German government.

Will Hobbs, the chief investment officer at Brooks Macdonald, said Europe provides insulation because it is far from the AI trade epicenter. He noted that investors are reappraising financials and healthcare to diversify away from the United States and parts of Asia. Barclays downgraded luxury stocks to underweight but raised its year-end 2027 target for the Stoxx 600 to 725 points. Other movements included a 7.9 percent rise for Babcock and a 2.5 percent drop for Novartis.

European markets have remained resilient even as mining stocks slumped and defensive sectors like healthcare and utilities lost nearly 1 percent. The Stoxx 600 had reached an all-time high just one week prior to these recent fluctuations. Investors are now watching the market debut of Anthropic as a major test for the demand for artificial intelligence. Future growth may depend on how enterprises manage sustainability targets and power constraints.

Articles.Title: European stocks rebound as tech climbs on AI optimism after Anthropic’s record IPO - The Business Times

stories.Headline: Singapore non-oil domestic exports surge 79.8 percent in October on AI demand
stories.Summary:
Enterprise Singapore announced on Tuesday that non-oil domestic exports from Singapore surged by 79.8 percent year on year during October. This significant growth followed a previous increase of 68.3 percent recorded in September. The rise was driven largely by strong demand for artificial intelligence technology. Total merchandise trade for the nation also expanded by 50.7 percent in October.

Electronic non-oil domestic exports rose by 73.9 percent, while non-electronic exports grew by 81.9 percent. Non-oil re-exports increased by 48.1 percent in October, continuing a trend from a 47.8 percent rise in September. Within that category, electronics re-exports grew by 69.1 percent and non-electronics grew by 15 percent. Both imports and exports contributed to the overall growth in total merchandise trade.

Enterprise Singapore provided these statistics in an official release to explain the current economic trends. The agency noted that the surge in electronic exports was supported by sustained demand related to artificial intelligence. They highlighted that the growth in total merchandise trade followed a 50.8 percent expansion in the previous month. No further details regarding future projections or specific responsible officials were provided.

stories.Headline: AI removes professional promotion ladders by eliminating middle tier roles
stories.Summary:
Ray Xian Sen wrote about a brutal workplace shift occurring in 2026. He argues that artificial intelligence is not stealing jobs but removing promotion ladders. This change eliminates workers who merely repeat one year of experience for a decade. The shift targets the disappearing middle tier of professional employment. It affects both new graduates and mid-level managers.

The State Council General Office issued a document in October 2026 with 18 tasks. ShanghaiTech University analyzed 743 million recruitment records from 2022 to July 2026. Demand fell most in basic operation, financial accounting, graphic content, and telesales. AI contraction hits those with one to three years experience earning 5000 to 8000 yuan. A Hangzhou e-commerce company saved 4 million yuan by cutting PMO, data, and test teams.

Tencent headquarters released internal notes on November 16 proposing accelerated organizational flattening. They stated that cadres who only pass on messages and occupy resources should not be obstacles. An International Labour Organization chief macroeconomist introduced the term verification tax for checking AI hallucinations. Ray Xian Sen says the real change is re-pricing people as either costs or assets. He believes value depends on taking responsibility for things AI cannot do.

New graduates are affected because companies now hire people who can take real responsibilities. Junior developers are decreasing in number while senior developers are increasing. People with three to five years of experience find the path upward has become narrower. Positions requiring over three years of experience now account for more than 70 percent. Recruitment for those with less than one year of experience decreased by about 20 percent.

The civil service examination relaxed age limits for the first time since 1994. Application limits moved from 35 to 38 years old for general applicants. Limits for fresh master and doctoral graduates moved from 40 to 43 years old. Over 20 provinces followed this loosening of the age rules. A cloud vendor now requires five years of experience instead of three for solution positions.

The articles leave open how many workers can successfully transition to roles requiring human judgment. They do not state if the civil service age relaxation will permanently solve youth unemployment. The text does not specify which other industries will follow the programming pyramid effect. It remains unclear how many companies will adopt the Tencent flattening model. The future safety line for employees depends on their ability to take overall charge.

stories.Headline: Anthropic plans a Nasdaq IPO to raise over 90 billion dollars for AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Anthropic plans to debut on the Nasdaq stock market this coming Thursday to test investor confidence in the global artificial intelligence boom. The five year old company develops the Claude family of models and expects the initial public offering to generate over 90 billion dollars. Technology companies are committing billions of dollars to the offering despite concerns over financing risks and the sustainability of the investment boom. This arrival occurs during a difficult moment for the sector following a decline in technology shares and a leadership crisis at Nvidia. The company reported a net loss of 104 billion dollars during the first nine months of 2026 but holds 132 billion dollars.

The offering price is expected to be 70 to 78 dollars per share with investments of 26 billion dollars from several major firms. These investors include Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, while Amazon holds a substantial stake. Anthropic has over 900 billion dollars in spending commitments, including 110 billion dollars with Amazon over 10 years and 400 billion dollars elsewhere. It will spend 125 billion to 150 billion dollars on Google chips by 2028 and lease a data centre starting 2027. Amazon also built an 11 billion dollar data centre in Indiana for Anthropic using custom chips, and Google guaranteed 19 billion dollars.

Anthropic stated in its prospectus that it previously underestimated computing requirements, which left the company short of capacity and affected product deployment. Joe Fath of Eclipse called the staggering numbers hard to wrap one's head around, while David Tollen called it smart investing. Subhadeep Chatterjee, a former Google executive, said that everybody knows Anthropic is going to be the future of the Google company. Broadcom provided a financial backstop with a maximum liability of 43 billion dollars to support the rental of artificial intelligence chips. Bank of America, Blackstone, Citigroup and Morgan Stanley offered 63 billion dollars to purchase the racks of chips that Anthropic will rent.

Corey Quinn of Duckbill questioned if the long agreements could remain unchanged, stating that anything past four years is like throwing darts. The Nasdaq fell 5.3 percent in October, which was its worst monthly performance since March 2025, adding pressure to debt heavy providers. Rising interest rates and new United States ballot measures could further restrict the development of new data centres across the entire country. Investors are also concerned by Nvidia, where shares fell 13 percent after chief executive Jensen Huang resigned following reports of extramarital affairs. Colette Kress was appointed interim chief executive after Huang was linked to a woman suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence.

The company is committing to infrastructure well in advance because it needs computing power to develop advanced models and expand its services. Cloud providers Amazon, Google and Microsoft account for 31 percent of the contractual obligations listed in the latest official company prospectus. Google is expected to hold an ownership stake of approximately 13 percent following the completion of the initial public offering process. The 10 year agreement with Amazon is twice the length of typical contracts, which has attracted questions about the financial exposure. These investments occur as the broader technology sector faces mounting pressure from indebted cloud infrastructure companies and volatile global stock market trends.

The initial public offering will provide funding for the computing infrastructure needed to operate advanced models and expand the company's current services. The articles leave open whether the long term infrastructure commitments and the 20 year data centre lease will remain financially sustainable. It remains uncertain if the arrangements with cloud providers will be renegotiated before the contracts expire as suggested by some industry experts. The market will see if the 90 billion dollar debut can redefine the scale of technology listings despite the current sector turmoil. Investors must wait to see if the calculated exposure to these staggering costs will result in the predicted future for Google.

stories.Headline: Chinese cement producers adopt AI and digital sensors to create smart green factories
stories.Summary:
Major Chinese cement producers are integrating artificial intelligence and digital sensors to transform their energy-intensive plants into smart, green factories. Anhui Conch Group Co., Ltd. in Wuhu, Anhui Province, now utilizes driverless trucks and real-time monitoring to optimize production and reduce environmental impact. This shift is part of a broader national drive to embed low-carbon technologies into traditional manufacturing across the country. Other industry leaders, including CR Cement and BBMG Jidong Cement Group Co., Ltd., are also implementing these advanced intelligent systems.

The transition requires the adoption of computer vision, predictive analytics, and natural language processing to manage the entire production chain. Anhui Conch Group Co., Ltd. collaborated with Huawei to develop an AI model covering 15 categories and over 200 potential scenarios. This system includes more than 40 mature applications, such as a clinker strength prediction model and a carbon capture project handling 50,000 tonnes of gas annually. Meanwhile, the Tongchuan plant of BBMG Jidong Cement Group Co., Ltd. has established a zero-employee production line with a daily capacity of 10,000 tonnes.

Company officials and industry experts believe these upgrades significantly improve efficiency and reduce coal consumption. Xu Yue, assistant general manager of Conch Cement, noted that predictive models allow operators to adjust kiln parameters in real time. Kong Xiangzhong, former executive president of the China Cement Association, stated that nearly 70 companies have become demonstration factories since 2021. Peng Shou, an academician of the Chinese Academy of Engineering, explained that policy and market forces are pushing the sector toward circular resource use.

This industrial evolution aligns with a government initiative where over 30 percent of large manufacturing firms adopted AI by the first half of this year. The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology reports that tens of thousands of smart factories have been built nationwide. The World Economic Forum recently recognized the Tianyang plant of CR Cement in Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region as the first lighthouse factory in the building materials sector. These developments signal a strategic transition toward higher-end products and lower carbon emissions for the entire industry.

Articles.Title: China's cement sector goes digital, green amid nationwide AI drive - Xinhua
