stories.Headline: Pierre du Preez says human-centered design counters AI blandness by making thinking collaborative and visible
stories.Summary:
Pierre du Preez, director of Notitia, wrote in an article published by IT Brief Australia on 19 November 2026 that human-centered design is the antidote to what he called "AI blandness." He said AI works well for known solutions to known problems, where the requirement is well documented and understood. He said that as requirements become less straightforward, solutions become less defined and innovation becomes key. He defined innovation as the practical implementation of new ideas, methods or products that create measurable value, solve problems or improve efficiency. He said AI is becoming inward-looking, rehashing the same content with variation driven only by how the prompt is written.

He said this generates increasingly bland output of ever diminishing value. He said innovation begins at the discovery phase, including the context of the requirement and what is actually needed in the context of the business. He said this includes how the requirement affects the rest of the business and the practical people and process implications to deliver it. He said humans are very good at innovation and largely responsible for all innovation in recorded history, save for a few happy accidents. He said innovation comes from inspired leaps of understanding that bring loosely connected ideas and threads together to create something new.

He said discussion, exploration of ideas, challenging assumptions and arguing competing viewpoints evolve both the requirement and the solution, especially in complex, overlapping or interconnected problems. He said the most effective approach is where the requirement and solution are developed together, with time and environment allowing the best overall solution to be reached by the humans who require and use it. He said this human-centered approach can be very effective for solutions required to operate across departments, complex solutions, solutions that have failed before, solutions driven by material changes in operating environment, systems or competitive environment, and prior to a major software buy or build decision. He said a very clear understanding of future requirements at that stage reduces the risk of an expensive software project that isn't fit for purpose and ultimately fails. He said human-centered design is a collaborative approach to problem-solving that involves the people who experience, understand or are affected by a problem.

He said the process brings people together to create an agreed upon solution. He said incorporating the design of the solution into the outcome, capturing the workflow, practical real world use and look and feel, lets the result serve as a design specification, changing "Can it do X?" to "We need X to be done this way." He said human-centered design can include facilitated workshops, interviews, user persona creation, process mapping, and prototyping or iterative wireframing. He said its purpose is to make people's internal knowledge of how the business works visible, challenge assumptions, and develop a shared understanding of the problem before choosing or building a solution.

He said it confirms at a practical, day-in-the-life level what is actually required to deliver an outcome. He said the valuable part is the interaction, where people challenge assumptions, explain why something works the way it does, add context and practical experiences, make connections and reach decisions together. He said that context is often where the real insight sits and is very difficult to recover once flattened into a generic brief or fed into an AI tool without sufficient thought. He said the risk of AI is not simply that organisations will begin producing similar-looking strategies, but that we substitute pre-generated outputs for the harder process of drawing out the knowledge, experience and judgement of people. He said human-centered design is an antidote to "AI blandness" because it makes the thinking collaborative and visible and allows a better, practical solution to be developed.

He said reducing the uncertainty from the cost of developing a solution is achieved through a robust requirements confirmation process. He said mapping out requirements with human-centered design creates practical outputs that confirm in absolute detail what is required by a user or team to deliver an outcome. He said this output, in the form of mock-ups and wireframes, allows a day-in-the-life walk-through of the proposed solution, uncovering inconsistencies, missing or overlapping authority, data or other departmental or workflow dependencies. He said the approach ensures the solution meets both individual and organisational objectives and is fit for purpose in the context of the organisation. He said the output allows more informed decisions on collaboration, cost, planning of a Minimum Viable Product and additional phases, and buy-in from executives or key users.

He said clients told Notitia the design process allowed them to better "understand how other departments use our data" and how the organisation uses data for its mission. He said clients described the approach as low stress and said it allowed them time to work through the changes they needed to make to "deliver better outcomes for our customers." He said clients reported a more intuitive and effective solution that aligns with their day-to-day workflow. He said clients described the booking and appointments process as super easy and a stress-free exercise for their customers, with clear feedback and proactive status updates. He said clients described the solution as "sophisticated and elegant" and said it "nailed the brief."

He said Notitia uses human-centered design to work through complex requirements by creating a collaborative environment for discovery and innovation. He said this delivers a detailed design specification with context to allow a deliberate assessment of strategic options, build versus buy versus augmenting existing systems, as well as tactical options such as which solutions to assess if buying. He said human-centered design ensures that the human remains fundamental to the process. The article carried no further statements on what happens next.

stories.Headline: IDC names Cloudinary a Leader in AI-enabled digital asset management for the second time
stories.Summary:
Cloudinary has been named a Leader in the IDC MarketScape for Worldwide AI-Enabled Digital Asset Management 2026, the second time it has received that ranking, according to IT Brief Australia. The assessment highlighted Cloudinary's combination of asset management, media delivery and activation, and it also cited the breadth of its API and extensibility tools, including REST APIs, SDKs, command-line tools, webhooks and user interface extensions. Digital asset management software helps companies organise, store and distribute images, video and other media across websites, apps, marketing systems and commerce platforms. Artificial intelligence has become a key focus for vendors as businesses look to manage larger volumes of content and automate more of the work around it.

IDC said Cloudinary's product was suited to organisations handling high volumes of image and video content and connecting digital asset management systems to wider business functions. Jordan Jewell, senior research director for content and digital experiences at IDC, said Cloudinary is well suited for midmarket and enterprise organizations with high volumes of image and video content that need to connect DAM directly to commerce, marketing, product content, and digital experience delivery. The report also said Cloudinary stands out for combining asset management with dynamic media delivery and activation, and it added that the company shows notable depth in API coverage and extensibility. More than 4.5 million developers and 14,000 customers use its platform, according to the company, which lists customers including Adidas, Etsy, Grubhub, Mattel, Minted, Paul Smith and Zalando.

Cloudinary also says it works with more than 300 partners, integrations and plug-ins. Rob Daynes, vice president of global new business at Cloudinary, said the company viewed the ranking as recognition of a broader shift in how businesses use digital asset management. He said Cloudinary was proud to be named a Leader by IDC MarketScape for the second time, and that he believes it reflects what DAM has become, which he described as a business-critical content operations engine. He said that when teams can manage, transform, and deliver images and video from one platform, at any scale and alongside AI agents, they create visual experiences that engage and convert across every channel.

The latest ranking comes as software suppliers across the content and marketing stack push AI-based features into their products. In digital asset management, that includes tools for tagging, searching, transforming, routing and delivering visual content, as well as support for automated workflows. Cloudinary sells software for managing and delivering image and video content, an area that sits between content operations, eCommerce and digital marketing, and businesses use these systems to maintain a central library of approved assets while adapting files for different devices, channels and customer experiences. That ecosystem matters in a market where buyers often want digital asset management software to connect with content management systems, retail platforms, product information tools and internal workflows.

Articles.Title: Cloudinary named a leader in IDC AI asset management - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Interpreters, designers and voice actors lose work to AI and fight back
stories.Summary:
Berlin interpreter Sara Campos recently lost a longtime client to AI, according to a DW report published on November 21, 2026. The company switched to AI because it is cheaper and can translate into several languages at once. Graphic designer Adrian Romero helped introduce AI tools at his agency, and then he lost his job. After six months of job hunting, he is now moving to an insurance company.

Voice actor Matti Klemm is taking legal action against Netflix, claiming his voice was used to train AI without his permission. As AI reshapes creative work, many people are asking what is left for humans. Interpreters, designers and voice actors fear AI could replace them, and they are fighting back. The report does not say what the legal action seeks or when it was filed.

The articles do not name who is responsible beyond the companies involved, and they do not give direct statements from Campos, Romero or Klemm. The report frames the changes as part of a broader shift in creative work rather than a single event. It does not say what happens next in Klemm's case or how the others' stories end. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Karnataka hosts nearly half of India's AI centres of excellence, Zinnov-KDEM report finds
stories.Summary:
Karnataka hosts more than 120 artificial intelligence and machine learning Centres of Excellence across over 100 global capability centres, which amounts to nearly half of India's AI and machine learning CoE base, according to a Zinnov-KDEM report. That network is around four times the size of the next-largest hub in the country, and one in three of these centres now works on generative AI or agentic AI mandates. These centres help global capability centres develop AI products and platforms for global enterprises. The report was published on 19 November 2026.

Karnataka is home to 1,088 global capability centres, or 51% of India's total, including 320 Global 2000 centres, the report says. Between FY2021 and FY2026E the state added 90 software and internet global capability centres, accounting for 51% of India's additions. The state also has 111,000 global capability centre AI and machine learning professionals, or 43% of the national total. India's global capability centre ecosystem has 1.1 million emerging tech professionals and 259,000 AI and machine learning professionals, representing 47% and 11% of total global capability centre headcount.

In Karnataka, emerging-tech talent makes up 54% of global capability centre employees, while AI and machine learning professionals account for 13%, and the state has 451,000 emerging-tech professionals, or 41% of India's global capability centre pool. Nitika Goel, CMO and Managing Partner at Zinnov, said in the report that the industry is now in a third wave, which she called Value 2.0, where value is measured by AI itself, not by pilots and proofs of concept but by large-scale enterprise value created and deployed in production. The report identified four drivers of Karnataka's AI position: global capability centre ownership of AI architecture and platforms, specialist talent and leadership, dedicated centres of excellence, and an ecosystem of start-ups, investors, research institutions and policy support. Surveyed Karnataka global capability centres scored 1.12 times India's average in AI maturity.

Bengaluru's AI hiring intensity reached 13.6% of global capability centre job postings in 2026, against 9.8% at the same companies' offices elsewhere in India, and around 69% of surveyed Karnataka global capability centres provide role-specific AI training, compared with 53% nationally. Between 2024 and 2026, GitHub Copilot's share of AI-related postings grew 26 times, prompt engineering 8.1 times, LangChain 7.8 times, and Vertex AI six times. The centres are applying AI across software development, finance, chip design, retail, telecom, industrial maintenance, healthcare, and IT services. The report describes a cycle in which AI talent attracts global mandates, which in turn creates demand for specialist engineers and architects.

stories.Headline: Wadhwani AI and LinkedIn launch a 12-month programme to train 2,000 Northeast India entrepreneurs in AI
stories.Summary:
Wadhwani AI and LinkedIn signed a memorandum of understanding to launch a programme called AI for Future SMEs, which will train 2,000 small and micro entrepreneurs across Northeast India in using artificial intelligence for their businesses. The partnership was announced in an article published by Analytics India Magazine on 19 November 2026, and the initiative is set to run for 12 months. The programme covers five states, namely Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Meghalaya and Manipur, and it targets businesses in sectors such as handloom, handicrafts, bamboo, food processing, tourism and agriculture-linked activities. The training is meant to help these entrepreneurs build digital skills and apply AI tools in everyday tasks including marketing, customer communication and inventory management.

The curriculum is divided into two tracks, with the first covering foundational AI and digital literacy, including machine learning, generative AI, prompt engineering and responsible AI practices, as well as privacy, misinformation and digital safety. The second track focuses on applying generative AI to small-business operations, ranging from market research to workflow automation, and the training will include practical examples of creating product catalogues, developing social media campaigns, researching competitors and engaging with customers. To reach entrepreneurs in areas with limited connectivity, the initiative will use a mobile-first learning model, open-source AI tools and offline-friendly materials, alongside classroom sessions and continued mentorship with content adapted to local business needs. Participants will present their work through a project showcase and receive joint certification, and the organisations will assess changes in digital fluency, understanding of responsible AI, confidence in using the technology and adoption of AI tools through baseline and endline evaluations.

Shekar Sivasubramanian, Head of Wadhwani AI, said in a statement that AI can become a meaningful growth enabler for small businesses when it is practical, accessible and rooted in real economic needs, and he said the partnership with LinkedIn aims to bridge the digital gap by equipping entrepreneurs with practical, business-focused AI capabilities that can be applied immediately. Kumaresh Pattabiraman, Country Manager of LinkedIn India, said the Northeast is home to a new wave of entrepreneurs building businesses rooted in the region's craft, culture and communities, and he said the partnership will help them use AI to reach new customers, run their businesses more efficiently and grow well beyond their local markets. The article does not name any other officials or give any further statements from the two organisations about the programme. It also does not say what happens after the 12-month period ends or whether the initiative will be extended to other regions.

stories.Headline: French health data chief says hospitals worldwide cannot measure whether medical AI improves patient outcomes
stories.Summary:
Emmanuel Bacry, Scientific Director of France’s Health Data Hub, said at the Bengaluru Tech Summit on November 20, 2026, that hospitals worldwide are ill-equipped to assess whether artificial intelligence systems deployed in their facilities actually improve patient outcomes. He estimated that there are perhaps only six or seven hospitals in the whole world today that are able to evaluate medical devices deployed in their systems. Hospitals struggle to access and integrate patient information to track outcomes after discharge, including recovery rates and mortality, which makes it difficult to establish the real impact of AI-based medical technologies. He said hospitals do not know how to compute the return on investment of such technologies, and asked what would happen if they adopted AI.

Mr. Bacry cited an alert system based on rules-based AI, or an expert system, designed to warn intensive care unit staff about severe kidney failure. Despite functioning effectively, the system was associated with a doubling of deaths in two of the six US hospitals where it was deployed in 2022, and he did not identify the study. While researchers had offered hypotheses, the precise cause remained unknown, and he suggested that the absence of a tested response protocol among hospital personnel could have contributed. He said replacing a human alert with a device alert changes the whole thing, and stressed integrating AI into clinical workflows rather than treating it as a standalone technology. He also cautioned against judging diagnostic AI tools solely by laboratory accuracy, saying a system with 95% accuracy against a doctor’s 90% might not perform better in clinical settings, and that once deployed in real life those scores can be forgotten.

He flagged that AI systems can identify patterns even their developers cannot explain, citing research in which one model predicted ethnicity from chest X-rays with approximately 85% accuracy and another inferred sex from eye images with 95% accuracy. Such hidden correlations could influence medical decisions without clinicians understanding the basis, potentially introducing unintended bias into diagnosis and treatment. In a separate interaction with The Hindu, he warned that healthcare AI development is heavily skewed towards Western populations, estimating that nearly 70% of global healthcare AI training data came from male, white and Western populations. He said the field is developing an Occidental AI and even narrow types of Occidental AI, and advocated smaller, locally tailored models trained on representative population data, arguing that deploying large general-purpose models without adaptation could have disastrous consequences, particularly in developing countries. Mr. Bacry heads the Health Data Hub, established under French law in 2019 to facilitate secondary use of health data for research, and is also a research director at France’s National Centre for Scientific Research at Université Paris Dauphine, PSL.

stories.Headline: Vectorial AI models 2.5 million users with SAPIENS to test products before launch
stories.Summary:
Vectorial AI, a startup founded in 2024 and headquartered in San Francisco with a 12-member team across the US and India, has built a model called SAPIENS that creates virtual representations of target audiences so product, design and marketing teams can test ideas before launch, and it raised $3 million in seed funding in October 2026 from SenseAI Ventures, Smilegate and investors associated with the Berkeley and Stanford ecosystems. The company says it has modelled more than 2.5 million users, including 500,000 in India, and run more than 30,000 simulations, and it reports that SAPIENS is 87% accurate in predicting behaviour and has matched previous customer research by 85 to 95% in some comparisons. The founders began exploring commercial uses in 2024, worked with design partners from mid-2025 and launched in January 2026, and SAPIENS began as a question-and-answer interface that worked like a focus group with a simulated audience before expanding to let businesses test software interfaces, physical product concepts and advertising campaigns. Its announced customers include boAt, GoodRx, Suki AI, MIDI Health and Concrete Software, and it targets healthcare, gaming and technology companies building software products and digital experiences. Co-founder and CEO Taranveer Singh, who spent the last 10 years modelling human behaviour and worked with Andrew Ng's team at Coursera while at Carnegie Mellon University before joining Berkeley AI Research as a visiting research fellow, says a traditional study can take three to 12 weeks depending on scope and that user research becomes a bottleneck as AI speeds up product development.

Singh says some companies skip research because of time or cost, which he said can waste millions of dollars on failed products, and he argues that simulations can replace conventional research for many decisions while still encouraging calibration against live participants. He says the company encourages customers to run studies with live people during the calibration phase so it can show how accurate it is, and he insists that it is not making up users but modelling real people against real behavioural data. Jasmine Kaur, the chief business officer, graduated from Stanford Graduate School of Business and worked on synthetic users for marketing at Pfizer, while Rahul Garg, the chief product officer, has worked in product leadership at Blinkit and Housing.com and on a behaviour graph for sales conversations at Zime AI. SAPIENS is built on behavioural data from partners and AI-moderated interviews with paid participants, which the company uses to profile how people behave across locations, lifestyles and income groups, and Vectorial aims to deliver feedback within hours at around one-twentieth of the cost of a conventional study, charging a base platform fee to develop an audience model and then running additional simulations. Researchers remain cautious, with a 2026 survey by User Interviews finding that 47% were sceptical and wanted more evidence and 88% cited quality and accuracy of insights as a concern, and Singh notes that it is one thing to have a model accurate sometimes for some audiences but another to have it accurate in all possible scenarios a customer can influence.

Vectorial addresses this with a broader pipeline of behavioural data and a calibration period that compares simulated responses against previous studies and interviews with real people, gathering more data where it finds gaps. Its competitors include Maze and UserTesting along with AI-moderated research companies Listen Labs and Outset AI, and Singh says AI-moderated interviews can accelerate research but are limited to about 100 people and each new question requires a new study, whereas Vectorial keeps a model of the audience that customers can query repeatedly. Vectorial will use the seed funding to develop SAPIENS 2.0, expand behavioural data partnerships and invest in product-led growth, and its tools include a Chrome Web Store beta and a Figma plugin, with an MCP server planned so compatible AI tools can interact with simulated audiences. The company adds around five customers per quarter and expects that to accelerate, with a lower-cost product for individual developers planned, and it is targeting double-digit million-dollar revenue by the end of 2027 while not having disclosed its current revenue or run rate. Singh says that when the company first pitched SenseAI Ventures, the firm clearly understood that Vectorial is a category creator and that behaviour models and simulations are going to be the new way to build and launch products.

stories.Headline: Infosys invests JPY 1.59 billion for a 10.1% stake in NTT DOCOMO Playspace joint venture
stories.Summary:
Infosys said on 19 November 2026 that its Singapore subsidiary, Infosys Singapore Pte Ltd, would enter into a joint venture agreement with the Japanese telecommunications company NTT DOCOMO, and that it would invest JPY 1.59 billion, or about ₹92.75 crore, in the venture called NTT DOCOMO Playspace. Under the deal, Infosys will acquire a 10.1% stake in the joint venture and serve as its technology and AI partner, according to the company's exchange filing. The investment will also give Infosys the right to nominate one director to the board of the joint venture. The venture will focus on developing metaverse-based experiences, digital twins and virtual commerce, and it aims to build a virtual economic ecosystem in Japan that connects immersive digital experiences with businesses and real-world commerce.

Infosys would contribute its AI engineering capabilities alongside its Topaz and Metaverse Foundry capabilities to the partnership. The company did not disclose the venture's expected revenue, its commercial launch timeline or its projected financial returns. Infosys also did not specify which businesses or customers the NTT DOCOMO venture would initially target, or how it plans to generate revenue from its virtual ecosystem. The venture's virtual commerce focus comes as AI agents begin to take on more tasks in online shopping, an emerging model called agentic commerce in which AI agents handle product discovery, checkout and payments with user consent.

The investment comes as Infosys expands its AI partnerships, having partnered with OpenAI in April to deploy the latter's Codex coding agent across enterprise workflows, combining it with Infosys Topaz for software engineering, legacy system modernisation and DevOps automation. In March, Infosys expanded its collaboration with Intel to help enterprises move AI projects from pilot stages into production. Digital twins are also finding applications outside conventional enterprise software, and in February The ePlane Company announced plans to develop a digital twin of its electric air taxi using NVIDIA Omniverse to simulate flight conditions, aerodynamic interactions and aircraft systems before physical testing. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the signing of the joint venture agreement.

stories.Summary:
AI healthtech startup August AI has raised $12 Mn from Accel, Peak XV Partners, and Claypond Capital to expand its healthcare assistant in the US. Founder and CEO Anuruddh Mishra announced the fundraise on social media alongside the rollout of the new capabilities. August AI previously raised $3 Mn in seed funding from Accel and Claypond Capital in October 2025.

The $12 Mn fundraise is from Accel, Peak XV Partners, and Claypond Capital, the family office of Manipal Group chairman Ranjan Pai. The new capabilities are available in beta in the US, with users able to join a waitlist for access. He said it can also call nearby pharmacies to compare medicine availability and prices, review medical bills for potential errors and savings, and follow up with insurers and hospitals on denied claims. stories.Headline: Baker Tilly's Millet says AI amplifies poor data hygiene without regular cleanup
stories.Summary:
Chris Millet, managing director of digital advisory services for the NetSuite practice of Top 10 firm Baker Tilly, spoke at the Finance and Accounting Technology Expo in New York. He said AI tools without a strong data foundation can amplify the classic garbage-in-garbage-out problem for data analysis. He said AI just reports what it is given and can technically learn bad habits if not trained appropriately. He said this includes all the errors in a dataset. Chris Gaetano reported the remarks for Accounting Today on November 19, 2026.

Millet raised the example of a vendor master record, which he said commonly has data hygiene issues. A record might contain duplicate vendors, which can lead to the wrong people being paid or the right people being paid improperly. Duplicates can also kneecap spend analysis because the AI will treat the same company as separate ones. Another common issue is inconsistent general ledger mapping, meaning the organization cannot map expenses to the right accounts, which will impede AI automation. Outdated information can lead to errors and disconnected systems that gum up workflows.

Millet said AI can amplify these problems and lead to recurring costs for the organization, and it will get worse the longer it goes on. He said it will learn patterns of inconsistent coding, so the more you use the automation the worse the problem gets. He said AI can also get you out of the mess, provided an organization approaches things deliberately and methodically and with plenty of human supervision. He recommended running datasets through an AI hygiene analysis, instructing the model to look for missing, incorrect, outdated or incomplete data. He said the user can then tell the agent to go fix the dataset if confident about the agentic AI work.

Millet said this should be done across multiple systems, ranging from AP to bank recs and anywhere else clean data is especially important. He said it should be done again and again because even clean data can get dirty over time. He equated data hygiene cleanliness checking to inventory counts, something you do not do once at the end of the year but constantly stay up on. He said it is something an organization could do every 90 days to help build and maintain a good data foundation. He said the process would first involve profiling and prioritizing what is most valuable for cleanup and assigning an owner for each dataset who is ultimately responsible for its accuracy.

Millet said the organization should then review the data in the most important set, cleaning files to get rid of duplicates or inaccuracies while filling in missing information. He said controls should then be put in place to make it easier the next time and to keep data AI-ready between cleanups. He said the controls include named ownership so each domain has an owner responsible for the dataset's accuracy, who could be a vendor, a processor, a controller or someone else. He said the controls also include consistent rules for data entry such as required fields, continuous monitoring of the dataset, and maintenance of a proper audit trail that includes not just the numbers but the context and logic behind them. He said the organization should then move on to the next set and do it again, and when finished with all the sets, prepare for the next cleanup.

Millet repeatedly stressed the importance of doing this regularly versus annually or only when things get dire. He said this is never done, that you cleanup once and automatically start again. He said that while AI can automate much of the data cleanup process, it is important to assign the proper level of automation to each step. He said an AI might fix a simple typo automatically, but for more important changes it needs to ping the human for confirmation. He said there are certain tasks, such as changing bank or remittance details, that AI should never do, and that automated processes always have to happen within an agreed-upon rule.

stories.Headline: India's NIA conference closes with sessions on drones, crypto and AI misuse in terrorism
stories.Summary:
India's National Investigation Agency held its sixth anti-terror conference on November 19 and 20 at DRDO Bhawan in New Delhi, organised around the theme of cross-border terrorism, and it concluded on Friday with discussions dominated by drones, cryptocurrencies, radicalisation and the misuse of artificial intelligence. NIA Director General Rakesh Aggrawal told reporters that the first technical session dealt with the nexus between organised crime and terrorism, with particular emphasis on the threat posed by drones, which he described as a very low-cost but highly effective tool for transporting narcotics, arms, cash and explosives. He said shooting such drones down was an asymmetric situation because of their low cost, and that the challenge was to develop an effective mechanism to block unauthorised drones from entering the country, similar to physical barriers that stop people from crossing the border. Punjab has faced the maximum drone threat, with the highest number of drone crossings recorded in the state, he said. The second session focused on radicalisation, particularly the use of online platforms to spread extremist content, and Aggrawal highlighted radicalising material available on platforms including Facebook, Meta, Telegram and Signal, besides other websites and open-source material.

He said magazines and newsletters published by terrorist groups, along with glorification of their activities or exaggerated accounts of atrocities against some people, were also being projected on these platforms, and that radicalisation also took place through physical means such as gatherings and through prisons being used for networking. The third session covered cross-border terror financing, with a focus on the challenges posed by cryptocurrencies, which he said are difficult to crack and can conceal the identities of senders and receivers without leaving any trail. The fourth session was on international cooperation, where Aggrawal said India had achieved good successes in securing the return of fugitives from other countries, with 303 brought back since 1999, including 72 so far this year, against 69 in 2025, 43 in 2024, 37 in 2023, 40 in 2022, 23 in 2021, 8 in 2020 and 11 in 2019. Aggrawal said the fifth session was on the use of technology in countering cross-border terror offences, particularly artificial intelligence, and discussions covered the use of AI by terrorist groups and law enforcement agencies to counter propaganda as well as challenges related to SIM cards.

He said securing international cooperation remained a technical subject involving formal mechanisms of mutual legal assistance requests and letters rogatory, and that discussions were held on how to use these channels more effectively. Union Home Minister Amit Shah attended two technical sessions, one on the nexus between organised crime and terrorism and the other on the use of technology to counter cross-border terrorism, and he inaugurated the conference in the presence of Minister of State for Home Bandi Sanjay Kumar and Union Home Secretary Govind Mohan. The conference was attended by 40 DGs and heads of state police and central agencies and 230 participants from anti-terror investigation units of the states, according to an NIA statement. It concluded with a renewed commitment to strengthening India's collective counter-terrorism architecture through closer coordination between central and state agencies, intelligence-led investigations and effective prosecution of terror cases, the statement said.

stories.Headline: Acceldata expects agentic AI products to grow three times faster than its core data business
stories.Summary:
Acceldata, a Campbell, California-based startup that sells data observability software to enterprises, expects its agentic AI offerings to grow faster than the core products it launched with in 2018, according to chief executive Rohit Choudhary. Choudhary said he would not be surprised if the AI offerings grow at three to three and a half times year over year. Data observability remains Acceldata's core business and is still growing at 100% year on year, though it is a relatively smaller market. Founded in 2018, the company initially started with a suite of products that provided visibility into enterprises' data lakes, helping businesses monitor the accuracy and reliability of their data. Since the beginning of 2025, Acceldata has also been adding agentic AI observability to its product suite.

According to Mordor Intelligence, the data observability market is estimated to be worth $3.5 billion this year and is projected to reach $6 billion by 2031, at a compound annual growth rate of 11.4%. In comparison, agent observability and data governance together are estimated to be a $1 billion market in 2026 but are expected to grow to $8.6 billion by 2031, at a CAGR of 38.6%. Acceldata was founded in 2018 and raised $2 million in seed funding, then raised $8.5 million two years later in a round led by Sorenson Capital, with participation from Emergent Ventures, Lightspeed and Freshworks founder Girish Mathrubootham. In 2021 it raised $35 million from Insight Partners, with March Capital joining its cap table, and in 2023 it raised $50 million in a round led by March Capital, followed by another $10 million in a round led by Prosperity7 Ventures.

The company was last valued at between $351 million and $360 million, according to several media reports. Choudhary said every Indian company is concerned about such kinds of attack vectors and that the heightened level of sensitivity is causing people to purchase really rapidly right now. He said Indian enterprise clients are now willing to pay the same rates the company commands in the US, adding that the numbers are matching at this point and that he would not have been able to say this five years ago, though he declined to provide a range for Acceldata's average contract sizes. He said traditional companies have put in effort into digitising their operations, and that this is now being followed by their efforts into putting it all into AI.

The demand is being driven by security concerns around agentic AI, which is widely seen as the next step in the evolution of AI, with systems that can set goals, reason through multi-step problems, use tools and take autonomous actions with minimal human supervision. OpenAI's agents broke into Hugging Face, a platform that allows users to share datasets and machine-learning models, in July, and its rival Anthropic has also recorded at least three publicly announced security incidents that took place that month. Earlier this week, the Google Threat Intelligence Group said its analysts had identified what they described as the first fully autonomous cyberattack carried out by artificial intelligence. On 22 May this year, Mint had reported that India's business-to-business AI startups were beginning to see a surge in business as enterprises race to deploy the technology into their ecosystems, a marked shift from previous years when startups would often struggle with long sales cycles with clients in India.

stories.Headline: KPMG trials over 100 AI agents on a UK-listed company audit
stories.Summary:
EY rolled out enterprise-scale agentic AI across its Assurance division in April 2026, built with Microsoft technology and plugged into a global audit platform that reportedly processes more than 1.4 trillion lines of journal-entry data each year. Deloitte followed on 24 June with a linked network of agents inside its Omnia platform, which handles early-stage chores such as scraping data, sifting through evidence and writing first-draft paperwork. KPMG then ran a live trial called Project Exponential in November, putting more than 100 AI agents to work alongside humans on the audit of an unnamed UK-listed company. PwC US took a different route, focusing on training more than 85,000 employees to interrogate AI outputs rather than simply accept them. KPMG plans to expand its agent approach to as many as 20 larger audits, while every tentative finding from the Deloitte agents is routed to a human professional for a reality check.

PwC's Critical Thinking and Judgment certificate programme starts in December with a target of June 2027, and it is built to sharpen employees' ability to challenge what AI tells them. Across the firms the official line stays the same: algorithms do the legwork, but humans still carry the legal liability and sign the opinion. The companies say they are not trying to have AI issue audit opinions, and the UK's Financial Reporting Council has warned that sharing AI-derived insights with audit clients can threaten an auditor's objectivity and independence. KPMG's trial showed the agents are not flawless, because one agent could not match regulations to the documents it was checking, which is why people stay in charge of the result. The firm also found that the bots occasionally asked more probing questions and dug deeper into tricky financial details than the humans in the room, though the pilot ran alongside a traditional audit with reviewers checking every conclusion.

PwC's stated worry behind its training programme is over-reliance, since AI is fast, fluent and extremely sure of itself even when its output is incomplete or flat-out wrong. An auditor who takes a confident answer at face value without enough evidence is quietly wearing down the scepticism an opinion depends on, and junior work is shifting toward reviewing and interpreting whatever the agents produce. The Big Four are working to a simple rule for now, in which the agent drafts and the human signs, and KPMG's plan to move to as many as 20 larger audits will test how far that rule goes when the workload gets heavier. There is no evidence yet that these digital assistants are cutting client bills or thinning out audit teams, and the loud emphasis on human oversight hints that the industry still does not trust algorithms to master audit evidence, independence and healthy scepticism on their own. The next round of audits will show how quickly that doubt starts to melt away.

stories.Headline: Blue J signs multi-year deal to bring AI tax research to Deloitte Canada
stories.Summary:
Blue J announced a multi-year enterprise agreement with Deloitte Canada on November 19, 2026, to deliver AI-powered tax research capabilities across Canada. The Toronto, Ontario, Canada company said the deal deepens its relationship with Deloitte Canada through content and MCP integration. The agreement re-engineers the practitioner experience across Deloitte Canada's tax practice. Blue J's purpose-built AI-powered tax research solution is trusted by more than 6,500 organizations worldwide. Deloitte Canada announced the deal on Thursday, according to The Logic.

The collaboration equips Deloitte Canada's multidisciplinary team of over 1,500 Tax & Legal professionals serving governments, corporations, Indigenous communities, nonprofit and private organizations. Select Deloitte Canada proprietary research and knowledge content, excluding client-specific information, will be integrated directly into Deloitte's practitioner experience through the Blue J platform. MCP integration will let Blue J connect within Deloitte's proprietary connected practitioner experience, bringing together research tools, tailored agentic workflows, and over 150 Deloitte-built codified skills and sub-agents for all Deloitte tax practitioners. The partnership gives Deloitte Canada's 150 internal AI tools access to Blue J's tax library and lets Blue J generate responses tailored to Deloitte's standards. No client-specific information will change hands, the companies said.

Benjamin Alarie, CEO and Co-Founder of Blue J, said tax is complex, global and high-stakes, and professionals need clarity they can stand behind. Alarie said Deloitte Canada's tax practice has been a clear market leader in transforming how practitioners and clients experience tax outcomes. He said Blue J has been excited to work with Deloitte over the years, calling the firm a great product collaborator that helped define many experiences enabled on Blue J. Alarie said he believes custom, fact-based content is becoming the trade secret that sets some AI apart. Stephen Lopes, Tax Technology Commercialization Leader for Deloitte Canada, said Deloitte is deliberate in how it adopts AI, particularly in high-stakes areas like tax where accuracy and defensibility are paramount.

Lopes said that after seeing the impact on research efficiency and confidence in practice, expanding Blue J to create a more unified practitioner experience anchored on proprietary IP was a natural next step. He said Deloitte is proud to support and collaborate with a Canada-based AI company setting the global standard for responsible, domain-specific AI in tax. Jean-Luc Ratté-Boulianne, chief technology officer for Deloitte Canada's tax and legal division, said the firm increasingly turns down tech tools and prioritizes AI companies that connect into its existing systems. Ratté-Boulianne said that even if a product is great, if it does not offer integration as a feature, Deloitte more and more says thanks but no thanks. He said Deloitte wants authoritative data sources, which is what Blue J does out of the box, and does not want to add more tools.

The collaboration follows Blue J's US$176M Series E funding round in November 2026, led by JMI Equity, a leading growth equity investment firm. Annual recurring revenue grew 165% in the 15 months after Blue J's 2025 Series D, and more than 6,500 organizations now use Blue J, including Big Four firms and Fortune 100 companies. Blue J has doubled its team over the past year and expects to exceed 200 employees by year-end. In October, Blue J partnered with Legora to bring its tax research into Legora's agentic operating system for legal work, used by more than 140,000 legal professionals. Blue J was founded in 2015 and is trusted by more than 45,000 tax professionals at over 6,500 organizations, including leading law firms, Big Four accounting firms and Fortune 100 companies, with over 15 million tax questions answered to date.

Deloitte Canada has 181 years' worth of files, and Blue J keeps data processing in Canada at a time when Deloitte is getting more client inquiries about the issue, Ratté-Boulianne said. After allegations of AI hallucination flubs at several big professional services firms, including Deloitte, the firm has tightened controls around AI governance, training and accountability, Ratté-Boulianne said. Thomson Reuters is building custom products for law firm Skadden, while Intuit is working with Anthropic on a similar venture. Ratté-Boulianne said having one-of-a-kind software that relies on Deloitte's proprietary content and intellectual property gives Deloitte a leg up over competitors using the vanilla version of the technology. Alarie said he hopes the partnership makes it slightly easier for accountants to dig up information without feeling they are digging ditches by hand, and that a lot of tax professionals feel they do not see enough of their loved ones for a few months a year, a huge human cost.

The deal's dollar value was not disclosed. Blue J raised its Series E round last week before announcing the multi-year deal with Deloitte, The Logic reported. Alarie said the partnership is about making tax work more pleasant to do. Deloitte Canada calls the approach re-engineered and deliberate.

stories.Headline: AINU AI launches a creation platform to standardize short video production for e-commerce marketing
stories.Summary:
AINU AI launched a one-stop creation platform in September 2026 to help short video creators. The platform aims to turn viral hit videos into a standardized production pipeline for users. It focuses on the entire workflow from topic selection to final production for e-commerce marketing. This system integrates script writing and generation into one single interface for its users. The platform has already served 540,000 merchants and 2.2 million influencers globally.

The platform uses a Global Viral Data Dashboard to aggregate real time videos from TikTok, Douyin, and Xiaohongshu. It includes data from TikTok influencers like ash tervino vs bri and popular Douyin food accounts. The Script Master tool offers 8 built-in official preset skills and supports storyboard scheme output. Video generation is powered by models including Wan 3.0, Seedance 2.0, and Seedance 2.5. The system also provides specialized templates for clothing detail images and product selling point images.

The AINU AI team consists of nearly 100 members who manage core research and development. They stated that the platform is designed to enable one person to do the work of three. The team independently controls model iteration and computing power operation and maintenance for the system. They believe the next stage of competition lies in connecting the whole process from start to finish. This approach relies on a self-built computing power server room to support large-scale delivery.

E-commerce practitioners, individual merchants, and small teams are the primary groups targeted by this tool. These users prioritize a fast assembly line over having the single best generation model. Professional creators may still prefer single-point depth, which the platform might not provide in every link. The system affects how users create content for catering, entertainment, tourism, and domestic services. It allows visitors to create secondary works based on others' content via AINU TV.

The platform was built on existing industry content production experience and a large computing infrastructure. It has achieved a total accumulated content play volume of over 500 million views. The system supports an annual AI content production capacity of nearly 2 million hours. It differs from Kling, Jimeng, and Runway by focusing on workflow rather than just model capability. These other tools focus on character movement, ecological collaboration, or professional film and television post-production.

AINU AI will continue to bet on the workflow as generation capability becomes public infrastructure. The company must manage risks if upstream model providers tighten authorization or raise their prices. It remains to be seen if the platform can compete with editing software developers. The articles do not state how the platform will scale its user base further. They leave open whether the tool can achieve industry-leading performance in every single production link.

stories.Headline: U.N. talks extend debate on killer robots to 2028 without binding rules
stories.Summary:
Efforts to set firm rules on AI-powered killer robots and drones ran aground on Saturday when U.N.-backed talks in Geneva produced a softened agreement to extend discussions for two more years. Scores of countries ended the week-long U.N. conference on weapons by agreeing to elaborate a possible accord on lethal autonomous weapons systems by 2028. But they did not commit to the binding rules sought by U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres, many countries and activists. The outcome underscored the difficulty of achieving concrete results in diplomacy amid global conflicts and major military powers jockeying for dominance.

Before the meeting, seven countries proposed launching negotiations on a rulebook that could prevent or limit the ability of machines to kill without human control or accountability. That effort fell short, and the agreement instead calls for elaborating a possible accord by 2028 without binding rules. Izumi Nakamitsu, the U.N. high representative for disarmament affairs, hailed a significant achievement but acknowledged a glass half full or half empty scenario, citing Guterres' hopes for a legally binding deal this year. Guterres, who leaves office at the end of the year, had set a 2026 deadline for launching negotiations toward an agreement on autonomous weapons systems.

Activists accused military powers like Russia and the United States of blocking stronger language, and Stop Killer Robots lamented a watered-down mandate. Beatrice Fihn, founder of the international law advocacy group Lex International, said the decision amounts to pushing the can down the road for two more years. Max Tegmark, a machine learning specialist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and founder of the Future of Life Institute, said states have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about the issue for the 14th year while these weapons enable atrocities. Ambassador Frederico Meyer of Brazil, which joined Austria, Belgium, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama in proposing negotiations, said technology is moving faster than diplomacy and diplomats are very slow.

Advocacy groups bemoaned obstructionism largely by Russia, which, like other top AI weapons-developing countries such as the United States, wants a freer hand to develop such high-tech weapons. Pope Leo XIV and many advocacy and humanitarian groups have framed the issue as an existential debate, urging quick action to rein in AI weapons before they become too commonplace to regulate easily. Activists say armed drones that can independently strike targets have already been deployed in some select instances in conflict zones, but widespread rollout has not happened. The talks will continue for two more years under the softened agreement.

stories.Headline: Greenland starts bulk shipments of TMAH products to overseas advanced packaging supply chains
stories.Summary:
China's Greenland confirmed during earnings briefings on November 18 and 19, 2026, that its TMAH series products have entered the overseas advanced packaging supply chain. The company completed production-line testing and validation with international customers, passed system certification, and has now started bulk shipments. This expansion follows the company's successful entry into the supplier systems of various pan-semiconductor enterprises, including stable volume supply to customers located in Taiwan. These developments require Greenland to accelerate its new product expansion to meet changing market demands and build a diversified product matrix. The company has already achieved full-factory scale supply of strippers at the Yungu facility of Visionox and completed introduction at the new Hefei Guoxian high-generation OLED plant.

Additionally, Greenland serves as a strategic supplier to MetaX, providing semiconductor developers and diluents to power device makers. Meanwhile, ACM Research reported that new orders rose 147 percent year on year in the first three quarters, with orders in hand reaching 17.073 billion yuan, or approximately 2.6 billion dollars, as of September 29. Company representatives stated that they are focusing on independent research and development while remaining open to collaborations with partners who possess mature technologies. Greenland noted that its developers provide a stable base, while strippers and advanced packaging materials represent new growth directions for the business. ACM Research officials explained that Plant A at the Lingang R&D and Manufacturing Center is nearly at full capacity, and Plant B will begin production in the fourth quarter.

They believe that once both plants reach full output, they can support an annual output value of about 20 billion yuan, which is approximately 3.0 billion dollars. The growth of these companies is driven by the increasing demand for chips and new display devices fueled by artificial intelligence and the Internet of Things. Both firms are benefiting from a broader trend of domestic substitution and supply chain self-reliance within the Chinese semiconductor and display industries. ACM Research plans to ship more than 20 units of its upgraded high-temperature SPM cleaning system to multiple customers in 2026. The companies continue to navigate challenges such as long customer validation cycles and volatility in the global components market.

stories.Headline: SK Hynix invests 1.4 trillion won to support domestic semiconductor suppliers
stories.Summary:
SK Hynix announced that high-bandwidth memory helped push South Korean semiconductor exports to 42.8 percent of total exports from January to October. The company reported record third-quarter revenue of 104.6155 trillion won and an operating profit of 83.3338 trillion won during that period. South Korea became the fourth country to surpass one trillion dollars in annual exports after the United States, Germany, and China. Semiconductor exports jumped 257.5 percent in October alone to reach 56.7 billion dollars, which is the highest ever for that month. These results were driven by the spread of generative AI and the company's focus on advanced memory technology and supplier alliances.

The company will invest 1.4 trillion won over five years to support domestic suppliers of semiconductor materials, parts, and equipment. Trinity Fab, a shared test facility at the Yongin Semiconductor Cluster, will open in May 2027 with a 1,000-pyeong clean room. This 874.6 billion won project includes 55 tools, with SK Hynix contributing 443.2 billion won and the central government adding 373.6 billion won. Local governments will provide 57.7 billion won, while the facility incorporates the specific needs of 217 different materials, components, and equipment suppliers. SK Hynix also plans to invest 600 trillion won to construct four chip fabrication plants at the Yongin semiconductor cluster site.

A company official stated that reaching one trillion dollars in exports resulted from the solidarity of the entire South Korean ecosystem. The official said the company will work with partners to raise competitiveness, drive shared growth, and contribute to national exports. SK Hynix explained that producing top-tier memory requires converging supplier technologies in specialty chemicals, advanced packaging equipment, and precision metrology tools. The company aims to help smaller firms overcome financing and technology challenges through a program covering research, testing, production, and sales. They provide upfront support for early research costs and compensate suppliers even if a project does not meet its targets.

Smaller suppliers are affected because they can now validate new technologies in mass-production environments at a minimum actual maintenance cost. This facility is expected to lower the verification burden for companies that struggle to build their own expensive production equipment. The program also provides 2 trillion won in financing backed by the Korea Trade Insurance Corporation to help these domestic partners. Other support includes the Technology Innovation Company program, a Semiconductor Academy, and youth hiring-linked programs to strengthen the overall workforce. These initiatives aim to bolster the supply chain as competition intensifies within the global market for artificial intelligence chips.

SK Hynix developed the first high-bandwidth memory in 2013 using through-silicon via technology but initially struggled with high costs and demand. The company later applied its proprietary mass reflow-molded underfill process to HBM2E to solve productivity and heat issues for its customers. It expanded its lineup to HBM3, HBM3E, and HBM4, and began supplying samples of a 12-layer HBM4E product this year. In 2024, the firm developed DDR5 using a 10-nanometer-class sixth-generation process and mass-produced 321-layer NAND flash and SOCAMM2 DRAM modules. National semiconductor export shares grew from 15.6 percent in 2023 to 20.8 percent in 2024 and 24.4 percent last year.

The market expects demand for high-bandwidth memory to continue through next year, potentially accelerating the localization of the supply chain. Future export momentum depends on the pace of AI infrastructure investment and changes in the procurement plans of major customers. The technological self-reliance of the supplier ecosystem is another variable that will determine if the current growth trend can be maintained. If Trinity Fab begins operations as scheduled, equipment and materials companies will gain more opportunities for critical mass-production validation. The articles leave open how these variables and the global competition for AI chips will impact long-term semiconductor export figures.

stories.Headline: Kulicke and Soffa beats Q3 estimates and guides Q4 revenue above consensus on AI packaging demand
stories.Summary:
Kulicke and Soffa reported revenue for calendar Q3 2026, its fiscal Q4 2026, that beat Wall Street expectations, with sales up 131% year on year to $410.3 million against an S&P analyst consensus of $377.7 million, an 8.6% beat. The company also posted non-GAAP profit of $1.52 per share, which was 6.3% above the $1.43 consensus, and adjusted operating income of $96.5 million against analyst estimates of $93.23 million, a 3.5% beat at a 23.5% margin. Its operating margin came in at 21.2%, up from 0.5% in the same quarter last year, while inventory days outstanding fell to 101 from 120 in the previous quarter. The results were reported on 19 November 2026, and the company's market capitalization stood at $3.51 billion.

For the next quarter, Q4 CY2026, Kulicke and Soffa guided revenue to $410 million at the midpoint, which is above analyst estimates of $380 million and 7.9% higher than what analysts were expecting. It also guided adjusted EPS to $1.65 at the midpoint for Q4 CY2026, above analyst estimates of $1.43. Management said the outlook rests on expectations that AI-driven data center expansion and broader adoption of advanced packaging will remain robust, and it believes its expanded portfolio in thermal compression bonding and hybrid bonding positions it for technology transitions in memory and logic chips. The company plans to ship more than twice as many TCB systems as in the prior year, and it expanded its manufacturing footprint in Singapore to triple advanced solutions capacity, with factory utilization above 90%.

CEO Raj Talluri said the company expects to ship more than twice as many TCB systems as in the prior year, reflecting plans to increase capacity and respond to growing customer demand, while also acknowledging ongoing supply chain and investment requirements. Management attributed the quarter's performance to widespread demand in wire bonding, major traction in advanced solutions and improved operational leverage amid technology transitions, and it reported that approximately 75% of semiconductor package units deployed in data centers still rely on wire bonding. The company saw advanced solutions revenue nearly double over the past year, driven by adoption of fluxless thermal compression bonding and the launch of new panel-level packaging systems. Its wedge segment, which serves automotive and industrial markets, benefited from improving demand in power semiconductors and electric vehicle-related applications, with management noting sequential growth and signs of cyclical recovery even though these markets are not yet at long-term averages.

Investors reacted negatively despite the beat, as they scrutinized the sustainability of recent growth and the cyclical nature of the core businesses, and the stock traded at $63.03, down from $66.99 just before the earnings. Management was cautious about visibility beyond the next couple of quarters, citing the cyclical nature of the core wire bonding business, ongoing supply chain constraints and uncertainties in end-market demand, particularly outside of data center and memory. It also recognized that the timing of large panel tool adoption could be uneven, depending on customer readiness and technical challenges related to scaling. In upcoming quarters, attention will focus on the ramp and adoption of panel-level and hybrid bonding systems, sustained utilization and demand for wire bonding as AI infrastructure buildouts continue, and signs of recovery in automotive and industrial segments.

stories.Summary:
TradingView published a comparison of semiconductor stocks Onto Innovation and KLA Corporation on November 19, 2026. The report analyzes how both companies benefit from AI and advanced chip manufacturing. It examines their growth opportunities, business models, and current market valuations. The analysis focuses on the inspection and metrology equipment market. It evaluates which company offers a better investment opportunity for shareholders.

The global metrology market should grow from 16.26 billion dollars in 2026 to 29.57 billion dollars by 2034. Onto Innovation reported third quarter revenue of 410 million dollars and a backlog over 1.3 billion dollars. KLA Corporation reported fiscal first quarter revenue of 4.14 billion dollars and 1.34 billion dollars in free cash flow. KLA ended September 2026 with 4.74 billion dollars in cash and 5.72 billion dollars in debt. Onto Innovation expects Dragonfly platform revenue to increase more than 80 percent in 2026.

Onto Innovation management expects fourth quarter revenue between 430 million and 450 million dollars. They anticipate that growth from advanced logic, DRAM, and NAND nodes will exceed 35 percent in 2027. KLA management expects the wafer fabrication equipment market to exceed 200 billion dollars in calendar 2027. They target returning more than 90 percent of free cash flow to shareholders through 2030. KLA also aims for a gross margin of 63 to 64 percent in 2027.

Zacks Investment Research ranks KLA as a Buy while ranking Onto Innovation as a Hold. Investors are affected by Onto Innovation's high customer concentration, with four customers providing 57.1 percent of revenue. KLA shareholders received 936 million dollars in buybacks and 305 million dollars in dividends. Onto Innovation investors face risks from tariff uncertainty and rising costs for fuel and freight. KLA investors may see China revenue decline to the low 20 percent range by 2027.

The industry is driven by AI, high performance computing, and advanced packaging like 2.5D and 3D integration. Onto Innovation spent 45.1 million dollars on research and development in the third quarter. Its Semilab USA unit recorded an operating loss of 2.8 million dollars in that quarter. Onto Innovation also had a 40.8 million dollar unrealized loss on its Rigaku investment. KLA's process control services revenue grew 14 percent due to a larger installed base.

KLA expects advanced packaging revenue to reach approximately 1.1 billion dollars in 2027. Onto Innovation expects its Atlas G6 OCD platform to support sub 2nm technologies. KLA plans annual capital expenditures between 600 million and 800 million dollars for capacity expansion. The report leaves open whether Onto Innovation can sustain its improving margins. It also questions if the company can successfully convert its large backlog into revenue.

stories.Headline: Chinese chip firms import equipment via Singapore to bypass US export controls
stories.Summary:
Chinese semiconductor companies imported large volumes of manufacturing equipment from Singapore between January and July of this year to evade United States export controls. These imports reached 3.456 billion dollars across the production hubs of Shanghai, Beijing, and Anhui, which is double the amount recorded during the same period last year. This strategic shift caused the share of imports from the United States to plunge from 16.0 percent to 4.3 percent. The procurement network has expanded beyond back-end processes to include front-end tools like etching and deposition equipment.

The shift requires a reliance on Singapore-routed tools, including 1.9344 billion dollars in chemical vapor deposition equipment and 405.68 million dollars in physical vapor deposition tools. Imports of etching equipment rose 33 percent to 2.3376 billion dollars, while mounting and bonding tools increased fivefold to 6.39 million dollars. In Anhui Province, where ChangXin Memory Technologies is headquartered, the Singapore share of heat-treatment equipment soared from 3.9 percent in 2022 to 58.5 percent. These tools target the MR-MUF packaging process used by SK Hynix to lead the high-bandwidth memory market.

Analysts from the Korea Institute for International Economic Policy and university professors are responsible for these findings. Kim Hyung-jun stated that core equipment likely used circumvention channels because direct supplies from major companies were blocked. Bae Young-ja noted that circumvention trade through Southeast Asia expanded after United States controls tightened around 2022. Industry officials added that while Chinese memory currently lags South Korea by one to two generations, a strong domestic market could close that gap quickly.

This trend follows United States export controls that took full effect around 2022 to limit China's access to advanced logic chips. Singapore is now viewed as a substantive base for supplying core equipment, specifically through firms like ASMPT. ChangXin Memory Technologies is reportedly mass-producing its fifth-generation HBM3E product using these acquired technologies. The market now watches to see if the United States will tighten controls on these Southeast Asian circumvention channels.

stories.Headline: SemiFive and Preferred Networks stack DRAM on logic to create an AI inference chip alternative to HBM
stories.Summary:
South Korea's SemiFive and Japan's Preferred Networks collaborated to develop a new AI inference chip. These two companies showcased their joint effort known as the MN-Core L2000 project at the SC26 event in Chicago. This announcement took place on November 19, 2026, according to the report from Taipei. The project aims to provide a different approach to memory integration for artificial intelligence hardware. The design requires stacking DRAM directly above a logic die to improve efficiency.

This vertical arrangement changes the conventional 2.5D package layout where processors and HBM sit side by side. By moving the memory on top of the logic, the companies offer a viable alternative to high bandwidth memory. This structural shift is intended to optimize how data moves within the AI inference chip. The development is led by SemiFive and Preferred Networks, who are both seeking better hardware performance.

While the provided text does not include direct quotes, the companies presented the MN-Core L2000 as a solution for inference needs. They are positioning this technology to compete with the standard layouts used in current data center technology. The partnership combines South Korean and Japanese engineering to challenge existing semiconductor packaging norms. More to follow.

stories.Headline: TrendForce attributes falling NAND spot prices to weak smartphone and PC demand and module maker inventory clearance
stories.Summary:
NAND spot prices fell about 20 percent since the second half of last month. This price drop happened despite a general boom in artificial intelligence memory chips. Commodity NAND used in PCs and smartphones is falling while AI data center products remain firm. Bank of America reported that NAND is most likely to face price correction first. Industry sources shared this information on November 16, 2026.

A 512-gigabit NAND wafer dropped 32 percent from the previous quarter to 14.30 dollars. One-terabit products fell 19 percent to 24.90 dollars. Counterpoint Research expects global smartphone shipments to fall 13.9 percent this year to 1.08 billion units. Gartner says third quarter PC shipments fell 22.4 percent to 55.35 million units. YMTC revenue share reached 14 percent in the second quarter, up 5 percentage points.

TrendForce attributed the price drop to weak smartphone and PC demand and module maker inventory clearance. Bank of America stated that older fabrication lines cannot be quickly converted to high-value production. One memory industry official said that NAND cannot sustain the steep price gains seen so far. These sources explain why commodity chips face a supply-demand gap. They note that buyers are now demanding discounts on some products.

Consumers are delaying upgrades because higher memory costs feed into retail prices. Smartphone makers are reducing base storage capacity or charging more for higher-capacity models to contain costs. PC makers are drawing down existing inventory rather than placing new memory orders. Module suppliers are unloading stock as orders from device makers dry up. This process accelerates the price decline in the short-term spot market.

The NAND market includes Samsung Electronics, SK hynix, Micron, Kioxia, SanDisk, and Yangtze Memory Technologies Corp. Samsung Electronics holds 28 percent of revenue and SK hynix holds 19 percent. Enterprise SSDs accounted for 48 percent of total NAND bit shipments in the second quarter. This is up from 26 percent a year earlier according to Counterpoint Research. Older fabrication lines account for 20 to 30 percent of global NAND wafer capacity.

TrendForce expects enterprise SSD contract prices to rise 15 to 20 percent in the fourth quarter. Bank of America expects smartphone and PC NAND prices to fall 5 to 10 percent next quarter. Enterprise products may hold flat or rise slightly during that same period. It remains unclear if spot prices have already translated into lower contract prices. Future conditions depend on if AI data center growth can offset commodity chip weakness.

stories.Headline: ASI Foundry chairman Jimmy Lee promotes physical AI development for the manufacturing industry
stories.Summary:
Jimmy Lee, the chairman of ASI Foundry, promoted the development of physical AI for the manufacturing industry during an interview. He spoke with the Seoul Economic Daily in Palo Alto, California, on November 17. Lee urged Korea to use industrial data aggressively to become a leader in this new market. He believes that Korea can lead because it is a global manufacturing powerhouse. This shift involves integrating AI technology with the physical world, such as machines and cars.

ASI Foundry acts as a bridge for companies to combine their data with AI while maintaining governance. Lee noted that Korea leads globally in semiconductors, autos, and shipbuilding, which are key areas for physical AI. He mentioned that the Korean government is promoting policies like the Saemangeum AI data center to launch this industry. Lee also discussed how Loudoun County, Virginia, uses data center tax revenue to lower property tax burdens for residents. He noted that gas turbines from Korea's Doosan currently have a delivery lead time of four or five years.

Jimmy Lee, a former Maryland cabinet secretary and Virginia deputy secretary of commerce, is responsible for leading ASI Foundry. He stated that Korea must be a first mover in physical AI to maintain its position as a manufacturing power. Lee explained that while the United States and China lead AI models, Korea has more manufacturing data. He argued that the cost of inaction is greater than the cost of taking action during rapid change. He believes that data will eventually be exchanged like trade under a system that also protects sovereignty.

Korean manufacturers and small suppliers of parts, such as screws and pipelines, are the primary parties affected by this shift. Lee suggested that U.S. AI firms in Silicon Valley need the factory data that Korean companies possess. He mentioned that the AI Alliance, including Yann LeCun, and Project Tapestry support participants retaining control of their data. Some critics argue that data must be strictly protected to ensure AI sovereignty for the nation. Lee responded that horizontal information can be shared while vertical, sensitive information remains closed.

Lee is a 1.5-generation Korean-American and the son of Jhoon Rhee, who is known as the godfather of taekwondo. He previously served on the energy advisory council for the governor of Virginia and worked at the Livingston Group. He was appointed as Maryland's first Korean-American cabinet secretary by former Governor Larry Hogan. The articles explain that physical AI requires structuring unstructured factory data so that AI engines can read it. This process creates a flywheel ecosystem involving data centers, chips, and autonomous vehicles.

The next steps involve building the infrastructure for data centers and securing power sources like small modular reactors. Lee predicts that AI infrastructure buildout will continue despite recent Democratic gubernatorial wins in the United States midterms. He suggests that Korea could eventually manufacture GPUs if the flywheel ecosystem takes shape. The articles leave open how exactly the global system for data exchange and sovereignty will be structured. They also leave open when the shift from gas turbines to nuclear power will fully occur.
