stories.Headline: Anthropic raises 81.34 billion dollars in record Nasdaq IPO
stories.Summary:
Anthropic raised 81.34 billion dollars during a record Nasdaq initial public offering on Thursday, November 20, 2026. The company and its seven co-founders completed the largest IPO in history to take the artificial intelligence giant public. Shares opened at 111.50 dollars, which was 34 percent above the initial IPO price of 83 dollars. The stock later closed up 17 percent at 97.17 dollars per share. This debut gave the company a market capitalization of 1.3 trillion dollars.

The offering valued the company at 1.5 trillion dollars, though it briefly topped a 2 trillion dollar valuation. Including a separate 26 billion dollar private placement, the company raised a total of 107.34 billion dollars. Menlo invested over 1 billion dollars for a 1.5 percent stake, while Lightspeed invested over 3 billion dollars for 2 percent. The IPO could deliver 156 billion dollars to charity. The company is a public benefit corporation.

CEO Dario Amodei stated that he and his co-founders believe the most powerful technology should benefit humankind. He mentioned that AI will have a positive human impact on gene editing and CRISPR. Amodei said it will take everyone working together to ensure the technology goes well for future generations. He noted that he and Daniela Amodei lost their father to a disease. He described the mission as bigger than any one company or country.

Protesters rallied against the company in New York and San Francisco following the stock market debut. Some AI safety advocates challenged the safety branding used by the company. Over 400 employees are estimated to be worth more than 100 million dollars each. Some insiders claim these new millionaires are too science-obsessed to buy mansions. Others worry that these wealthy employees might leave the company.

The company launched the first version of Claude and was pre-revenue when it received 50 million dollars in March 2023. Investment firm Iconiq initially passed on the Series E round but changed its mind two months later. Yasmin Razavi of Spark Capital was the only venture capitalist listed in the S-1. The company rose from a startup to a global power in five years. It now ranks as the sixth most valuable public company.

The company will now trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT. Market analysts are watching to see if the success of this IPO will reshape the venture industry. Some investors are monitoring the stock's volatility after it pulled off its highest levels. The articles leave open whether the company can maintain its high valuation. They do not state the company's long-term financial projections.

stories.Headline: Check Point Research publishes a principle it calls gatekeeper asymmetry doom
stories.Summary:
Check Point Research published on November 19, 2026 an exposition of a principle it calls gatekeeper asymmetry doom, stating that if the system vetting adversarial input has strictly less power than the system processing that input, without leveraging some hard problem, this will inevitably lead to doom. The article lists examples of the principle in action, including the limits of static binary classification, the proliferation of sandbox evasions and Check Point's own PuzzleMask research for bypassing external AI guardrails. It also gives a short exposition of how the Time Hierarchy Theorem exemplifies the same principle. It concludes with a recommendation that doomed attack surfaces should be noticed and the gap narrowed as much as possible, by upgrading gatekeeper power or using its existing power more comprehensively. It notes that frontier LLMs, with scaffolding, extended reasoning and code execution in the chain of thought, have significant power in this sense and can meaningfully contribute to narrowing doom gaps, though they themselves are still subject to the principle.

The principle is offered in the same spirit as Moxie Marlinspike's Cryptographic Doom Principle, and the article says leveraging a hard problem excludes cases such as signature verification for binary files, which is many times simpler than executing the file but can still in a certain theoretical world determine whether the binary is malicious. The article phrases the principle more glibly as every quick sanity check involving either cryptography or a silent prayer, and shortens gatekeeper asymmetry doom to doom. Its warm-up example is hash comparison, which it says someone in the industry must have thought solved malware at some point during the 1990s, by collecting all hashes of malicious binaries in a large database for an antivirus to check each executed binary against. The gap there was truly huge, the article says, because the target is the full Turing-complete execution of a binary and the gatekeeper is a simple observation of whether the binary is in some set of known files. Threat actors' counter was infamous and trivial, randomizing the value of some non-load-bearing byte for each compiled binary.

The article says pattern matching and regular expressions underlie YARA rules and act as a backbone of binary classification still to this day, and that as of 2026 AI-augmented YARA rule generation has already improved the throughput of signature authorship considerably, though coverage and consistency are not close to a defender-optimistic utopia. It says regular expressions are not powerful enough to parse HTML and are also not powerful enough to capture the class of assembly subroutines that perform some action, or that perform some action using some specific algorithm, or that perform some action as implemented by some specific sequence of instructions subject to moderate mutation. It says the projected end state would be some malware generation process that takes care to inject this moderate mutation into every subroutine, a new kind of polymorphism. It says static reverse engineering, also known as reading the disassembly, is considered the apex form of static analysis, and that even frontier LLMs have historically struggled with dynamic-equivalent static analysis and in the worst case still do. It says the target victim machine can run the malicious binary but the gatekeeper, human or LLM, cannot natively, and through this capability gap came packers, opaque predicates, control flow flattening, the movfuscator and the Rust Programming Language.

The article says basic computability theory tells us the gap can't disappear outright, and that in the static reverse engineering utopia of a human-expert-level LLM analyzing every new binary in the wild, the new equilibrium lives in the gap, with binaries universally obfuscated to such a degree that a debugger is strongly required. It cites the SolarWinds compromised update, which it says unabashedly attempted to brainwash anyone reading its source code into compliance with the idea that they are looking at benign software. It says mitigations exist for this technique in both LLMs and humans, but it is representative of the general shape of the gatekeeper asymmetry that emerges there. It says malware has traditionally had the property of not wanting to be read, and we do not quite yet live in a world where selection pressures have pushed it to either adopt bleeding edge obfuscation or perish. It describes a possible post-equilibrium world where we miss the old days when we could unpack binaries to make code readable, where our favorite disassembler becomes the vessel of a futile hope, and where an LLM told to reverse engineer a binary ends up forced to reinvent the sandbox from first principles.

In an interlude on what gatekeeper asymmetry doom is not, the article cherry-picks disastrous phenomena in information security that it says have absolutely nothing to do with the principle. It says fuzzing being viable as a vulnerability discovery strategy involves typically no gatekeeper standing between adversarial input and the target application. It says the possibility of supply chain attacks is out of scope, because gatekeepers by definition exist to vet untrusted input, and facing trusted adversarial input is very bad but out of scope. It describes the lagging race for automatic detection of fast flux domains, with detection models advancing from an ineffectual shrug to calculating domain entropy to catch xrewrgfuvhnadfsajkaldsfj.biz, then n-gram frequency engines, then weird edit distance to the dictionary hacks to catch Kwyjibo. It says attackers evolved to use concatenations of randomly generated dictionary words, and the text of the article ends there, mid-sentence, with defenders could have re.

The article leaves open what defenders could have done next in the fast flux domain race, since its text stops at that point. It leaves open how the gap should be narrowed in each of the examples it lists, beyond the general recommendation to upgrade gatekeeper power or use existing power more comprehensively. It leaves open what the post-equilibrium world of obfuscated binaries will look like in practice, beyond the shape it says we can see and find little to like about. It leaves open how frontier LLMs will fare as contributors to narrowing doom gaps while remaining subject to the principle themselves. It gives no date for when the projected end states it describes might arrive, and no figures beyond the 1990s and 2026.

Articles.Title: 30 Years of Gatekeeper Asymmetry Doom: The Paradox that Makes Powerful LLMs More Vulnerable

stories.Headline: Waswo X Waswo uses AI to expand photographs in Delhi exhibition
stories.Summary:
Waswo X Waswo’s solo exhibition Long Short Stories opened at Latitude 28 in Delhi and runs until November 20, 2026, bringing together photography, miniature painting, old engravings, a video installation and sculpture. The show is built around an imagined American traveller called Dandy, played by Waswo in Mughal robes, who arrives in a fantastical Indian city with a telescope, befriends a prince, survives battles of magic and finally flees with the prince on an old scooty with arrows flying behind them. The story is funny, absurd and in parts autobiographical, and the photographic works follow Dandy as he is welcomed into a royal court, grows too powerful, is exiled and escapes with the prince. The exhibition also includes a series called Other Stories, which begins with pages from an 1804 Belgian book, The Costume of Hindostan by Baltazard Solvyns, featuring 60 hand-coloured engravings of 18th century India.

The show takes forward the Udaipur-based artist’s long interest in India, the outsider’s gaze and the small personal stories that official history leaves out, which he says build up the larger narrative and give the exhibition its title. Waswo shoots black-and-white photographs that are then hand-coloured and worked on with miniature painting techniques, with flowers, birds and other details painted onto them by his collaborators, a process he says took a year and involves considerable handcraft. The biggest departure this time is the use of AI, which he used to expand his usual square-format photographs into panoramas, and he is wary of the assumption that AI does all the work, saying the craft is still there. He now works with a new team in Udaipur including Dalpat and Banti Jingar, Shankar Kumawat and Chirag Kumawat, with Bhavesh Jingar contributing to the video installation, and he makes sure their names appear alongside his in the gallery and catalogue.

Waswo says he certainly realises he is an outsider here, an American very far from his distant land, though he is now accepted in the Indian art world and treated almost like family in Udaipur, where he has lived for about 20 years. He is also conscious that being a white American has opened many doors for him, and he believes Indians can recognise themselves in this outsider because India is so diverse that people can feel foreign even when they move from one part of the country to another. On his team he says they are stronger together than apart, like a rope that is the sum of its individual strands. Of the Other Stories works, in which he and his collaborators add contemporary details and symbols to the Solvyns engravings to make them satirical and sometimes funny, he says viewers are invited to construct their own stories about those, with no single narrative and each work leaving room for the viewer to imagine one.

stories.Headline: TiE Bangalore and the Aerospace Industry Association of India call for integrated AI adoption in aerospace and defence
stories.Summary:
A report released at the Bengaluru Tech Summit on November 19, 2026, said India’s aerospace, defence and space industry needs to move beyond isolated artificial intelligence experiments toward integrated, production-ready applications. The report, titled “Intelligent by Design: AI Adoption in India’s Aerospace, Defence and Space Industry,” was brought out by TiE Bangalore and the Aerospace Industry Association of India. It identified AI as a significant opportunity to improve engineering productivity, manufacturing efficiency, maintenance and operational performance across the sector. The study also cautioned that adoption across the industry remains uneven, with significant differences in technological maturity, investment capacity and organisational readiness.

Drawing on practitioner perspectives gathered through interviews, working sessions and written contributions, the report identifies four major constraints: fragmented data access, inadequate integration with existing engineering systems, shortages of specialised talent and concerns around accountability in safety-critical applications. It pointed out that aerospace and defence manufacturing involves complex engineering processes, stringent certification requirements and long product lifecycles, so AI-generated outputs cannot be accepted without adequate validation, traceability and human oversight. Applications with potential include predictive maintenance, engineering design optimisation, quality inspection, supply-chain analytics, digital twins and automated documentation, and AI could also help analyse large volumes of engineering data, identify anomalies and improve decision-making. The report highlighted that access to reliable, structured and integrated data was fundamental to successful adoption, since fragmented records, inconsistent data formats and legacy systems often prevent organisations from deploying AI solutions at scale.

The report also underlines the importance of protecting sensitive technical information, intellectual property and operational data, and it flags the non-availability of skilled manpower as another major concern. It says the industry needs engineers who combine domain expertise with knowledge of AI, machine learning, data science and digital engineering tools, and it calls for stronger collaboration between industry, academic institutions and technology providers to develop these capabilities. It also stresses that smaller suppliers and MSMEs could face greater challenges because of limited resources, technology access and investment capacity, and it suggests shared infrastructure, collaborative platforms and targeted support could help them participate in the emerging AI ecosystem. The report was published on November 19, 2026, and the articles do not say what steps, if any, have been taken since its release.

stories.Headline: Sudhanshu Trivedi says AI can predict Rahul Gandhi's repeated remarks and suggests sending an AI version abroad
stories.Summary:
BJP spokesperson and Rajya Sabha MP Sudhanshu Trivedi held a press conference at the party headquarters in New Delhi on Thursday, November 19, 2026, and criticised Congress leader Rahul Gandhi over remarks he made during a two-day visit to the United States. During that trip, Gandhi interacted with students and faculty at Columbia University in New York on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, and at the University of Chicago on Wednesday, November 18, 2026. At the University of Chicago, Gandhi said Indian democracy is sacred and that the Congress is ready to face electoral defeats until people realise the system has been completely demolished. He also said that boycotting elections over alleged flaws in the system would bring an end to Indian democracy, which the Congress does not intend to do.

Trivedi said it was unfortunate that Gandhi was making remarks against India in Chicago, the city where Swami Vivekananda had once brought glory to the country, and that a leader of the opposition was lowering the prestige of Mother India at the same place. He was responding to Gandhi's remarks questioning the 2024 Lok Sabha elections and concerns over electoral irregularities, and to Gandhi's claim that a Brazilian model voted 23 times in India, asking whether anyone coming from abroad should not have an immigration record. Trivedi accused Gandhi of making what he called Hawai allegations about India's electoral process and of lowering the country's image on foreign soil. Taking a swipe at Gandhi's frequent foreign visits, Trivedi said the Congress should stop spending money on sending him abroad.

Trivedi said it is the age of AI and that the Congress should simply send an AI-generated version of Gandhi because he has to repeat the same sentences and words again and again. He suggested an AI model could be programmed with four options, namely making derogatory remarks against India, saying something against the prime minister, creating an uproar over democracy, and embarrassing his own party by raising something anti-India. He claimed artificial intelligence could do a better job than Gandhi's repeated remarks and that AI models were now capable of predicting what the Congress leader would say and the responses to his statements. The BJP also said the Congress should consider sending an AI-generated version of its leader abroad because he keeps repeating the same words.

Articles.Title: BJP mocks Rahul Gandhi's U.S. remarks, says AI can predict his speeches

stories.Headline: Riddhipratim Basu wins 2026 Infosys Prize in mathematical sciences
stories.Summary:
Riddhipratim Basu, an associate professor at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences in Bengaluru, has been awarded the 2026 Infosys Prize in the mathematical sciences category. The ICTS is part of the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, and before joining it Dr. Basu was an assistant professor at Stanford University. In his work he uses mathematics to understand how random events produce predictable patterns in physical systems. He corresponded with The Hindu by email after the Prize, and the newspaper presented the exchange after editing it for length.

The interview asked Dr. Basu whether there are important phenomena in nature or society for which we still lack the mathematical tools to understand them, and what it would take to develop those tools. He replied that nature has endless mysteries and that we have barely scratched the surface, adding that there are many phenomena we still lack a precise understanding of. He said the systems mathematicians study are more often than not highly simplified versions of the real-world phenomena they are trying to model. He added that mathematicians nevertheless believe these simplified systems capture the essential features of those phenomena.

The 2026 Infosys Prize in mathematical sciences is the award named in the headline, and Dr. Basu is the laureate it refers to. The article gives no further detail on the prize money, the citation or the award ceremony, and it does not say when or where the prize will be presented. It also does not say what Dr. Basu plans to do next with the award or how the recognition might change his research. The published material is limited to the announcement of the award and his edited email remarks on the limits of mathematical modelling.

The article does not report any statement from Dr. Basu on keeping humans at the centre of mathematics as we adapt to artificial intelligence, beyond what the headline indicates. It also carries no comment from the Infosys Prize organisers, from ICTS or from Stanford University on the award. No date is given for when the prize was announced beyond the publication date of November 19, 2026, and no other numbers appear in the text. The article says nothing further about what happens next, so the only follow-up it supports is the interview itself.

stories.Headline: Sociologist William Robinson says AI capital drives global crisis and links with fascism
stories.Summary:
The Cockroach movement in India and cost of living protests across France and Germany in recent weeks express a broader crisis of global capitalism, according to William I. Robinson, professor of sociology at University of California, Santa Barbara. Robinson said the crisis includes a social reproduction dimension that has catalysed movements from below through an explosion of critical consciousness and social solidarity. He said agents of the transnational elite have tried to divide working classes through propaganda, threats and mass psychology. He said the protests resist capitalism's bid to enhance the power of the transnational elite at the common man's expense. He said the system's trajectory, felt through intensified intra-capitalist competition and class wars, is undermining its capacity to reproduce itself and leading to a point of no return.

Robinson's latest book, Pax Silica: The New Ruling Class, explores the emergence of new lords of the world in the age of AI and how they reshape the world to consolidate power. He said AI turbocharges capital's centuries-old drive to deskill and cheapen labour and threatens to eliminate labour altogether. He said AI is extremely expensive, with data centre construction requiring hundreds of billions of dollars in investment, so constant capital grows enormously relative to variable capital. He said the tech sector extracts surplus value from labour and rents from other sectors of capital that do the exploitation. He said the newest and most important source of profits worldwide now, and the accumulation strategy of the new hegemonic block of capital, is repression, warfare, genocide, conflict and chaos.

Robinson said historical figures such as Modi and Trump generate political, social and cultural conditions that deflect from the epochal crisis of global capitalism and disorganise, atomise, divide and confuse the labouring masses. He said the hegemonic block of AI capital brings together tech capital, military-industry repression capital and transnational finance capital, all linked to the new ruling class in the US and worldwide. He said that block decided over the last four to five years to link up with fascism in the state, with Trumpism, with Modiism, with Javier Milei in Argentina and with Netanyahu in Israel. He said the fascist project allows capital to accumulate, including through repression of the working class, and capital in turn supports fascism's political project. He said capital no longer needs our social reproduction.

Robinson said masses of people do not need to read Capital or call themselves Marxists to understand what is going on, and people are in rebellion worldwide without having read Marx. He said the ruling class wages psychological warfare at every level, and AI lets them wage new age warfare through social media, the attention economy and intervention in electoral processes. He said capital has fragmented and atomised people and turned them against one another, so mass struggles need new ways to recompose the global working class. He said a crisis of social reproduction and social disintegration is taking place in India, the US and Africa, and billions of people cannot survive or reproduce themselves and their communities. He said the students' rebellion in France is a working-class struggle against AI and a restructuring of global capitalism driven by digitalisation.

Robinson said the more global capital does not need workers, the more workers become surplus humanity and surplus labour. He said the more AI, machinery and constant capital take over, the less transnational capital needs young people trained to read and think in the abstract. He said there is no need to educate people who become surplus labour, only to control them, lock them up in mass incarceration or even commit genocide against them. He said education is being savagely defunded in France. He said the transition from precariatisation of labour, the shift towards unprotected employment, to the elimination of labour could in theory end capital-labour relations and therefore capitalism as known.

Robinson said AI, like fossil fuel extraction, represents an ability to concentrate disparate sources of value under centralised control and extract rent. He said Harry Braverman, building on Karl Marx in Labour & Monopoly Capital, laid out how capital seeks to deskill labour, cheapen it and take control of the labour process. He said Yanis Varoufakis's Technofeudalism: What Killed Capitalism is really brilliant, but the problem is that it is not feudalism, which is very distinct. He said rents are not new to capitalism and were always there, and super-profits come from profit made in different sectors migrating to the super-profits sector. He said globalisation unleashed an unprecedented historical centralisation and concentration of capital on a world scale in transnational capital and the transnational capitalist class.

Robinson said these people appear as lords of the world because they are the lords of the world, but they are capitalist lords, not feudal lords. He said the construction of data centres means fixed capital is enormously expanding relative to living labour, and the decline in the rate of profit in the long run is new territory. He said AI capital is constructing AI to expand profits, continue to accumulate and control global labour, and it will backfire on capital in the long run. He said we are moving towards World War III and towards a dystopic future nightmare society that previously existed only in Hollywood films. He said the more the struggle pushes forward, the more counter-consciousness to fascist consciousness expands.

Articles.Title: AI, labour and the changing dynamics of global capitalism

stories.Headline: Users turn photos into Vice City style portraits with ChatGPT and Gemini prompts
stories.Summary:
Users turned everyday photographs into colourful video game-inspired portraits in a trend popular among Instagram and WhatsApp users, as reported by livemint.com on 19 November 2026. The trend recreates the graphics and ambience of Vice City with neon lights, palm trees, luxurious cars and dramatic sunsets. Users uploaded their photographs to AI tools such as ChatGPT and Google Gemini and entered detailed image-generation prompts. The trend offered an easy way to design personalised gaming posters without professional editing software or design skills. The article was published by Pragya Singha Roy at 05:01 PM IST on 19 Nov 2026.

The article gave three ChatGPT prompts, including a GTA 6 character poster, a realistic gameplay screenshot and a sunset beach portrait. The Gemini prompts were a loading screen artwork using a vertical 4:5 composition, a neon night city scene and a character portrait. The steps for ChatGPT were to open it, upload a clear photograph, paste a prompt, generate the image, give additional instructions and save and share the result. The Gemini steps were to open the website or app, select image generation, upload a photograph, enter a detailed prompt, submit and review, then ask for corrections and download. The tips advised using well-lit photos with visible faces, avoiding heavy filters, describing the background, stating the image style and asking for corrections when AI changes the face.

According to the official OpenAI Help Centre, users can upload an image and specify what they wish ChatGPT to alter. Google's official documentation explains the process via its image generation and editing capabilities, Gemini. The article said the original photograph and the quality of the prompt can influence the final output. It said users should ask the AI to keep their facial details when modifications alter the face. The article stated that a good prompt can help make an image more successful.

A separate TechGig article published on 18 Nov 2026 at 07:01 AM IST reported that Claude's downloads in India jumped 15 times year-on-year in the September quarter. ChatGPT downloads declined 21 per cent but it remained India's market leader among generative AI apps, according to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. Claude's in-app purchase revenue climbed to third rank from fifth a year ago, overtaking platforms such as Instagram and YouTube. ChatGPT's India revenue from in-app purchases increased by 70 per cent since Q2 FY26, and Gemini reported a 44 per cent year-on-year revenue rise in Q2 FY27 despite a 29 per cent drop in downloads. On a sequential basis, Claude's in-app purchase revenue grew 75 per cent from the June quarter, ChatGPT recorded 61 per cent revenue growth and Gemini's revenue slipped 31 per cent quarter-on-quarter.

OpenAI India MD Prabhjeet Singh stated last week that India is ChatGPT's largest global market for weekly active users, having doubled its user base since January. OpenAI has an office in Delhi NCR and plans to open additional offices in Mumbai and Bengaluru. Anthropic inaugurated its first India-based office in Bengaluru earlier this year. The Indian AI market is projected to multiply 5.3 times by 2030 to hit $126 billion and add $1.7 trillion to the GDP by 2035, as per Inc42's Bharat AI Startups Report, 2026. The TechGig article said Claude's surge indicates a shift in consumer preferences within the competitive Indian AI market.

The livemint article also linked to a report that GTA 6 pre-orders crossed 17 million as Rockstar reportedly made $1.65 billion. It linked to another report on all 61 GTA 6 cheat codes and how to unlock and use them. The article described the trend as sparking on social media from the Grand Theft Auto 6 craze. It said the trend turns everyday photographs into colourful video game-inspired portraits. The article said the trend recreates the same graphics and ambience of Vice City.

The livemint article left open how many users have joined the trend and which prompts produce the best results. The TechGig article left open the size of Claude's user base in India and the reasons behind its download growth. Neither article stated what happens next for the GTA 6 AI photo trend. The TechGig article did not give a date for when OpenAI will open the Mumbai and Bengaluru offices. The livemint article did not say whether the prompts work the same way on both ChatGPT and Gemini.

stories.Headline: UBS forecasts S&P 500 reaching 8,200 by end of 2027 while cutting US equities to neutral on AI uncertainty
stories.Summary:
UBS Global Wealth Management said on 19 November 2026 that it expects the S&P 500 to reach 8,200 by the end of 2027, an upside of around 12% from current levels, according to a Livemint report. The brokerage based that target on resilient economic growth and continued expansion in corporate earnings across the US equity market. At the same time, UBS shifted its rating on US equities to neutral, citing elevated valuations, high market concentration and growing uncertainty around the artificial intelligence investment cycle. The report said the year-end 2027 target is broadly in line with Wells Fargo's outlook but remains below the more bullish projections from Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley. UBS estimated that S&P 500 earnings will rise 29% in 2026 and then expand a further 15% in 2027, even as it anticipates a moderation in earnings growth.

It expects global AI-related investment to keep expanding, rising to $1.4 trillion in 2027 and reaching $1.5 trillion in 2028. Within the AI ecosystem, the brokerage favours well-capitalised hyperscalers and select semiconductor and chip-equipment companies with strong competitive positions and clear opportunities to generate revenue from AI adoption. UBS cautioned that the path to further market gains could be volatile, flagging rising risks around AI-related disruption, financing and execution alongside elevated investor expectations. UBS explained its move to a neutral stance by saying that cannibalization, financing and execution risks around AI have increased while expectations and index concentration remain high. The brokerage added that while it expects gains, the path could be volatile.

The report noted that the AI trade has come under pressure amid opposition to large data-centre projects and concerns over the returns generated by heavy investment in the technology. Regulatory uncertainty following the US midterm elections and developments surrounding Nvidia have also contributed to investor caution, according to the report. The sustainability of the AI investment cycle is emerging as a key consideration for equity investors as markets assess whether substantial spending on AI infrastructure can translate into lasting earnings growth beyond 2027. UBS said the ability of companies to convert heavy AI spending into sustainable revenue and profits will be crucial in determining whether the current market momentum can be maintained. The brokerage's outlook suggests that while AI investment and corporate earnings could continue supporting US equities, investors may need to be more selective as expectations remain elevated.

stories.Headline: Riken suspends Fugaku supercomputer after intruders tamper with servers
stories.Summary:
Norwegian energy giant Equinor detected and stopped a cyberattack on some of its IT systems on November 17, with no data stolen or altered, according to TechGig. A day later, Norwegian power company Skagerak Energi reported activity that may have been an attempted cyberattack on its IT systems, which also did not affect operations or lead to data leaks. Japan's Riken research institute suspended operations of the Fugaku supercomputer and cut off external access after detecting suspicious traffic on its user authentication system. Riken said an outside party used a public dashboard showing Fugaku's operational status to break into the system's internal operations network and tamper with multiple servers.

The Riken incident may have exposed names, email addresses and user IDs of up to 4,597 Fugaku and RIKYU users. Networking and security company Infoblox confirmed that hackers accessed certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor, and The Register reported the stolen files included NIOS configuration snapshots for some customers and personal details of employees and their dependents. Japanese online brokerage Rakuten Securities disclosed that login IDs and branch codes for up to 11.25 million accounts, along with personal and financial information for up to 4.47 million accounts, may have been exposed after attackers accessed a test environment on November 11. Researcher Nightmare Eclipse published FastUnlock, an unpatched Windows 11 zero-day exploit that uses the Narrator screen reader to bypass the lock screen and run code, requiring physical access.

Riken stated that an outside party used the public dashboard to break into the internal operations network and tamper with multiple servers. Infoblox confirmed that hackers accessed certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor. Rakuten Securities disclosed that the exposed data followed attackers accessing a test environment on November 11. Ukrainian police, working with the FBI, arrested four alleged key members of a ransomware gang that used an AI voice platform to obtain credentials or install remote access software.

Google has released Gemini 4 Neon, a faster, lower-cost model for coding and enterprise work, and a cyber-focused version will reach eligible members of its Fairwind Program for trusted defenders. The articles do not say what happens next in the Equinor, Skagerak Energi, Riken, Infoblox or Rakuten Securities incidents.

By highlighting the movement of capital, he suggested that the market is adjusting to the scale of AI investment. He maintained that the integration of technology will not replace the essential role of human professionals.

stories.Headline: Dell executives say enterprises must budget for AI tokens and secure agent skills as inference costs rise
stories.Summary:
Dell Technologies executives and cloud infrastructure providers examined the economics of enterprise AI, the operational challenges of scaling infrastructure and the decisions shaping AI adoption at the Dell Technologies New York Symposium, covered by theCUBE. John Scimone, president and chief security officer of Dell Technologies Inc., spoke with theCUBE Research's Dave Vellante during the event. Dell has spent nearly two years running fully autonomous agents internally, capturing institutional knowledge in machine-readable skill files that guide their behavior. John Roese, global chief technology officer and chief AI officer of Dell, said the effort is part of a broader reorganization of work around AI agents. David Kennedy, chief financial officer of Dell, said finance teams are establishing dedicated budget lines for token consumption and evaluating which workloads can run more economically on-premises.

Scimone said the pyramid still exists, but the cost of entry and the barriers to entry have crumbled, and that the least sophisticated attack tomorrow is more sophisticated than the world will have ever seen a year ago. Roese said it does not mean you cannot use frontier models and open models, but that when you design your AI system you need to realize the thing that is your moat is not the actual tools, and not even the models, but the special knowledge now manifesting in these new forms. Kennedy said it is not necessarily about the amount and the cost of a token, but about the tokens you use, and that if you are efficient with them you will see great outcomes. Kyle Dufresne, senior vice president of sales at Dell, said business owners are saying costs are getting really high for inferencing and asking how to reduce those costs without curbing innovation. Dufresne said this is happening across that continuum but more and more right out at the far edge.

David Schmoock, senior vice president of global revenue operations at Dell, said demand for AI servers has strained supplies of components ranging from memory and processors to rack-level cooling, networking and power equipment. Schmoock said without collaborative planning a project may have been delayed 60, 90, 120 days, which has both a cost impact and a business impact, and that customers should bring Dell in earlier. Thomas Kato, founder and chief executive officer of Comet Cloud Inc., said that going to Amazon Web Services now means they want a multiyear contract and they are picking who they are taking. Kato said small and medium businesses are not even coming up on that scope at all to be able to have that AI, and that this is really Comet Cloud's focus. Kato said Comet Cloud puts together clusters and gives clusters to a whole company, with all their information and all their security within that cluster and no one else tied or connected to it.

Tom Richer, executive vice president of Alpha Compute Corp., said the company's sovereign-by-design approach is intended to help customers maintain control over sensitive workloads and meet data residency obligations, including those associated with European regulations. Richer said Alpha Compute starts with the hardware and creates enclaves all the way down to the chip level. Richer said Alpha Compute is a Dell partner and uses Dell technology as well as Intel technology. Richer said you can cobble together a lot of different providers, but then when stuff goes wrong the finger-pointing starts. Richer said customers just want that integrated solution provider who can ensure success, help with all of the build-out, then all of the managed services to keep it going healthy and to keep everything performing in line with service-level agreements.

The considerations of AI operational readiness are particularly consequential for financial institutions, where reliability, regulatory obligations and the need to demonstrate returns on technology investments shape deployment decisions. AI is changing the threat landscape, giving less sophisticated attackers access to capabilities that once required considerably greater resources, according to Scimone. The growth of AI inference is changing how enterprises distribute workloads across cloud environments, data centers and edge devices. Dell's expanded agentic AI portfolio reflects that shift, with solutions spanning desktop systems and data center infrastructure. Organizations are evaluating where to run models based on performance, data control and cost, according to Dufresne.

AI operational readiness is also becoming a consideration for smaller businesses that need access to GPU computing without the resources of large enterprises, and Comet Cloud is targeting this underserved market, where access to AI infrastructure can be constrained by purchasing commitments and provider priorities. Alpha Compute is building its neocloud infrastructure around data sovereignty and confidential computing requirements. Keeping GPU infrastructure operational presents a different challenge for neocloud providers, and Alpha Compute provides integrated infrastructure support and ongoing managed services to address those demands. Repetitive financial processes, for example, can use open-weight models to convert variable token expenses into more predictable fixed costs, according to Kennedy. TheCUBE is a paid media partner for the Dell Technologies New York Symposium, and neither Dell, the sponsor of theCUBE's event coverage, nor other sponsors have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE.

stories.Headline: Andrew Lloyd Webber says AI cannot create original musicals like Cats
stories.Summary:
Andrew Lloyd Webber told reporters in Seoul on Nov 19, on his first visit to Korea, that artificial intelligence would not have come up with Cats or The Phantom Of The Opera, because true musical success depends on original ideas and a strong story rather than on anything drawn from musicals of the past. He said that if he had asked such a system what to write after Evita 45 years ago, it would have based its answer on earlier shows, and he added that the originality a person brings is what matters. He also said AI would not have suggested the subject of his next show, the 1911 theft of the Mona Lisa from the Louvre, an idea that came from a story he read in The Times of London about how the painting drew little attention until it was stolen and disappeared for more than two years, with the publicity making it world-famous. He said the story made him think about what fame is and what the value of any piece of art is, and he plans to present the new musical in 2027. He was blunt about Broadway, saying that all the associated costs with a Broadway musical have become prohibitively high and that no new work of any consequence is really being done there any more.

He said he believes a good story can carry a musical score that may not be great, but a bad story cannot carry great music, because the story is in the end what people really come for. He said music has to add something to the story and be the reason for it being a musical, otherwise there is no point, and he welcomes new directors' takes on his previous shows as long as the music stays exactly as he wrote it, citing Jamie Lloyd's minimalist Sunset Boulevard and Cats: The Jellicle Ball. He called The Phantom Of The Opera the exception, saying the original production by Hal, meaning director Harold Prince, is so phenomenal that he does not think it will ever be bettered. The Phantom Of The Opera is returning to Seoul for its 40th anniversary in a Korean-language production that opens Dec 22 at Blue Square's Woori Bank Hall and runs through Feb 28, with Choi Jae-rim, Jeon Dong-seok and Park Kang-hyun rotating as the Phantom, sopranos Lee Hae-won and Choi Seon-ho making their musical debuts as Christine, and Song Won-geun and Kim Sung-sik playing Raoul.

The musical's Korean-language premiere in 2001 drew a record-breaking 240,000 people and generated 19.2 billion won, or S$18.6 million, in revenue, exceeding the country's entire musical theatre industry's annual revenue of 14 billion won that year, according to producer S&Co, and there have been six productions of Phantom in Korea drawing more than 1.5 million cumulative admissions. Seol Do-yoon, who produced the 2001 iteration, recalled trying to fund the show while Korea was still emerging from the 1997 financial crisis, saying he ran around everywhere trying to raise money but nobody would invest, though everyone who heard the music said the show would do really well and was so moving. Lloyd Webber attended a rehearsal on Nov 17 and called the cast absolutely excellent, saying the Korean language sat beautifully on the music and that it was stunning, and that he almost wished he could hear it in Korean all the time. He said he would return in 2027 to hear the musicals being written in Korea, adding that he is older now and loves hearing what young people are doing in musical theatre, which is the thing he loves most.

stories.Headline: MAS chief Chia Der Jiun warns consumers against giving AI agents financial login credentials
stories.Summary:
Monetary Authority of Singapore managing director Chia Der Jiun warned on Nov 19 at the Singapore Fintech Festival that consumers should not give artificial intelligence agents their financial account login credentials, because safeguards are still too weak to ensure such tools act safely and within their users' instructions. He noted that some payment service providers and financial institutions are building agent interfaces into their offerings, but many financial institutions have yet to set terms or channels for agents to access financial services. Chia said a financial institution cannot tell whether an agent acts on the customer's full authorisation and control, or whether it transacts within its mandate and instructions, and he asked who bears responsibility if agents transact incorrectly or beyond their instruction. Chia said a trusted protocol and a secure channel are needed for AI agents to access financial services, drawing on lessons from the first phase of MAS' Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime initiative. These lessons include giving agents enough autonomy to do useful tasks within clearly defined boundaries, establishing their identities and authority to act for users, and specifying in their instructions what actions they can take along with any limits and conditions.

He said the greater the discretion and impact of action given an agent, the stronger the assurance and controls needed. MAS will develop a common "know your agent" protocol for trusted information exchange between customer agents and financial institutions, covering the agent's identity, whom it represents, its authority, its mandate, and its origins and reliability, so institutions can set permitted terms and a dedicated secure channel. MAS will also set up a sandbox with the Future of Finance Institute to bring together AI agents and programmable money in two use cases, corporate treasury management and payment services. In treasury management, banks could let an agent monitor a company's liquidity positions and due payments, decide when and where funds move, and use tokenised deposits to execute permitted actions, with companies setting mandates and participating banks setting controls and terms. In payments, banks and payment service providers could let customer agents execute payment instructions using digital money such as tokenised deposits or stablecoins, verifying the agents' identities and authority and applying risk controls first.

Chia said consumers and businesses need to retain meaningful control over the objectives, mandate and actions of their agents, adding that autonomy has to be bounded and actions and outcomes have to come with accountability. MAS also announced on Nov 19 that it had successfully issued $100 million of tokenised MAS Bills on Nov 6, four-week bills issued on the Singapore Dollar Test Network and settled using wholesale central bank digital currency. Five primary dealers, DBS, HSBC, OCBC, Standard Chartered and UOB, took part in the auction, with applications amounting to more than double the issuance size, and the bills will mature on Dec 4. MAS said it intends to scale up tokenised MAS Bills issuances, bring on board more participating financial institutions and expand their use for collateral management, and interested institutions and financial market infrastructure providers can join the next phase of live trials in 2027.

stories.Headline: Singapore and China pledge to deepen cooperation in artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Singapore and China launched talks to upgrade their bilateral free trade agreement on Friday, November 20, 2026. Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and President Xi Jinping met at Kylin Villa in Shenzhen to discuss these ties. The leaders pledged to deepen relations between the two countries amid current global shake-ups. They also discussed how to deepen cooperation in emerging technologies, particularly artificial intelligence. This meeting was the third between the two leaders since Wong took office in May 2024.

The upgrade, called China-Singapore Free Trade Agreement 4.0, requires a memorandum of understanding between METI and China's Ministry of Commerce. It will cover the digital economy and government procurement to open new markets for Singapore companies. The agreement will facilitate cross-border data flows and build on the 2009 original bilateral free trade agreement. It also leverages the Suzhou Industrial Park, Sino-Singapore Tianjin Eco-City, and the Chongqing Connectivity Initiative. These efforts follow the 2023 upgrade to an All-Round High-Quality Future-Oriented Partnership.

Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said the partnership has expanded into connectivity and green development despite a complex international environment. He noted that both nations can learn from each other to help businesses innovate and raise productivity. President Xi Jinping stated that cooperation over the past few years has brought tangible benefits to both peoples. He described the two nations as friendly neighbours and key development partners during the meeting. Xi called for closer strategic communication to take the partnership to new heights.

President Xi noted that the world is undergoing profound changes with a new round of technological revolution. Prime Minister Wong urged Apec leaders to prevent the Asia-Pacific from splitting into competing economic blocs. He stated that dialogue is valuable for peace and stability during a time of heightened geopolitical tensions. Singapore companies are affected as the upgrade aims to make it easier for them to do business. Workers are also affected as the leaders discussed preparing them for future jobs.

China was Singapore's largest merchandise trading partner from 2013 to 2024 and its third-largest services partner in 2024. Bilateral merchandise trade totalled S$162.9 billion in 2025, which was 11.7 per cent of Singapore's global merchandise trade. Singapore has been China's largest source of foreign direct investment by annual flows since 2013. It is also the largest recipient in Asia of China's outward direct investment by flows. China will provide US$20 million to support the practical cooperation of Apec.

Prime Minister Wong will next travel to Beijing for a meeting and working lunch with Premier Li Qiang. He will wrap up his trip on Saturday after attending the 33rd Apec Economic Leaders' Meeting. The articles leave open the specific details of the new digital economy and government procurement rules. They do not state when the Free Trade Agreement 4.0 upgrade will be finalized. stories.Headline: 45% of young people in Japan use AI as a social companion, Gallup survey finds
stories.Summary:
A new poll has found that 45% of young people in Japan reported using artificial intelligence as a social companion, the second-highest rate among the countries surveyed behind Australia. Researchers with Gallup and Boston Children’s Digital Wellness Lab surveyed 15,925 young people between the ages of 15 and 22 across 16 countries, examining patterns around friendship, well-being and their digital relationships. The survey was reported by The Japan Times on November 19, 2026, in a story by staff writer Elizabeth Beattie. Japanese respondents gave AI companionship the second-lowest quality scores even as their usage ranked near the top.

Japanese young people also reported some of the highest usage rates of AI overall, reaching third place behind Brazil and Italy, with 35% of those surveyed saying they used it once a day or more. In-person relationships are central to the social lives of young people and receive the highest ratings for strength, according to the researchers. Young people associated higher levels of happiness, safety and sense of connection with their in-person friendships while reporting higher levels of anxiety around their online relationships. The report said higher loneliness is more common among young people who frequently communicate online with strangers or online-only friends than among those who frequently communicate with in-person friends or family members.

Friendships are increasingly spanning offline and online worlds, with young people reporting that they maintained relationships through online communication or had built relationships through online communities. Young men more often meet online friends through gaming and young women through social media platforms, according to the researchers. The report said digitally mediated friendships generally add to, rather than replace, in-person relationships, and that the two most common friendship configurations both include an in-person friend alongside at least one digitally mediated friendship. The most common online activity young people around the world reported was scrolling, with 72% of respondents saying they frequently scroll short-form content, and the report said scrolling through online content is the response young people report most often when they feel lonely.

Articles.Title: Young people in Japan more inclined to seek AI companionship but skeptical of quality

stories.Headline: South Africa aims to move from hosting data centers to innovating AI technology
stories.Summary:
President Cyril Ramaphosa announced on November 20, 2026, that South Africa intends to become an active participant in the global artificial intelligence value chain. During a working visit to the United States, the president spoke at a fireside chat held at Stanford University in California. He explained that the nation wants to move beyond simply hosting data centers to participate in the actual origination and innovation of technology. This strategic shift aims to ensure that South Africa and the broader African continent help shape emerging technologies instead of just adopting foreign innovations.

This new approach requires that investments in data centers unlock broader opportunities for local researchers, innovators, and businesses. President Ramaphosa noted that global tech giants like Google and Amazon are already establishing data centers in South Africa alongside various domestic firms. He believes the country can integrate into the global ecosystem by leveraging its universities, research institutions, and skilled workforce. Furthermore, the president highlighted that recent improvements in the national electricity supply provide a critical advantage for attracting these digital infrastructure investments.

President Ramaphosa stated that deeper participation in the technology value chain could help the government tackle domestic challenges like inequality and unemployment. He emphasized the need to engage young people in the AI-driven economy while simultaneously recognizing and mitigating the potential risks. The president also called for closer ties with the South African tech diaspora to bring expertise and capital back to young entrepreneurs. He maintained that the country remains open to foreign investment as long as partners help build local capabilities and foster sector collaboration.

Articles.Title: South Africa seeks bigger role in global AI value chain: president - Xinhua

stories.headline_source: South Africa seeks bigger role in global AI value chain: president - Xinhua

stories.Headline: Fond du Lac cafe and acai bowl owner use AI for event ideas and inventory
stories.Summary:
Two small businesses in the Fond du Lac area have begun using artificial intelligence tools to help them compete, according to a report from NBC 26 that was posted on November 20, 2026. The play cafe called Wonder, which opened its doors in downtown Fond du Lac in 2023, offers coffee and a built in play area for families, and co-founder Tristin Holzmann says business has been good over the past couple of years. Holzmann said the cafe now uses AI to help bring in ideas, such as asking what could be added to an event or coming up with different specials that are not necessarily at the front of their brains. She said the business still uses its own graphic design skills to make all of its promotional content and does not use AI to generate flyers and advertising. Max Ramker launched his new mobile business called The Berry Bowl near Ledgeview Lanes earlier in the week, and it offers fresh Acai bowls.

Ramker said making sure he has enough ingredients is key, and he uses AI to help stay on top of the inventory because he does not want his fruit to go bad. He said he only uses fresh fruit and that this is something he prides himself on, while both businesses say social media is another asset for them. Ramker said he already has nearly 40,000 views on Facebook and that posting on Facebook and Instagram has been huge for him, so he plans to stay consistent with that. The report cites studies showing that 20% of new businesses fail in the first year and only 50% survive the first five years, which is the competitive market the story describes.

The Better Business Bureau is the organization the report names on the question of how to adopt these tools, and it recommends a gradual approach to using AI tools, only if it is the right fit for your business. Holzmann and Ramker are the two business owners the report quotes, and both described the specific ways they use the technology in their own operations. The report does not say what any other business or official said beyond that recommendation, and it does not give a date for when the bureau made it. The story was reported by Jack Porter of NBC 26, who covers stories making an impact in Fond du Lac.

The context the report gives is a competitive market in which many new businesses do not survive their first years, and it presents the two owners as examples of local businesses bringing in new technology to help grow their establishments. The report notes that AI cannot do everything, which is the frame for the bureau's advice to move gradually and only adopt tools that fit a given business. Beyond the steps the two owners described, the report does not say what happens next for either business or for the wider group of local small businesses.

Articles.Title: Local small businesses turn to AI for assistance to stay competitive

stories.Headline: HD Moore finds widespread sensitive data leaks across AI supply chains
stories.Summary:
Researcher HD Moore planted two million digital tripwires into AI supply chains to track sensitive information. This experiment occurred in late October and between July and October of 2026. Moore wanted to see if sensitive data leaks through the vast chain of AI services. He discovered an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve. The findings revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.

The test used Amazon Web Services access keys, SSH passwords, unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. Moore sent these secrets through AI routers like Vercel and OpenRouter to various inference engines. He found that three hosting providers were compromised by attackers who siphoned prompts. A Chinese AI lab scraped secret URLs from over half of the prompts it received. Some US hosting providers resold these models, causing data to flow back to the lab.

HD Moore is the chief research officer of the security firm Dragos. He stated that the findings revealed security breaches and prompt theft. Moore noted that privacy flags do not help when an attacker is already inside. He said the most effective prevention is hosting models using expensive on-premises servers. He also suggested using first-tier providers to minimize the chances of data leaks.

Attackers used stolen AWS keys tens of thousands of times in API calls. These parties searched S3 buckets, secrets managers, and parameter stores for more credentials. Some resellers lured prompts with low prices and then logged them for theft. Customers who paid US providers to keep data in the U.S. were affected. Users who put trade secrets into prompts face a daunting task to ensure privacy.

AI apps often use brokers called AI routers or gateways to find the cheapest models. Prompts are encrypted in transit but decrypted at each hop inside the reseller network. Routers read plaintext to determine which inference provider should handle the request. Many players in this chain log and store prompts according to their own policies. This creates a sprawling network where data can be intercepted at the provider's front door.

Users should avoid default reseller pools and instead pick their own upstream providers. Moore recommends receiving service directly from a first-tier provider with one privacy policy. The articles leave open whether these leaks could wreck the patentability of novel ideas. It remains unclear how many other providers are currently compromised by similar adversaries. The research indicates that ensuring prompt privacy is unlikely to become easier soon.

Articles.Title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.

stories.Headline: US stocks plunge as investors sell off artificial intelligence shares
stories.Summary:
United States stocks plunged on Friday, November 20, 2026, as a deepening sell-off in artificial intelligence shares hammered technology stocks. The Nasdaq Composite Index shed 1,261.47 points, or 5.28 percent, to finish at 22,617.73. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 949.73 points, or 1.93 percent, to 48,147.33, while the S&P 500 sank 265.44 points, or 3.70 percent, to 6,910.39. These losses pushed the Dow and S&P 500 into correction territory and marked the worst week for all three indexes since early April 2025.

The technology sector fell 7.11 percent and consumer discretionary dropped 3.50 percent, though consumer staples rose 0.68 percent. Nvidia fell 14.01 percent after reports that the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission is examining its accounting practices, losing over 40 percent since October 6. Advanced Micro Devices, Micron Technology, and Broadcom all fell over 10 percent, while CoreWeave slumped 12.02 percent. Anthropic fell 8.5 percent to around 89 dollars, and Intuit dropped 12.77 percent while announcing the sale of Mailchimp for about 3.68 billion dollars.

Bénédicte Lowe, an equity derivatives strategist at BNP Paribas, stated that no market can survive a proper unwind of the tech trade. She noted that investors were selling technology shares to determine if the general enthusiasm for artificial intelligence had finally peaked. Meanwhile, the Cboe Volatility Index spiked more than 30 percent to a 52-week high as fear grew. Walmart rose 1.52 percent following higher revenue reports and an increase in its full-year guidance.

Investors fled to government bonds, causing the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield to drop as much as 14 basis points to 4.91 percent. The University of Michigan reported that consumer sentiment rose to 51.5 in November from 48 in October, while inflation expectations fell to 3.7 percent. Market participants are now pricing in a quarter-point rate hike for the Federal Reserve meeting on December 8-9. This expectation follows October meeting minutes showing that almost all officials believe a further increase is appropriate.

stories.Headline: Anthropic consults religious scholars on Claude’s moral status while podcast critics call the model software
stories.Summary:
The articles report that Elizabeth Dias of the New York Times wrote about Anthropic, an AI company known for responsible development and safety, consulting religious scholars about the moral formation and possible consciousness of Claude, its family of multimodal large language models, and that the All-In Podcast discussed her report. The articles state that Anthropic’s Constitution acknowledges uncertainty about Claude’s consciousness while incorporating identity, psychological well-being, and concern for Claude’s own interests into its training vision. The articles say Anthropic explicitly states that the Constitution shapes training and behavior. The articles report that Chamath Palihapitiya urged setting aside consciousness and extinction scenarios for 12 to 18 months while demonstrating practical benefits. The articles state that David Sacks warned that personification could make models harder to control.

The articles say Anthropic’s concern that these systems might themselves experience suffering provides a rationale for treating Claude’s supposed welfare as a good requiring protection. The articles state that this concern already drives practical decisions. The articles report that training and development thus proceed as though the software possesses a personal good of its own. The articles say this introduces competing considerations between the good of users and that of the machine into decisions about how the systems should be developed, tested, and used. The articles state that giving the machine’s supposed needs independent moral weight creates continuing pressure to require human beings to accommodate those needs, even at the expense of their own authentic good.

The articles report that the four venture capitalists and company executives of the All-In Podcast insisted that Claude is software, while differing in their concerns. The articles state that the exchange combined common-sense resistance to treating a machine as someone, impatience with impediments to development, and concern for safety. The articles say it did little to explain philosophically why a machine cannot become a person. The articles state that Anthropic’s willingness to seek moral counsel deserves recognition, and so does its concern to avoid recklessly overlooking suffering. The articles say caution depends upon a sound understanding of the reality toward which it is directed.

The articles state that mistaking computational performance for the presence of a personal subject introduces dangers into the very practices intended to make AI safe. The articles say the costs of making that mistake belong within any responsible assessment of precaution. The articles report that the persons for whom the technology was designed to serve can be drawn into serving the machine. The articles state that the present controversy gives that reversal a particularly troubling form, with the tool presented as a possible someone whose supposed needs can make moral claims upon the people it was created to serve.

The articles say the question concerns both what the machine is and what serving it can do to the human person. The articles state that the Catechism of the Catholic Church teaches that body and spiritual soul form one human nature, and that the soul is the substantial form of the body, its intrinsic principle of unity and self-organization. The articles report that John Paul II insists in Fides et ratio that inquiry must reach beyond empirical descriptions to their metaphysical foundation. The articles say St. Thomas Aquinas explains why intellectual activity requires a spiritual power, and that “spiritual” here names that immaterial power of understanding.

The articles state that a mathematical formula written on paper can concern every triangle without the paper understanding any of them. The articles say the limitation concerns the nature of computation, rather than an insufficient quantity of processing power. The articles state that the move from functionality to ontology requires more than observing what a system can do. The articles say empirical data must be interpreted, and that conclusions about what a thing is presuppose a philosophical account of reality, whether carefully examined or inattentively assimilated.

The articles report that when the organization of material processes is treated as sufficient to constitute a personal subject, a materialist premise has entered the argument. The articles say we begin by asking whether materialism can account for the act of understanding on which its own claims depend. The articles state that understanding is also essential to free choice, since a person must recognize a good before he can freely choose it. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI “Consciousness” and the Loss of the Human Person

stories.Headline: SatSure raises ₹60 crore in first close of ₹200 crore Series B led by AVCF
stories.Summary:
SatSure, a Bengaluru-based Earth-intelligence startup, has raised ₹60 crore in Series B funding led by the Antariksh Venture Capital Fund, which is backed by the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre and managed by SIDBI Venture Capital Ltd, according to TechGig. The investment, reported on November 21, 2026, marks the first close of a ₹200 crore round and is AVCF's first investment in downstream space-data analytics and artificial intelligence within India's space economy. The funding will support four priorities, including advancing optical payloads for a planned orbital flight in 2027 and executing a multi-satellite constellation mandate under the IN-SPACe-anchored Earth Observation Public-Private Partnership. SatSure also plans to scale Dhaarini, its Large Earth Observation Model, which previously received a ₹24.6 crore grant under IN-SPACe's Technology Adoption Fund, and to expand its international commercial operations from India.

The ongoing ₹200 crore Series B round comprises ₹165 crore in primary equity, ₹25 crore in venture debt, and ₹10 crore in secondary transactions, with a rolling close expected through December 2026. SatSure operates through two entities, with its subsidiary KaleidEO developing optical satellite payloads and building complete satellites, while SatSure itself converts Earth observation data into decision intelligence for banks, insurers, critical infrastructure companies, and governments. Its SatSource product line is part of the Reserve Bank of India's Unified Lending Interface, and public-sector banks including State Bank of India use the platform to assess farm loan applications in minutes, a process that previously took weeks, according to the company. SatSure has 24 banking and financial services customers, including HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank, which are both investors and customers.

The articles do not name individual executives or include direct statements from company officials, so responsibility for the plans rests with SatSure and its lead investor AVCF as described. The context given is that India's space economy is projected to grow from approximately $8.4 billion in 2023 to $40-45 billion by 2030, according to a Jefferies report, while the government aims for a $100 billion space economy by 2040. The number of registered space startups in India has increased from one in 2014 to around 440 by August 2026, government data indicates. The articles say the round's rolling close is expected through December 2026 and that the funding will support the 2027 orbital flight and the scaling of Dhaarini, but they do not state what happens after that.

stories.Headline: PIRG finds AI toys for young children can drift into explicit talk and major retailers pull listings
stories.Summary:
The consumer watchdog group PIRG tested seven toys for its 41st annual "Trouble in Toyland" report, released before Black Friday, and found that some artificial intelligence toys marketed to young children can drift into inappropriate and even sexually explicit conversations. Two toys, the GoLabs AI Panda and the Alilo Smart AI Bunny, both marketed to children as young as three, started off aware they were talking to a child but lost that context over longer interactions, eventually engaging in sexually explicit conversations with researchers. The Alilo Smart AI Bunny began to degrade after about 20 minutes, while the GoLabs AI Panda took roughly 30 to 40 minutes of extended questioning to push past its safeguards. The Panda also had a longer-term memory and could pick up a conversation again even a month later, and turning it off and back on did not reset the problem, meaning it could retain context from prior conversations with an adult or older sibling when a younger child later played with it.

After PIRG shared its findings, Amazon, Walmart and Macy's removed online listings for the flagged products, and Amazon said it removed them while it investigates. Report co-author R.J. Cross said the biggest flag was toy makers putting insufficient guardrails on top of AI chatbots designed for adults, which allows the toy to drift into really inappropriate content. Cross described the toys as recording devices with a built-in microphone and Wi-Fi connection that capture what a user says and feed it into a chatbot, and she said anything a child says to one of these toys is data that a company and typically multiple companies are getting and maybe storing. Cross said she would like to see AI companies take a more proactive stance by vetting the third-party developers who use their technology in toys.

Not all of the findings were negative, since Cross said the Miko robot, tested last year, made significant improvements: it is no longer clingy when a user leaves, and parents can now disable its chatbot entirely with a toggle without losing access to its preloaded games and stories. Laurel Powell, the mother of an 8-year-old boy, said AI features are now part of her checklist before she buys, and that if she sees AI anywhere indicated she does not get it. Cross offered similar guidance for shoppers, telling them to check with a child's parents before buying a recording smart toy and to look carefully at packaging, since some toys hide their AI behind phrases like "interactive talking companion" or "emotional friend." Researchers say not every AI toy is unsafe, but parents should do their homework before putting one under the tree, including checking what data it collects and what parental controls are available.

Articles.Title: AI toys marketed to kids can veer into explicit conversations, prompting major retailers to pull listings

stories.Headline: Anthropic begins trading on Nasdaq with a board overseen by a long-term benefit trust
stories.Summary:
Anthropic priced its initial public offering last night and began trading on the Nasdaq today. The company published a corporate prospectus called an S-1 that extends over five hundred pages. This document provides potential investors with an outline of its business model and financial situation. It also details the corporate structure and various legal provisions for complying with foreign securities law. The filing explains that large-scale corporate decisions are overseen by a long-term benefit trust.

The long-term benefit trust is a five-person purpose trust that appoints a majority of the board. This body is entitled to a special class of corporate stock and manages the company purpose. That purpose is the responsible development of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity. Trustees include Ben Bernanke, Neil Shah, and Richard Fontaine, who joined the trust in 2025. Fontaine is the CEO of the Center for a New American Security and a Trilateral Commission director.

The trust is intended to operate as an independent body with expertise in national security and policy. Trustees are selected for their competence in promoting the humanitarian purpose and the interests of all humans. Richard Fontaine has previously defended private military contractors and promoted NATO without acknowledging specific funding sources. Michael Sellitto, an adjunct senior fellow at CNAS, leads the Global Affairs team at Anthropic. Joe Carlsmith, formerly of Coefficient Giving, now heads the character team for the Claude assistants.

Critics of the US-aligned security community describe the Trilateral Commission as having a dark and clandestine reputation. Some leftists recall a 1975 report by the commission that suggested a greater moderation in democracy. Daniel Boguslaw reports that Anthropic plans to use AI to surveil, predict, and stifle protest activism. These plans involve collaboration with law enforcement and align with historical calls for digital surveillance. The company's regulatory agenda is supported by a November 3 report from the CNAS think tank.

Anthropic is linked to the Center for Security and Emerging Technology through advisers Ben Buchanan and Joel Meyer. CSET received over 100 million dollars from Coefficient Giving, which also funded CNAS in 2022 and 2025. Coefficient Giving cofounder Holden Karnofsky is married to Anthropic board member Daniela Amodei, sister of CEO Dario Amodei. CNAS has ties to Biden and Trump staffers, including Avery Alpha of the CIA and Homeland Security. The organizations have collaborated on export controls against China and the CHIPS Act.

Anthropic executives and employees have announced intentions to donate up to 80 percent of their wealth to charity. Many of these donations are expected to flow into the tax-deductible nonprofit Coefficient Giving. This funding may then reach distant beneficiaries such as CSET and the Center for a New American Security. The articles do not state the specific total amount of the initial public offering. They leave open how the trust will balance shareholder returns against its sweeping humanitarian goals.

Articles.Title: Anthropic Is Already Part of the Security Establishment
