stories.Headline: GC Evans president Mark McNamer uses AI to help small manufacturers compete globally
stories.Summary:
GC Evans, an automated packaging manufacturer tucked into a wooded area just off Interstate 530 in Little Rock, has been building custom systems for the food and beverage industry since the 1950s, and it is now using artificial intelligence to reshape both what it builds and how it operates, according to a November 19, 2026 article by Jeremy Harper in Arkansas Money & Politics. Company president Mark McNamer said that with AI, GC Evans can offer the same resources and capabilities that previously only very large companies could offer, and that work a staff of 10 once did can now be done more efficiently by just one or two engineers. AI-assisted tools let the company's engineers create three-dimensional floor plans and visualize custom packaging solutions with considerably less time and effort, while tasks that once required hours of coding can increasingly be accomplished through simple prompts. Manuals, instructions and technical documentation can also be generated in a fraction of the time, which the article says leaves a smaller company capable of offering services, speed and pricing that can compete with much larger international manufacturers.

Artificial intelligence is also becoming part of the machinery itself, with GC Evans manufacturing inspection and rejection systems that identify flaws in packaging as products move through a production line. Those systems can increasingly incorporate AI cameras, meaning machine-vision cameras paired with artificial-intelligence software capable of analyzing products and packaging almost instantaneously, and rather than relying exclusively on traditional programming, the systems can be trained to recognize acceptable products and identify defects or inconsistencies. On a beverage line, that might include damaged cans, improper labels, faulty closures or other packaging problems, and McNamer said the AI cameras enable the systems to process 2,000 12-ounce standard aluminum cans per minute. He said the cameras are programmed through prompting rather than tedious coding, which means a person does not need to be a computer scientist to make an adjustment.

McNamer is the person responsible for the effort described in the article, and he said many food and beverage companies would very much like to work with USA-based manufacturers, but overseas conglomerates have acquired many of the companies providing automated packaging solutions. He said AI is one tool GC Evans uses to even the playing field and bring manufacturing to Arkansas, and he believes the effect on jobs could look very different for small and midsize companies than for large ones. While very large companies will likely reduce workforce, he said, smaller companies like GC Evans will increase hiring due to added productivity, and what is happening is a shift of workforce to where it is most needed. He added that like any technology, companies will adapt to it and be better for it.

The article places GC Evans in the context of a national conversation that has focused on the possibility that automation will eliminate jobs, and it says the combination of speed and accessibility shows why AI could prove especially consequential for smaller manufacturers. It is not simply automating individual tasks but giving smaller teams access to capabilities that once required significantly more personnel, specialized expertise and capital. For Arkansas manufacturers, the article says, that may ultimately be one of AI's greatest opportunities, because the technology can give smaller companies productivity, engineering capabilities and sophisticated tools once available primarily to multinational corporations. That allows Arkansas businesses not simply to compete globally but to bring more of that work home, according to the article.

stories.Summary:
The Office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Violence Against Children and the Permanent Mission of Sweden to the United Nations organized a side event on 19 November 2026 at the United Nations in New York. The event was titled Ending Violence Against Children: Risks and Opportunities of Artificial Intelligence, and a participant is shown attending it in a photograph credited to UN Photo and taken by Manuel Elías. The photograph carries the unique identifier UN71161266 and is categorized under meetings and events, side events, with topical subjects listed as violence, domestic violence, children and participants. The location is given as New York in the United States of America, and the production date matches the event date of 19 November 2026.

The event was held as a side event during the United Nations General Assembly period in New York, and it brought together participants to discuss how artificial intelligence relates to ending violence against children. stories.Headline: Google AI search answers push marketer Marshall Evans to cut search ad spending
stories.Summary:
Marshall Evans, a North Carolina marketer who has bought Google search ads for small businesses like home repair companies and fitness studios for more than a decade, has moved ad dollars away from those ads over the past six months because AI-written responses now often appear above the usual links and ads. For one trophy company he now allocates $500 a month to search ads, down from $2,000 a month about a year ago when Google introduced a feature called AI Mode, and he is shifting money toward streaming services such as Tubi, other search engines like Bing and social media sites like Reddit and Nextdoor. Last month Google reported for the first time that search advertising had fallen to less than 50% of its $128 billion in quarterly revenue, with search ad revenue rising 12% and falling short of the 15% Wall Street expected. Google CEO Sundar Pichai said during the earnings call that the company is focused on building the best search user experience, followed by monetization, and Google has said it wanted to make AI search features appealing to users and would think about advertising later.

Users now often see AI Overviews, an AI-written answer to their query, at the top of the search results page, and the bottom of the summary invites them to interact with a chatbot through AI Mode, but advertising in those AI answers and chatbots has not yet taken off. Advertisers can pay more for the chance to feature their ads in AI Mode, but there is no guarantee the promotion will show up, and Google does not offer advertisers a way to buy guaranteed placement in AI Overviews. Google spokesperson Thomas Schoenfelder said AI is driving an expansionary moment for Search, with AI features leading to increased usage and overall query growth including commercial queries, and that the company's ads experiments have shown promising results. Google also said users were flocking to its AI search tools and that the number of search queries was growing faster than it had in the past five years.

Thomas Monteiro, a senior analyst at Investing.com, said Google is trying to take a business that was the best in the world for 10 years and transform it into a different business without the same advantages, and that making the transition is a lot harder than management thought it would be. Valerie Schlosser, a marketing executive at the global creative agency VML in New York, said what is being seen is arguably the biggest change in searcher behavior, with people spending more time in conversation with chatbots and less time surfing the web. She added that advertisers are not abandoning Google search but are trying to figure out how to survive in the new system, and that clients want to test new things like ChatGPT and Perplexity without totally pulling back from Google. Max Anderson, CEO of OnlyFinder, a service that helps users find creators on the adult entertainment site OnlyFans, said his ads either will not show on the page at all or will show down the page below an AI Overview, and that his costs have probably tripled or quadrupled in the last three years.

Anderson said he is gradually and mathematically pulling back as costs rise and now devotes about half as much spending to Google ads as he did in the early days of the business, declining to discuss specific spending because the numbers were proprietary. He is not planning to abandon Google but is flummoxed by how to get his business mentioned in AI Overviews, saying he would love a way as a business to predictably play there but has not seen one yet. The article describes AI as a double-edged sword for even the biggest companies, with Google standing to benefit enormously from the technology including in its booming cloud computing business while AI takes a toll as the company adjusts. The articles do not say what happens next beyond Google's stated focus on the user experience first and its confidence about its trajectory.

stories.Headline: Researchers present BTG framework for multilingual translation in cross-border firms
stories.Summary:
Jinsheng Wei, Song Cheng, Bo Xiao and Ke Zeng posted a paper on arXiv on 21 November 2026 describing a data-centric framework called Bridging the Terminology Gap, or BTG, for multilingual translation in cross-border corporations. The authors say multilingual translation for cross-border enterprise collaboration is held back by insufficient domain-specific terminology, rigid terminology translation, weak instruction-following and high inference latency in long-instruction scenarios. Their framework first mines cross-lingual term alignments from domain documents and uses large language models to synthesize terminology-rich parallel corpora. A hybrid filtering strategy that combines heuristics with XCOMET scoring is then used to keep the data faithful, and a two-stage training paradigm follows.

The two-stage training starts with supervised fine-tuning for targeted terminology injection and is followed by reinforcement learning to refine output preferences, which the authors say balances domain knowledge integration with model reliability. The paper reports extensive offline evaluations using measures such as XCOMET, GEMBA and Acc@T, alongside online human assessments, and says these show significant improvements in terminology accuracy and instruction-following capabilities. The authors state that the framework is now deployed on their cross-border collaboration platform. The abstract does not give the size of the corpora, the scores achieved or the dates of the evaluations.

The four authors present BTG as a response to the barriers listed in their abstract, and they describe the combination of mined alignments, synthesized corpora, hybrid filtering and two-stage training as the way their framework overcomes them. They say the offline and online results validate the effectiveness of the framework, and they point to its deployment on the cross-border collaboration platform as evidence of that validation. The paper appears on arXiv under the identifier 2611.19858, and the listing offers a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source. Beyond the abstract, the articles give no further statements from the authors.

The context the articles provide is the growing demand for seamless cross-border enterprise collaboration as globalization accelerates, which the authors say multilingual translation has not kept up with. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the deployment already described, and they give no further plans, timelines or follow-up work. No independent evaluation or outside comment on the framework appears in the material.

Articles.Title: Bridging the Terminology Gap: A Data-Centric Alignment Framework for Multilingual Translation in Cross-Border Corporation

stories.Headline: Amazon says Connect Talent uses structured questions and evidence-based scoring to run AI-led job interviews at scale
stories.Summary:
Amazon published a blog post on November 19, 2026 describing Amazon Connect Talent, an AI-led structured interview service. The post says Connect Talent uses structured questions, adaptive follow-ups and evidence-based scoring to gather consistent, job-related information. Amazon built the service around three core design principles and evaluated it through internal research and independent expert review. The post says the service brings established hiring science to AI-led interviews at scale. The article appears on the AWS blog under the Artificial Intelligence topic.

Connect Talent builds each interview around the competencies required for the role, using job requirements and established occupational frameworks to create behaviorally anchored scorecards. The AI interviewer checks after every answer whether the candidate has provided enough evidence and asks targeted follow-up questions when details are missing. A separate evaluation process identifies demonstrated behaviors, cites supporting transcript passages and calculates each competency score from 1 to 5 using a fixed formula. When the transcript lacks sufficient evidence, Connect Talent flags the competency instead of producing a score, and missing evidence does not automatically count against the candidate. The service evaluates transcribed responses without video, voice tone or physical appearance, excludes candidate identity information from scoring and evaluates each competency separately.

An independent I-O psychology firm reviewed Connect Talent's baseline output before human editing and found it retained critical job information in 100% of the job descriptions reviewed. The firm found 91% of generated competencies were clearly traceable to the job description, 98% of interview questions targeted the intended competencies and 94% of rubric signals clearly measured the intended competency. Hiring teams can review, select and edit the competencies, scorecards and questions before using them. The post says this human oversight gives organizations control over the interview process while helping them apply structured hiring practices at scale.

A second independent review covered 36 interviews assessing specific strengths and concerns, creating 252 rubric signals, and Connect Talent aligned with expert scoring decisions in 89.3% of cases. Scoring alignment reached 97.6% when candidates provided clear evidence and 92.9% when only considering candidate concern signals. The evaluation produced a Cohen's kappa of 0.79, which the post calls substantial agreement and just under the 0.81 standard for almost perfect agreement. In a preliminary evaluation, scores based only on the first response were up to 1.14 points lower on a five-point scale than scores based on the full conversation. Connect Talent's structured scoring used all five points of the rating scale, while holistic LLM-as-judge scoring concentrated its ratings within the middle three points.

The post cites decades of research in industrial-organizational psychology, including Schmidt and Hunter, 1998, and Sackett et al., 2022, showing structured interviews help organizations evaluate candidates and predict job performance. It says delivering structured interviews at scale requires significant time and expertise to develop competencies, create questions, train interviewers and evaluate responses consistently. It cites Zhu et al., 2026, finding that some AI scoring approaches concentrate ratings within a narrow range, making differences harder to recognize. It also lists Booth et al., 2021, on bias and fairness in multimodal machine learning, as a reference. The post says a traditional one-way video interview gives a candidate a fixed question and only one opportunity to answer it.

Amazon will present BIZ332, "Every Candidate, Every Time: AI-Led Structured Interviews with Amazon Connect Talent," a Chalk Talk led by Sunitha Srivatsa and Gerald Friedland at AWS re:Invent 2026. Session 1 runs Monday, November 30, 2026, 10:00, 11:00 AM at Caesars Forum, Level 1, Academy 409, with a repeat Thursday, December 3, 2026, 3:00, 4:00 PM at MGM Grand, Premier 309. The post says the session will explore structured interviewing, adaptive follow-up questions and evidence-based scoring. The post does not give pricing, availability dates or customer names for Connect Talent. The post does not say how many candidates or organizations have used the service.

stories.Headline: Fang, Wang, Zeng and Zhou stabilize variance in Gaussian smoothing estimators for high-order derivatives
stories.Summary:
Shuixin Fang, Xuerui Wang, Hang Zeng and Tao Zhou posted a paper on arXiv on 21 November 2026 describing a variance stabilization technique for Gaussian smoothing estimators of high-order partial derivatives. The authors note that computing high-order partial derivatives in high dimensions by automatic differentiation can be costly in both computation and memory. Stein's identity offers an alternative through Gaussian smoothing, but the variance of the resulting estimators can diverge as the step size tends to zero, even with antithetic sampling. Their method extends antithetic sampling from a reflection pair to n equally spaced points on a circle in the complex plane.

Under local analyticity, the authors prove that when n is at least the derivative order, the bias is of order O of sigma to the n and the variance remains bounded as the smoothing step size sigma tends to zero. Numerical experiments support these predictions and demonstrate the effectiveness of the estimator in physics-informed neural networks for polyharmonic and Cahn-Hilliard equations. The technique mitigates the bias-variance trade-off in smoothing-based derivative estimation and is useful for physics-informed neural networks solving high-order partial differential equations. The paper is listed as arXiv 2611.19909.

The work is credited to the four named authors, and the abstract presents the variance stabilization claim and the bounded-variance result as their contribution. The abstract states that the bias is of order O of sigma to the n when n is at least the derivative order, and that the variance stays bounded as sigma tends to zero. The authors report that numerical experiments support these predictions and show the estimator working in physics-informed neural networks for polyharmonic and Cahn-Hilliard equations. They describe the technique as mitigating the bias-variance trade-off in smoothing-based derivative estimation.

The context given in the abstract is the high cost of computing high-order partial derivatives in high dimensions by automatic differentiation, in both computation and memory. Stein's identity is presented as an alternative through Gaussian smoothing, with the drawback that estimator variance can diverge as the step size tends to zero, even with antithetic sampling. The proposed fix moves antithetic sampling from a reflection pair to n equally spaced points on a circle in the complex plane. The abstract does not say what happens next beyond the reported experiments and the stated usefulness for physics-informed neural networks solving high-order partial differential equations.

stories.Headline: Texas regulator restarts data center permits before ERCOT audit finishes
stories.Summary:
Texas environmental regulators restarted data center permit reviews in November 2026. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality resumed processing after the Governor's office gave notice on November 13. This action ended a pause that began with Governor Greg Abbott's September 21 directive. The agency issued an air permit for a data center and gas plant on November 16. This restart occurred before the grid operator ERCOT finished its full audit.

The pause required the agency to halt permits until ERCOT completed an audit of data centers. ERCOT plans to file two reports by December 10, including the Community Impact Review Report. The Batch Zero Eligibility Verification Report will decide which loads of 75 MW and above remain eligible. The Public Utility Commission of Texas is expected to discuss these reports on December 17. A new Democratic governor, Gina Hinojosa, takes office on January 19, 2027.

The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality is responsible for evaluating applications under state and federal laws. A spokesperson for the agency stated that they will follow all applicable laws during reviews. Governor Greg Abbott previously directed the agency to stop permits until the ERCOT audit was finished. The Governor's office later told the agency that ERCOT finished gathering information on community impacts. Gibson Dunn confirmed that the permit pause described in its alerts has ended.

Public Citizen and other watchdogs claim that the agency is issuing permits unilaterally and prematurely. Kathryn Guerra of Public Citizen said that agency leadership began issuing these permits on its own. These critics argue the restart is early because the final audit reports are not yet filed. Developers waiting on the grid are affected by the ERCOT study and the April 9, 2027, deadline. AI builders who depend on Texas capacity must track these changing regulatory and political conditions.

Governor Abbott directed the PUC and ERCOT to audit data centers in August 2026. The agency took its electronic filing system, STEERS, offline after some approvals were flagged in October. ERCOT reviewed responses from 257 developers and about 5,140 questions by November 5. Bipartisan proposals filed between November 9 and March 12, 2027, seek to repeal data center sales tax exemptions. These proposals also aim to require water-use disclosure and bar local tax incentives.

The 90th Texas Legislature convenes on January 12, 2027, and the regular session ends May 31, 2027. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa may rescind or replace the directives issued by Governor Greg Abbott. TCEQ chair Paup's term expires August 31, 2027, and two PUC terms expire September 1, 2027. It remains open whether the restart covers every permit type or only some specific ones. The articles leave open which specific projects will benefit from the resumed permit reviews.

stories.Headline: KPMG runs over 100 AI agents in a second audit of a FTSE 250 company
stories.Summary:
KPMG deployed more than 100 AI agents alongside its conventional audit of an unnamed FTSE 250 company, according to the Financial Times. The agents gathered and analysed information, documented their work and produced draft conclusions. They also suggested next steps. KPMG ran the experiment as a second, AI-assisted audit called Project Exponential. An audit partner signed off the experimental work, but KPMG based its statutory audit opinion on the conventional audit.

KPMG built the agents in four months. Two partners and a director worked with senior managers and junior staff to build and run them, and the firm declined to disclose the team's exact size. Humans set the agents' objectives, supplied information about the business and previous audits, reviewed their work and challenged their conclusions. In one area, a person intervened after an agent failed to match regulations to company documents. KPMG did not rely on the AI-assisted exercise when issuing its audit report.

KPMG's UK head of audit, Cath Burnet, said the technology asked better questions than the human team in some situations. She described instances in which the agents investigated issues more deeply, saying the AI was able to go so much deeper. PwC argued in its 5 August submission to the PCAOB that the use of AI by companies and auditors should become the board's foremost priority. PwC sought guidance on automation bias, explainability, traceability and the ability to reconstruct AI-generated work. PwC identified the need to assess the relevance and reliability of audit evidence and to maintain professional scepticism even when an AI output appears plausible.

Wayne Banks has warned about automation deference, the weakening of scepticism when reviewers become accustomed to plausible, professionally presented AI output. KPMG US has redesigned its audit internship training around fraud scenarios, incomplete information and critical thinking. PwC is introducing critical-thinking and judgement certification for more than 85,000 professionals, including simulations that require employees to challenge AI-generated conclusions. William Englehaupt argues that firms must reconsider staffing, promotion and incentives alongside formal instruction. The traditional audit pyramid distributes work across levels of experience and provides a route through which recruits become managers, directors and partners.

KPMG's pilot does not establish better audit quality overall. The firm's confidence in the technology may encourage employees to regard its conclusions as authoritative. Claims that agents ask better questions than human teams could reinforce that perceived authority. The commercial risk is that firms reduce their staffing pipeline before they understand the sustained demand for human expertise. Firms may need fewer people to produce the work, but they will still need people capable of challenging it.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Cloud host reports AI API key exposure as PHP fixes critical flaws
stories.Summary:
A cloud hosting platform disclosed in October that an unauthorized third party may have accessed encrypted environment variables and, for some of them, obtained the decrypted contents. The platform said those variables may contain secrets such as API keys or database and registry credentials. It advised customers to immediately roll all environment variables. The platform said the impact may be limited to a subset of users. It said it believes the incident is part of a series of attacks on platform companies aimed at compromising AI inference providers.

The platform said it has since invalidated all of its API tokens. In a preliminary report, it said the attack was attempting to obtain AI provider API keys. It said at most 1.85% of workspaces had some environment variables potentially compromised. It said it is not yet able to share the specific details and scale of the exploits. The same day, the PHP project released fixes for two critical flaws that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution.

Both PHP flaws are rated 9.2 under CVSS v4.0 and affect all PHP installations serving web requests. The PHP project says there are no complete mitigations and updating is the only safe choice. Versions 8.1 and older are past end of life and get no new official release. For 7.4 through 8.1, the project posted only minimal source patches. Steven de la Fe wrote the Accounting Today article published November 20, 2026, at 9:00 a.m.

EST. De la Fe said an API key is a password that software uses, and an agent often uses one to pull a trial balance or read a client file. He said that if a key leaks from a breached host or an unpatched server, whoever holds it can get whatever the agent could get. He said that makes it a Safeguards Rule issue. In July, the IRS Office of Professional Responsibility said firms in the business of completing income tax returns are defined as covered financial institutions under the FTC Safeguards Rule.

IRS Publication 5708 adds that this holds regardless of size and that a written information security plan is required. De la Fe said the rule requires each authorized user to get only the customer information they need, and customer information to be encrypted at rest and in transit. He said the rule also requires multifactor authentication, monitoring and logging of user activity, and contract oversight of service providers with periodic checks. He said firms that do not qualify for the small-institution exception (314.6) must also run continuous monitoring or periodic penetration testing and vulnerability assessments.

He said none of that mentions AI agents, and he would treat an agent's key like an authorized user. He said the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications names excessive functionality, excessive permissions and excessive autonomy as typical root causes when agents overreach. De la Fe cited a January 2025 technical blog in which NIST's AI safety team, now its Center for AI Standards and Innovation, wrote that many AI agents are vulnerable to agent hijacking. He said the finding came from lab tests in simulated environments, not field data.

He said an attacker hides instructions in data the agent reads, which in a firm includes client emails and uploads. He proposed a one-page AI key and patch policy for a partner to sign, with seven of 10 lines tied to the rule or IRS guidance. He said line 7 follows CISA's advice and lines 4 and 5 are his recommendations. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Researchers replicate and extend weight-space programming in frontier LLMs
stories.Summary:
Researchers at MIT had recently reported that GPT-6 Astra, a frontier large language model, could write the weights of small neural networks directly in a single reply and could read the raw weights of small networks to say what they were trained to do. In a three-day sprint, Roksana Goworek, Alexander Hickey, Federico Nanni and Martin O'Reilly replicated and extended those results, posting their paper on arXiv on 21 November 2026. Their first finding is that writing weights reproduces, because Astra's networks for the game Breakout scored 514, 550 and 307 against MIT's 517 and scored just as well on two modified versions of Breakout. Claude Opus 5.5 can also write working networks, but it often runs out of output tokens before finishing.

The new element is translating programs into weights, since earlier models could write a good policy as code a generation before they could write network weights. The networks the models write behave like compiled programs, and two models independently decompiled Astra's Breakout network into Python that matched its actions in all tested states. On classifying handwritten digits, Astra's networks scored 50% on average, which is below a simple classifier at 82%. Reading weights turns out to be mostly reading the input layer, because Astra and Opus 5.5 identify which game a network plays almost perfectly.

On three new games the team designed and trained themselves, Astra recovered where things are on the board while mostly missing how the game works. Auditing from weights alone is possible but shallow, because without executing code Astra picked out a small language model poisoned during training in 10 of 10 runs and one poisoned by extra training afterwards in 7 of 10. Astra also flagged a malicious adapter in 23 of 32 cases, but it never identified the trigger or the malicious behaviour. Open-weight models lag behind on these tasks.

The authors conclude from this early study that LLMs can read and write small networks, but that this currently amounts to compiling hand-designed programs and reading the layout of the input layer. They describe it as a promising but early tool for interpretability.

Articles.Title: Replicating and Extending Weight-Space Programming: Frontier LLMs Compile Programs into Weights and Read Input Layers

stories.Headline: Mike Diegel argues AI oversight must govern actions as he builds Pulpo in Arizona
stories.Summary:
A letter published on November 19, 2026 in The Gila Herald, written by Mike Diegel of Pima, Arizona, responded to a November 18 article about Senator Mark Kelly’s new framework to protect Americans from the most advanced AI models. Diegel wrote that Senator Kelly is right about the problem, saying companies should not grade their own homework and that self-regulation has failed. He added that oversight which only arrives after an incident is not oversight at all. The letter argued that Kelly’s proposed fix still misses the core issue because it governs the model rather than the action.

The framework described in the letter calls for a rulebook of hazard levels, independent examiners embedded at AI companies to review safeguards as models are built, and testing and liability before and after deployment. Diegel wrote that none of that stops a consequential action at the moment it happens, because a test can pass, an examiner can sign off, and a company can disclose a risk while the AI system still makes the transfer, deletes the file, or sends the data. He argued the danger is not only how smart a model is but what authority it has been given to act, since a safe model with write access is dangerous and a dangerous model with no authority does nothing. For that reason he said his team is building Pulpo in Arizona, with governance sitting before execution as a narrow, one-use permit for one specific action, with durable evidence afterward.

Diegel wrote that no permit should mean no governed effect, and that anything else is monitoring dressed up as prevention. He said he respects Senator Kelly’s intent and his service, but that protecting Americans requires governing what AI is allowed to do, not just how it is tested or watched. The letter was signed by Mike Diegel of Pima, Arizona. The articles give no further details on the framework, on Pulpo, or on what happens next.

stories.Headline: Sara Jacobs and Don Beyer introduce bipartisan AI safety framework
stories.Summary:
Representatives Sara Jacobs of California and Don Beyer of Virginia introduced a new artificial intelligence framework on November 19, 2026. This legislative outline aims to establish essential guardrails for the development and deployment of advanced technology. Representative Celeste Maloy of Utah joined the Democratic lawmakers to support this bipartisan effort. The proposal represents the second attempt by members of the House to address these issues.

The proposed SAFE AI Act would require the federal government to establish a set of minimum safety standards. These baseline requirements would then allow individual states to build their own additional regulations upon the federal foundation. This structured approach seeks to balance national consistency with the specific needs of different state jurisdictions. The framework focuses on creating a reliable safety net for the rapid evolution of artificial intelligence.

Representatives Jacobs and Beyer are responsible for the outline as they prepare to advance the issue during the next Congress. While the provided text does not include direct quotes, the lawmakers intend to create a bipartisan path for AI oversight. This initiative follows other House efforts, such as a separate framework by Sam Liccardo and Kevin Kiley regarding engagement with China. The broader goal is to mitigate risks while maintaining technological progress through legislative cooperation.

stories.Headline: CPA and learning chief Akhila Chandrashekar argues AI literacy should become a core competency for accountants
stories.Summary:
Akhila Chandrashekar, chief learning officer and a qualified CPA, CMA, CIA and CFE, published an opinion article on November 20, 2026, in Accounting Today arguing that AI literacy should become a core competency for certified public accountants. She opened with a hypothetical in which a CPA asks an AI tool to research a complex tax issue and receives a polished report with regulatory citations and a confident recommendation, only for the CPA to discover the regulation does not exist because the AI fabricated it. She wrote that when something goes wrong the client will not sue the AI company but the CPA, because the accountant remains accountable. The article asks whether AI literacy should become a core CPA competency and notes that the profession's exam already acknowledges AI. The article states that the AICPA's 2026 CPA Exam Blueprints explicitly added artificial intelligence to the Auditing and Attestation section, where students are expected to understand confidentiality risks in using AI tools, recognize how AI adoption could affect the risk of material misstatement, and evaluate the accuracy, completeness, authenticity and potential bias of AI-prepared information.

The 2027 CPA Exam Blueprints, effective January 2027, make what the article calls a nuanced but meaningful change, shifting terminology in AUD17 from information prepared using technologies including AI to information generated using those technologies, and AUD18 explicitly identifies AI-generated information among potential sources of audit evidence. The article stresses that the 2027 blueprint did not introduce AI verification for the first time, since those responsibilities were already reflected in 2026, and it does not create a separate AI examination. Chandrashekar describes the change as a step forward but not a leap, and she argues that foundational AI literacy should be assessed across the CPA exam's Core sections, with more advanced competencies addressed through specialization. Chandrashekar illustrates AI literacy by contrasting two accountants using the same tool, one who copies results into a report and sends it to management and another who checks the underlying data, questions unusual assumptions, verifies calculations, investigates inconsistencies and documents the review. She defines AI literacy not as writing clever prompts or knowing which tool is trending but as understanding AI's limitations, detecting fabricated information, protecting confidential data, recognizing bias and knowing when human judgment must override a machine's recommendation.

She gives sample exam scenarios, including an AI-recommended tax deduction supported by three authoritative-looking citations where one is fabricated, one is outdated and one does not apply, and an AI system that finds no significant revenue anomalies in a dataset that excludes the final month of the financial year. She also raises the case of a CPA who passed the exam 15 years ago and may never have studied generative AI, hallucinations or algorithmic bias yet could now be approving AI-assisted tax advice, supervising automated audits or signing off on AI-prepared financial reports, and she asks whether continuing professional education should evolve to teach identifying errors, challenging outputs, protecting client information and remaining accountable. The article credits the AICPA for recognizing AI-related risks in the 2026 blueprints and for making AI-generated evidence more explicit in 2027, and it concludes that there is a burning need for AI literacy to become a core competency for every CPA. Chandrashekar writes that in a profession built on skepticism, evidence and trust, the greatest risk is not what AI does not know but that accountants may not know what AI does not know. The article does not say what action, if any, the AICPA or state boards plan to take on making AI literacy a core competency or on changing continuing professional education requirements.

stories.Headline: Local authority teams learn to assess AI risks to human rights at Paris academy
stories.Summary:
Teams from 20 local and regional authorities took part in the first HUDERIA Academy for Local Authorities, held in Paris from 17 to 19 November 2026, where they learned to assess the risks that artificial intelligence poses to human rights, democracy and the rule of law. The event was organised by the Centre of Expertise for Multilevel Governance at the Congress of Local and Regional Authorities, working closely with the Council of Europe's Steering Committee for New and Emerging Digital Technologies. Over the three days, participants from 18 member states applied HUDERIA, the Council of Europe's methodology for assessing the impact of AI systems, to a fictional AI-supported public consultation. They identified risks, mapped stakeholders and designed measures to mitigate those risks. The authorities represented included Camden from the United Kingdom, Fingal County from Ireland, Amaroussion from Greece, Bergen from Norway, Valongo from Portugal, Lviv and Rivne from Ukraine, Arezzo from Italy and Harghita County from Romania.

The list also included Ventspils from Latvia, Vigo from Spain, Diyarbakır from Türkiye, Bitola and Resen from North Macedonia, Bălți from the Republic of Moldova, Shkodër from Albania, Kutaisi from Georgia, Szentendre from Hungary, Turnišče from Slovenia, Nõo from Estonia and the Association of Netherlands Municipalities. Participants described HUDERIA as practical and relevant, and several began applying it to their own projects while obtaining feedback from their peers. They committed to maintaining an alumni network and called for follow-up and continued opportunities to engage with HUDERIA. The Academy is an official event on the Road to Geneva AI Summit 2027 and a contribution to the Council of Europe's New Democratic Pact for Europe, and it supports implementation of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence.

Annika Vaikla, the Congress co-rapporteur on AI and Deputy Mayor of Viimsi in Estonia, urged authorities to use AI to give public servants more time for people while keeping people in control. She called for AI literacy among political leaders, staff and citizens, and for smaller municipalities to have access to shared expertise. The articles say several themes ran through the Academy, including that local AI should be human-centred, socially anchored and community-led, and that public trust has to be earned through openness and clear accountability by keeping humans in the loop. The articles do not say what specific follow-up measures were agreed beyond the alumni network and the calls for continued engagement.

stories.Headline: Mid-cap Indian IT firms buy AI skills as acquisitions outpace organic growth
stories.Summary:
During Coforge's Q2 earnings call, an analyst asked Chief Financial Officer Saurabh Goel to explain the gap between consolidated and organic growth. Revenue grew 10.9% sequentially in constant currency, against organic growth of 3.8%, indicating how much acquisitions are supplementing the company's growth. Goel attributed the difference partly to the consolidation of a full quarter of Encora's revenue in Q2, compared to only two months in Q1. Encora, the digital engineering firm Coforge acquired for ₹22,090 crore, contributed ₹1,382, 1,391 crore in revenue. It contributed about ₹940 crore during the two months included in Q1.

Q2 was busy not just for Coforge, but also for Cyient and Mphasis, which acquired data engineering and decision intelligence firms. Meanwhile, Persistent is expected to complete its acquisition of Nagarro in the first quarter of 2027. Coforge said its AI-led engineering, data integration, and cloud businesses contributed 86% of consolidated revenue. Mphasis said AI-led deals accounted for 66% of its ₹4,380 crore in net new total contract value. Zensar reported that AI-influenced deals made up 36% of its order book, while Sonata Software put AI-led order bookings at 25%.

Gartner's Distinguished Vice President Analyst Milind Govekar tells AIM that most mid-tier companies are acquiring to get new skills and new technology. Coforge has already integrated Encora into its business, and the company no longer distinguishes between the two entities. Coforge's consolidated EBIT margin stood at 16%, against 17% for its standalone business. Integration costs reached about ₹160 crore, exceeding the company's guidance of ₹141 crore to ₹150 crore. Cyient acquired AI-native data engineering firm TAO Digital for ₹2,049 crore, and TAO contributed ₹90 crore in its first month.

Excluding the acquisition, organic revenue grew 1.6% sequentially and 0.4% year-on-year in constant currency. CFO Shrinivas Kulkarni said TAO's annual revenue run rate had risen from about $80 million (₹752 crore) at acquisition to nearly $100 million (₹940 crore). He expects it to reach ₹1,034 crore over the next 12 months, while cautioning against extrapolating from one month's revenue. Cyient now plans to take TAO's AI data engineering capabilities to existing customers.

The company's technology order intake rose 39.7% during the quarter. Persistent secured approximately 94.04% of Nagarro's share capital and voting rights, excluding treasury shares and including its existing holding. The deal awaits RBI approval and foreign investment clearances in Austria and Spain. The acquisition would expand Persistent's European presence through Nagarro's delivery centres in Romania, Portugal, Hungary, and Poland.

Persistent's European revenue fell 8.5% year-on-year in Q2 in US dollar terms, which it attributed to two client-specific events. North American revenue grew 22.5%. Persistent booked ₹185 crore in Nagarro-related transaction costs in Q2, including advisory, financing, and legal expenses. Its PAT margin was 7.5% and operating PAT margin 10.6%.

It expects another ₹235, 282 crore in costs over the next two quarters, taking cumulative one-time expenses to approximately ₹420, 467 crore. Mphasis acquired Canadian decision-intelligence firm Theory and Practice Business Intelligence (TAP) in April and expects to complete its acquisition of IT staffing firm Red Oak Tech's customer contracts, worth up to ₹265 crore, in November. CFO Aravind Viswanathan cited TAP-related amortisation as a pressure on margins during the earnings call. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Bajaj Finserv and Pennant Technologies invest $4 million in Soket AI as it launches EKA-1 model
stories.Summary:
Bajaj Finserv's applied research initiative Finserv Intelligence invested about $2 million in AI research company Soket AI, and its investee firm Pennant Technologies put in a further $2 million in the same round, for a total of $4 million. Soket AI, which is backed by the IndiaAI Mission, also launched EKA-1, a 26-billion-parameter foundation model under Project EKA, its flagship sovereign AI initiative focused on math, code and reasoning. The model is being built to support over 100 languages, including Indian and Global South languages, alongside programming languages. The investment supports Soket AI's work on indigenous AI solutions for applications where data security, reliability and technological sovereignty are critical.

Sanjiv Bajaj, Chairman and Managing Director of Bajaj Finserv, said in a statement that demand is for AI systems that are not only intelligent but also reliable, secure, auditable and able to operate within trusted environments. He said the group is investing in indigenous research that meets these requirements. Rajeev Jain, Vice Chairman and Managing Director of Bajaj Finance, said the next phase of AI will be defined by outcomes delivered at sustainable cost. He said Soket AI's efficient reasoning-led models can make advanced AI economically viable for financial services while allowing the firm to deploy it securely within its own infrastructure, with full control over data. He added that the startup's depth in Indian languages can help the firm serve customers in the language they are comfortable with.

Abhishek Upperwal, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Soket AI, asserted that the backing of Bajaj Finance and Pennant Technologies reinforces the company's belief that India has the talent and capabilities to develop foundational AI technologies at a global scale. Pradeep Verma, Founder and Managing Director of Pennant Technologies, said the firm is building agentic AI into its lending platform so banks can use AI across their operations while retaining control over their data and decisions. He said there is a clear need for locally built large language models that regulated institutions can run on their own infrastructure and govern under their own policies. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the launch and the funding.

stories.Headline: House committees warn US companies against using Chinese open weight AI models
stories.Summary:
The House Homeland Security Committee and the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party released a report on November 20, 2026, regarding American companies using Chinese open weight artificial intelligence. This joint investigation found that firms like Airbnb, DoorDash, and Anysphere, the owner of the Cursor coding platform, embedded these models into their tech stacks for inventory, coding, and customer assistance. The report warns that allowing these models to take root could cost taxpayers billions of dollars and take years to resolve, similar to the threats posed by Huawei and ZTE. The 50-page document proposes twelve policy recommendations, including the creation of an American open-weight AI initiative and a standard for sourcing models. It suggests establishing an AI bill of materials and banning China-developed models from sensitive critical infrastructure and federal contract work.

The report also calls for the systematic evaluation of Chinese models to mitigate risks. These changes aim to prevent the long-term integration of foreign technology that could compromise national security. Representatives Andrew Garbarino and John Moolenaar, both from New York, authored the report based on agency advisories, classified briefings, and hearings. They stated that the investigation revealed risks that national security officials and American businesses can no longer afford to downplay or overlook. The lawmakers noted that while the United States invests billions in super intelligence, Beijing is utilizing stolen intelligence to close the technological gap.

They highlighted that Chinese developers used fraudulent accounts and proxy networks to replicate the capabilities of American frontier models. Cybersecurity expert Mark Montgomery of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies explained that China is expanding global dependence on its open-source AI to kill competition. He noted that companies often ignore safety and security issues to achieve lower front end costs, a strategy that Chinese leaders understand well. Because American firms like OpenAI and Anthropic dominate the frontier model space, China is focusing on the low cost open-source marketplace. The report emphasizes the urgent need for the United States to compete more seriously in this specific sector.

Articles.Title: US companies’ use of Chinese open weight AI draws rebuke from House chairmen - The Record from Recorded Future News

stories.Headline: Researchers present MAGE framework for transferable multimodal graph learning without target-domain parameter updates
stories.Summary:
Haiyang Jiang, Tong Chen, Xinyi Gao, Hao Wang and Hongzhi Yin posted a paper to the arXiv preprint server on 21 November 2026 describing a framework they call MAGE, which stands for Meta-path Adaptive Graph Evidence Prompting, and which is built for transferable multimodal graph learning. Multimodal graphs combine textual and visual attributes with relational structures, giving a rich representation of complex real-world data, and the authors argue that models trained on source graphs need to generalize to unseen graph domains so that graph models can be broadly applied and reused. The authors say this is hard because cross-modal interactions among neighbors and the neighboring information needed for prediction can vary across target nodes and graph domains. They frame the problem as two key challenges, adaptive cross-modal neighborhood fusion, which captures and integrates cross-modal interactions among neighbors to accommodate variation across nodes and domains, and target-specific evidence selection, which identifies the neighboring textual and visual information each target node needs to support prediction by a large language model.

MAGE represents textual and visual node views separately in a heterogeneous graph and introduces two complementary components. Meta-path Adaptive Multimodal Propagation, or MAMP, adaptively aggregates neighborhood information along heterogeneous meta-paths and compresses it into graph-aware soft tokens. Evidence-Guided Instruction Tuning, or EGIT, selects relevant neighboring evidence for each query and incorporates its graph-aware representations into instructions for a frozen multimodal large language model. Together, the authors say, these components support transfer from multiple source graphs to unseen target graphs without any parameter updates on the target domains.

The authors report experiments with three source graphs and four unseen target graphs that show strong cross-domain transfer performance on node classification and link prediction, again without requiring parameter updates on the target domains. The paper lists five authors, Haiyang Jiang, Tong Chen, Xinyi Gao, Hao Wang and Hongzhi Yin, and is identified on arXiv as 2611.20449. The abstract presents the work as a response to the two challenges of adaptive cross-modal neighborhood fusion and target-specific evidence selection, and it describes the frozen multimodal language model as the component that receives the selected evidence through instructions. The posting page offers the paper as a PDF, as experimental HTML and as TeX source, and it also carries the standard arXivLabs notice about collaborators who develop and share features on the site.

The articles do not say what happens next, beyond the posting of the preprint and the results the authors report. No venue, publication date or peer review outcome is given, and the articles do not describe any deployment or follow-up work. The only stated plan is the framework itself, which the authors present as a way to transfer from multiple source graphs to unseen target graphs without target-domain parameter updates.

Articles.Title: MAGE: Meta-path Adaptive Graph Evidence for Transferable Multimodal Graph Learning

stories.headline_source: MAGE: Meta-path Adaptive Graph Evidence for Transferable Multimodal Graph Learning

stories.Headline: Justice department launches Super Intelligence Task Force to coordinate AI enforcement
stories.Summary:
The Department of Justice has launched a Super Intelligence Task Force, known as DOJ-SITF, to promote American artificial intelligence and to coordinate criminal and civil enforcement against actors who misuse AI, according to a November 19, 2026 article by McCarter & English attorneys Lindsey R. Harteis, Zachary Myers and Erin Prest. The Attorney General’s press release announcing the Task Force signals that enforcement will be forthcoming for those who use AI to engage in fraud or other criminal conduct. The new body merges the Artificial Intelligence Task Force that the former Attorney General announced in January 2026. Under Executive Order 14434, the executive branch uses the terms Super Intelligence and SI instead of Artificial Intelligence or AI.

The Task Force is charged with organizing the Department’s criminal and civil enforcement efforts involving AI and with deconflicting investigations, cases and other matters among Department components and United States Attorneys’ Offices. It will recommend enforcement priorities meant to promote public safety and prevent misuse of AI, serve as the Department’s point of contact with the President’s separate AI Task Force and other federal agencies, and coordinate the Department’s affirmative civil litigation involving AI. It will also develop guidance on prosecuting AI-related unlawful conduct and on evaluating compliance measures, and advise on legislative or regulatory proposals that promote AI innovation without burdensome regulation. The announcement does not establish a new regulatory or legislative framework for AI, so potential enforcement would proceed under existing laws.

The Task Force will be led by the Attorney General or his designees, with the Associate Attorney General and Associate Deputy Attorney General serving as co-chairs. Additional members will include representatives of the Antitrust Division, the Attorney General’s Advisory Committee, Civil Division, Criminal Division, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the National Fraud Enforcement Division, the National Security Division and the Office of the Solicitor General. The DOJ release says the Task Force will ensure a comprehensive approach across the Department and will ensure that America’s leadership in AI is not compromised by misuse by foreign state and state-sponsored actors, transnational criminal organizations, and individual or corporate actors engaged in fraud or other unlawful conduct. The Task Force will work in partnership with the separate AI Task Force established by President Trump.

The article says the DOJ does not explain what constitutes misuse of AI or establish the precise scope of conduct that could result in civil or criminal liability. It says companies’ use of AI in connection with government payment claims, cybersecurity controls, and representations made while negotiating and performing government contracts could present potential exposure under existing federal statutes. Using AI to present false claims for payment from the government, failing to maintain necessary cybersecurity controls while using AI resources, and making material misrepresentations about AI use in government contracts might conceivably result in liability, according to the article. The authors write that companies should understand the Task Force’s objectives and composition and should consider steps to mitigate potential civil or criminal exposure from their use of AI technologies and platforms.

stories.Headline: NTT DATA finds Asia Pacific clients more open to outcome-based AI deals than Western markets
stories.Summary:
Nitin Bajaj, the global head of AI strategy and product at NTT DATA, announced at the NTT R&D Forum 2026 in Tokyo that Asia Pacific clients are more open to outcome-based AI deals than those in Europe or North America. This shift is part of a broader strategy called services as software, where AI agents perform tasks that were previously billed by the number of hours or people assigned to the work. The company is moving away from traditional headcount models to focus on measurable results, noting that this appetite for performance-based arrangements has grown over the last two years. The new approach requires different pricing models, including consumption-based fees for high-volume tasks and fees tied to specific results, such as increasing system uptime from 90% to 98.5%. Some contracts involve revenue or profit sharing, such as taking a percentage of profits from a telecommunications call center that exceeds a baseline for new customers.

Bajaj noted that NTT DATA ran over 600 AI pilot projects in 2024, which eventually led to 1,350 paid projects last year. While only about 20% of those specific pilots went into production, the region now accounts for 15 to 20% of pilot volume and is growing quickly. Bajaj explained that the openness in Asia Pacific stems from a diverse mix of frontier, privately developed, and Chinese open-weight models, as well as specific regional capital structures. He admitted that outcome-based contracts are difficult to manage because providers cannot control every variable within a client's business that might affect the final result. He also mentioned that many AI projects fail due to fragmented data in old systems rather than the models themselves, citing estimates that 80% of such projects fail to deliver.

To improve efficiency, the company uses its Silicon Valley firm, AIVista, to reduce document processing costs from a benchmark of 43 cents to about 17 cents. The company is expanding its partnerships with hyperscalers like Amazon Web Services, which has significant influence in the Asia Pacific banking market, and Databricks. NTT DATA is also strengthening its relationship with Google Cloud and expects to have more than 5,000 engineers certified on the Gemini Enterprise platform within a few months. By integrating these tools into a full software stack, the company aims to guarantee the variables that impact client outcomes. This strategy allows them to offer sovereign AI solutions that keep data and control within a specific organization or country.

stories.Headline: Brazil's Senate approves an AI regulation bill while Peru enacts a general AI law
stories.Summary:
Brazil’s Senate approved a bill on December 10, 2024 regulating the use, development, and deployment of AI, and that general framework remains before a special committee in the Chamber of Deputies with no vote date confirmed. On February 25, 2026, another law turned Brazil’s National Data Protection Authority into a full regulatory agency with greater technical, administrative, and financial authority. Peru passed legislation in 2023 establishing principles including data privacy, the development of national AI talent, and cooperation on AI development at home and abroad. In 2025, a supreme decree approved regulations implementing Peru’s law, setting out financing provisions, accountability mechanisms, and implementation periods. The Atlantic Council published the analysis on November 19, 2026, written by Olivia Torres, a project assistant at its GeoTech Center, and Angel Ortega, a Panamanian attorney and policy researcher.

An attached proposal in Brazil would expand the role of the National Data Protection Authority, making it the default AI regulator alongside sectoral regulators. Peru’s 2023 law designates regulatory authority to the existing Secretariat of Government and Digital Transformation. Peru’s 2025 decree clarifies how responsibilities are divided among government institutions and enforcement authorities, and provides that when the Secretariat encounters a regulatory breach it has authority to consult the competent authorities. In Peru, the National Data Protection Agency handles AI-related personal data breaches, the National Institute for the Defense of Competition and Protection of Intellectual Property handles industry competitiveness and consumer protection, and the National Police specializes in cybercrimes. The Organization of American States launched the Inter-American Framework on Data Governance and Artificial Intelligence, known as MIGDIA, a regional initiative developed by multisector stakeholders and governments.

Ahead of the 2026 Brazilian elections, Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court issued fourteen resolutions governing the electoral process, including restrictions on AI use. The resolutions barred AI systems from recommending candidates or signaling voting preferences and required disclosure of AI-generated or digitally manipulated campaign content. The court was able to enforce the resolutions through the suspension of profiles. Dilmar Villena, director of Hiperderecho, one of Peru’s leading digital safety organizations, warned the authors in an interview that without additional resources institutions will have limited bandwidth to oversee all emerging AI technology concerns. Villena noted that oversight of most emerging technologies, including cloud computing and platform regulation, falls under the Secretariat of Government and Digital Transformation, which faces concerns around its budgetary capacity due to its reliance on funding from the Presidency of the Council of Ministers.

Brazil’s first AI proposal was criticized for insufficient inclusion of Indigenous voices in the legislative debate and failure to consider structural racism in public security. São Paulo’s Smart Sampa city surveillance pilot project was heavily scrutinized by civil society since its presentation in 2022, as it was found to disproportionately profile black individuals. Brazil’s legislative debates incorporated concerns about racial discrimination and other contextual issues. Peru has launched digital government indicators that track the implementation of digital government initiatives and institutional capabilities and show where administrative capacity is thin. The indicators do not yet measure whether AI implementation itself is working, but are described as an important building block for future institutional readiness assessments.

Countries in Latin America are developing AI regulatory frameworks, many drawing on European regulatory traditions, from data protection to emerging risk-based AI rules. Brazil and Peru have become regional leaders in regulation while still at an early stage of AI governance, pioneering different approaches. Brazil has begun strengthening its institutions while its general AI framework remains in development, and Peru has become one of the first Latin American countries to pass a general AI law coupled with implementation mechanisms. One MIGDIA recommendation is to clearly define the processes, roles, and responsibilities of actors involved across the data lifecycle. Brazil has already taken steps in this direction by assigning a role of AI regulator to the National Data Protection Authority.

Brazil is developing authority before its regulatory framework is concretized into law, while Peru has a more clearly assigned authority now that AI legislation has been approved and is beginning to be applied. The articles leave open whether Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies will vote on the general AI framework and when. They leave open whether the attached proposal making the National Data Protection Authority the default AI regulator will be adopted. They leave open whether Peru will scale up institutional resources as regulatory responsibilities expand. They leave open whether Peru’s digital government indicators will later measure whether AI implementation itself is working.

stories.Headline: MIT and Mecalux find 57% of firms expect AI to make over a quarter of warehouse decisions autonomously by 2028
stories.Summary:
A study by the MIT Centre for Transportation & Logistics and Mecalux found that 57% of organisations expect AI to make or execute more than a quarter of warehouse operational decisions autonomously by 2028, based on a survey of nearly 2,000 supply chain and warehousing professionals across 21 countries. The report, published on 20 November 2026, examined generative and agentic AI in warehouse operations and found that 61% of organisations reported using generative AI at large-scale deployment or full integration, compared with 56% for agentic AI. About three in four deployments had been at their current stage for less than a year, yet 87% of generative AI applications and 81% of agentic AI applications showed at least moderate improvement in their target metrics. Only 39% of generative AI use cases and 36% of agentic AI use cases had significant gains that were both quantified and documented, and where respondents could estimate the scale, the typical gain was about 20% on the main target metric.

Companies are giving AI systems authority in selected areas while keeping tighter controls elsewhere, with inventory movements the area where agents were most often allowed to decide without human approval at 51% of agentic AI use cases, followed by data corrections at 42%. Only 22% of these systems were allowed to make customer-facing commitments and 12% were permitted to make financial decisions, and the most common oversight model was human-on-the-loop, in which AI operates within defined limits while employees monitor and can intervene. Organisations with comprehensive, actively enforced AI governance were about twice as likely to report significant, documented improvements, at 51% versus 26% for generative AI and 46% versus 23% for agentic AI, a pattern that held after accounting for deployment status, region, industry and budget, though the study noted association rather than proof of causation. Legacy system integration was the biggest constraint on scaling generative AI for 40% of respondents, while 54% said better integration with warehouse management and ERP systems would have the greatest effect on adoption.

Matthias Winkenbach, Director of the Intelligent Logistics Systems Lab, said the objective was to move beyond general sentiment and provide practical guidance on where these technologies deliver operational value today and where they remain experimental. Javier Carrillo, Chief Executive Officer of Mecalux, said warehouse decision-makers need AI they can measure and that the research gives clients a clear map of where the technology is working and what it takes to prove it. On employment, 56% of organisations said the technology had mainly shifted staff towards higher-value tasks, while 11% reported reduced headcount and 9% reported increased headcount, and 73% said they were upskilling warehouse-floor staff while 61% were creating new technical roles. Ninety per cent anticipated an increase in AI investment over the next two to three years, with 29% expecting that rise to exceed 25%, broadly in line with the previous year's study, and among companies that had fully integrated the technologies, 70% expected agentic AI to make or execute more than a quarter of warehouse operational decisions autonomously by 2028.

Articles.Title: Study finds AI will run more warehouse decisions by 2028 - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Texas senator Sarah Eckhardt urges statewide AI safeguards for schools as lawmakers convene
stories.Summary:
Last year, Texas lawmakers required public schools to restrict students' use of cell phones throughout the school day, including between classes, according to a Nov 19, 2026 Houston Chronicle opinion piece by Kris Perry. Artificial intelligence is now moving into classrooms, homework assignments, school-issued computers and the software teachers use every day, Perry wrote. When the Legislature convenes in January, Texas has an opportunity to lead the country again, she wrote. A 2026 Stanford University review examined a research repository containing over 1,600 papers on AI in K-12 education, Perry wrote. Only 52 studies met its standards for strong causal evidence, few examined long-term learning outcomes, and only five of the high-quality studies of student AI use took place in American K-12 classrooms, she wrote.

Perry called for statewide standards for AI products used by students, with providers required to demonstrate evidence of educational effectiveness and safeguards for student privacy, data security and developmental well-being before schools adopt a tool. Schools should know what information is collected, how it is used and whether students' interactions are retained or used to train AI systems, she wrote. A law should require meaningful human oversight, with teachers remaining responsible for instruction, assessment and decisions affecting students, and AI should never independently determine a child's academic progress, disciplinary consequences or access to educational opportunities, she wrote. Students should not be required to engage in unrestricted, emotionally responsive conversations with AI systems as part of their education, she wrote. The Texas Education Agency could establish an independent review process, publish approved-use guidance and maintain a transparent list of evaluated products, and schools should have the right to disable unnecessary AI features without losing access to essential educational services, she wrote.

Perry, executive director of Children and Screens: Institute of Digital Media and Child Development, wrote that Google has made access to search on school-managed devices contingent on accepting AI features built into the search engine. That puts schools in the position of accepting AI features they may not want simply to preserve access to a basic educational resource, she wrote. She asked who should determine how children learn: their teachers and communities, or the companies supplying their software. She wrote that a small rural district and a large urban district may have different educational needs, but children in both deserve the same basic safeguards and access to high-quality resources. She wrote that none of this requires banning every use of AI.

Perry wrote that some early studies suggest students can perform better on assignments when AI is available, but when the technology is removed, evidence of lasting learning is mixed. She wrote that evidence shows general-purpose chatbots do not support learning as well as tools designed to align with core pedagogical theory and practice, supporting learning through guided reasoning rather than supplying answers. She wrote that early research suggests AI may help teachers reduce preparation time, but schools should evaluate whether those savings preserve instructional quality. She wrote that carefully designed tutoring systems that guide students through problems rather than simply supplying answers may also prove useful, with educators directing their use and evidence determining whether they belong in classrooms.

She wrote that AI cannot solve budget shortfalls, academic struggles and shortages of individual attention, and that effective education depends on relationships with teachers, meaningful interaction with classmates and opportunities to work through difficult material with support. Perry wrote that a 2026 letter to Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick from State Sen. and Comptroller-elect Sarah Eckhardt calls for examining AI literacy, student safety and statewide guidance. She wrote that the work should become enforceable protections, not simply another set of recommendations schools are left to interpret on their own.

She wrote that parents should ask their state representatives and senators to support legislation establishing independent AI product review, strong student-data protections, meaningful teacher oversight and the ability for schools to reject unwanted AI features. She wrote that local school boards should be required to disclose which AI tools students encounter and how those tools are evaluated. She wrote that with its school phone law, Texas showed that protecting children can be a bipartisan priority. Perry wrote that the question is not whether children should learn about artificial intelligence, because they should.

She wrote that the question is whether we will allow companies to determine how children experience it before parents, teachers and researchers have established what is safe and educationally sound. She wrote that Texas still has time to make that choice. She wrote that Texas faces a harder version of the same question it answered with its phone law. She wrote that the goal should be to establish clear statewide guardrails for the use of AI in schools before a piecemeal approach becomes so widespread that meaningful oversight is difficult.

Articles.Title: Texas got cell phones out of classrooms. Now it’s time to confront AI. | Opinion - Houston Chronicle

stories.Headline: Lenexa Medical wins three VIC AI Awards including Best in Australia
stories.Summary:
Lenexa Medical, a Victorian health technology startup, won three prizes at the VIC AI Awards 2026 in Melbourne, where it was named Best Use of AI in Healthcare, AI Startup of the Year and Best in Australia, the awards recognising projects across technical and creative artificial intelligence categories with winners drawn from Victoria, elsewhere in Australia and overseas. The company was the biggest winner on the technical side of the program through its LenexaCARE product, and it has also been recognised by TIME Magazine as one of the world's top Health Technology companies. Other technical winners included Rostrum AI, which took the Best Enterprise AI Tool award for RostrumLink with Orato, and SPQR Technologies, which won Best AI for Safety for Aegis Runtime Control: Independent Execution Authority for AI Agents. The creative awards covered art, film, music and advertising made with AI tools, with Annelise (Wink.) Clark winning Best in AI Art for Cul-de-Sac Couture and the Best AI Campaign/Commercial prize going to Chapel Street Precinct Film, created by Toby Goodman and the team at CoastGen.

In the film categories, Glamourexia by John Paul DeFazio won Best in AI Short Films, while Edmond Yang took Best in AI Animation for When You Run From Your Mom, and the Best AI Music / Music Videos award went to Is This Not real? by Jason Joseph Dainter. A special Rising Star award went to Peek-a-Boo! A Bunny's Halloween Night, directed by Guillaume Descamps. Matt Kirby, Director of the VIC AI Awards and VIC AI Boom, said the quality of entries stood out before judging began, noting that submissions came from local Victorian individuals and companies alongside international ones and that startups without a profile yet sometimes blew the judges away.

He also pointed to the commercial focus of the technical category winners, saying they are all driven by a real-world need and that it is easy to fall in love with the power of AI but there must be a worthwhile outcome for it to stack up commercially. Kirby said two of the winning filmmakers showed how AI-assisted work could still rely on traditional storytelling strengths, saying both know how to tell a story and that AI is supporting their ideas but it is still driven by human emotion and creativity. The winners reflected a mix of Victorian startups, Australian creatives and international entrants, and the awards were intended to recognise achievements in AI innovation, creativity, consumer work and large-scale business applications. For Victoria's startup scene, Lenexa Medical's result is likely to draw the most attention because of the breadth of its wins, taking category honours in healthcare and the startup competition and then securing the overall Best in Australia award, which placed the company at the centre of this year's judging.

Rostrum AI's award underlined the presence of local business software developers in the field, while SPQR Technologies' win highlighted the attention being paid to AI safety tools as the use of autonomous systems expands. The results come as Australian AI activity continues to spread beyond large technology companies to specialist startups, creative studios and individual artists, and the list of winners suggests judges weighed both commercial application and creative execution across a wide range of work. Kirby said the event left him encouraged by what he had seen from participants, saying VIC AI Boom and the VIC AI Awards came along at the right time and that when everyone else is feeling tired at the end of the year he is feeling inspired by what he is seeing. He added that he cannot wait for the next event.
