stories.Headline: Snowflake engineer says enterprises should fix data layers rather than prompts to make AI answers trustworthy
stories.Summary:
Arjun Danda Sureshbabu, a Staff Software Engineer at Snowflake, wrote in SD Times on 2026-11-20 that a few months into building an AI assistant for finance teams, someone asked it what bookings looked like for one region last quarter. The assistant answered in a few minutes with a table and a summary explaining how it got there, and the number was inaccurate. His first instinct was to blame the prompt, into which the team had put role instructions, worked examples and a long description of the schema. When he analyzed the query, the model had done exactly what was asked, finding a table with an AMOUNT column, a REGION_CD column and a date, and summing it up. The model could not know that the amounts included reversals, that region codes had been remapped after a reorg, and that bookings there means something narrower than every row in that table.

The article says most enterprise data was designed for applications and reports, not for a language model reading it cold, and that a finance table is mostly surrogate keys, status codes, amounts and timestamps. It says what those things mean is written down somewhere else, if at all, in a reporting team's SQL, a spreadsheet of code mappings, or the memory of an analyst who has been around for six years. It says a STATUS column with values 1 through 7 will lead the model to decide for itself what they mean, and it won't ask. It says describing the data in the prompt holds up in a demo with five tables and gets shaky at enterprise scale, because definitions and mappings change every quarter and nobody updates the prompt with each mapping change. It says a rule in the ninth paragraph can stop being honoured after a model upgrade, and you find out when a user does.

The article says the teams that get this right stop trying to explain the business to the model in prose and put that knowledge in the data layer, where developers already have tools to build, review and version it. It says that starts with a semantic layer instead of raw tables: named business entities, ontologies, metric definitions, plain-language descriptions of columns and their allowed values, their synonyms and accurate joins. It says bookings gets defined once, in code, and any change to that definition goes through review like everything else, and the model picks from definitions business teams have agreed on rather than creating on its own. It says access control stays in the database, enforced by the same row- and column-level policies that apply to every other query, so the data the model can reach has already been filtered. It says the third piece is making answers checkable, with verified queries reviewed by the owners of those numbers, and when the model writes something new it shows the query, definitions and filters it used.

The article says a prompt tends to belong to whoever wrote it, often one person tweaking it until the demo works, while definitions, policies and verified queries belong to an engineering team with code review, monitoring and someone on call when an answer goes wrong. It says the developers who do this well understand both the data model and the business it describes, sitting with a finance analyst to find out why a code was remapped two years ago and turning that into a definition the system enforces using patterns such as a verified query repository. It says data engineers and domain experts, who often sit at the edge of AI projects, end up doing some of the most important work. It says a better bar than a good demo is whether known or frequently asked questions return the same report the finance team consistently produces, which a human verifies, and whether each answer can be traced back to its definitions and source data. It says prompts still matter, setting the context surrounding the data and how the model asks a follow-up when it is unsure, but they sit on top of everything else.

The article says the author has seen versions of that failure many times since, and the usual response is to tune the prompt, which he thinks is the wrong place to look. It says you can tell the model not to show compensation data to the wrong person, but that is a request, not a permission check. It says moving to a bigger model does not help much, because it writes a more convincing guess and still has no idea when your fiscal year starts. It says you cannot really test a prompt the way you test code. It says most of this is ordinary engineering, schema design, contracts, authorisation and testing, and the unusual part is the consumer, which won't tell you when it's confused or fails silently.

The article says that when an enterprise AI system gives a confident wrong answer, the prompt is usually the last thing the author would change, and he would look first at what the data tells the model, the context layer and grounding factors, and at what it leaves the model to guess. It says the teams keep test sets of real questions with known answers, which is how they tell whether a change actually made things better or just felt like it did. It says the author designs and runs production AI systems that answer questions over enterprise finance data for finance teams and thousands of employees. It says a good answer in a demo tells you very little. It does not say what the finance teams did after the inaccurate answer, or when any of the changes it describes were made.

Articles.Title: Prompt engineering won’t make enterprise AI trustworthy. Data engineering will. - SD Times

stories.Headline: Researchers propose Onsager-based neural time-stepping framework for gradient-flow PDEs
stories.Summary:
Zhonghua Qiao, Xianmin Xu, Rukang You and Tao Zhou posted a paper to the arXiv preprint server on 21 November 2026 that proposes a unified Onsager-based neural time-stepping framework, which they call ONTS, for solving gradient-flow partial differential equations with conserved and nonconserved dynamics. Unlike conventional neural time-stepping methods that directly parameterize the evolving state, the framework uses spatial neural networks to approximate the Onsager process variables, namely the rates in nonconserved systems and the fluxes in conserved systems. Within this Eulerian framework, the authors develop three complementary schemes: an explicit least-squares scheme called E-ONTS, an implicit variational scheme called I-ONTS, and a predictor-corrector scheme called PC-ONTS that combines explicit prediction with safeguarded implicit correction. The paper is listed as arXiv identifier 2611.20563.

For conserved systems, the flux-based formulation guarantees discrete mass conservation under periodic or no-flux boundary conditions, according to the abstract. The authors also rigorously establish unconditional discrete energy stability for the implicit schemes, provided that a suitable descent criterion is satisfied, without requiring global minimization of the neural variational objective. Numerical experiments for the heat, Allen-Cahn, Cahn-Hilliard, Fokker-Planck, and coupled Poisson-Nernst-Planck equations demonstrate the accuracy, robustness, and structure-preserving properties of the proposed framework. The abstract does not give numerical error values or timing results for those experiments.

The paper is credited to Zhonghua Qiao, Xianmin Xu, Rukang You and Tao Zhou, and the arXiv listing names Qiao and two other authors in its byline for the PDF. The abstract states that the framework is unified and that the implicit schemes carry unconditional discrete energy stability under a suitable descent criterion. It describes the three schemes as complementary and the numerical experiments as showing accuracy, robustness and structure-preserving properties. The articles do not include separate comments from the authors beyond the abstract text.

The context given in the articles is limited to the abstract and the standard arXivLabs boilerplate about openness, community, excellence and user data privacy. The articles do not say whether the paper has been peer reviewed, accepted at a conference or journal, or revised since posting. They also do not describe planned follow-up work, code release, or applications beyond the five equation families named in the abstract. More to follow.

These writers explored the current state of AI engineering and model deployment. They focused on how agents function within various software development environments. The articles discuss the evolution of autonomous agents and their security.

The research by Jing, Chen, Sun, He, and Si requires provenance-gated tool invocation. This method defends agents against indirect prompt injection in the year 2026. The study appears in Advances in Engineering Innovation, volume 17, issue 12, pages 1 to 7. It references Toolformer from 2023 and InjecAgent from 2024 to explain security. The authors used specific datasets to analyze these tool-integrated large language model agents.

The authors of the provenance-gated study are responsible for the data provided. They stated that the datasets used in their current study are available. These security flaws impact any organization deploying autonomous agents in production.

Linus Torvalds used Claude Code to fix the Linux page cache in October. Anthropic ran AI on 15 cheap TV boxes during a red team exercise. These events show a broad trend toward integrating AI into core infrastructure.

stories.Headline: Medical students who use reasoning scaffolding before an AI assistant achieve higher diagnostic accuracy, trial finds
stories.Summary:
A randomised controlled trial involving 496 medical students, of whom 389 were analysed, tested whether the order in which trainees receive AI support affects their clinical reasoning, and the preprint by Yizhou Fan, Luzhen Tang, Mengyu Xia, Jiaqi Xu, Zijian Li, Naping Chen and 10 more was posted on Research Square on 21 November 2026 without peer review. The students worked through clinical reasoning tasks with virtual standardised patients and were assigned to six conditions: no intervention, an AI assistant alone, AI scaffolding alone, scaffolding followed by the assistant, the assistant followed by scaffolding, or both at once. The scaffolding prompted students to reflect on and evaluate their own reasoning without giving direct answers, while the assistant supplied requested information and answers. The study ran an AI-free baseline, two intervention phases and a final assessment after all AI support was withdrawn, and frontier large language models completed the same tasks as a benchmark. Students first performed below the language models but later exceeded them following the interventions.

Students who began with AI scaffolding reached higher diagnostic accuracy than those given the assistant from the outset, both during the later intervention phase at 75.2% versus 66.0% (OR 1.73, 95% CIs [1.12, 2.68]) and after withdrawal at 24.6% versus 14.4% (OR 2.19, 95% CIs [1.15, 4.14]). After withdrawal, the scaffold-first groups were the only ones to outperform both unsupported students, at 24.5, 24.7% versus 9.0% (ORs 3.77, 3.87, 95% CIs [1.25, 12.00]), and the language models, at 24.5, 24.7% versus 8.6% (ORs 3.48, 3.50, 95% CIs [1.22, 9.89]). Introducing the assistant after scaffolding lowered intrinsic cognitive load (t(50) = 3.25, p BH = .006, Cohen’s d z = 0.46, 95% CIs [0.17, 0.75]) and raised metacognitive evaluation (t(50) = 3.11, p BH = .019, Cohen’s d z = 0.44, 95% CIs [0.15, 0.73]). The authors state that there is no competing interest and provide supplementary information in an appendix file.

The authors conclude that their findings support a staged and human-first approach to AI use in medical training, in which reasoning-focused scaffolding comes before answer-providing assistance. They say this order strengthens diagnostic performance both while AI-supported learning is under way and after AI support is withdrawn. The abstract frames the question as whether trainees can develop the clinical reasoning needed to use generative AI effectively and independently, given that such tools could improve physicians' clinical performance. Because the paper is a preprint, it has not been peer reviewed by a journal, and the articles give no further details on publication or follow-up work.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave and Humatica release a study on scaling proprietary enterprise AI
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave and Humatica released a joint study on November 20, 2026, regarding the scaling of proprietary enterprise artificial intelligence. This research examines how large organisations turn technological ambition into durable competitive value through resilient data architectures and internal governance. The study drew on insights from 252 enterprises across 14 industries and more than 30 interviews with senior executives. The report finds that 66 percent of surveyed organisations operate models or processes that would fail if their systems were switched off. Only 35 percent of enterprises have a formal operating model, while executives cite organisational barriers 2.4 times more than technological limits.

Seventy-three percent move critical workloads to self-controlled infrastructure for proprietary intellectual property, followed by data security at 55 percent and control at 45 percent. Cost and predictability motivate 36 percent of these moves, while 42 percent of production use cases started in business units. Finally, 24 percent of these AI projects were launched independently by employees or small teams. Chen Goldberg, the CoreWeave Executive Vice President of Product and Engineering, stated that businesses are becoming dependent on AI faster than they can run it. She explained that bringing managed PostgreSQL into Kubernetes clusters reduces latency by keeping data calls local and handles replication, patching, and backups.

Goldberg also noted that the connections between compute and data require the same engineering attention as the components themselves. She highlighted that CoreWeave achieved target quality on DeepSeek-V3 2.7 times faster than its GB200 run in MLPerf results. Andy Knobloch, a Partner at Humatica, said that winning leaders are those who decide who owns each AI system and how it improves. He noted that almost half of production AI started in business units without a formal budget or an executive sponsor. The study affects enterprises that rely on AI for core functions but lack the governance to secure and monitor production systems.

These organisations face vulnerability as initial pilots transition into mission-critical applications that require scalable deployment and strict security. The articles state that CoreWeave is the first cloud to publish multi-rack Vera Rubin results in MLPerf and holds Platinum rankings in SemiAnalysis ClusterMAX. CoreWeave also holds first-place inference speed and price-performance rankings from Artificial Analysis for Moonshot AI's Kimi K2.6 and Kimi K2.7 Code. The company partners with CrowdStrike for security, VAST Data for storage, and ClickHouse for real-time analytics. Other partners include Wayve for autonomous driving and PhysicsX for industrial physics AI, while Humatica works with GloCoach for leadership development.

Next, enterprises can use CoreWeave Forge for scalable deployment and the ARIA tool to transform institutional knowledge into proprietary assets. The CoreWeave Zero Trust AI Framework provides security, while Mission Control offers real-time infrastructure visibility across the entire lifecycle. Companies may also use CoreWeave Direct-to-Expert support to pair internal domain knowledge with external engineering expertise. The articles leave open how many more enterprises will establish formal operating models to bridge the gap in organisational readiness.

stories.Headline: E2E Networks falls for a fourth day as AI financing worries hit Indian tech stocks
stories.Summary:
E2E Networks shares fell to the lower circuit limit for a second straight session on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, extending the stock's slide to four consecutive days since October 15. The shares dropped 5 percent to Rs 627.15 on the NSE, the lowest level permitted for the day. The weakness spread to other AI-related stocks in India as global AI shares came under selling pressure. Moneycontrol reported the story on the same day, with its report published at 12:53 pm.

Among the other Indian names, Black Box shares slipped 1.55 percent to Rs 880.75 on the NSE. Netweb Technologies India declined 0.36 percent to Rs 4,683 per share at around 12.50 pm. A related headline from the site said Netweb and Black Box had fallen by as much as 9 percent during the broader slide. The article itself gave the smaller figures for the two companies at the time of writing.

The selloff was tied to worries about how the rising costs of AI development and infrastructure will be financed around the world. Concerns about the debt burden carried by CoreWeave added to the pressure on global AI stocks. Fears that higher interest rates could curb spending on AI infrastructure also weighed on technology shares, particularly chipmakers and data centre operators. The article did not name any company or official as having announced a specific decision behind the moves, and it attributed the decline to investor sentiment.

The pattern appears to have built up over several sessions rather than a single day, since E2E Networks has now fallen every day since October 15. An earlier Moneycontrol piece from October 13 carried a headline saying that E2E Networks, Hitachi Energy India and other AI-related stocks had fallen by up to 5 percent amid global jitters over AI. The articles did not say what would happen next for these stocks. The reports left open whether the concerns over financing costs and interest rates would ease or continue to weigh on the sector.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang's foundation commits $350 million to buy CoreWeave computing time for open science
stories.Summary:
The charitable foundation of Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori, committed $350 million to buy computing time from CoreWeave, according to reporting on the foundation's tax disclosures. The arrangement gives universities and nonprofit research institutes access to powerful chips for open science and AI research. For CoreWeave, it brings in business from a foundation whose assets are largely tied to the company that supplies its chips. The commitment supports the Computing Initiative for Open Science.

Nvidia previously disclosed in a proxy filing that $108.3 million had already been donated under the arrangement. Researchers receive the computing time through grants, and Nvidia said it planned to offer certain recipients engineering help at no charge. Nearly 90% of the foundation's $12.7 billion in assets at the end of 2025 was held in Nvidia shares, according to GuruFocus. Nvidia also invested $2 billion in CoreWeave in January through a private placement of approximately 23 million Class A shares. CoreWeave rents access to Nvidia's graphics processing units, the chips that power many of its customers' AI workloads.

The pledge adds a source of demand from outside the commercial AI market, according to the investors takeaway in the report. Its value to CoreWeave's business will depend on when researchers use the computing time and how much revenue the company recognizes from it over time. Timing matters because CoreWeave has to fund servers before customers use them. The larger question for shareholders is whether demand from a broader range of customers can keep pace with the company's spending on infrastructure.

Articles.Title: CoreWeave Finds AI Demand Outside the Commercial Market - TradingView

stories.Headline: Together AI launches hosted API for Qwen3 TTS to support live assistants
stories.Summary:
Together AI added hosted Qwen3 TTS on November 20, 2026, to provide a managed API layer for the open weights model. The company launched this service to help builders create live assistants rather than focusing on batch narration alone. This release follows the open sourcing of the Qwen3-TTS weights by the Alibaba team earlier in the year 2026. The service is available through serverless inference and dedicated endpoints for users who need steady isolation. Together AI aims to pitch a full stack of services including agent eval work and a Storage Accelerator.

The Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B model costs 20 dollars per 1 million characters, which is more than Kokoro at 4 dollars. It offers nine preset voices including vivian, serena, ryan, aiden, uncle_fu, dylan, eric, ono_anna, and sohee. These voices support ten languages including zh, en, ja, ko, de, fr, ru, pt, es, and it. Users can provide plain language delivery instructions up to 500 characters in the extra_params.instructions field to control the style. The system supports wav, mp3, raw, and mulaw formats with sample rates of 24000 Hz or 8000 Hz.

Together AI claims that its inference team tuned serving so first audio can start in as little as 97ms. Authors Anthony Ji, Charles Duong, Sebastien Beurnier, Sahil Yadav, and Sonny Khan credited the launch post on the company blog. They stated that the model separates who speaks from how they speak by using fixed voices with flexible instructions. The company suggests that this allows one branded voice to work across different European and Asian locales. Together AI notes that the 97ms figure is a hosted claim on their own specific serving stack.

Hacker News commenters noted that the time to first audio does not cap the total end to end conversational delay. Product owners are affected by the pricing, with a call center prototype of 50 million characters costing 1,000 dollars. Builders comparing open TTS options may look at Nari Labs, Hugging Face speech to speech defaults, or Zyphra's ZONOS3-Mini. Some teams may prefer self-hosting to avoid the per character meter or to keep audio on premises for compliance. Others might choose HeyGen on OpenRouter or DeepL Voice Aure when emotional range and translation are more important.

Alibaba's Qwen team released the weights earlier in 2026, leading to various local CPU stacks and serving optimizations. Nari Labs previously reported sub 50ms p95 time to first audio using one H100 with a custom stack. Together AI now provides a single invoice for speech alongside Llama or DeepSeek calls for teams using their platform. The model is positioned as a mid tier option, being cheaper than Cartesia Sonic 2 at 65 dollars. This managed layer removes the need for users to operate their own GPUs for Qwen's instruction steered presets.

Users must now benchmark the latency in their own regions rather than trusting the single blog number provided by Together. The documentation leaves open whether instructions work identically across every language, though demos show aiden reading English and others. There is currently no support for word level alignment or opus, aac, and flac output formats on this model. Seed reproducibility is listed as best effort only when the input, voice, and seed match. The articles do not state if custom voice cloning will be added to the Qwen3 hosted offering.

stories.Headline: Samsung and SK hynix values dive as AI chip rally ends
stories.Summary:
The KOSPI index fell 30 percent from early October and 45 percent from its June peak. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix saw their values dive 32.82 percent and 39.33 percent respectively. These losses occurred as the AI chip rally ended in November 2026. Investors who bought equity products like ETFs now face mounting losses. The market downturn has caused a significant shift in market capitalization rankings.

Total KOSPI market capitalization shrank from 7,449.6 trillion won in June to 3,991.4 trillion won. This represents a loss of 3,458 trillion won, or 46.4 percent of the total. Samsung Biologics rose to fifth place, while Celltrion returned to the top ten at ninth. Hyundai Motor fell to eighth place as Samsung Securities cut its target price to 380,000 won. Investor deposits shrank to 81.5669 trillion won during this period of volatility.

Citibank estimates that household stock investment losses will reach 563 trillion won in the second half. This impact is comparable to a base rate increase of 0.50 to 0.75 percentage points. The South Korean government has not yet produced clear measures to stabilize the market. This differs from Taiwan's FSC, which tightened short-selling restrictions and used a stabilization fund. Officials have stood by while the market dropped 30 percent in six weeks.

Investors who used retirement savings for stocks are now affected by the market slide. Average daily KOSPI trading volume hit a 12 year low of 239 million shares on November 19. Hyundai Motor faces pressure from a stronger won and price competition with Chinese electric vehicles. Chinese passenger EV exports to South Korea jumped 99.2 percent to 3.35991 billion dollars. Korean-made passenger EV market share fell to 48.7 percent while Chinese vehicles reached 43.5 percent.

The market previously rallied in June during a surge in AI chip investments. Samsung Electronics previously trailed SK hynix in HBM3E, with its market share falling to around 20 percent. Samsung later restored its HBM market share to the high 30 percent range in the third quarter. The government is now pushing for production tax credits for domestically built electric vehicles. They also want to strengthen R&D support for autonomous-driving AI and computing hardware.

Samsung appointed President Hwang Sang-joon to lead memory and President Choi Won-joon to lead the MX division. AI glasses launch on December 10, and a humanoid robot will debut at CES 2027. Samsung aims for HBM4E next year and HBM5 in 2028 to regain its technology lead. The articles leave open the timing of the National Assembly's tax subcommittee decisions. It remains uncertain if the foundry business will turn profitable or if shares will rebound.

stories.Headline: Michael Burry claims he warned investors about AI companies following a market rout
stories.Summary:
Former Scion Asset Management fund manager Michael Burry claimed on X on November 19, 2026, that he had previously warned investors about several artificial intelligence companies. His comments followed a market rout on Thursday that saw shares of Nvidia, CoreWeave, and Nebius all decline. Nebius holders experienced a 9.4 percent loss, while CoreWeave and Nvidia holders lost 6.1 percent and 3.3 percent respectively. These losses occurred as Nvidia shares fell 19 percent since November 8, following the resignation of co-founder Jensen Huang.

The current market situation involves several specific financial positions and corporate changes for the mentioned firms. Michael Burry holds Nvidia puts with a 140 dollar strike price expiring in February 2027, and he doubled his put options on the Nasdaq-100 index on November 12. He also rebuilt a put position in the VanEck Semiconductor ETF, which includes Nvidia as a top holding. Meanwhile, Nvidia reported that revenue jumped 103 percent to 115.8 billion dollars in its first earnings report after Jensen Huang left the company.

Michael Burry stated that while he never explicitly told anyone to short these stocks, he provided the necessary information for investors to sell. He argued that equipment maker ASML, chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, and neoclouds CoreWeave and Nebius relied too heavily on the market power of Nvidia. In contrast, interim CEO Colette Kress rejected these concerns by stating that the largest cloud operators are not pulling back. Burry continues to bet against the market with positions that run into early 2027.

This volatility follows a period where Nvidia shares dropped 39 percent from their October high despite the massive increase in quarterly revenue. The broader market is also facing pressure, with the S&P 500 dropping below 7,000 as Nvidia deals with an accounting investigation. Investors are now watching to see if Burry's bearish outlook on the Nasdaq-100 and semiconductors will be proven correct. The coming months will test his theory that the market power of Nvidia has entered a new phase.

stories.Headline: South Korea surpasses one trillion dollars in annual exports driven by AI chip demand
stories.Summary:
South Korea surpassed one trillion dollars in annual exports for the first time this year on Thursday, driven largely by a boom in artificial intelligence chips. This milestone makes the nation the fourth country ever to reach this threshold, following the United States and Germany in 2006 and China in 2007. The achievement occurred despite significant global trade headwinds, including higher tariffs from the administration of President Donald Trump and ongoing conflicts in the Middle East. This growth follows a previous record of 709.3 billion dollars last year, which narrowed the gap with Japan's 738.3 billion dollars. The surge was led by semiconductor exports, which rose 193.1 percent to 396.8 billion dollars between January and October, representing 42.7 percent of total exports.

This demand for memory chips used in data centers benefited major companies like Samsung Electronics Co. and SK hynix Inc. The cumulative trade surplus for the first ten months reached 294.9 billion dollars, more than triple the 2017 record of 95.2 billion dollars. Consequently, the economy is expected to grow by more than 3 percent in 2026, the first such expansion since 2021. Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan credited the workers and businesses for this success and promised continued government support for exporters. He stated that the government would help companies overcome various challenges in financing, logistics, and trade to maintain this growth. Meanwhile, Professor Lee Jae-min of Seoul National University School of Law called the event historic but warned about potential trade restrictions.

He noted that managing these risks is essential to ensure the sustainability of growth driven by semiconductors and artificial intelligence. While shipbuilding, defense, and biohealth industries grew, automakers and electronics manufacturers faced pressure from Chinese rivals and American tariffs. Experts warn that a heavy reliance on semiconductors makes the economy vulnerable to price drops or a slowdown in global AI investment. To mitigate these external shocks, the country must develop new markets and diversify its export industries beyond traditional heavy manufacturing. South Korean companies are currently reviewing their supply chains and overseas production plans to adapt to these uncertainties.

stories.Headline: Commerce Department approves sales of over 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies
stories.Summary:
The Commerce Department approved sales of over 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies as of May 2026. The Bureau of Industry and Security handled these approvals for Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices. Documents released on Thursday by the House Foreign Affairs Committee revealed these specific sales figures. This news emerged following the resignation of Nvidia chief Jensen Huang. The release occurred amid increasing scrutiny regarding the export of chips to China.

The Bureau of Industry and Security licensed H200 sales to ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent. Approvals included sales to firms the Department of Defense designated as Chinese Military Companies. Between December and May, companies requested 3.4 million AI chip sales to China. License requests also included firms like Baidu and Tesla Shanghai. Some approvals went to Maginfra and New Matrix, which are suspected smuggling fronts.

Representative Gregory Meeks said the administration's handling of export controls put national security at risk. He stated the Bureau of Industry and Security failed to enforce rules and requires oversight. A Bureau of Industry and Security spokesperson said licensing decisions resulted from multiple agency consultations. Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo stated that approvals were subject to strict conditions and limited volumes. AMD stated it maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance with all export laws.

Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon said the number of approved chips is not that many. He noted that the government approved about one out of every four requested sales. Analyst Patrick Moorhead said Beijing did not approve large scale imports, which limited sales. Hunterbrook Media alleged AMD has a China problem involving firmware for blacklisted IEIT Systems. Lawmakers are concerned that Jensen Huang's relationship with a spy jeopardized American AI dominance.

Export controls on AI chips began under the Biden administration in 2022. In December, Trump said Nvidia could ship H200s if the U.S. got 25 percent. Nvidia reported 2.4 billion dollars in quarterly revenue from H200 sales in China. Former CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed. Investigators suspect Megaspeed diverted Nvidia chips to China before Alice Huang left in 2025.

Jensen Huang will have a closed door interview with three committees on December 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter is scheduled to appear before the panels December 2. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has also agreed to testify before the Senate banking committee. The Commerce Department issued a rule Monday to stop Chinese companies leasing computing power. The articles leave open whether the new rule will successfully close the leasing loophole.
